RIN 2120-AA64
(

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for all General Atomics AeroTec Systems GmbH (General Atomics) Model Dornier 228-100, Dornier 228-101, Dornier 228-200, Dornier 228-201, Dornier 228-202, and Dornier 228-212 airplanes. This AD was prompted by reports of specific part-numbered hydraulic pump motors becoming severely damaged by excessive heat. This AD requires replacing the affected hydraulic pump motor with an improved design hydraulic pump motor. This AD also prohibits installing an affected hydraulic pump motor on any airplane. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective December 24, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2025-5401; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Doug Rudolph, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (816) 329-4059; email:
doug.rudolph@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to all General Atomics Model Dornier 228-100, Dornier 228-101, Dornier 228-200, Dornier 228-201, Dornier 228-202, and Dornier 228-212 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on January 5, 2026 (
91 FR 205
). The NPRM was prompted by AD 2025-0172, dated August 4, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0172) (also referred to as the MCAI), issued by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. The MCAI states that several occurrences were reported where the hydraulic pump motor became severely damaged by excessive heat. The MCAI further states that it was determined that carbon brushes installed on the affected hydraulic pump motor were the root cause of the failures. This condition, if not corrected, could lead to an uncontained fire, possible injury to passengers and crew, and consequent loss of control of the airplane.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require replacing the affected hydraulic pump motor with an improved design hydraulic pump motor. The proposed AD also prohibits installing an affected hydraulic pump motor on any airplane. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2025-5401.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from two commenters. The commenters were Bighorn Airways (Bighorn) and Consolidated Aircraft Supply Company, Inc. (Consolidated Aircraft). The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Withdraw the NPRM
Bighorn requested that the FAA withdraw the NPRM since it has not encountered the unsafe condition addressed by the NPRM. Bighorn based its request on its extensive operational experience of a multi-airplane fleet with over 14,000 hours.
The FAA disagrees with the request to withdraw the NPRM. The condition is based on data extrapolated from the worldwide fleet by EASA and the type certificate holder and confirmed by the FAA. The FAA has determined that this condition is unsafe and could exist or develop on other airplanes of the same type design. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Withdraw the NPRM
Consolidated Aircraft stated that it has not experienced high motor failures in other motor assembly types with the 1259A motor.
The FAA infers that the commenter wants the NPRM withdrawn and disagrees to withdraw the NPRM based on other motor assembly types not having the same failure issues. Service history of the motor assemblies on the affected airplanes reveals failure issues. Therefore, an unsafe condition exists or could develop on other airplanes of this same type design that must be addressed by AD action. If other motor assemblies develop a similar condition, the FAA will consider additional rulemaking action. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Redefine the Actions of AD
Consolidated Aircraft disagreed with changing the part number of the pump motor as required per the service material. Consolidated Aircraft stated that this limits available support, which affects safety. Additionally, Consolidated Aircraft stated that changing the base part number prevents unmodified hydraulic pump motors from being installed, but pointed out that this could have been done by adding a dash to the base number of the old part number.
The FAA disagrees with this comment. The type certificate holder chose to change the part number of the modified pump motor after modification per their procedures to address this
(
printed page 74472)
unsafe condition. The FAA will consider alternative methods of compliance (AMOCs) to address this differently if the AMOCs are submitted following paragraph (i) of this AD. Therefore, the FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Extend the Compliance Time
Bighorn requested that the FAA revise the compliance time in paragraph (g), “Required Actions” of the proposed AD, from 200 hours time-in-service (TIS) to 600 hours TIS. The commenter stated that this interval should coincide with the next overhaul of the hydraulic pump motor to reduce the burden of an additional compliance time for replacing the hydraulic pump motor.
The FAA disagrees with the request to extend the compliance time. In developing an appropriate compliance time for this action, the FAA considered the recommendations of the manufacturer and EASA, the risk associated with the subject unsafe condition, the availability of required parts, and the practical aspect of accomplishing the required modification within a period of time that corresponds to the normal scheduled maintenance for most affected operators. According to the manufacturer, an ample number of required parts will be available to modify the U.S. fleet within the proposed compliance time. In consideration of these items as well as the reports of severely heat damaged hydraulic pump motors, the FAA has determined that the 200-hour TIS compliance time is necessary to provide an acceptable level of safety. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Mandate Removal Time
Consolidated Aircraft requested that the FAA add a mandatory removal time for overhaul of the hydraulic pump assembly in the NPRM.
The FAA disagrees with adding a mandatory removal time for overhaul of the hydraulic pump assembly in the NPRM. Per data supplied by the type certificate holder, the motor of the pump assembly is the focus of the unsafe condition and thus the replacement of the motor per paragraph (g) of this AD is the action that addresses the unsafe condition. The pump part of the assembly is replaced on condition as opposed to a time limit replacement schedule.
Request To Require Pump Part Numbers
Consolidated Aircraft stated that it often receives the pump for overhaul, separate from the motor, resulting from extensive wear.
The FAA infers that the commenter wants the FAA to include the part numbers of the pump in the Applicability of this AD. Although there may be signs of extensive wear on the pumps of hydraulic pump assemblies, the pump motor of the assembly is specifically the focus of the MCAI and this AD. The FAA has no data, including nothing from the type certificate (TC) holder, that indicates that wear on the pumps leads to pump motor issues on affected airplanes, so the hydraulic pump part numbers are not included within the scope of the MCAI and this AD. The TC holder has not identified any instances or reports of extensive wear in these pumps. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Add Time Between Overhaul (TBO) for Hydraulic Pump Motor and Pump/Motor Assembly
Consolidated Aircraft asked if the hydraulic pump motor [part number 1259A], and pump/motor assembly, part numbers 40178-02 and -03, have a TBO.
The FAA has confirmed there is no TBO for the hydraulic pump motor addressed by this AD, which is part number 1259A. This AD does not address the hydraulic pump/motor assembly. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Concern Not To Allow Pilots To Handle Tripped Circuit Breakers
Consolidated Aircraft expressed concern about the possibility that pilots having less training could incorrectly handle a hydraulic pump motor circuit breaker when it trips and mentioned that if it does trip, there should be no resetting but instead to tow the airplane if necessary.
It is common airmanship for pilots to be trained to handle not resetting the circuit breaker unless it is deemed necessary. This situation is also addressed in the “Pilot's Operating Handbook.” There is no additional need to include pilot actions for tripped circuit breakers within this AD. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Include the Pump Assembly in the AD Applicability
Consolidated Aircraft stated that motor and pump serial numbers are sequential when produced and that traceability of the pump assembly is lost when the pairing of the pump assemblies and hydraulic pump motors are changed.
The FAA infers that the commenter wants the FAA to include the pump assembly in the Applicability of this AD. The FAA disagrees with including the pump assembly in the Applicability of this AD. Since there is no data indicating a safety risk with the pump assemblies paired with the hydraulic pump motors, the FAA has determined that the unsafe condition is only on the pump motor. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Include a Placard in the Cockpit
Consolidated Aircraft requested that the FAA require a placard in the cockpit for pilots to have an observable message regarding the hydraulic pump motor duty cycle.
The FAA disagrees with requiring a placard. Since the pump assembly and the hydraulic pump motor do not continuously operate and are not used more than specified, there would be no need for an additional placard in the cockpit. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Allow FAA-Approved Repair Stations To Complete the Modification
Consolidated Aircraft requested that FAA-approved repair stations be allowed to complete the modification to the hydraulic pump motor assembly.
The FAA infers that the commenter is wanting to modify the internal components of the old motor part number (P/N) 1259A to make it a new P/N A-752511A00B. The FAA disagrees. Currently the General Atomics service bulletin (SB) states to contact the company for a slot for modification of the pump motor to make it a new part number motor or exchange old part number motor for the new part number motor. The SB and this AD do not allow the modification/re-identification of these motors by non-company outside sources. The repair station can still modify the hydraulic pump assembly per General Atomics AeroTec Dornier 228 Service Bulletin No. SB-228-360, Rev. 0. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority
(
printed page 74473)
has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD affects 16 airplanes of U.S. registry.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
This AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify that this AD:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
,
(2) Will not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
(3) Will not have a significant economic impact, positive or negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Accordingly, under the authority delegated to me by the Administrator, the FAA amends
14 CFR part 39
as follows:
PART 39—AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVES
1.
The authority citation for part 39 continues to read as follows:
Authority:

2.
The FAA amends § 39.13 by adding the following new airworthiness directive:
2026-24-01 General Atomics AeroTec Systems GmbH (Type Certificate Previously Held by RUAG Aerospace Services GmbH):
Amendment 39-23525; Docket No. FAA-2025-5401; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01313-A.
(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective December 24, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to all General Atomics AeroTec Systems GmbH (type certificate previously held by RUAG Aerospace Services GmbH) Model Dornier 228-100, Dornier 228-101, Dornier 228-200, Dornier 228-201, Dornier 228-202, and Dornier 228-212 airplanes, certificated in any category.
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 2913, Hydraulic Pump, (Elect/Eng), Main.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by reports of several occurrences of hydraulic pump motors becoming severely damaged by excessive heat. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent the overheating of the hydraulic pump motor. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in an uncontained fire, possible injury to passengers and crew, and loss of control of the airplane.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Required Actions
For airplanes with an installed hydraulic pump motor having part number (P/N) 1259A, within 200 hours time-in-service of the hydraulic pump motor (for airplanes equipped with a hydraulic system elapsed time indicator), or 600 landings (for airplanes not equipped with a hydraulic system elapsed time indicator), as applicable, after the effective date of this AD, replace the hydraulic pump motor with a hydraulic pump motor having P/N A-752511A00B.
Note to Paragraph (g):
General Atomics AeroTec Dornier 228 Service Bulletin No. SB-228-360, Rev. 0, dated May 28, 2025, contains information related to this AD.
(h) Installation Prohibition
As of the effective date of this AD, do not install a hydraulic pump motor having P/N 1259A on any airplane.
(i) Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs)
The Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA, has the authority to approve AMOCs for this AD, if requested using the procedures found in
14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with
14 CFR 39.19
, send your request to your principal inspector or local Flight Standards District Office, as appropriate. If sending information directly to the manager of the International Validation Branch, send it to the attention of the person identified in paragraph (j)(1) of this AD and email to:
AMOC@faa.gov
.
Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the local flight standards district office/certificate holding district office.
(j) Additional Information
(1) For more information about this AD, contact Doug Rudolph, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (816) 329-4059; email:
doug.rudolph@faa.gov
.
(2) For material identified in this AD that is not incorporated by reference, contact General Atomics AeroTec Systems GmbH, Galileostraße 396, D-82131 Gauting, Germany; phone: +49 8153 302280; email:
(

;

ga-ats.com/.

None.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Table of Contents
I. Background
II. Ordering Paragraphs
I. Background
This complaint stems from a dispute between the Postal Service and Complainant regarding delivery of mail to his home. Complainant asserts three causes of action in his Complaint. Specifically, Count I alleges that the Postal Service has breached a settlement agreement between the parties. Counts II alleges that the Postal Service violated
39 U.S.C. 403(1)
by failing to maintain an efficient system of sorting and delivering the mail. Count III alleges that the Postal Service violated
39 U.S.C. 403(c)
by discriminating against him in the delivery of his mail.
After determining that Complainant has raised sufficient issues of material law and fact as to Count III, the Commission appointed a presiding officer to preside over the conduct of the proceedings, including but not limited to scheduling, discovery, potential hearings, and briefing in this matter. The Presiding Officer therefore enumerates the provisions that will govern discovery as well as other related procedures. The Presiding Officer also denies certain procedural motions as moot or premature.
II. Ordering Paragraphs
It is ordered:
1. The deadline to file a notice of intervention pursuant to
39 CFR 3010.142
is December 1, 2026.
2. The parties and counsel shall follow the procedural schedule and case management procedures established by this Presiding Officer's Ruling.
3. The United States Postal Service's Motion to Strike Complainant's Premature Discovery, filed September 25, 2026, is denied.
4. Commission dockets staff shall remove the Complainant's Response in Opposition to Respondent's Answer to the Complaint, filed September 22, 2026, from this docket.
5. United States Postal Service's Motion to Strike Complainant's Opposition to the Answer to the Complaint, filed September 25, 2026, is denied.
6. This Order, or an abstract thereof, shall be published in the
Federal Register
.
By the Commission.
Mallory Richards,
Attorney-Advisor.

title: Privacy Act of 1974; Matching Program
abstract: This matching program will support the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and the Department of War (DoW) in meeting the requirements set forth in Section 559(b) of the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, which requires the Secretary of Education and the Secretary of War to enter into a matching program to identify servicemembers and staff eligible for certain public service loan forgiveness programs. Under this matching program, DoW (source agency) will disclose to the ED, Federal Student Aid (FSA), (recipient agency), information on individuals who, at any time beginning on or after October 1, 2007, were members of the Armed Forces serving on active duty for a period of more than 30 consecutive days or civilian employees of DoW, for the purposes of: (1) identifying whether they made one or more student loan payments eligible to be counted for purposes of the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) Program under subsection 455(m) of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA) and Temporary Expanded PSLF (TEPSLF) program; and (2) without requiring further information from them, certifying the total period of such service or employment for purposes of such program and counting the total number of qualifying payments made by them for purposes of such program during such period. ED will evaluate the information that it receives from DoW to create a count of qualifying payments under PSLF made by covered employees on their respective Title IV Loans (as defined herein). In addition, ED will create customized notifications for covered employees based on the status of their respective Title IV Loans and whether they have already submitted a PSLF and TEPSLF Certification and Application (PSLF form).

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of a new matching program.
SUMMARY:
This matching program will support the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and the Department of War (DoW) in meeting the requirements set forth in Section 559(b) of the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, which requires the Secretary of Education and the Secretary of War to enter into a matching program to identify servicemembers and staff eligible for certain public service loan forgiveness programs. Under this matching program, DoW (source agency) will disclose to the ED, Federal Student Aid (FSA), (recipient agency), information on individuals who, at any time beginning on or after October 1, 2007, were members of the Armed Forces serving on active duty for a period of more than 30 consecutive days or civilian employees of DoW, for the purposes of: (1) identifying whether they made one or more student loan payments eligible to be counted for purposes of the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) Program under subsection 455(m) of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA) and Temporary Expanded PSLF (TEPSLF) program; and (2) without requiring further information from them, certifying the total period of such service or employment for purposes of such program and counting the total number of qualifying payments made by them for purposes of such program during such period. ED will evaluate the information that it receives from DoW to create a count of qualifying payments under PSLF made by covered employees on their respective Title IV Loans (as defined herein). In addition, ED will create customized notifications for covered employees based on the status of their respective Title IV Loans and whether they have already submitted a PSLF and TEPSLF Certification and Application (PSLF form).
DATES:
Submit your comments on the proposed establishment of the matching program on or before December 21, 2026.
The matching program will become effective on the later of the following two dates: (1) December 1, 2026, or (2) 30 days after the publication of this notice, on November 19, 2026, unless comments have been received from interested members of the public requiring modification and republication of the notice. The matching program will continue for 18 months after the effective date and may be renewed for up to an additional 12 months if, within 3 months prior to the expiration of the 18 months, the respective Data Integrity Boards of ED and the DoW determine that the conditions specified in
5 U.S.C. 552a(o)(2)(D)
have been met.

U.S. Department of Education and the Department of War.
Authority for Conducting the Matching Program
ED's legal authority to enter into this matching program is provided by subsection 455(m) of the HEA (
20 U.S.C. 1087e(m)
), and the regulations set forth in
34 CFR 685.219

This matching program will assist DoW and ED in sharing information on individuals who, at any time beginning on or after October 1, 2007, were members of the Armed Forces serving on active duty for a period of more than 30 consecutive days or civilian employees of DoW (collectively referred to as “covered employees”), for the purposes of: (1) identifying whether they made one or more student loan payments eligible to be counted for purposes of the PSLF program under subsection 455(m) of the HEA (

Notice of meeting.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service gives notice of a virtual public meeting of the Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force (ANSTF) in accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act.
DATES:
The ANSTF will meet virtually Tuesday through Wednesday, December 1-2, 2026, from 12:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. (eastern time) each day.
Registration:
Registration is required. The deadline for registration is November 27, 2026.
Accessibility and Other Accommodations:
The deadline for accessibility and other accommodation requests is November 27, 2026. Please see
Requests for Accommodations,
below.
ADDRESSES:
The meeting will be held virtually. Participation will be available via teleconference and broadcast over the internet. To register and receive the telephone number or web address for virtual participation, contact the Executive Secretary (see
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
) or visit the ANSTF website at
https://www.fws.gov/​program/​aquatic-nuisance-species-task-force
.

Susan Pasko, Executive Secretary, ANSTF, by telephone at (571) 623-0608, or by email at
susan_pasko@fws.gov
.
Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The ANSTF was established by the Nonindigenous Aquatic Nuisance Prevention and Control Act of 1990 (
16 U.S.C. 4701
et seq.
) and is composed of Federal and ex-officio members. The purpose of the ANSTF is to develop and implement a program for U.S. waters to prevent introduction and dispersal of aquatic invasive species; to monitor, control, and study such species; and to disseminate related information. This virtual meeting is open to the public.
Meeting Agenda
The meeting agenda will focus on identifying and establishing priority objectives and strategies to inform and guide the development of the next ANSTF Strategic Plan. The agenda also includes reports from ANSTF members, reports and recommendations from regional panels and subcommittees, and a public comment period. The final agenda and other related meeting information will be posted on the ANSTF website,
https://www.fws.gov/​program/​aquatic-nuisance-species-task-force

) no later than November 27, 2026, to give the

31 CFR Part 1010

AGENCY:
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Treasury.
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
FinCEN is issuing this proposed rule to strengthen customer due diligence requirements under the Customer Due Diligence Rule consistent with the policy goals of, and as directed by,
Executive Order 14406
,
Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System.
Specifically, the proposal ensures financial institutions covered by the Customer Due Diligence Rule collect sufficient information to verify the identities of beneficial owners of legal entity customers and maintain the authority, where warranted, to obtain additional information, including information relevant to whether the beneficial owners of legal entity customers possess lawful immigration status and employment authorization in the United States when such information is relevant to assessing risks.
DATES:
Comments must be received by January 19, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Comments must be submitted in one of the following two ways (please choose only one of the ways listed):
Electronically at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions under Docket FINCEN-2026-0298. If you are reading this document on federalregister.gov, you may use the green “SUBMIT A PUBLIC COMMENT” button beneath this rulemaking's title to submit a comment to the
regulations.gov
docket.
You may mail written comments to the following address: Regulatory and Strategic Affairs Division, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, P.O. Box 39, Vienna, VA 22183. Mailed comments must be received by the close of the comment period.
All comments will be made available to the public. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication a comment that contains threats of violence, classified information, or information potentially related to a whistleblower submission or that identifies a whistleblower. Comments may be submitted anonymously. When multiple comments are submitted with identical or near-identical content, FinCEN may post only a single representative example of identical or substantially identical comments. All related documents and comments are posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a summary of this proposed rule may be found at
www.regulations.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
FinCEN's Regulatory Support Section by submitting an inquiry at
www.fincen.gov/​contact
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Scope
This proposed rule would amend the Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Rule, which was promulgated under authorities provided by the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), to strengthen certain customer due diligence requirements. This proposed rule supports the efforts of the Department of the Treasury to make the CDD Rule more effective, risk-based, and focused on the greatest threats to financial institutions and national security, as well as promote Treasury's efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden consistent with
Executive Order 14192
,
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
This proposal implements the directive in
Executive Order 14406
,
Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System
(hereinafter “
Executive Order 14406
”) to propose changes to applicable BSA regulations to strengthen risk-based customer due diligence requirements.
II. Background and Authority
A. The Bank Secrecy Act
Enacted in 1970 and amended several times since, the BSA is designed to combat money laundering, the financing of terrorism, and other illicit finance risks.
[
1
]
Congress has authorized the Secretary of the Treasury to administer the BSA. The Secretary has in turn delegated the authority to implement, administer, and enforce compliance with the BSA and its associated regulations to the Director of FinCEN.
[
2
]
Since its original enactment, Congress has expanded the BSA to address various aspects of anti-money laundering (AML) and countering the financing of terrorism (CFT) compliance, including through expansion of the BSA. In 1992, the Annunzio-Wylie Anti-Money Laundering Act
[
3
]
gave the Secretary authority to require financial institutions, as defined in the BSA regulations, to “carry out” AML programs and to prescribe minimum standards for such programs, including: “(A) the development of internal policies, procedures, and controls; (B) the designation of a compliance officer; (C) an ongoing employee training program; and (D) an independent audit function to test programs.”
[
4
]
Later, the USA PATRIOT Act further amended the BSA, reinforcing the Annunzio-Wylie framework by making it mandatory for financial institutions to maintain AML programs that meet minimum prescribed standards.
[
5
]
The USA PATRIOT Act also, among other things, directed the Secretary to set minimum standards for financial institutions regarding customer identity in connection with the opening of accounts, commonly referred to as customer identification program (CIP) requirements,
[
6
]
and expanded the definition of “financial institution” under the BSA, and by extension the AML program requirement, to cover certain other financial industry participants (
e.g.,
credit unions and futures commission merchants).
[
7
]
(
printed page 74515)
Finally, on January 1, 2021, Congress enacted the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (FY 2021 NDAA), of which the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AML Act) was a component.
[
8
]
Among the purposes of the AML Act, as stated by Congress, was to reinforce that required policies, procedures and controls should support the need for AML/CFT programs to be “risk-based.”
[
9
]
Consistent with the goals of the AML Act, Treasury recognizes the urgent need to modernize the AML/CFT regime in the United States so that it is effective, risk-based, and focused on the greatest threats to financial institutions and national security.
[
10
]
B. The Customer Due Diligence Rule
FinCEN has implemented these statutory mandates and authorities by promulgating program rules, among other requirements. Most notably in a 2016 rulemaking, FinCEN, in consultation with the Federal functional regulators, incorporated both general and specific customer due diligence (CDD) requirements into FinCEN's regulations.
[
11
]
First, the 2016 rulemaking required banks, brokers and dealers in securities, mutual funds, and futures commission merchants and introducing brokers in commodities (collectively “covered financial institutions”) to implement and maintain, as part of their AML programs, “appropriate risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence,” including “[u]nderstanding the nature and purpose of customer relationships for the purposes of developing a customer risk profile” and “[c]onducting ongoing monitoring” both “to identify and report suspicious transactions” and “on a risk basis, to maintain and update customer information.”
[
12
]
This became what is now colloquially known as the “fifth pillar” of an AML compliance program.
[
13
]
Second, the CDD rulemaking codified at
31 CFR 1010.230
a requirement that covered financial institutions “identify and verify beneficial owners of legal entity customers.”
[
14
]
Under what became known as the “ownership prong” of this requirement, covered financial institutions collect the names and identifying information of “[e]ach individual, if any, who, directly or indirectly . . . owns 25 percent or more of the equity interests” of the legal entity customer.
[
15
]
Under what became known as the “control prong” of this requirement, covered financial institutions collect the name and identifying information of “[a] single individual with significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct a legal entity customer.”
[
16
]
For the status of the specified individuals as beneficial owners of the legal entity customer, covered financial institutions could “rely on the information supplied by the legal entity customer . . . provided that [the covered financial institution] has no knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of such information.”
[
17
]
For verification of the identity of the individual beneficial owners, covered financial institutions, at a minimum, would have to follow procedures containing all of the elements required for verification of individual account-holders under applicable CIP regulations.
[
18
]
Covered financial institutions were required to undertake this identification and verification “at the time a new account is opened,” meaning every time that a legal entity customer opened a new account.
[
19
]
C. Recent Modifications to CDD Rule Obligations
In 2026, FinCEN used its authority under the BSA to grant exceptive relief to covered financial institutions from the requirement to identify and verify the identities of beneficial owners of legal entity customers at each new account opening.
[
20
]
That order, FIN-2026-R001, acknowledged that the CDD Rule requires a covered financial institution to identify and verify a legal entity customer's beneficial owners each time that customer opens an account with the covered financial institution, regardless of how little time passes between account openings or whether the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information last obtained about the customer. Consistent with the Trump Administration's policy of reducing unnecessary regulatory burden and enhancing the risk-based framework of the AML/CFT regulations, FinCEN granted relief so that a covered financial
(
printed page 74516)
institution—instead of being required to undertake identification and verification “at the time a new account is opened”—“may instead limit its identification and verification of the identities of beneficial owners . . . to the following scenarios: (1) when a legal entity customer first opens an account with a covered financial institution; (2) any time thereafter when the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer; and (3) as needed based on a covered financial institution's risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence.”
[
21
]
FinCEN noted in its exceptive relief order that it would consider whether to codify this relief via a rulemaking.
D.
Executive Order 14406
: Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System
On May 19, 2026, President Donald J. Trump issued
Executive Order 14406
to further the Administration's policy of “restor[ing] integrity to America's financial system, safeguard[ing] financial institutions against structural risks, and deter[ring] fraud and abuse.”
[
22
]
The Executive Order highlighted risks to the financial system caused by illicit cross-border financial activity and extension of credit or financial services to the inadmissible and removable alien population. To address these risks, it emphasized the importance of the Federal government adopting tailored measures to safeguard the financial system from illicit use and promote safe and sound lending and other practices by financial institutions and stated the need for financial institutions to have in place “proper know-your-customer practices” to prevent abuse of the system and be attentive to “credit risks posed by the extension of . . . consumer credit to the inadmissible and removable alien population.”
[
23
]
The Executive Order requires actions by various Federal agencies, including changes to the CDD Rule and consideration of changes to CIP rules.
[
24
]
This proposal would implement section 3(b) of
Executive Order 14406
. Section 3(b) directs the Secretary—in consultation with the “appropriate Federal functional financial regulators,” defined in the Executive Order as the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (FRB), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), and the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA)—to propose changes to applicable implementing regulations of the BSA to strengthen risk-based customer due diligence requirements for covered financial institutions. Section 3(b) of the Executive Order specifies that such changes should ensure that “(i) institutions collect and verify sufficient customer identity information to reasonably identify the nominal and beneficial owners of accounts in order to assess risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, or other unlawful activity; and (ii) institutions maintain the authority, where warranted by other risk indicators or supervisory concerns, to obtain additional information necessary to resolve material compliance concerns, including information relevant to whether account holders possess lawful immigration status and employment authorization in the United States when such information is relevant to assessing risks associated with fraud, identity misrepresentation, sanctions evasion, or other illicit financial activity, as part of a risk-based customer due diligence program.”
E. Other FinCEN Proposed Rules
In developing its proposal to implement section 3(b) of
Executive Order 14406
, FinCEN has considered other relevant FinCEN regulations—both those in effect and those in consideration—that are relevant to customer due diligence and mitigation of customer risk to inform the specifics of this proposed rule.
FinCEN has issued proposed rules further emphasizing the risk-based approach to AML/CFT programs for covered financial institutions, as well as permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs).
[
25
]
Those rules, if finalized as proposed, would, among other things, require each covered financial institution and PPSI to establish a risk-based set of internal policies, procedures, and controls that must be reasonably designed to conduct ongoing customer due diligence. Under these proposed requirements, if finalized, covered financial institutions must establish and maintain a written AML/CFT program that includes appropriate risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence, to include, but not be limited to, understanding the nature and purpose of customer relationships for the purpose of developing a customer risk profile.
Notably, those proposals are consistent with
Executive Order 14406
's directive to adopt tailored measures to safeguard the financial system from illicit use and ensure that institutions maintain risk-based customer due diligence programs.
[
26
]
Most importantly,
(
printed page 74517)
the proposals would, if finalized, ensure internal policies, procedures, and controls—including those relating to conducting ongoing customer due diligence—must be reasonably designed to mitigate assessed risk, including by allocating more attention and resources toward higher-risk customers and activities rather than toward lower-risk customers and activities.
[
27
]
III. Overview of the Proposal
In drafting this proposed rule, FinCEN has considered how it can best strengthen the CDD Rule by adopting tailored measures to safeguard the financial system, including by ensuring that covered financial institutions have risk-based collection and verification requirements and direct compliance resources towards higher risk customers as directed by
Executive Order 14406
. In addition to implementing the directive in section 3(b) of
Executive Order 14406
, FinCEN also seeks to further the Trump Administration's efforts to modernize the AML/CFT regime by making it more effective, risk-based, and focused on the greatest threats to national security, while reducing unnecessary regulatory burden.
After considering the existing regulations, proposals, and obligations, as well as the directives in
Executive Order 14406
, FinCEN assesses that targeted amendments to the CDD Rule—specifically, § 1010.230—best effectuate the goals of
Executive Order 14406
. Specifically, this proposal includes three targeted revisions to the CDD Rule codified at § 1010.230, in addition to other minor regulatory clarifications.
First,
consistent with
Executive Order 14406
, the proposal would strengthen risk-based customer due diligence requirements for covered financial institutions by making explicit that, where warranted by other risk indicators or supervisory concerns, a covered financial institution may obtain additional information necessary to resolve material compliance concerns, including information relevant to whether account holders possess lawful immigration status and employment authorization in the United States when such information is relevant to assessing risks associated with fraud, identity misrepresentation, sanctions evasion, or other illicit financial activity, as part of a risk-based customer due diligence program.
Second,
FinCEN is proposing to formally incorporate the exceptive relief provided in FIN-2026-R001. This change would formally eliminate the requirement for covered financial institutions to repeatedly collect and verify beneficial ownership information in cases where there is no reason to believe that the customer's beneficial ownership information has changed since it was last collected, and the circumstances do not indicate a risk-based need to collect and verify beneficial ownership information. By codifying this relief, FinCEN is ensuring that covered financial institutions will continue to benefit from the flexibility to direct compliance resources consistent with their own assessments of risk.
Third,
the proposal would specify in § 1010.230 the pieces of information a covered financial institution must collect relating to beneficial owners. This would involve moving the specific details of the requirement to collect information about beneficial owners from the rule's Appendix A into the rule itself. Most, but not all, of those details would not change. The proposal would, however, restrict the ability to satisfy the information collection requirement by collecting a beneficial owner's Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN). Additional flexibilities described in the proposal would allow institutions to obtain information from third parties. FinCEN assesses that these proposed changes would ensure that covered financial institutions collect sufficient, appropriate information to be able to verify the identities of beneficial owners while making it less burdensome for covered financial institutions to reasonably identify beneficial owners. As a result, FinCEN expects covered financial institutions will be both able to use their resources more efficiently and better positioned to assess risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, or other unlawful activity.
In developing this proposal, as directed by
Executive Order 14406
, FinCEN consulted with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the National Credit Union Administration. Additionally, FinCEN consulted the staff of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which are the primary Federal functional regulators for additional categories of institutions covered by the CDD Rule, specifically brokers and dealers in securities, mutual funds, and futures commission merchants and introducing brokers.
[
28
]
IV. Section-By-Section Analysis
A. Proposed Amendment to
31 CFR 1010.230(a)
—In General
As mentioned above, this rulemaking is rooted in FinCEN's authority to “prescribe minimum standards for programs” intended to “guard against money laundering and the financing of terrorism through financial institutions . . . including . . . the development of internal policies, procedures, and controls[.]”
[
29
]
Consistent with
Executive Order 14406
's emphasis on assessing the risk associated with beneficial owners, the proposed language would clarify that covered financial institutions are required to establish and maintain written procedures reasonably designed to identify and verify
the identity of
beneficial owners of legal entity customers. This proposed addition of the words “the identity of” to § 1010.230(a) is intended to make clear that covered financial institutions are required to collect and verify
identifying information
on a beneficial owner (
i.e.,
to verify the individual's existence and identity), not whether that individual is actually a beneficial owner of the legal entity that is the covered financial institution's customer. This is consistent with language in the current rule that a covered financial institution may rely on the information supplied by the legal entity customer regarding the identity of its beneficial owner or owners, provided that it has no knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of such information.
[
30
]
This proposed language is intended as a clarification and does not change covered financial institutions' existing obligations to verify the identities of beneficial owners.
FinCEN is also proposing to add “countering the financing of terrorism” to the reference in § 1010.230 to “anti-
(
printed page 74518)
money laundering compliance programs.” The inclusion of countering the financing of terrorism is a technical change, consistent with other FinCEN proposals, which reflects a statutory change requiring institutions to account for risks related to terrorist financing.
[
31
]
B. Proposed Amendment to
31 CFR 1010.230(b)
—Identification and Verification
1. Proposed
31 CFR 1010.230(b)(1)(i)
—Timing
The proposal would codify the exemptive relief provided in FIN-2026-R001 by amending § 1010.230(b)(1)(i). FinCEN expects that this proposed change, if finalized, will ensure covered financial institutions continue to benefit from the flexibility to allocate compliance resources to focus on customers that present higher risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, and other unlawful activity as indicated in
Executive Order 14406
.
The current rule requires a covered financial institution to identify the beneficial owner(s) of each legal entity customer every time a new account is opened, subject to certain limited exemptions. Covered financial institutions and their trade associations have characterized this requirement as unnecessarily burdensome, particularly in situations involving legal entity customers whose business happens to involve the frequent creation of new accounts. Where there is no reason to think that the customer's beneficial ownership information has changed since last collected, they have pointed out, repeated collection and verification of the same information wastes resources that, deployed in a more risk-conscious manner, could improve overall risk management.
The proposed rule would address these concerns by replacing the rigid account opening requirement with a more flexible, risk-based approach. The proposed rule provides that a covered financial institution must identify the beneficial owner(s) of a legal entity customer: (1) when the legal entity customer first opens an account with the covered financial institution; (2) any time thereafter when the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer; and (3) as needed based on a covered financial institution's risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence. The proposal would eliminate the requirement for covered financial institutions to collect a legal entity customer's beneficial ownership information at each new account opening except, among other circumstances, as needed based on a covered financial institution's risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence. Whether a financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of previously obtained beneficial ownership information would depend upon the facts and circumstances. Notably, if a covered financial institution elects, as part of its risk-based procedures, to continue collecting beneficial ownership information at each account opening, it would be permitted to do so under the proposed rule. FinCEN expects this change would, consistent with the policy goals of
Executive Order 14406
, improve the risk-based nature of the CDD Rule by allowing financial institutions to focus on higher risk customers, including those that present risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, and other unlawful activity.
FinCEN requests comment on the timing element of the proposal. Specifically, FinCEN seeks comment on whether “any time thereafter when the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer” is an appropriate trigger for identification and verification of beneficial owners.
Additionally, one of the three circumstances in which FinCEN's exceptive relief specifies that beneficial ownership information should be collected—and therefore one of the circumstances in which this proposal requires that it be collected—is “when the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer.” FinCEN requests comment on its use of “reliability.” If, for example, the covered financial institution has reason to believe there has been a change in ownership of the legal entity, the covered financial institution might not be questioning the “reliability” so much as the continuing accuracy of the information originally provided. FinCEN therefore requests comment on whether “reliability” should be used, defined in a more specific fashion, or supplemented.
2. Proposed
31 CFR 1010.230(b)(1)(ii)
—Information To Collect
The proposed rule would make two changes relating to the information potentially collected by financial institutions under § 1010.230. Both changes support the policy directives of
Executive Order 14406
by ensuring institutions collect information sufficient to reasonably identify the beneficial owners of legal entity customers for the specific purpose of assessing risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, or other unlawful activity. One change would make explicit the information a covered financial institution must collect, while the second would ensure that covered financial institutions can collect additional information, where warranted by other risk indicators or supervisory concerns, to assess risks associated with fraud, identity misrepresentation, sanctions evasion, or other illicit financial activity.
This combination reinforces the original CDD Rule's balancing of categorical and risk-based elements. FinCEN has assessed that this balance not only ensures that a covered financial institution will collect sufficient information with regard to beneficial owners of its legal entity customers, but also provides flexibility for a covered financial institution to collect additional information for particular beneficial owners where warranted by risk. In doing so, FinCEN aims to strengthen the risk-based element of the CDD Rule, including by ensuring that institutions maintain the authority to collect additional information based on risk, while still maintaining the categorical aspect of the CDD Rule.
The proposed rule in general requires that a covered financial institution must obtain information about each beneficial owner of a legal entity customer sufficient to allow the institution to identify, and to verify the identity of, the beneficial owner. FinCEN proposes these changes to make plain the specific information that covered financial institutions are required to obtain about beneficial owners of legal entities. The proposed rule specifies a discrete list of information that a covered financial institution must obtain about each beneficial owner of a legal entity customer, which includes a qualifying identifying number for the individual.
(
printed page 74519)
Under this proposal the regulatory text would set out a list of identifying numbers that may be used to satisfy this requirement, including a Social Security number, or for non-U.S. persons a passport number with country of issuance, an alien identification card, or a number and country of any other government-issued document evidencing nationality or residence and bearing a photograph—all of which are included in the existing certification form in Appendix A to the current rule. The proposal also specifies that an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) is not an acceptable substitute for a Social Security number.
[
32
]
This specification recognizes that an ITIN, as the IRS has noted, is “issued . . . for federal tax purposes only.”
[
33
]
It also reinforces the analysis set forth in FinCEN's recent advisory that recognized the use of an ITIN in lieu of a Social Security number or valid employment authorization document may be identified as a risk factor requiring enhanced due diligence.
[
34
]
Recognizing the risk associated with ITINs, FinCEN proposes to exclude their use as an identifying number for a beneficial owner. It expects that ITIN holders legally in the United States and authorized to work will have alternative identification including, for example, a foreign passport or an alien identification card.
While new in the rule itself, the proposed language identifying core pieces of information is substantively the same as the current rule's optional Appendix A form. The proposed rule returns the appendix to its proper function of providing material supplementary to the regulation, rather than stating the regulatory requirement itself. In maintaining that continuity, FinCEN seeks to preserve a workable level of flexibility for covered financial institutions in complying with this requirement. FinCEN seeks comment on the workability of its specific proposal that an ITIN cannot substitute for a Social Security number under this provision, as well as whether it should make other changes, either specifically to permit or to prohibit acceptance of other identification numbers or documents.
As noted earlier in this section, the proposed rule has a second goal: that covered financial institutions maintain the authority to collect additional information. The proposed rule does this by proposing regulatory text stating that, where warranted by other risk indicators or supervisory concerns, a covered financial institution may obtain additional information necessary to mitigate indicated risk or address supervisory concerns, including when relevant to assessing risks associated with fraud, identity misrepresentation, sanctions evasion, or other illicit financial activity, lawful immigration status or employment authorization in the United States. This is intended to make clear that, in situations of heightened risk or supervisory concern, a financial institution may consider obtaining additional information in order to confirm a beneficial owner's identity. It is also intended to make clear that such additional information can include immigration status and employment authorization information.
FinCEN anticipates providing additional guidance, alerts, or advisories to financial institutions, including highlighting new and emerging threats and typologies that may further feed into financial institutions' risk-based assessments. Providing this type of feedback through supplemental documents, rather than in specific regulatory text, will allow both Treasury and the financial institutions to more quickly adapt to address new and emerging threats and typologies and allow financial institutions to assess risks associated with fraud, identity misrepresentation, sanctions evasion, or other illicit financial activity, including illicit activity relating to a lack of lawful immigration status or employment authorization in the United States.
This proposal does not specify situations that present heightened risks, instead deferring that judgment to financial institutions and allowing them greater flexibility to identify such situations, relying on appropriate risk-based practices. However, such situations may well be judged to include instances where the identifying information for a beneficial owner residing in the United States presented to covered financial institutions includes documentation issued by a foreign government, rather than an identity document issued by a United States federal or state government agency. An individual may even present an ITIN and represent it to be a Social Security number, which could be a risk factor warranting additional inquiry.
Moreover, the CDD Rule is critical to aiding a covered financial institution's efforts to detect and report suspicious activity, including activity that could expose the institution to loss. Immigration and employment status would also be germane to reasonably assessing risk if the beneficial owner were providing a financial guarantee based on the beneficial owner's income from U.S. employment—income that might be in jeopardy if the beneficial owner were not legally authorized to work in the United States. Thus, a covered financial institution's compliance with the CDD Rule and its efforts to detect and report suspicious activity may aid the institution in evaluating risk outside of illicit finance.
[
35
]
This permissiveness, however, should not be misinterpreted. The proposed language providing that a covered financial institution “may” obtain such additional information is not intended to suggest any reduction of the requirement to conduct ongoing due diligence or to verify the identity of each beneficial owner according to risk-based procedures that contain, at a minimum, the same elements financial institutions are required to use to verify the identity of individual customers under applicable CIP requirements. It is intended to reinforce the individual covered financial institution's authority, where warranted by other risk indicators or supervisory concerns, to demand additional information as part of a risk-based customer due diligence program.
FinCEN is interested in receiving comments on whether this rulemaking strikes an appropriate balance between mandating information collection and recognition that covered financial institutions may be better placed to assess what information they should
(
printed page 74520)
collect. FinCEN is also interested in receiving comments on whether its proposed approach mitigates the risks identified in
Executive Order 14406
, including by providing covered financial institutions sufficient authority to collect necessary information.
3. Proposed
31 CFR 1010.230(b)(1)(iii)
—Sources of Information
The proposed rule also would improve the risk-based nature of the CDD Rule by providing more flexibility in how a covered financial institution obtains information, which is expected to reduce compliance burden. In doing so, this change supports
Executive Order 14406
by allowing those financial institutions to direct resources to higher risk customers and activities, including customers that present risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, and other unlawful activity as indicated in
Executive Order 14406
.
The CDD Rule specifies that covered financial institutions must obtain information about a legal entity customer's beneficial owners “from the individual opening the account on behalf of the legal entity customer,” using the optional certification form found at Appendix A to the rule or its substantive equivalent.
[
36
]
Some have attempted to read the regulation as allowing the collection of information from third parties along the lines of the bank-specific CIP Rule's special provision for the opening of individual credit card accounts, provided that a representative of the legal entity customer certified the accuracy of the information.
[
37
]
However, given the equivocal support that the CDD Rule's preamble provides for this interpretation, many covered financial institutions have been collecting beneficial ownership directly from their customers every time it was required, despite the time and expense of this practice.
[
38
]
The proposed addition of paragraph (b)(1)(iii) would offer covered financial institutions clarity by providing that a covered financial institution may obtain any information described in paragraph (b)(1)(ii) by acquiring it from a third-party source. Regardless of the source from which information is obtained, a covered financial institution must comply with the certification requirement set forth in paragraph (b)(1)(iv). Similarly, regardless of the source from which information was obtained, a covered financial institution must comply with the requirement to identify the beneficial owner(s) of a legal entity customer any time after the legal entity customer first opens an account with the covered financial institution when the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer.
4. Proposed
31 CFR 1010.230(b)(1)(iv)
—Certification
Relatedly, the proposed rule also would improve the risk-based nature of the CDD Rule by providing more flexibility about when an institution must obtain a new certification for an existing legal entity customer. This enables a covered financial institution to rely on beneficial ownership information previously obtained from a certification provided in connection with the initial opening of an account by the legal entity customer with the covered financial institution. This change supports
Executive Order 14406
by allowing financial institutions to focus on higher risk customers and activities, instead of activities that result in unnecessary information collection untethered from the risk of a particular customer.
The proposal provides that when a legal entity customer first opens an account with a covered financial institution, the covered financial institution obtaining information on the legal entity customer's beneficial owners must obtain a certification from the individual opening the account on behalf of the legal entity customer that the information obtained is accurate to the best of the individual's knowledge. A covered financial institution may, but is not required, to use the standardized certification form contained in Appendix A to § 1010.230. If the standardized certification form is not used, a covered financial institution must obtain from the individual opening the account the information required by the standardized certification form by another means.
The proposal also provides that, when obtaining information on beneficial owners as needed based on a covered financial institution's risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence, a covered financial institution may rely on beneficial ownership information previously obtained from a certification provided in connection with the initial opening of an account by the legal entity customer with the covered financial institution. In order to rely on such a prior certification, the covered financial institution must obtain from a representative of the legal entity customer either oral or written confirmation that such information is up to date and accurate to the best of the individual's knowledge. This confirmation may, but is not required to, take the form of the standardized certification form in Appendix A of this section. Thus, certification remains essential to collection of beneficial ownership information, but the proposal grants flexibility to institutions with respect to the form of certification obtained.
The covered financial institution must maintain a record of such certification or confirmation, whether the certification or confirmation is oral or written. If a covered financial institution is unable to obtain a necessary certification or confirmation that previously obtained beneficial ownership information is up-to-date and accurate, or if the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer, the covered financial institution must identify and verify the identities of the beneficial owners of the legal entity customer in accordance with the general requirements of § 1010.230.
5. Proposed
31 CFR 1010.230(b)(2)
—Verification
Under this proposal, § 1010.230 would contain a discrete list of information that covered financial institutions must collect, which would serve as the factual basis for their verification of the identities of the beneficial owners of their legal entity customers. The presence of this list could create confusion given § 1010.230's current cross-reference to the CIP rules, which encompass those rules' own list of information that must
(
printed page 74521)
be collected for CIP compliance purposes. The cross-reference currently requires covered financial institutions to have procedures that “contain the elements required for verifying the identity of customers that are individuals under § 1020.220(a)(2) of this chapter (for banks); § 1023.220(a)(2) of this chapter (for brokers or dealers in securities); § 1024.220(a)(2) of this chapter (for mutual funds); or § 1026.220(a)(2) of this chapter (for futures commission merchants or introducing brokers in commodities).”
[
39
]
Sections (a)(2)(ii) and (a)(2)(iii) of the CIP rules concern procedures for customer verification and procedures in situations where verification is impossible. Section (a)(2)(i) of those rules, however, is a list of customer information that a financial institution is required to collect about each individual or corporate customer. Among other things, section (a)(2)(i) of those rules specifically allows use of “a taxpayer identification number,”
i.e.
an ITIN, for a non-U.S. person, which would not be permitted under this proposal and should not be misinterpreted to apply to the CDD Rule.
To clarify which aspects of the CIP rules do and do not apply for purposes of the CDD Rule, FinCEN proposes amending § 1010.230(b)(2). That change will clarify that a covered financial institution must have customer due diligence verification procedures that reflect the requirements of that institution's CIP rule, but also that covered financial institutions must adhere to proposed § 1010.230(b)(1)(ii), which specifies the information to be collected. This change is designed to clarify but not change the current CDD Rule's adoption of CIP verification procedural standards while recognizing that the information a financial institution can use to verify an identity will, if this proposal is adopted, be different under the CIP and CDD Rules. FinCEN requests comment on challenges that may arise from different information collection requirements for CIP and CDD obligations, and whether the revised cross-reference is sufficiently clear.
In addition, given the continuing reference to, and incorporation of the standards of, the CIP rule, FinCEN solicits comments about the need for the CDD Rule itself to qualify the compliance standard of its verification requirement with the phrase “to the extent reasonable and practicable”—a phrase that is already found in the CIP rule.
[
40
]
Alternatively, FinCEN solicits comments on whether it should dispense with cross-references altogether and insert in the CDD Rule all of the specific appropriate procedural language now found in the CIP rule itself, even if such insertion simply reproduces relevant CIP rule language.

VI. Requests for Comment
FinCEN seeks comments on all aspects of the proposed rule and specifically seeks comments on the following topics. For all responses, commenters are encouraged to provide the basis for any conclusions drawn in their comments.
1. Do the information collection requirements proposed in this rulemaking strike an appropriate balance, including between providing covered financial institutions sufficient direction in information collection, as well as discretion to require more information when risk warrants additional collection?
2. Is the information that the proposal requires covered financial institutions to collect and verify sufficient for them to reasonably identify most beneficial owners and assess beneficial ownership-related risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, or other unlawful activity? If not, what additional or alternative information should covered financial institutions be required to collect?
3. Does the proposal provide covered financial institutions sufficient certainty that, where warranted, they maintain the ability to collect additional information, including relating to whether beneficial owners possess lawful immigration status and employment authorization in the United States? Should the proposed text be refined in any way?
4. Under the proposal, a covered financial institution may be required to collect beneficial ownership information “any time thereafter [that is, after the initial collection] when the covered financial institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of beneficial ownership information previously obtained about the legal entity customer.” Is this circumstance an appropriate trigger for identification and verification of beneficial owners? Does it need to be refined or clarified, and if so how? For example, could “reliability” be supplemented with another measure, such as “accuracy” or “continuing accuracy,” given that, if the covered financial institution has reason to believe there has been a change in ownership of the legal entity, the covered financial institution might not be questioning the “reliability” so much as the continuing accuracy of the information originally provided?
5. Does the proposal's prohibition on use of an ITIN in lieu of a Social Security number appropriately balance risk? Does it represent any compliance challenges for covered financial institutions, including because of the potential divergent approach between the information permitted to be collected under the CIP rules and the CDD Rule? Would additional FinCEN guidance help address those challenges?
6. Should FinCEN consider alternatives to prohibiting use of an ITIN? For example, should FinCEN allow collection of an ITIN for verification purposes but require a covered financial institution to undertake additional steps, such as further due diligence measures or submission of additional information or documentation? Describe benefits and drawbacks of such alternatives.
7. Are there circumstances where an individual lawfully present in the United States would have an ITIN, but no other number or document specified in the proposal? If yes, how could FinCEN account for such scenarios while still accounting for the risk addressed by
Executive Order 14406
?
8. The CDD Rule incorporates some language borrowed from the CIP rules, and it also cross-references the CIP rules. In general, should FinCEN dispense with cross-references altogether and insert in the CDD Rule all of the specific appropriate procedural language of the CIP rule itself? Whether or not FinCEN adopts this global solution, should FinCEN retain the phrase “to the extent reasonable and practicable,” borrowed from the CIP rules, in the verification section of the CDD Rule? Should it use an alternative standard? If the phrase is deleted, what will be the effect?
9. The CDD Rule requirement is, generally speaking, “categorical,” imposing essentially the same core requirements with respect to all of a covered financial institution's non-exempt legal entity customers. Should FinCEN provide greater flexibility to covered financial institutions to adjust their due diligence efforts with respect to legal entity customers and their beneficial owners downward with decreased risk, not simply upward with
(

respect to increased risk? What lower risk scenarios might be identified, under which on a risk-basis financial institutions should be permitted to collect less or different information related to beneficial ownership?
10. Should the recordkeeping requirement of the CDD Rule,
31 CFR 1010.230(i)
, be amended to better account for written or verbal confirmations contemplated under the proposed revisions to
31 CFR 1010.230(b)(1)(iv)(B)

VII. Severability
As part of this proposal, FinCEN proposes that if one portion of the proposed regulation, if finalized, is found to be invalid, the invalidated portion of the regulation should be severed with the remaining portions of the regulation remaining in full force and effect. FinCEN's position is that invalidation of any one provision, or application thereof to any one person or circumstance, does not, and should not, affect any other provision in this proposed regulation. Each provision serves an important, related, but distinct purpose and application, designed to benefit the public by protecting the U.S. financial system from illicit financial activity. FinCEN accordingly has proposed each provision such that invalidity to one provision would not undermine the operability or usefulness of the other provisions.
