IX. Regulatory Impact Analysis
FinCEN has analyzed this proposed rule as required under Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192; the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA); the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA); and the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA). This section presents the findings of its analysis, including a discussion of the expected incremental economic effects of the proposed rule relative to the current regulatory baseline and invites comment on all aspects of this analysis, including any data or information that would assist FinCEN in better quantifying the costs, cost savings, or other effects of the proposed rule.
The proposed rule would amend the CDD Rule,
31 CFR 1010.230
, primarily by making three overarching revisions, and introduce certain minor regulatory clarifications. These revisions, as discussed in section III: (1) make it explicit that covered financial institutions may obtain additional information necessary to mitigate indicated risk or address supervisory concerns; (2) incorporate FinCEN's exceptive relief and required information, permissible sources, and certification; and (3) specify pieces of information required to be collected, while providing additional flexibility in how such information is obtained. The following analysis focuses on the expected incremental economic effects of these revisions.
As a threshold matter, FinCEN does not expect the proposed amendments would have a significant economic effect. Among other things, the proposal would not expand the set of covered financial institutions, would not expand the definition of legal entity customer, would not require covered financial institutions to collect beneficial ownership information from a new class of customers, and would not impose a new mandatory reporting or recordkeeping requirement. Instead, the proposal would codify regulatory flexibility that reduces duplicative beneficial ownership identification and verification at repeat account openings while identifying select risk-based triggers for obtaining and updating information when appropriate. The proposed clarification regarding the collection of additional information in heightened-risk circumstances is itself risk based; it does not impose a categorical obligation to collect any particular additional document or information, nor does it expand the pre-existing authority or obligation of covered financial institutions to collect risk-relevant information.
[
44
]
A. Analysis of Impact
1. Broad Economic Considerations
As it proposes these amendments to § 1010.230, FinCEN remains mindful of the fundamental economic tensions observed in the original rule. The analysis in the CDD Rule framed beneficial ownership requirements as addressing externalities associated with
(
printed page 74523)
illicit finance. Covered financial institutions bear the private costs of collecting and verifying beneficial ownership information, while many of the benefits of improved transparency, including reduced money laundering, terrorist financing, fraud, sanctions evasion, and related illicit activity, accrue broadly to the public, law enforcement, national security agencies, and the financial system as a whole. Absent a standard of collection requirements, covered financial institutions may underinvest in beneficial ownership information collection, particularly if they believe more rigorous requirements could place them at a competitive disadvantage relative to institutions with less comprehensive practices.
Prior FinCEN analysis also recognized cross-border spillovers.
[
45
]
Jurisdictions with less stringent AML/CFT standards may become more attractive destinations for laundering proceeds generated by illicit activity elsewhere, allowing those jurisdictions to receive capital inflows without bearing the full social costs of the underlying crimes. A clear and consistent CDD framework can help mitigate this concern by improving beneficial ownership transparency and making it more costly for illicit actors to misuse legal entities to access the U.S. financial system.
The proposed revisions build on that same general framework but are expected to have more limited incremental economic effects than the original CDD Rule. Rather than creating a new beneficial ownership information-collection obligation, the proposal would clarify and refine existing CDD requirements, reduce duplicative collection at repeat account openings, and preserve risk-based authority to obtain additional information when warranted by risk indicators or supervisory concerns. Thus, the relevant economic trade-off is not whether to impose a new beneficial ownership framework, but how best to preserve the benefits of beneficial ownership transparency while reducing unnecessary or duplicative compliance activity.
Having taken the original animating concerns into consideration, FinCEN believes the proposed amendments would enhance the balance of imposing private costs on financial institutions for the public benefit of standardized due diligence practices.
2. Institutional Baseline and Affected Parties
a. Regulatory Baseline
The anticipated incremental economic effects of the proposed rule were analyzed against a counterfactual state of the world in which a covered financial institution's obligations under the BSA would maintain the
status quo.
For purposes of this analysis, FinCEN considered the most salient component of the regulatory baseline to be comprised of both the original CDD Rule, as currently implemented and interpreted, and FinCEN's February 2026 exceptive relief.
[
46
]
Additionally, the impact analysis takes into account that covered financial institutions continue to be subject to, among other obligations, applicable AML/CFT program, customer identification, suspicious activity reporting, and recordkeeping requirements under the BSA. FinCEN further took into consideration that covered financial institutions' business practices may be subject to other regulatory standards and requirements that govern operating risks.
[
47
]
Using this baseline, FinCEN does not expect the proposed rule to impose significant incremental costs because the primary change is to codify and make durable an existing form of relief, while clarifying that covered financial institutions may obtain additional information in risk-based circumstances. In the alternative, if the proposed rule were evaluated relative to the pre-relief requirement to identify and verify beneficial owners each time a legal entity customer opened a new account, the proposed rule would be expected to generate cost savings by eliminating duplicative beneficial ownership collection and verification at repeat account openings.
b. Baseline of Affected Parties
The primary affected parties of the proposed amendments are the covered financial institutions already subject to the CDD Rule and, indirectly, their current and prospective legal entity customers and beneficial owners. Because the proposal would not expand the definition of covered financial institution, legal entity customer, account, or beneficial owner, FinCEN does not expect the proposal to impose new compliance costs on any newly affected population. FinCEN encourages commenters who do not share this expectation to submit comments on the subject, ideally supported by specific information.

c. Current Market Practices
Covered financial institutions currently use a range of processes to manage account-opening, customer due diligence, customer identification, and beneficial ownership information-related activities. 4. Anticipated Economic Effects
a. Expected Benefits
FinCEN expects the proposed rule to produce several categories of benefits. First, codifying the relief from beneficial ownership identification and verification at every repeat account opening should reduce duplicative compliance activity. Covered financial institutions would be able to rely on beneficial ownership information obtained at the first account opening unless facts reasonably call the reliability of that information into question or risk-based procedures otherwise require additional or updated information. This should reduce repetitive customer outreach, duplicative collection of identification information, and associated account-opening delays.
Second, the proposed rule should improve regulatory clarity. Codifying the February 2026 exceptive relief in the CDD Rule would reduce uncertainty about the continued availability and operation of that relief and would allow covered financial institutions to design policies, procedures, systems, and training around the text of the regulation. Clearer regulatory text may also promote more consistent supervisory expectations across covered financial institutions and functional regulators, possibly reducing examination costs.
Third, the proposal should better align the CDD Rule with a risk-based
(
printed page 74526)
approach to AML/CFT compliance. The proposal would preserve the ability, and where applicable the obligation, of covered financial institutions to update or obtain additional information when facts call previously obtained beneficial ownership information into question or when risk-based procedures indicate that additional or updated information is appropriate. At the same time, the proposal would avoid requiring covered financial institutions to repeat the same identification and verification steps at every account opening without regard to risk or whether the institution already has reliable information about the legal entity customer.
Fourth, the proposed clarification concerning additional information in heightened-risk or supervisory-concern circumstances may help covered financial institutions resolve material compliance concerns involving fraud, identity misrepresentation, sanctions evasion, or other illicit financial activity. By clarifying that covered financial institutions may obtain additional information where warranted by risk indicators or supervisory concerns, the proposal may support more effective risk assessment while avoiding a categorical, one-size-fits-all requirement.
FinCEN has not quantified these benefits at this stage because public data are limited regarding the number of repeat account openings by the same legal entity customer at the same covered financial institution and regarding the degree to which institutions have already implemented the February 2026 exceptive relief.
b. Expected Costs
FinCEN does not expect the proposed rule to impose significant economic costs. The proposal would not impose a new obligation to file reports with FinCEN, would not require covered financial institutions to retain a new category of records, would not expand the population of covered financial institutions, and would not impose a new mandatory customer due diligence procedure for all accounts or all customers.
Covered financial institutions may incur limited one-time costs to review the final rule and revise policies, procedures, forms, account-opening workflows, monitoring processes, or training materials. FinCEN expects these costs to be small because covered financial institutions already maintain CDD policies and procedures and because the proposed rule generally aligns with existing exceptive relief and ordinary-course risk-based due diligence practices. To the extent an institution has already implemented the February 2026 exceptive relief, any incremental implementation cost attributable to this proposal should be further reduced.
FinCEN does not expect that its specification of information covered financial institutions must collect and exclusion of ITINs will impose significant costs. FinCEN believes its proposed regulatory text largely aligns with current practices, though some institutions may incur limited one-time costs to review the final rule and revise policies, procedures, forms, account-opening workflows, monitoring processes, or training materials accordingly.
FinCEN does not expect the proposed clarification regarding additional information in heightened-risk circumstances to require covered financial institutions to collect additional information in every case. The proposed language would clarify that an institution may consider obtaining additional information where warranted by risk indicators or supervisory concerns and where the information is relevant to resolving material compliance concerns. FinCEN does not expect this clarification to result in significant recurring costs.
FinCEN also does not expect the proposed rule to have significant adverse effects on competition, innovation, access to financial services, or market structure. By reducing duplicative collection and verification requirements, the proposal may reduce account-opening friction for legal entity customers, including small businesses.
5. Consideration of Alternatives
In developing the proposed rule, FinCEN considered several policy alternatives, including alternatives specifically tailored to accommodate small entities that may otherwise be disproportionately burdened by regulatory compliance. FinCEN invites comment on these alternatives, and on any other alternatives that were not considered here but could reasonably be expected to accomplish the same policy objectives with equal or greater efficiency.
a. Alternative 1: Strictly Risk-Based Information Collection
First, FinCEN considered adopting an entirely risk-based approach to the determination of the types of information that covered financial institutions would have to collect in order to identify and verify the identity of beneficial owners of legal entity customers.
[
52
]
In contrast to the proposed rule, the alternative considered would eliminate the proposed list of required information and instead grant covered financial institutions complete discretion to determine what information to obtain from a beneficial owner of a legal entity customer, based upon the institution's own risk-based analysis.
FinCEN believes that the proposed rule, which specifies certain information that a covered financial institution must collect, appropriately acknowledges a continuing need for a minimum standard, supplemented, rather than replaced, by tailoring based on risk. FinCEN is concerned that declining to set a minimum requirement for information to be collected across covered financial institutions would make it easier for illicit actors to enter into the financial system by persuading covered financial institutions that they are low-risk customers and therefore should not provide much, if any, identifying information, or by targeting covered financial institutions with less comprehensive CDD programs or less sophisticated risk-analysis capabilities. In return for focusing on heightened risks, the financial services industry as a whole might obtain some regulatory relief, but in FinCEN's judgment not significantly more than the proposal itself provides. Accordingly, FinCEN has opted against this alternative. This alternative could reduce compliance costs for some covered financial institutions by allowing them to collect less information for beneficial owners they determine to present lower risk. The cost savings would likely arise from reduced customer outreach, fewer information fields collected, and potentially shorter account-opening processes in low-risk cases. The magnitude of those savings, however, is uncertain and may be limited because the proposed rule already reduces duplicative compliance activity by eliminating repeated beneficial ownership identification and
(
printed page 74527)
verification at repeat account openings unless facts or risk-based procedures call for updated information. The proposed rule also already permits covered financial institutions to obtain additional information only where warranted by risk indicators or supervisory concerns, rather than imposing a categorical obligation to collect additional information in every case.
This alternative would also likely provide greater discretion and potentially greater burden reduction in some low-risk circumstances, but at the cost of reduced uniformity, less regulatory certainty, and potentially weaker beneficial ownership transparency. This trade-off may be particularly important for smaller or less technologically sophisticated covered financial institutions. Although the alternative could appear less burdensome because it would allow such institutions to collect less information in some cases, it could also require them to make and document more case-specific judgments about what information is sufficient to identify and verify beneficial owners. That added discretion could increase uncertainty, training needs, supervisory risk, and inconsistency in implementation.
FinCEN therefore expects that the proposed rule would better balance costs and benefits. Compared with the alternative, the proposed rule is expected to preserve more of the AML/CFT, countering fraud, countering sanctions-evasion, and countering illicit-finance benefits associated with a uniform beneficial ownership identification baseline, while still reducing burden through relief from duplicative collection at repeat account openings, greater flexibility to use third-party sources, and risk-based authority to obtain additional information when warranted. Accordingly, FinCEN preliminarily assesses that the alternative would likely provide, at most, modest additional compliance cost savings relative to the proposal, while presenting greater risks to regulatory consistency and the effectiveness of customer due diligence.
b. Alternative 2: Additional Data Collection Requirements
FinCEN separately considered a version of the proposed rule that would have required covered financial institutions to collect additional information beyond what this proposal would require by expanding the list of information an institution must obtain about each beneficial owner of a legal entity customer beyond the beneficial owner's name, date of birth, address, and qualifying identifying number. The goal of such an enhanced data collection requirement would be to reduce uncertainty about whether the information that a covered financial institution can be relied upon to collect will be sufficient to perform a meaningful analysis of beneficial ownership-related risks.
FinCEN believes that such an approach would be overly prescriptive and inconsistent with the aim of
Executive Order 14406
to improve the risk-based nature of the CDD Rule by allowing financial institutions to focus on higher-risk customers, including those that present risks related to illicit finance, sanctions evasion, fraud, and other unlawful activity. FinCEN believes that the proposed rule would ensure that covered financial institutions collect sufficient information concerning the beneficial owners of their legal entity customers, while providing the necessary flexibility for a covered financial institution to collect additional information for specific beneficial owners where such collection is warranted by risk. The small benefit in terms of increased regulatory certainty that the alternative would achieve would come at significant cost to covered financial institutions. Thus, FinCEN rejected this alternative approach.
This alternative would likely produce greater regulatory certainty than the proposed rule by specifying additional information that covered financial institutions must obtain from each beneficial owner of a legal entity customer. A more prescriptive information-collection requirement could reduce ambiguity about whether an institution has collected enough information to conduct a meaningful beneficial ownership risk assessment and could promote more uniform practices across covered financial institutions.
However, relative to the proposed rule, this alternative would likely impose materially greater costs, by requiring additional information in all cases, including for legal entity customers and beneficial owners that present lower risk and for whom the additional information may have limited marginal value. The principal costs of this alternative would likely include increased customer outreach, longer account-opening processes, additional form and system changes, additional training, and greater compliance and quality-control burdens. These costs would be recurring because institutions would have to collect any additional information for each covered beneficial owner whenever beneficial ownership information is required. The alternative could also increase burden on legal entity customers and beneficial owners by requiring them to provide additional information even when no risk-based factor suggests that the information is needed.
FinCEN preliminarily assesses that the proposed rule better balances costs and benefits. Compared with the alternative, the proposed rule preserves a clear minimum standard, maintains flexibility to collect additional information in higher-risk circumstances, and avoids imposing additional recurring burden on all covered financial institutions, legal entity customers, and beneficial owners.
c. Alternative 3: Delayed Effective Date for Small Financial Institutions
FinCEN separately and additionally considered modifying the proposed rule to provide a delayed effective date for small financial institutions as defined by the RFA, as a way of minimizing costs to small businesses. However, FinCEN does not believe that implementation of the proposed rule would impose a significant burden on small financial institutions, as much of the proposal is permissive rather than prescriptive or captures existing industry practices. Additionally, FinCEN is mindful that by introducing a staggered effective date by financial institution size, this may inadvertently create confusion or unequal burdens for the small businesses that are the legal entity customers of covered financial institutions by causing them to face different standards of information provision based on the size of the institutions where they maintain an account. Accordingly, FinCEN has opted against this alternative.
This alternative could reduce near-term implementation burden for small covered financial institutions by giving them additional time to review the final rule and make any needed updates to policies, procedures, forms, workflows, systems, or training materials. A delayed effective date could be most useful in providing additional time for small institutions with less automated account-opening systems, fewer compliance personnel, or greater reliance on third-party vendors or core processors whose services might be more difficult to obtain or more expensive for small financial institutions if required to compete with larger institutions in the run-up to a universal, industry-wide effective date.
FinCEN expects, however, that the incremental benefit of this alternative
(
printed page 74528)
would be limited. The proposed rule is not expected to impose significant costs because it would not expand the population of covered financial institutions, legal entity customers, accounts, or beneficial owners, and would not impose new mandatory reporting, recordkeeping, or customer information collection requirements. A delayed effective date for small financial institutions would also delay the benefits of regulatory clarity and burden reduction for those institutions.
FinCEN preliminarily assesses that the proposed rule better balances costs and benefits. A delayed effective date for small financial institutions could provide some additional implementation flexibility, but the likely cost savings would be modest because the proposal is expected to reduce, rather than increase, recurring beneficial ownership collection and verification obligations. The proposed rule also aligns with practices that at least some institutions have already revised or begun revising in response to the February 2026 exceptive relief.
B. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, to the extent permitted by law, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits, including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety, distributive, and equity effects.
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility.
FinCEN has considered the expected costs and benefits of the proposed rule and does not anticipate that it would introduce an effect of $100 million or more on the economy in a given year. Notwithstanding a lack of expected economic significance under section 3(f)(1) of
Executive Order 12866

Executive Order 12866
. Accordingly, FinCEN has conducted the requisite regulatory impact analysis and included a summary thereof in section IX.A.
FinCEN expects that this action, when finalized, would be an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action because it is expected to reduce compliance burden and to have total costs less than zero. The proposal would codify relief from duplicative beneficial ownership identification and verification at repeat account openings and would not impose a new mandatory reporting, recordkeeping, or customer information collection requirement.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The RFA requires an agency either to provide an initial regulatory flexibility analysis with a proposed rule or to certify that the proposed rule, if promulgated, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The proposed rule would apply to covered financial institutions, some of which are small entities. However, the proposal would not expand the categories of covered financial institutions, would not impose a new reporting or recordkeeping requirement, and would not require covered financial institutions to collect additional information in all cases.
FinCEN expects that any one-time costs for small covered financial institutions would be limited to ordinary-course review of the final rule and conforming updates to policies, procedures, forms, training, or workflows. FinCEN expects those costs to be small because small covered financial institutions already maintain CDD procedures and because the proposal is expected to reduce rather than increase recurring beneficial ownership collection and verification obligations for repeat account openings. Accordingly, FinCEN certifies that the proposed rule, if finalized, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.

(iii)
Sources of Information.
Subject to compliance with the certification requirement in paragraph (b)(1)(iv) of this section, a covered financial institution may obtain any information described in paragraph (b)(1)(ii) of this section by acquiring it from a third-party source.
(iv)
Certification.
(A) When obtaining information at a time described in paragraph (b)(1)(i)(A) of this section, a covered financial institution must obtain a certification from the individual opening the account on behalf of the legal entity customer that the information obtained is accurate to the best of the individual's knowledge. This certification may, but is not required to, take the form of the certification in Appendix A of this section.
(B) When obtaining information at a time described in paragraph (b)(1)(i)(C) of this section, a covered financial institution may rely on information to which a certification provided in connection with obtaining information at a time described in paragraph (b)(1)(i)(A) of this section applies, provided that a representative of the legal entity customer provides oral or written confirmation that such information is up to date and accurate to the best of the individual's knowledge. Written confirmation may, but is not required to, take the form of the certification in Appendix A of this section.
(2) Verify the identity of each beneficial owner identified to the covered financial institution, according to risk-based procedures, to the extent reasonable and practicable. At a minimum, these procedures must require collection of information specified in paragraph (b)(1)(ii) and contain the elements required for verifying the identity of customers that are individuals under § 1020.220(a)(2), other than § 1020.220(a)(2)(i), of this chapter (for banks); § 1023.220(a)(2), other than § 1023.220(a)(2)(i), of this chapter (for brokers or dealers in securities); § 1024.220(a)(2), other than § 1024.220(a)(2)(i), of this chapter (for mutual funds); or § 1026.220(a)(2), other than § 1026.220(a)(2)(i), of this chapter (for futures commission merchants or introducing brokers in commodities); provided, that in the case of documentary verification, the financial institution may use photocopies or other reproductions of the documents listed in paragraph (a)(2)(ii)(A)(
1
) of § 1020.220 of this chapter (for banks); § 1023.220 of this chapter (for brokers or dealers in securities); § 1024.220 of this chapter (for mutual funds); or § 1026.220 of this chapter (for futures commission merchants or introducing brokers in commodities). A covered financial institution may rely on the information supplied by the legal entity customer regarding the identity of its beneficial owner or owners, provided that it has no knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of such information.

Title:
Stopping Threats on Pedestrians (STOP) Grant Program, also known as the Bollards Competitive Grant Program.
Background:
The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) administers the Stopping Threats on Pedestrians (STOP) program. It was established by Congress in Section 11502 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA),
Public Law 117-58
.
The purpose of the Bollards Competitive Grant program is to provide competitive grants to local government entities and State Departments of Transportation to install bollards and other physical barriers designed to prevent death and injury from motor vehicle-pedestrian accidents. The program's goals include hardening “soft targets” in high-pedestrian areas, enhancing public safety in crowded spaces such as plazas and transit hubs, and reducing the frequency of vehicle-ramming incidents.
The program provides competitive grants for which the Federal share of the cost of an installation project may be up to 100 percent. The FHWA has authorized $5 million for fiscal year 2026 grants to support these critical safety and security infrastructure efforts.

. FHWA is expecting roughly 50 applicants to apply for STOP grant funding, 15 grant agreements, and 30 respondents during the project management phase.

4 hours per respondent per applicant during the application and project management phase and 2 hours per respondent during the grant agreement phase.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
It is expected that there will be an estimated total of 350 annual burden hours.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, FAA invites public comments about our intention to request the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval for a renewed information collection. The
Federal Register
Notice with a 60-day comment period soliciting comments on the following collection of information was published on July 20, 2026. FAA received five comments to this notice. The collection involves a request that airplane operators subject to the applicability of Annex 16, Volume IV of the Convention on Civil Aviation (hereinafter the “Chicago Convention”) submit electronically an Emissions Monitoring Plan (EMP), an annual Emissions Report (ER), and an optional annual ER Eligible Fuels Annex (EFA) to the FAA. The information to be collected is necessary because FAA will use the information to fulfill the United States' responsibilities under the Chicago Convention.
DATES:

;

Public Comments Invited:
You are asked to comment on any aspect of this information collection, including (a) Whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for FAA's performance; (b) the accuracy of the estimated burden; (c) ways for FAA to enhance the quality, utility and clarity

Title:
CORSIA Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) Program.
Form Numbers:
1. Emissions Monitoring Plan (EMP) Template; 2. Emissions Report (ER) Template; 3. ER Eligible Fuels Annex (EFA).
Type of Review:
Clearance of a renewal of an information collection.
Background:
The
Federal Register
Notice with a 60-day comment period soliciting comments on the following collection of information was published on July 20, 2026 (
91 FR 45317
). FAA received five comments in response to this notice.
The FAA MRV Program is a voluntary program for certain U.S. air carriers and commercial operators (collectively referred hereinafter as “operators”) to submit certain airplane emissions data to the FAA to enable the United States to establish uniformity with ICAO Standards And Recommended Practices (SARPs) for Annex 16, Volume IV of the Chicago Convention, which were adopted in June 2018, as Annex 16, Volume IV to the Chicago Convention. Facilitating voluntary reporting by U.S. operators will ensure fair and reciprocal commercial competition by avoiding a patchwork of country- or regionally-based regulatory measures that are inconsistently applied, bureaucratically costly, and economically damaging.
According to Annex 16, Volume IV, all ICAO Member States whose airplane operators undertake international flights were required to develop an MRV system for emissions from those international flights starting January 1, 2019. The FAA MRV Program is intended to be the United States' MRV system for monitoring, reporting, and verification of U.S. airplane operator emissions from international flights.
Operators that are subject to the applicability of Annex 16, Volume IV will submit their EMPs, ERs, and optional ER EFAs electronically.
[
1
]
Each document uses Microsoft Excel-based templates and can be transmitted via email. EMPs that are submitted by operators will be used as a collaborative tool between the operator and FAA to document a given operator's chosen fuel use monitoring procedures. FAA will retain a copy of the EMP and will share with ICAO a list of operators that submit EMPs. FAA will not submit any specific EMPs from U.S. operators to ICAO. Operators may gather data through a “fuel use monitoring method” or a simplified monitoring method depending on the scale of their operations. Annual ERs that are submitted to FAA by operators and verifiers will be used to document each operators' international emissions. FAA will use the ERs, and optional ER EFAs, to calculate aggregated emissions data for all U.S. operators. FAA will submit the aggregated emissions data to ICAO to demonstrate U.S. implementation of Annex 16, Volume IV.
Respondents:
Respondents will be airplane operators subject to the applicability of Annex 16, Volume IV of the Chicago Convention. FAA expects between 40 and 50 operators to submit an EMP and ER. Some additional operators could submit an EMP and ER over time based on their international aviation activities.
Frequency:
An EMP is a one-time submission. An ER and optional ER EFA is an annual submission.
Estimated Average Burden per Response:
—For an EMP (one-time submission), FAA expects that filling and submitting an EMP could on average take approximately 28.6 hours.
—For an ER (annual submission), FAA expects that the reporting burden could be approximately 68 hours per operator using a Fuel Use Monitoring Method, inclusive of approximately 8 hours per operator that chooses to voluntarily submit an optional ER EFA. FAA expects the reporting burden could be approximately 21.5 hours per operator for operators using a simplified Monitoring Method, inclusive of approximately 4 hours per operator that chooses to voluntarily submit an optional ER EFA.
Estimated Total Annual Burden:
Based on the above, FAA expects that the annual submission of an EMP and ER, including optional ER EFA, could take approximately 37.5 to 115.5 hours for each of the 40-50 operators.
Issued in Washington, DC, on November 17, 2026.
Julie Ann Marks,
Executive Director, Office of Environment and Energy.

—Operations using an airplane with a maximum certificated take-off mass equal to or less than 5,700 kg;
—Operations on behalf of the military.

On November 4, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) filed a preliminary answer opposing fast-track processing and a motion requesting a four-week extension of time, until December 21, 2026, to answer the complaint filed by Exelon Corporation (Exelon) in the above-captioned proceeding. PJM argues that there is good cause to grant the extension because the additional time will permit PJM to incorporate into its response the outcome of the deliberations by the PJM Board, which will meet on November 17, 2026. PJM also argues that Exelon has failed to demonstrate any compelling reason for Commission action by the requested January 31, 2027, date and therefore a four-week extension of the answer deadline will not impair the Commission's ability to act.
On November 9, 2026, Exelon filed a motion for leave to answer and answer. Exelon supports an extension of the comment period to December 7, 2026, but argues that the scale of PJM's proposed extension is excessive for the narrow scope of the allegations it must answer. Exelon also urges the Commission to act sufficiently in advance of the May 2027 Base Residual Auction.
Upon consideration, notice is hereby given that PJM's motion for extension of time is granted and the deadline to file the answer to Exelon's complaint, comments, and interventions is December 21, 2026.

If a Notice of Schedule for Environmental Review is issued, it will indicate, among other milestones, the anticipated date for the Commission staff's issuance of the final environmental impact statement (FEIS) or environmental assessment (EA) for this proposal. The filing of an EA in the Commission's public record for this proceeding or the issuance of a Notice of Schedule for Environmental Review will serve to notify federal and state agencies of the timing for the completion of all necessary reviews, and the subsequent need to complete all federal authorizations within 90 days of the date of issuance of the Commission staff's FEIS or EA.
Public Participation
There are three ways to become involved in the Commission's review of this project: you can file comments on the project, you can protest the filing, and you can file a motion to intervene in the proceeding. There is no fee or cost for filing comments or intervening. The deadline for filing a motion to intervene is 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on December 7, 2026. How to file protests, motions to intervene, and comments is explained below.
For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions, comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation (OPP) at (202) 502-6595 or
OPP@ferc.gov

6

AGENCY:
Bureau of Land Management, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of application.
SUMMARY:
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) has received a right-of-way (ROW) application from Coastal Connect Services, LLC for a proposed intrastate natural gas pipeline in Cape Canaveral, Florida. The BLM will complete environmental analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) before deciding whether to authorize the pipeline ROW.
DATES:
The application was accepted by BLM Southeastern States District Office on September 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The ROW application and maps of the project are available for review at the BLM Southeastern States District Office located at 273 Market Street, Flowood, Mississippi 39232.
NEPA documents associated with this proposal will be released to the public upon completion. Once available, these documents may be accessed online via the following link:
https://eplanning.blm.gov/​Project-Home/​?id=​c6d2b2a5-c9bd-f111-aaae-001dd8029bbb
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shayne Banks, Acting District Manager, telephone: (601) 919-4652; address: 273 Market Street, Flowood, MS 39232; email:
sbanks@blm.gov
.
Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services for contacting Ms. Banks. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The applicant seeks a ROW for a 16-inch diameter natural gas pipeline and related facilities totaling approximately 20.3 miles, including temporary workspaces and minor above ground components such as mainline valves and rust-prevention equipment. The pipeline would provide natural gas services to Space Launch Complex 37 and Launch Complex 39A at Cape Canaveral, Florida, to support future launch operations, and eliminate the need for fuel truck deliveries at these locations. For more detailed information regarding the application, maps, and overall project, refer to

title: Medicare Program; CY 2027 Part A Premiums for the Uninsured Aged and for Certain Disabled Individuals Who Have Exhausted Other Entitlement
abstract: This notice announces Medicare's Hospital Insurance Program (Medicare Part A) premium for uninsured enrollees in calendar year (CY) 2027. This premium is paid by enrollees aged 65 and over who are not otherwise eligible for benefits under Medicare Part A (hereafter known as the "uninsured aged") and by certain individuals with disabilities who have exhausted other entitlement. The monthly Medicare Part A premium for the 12 months beginning January 1, 2027 for these individuals will be $597. The premium for certain other individuals as described in this notice will be $328.

Department of Health and Human Services
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
[CMS-8093-N]
RIN 0938-AV85
AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), HHS.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces Medicare's Hospital Insurance Program (Medicare Part A) premium for uninsured enrollees in calendar year (CY) 2027. This premium is paid by enrollees aged 65 and over who are not otherwise eligible for benefits under Medicare Part A (hereafter known as the “uninsured aged”) and by certain individuals with disabilities who have exhausted other entitlement. The monthly Medicare Part A premium for the 12 months beginning January 1, 2027 for these individuals will be $597. The premium for certain other individuals as described in this notice will be $328.
DATES:
The premium announced in this notice is effective on January 1, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Yaminee Thaker, (410) 786-7921.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Section 1818 of the Social Security Act (the Act) provides for voluntary enrollment in Medicare Part A, subject to payment of a monthly premium, of certain persons aged 65 and older who are uninsured under the Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) program or the Railroad Retirement Act and do not otherwise meet the requirements for entitlement to Medicare Part A. These “uninsured aged” individuals are uninsured under the OASDI program or the Railroad Retirement Act, because they do not have 40 quarters of coverage under Title II of the Act (or are/were not married to someone who did). (Persons insured under the OASDI program or the Railroad Retirement Act and certain others do not have to pay premiums for Medicare Part A.)
Section 1818A of the Act provides for voluntary enrollment in Medicare Part A, subject to payment of a monthly premium for certain individuals with disabilities who have exhausted other entitlement. These are individuals who were entitled to coverage due to a disabling impairment under section 226(b) of the Act, but who are no longer entitled to disability benefits and premium-free Medicare Part A coverage because they have gone back to work and their earnings exceed the statutorily defined “substantial gainful activity” amount (section 223(d)(4) of the Act).
Section 1818A(d)(2) of the Act specifies that the provisions relating to premiums for the aged under section 1818(d) through section 1818(f) of the Act will also apply to certain individuals with disabilities as described above.
Section 1818(d)(1) of the Act requires us to estimate, on an average per capita basis, the amount to be paid from the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund for services incurred in the upcoming calendar year (CY) (including the associated administrative costs) on behalf of individuals aged 65 and over who will be entitled to benefits under Medicare Part A. We must then determine the monthly actuarial rate for the following year (the per capita amount estimated above divided by 12) and publish the dollar amount for the monthly premium in the succeeding CY. If the premium is not a multiple of $1, the premium is rounded to the nearest multiple of $1 (or, if it is a multiple of 50 cents but not of $1, it is rounded to the next highest $1).
Section 13508 of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993 (Pub. L. 103-66) amended section 1818(d) of the Act to provide for a reduction in the premium amount for certain voluntary enrollees (sections 1818 and 1818A of the Act). The reduction applies to an individual who is eligible to buy into the Medicare Part A program and who, as of the last day of the previous month:
Had at least 30 quarters of coverage under Title II of the Act;
Was married, and had been married for the previous 1-year period, to a person who had at least 30 quarters of coverage;
Had been married to a person for at least 1 year at the time of the person's death if, at the time of death, the person had at least 30 quarters of coverage; or
Is divorced from a person and had been married to the person for at least 10 years at the time of the divorce if, at the time of the divorce, the person had at least 30 quarters of coverage.
Section 1818(d)(4)(A) of the Act specifies that the premium that these individuals will pay for CY 2027 will be equal to the premium for uninsured aged enrollees reduced by 45 percent.
Section 1818(g) of the Act requires the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (the Secretary), at the request of a State, to enter into a Medicare Part A buy-in agreement with a State to pay Medicare Part A premiums for Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (QMBs). Under the QMB program, State Medicaid agencies must pay the Medicare Part A premium for those not eligible for premium-free Medicare Part A if those individuals meet all of the eligibility requirements for the QMB program under the State's Medicaid State plan. Entering into a Medicare Part A buy-in agreement would permit a State to avoid any Medicare Part A late enrollment penalties that the individual may owe and would allow States to enroll persons in Medicare Part A at any time of the year, without regard to Medicare enrollment periods. Other individuals may be eligible for the Qualified Disabled Working Individuals program, through which State Medicaid programs provide coverage of Medicare Part A premiums for individuals eligible to enroll in Medicare Part A by virtue of section 1818A of the Act who meet certain financial eligibility criteria.
II. Monthly Premium Amount for CY 2027
The monthly premium for the uninsured aged and certain individuals with disabilities who have exhausted other entitlement for the 12 months beginning January 1, 2027, is $597. The monthly premium for the individuals eligible under section 1818(d)(4)(B) of the Act, and therefore, subject to the 45 percent reduction in the monthly premium, is $328.
(
printed page 74557)
III. Monthly Premium Rate Calculation
As discussed in section I of this notice, the monthly Medicare Part A premium is equal to the estimated monthly actuarial rate for CY 2027 rounded to the nearest multiple of $1 and equals one-twelfth of the average per capita amount, which is determined by projecting the number of Medicare Part A enrollees aged 65 years and over, as well as the benefits and administrative costs that will be incurred on their behalf.
The steps involved in projecting these future costs to the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund are:
Establishing the present cost of services furnished to beneficiaries, by type of service, to serve as a projection base;
Projecting increases in payment amounts for each of the service types; and
Projecting increases in administrative costs.
We base our projections for CY 2027 on—(1) current historical data; and (2) projection assumptions derived from current law and the Midsession Review of the President's Fiscal Year 2027 Budget.
For CY 2027, we estimate that 63,981,910 people aged 65 years and over will be entitled to (enrolled in) benefits (without premium payment) and that they will incur about $458,587 billion in benefits and related administrative costs. Thus, the estimated monthly average per capita amount is $597.29 and the monthly premium is $597. Subsequently, the full monthly premium reduced by 45 percent is $328.
IV. Costs to Beneficiaries
The CY 2027 monthly premium of $597 is approximately 5.7 percent higher than the CY 2026 premium of $565. We estimate that approximately 904,000 enrollees will voluntarily enroll in Medicare Part A by paying the full premium. We estimate that over 90 percent of these individuals will have their Medicare Part A premium paid by States, since they are enrolled in the QMB program. Furthermore, the CY 2027 reduced monthly premium of $328 is approximately 5.5 percent higher than the CY 2026 premium of $311. We estimate that an additional 129,000 enrollees will pay the reduced premium. Therefore, we estimate that the total aggregate cost to enrollees paying these premiums in CY 2027, compared to the amount that they paid in CY 2026, will be about $373 million.
V. Waiver of Proposed Rulemaking
We ordinarily publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
and invite public comment prior to a rule taking effect in accordance with section 1871 of the Act. Section 1871(a)(2) of the Act provides that no rule, requirement, or other statement of policy (other than a national coverage determination) that establishes or changes a substantive legal standard governing the scope of benefits, the payment for services, or the eligibility of individuals, entities, or organizations to furnish or receive services or benefits under Medicare shall take effect unless it is promulgated through notice and comment rulemaking. Unless there is a statutory exception, section 1871(b)(1) of the Act generally requires the Secretary to provide for notice of a proposed rule in the
Federal Register
and provide a period of not less than 60 days for public comment before establishing or changing a substantive legal standard regarding the matters enumerated by the statute. Section 1871(b)(2)(C) of the Act also provides exceptions from the notice and 60-day comment period, under the good cause standard set forth in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
. Section 553(b)(B) authorizes an agency to dispense with notice and comment rulemaking for good cause if the agency makes a finding that notice and comment procedures are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
The annual Medicare Part A premium announcement set forth in this notice does not establish or change a substantive legal standard regarding the matters enumerated by the statute or constitute a substantive rule which would be subject to the notice requirements in section 1871(b) of the Act. However, to the extent that an opportunity for public notice and comment could be construed as required for this notice, we find good cause to waive this requirement.
Section 1818(d) of the Act requires the Secretary during September of each year to determine and publish the amount to be paid, on an average per capita basis, from the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund for services incurred in the impending CY (including the associated administrative costs) on behalf of individuals aged 65 and over who will be entitled to benefits under Medicare Part A. Further, the statute requires that the agency determine the applicable premium amount for each CY in accordance with the statutory formula, and we are simply notifying the public of the changes to the Medicare Part A premiums for CY 2027. We have calculated the Medicare Part A premiums as directed by the statute; the statute establishes both when the premium amounts must be published and the information that the Secretary must factor into the premium amounts, so we do not have any discretion in that regard. We find notice and comment procedures to be unnecessary for this notice and we find good cause to waive such procedures under section 553(b)(B) and section 1871(b)(2)(C) of the Act, if such procedures may be construed to be required at all. Through this notice, we are simply notifying the public of the updates to the Medicare Part A premiums, in accordance with the statute, for CY 2027.
VI. Collection of Information Requirements
This document does not impose information collection requirements, that is, reporting, recordkeeping or third-party disclosure requirements. Consequently, there is no need for review by the Office of Management and Budget under the authority of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C.
3501 et seq.
).
VII. Regulatory Impact Analysis
We have prepared this Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) section in the interest of ensuring that the impacts of this notice are fully understood.
A. Statement of Need
This notice announces the CY 2027 Medicare Part A premiums for the uninsured aged and for certain disabled individuals who have exhausted other entitlement, as required by sections 1818 and 1818A of the Act. It also responds to section 1818(d) of the Act, which requires the Secretary to provide for publication of these amounts in the
Federal Register
during the September that precedes the start of each CY. As this statutory provision prescribes a detailed methodology for calculating these amounts, we do not have the discretion to adopt an alternative approach to these issues.
B. Overall Impact
We have examined the impacts of this rule as required by
Executive Order 12866
, “Regulatory Planning and Review”;
Executive Order 13132
, “Federalism“;
Executive Order 13563
, “Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”;
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”; the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (Pub. L. 96-354); section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act; section 202 of the Unfunded
(
printed page 74558)
Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-4
); and the Congressional Review Act (
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
).
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select those regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety, and other advantages; distributive impacts.). Section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
defines a “significant regulatory action” as any regulatory action that is likely to result in a rule that may: (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, or tribal governments or communities; (2) create a serious inconsistency or otherwise interfere with an action taken or planned by another agency; (3) materially alter the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user fees, or loan programs or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof; or (4) raise novel legal or policy issues arising out of legal mandates, or the President's priorities.
An RIA must be prepared for a regulatory action that is significant under section 3(f)(1) of
Executive Order 12866
. As stated in section IV. of this notice, we estimate that the overall effect of the changes in the Medicare Part A premium will be a cost to voluntary enrollees (sections 1818 and 1818A of the Act) of about $373 million. Based on our estimates, Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined this notice is significant under section 3(f)(1). Accordingly, we have prepared an RIA that to the best of our ability presents the costs and benefits of this notice.
In accordance with subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (also known as the Congressional Review Act), OIRA has determined that this notice meets the criteria set forth in
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. For the reasons given, however, we find for good cause that notice and public procedure are impracticable, unnecessary, and contrary to the public interest and have determined that this policy will take effect on January 1, 2027, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 808(2)
.
C. Accounting Statement and Table
Consistent with OMB Circular A-4 (available at
https://www.whitehouse.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​2025/​08/​CircularA-4.pdf
), in the Table 1, we have prepared an accounting statement showing the total aggregate cost to enrollees paying premiums in CY 2027, compared to the amount that they paid in CY 2026. This amount is approximately $373 million. As stated in section IV. of this notice, the CY 2027 premium of $597 is approximately 5.7 percent higher than the CY 2026 premium of $565. We estimate that approximately 904,000 enrollees will voluntarily enroll in Medicare Part A by paying the full premium. We estimate that over 90 percent of these individuals will have their Medicare Part A premium paid by States, since they are enrolled in the QMB program. Furthermore, the CY 2027 reduced premium of $328 is approximately 5.5 percent higher than the CY 2026 premium of $311.

D. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The RFA requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small entities, if a rule has a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities. For purposes of the RFA, small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions. Most hospitals and most other providers and suppliers are small entities, either by being nonprofit organizations or by meeting the Small Business Administration's (SBA) definition of a small business (having revenues of less than $9.0 million to $47 million in any 1 year). Individuals and States are not included in the definition of a small entity. This annual notice announces the Medicare Part A premiums for CY 2027 and will have an impact on certain Medicare beneficiaries, but not on small entities as defined by the SBA. As a result, we are not preparing an analysis for the RFA because the Secretary has certified that this notice will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare an RIA if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 604 of the RFA. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. This annual notice announces the Medicare Part A premiums for CY 2027 and will have an impact on certain Medicare beneficiaries. As a result, we are not preparing an analysis for section 1102(b) of the Act, because the Secretary has certified that this notice will not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals.
E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million. This notice would not impose a mandate that will result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal Governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of more than $193 million in any 1 year.
F. Federalism
Executive Order 13132
establishes certain requirements that an agency must meet when it promulgates a proposed rule (and subsequent final rule) that imposes substantial direct requirement costs on State and local governments, preempts State law, or otherwise has Federalism implications. This notice will not have a substantial direct effect on State or local governments, preempt State law, or otherwise have Federalism implications.
G. Congressional Review
This notice is subject to the Congressional Review Act and has been transmitted to the Congress and the Government Accountability Office's Comptroller General for review. Mehemet Oz, Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid
(
printed page 74559)
Services, approved this document on November 16, 2026.
Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.,
Secretary, Department of Health and Human Services.

RIN 0938-AV84
AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), HHS.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces the inpatient hospital deductible and the hospital and extended care services coinsurance amounts for services furnished in calendar year (CY) 2027 under Medicare's Hospital Insurance Program (Medicare Part A). The Medicare statute specifies the formulae used to determine these amounts. For CY 2027, the inpatient hospital deductible will be $1,776. The daily coinsurance amounts for CY 2027 will be as follows: $444 for the 61st through 90th day of hospitalization in a benefit period; $888 for lifetime reserve days; and $222 for the 21st through 100th day of extended care services in a skilled nursing facility in a benefit period.
DATES:
The deductible and coinsurance amounts announced in this notice are effective on January 1, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Suzanne Codespote, (410) 786-7737 or Yaminee Thaker (410) 786-7921.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Section 1813 of the Social Security Act (the Act) provides for an inpatient hospital deductible to be subtracted from the amount payable by Medicare for inpatient hospital services furnished to a beneficiary. It also provides for certain coinsurance amounts to be subtracted from the amounts payable by Medicare for inpatient hospital and extended care services. Section 1813(b)(2) of the Act requires the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (the Secretary) to determine and publish each year the amount of the inpatient hospital deductible and the hospital and extended care services coinsurance amounts applicable for services furnished in the following calendar year (CY).
II. Computing the Inpatient Hospital Deductible for CY 2027
Section 1813(b) of the Act prescribes the method for computing the amount of the inpatient hospital deductible. The inpatient hospital deductible is an amount equal to the inpatient hospital deductible for the preceding CY, adjusted by the Secretary's best estimate of the payment-weighted average of the applicable percentage increases (as defined in section 1886(b)(3)(B) of the Act) used for updating the payment rates to hospitals for discharges in the fiscal year (FY) that begins on October 1 of the same preceding CY, and adjusted to reflect changes in real casemix. The adjustment to reflect real casemix is determined on the basis of the most recent case-mix data available. The amount determined under this formula is rounded to the nearest multiple of $4 (or, if midway between two multiples of $4, to the next higher multiple of $4).
Under section 1886(b)(3)(B)(i)(XX) of the Act, the percentage increase used to update the payment rates for FY 2027 for hospitals paid under the inpatient prospective payment system (IPPS) is the IPPS operating market basket percentage increase, otherwise known as the IPPS market basket update, reduced by an adjustment based on changes in the economy-wide productivity (productivity adjustment) (see section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act). Under section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii) of the Act, for FY 2027, the applicable percentage increase for hospitals that do not submit quality data as specified by the Secretary is reduced by one quarter of the market basket update. We are estimating that after accounting for those hospitals receiving the lower market basket update in the payment-weighted average update, the calculated deductible will not be affected, since the majority of hospitals submit quality data and receive the full market basket update. Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(ix) of the Act requires that any hospital that is not a meaningful electronic health record (EHR) user (as defined in section 1886(n)(3) of the Act) will have three-quarters of the market basket update reduced by 100 percent for FY 2017 and each subsequent FY. We are estimating that after accounting for these hospitals receiving the lower market basket update, the calculated deductible will not be affected, since the majority of hospitals are meaningful EHR users and are expected to receive the full market basket update.
Under section 1886 of the Act, the percentage increase used to update the payment rates (or target amounts, as applicable) for FY 2027 for hospitals excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system is as follows:
The percentage increase for long term care hospitals (LTCH) is the LTCH market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment (see section 1886(m)(3)(A) of the Act). In addition, these hospitals may also be impacted by the quality reporting adjustments and the site-neutral payment rates (see section 1886(m)(5) and (6) of the Act).
The percentage increase for inpatient rehabilitation facilities (IRF) is the IRF market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment in accordance with section 1886(j)(3)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act. In addition, these hospitals may also be impacted by the quality reporting adjustments (see section 1886(j)(7) of the Act).
The percentage increase used to update the payment rate for inpatient psychiatric facilities (IPF) is the IPF market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment (see section 1886(s)(2)(A)(i) of the Act). In addition, these hospitals may also be impacted by the quality reporting adjustments (see section 1886(s)(4) of the Act).
The percentage increase used to update the target amounts for other types of hospitals that are excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system and that are paid on a reasonable cost basis, subject to a rate-of-increase
(
printed page 74583)
ceiling, is the IPPS operating market basket percentage increase, which is described at section 1886(b)(3)(B)(ii)(VIII) of the Act and
42 CFR 413.40(c)(3)
. These other types of hospitals include cancer hospitals, children's hospitals, extended neoplastic disease care hospitals, and hospitals located outside the 50 States, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.
The IPPS operating market basket percentage increase for FY 2027 is 3.2 percent and the productivity adjustment is 0.9 percentage point, as announced in the final rule that appeared in the
Federal Register
on August 4, 2026 entitled, “Medicare Program; Hospital Inpatient Prospective Payment Systems for Acute Care Hospitals (IPPS) and the Long-Term Care Hospital Prospective Payment System and Policy Changes and Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 Rates; Requirements for Quality Programs; Other Policy Changes; and Adoption of Updated Versions of Certain Health Information Technology Standards” (
91 FR 49570
). Therefore, the percentage increase for hospitals paid under the inpatient prospective payment system that submit quality data and are meaningful EHR users is 2.3 percent (that is, the FY 2027 IPPS operating market basket update of 3.2 percent less the productivity adjustment of 0.9 percentage point). The average payment percentage increase for hospitals excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system is 2.48 percent. This average includes long term care hospitals, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, inpatient psychiatric facilities and other hospitals excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system. Weighting these percentages in accordance with payment volume, our best estimate of the payment-weighted average of the increases in the payment rates for FY 2027 is 2.32 percent.
To develop the adjustment to reflect changes in real casemix, we first calculated an average casemix for each hospital that reflects the relative costliness of that hospital's mix of cases compared to those of other hospitals. We then computed the change in average casemix for hospitals paid under the Medicare inpatient prospective payment system in FY 2026 compared to FY 2025. (We excluded from this calculation hospitals whose payments are not based on the inpatient prospective payment system because their payments are based on alternate prospective payment systems or reasonable costs.) We used Medicare bills from prospective payment hospitals that we received as of July 2026. These bills represent a total of about 5.6 million Medicare discharges for FY 2026 and provide the most recent case-mix-data available at this time. Based on these bills, the change in average casemix in FY 2026 is −0.2 percent. Based on these bills and past experience, we expect the overall FY 2026 casemix change to be −0.1 percent as the year progresses and more FY 2026 data become available.
Section 1813(b) of the Act requires that the inpatient hospital deductible be adjusted only by that portion of the case mix change that is determined to be real. Real casemix is that portion of casemix that is due to changes in the mix of cases and not due to coding optimization. We are assuming that this increase in casemix is real and not a result of coding optimization.
Thus, the estimate of the payment-weighted average of the applicable percentage increases used for updating the payment rates is 2.32 percent, and the real case-mix adjustment factor for the deductible is −0.1 percent. Therefore, using the statutory formula as stated in section 1813(b) of the Act, we calculate the inpatient hospital deductible for services furnished in CY 2027 to be $1,776. This deductible amount is determined by multiplying $1,736 (the inpatient hospital deductible for CY 2026) by the payment-weighted average increase in the payment rates of 1.0232 multiplied by the increase in real casemix of 0.999, which equals $1,774.50 and is rounded to $1,776 (based on rounding to the nearest multiple of 4).
III. Computing the Inpatient Hospital and Extended Care Services Coinsurance Amounts for CY 2027
The coinsurance amounts provided for in section 1813 of the Act are defined as fixed percentages of the inpatient hospital deductible for services furnished in the same CY. The increase in the deductible generates increases in the coinsurance amounts. For inpatient hospital and extended care services furnished in CY 2027, in accordance with the fixed percentages defined in the law, the daily coinsurance for the 61st through 90th day of hospitalization in a benefit period will be $444 (one-fourth of the inpatient hospital deductible as stated in section 1813(a)(1)(A) of the Act); the daily coinsurance for lifetime reserve days will be $888 (one-half of the inpatient hospital deductible as stated in section 1813(a)(1)(B) of the Act); and the daily coinsurance for the 21st through 100th day of extended care services in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in a benefit period will be $222 (one-eighth of the inpatient hospital deductible as stated in section 1813(a)(3) of the Act).
IV. Cost to Medicare Beneficiaries

The estimated total increase in costs to beneficiaries is about $770 million (rounded to the nearest $10 million) due to: (1) the increase in the deductible and coinsurance amounts; and (2) the change in the number of deductibles and daily coinsurance amounts paid. We determine the increase in cost to beneficiaries by calculating the difference between the 2026 and 2027 deductible and coinsurance amounts multiplied by the estimated change in the number of deductible and coinsurance amounts paid.
V. Waiver of Proposed Rulemaking
We ordinarily publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
and invite public comment
