under Docket No. FAA-2026-13820.
You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call 206-231-3195.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Yaser Osman, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: 860-386-1786; email:
9-AVS-AIR-BACO-COS@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under the
ADDRESSES
section. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13820; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01552-T” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Yaser Osman, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: 860-386-1786; email:
9-AVS-AIR-BACO-COS@faa.gov
.
Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2021-12-17, Amendment 39-21604 (
86 FR 34621
, June 30, 2021) (AD 2021-12-17), for certain ATR—GIE Avions de Transport Régional Model ATR42-300, -320, and -500 airplanes; and all Model ATR72-101, -102, -201, -202, -211, -212, and -212A airplanes. AD 2021-12-17 was prompted by an MCAI originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued AD 2020-0097R1, dated May 28, 2020 (EASA AD 2020-0097R1), to correct an unsafe condition.
AD 2021-12-17 requires a detailed visual inspection of each affected part for deficiencies (sealant blockage and out of tolerance ligaments), and depending on findings, accomplishment of applicable corrective actions. The FAA issued AD 2021-12-17 to address structural failure of the seat track
(
printed page 74500)
attachment during an emergency landing, possibly resulting in injury to occupants, and affecting emergency evacuation.
Actions Since AD 2021-12-17 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2021-12-17, EASA superseded EASA AD 2020-0097R1 and issued EASA AD 2025-0205R3, dated December 8, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0205R3) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition for all ATR—GIE Avions de Transport Régional Model ATR42-200, -300, -320, -400, and -500 airplanes; and all Model ATR72-101, -102, -201, -202, -211, -212, and -212A airplanes. Model ATR42-400 airplanes are not certificated by the FAA and are not included on the U.S. type certificate data sheet; this proposed AD therefore does not include those airplanes in the applicability. The MCAI states that since EASA AD 2020-0097R1 was issued it was determined additional seat track part numbers might be affected and additional airplanes need to be inspected. EASA AD 2025-0205R3 also specifies that airplanes with certain configurations do not need to do the inspection and corrective actions.
The FAA is proposing this AD to address a structural failure of the seat track attachment during an emergency landing, possibly resulting in injury to occupants, and affecting emergency evacuation. You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13820.
Explanation of Retained Requirements
Although this proposed AD does not explicitly restate the requirements of AD 2021-12-17, this proposed AD would retain all of the requirements of AD 2021-12-17. Those requirements are referenced in EASA AD 2025-0205R3, which, in turn, is referenced in paragraph (g) of this proposed AD.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2025-0205R3, which specifies procedures for a detailed visual inspection of each affected seat track for deficiencies (sealant blockage and out of tolerance ligaments), and corrective actions if necessary. These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2025-0205R3 described previously, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some civil aviation authority (CAA) ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate EASA AD 2025-0205R3 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2025-0205R3 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2025-0205R3 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2025-0205R3. Material required by EASA AD 2025-0205R3 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13820 after the FAA final rule is published.

The FAA does not control warranty coverage for affected individuals. As a result, the FAA has included all known costs in the cost estimate.
Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

[EPA-R06-OAR-2023-0478; FRL-12671-02-R6]
AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
Pursuant to the Federal Clean Air Act (CAA or the Act), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is approving the CAA section 111(d) State plan submitted by the State of Texas for sources subject to the Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) Landfills Emission Guidelines (EG). The Texas MSW landfills plan was submitted to fulfill the State's obligations under CAA section 111(d) to implement and enforce the requirements under the MSW Landfills EG. The EPA is approving the State plan and amending the agency regulations in accordance with the requirements of the CAA.
DATES:
This rule is effective on December 21, 2026. The incorporation by reference of certain material listed in this rule is approved by the Director of the Federal Register as of December 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The EPA has established a docket for this action under Docket ID No. EPA-R06-OAR-2023-0478. All documents in the docket are listed on the
https://www.regulations.gov
website. Although listed in the index, some information is not publicly available,
e.g.,
Confidential Business Information or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Certain other material, such as copyrighted material, is not placed on the internet. Publicly available docket materials are available electronically through
https://www.regulations.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kevin Kim, EPA Region 6 Office, SO
2
and Regional Haze Section; telephone number: 214-665-8554; email address:
kim.kevin@epa.gov
.
Please call or email the contact listed above if you need alternative access to material indexed but not provided in the docket.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Throughout this document “we,” “us,” and “our” means the EPA.
I. Background
The background for this action is discussed in detail in our March 4, 2026, proposed rule (
91 FR 10556
) and accompanying Technical Support
(
printed page 74496)
Document (TSD). In that document, we proposed to approve the Texas MSW landfills plan submitted by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) in accordance with the requirements of CAA section 111(d) and to amend
40 CFR part 62, subpart SS
, to codify the EPA's approval. We proposed to find that the Texas MSW landfills plan, submitted by TCEQ on September 15, 2023, is as protective as the Federal requirements provided under the MSW landfills EG, codified at
40 CFR part 60, subpart Cf
.
II. Response to Comments
We received three comments on our proposed rule: two in support and one in opposition. We appreciate the supportive comments and have noted them in the record; no changes are made in response. A summary of the adverse comment and our response to it are provided below.
Comment:
The commenter asserted that proposed rules must secure stronger landfill gas capture and monitoring, faster organics diversion so that less methane is generated, and more public transparency about which sites may get exemptions. The commenter additionally provided their perspective on the landfill industry and operators and expressed concern for nearby communities while providing their comments. The commenter asked why the EPA is allowing less stringent rules from the State and stated that landfill operators should be accountable for their landfill emissions and put up safeguards for methane capture.
Response:
The EPA acknowledges the commenter's concerns on addressing landfill emissions and protecting affected communities. Under CAA section 111(d), the EPA must approve a State plan that meets Federal requirements and appropriately implements the applicable emission guidelines, including provisions for enforceable limits, monitoring, reporting, and compliance schedules. Under
40 CFR 60.24(f)
, a State may apply less stringent emission standards or longer compliance schedules than otherwise required if the State demonstrates one or more of the following: (1) that, due to plant age, location, or basic process design, the cost of control is unreasonable; (2) that installing the necessary control equipment is physically impossible; or (3) that other factors specific to the facility (or class of facilities) make a less stringent standard or a later final compliance date significantly more reasonable.
Texas adopted 30 TAC section 113.2406(a) to explicitly exempt MSW landfills that have not accepted waste since October 9, 1993, and have no remaining design capacity from State regulations at Chapter 113, Subchapter D, Division 6, continuing an existing Division 1 exemption (30 TAC section 113.2060(2)(A)) but rephrasing it as a stand-alone exemption rather than embedding it in the definition of “existing MSW landfill.” This exemption is less stringent than the default Federal applicability in
40 CFR part 60, subparts Cc
and
Cf
, because it excludes landfills that stopped accepting waste between November 8, 1987, and October 9, 1993.
[
1
]
TCEQ justifies the change under
40 CFR 60.24(f)
, which allows less stringent standards or longer compliance schedules for any of the three potential justifications detailed in the previous paragraph. In 1998, TCEQ
[
2
]
found only one landfill (City of Killeen) was briefly above the 50 megagrams per year (Mg/yr) nonmethane organic compound (NMOC) control threshold (to install a gas collection and control system for closed landfills) and projected that landfill would fall below this threshold by 2004. The EPA's 1999 approval likewise concluded that controlling these closed landfills would yield little emission benefit relative to cost. Given the passage of time, TCEQ asserts that none of the landfills that closed between 1987-1993 would currently exceed 50 Mg/yr NMOC, and TCEQ includes the prior State plan analysis
[
3
]
in support of maintaining the exemption. Therefore, these closed landfills in Texas would not be subject to gas collection and control system requirements nor would it likely result in a reduction in NMOC or landfill emissions even if Texas did not exempt these landfills as part of its current MSW landfills plan. The EPA finds that TCEQ has adequately demonstrated, consistent with
40 CFR 60.24(f)
, that a less stringent standard is reasonable for the applicable facilities, and approves of the provision, as adopted at 30 TAC section 113.2406(a).
In its assessment of Texas's plan, the EPA concluded that Texas's plan met Federal requirements under CAA section 111(d), the CAA section 111(d) implementing regulations at
40 CFR part 60, subpart B
, and
the
applicable provisions under the MSW landfill emission guidelines at
40 CFR part 60, subpart Cf
. While the EPA's action does not mandate organics diversion or rules beyond the landfill emission guidelines, the plan requires landfill gas collection and control, surface monitoring, corrective action, and reporting, with the EPA and TCEQ retaining full enforcement authority alongside citizens' recourse. Approving this plan would allow State implementation of substantively similar requirements from the Federal Plan that are already in effect and would provide for better enforcement oversight of landfill gas regulation. The EPA would continue to provide Federal oversight of landfill requirements under the emission guidelines.
III. Final Action
In this final action, the EPA is amending
40 CFR part 62, subpart SS
, to reflect approval of the Texas MSW landfills plan from TCEQ, received on September 15, 2023, in accordance with CAA section 111(d). As part of that plan approval, the EPA is approving the State regulations at Texas Administrative Code Title 30, Chapter 113: Standards of Performance for Hazardous Air Pollutants and for Designated Facilities and Pollutants, Subchapter D: Designated Facilities and Pollutants, Division 6: 2016 Emission Guidelines For Existing Municipal Solid Waste Landfills, sections 113.2400 through 113.2412 (30 TAC sections 113.2400 through 113.2412) as the enforceable mechanism of the State plan.
IV. Incorporation by Reference
In accordance with the requirements of
1 CFR 51.5
, we are finalizing regulatory text that includes the incorporation by reference of Texas Administrative Code Title 30, Chapter 113: Standards of Performance for Hazardous Air Pollutants and for Designated Facilities and Pollutants, Subchapter D: Designated Facilities and Pollutants, Division 6: 2016 Emission Guidelines For Existing Municipal Solid Waste Landfills, sections 113.2400 through 113.2412, adopted July 14, 2023, and effective July 19, 2023 (30 TAC sections 113.2400 through 113.2412), which is part of the CAA section 111(d) Plan applicable to existing MSW landfills subject to the MSW Landfills Emission Guidelines, at
40 CFR part 60, subpart Cf
, within TCEQ's jurisdiction in the State of Texas. The regulatory provisions of 30 TAC sections 113.2400 through
(
printed page 74497)
113.2412 incorporate the MSW Landfills Emission Guidelines promulgated by the EPA at
40 CFR part 60, subpart Cf
, and establish emission standards and compliance times for the control of municipal solid waste landfills, as defined in subpart Cf, that commenced construction, modification, or reconstruction on or before July 17, 2014. The EPA has made and will continue to make 30 TAC sections 113.2400 through 113.2412 generally available at the EPA Region 6 office (please contact the person identified in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this preamble for more information). They are also available at:
https://www.regulations.gov
and
http://www.sos.texas.gov/​tac/​index.shtml
.
This incorporation by reference has been approved by the Director of the Federal Register and the State plan is federally enforceable under the CAA as of the effective date of this final rulemaking.
V. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a CAA section 111(d)/129 submission that complies with the provisions of the Act and applicable Federal regulations.
42 U.S.C. 7411(d)
;
42 U.S.C. 7429
;
40 CFR part 60, subparts B
and
Cf
; and
40 CFR part 62, subpart A
. Thus, in reviewing CAA section 111(d)/129 State plan submissions, the EPA's role is to approve State choices, provided that they meet the criteria of the Act and implementing regulations. Accordingly, this action merely approves State law as meeting Federal requirements and does not impose additional requirements beyond those imposed by State law. For that reason:
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review
This action is not a significant regulatory action as defined in
Executive Order 12866
(
58 FR 51735
, October 4, 1993) and was therefore not subject to a requirement for
Executive Order 12866
review.
B.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This action is not an
Executive Order 14192
(
90 FR 9065
, February 6, 2025) regulatory action because this action is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
This action does not impose an information collection burden under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
) because it does not contain any information collection activities.
D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
This action is certified to not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
). This action will approve a State plan pursuant to CAA section 111(d) and will therefore have no net regulatory burden for all directly regulated small entities.
E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
This action does not contain any unfunded mandate as described in UMRA,
2 U.S.C. 1531
through
1538
, and does not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. This action imposes no enforceable duty on any State, local, or Tribal governments or the private sector.
F.
Executive Order 13132
: Federalism
This action does not have federalism implications as specified in
Executive Order 13132
(
64 FR 43255
, August 10, 1999). It will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
G.
Executive Order 13175
: Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
This action will not apply to areas of Indian country within Texas and therefore does not have Tribal implications as specified in
E.O. 13175
(
65 FR 67249
, November 9, 2000). This action will neither impose substantial direct compliance costs on federally recognized Tribal governments, nor preempt Tribal law. This action will not impose substantial direct compliance costs on federally recognized Tribal governments because no actions will be required of Tribal governments. This action will also not preempt Tribal law as no Texas Tribe implements a regulatory program under the CAA and thus does not have applicable or related Tribal laws.
H.
Executive Order 13045
: Protection of Children From Environmental Health Risks and Safety Risks
The EPA interprets
Executive Order 13045
(
62 FR 19885
, April 23, 1997) as applying only to those regulatory actions that concern environmental health or safety risks that the EPA has reason to believe may disproportionately affect children, per the definitions of “covered regulatory action” in section 2-202 of the Executive Order. Therefore, this action is not subject to
Executive Order 13045
because it approves a State program.
I.
Executive Order 13211
: Actions That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution and Use
This action is not subject to
Executive Order 13211
(
66 FR 28355
, May 22, 2001), because it is not a significant regulatory action under
Executive Order 12866
.
J. National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act
This rulemaking does not involve technical standards. This action is not subject to requirements of section 12(d) of the National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (
15 U.S.C. 272 note
) because application of those requirements would be inconsistent with the Clean Air Act.
This action is subject to the Congressional Review Act, and the EPA will submit a rule report to each House of the Congress and to the Comptroller General of the United States. This action is not a “major rule” as defined by
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
.
Under section 307(b)(1) of the Clean Air Act, petitions for judicial review of this action must be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the appropriate circuit by January 19, 2027. Filing a petition for reconsideration by the Administrator of this final rule does not affect the finality of this action for the purposes of judicial review nor does it extend the time within which a petition for judicial review may be filed, and shall not postpone the effectiveness of such rule or action. This action may not be challenged later in proceedings to enforce its requirements (see CAA section 307(b)(2)).

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-14-09, which applies to certain Dassault Aviation Model FALCON 7X, FALCON 900EX, and FALCON 2000EX airplanes. AD 2024-14-09 requires replacement of certain titanium screws, adds other locations for screw replacement, and revises the applicability from AD 2022-02-10. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-14-09, affected parts have been found in other areas of certain FALCON 7X airplanes as well as in additional FALCON 7X airplanes. This proposed AD would continue to require the actions in AD 2024-14-09 and would require expanding the applicability to additional airplanes, expanding the locations for screw replacement, and revising the compliance times for parts replacement. This AD would also limit the installation of affected parts under certain conditions. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this proposed AD by January 4, 2027.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under the
ADDRESSES
section. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13821; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01619-T” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Amanda F. Pieraccini, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: 516-228-7329; email:
9-AVS-AIR-BACO-COS@faa.gov
.
Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2024-14-09, Amendment 39-22790 (
89 FR 72966
, September 9, 2024) (AD 2024-14-09), for certain Dassault Aviation Model FALCON 7X, FALCON 900EX, and FALCON 2000EX airplanes. AD 2024-14-09 was prompted by MCAI originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2023-0207, dated November 21, 2023 (EASA AD 2023-0207), to correct an unsafe condition.
AD 2024-14-09 requires replacement of certain titanium screws, adds other locations for screw replacement, and revises the applicability. The FAA issued AD 2024-14-09 to address failure of an affected screw installed in a critical location, possibly resulting in reduced structural integrity of the airplane.
Actions Since AD 2024-14-09 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2024-14-09, EASA superseded EASA AD 2023-0207 and issued EASA AD 2025-0228R1, dated February 6, 2026 (EASA AD 2025-0228R1) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition for certain Dassault Aviation Model FALCON 7X, FALCON 900EX, and FALCON 2000EX airplanes. The MCAI states that since EASA issued EASA AD 2023-0207, it was determined that affected parts have been installed in additional areas of certain Model FALCON 7X airplanes already included in the applicability of EASA AD 2023-0207. The MCAI also states that it was
(
printed page 74512)
determined that additional Model FALCON 7X airplanes were not included in the applicability of EASA AD 2023-0207. The MCAI further states that the compliance time for parts replacement specified in EASA AD 2023-0207 can be defined in flight cycles (FC) only; therefore, the calendar-based compliance times were removed.
The FAA is proposing this AD to address failure of an affected screw installed in a critical location, possibly resulting in reduced structural integrity of the airplane. You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13821.
Explanation of Retained Requirements
Although this proposed AD does not explicitly restate the requirements of AD 2024-14-09, this proposed AD would retain all of the requirements of AD 2024-14-09. Those requirements are referenced in EASA AD 2025-0228R1, which, in turn, is referenced in paragraph (g) of this proposed AD.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
EASA AD 2025-0228R1 specifies procedures for replacing certain Decomatic titanium screws, including an inspection of the bore dimension and corrective actions (oversizing or repair). EASA AD 2025-0228R1 also limits installation of certain Decomatic titanium screws.
This proposed AD would also require Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Revision 2, dated March 20, 2023, which the Director of the Federal Register approved for incorporation by reference as of October 15, 2024 (
89 FR 72966
, September 9, 2024).
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI and material referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2025-0228R1 described previously, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some civil aviation authority (CAA) ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate EASA AD 2025-0228R1 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2025-0228R1 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2025-0228R1 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times”, compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2025-0228R1. Service information required by EASA AD 2025-0228R1 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13821 after the FAA final rule is published.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD, if adopted as proposed, would affect 52 airplanes of U.S. registry. The FAA estimates the following costs to comply with this proposed AD:
Estimated Costs for Required Actions

Up to 250 work-hours × $85 per hour = $21,250

* The FAA estimates that the rental of special tooling to accomplish replacement of any affected Decomatic titanium screw on Model FALCON 7X airplanes, serial number (S/N) 423 through 443 (inclusive), to be $524 per day.
According to the manufacturer, some or all of the costs of this proposed AD may be covered under warranty, thereby reducing the cost impact on affected individuals. The FAA does not control warranty coverage for affected individuals. As a result, the FAA has included all known costs in the cost estimate.
Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This proposed AD would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify this proposed regulation:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
,
(2) Would not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
(

(3) Would not have a significant economic impact, positive or negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

(b) Affected ADs

89 FR 72966
, September 9, 2024) (AD 2024-14-09).
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to Dassault Aviation airplanes identified in paragraphs (c)(1) through (3) of this AD, certificated in any category, as identified in European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2025-0228R1, dated February 6, 2026 (EASA AD 2025-0228R1).
(1) Model FALCON 7X airplanes.
(2) Model FALCON 900EX airplanes.
(3) Model FALCON 2000EX airplanes.
(d) Subject
Air Transport Association (ATA) of America Code 51, Standard Practices/Structures.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a report of an improper heat treatment process applied during the manufacturing of certain Decomatic titanium screws, and by the determination that affected parts in additional areas on certain airplanes, as well as additional airplanes, are subject to the unsafe condition. The FAA is issuing this AD to address failure of an affected screw installed in a critical location, possibly resulting in reduced structural integrity of the airplane.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Requirements
Except as specified in paragraph (h) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, EASA AD 2025-0228R1.
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2025-0228R1
(1) Where EASA AD 2025-0228R1 refers to October 30, 2025 (the effective date of the original issue of EASA AD 2025-0228), this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where the “Ref Publications” section of EASA AD 2025-0228R1 specifies “Dassault SB 7X-467 original issue dated 16 November 2020, Rev. 1 dated 12 December 2022, Rev. 2 dated 20 March 2023, Rev. 03 dated 11 March 2024, Rev. 04 dated 22 April 2024, Rev. 05 dated 09 September 2024 and Rev. 06 dated 10 April 2025 (including its Erratum dated 09 June 2025)”, this AD requires replacing that text with “Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Rev. 06 dated April 10, 2025 (including its Erratum dated June 09, 2025)”.
(3) This AD does not adopt the “Remarks” section of EASA AD 2025-0228R1.
(i) Credit for Previous Actions
(1) For Model FALCON 7X airplanes: This paragraph provides credit for the actions specified in paragraph (g) of this AD, if those actions were performed before October 15, 2024 (the effective date of AD 2024-14-09) using Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, dated November 16, 2020, provided the additional work specified in Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Revision 2, dated March 20, 2023, and the additional work specified in the applicable SB as defined in EASA AD 2025-0228R1 is accomplished within the applicable compliance time specified in EASA AD 2025-0228R1.
(2) For Model FALCON 7X airplanes: This paragraph provides credit for the actions specified in paragraph (g) of this AD, if those actions were performed before the effective date of this AD using Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Revision 2, dated March 20, 2023, Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Revision 3, dated March 11, 2024, Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Revision 4, dated April 22, 2024, or Dassault Service Bulletin 7X-467, Revision 5, dated September 9, 2024, provided the additional work specified in the applicable SB as defined in EASA AD 2025-0228R1 is accomplished within the applicable compliance time specified in EASA AD 2025-0228R1.
(j) Additional AD Provisions
The following provisions also apply to this AD:

Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs):

14 CFR 39.19

14 CFR 39.19
, send your request to your principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office, as appropriate. If sending information directly to the manager of the International Validation Branch, send it to the attention of the person identified in paragraph (k)(1) of this AD and email to:
AMOC@faa.gov
. Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office.
(2)
Contacting the Manufacturer:
For any requirement in this AD to obtain instructions from a manufacturer, the instructions must be accomplished using a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; or EASA; or Dassault Aviation's EASA Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.

title: Airworthiness Directives; Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Helicopters
abstract: The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3 and EC635T2+ helicopters. This proposed AD was prompted by a determination that the manufacturer's service material does not provide complete instructions for the inspections after a hard landing. This proposed AD would require a one-time inspection of the tail rotor control system and, depending on the inspection results, corrective actions. This proposed AD would also require revision of the existing aircraft maintenance manual (MM) or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA) and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3 and EC635T2+ helicopters. This proposed AD was prompted by a determination that the manufacturer's service material does not provide complete instructions for the inspections after a hard landing. This proposed AD would require a one-time inspection of the tail rotor control system and, depending on the inspection results, corrective actions. This proposed AD would also require revision of the existing aircraft maintenance manual (MM) or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA) and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this NPRM by January 4, 2027.

and

Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under
ADDRESSES
. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13819; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01531-R” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Shailesh Malla, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410 Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, has issued EASA AD 2020-0102, dated May 6, 2020 (EASA AD 2020-0102) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition on certain AHD Model EC135 P1, EC135 P2, EC135 P2+, EC135 P3, EC135 T1, EC135 T2, EC135 T2+, EC135 T3, EC635 P2+, EC635 P3, EC635 T1, EC635 T2+ and EC635 T3 helicopters. The MCAI states that the master service manual (MSM) for Model EC135 and EC635 does not provide complete instructions for the inspections after a hard landing. This condition, if not corrected, could lead to missed identification of tail rotor control damage, which could result in component or system failure and reduced control of the helicopter.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13819.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2020-0102, which specifies procedures for inspecting the tail rotor control system and, if a discrepancy is found, accomplishing the applicable corrective actions. EASA AD 2020-0102 also specifies that accomplishing the inspection of the tail rotor control system in accordance with the instructions of the aircraft MM is an alternative method for the inspection in accordance with the service material. Additionally, EASA AD 2020-0102 specifies that revising the Aircraft Maintenance Program (AMP) of a helicopter by incorporating the qualified instructions as defined in EASA AD 2020-0102 is a terminating action for recording compliance.
The FAA also reviewed Aircraft Maintenance Manual 05-51-00, 6-3, Conditional Inspections after Special Operational Incidents—Inspection,
(
printed page 74509)
Dated March 28, 2025, which specifies conditional inspections after a hard landing.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2020-0102, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. See “Differences Between this Proposed AD and the MCAI” for a discussion of the general differences included in this proposed AD.
Differences Between This Proposed AD and the MCAI
The MCAI applies to AHD Model EC635 P2+, EC635 P3, EC635 T1, and EC635 T3 helicopters, whereas this proposed AD would not because these model helicopters do not have an FAA type certificate. The MCAI requires accomplishing corrective actions in accordance with the qualified instructions as defined in the MCAI, whereas this proposed AD would require those corrective actions be accomplished in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; or EASA; or AHD Design Organization Approval (DOA).
Additionally, the MCAI requires for certain helicopters, inspecting the helicopter after each hard landing, whereas this proposed AD would require all applicable helicopters to perform these inspections within 12 months after the effective date of this proposed AD. Furthermore, the MCAI specifies that revising the AMP by incorporating the qualified instructions as defined in the MCAI is a terminating action for recording compliance, whereas this proposed AD would require revising the existing aircraft MM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, by incorporating certain qualified instructions.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate EASA AD 2020-0102 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2020-0102 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2020-0102 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2020-0102. Material required by EASA AD 2020-0102 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13819 after the FAA final rule is published.

The FAA estimates that this AD, if adopted as proposed, would affect 289 helicopters of U.S. registry.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This proposed AD would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify this proposed regulation:

,

The FAA amends § 39.13 by adding the following new airworthiness directive:
Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD):
Docket No. FAA-2026-13819; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01531-R.
(a) Comments Due Date
The FAA must receive comments on this airworthiness directive (AD) by January 4, 2027.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3 and EC635T2+ helicopters, certificated in any category, all serial numbers up to and including 1276.
Note 1 to paragraph (c):
Helicopters with an EC135P3H designation are Model EC135P3 helicopters, and helicopters with an EC135T3H designation are Model EC135T3 helicopters.
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 6720, Tail rotor control system.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a determination that the manufacturer's service material does not provide complete instructions for the inspections after a hard landing. The FAA is issuing this AD to address and correct incomplete inspection instructions. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in missed identification of tail rotor control damage, which could result in component or system failure and reduced control of the helicopter.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Requirements
Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2020-0102, dated May 6, 2020 (EASA AD 2020-0102).
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2020-0102
(1) Where EASA AD 2020-0102 refers to its effective date, this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where paragraph (1) of EASA AD 2020-0102 applies only to Group 1 helicopters, this AD requires paragraph (1) of EASA AD 2020-0102 to apply to Group 1 and Group 2 helicopters.
(3) This AD does not adopt paragraph (2) of EASA AD 2020-0102.
(4) Where paragraph (5) of EASA AD 2020-0102 specifies “Revising the AMP of a helicopter by incorporating the qualified instructions, as defined in this AD, ensures continued accomplishment of those instructions for that helicopter. Consequently, after that AMP revision, it is not necessary that accomplishment of any action as required by this AD is recorded for AD compliance demonstration on a continued basis.”, this AD requires replacing this text with “For Group 1 and Group 2 helicopters, within 30 days after the effective date of this AD, revise the existing maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, by incorporating the Aircraft Maintenance Manual 05-51-00, 6-3, Conditional Inspections after Special Operational Incidents—Inspection, Dated March 28, 2025”.
(5) Where the material referenced in EASA AD 2020-0102 specifies to contact the manufacturer prior to doing the special instructions after a hard landing, this AD requires corrective actions in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; or EASA; or Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
(6) Where the material referenced in EASA AD 2020-0102 specifies to perform an “Ease of Movement check”, this AD requires replacing that text with “Ease of movement inspection”.
(7) This AD does not adopt the “Remarks” section of EASA AD 2020-0102.
(i) No Reporting Requirement
Although the material referenced in EASA AD 2020-0102 specifies to submit certain information to the manufacturer, this AD does not require that action.
(j) Special Flight Permits
Special flight permits, as described in
14 CFR 21.197
and
21.199
, are not allowed.
(k) Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs)
(1) The Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA, has the authority to approve AMOCs for this AD, if requested using the procedures found in
14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with
14 CFR 39.19
, send your request to your principal inspector or local Flight Standards District Office, as appropriate. If sending information directly to the manager of the International Validation Branch, send it to the attention of the person identified in paragraph (l) of this AD and email to:
AMOC@faa.gov
.
(2) Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the local flight standards district office/certificate holding district office.
(l) Additional Information
For more information about this AD, contact Shailesh Malla, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410 Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (817) 222-5584; email:
shailesh.malla@faa.gov
.
(m) Material Incorporated by Reference
(1) The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of the material listed in this paragraph under
5 U.S.C. 552(a)
and
1 CFR part 51
.
(2) You must use this material as applicable to do the actions required by this AD, unless the AD specifies otherwise.
(i) European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2020-0102 dated May 6, 2020.
(ii) Aircraft Maintenance Manual 05-51-00, 6-3, Conditional Inspections after Special Operational Incidents—Inspection, Dated March 28, 2025.
(3) For EASA material identified in this AD, contact EASA, Konrad-Adenauer-Ufer 3, 50668 Cologne, Germany; phone: +49 221 8999 000; email:

airbus.com/en/products-services/helicopters/hcare-services/airbusworld.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is finalizing a limited approval and limited disapproval of three permitting rules as a revision to the San Joaquin Valley Unified Air Pollution Control District (SJVUAPCD or “District”) portion of the California State Implementation Plan (SIP). These are revisions to the District's New Source Review (NSR) air permitting program rules for new and modified sources of air pollution under Clean Air Act (CAA or “Act”) section 110(a)(2)(C) and part D of title I.
DATES:
This rule is effective on December 21, 2026.

I. Executive Summary
A. What action is the EPA taking?
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is finalizing a limited approval and limited disapproval of three permitting rules submitted by the San Joaquin Valley Unified Air Pollution Control District (SJVUAPCD or “District”) as a revision to the California SIP. The submitted rules address the District's New Source Review (NSR) air permitting program rules for new and modified sources of air pollution pursuant to CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) and part D of title I. This action will update the California SIP with rules that the District has revised to address deficiencies identified in a previous limited disapproval action and to incorporate other revisions related to Nonattainment New Source Review (NNSR) requirements. We proposed this action on January 21, 2025, and held a 30-day public comment period.
B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
CAA sections 110(k)(3) and 301(a) provide the EPA's statutory authority for finalizing a limited approval and limited disapproval of Rules 1020, 2020, and 2201. We have evaluated the rule revisions for compliance with CAA sections 172(c)(5), 173, 182(e), and 189(b), which establish the requirements for stationary source preconstruction permitting programs, including those specifically applicable for an Extreme ozone nonattainment area and Serious PM
2.5
nonattainment area, as well as the Federal regulations applicable to stationary source permitting at
40 CFR 51.160
through
51.165
. Additionally, the EPA reviewed the rules for consistency with other general CAA requirements for SIP submittals, including requirements at CAA section 110(a)(2)(A) regarding rule enforceability and requirements at CAA sections 110(l) and 193 for SIP revisions. We have also considered whether the rules meet the Federal visibility requirements related to State NNSR programs as described in
40 CFR 51.307
.
II. Background of the Proposed Action and Interim Final Determination To Defer Sanctions
On January 21, 2025 (
90 FR 6928
), the EPA proposed a limited approval and limited disapproval of three rules submitted for approval into the California SIP. Table 1 lists the rules addressed by this proposal with the dates they were amended or revised by the District and submitted by the California Air Resources Board (CARB), the agency that serves as the governor's designee for California SIP submittals.
(
printed page 74488)
Table 1—Submitted Rules
Rule No.

Adoption/amendment date

The October 13, 2023 submittal of these three rules was intended to resolve deficiencies identified in our July 10, 2023 final action (“2023 NSR Action”), which included a limited disapproval of a prior version of Rule 2201. In the 2023 NSR Action, specific issues included missing and deficient definitions, impermissible interprecursor trading provisions, unapprovable exemptions to offsetting and public notice provisions, among other assorted deficiencies. The EPA also identified concerns related to the “offset equivalency tracking system” used to ensure that the District's permitting program collected the federally-required amount of creditable emissions reductions.
In our January 21, 2025 action, we proposed to determine that the District had fully addressed the deficiencies identified in the 2023 NSR Action, but we also proposed a limited approval of the District's October 2023 submittal because we identified other aspects of the submitted rules that were not approvable. Specifically, we identified the following deficiencies:
1. Rule 1020—Definitions
The definition of VOC in Rule 1020 is deficient because it does not include an exemption for trans-1,1,1,4,4,4-hexafluorobut-2-ene (also known as HFO-1336mzz(E)). The EPA added trans-1,1,1,4,4,4-hexafluorobut-2-ene to the list of compounds
40 CFR 51.100(s)(1)
that are exempted from the definition of VOC at
40 CFR 51.100(s)
on February 8, 2023 (effective April 10, 2023).
[
1
]
While this compound was added to the Federal regulations nearly contemporaneously to the District's adoption of the amendments to Rule 1020 on April 10, 2023, the absence of trans-1,1,1,4,4,4-hexafluorobut-2-ene in the Rule 1020 list of exempt compounds creates a new rule deficiency. In addition, on November 12, 2024, the EPA proposed to add (Z)-1-chloro-2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene (also known as HCFO-1224yd(Z)) to the list of compounds exempted from the definition of VOC.
[
2
]
The District must revise the Rule 1020 definition of VOC to match the most recent Federal definition in effect at
40 CFR 51.100(s)
, including the exemptions listed at
40 CFR 51.100(s)(1)
.
[
3
]
2. Rule 2020—Exemptions
Several American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) test method citations provided in Rule 2020 are deficient because they do not include the revision or reissuance date of the specific ASTM methods.
3. Rule 2201—New and Modified Stationary Source Review Rule
The term “Emission Reduction Credit” is used in Rule 2201, but the term is not defined in the rule or in Rule 1020, “Definitions.” We note that the term is defined in Rule 2301—Emission Reduction Credit Banking, but this rule has not been submitted for SIP approval. Therefore, we find Rule 2201 deficient because it does not provide a definition for the term Emission Reduction Credit, and the term is a necessary component of an approvable NNSR program.
Please see our proposed rule for more information concerning the background for this action and for a more detailed discussion of the rationale for our limited approval and limited disapproval of the submitted rules. As described in the proposed rule, the rules listed in Table 1 are intended to replace older versions of the rules currently in the SIP.
In addition, on January 21, 2025, the EPA published an Interim Final Determination (IFD) to defer the imposition of the offset and highway sanctions triggered by the limited disapproval component of the 2023 NSR Action.
[
4 5
]
An EPA IFD to defer sanctions is an administrative action that temporarily pauses the automatic implementation of Federal penalties against a State for failing to meet specific CAA requirements.
III. Public Comments and EPA Responses
The EPA's proposed action provided a 30-day public comment period. During this period, we received three comment letters, which are included in the docket for this action. Two comment letters are from individuals; their comments are supportive and do not raise any discernable issues that are adverse to our action as proposed. The third comment letter was submitted by the Central Valley Air Quality Coalition, Committee for a Better Arvin, Committee for a Better Shafter, Delano Guardians, and the Center on Race, Poverty & the Environment (collectively, “Environmental Organizations”). Issues raised in this comment letter are summarized with responses below.
Comment 1:
The Environmental Organizations stated that the District has not corrected all deficiencies that the EPA identified in the 2023 NSR Action, and that the EPA's proposed limited approval of the revised rules and accompanying IFD deferring sanctions are therefore unlawful and arbitrary. The commenters highlighted the EPA's findings from the 2023 NSR Action that the prior version of Rule 2201 was less stringent than Federal requirements because it did not provide an equivalent amount of time-of-use surplus emissions reductions as would have been required under the Federal program and did not provide a remedy to correct the negative VOC and NO
X
balances from the District's 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 Annual Offset Equivalency Reports. According to the commenters, the revised Rule 2201 does not address this deficiency because it fails to provide sufficient offsetting emissions reductions and does not correct the VOC and NO
X
deficits in the offset equivalency program.
Response:
We disagree with the commenters' characterizations of our proposed action. As described below, neither the 2023 NSR Action nor the present action would require the District to provide additional offsetting emissions reductions as part of an approvable SIP submittal, and our review in each case is limited to
(
printed page 74489)
ensuring that the submitted rules meet applicable CAA requirements.
As an initial matter, comments relating solely to the 2023 NSR Action are outside the scope of this rulemaking because this action refers to the January 21, 2025 limited approval limited disapproval proposed action, not the 2023 NSR Action. However, we wish to clarify aspects of the 2023 NSR Action's characterization of deficiencies in the previous Rule 2201 to the extent that they are relevant to the present rulemaking. As the commenters have noted, the 2023 NSR Action includes a finding that the previous Rule 2201 equivalency system did not provide a mechanism to require the District to quantify or restore VOC and NO
X
negative balances from the District's 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 Annual Offset Equivalency Reports. We explained this deficiency in the proposal for that action as follows:
[B]ecause neither remedy provides a mechanism to require the District to quantify or restore a negative balance in the equivalency system, both remedies fail to ensure full Federal offset equivalency in the event of a shortfall. Thus, even where the District adopts all offset requirements of the Federal program in response to an equivalency failure, it will retain an historic deficit relative to the Federal program, which is not made whole under the rule. Therefore, the EPA finds that the District must revise the rule to address these deficiencies.
[
6
]
The proposal for the 2023 NSR Action also identified as deficiencies Rule 2201's failure to require sources to provide the federally-required quantity of offsets following an equivalency failure and the lack of requirements that would prevent the equivalency system from operating with a negative balance once creditable emissions reductions had been exhausted.
[
7
]
In describing these deficiencies, we noted that “several shortcomings in the District's equivalency system ha[d] become apparent” following the equivalency failures shown in the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 annual offset equivalency reports.
[
8
]
While these “shortcomings” were made prominent through the annual equivalency reports, the deficiencies identified in the 2023 NSR Action relate specifically to the content of the rule (and in particular, the rule's ability to address hypothetical future offset shortfalls). At the time, we noted that the “most straight forward way” to address the identified deficiencies would be to directly implement the Federal offset program requirements going forward.
[
9
]
We did not require the District to retroactively apply Federal offset requirements to past permitting actions or otherwise restore a negative balance in the equivalency system. As we stated in the 2023 NSR Action, there is nothing in the SIP-approved version of Rule 2201 to require this,
[
10
]
and we are similarly unaware of any other authority to require such action.
Turning to the present action, we have considered whether SJVUAPCD has fully addressed the Rule 2201 deficiencies identified in the 2023 NSR Action. As described elsewhere in this notice and in the proposal and TSD, which are included in the docket for this action, we find that it has.
[
11
]
Specifically, we find that changes to directly apply the Federal requirements to NOx and VOC and to revise the equivalency demonstration and remedies for other pollutants have sufficiently addressed the problems identified in the previous rule and will ensure equivalency with Federal requirements going forward. Importantly, contrary to the commenters' suggestion, our proposed action did not include a finding “that the District corrected the NSR program's negative balance of VOC and NOx offsets.” Rather, our review is limited to ensuring that the rule meets applicable Federal requirements for NSR permitting of new and modified sources, including those requirements that were the basis for our prior limited disapproval in the 2023 NSR Action.
Comment 2:
The Environmental Organizations noted that several of the commenting organizations have filed a CAA citizen suit alleging violations of Rule 2201 by the District. The commenters recounted and critiqued aspects of the 2023 NSR Action and argued that that action does not affect the enforceability of or otherwise diminish Rule 2201's requirements or remedies. The commenters indicated that the EPA should not construe their comments as waiving or conceding allegations in that suit.
Response:
Comments relating to the commenters' lawsuit against the District are outside the scope of this action. The EPA is not a party to the suit, and we take no position regarding the allegations or arguments raised. As noted previously, comments related solely to the 2023 NSR Action are also outside the scope of this action.
IV. EPA Action
The comments we received on our proposed action and on our interim final determination do not change our assessment of the submitted rules, as described in our proposed action. Therefore, as authorized in CAA sections 110(k)(3) and 301(a), the EPA is finalizing a limited approval and limited disapproval of Rules 1020, 2020, and 2201. This action incorporates the submitted rules into the California SIP, including those provisions identified as deficient.
This approval is limited because the EPA is simultaneously finalizing a limited disapproval of the rules under CAA section 110(k)(3). Our limited disapproval of Rules 1020, 2020, and 2201 triggers an obligation for the EPA to promulgate a Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) unless we approve subsequent SIP revisions that correct the rule deficiencies within 24 months of this final action. Additionally, because the deficiency relates to NNSR requirements under part D of title I of the Act, the offset sanction in CAA section 179(b)(2) will be imposed in the San Joaquin Valley nonattainment area 18 months after the effective date of this action, and the highway funding sanction in CAA section 179(b)(1) will be imposed in the area six months after the offset sanction is imposed, unless the EPA approves subsequent SIP revisions that correct the rule deficiencies prior to the implementation of the sanctions. The EPA intends to work with the District to correct the deficiencies in a timely manner.
Note that the rules have been adopted by the District, and the EPA's final limited disapproval does not prevent the local agency from enforcing them. The limited disapproval would also not prevent any portion of the rules from being incorporated by reference into the federally enforceable SIP.
[
12
]
V. Incorporation by Reference
In this rule, the EPA is finalizing regulatory text that includes incorporation by reference. In accordance with requirements of 1 CFR
(
printed page 74490)
51.5, the EPA is incorporating by reference the rules listed in Table 1 of this preamble. These rules are intended to address the CAA's statutory and regulatory requirements for NNSR permit programs for major sources emitting nonattainment air pollutants under CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) and part D of title I. The EPA has made, and will continue to make, these materials available through
https://www.regulations.gov
and at the EPA Region IX Office (please contact the person identified in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this preamble for more information).
VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a SIP submission that complies with the provisions of the Act and applicable Federal regulations.
42 U.S.C. 7410(k)
;
40 CFR 52.02(a)
. Thus, in reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to review State choices, and approve those choices if they meet the minimum criteria of the Act. Accordingly, this action merely approves State law as meeting Federal requirements and does not impose additional requirements beyond those imposed by State law.
Additional information about these statutes and Executive Orders can be found at
https://www.epa.gov/​laws-regulations/​laws-and-executive-orders
.
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review and
Executive Order 13563
: Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review
This action is not a significant regulatory action and was therefore not submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review.
B.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This action is not expected to be an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this action is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
This action does not impose an information collection burden under the PRA because this action does not impose additional requirements beyond those imposed by State law.
D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
I certify that this action will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA. This action will not impose any requirements on small entities beyond those imposed by State law.
E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
This action does not contain any unfunded mandate as described in UMRA,
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
, and does not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. This action does not impose additional requirements beyond those imposed by State law. Accordingly, no additional costs to State, local, or tribal governments, or to the private sector, will result from this action.
F.
Executive Order 13132
: Federalism
This action does not have federalism implications. It will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
G.
Executive Order 13175
: Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
This action does not have Tribal implications, as specified in
Executive Order 13175
, because the SIP is not approved to apply on any Indian reservation land or in any other area where the EPA or an Indian Tribe has demonstrated that a Tribe has jurisdiction, and will not impose substantial direct costs on Tribal governments or preempt Tribal law. Thus,
Executive Order 13175
does not apply to this action.
H.
Executive Order 13045
: Protection of Children From Environmental Health Risks and Safety Risks
The EPA interprets
Executive Order 13045
as applying only to those regulatory actions that concern environmental health or safety risks that the EPA has reason to believe may disproportionately affect children, per the definition of “covered regulatory action” in section 2-202 of the Executive Order. Therefore, this action is not subject to
Executive Order 13045
because it merely approves State law as meeting Federal requirements. Furthermore, the EPA's Policy on Children's Health does not apply to this action.
I.
Executive Order 13211
: Actions That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use
This action is not subject to
Executive Order 13211
, because it is not a significant regulatory action under
Executive Order 12866
.
J. National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act (NTTAA)
Section 12(d) of the NTTAA directs the EPA to use voluntary consensus standards in its regulatory activities unless to do so would be inconsistent with applicable law or otherwise impractical. The EPA believes that this action is not subject to the requirements of section 12(d) of the NTTAA because application of those requirements would be inconsistent with the CAA.
K. Congressional Review Act (CRA)
This action is subject to the CRA, and the EPA will submit a rule report to each House of the Congress and to the Comptroller General of the United States. This action is not a “major rule” as defined by
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
.
L. Petitions for Judicial Review
Under section 307(b)(1) of the CAA, petitions for judicial review of this action must be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the appropriate circuit by January 19, 2027. Filing a petition for reconsideration by the Administrator of this final rule does not affect the finality of this rule for the purposes of judicial review nor does it extend the time within which a petition for judicial review may be filed, and shall not postpone the effectiveness of such rule or action. This action may not be challenged later in proceedings to enforce its requirements (
see
section 307(b)(2)).

title: Veteran Readiness and Employment Program: Update to Reduced Work Tolerance and Basic Eligibility Period
abstract: The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposes to amend the Veteran Readiness and Employment (VR&E) regulations to align with current practice and statute. The rule would expand the list of approved providers for reduced work tolerance (RWT) documentation, allowing for more accurate and timely processing by a Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC). VA also proposes to clarify that a veteran who is subject to a basic period of eligibility would receive a new 12-year period of eligibility if such veteran obtains a compensable service-connected disability rating based on a subsequent period of active-duty service. Finally, the rule would remove the eligibility termination date for veterans discharged on or after January 1, 2013, consistent with the Johnny Isakson and David P. Roe, M.D. Veterans Health Care and Benefits Improvement Act of 2020.
dates: Comments must be received by January 19, 2027.

SUMMARY:
The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposes to amend the Veteran Readiness and Employment (VR&E) regulations to align with current practice and statute. The rule would expand the list of approved providers for reduced work tolerance (RWT) documentation, allowing for more accurate and timely processing by a Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC). VA also proposes to clarify that a veteran who is subject to a basic period of eligibility would receive a new 12-year period of eligibility if such veteran obtains a compensable service-connected disability rating based on a subsequent period of active-duty service. Finally, the rule would remove the eligibility termination date for veterans discharged on or after January 1, 2013, consistent with the Johnny Isakson and David P. Roe, M.D. Veterans Health Care and Benefits Improvement Act of 2020.
