SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Reduced Work Tolerance
In accordance with
38 U.S.C. 3100
, the purpose of the Chapter 31 VR&E program is to provide for all services and assistance necessary to enable veterans with one or more compensable service-connected disabilities to achieve maximum independence in daily living and, to the maximum extent possible, to become employable and to obtain and maintain suitable employment.
In some instances, a veteran's functional limitations, as a result of his or her disability(ies), impact his or her ability to participate in a rehabilitation program on a full-time basis. VA may approve a veteran for RWT following documentation from an approved medical provider. VA considers a veteran with an RWT to be pursuing his or her rehabilitation program full time when he or she is devoting as much time to the program as the effects of his or her disability(ies) permit. This allows VA, under certain circumstances, to pay the veteran a subsistence allowance at the full-time rate for the type of program being pursued when he or she meets the standard for full-time pursuit,
i.e.,
the rate of pursuit that VA considers to be equivalent to full-time pursuit, established for the veteran in his or her rehabilitation plan.
Section 21.312(e) of
title 38 Code of Federal Regulations
, currently requires a VA physician to make the RWT determination or redetermination. However, because an RWT determination or redetermination is an appealable benefits determination that is based on the evidence of record, VA proposes to revise the regulation to require a VRC to make the final determination or redetermination of RWT and to document such determination in the case file.
VA also proposes to amend
38 CFR 21.312(e)
to allow for documentation to support an RWT to be provided by a veteran's medical provider rather than being limited to a VA physician. The documentation is necessary for a VRC to determine the veteran's ability to pursue a rehabilitation program under the VR&E program and to specify the rate of pursuit that VA will consider to be equivalent to full-time pursuit, so that the veteran may participate in a program of rehabilitation and receive a subsistence allowance at the full-time rate. Expanding the list of approved medical providers to those who have knowledge of the veteran's disability conditions would allow a VRC to make a more accurate and timely RWT determination or redetermination that is consistent with the veteran's regular care.
Furthermore, VA seeks to clarify in proposed § 21.312(f) that a veteran generally may not be approved for RWT and also be employed, to include participating in work study, because it would further reduce the veteran's ability to fully participate in a program of rehabilitation. RWT is developed relative to the current impact of the veteran's disabilities and the amount of time the veteran needs to spend treating their disabilities. However, if a veteran accepts employment while receiving RWT, he or she may maintain the RWT rate until the end of the semester or term.
Finally, approval for an RWT redetermination under § 21.312(c) would be contingent on the veteran's documented cooperation and participation in line with his or her medical treatment plan and on his or her ability to participate in a rehabilitation plan. A feasibility determination would be required with each yearly evaluation. This is to ensure the veteran continues to benefit from, and is in need of, RWT. The RWT program is not intended for the life of the case, but only until such a time as when the veteran establishes enough stability in his or her condition to return to the normal rate of pursuit approved by his or her VRC or case manager, as established under
38 CFR 21.310
.
VA also proposes to amend § 21.312(d) to remove the outdated reference to electing benefits at the Chapter 34 rate. Chapter 34 benefits are not payable beyond December 31, 1989, and any previous election of benefits at the Chapter 34 rate terminated as of that date.
38 U.S.C. 3462(e)
;
38 CFR 21.334(e)
. VA also proposes grammatical updates to § 21.312.
Basic Period of Eligibility
Under
38 U.S.C. 3103(a)
, (b)(3), and (g), VA generally may not provide a Chapter 31 rehabilitation program to a veteran after the end of the 12-year period beginning on the date of the veteran's discharge or release from active military, naval, air, or space service or the date the veteran receives a compensable service-connected disability rating, whichever is later, if the discharge occurred before January 1, 2013. VA implemented section 3103(a) in
38 CFR 21.41(a)
by referring to the 12-year period as beginning on the date of the veteran's discharge or release from his or her “last” period of service, which is calculated at the time of the veteran's initial application for Chapter 31 benefits. Based on VA's interpretation of
38 U.S.C. 3102
and
3103(a)
, VA proposes adding § 21.41(d) to establish a new 12-year period of eligibility for a veteran who is subject to a basic period of eligibility and who has a subsequent period of service that independently gives rise to a new qualifying disability for Chapter 31 benefits.
Under
38 U.S.C. 3103(f)
and
38 CFR 21.46
, if VA determines that a veteran who is subject to a basic period of eligibility is prevented from participating in, or continuing in, a program of vocational rehabilitation as a result of being ordered to active duty, VA will extend the veteran's basic period of eligibility by the length of time the veteran serves on active duty plus 4 months. However, as reflected in proposed §§ 21.41(d) and 21.46, VA does not interpret section 3103(f) as precluding the application of section 3103(a) to establish a new 12-year period of eligibility when the veteran could qualify for Chapter 31 benefits based independently on the new period of service. This is a veteran-friendly interpretation that is consistent with both
38 U.S.C. 3103(a)
and
(f)
and would allow such veterans the time needed to pursue a rehabilitation program, despite being rated for their first condition potentially many years ago. We revised the authority citation for
38 CFR 21.46
to refer to both
38 U.S.C. 3102
and
3103
.
Additionally, on January 5, 2021, section 1025 of the Johnny Isakson and David P. Roe, M.D. Veterans Health Care and Benefits Improvement Act of 2020,
Public Law 116-315
, added
38 U.S.C. 3103(g)
. Section 3103(g) eliminated the 12-year eligibility termination date for veterans discharged or released from active military, naval, or air service on or after January 1, 2013. VA proposes adding
38 CFR 21.41(e)
to reflect the elimination of the eligibility termination date for veterans discharged or released from active military, naval, air, or space service on or after January 1, 2013. VA interprets section 3103(g) as eliminating the eligibility termination date for all veterans who were discharged or released on or after January 1, 2013,
(
printed page 74532)
including veterans who were discharged or released from space service. We note that section 3103(a) refers to an eligibility termination date applying to veterans “discharge[d] or release[d] from active military, naval, air, or space service” and believe that the omission of the reference to space service in section 3103(g) was a Congressional oversight. See
Public Law 116-283
, sec. 926 (adding space service to title 38 references to “military, naval, or air service”);
Public Law 116-315
, sec. 1025 (adding section 3103(g)). VA also proposes adding a reference to proposed paragraph (e) in § 21.41(a)(2).
We also propose a technical revision in proposed § 21.46 to refer to
10 U.S.C. 12304a
and
12304b
as additional authority under which a veteran may be ordered to active duty, to make the regulation consistent with
38 U.S.C. 3103(f)
, to which section 12034a and 12304b were added by
Public Law 115-48
after VA had promulgated § 21.46.
Executive Orders 12866, 13563 and 14192
VA examined the impact of this rulemaking as required by Executive Orders 12866 (Sept. 30, 1993) and 13563 (Jan. 18, 2011), which direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has determined that this rulemaking is not a significant regulatory action under
Executive Order 12866
, as supplemented by
Executive Order 13563
. This proposed rule is an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
Economic Impact:
VA has determined that this rule does not create any new entitlements, expand benefit levels, or alter existing payments under Chapter 31. All proposed regulatory updates reflect practices that VR&E has already implemented since fiscal year 2021, such as eliminating the eligibility termination date for veterans discharged on or after January 1, 2013, and applying the updated 12-year eligibility period when a new qualifying service-connected disability is incurred. Expanding the list of medical providers who may determine RWT also does not change the amount or nature of benefits; it simply allows more timely and accurate documentation by providers who already work with the veteran. Because the rule updates regulations to match current law and existing VA practice, there are no new expenditures, transfers, or burdens on veterans, providers, small entities, or governments.
VA characterizes the rule as deregulatory because it removes outdated restrictions and reduces administrative barriers. By eliminating unnecessary limitations, such as requiring RWT determinations solely from VA physicians and maintaining an obsolete eligibility termination date, the rule streamlines program administration and reduces compliance burdens on both veterans and VA. These changes make the regulations clearer, more efficient, and more aligned with current statutory authority, thereby reducing regulatory friction without imposing any costs.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Secretary hereby certifies that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities as defined in the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
). This certification is based on the fact that the technical changes made by this rule would affect individuals but would not affect any small entities. Therefore, under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
, the initial and final regulatory flexibility analysis requirements of
5 U.S.C. 603
and
604
do not apply.
Unfunded Mandates
This proposed rule would not result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any one year.
Paperwork Reduction Act
This proposed rule contains no provisions constituting a collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
).

(c)
Redetermination of work tolerance.
The veteran's work tolerance will be reevaluated one time per year, or more frequently if needed. The rate of pursuit required for VA to consider it equivalent to full-time pursuit will be modified if there is either an increase or decrease in the work tolerance of the veteran. Continued approval for reduced work tolerance is contingent on the veteran's documented cooperation and participation in line with his or her treatment plan and on his or her ability to participate in a rehabilitation plan. Feasibility determination is required with each yearly evaluation.
(d)
Payment of allowance.
A veteran with a reduced work tolerance will be paid a subsistence allowance at the full-time rate for the type of program being pursued when the veteran meets the standard for full-time pursuit established for the veteran in the rehabilitation plan.
(e)
Determining work tolerance.
Documentation must be submitted by a licensed or certified medical or mental health professional, to include but not limited to a physician, physician assistant, nurse practitioner, psychiatrist, or psychologist, and must support a determination or redetermination regarding the veteran's work tolerance. A Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor will make the final determination based on the evidence of record.
(f)
Limitations.
A veteran may not be approved for reduced work tolerance and participate in employment, including work study. If a veteran with a determined reduced work tolerance accepts employment, the veteran may maintain the reduced work tolerance rate until the end of the current term or semester.

Further classification changes are summarized as follows:
The Postal Service will apply a flat 11 percent fuel surcharge to domestic Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Parcel Select, and USPS Ground Advantage packages. Initially, the fuel surcharge will be static but eventually the Postal Service intends that it will adjust the surcharge on a weekly basis, based on average fuel prices reported by the Energy Information Administration (EIA). The new, permanent surcharge is set to take effect on the expiration date of the current time limited price change that has been in place since April 26, 2026.
The Postal Service will introduce a repricing fee for postage overpayments and underpayments caused by inaccurate dimensions or weight. For an underpayment, the fee will equal 20 percent of the unpaid amount and will be added to the postage due. For an overpayment, 20 percent will be deducted from the refundable amount, subject to Postal Service refund rules.
The Noncompliance Fee will be renamed the Dimension and Weight Noncompliance Fee and will apply only when dimensions or weight are missing.
The proposed changes to Premium Forwarding Service clarify that the online enrollment fee is annual. The Postal Service will also add Priority Mail Express as an option under Premium Forwarding Service Residential (PFSR) and Premium Forwarding Service Commercial (PFSC) and add Priority Mail Flat Rate Envelopes, Priority Mail Sacks, Priority Mail Express Flat Rate Envelopes, and Priority Mail Express Sacks options for PFSC. PFSC customers may control reshipment frequency for periods of up to 12 months.
The Postal Service will introduce a Shipping Label Noncompliance Fee under Domestic Competitive products for incorrect barcode symbology or constructs.
The Postal Service will expand the number of Price Groups for Priority Mail Express International (PMEI) Flat Rate Envelope from 8 to 20 groups and the number of Price Groups for Priority Mail International (PMI) Flat Rate Envelopes and Boxes from 8 to 20 groups.
The Postal Service will add USPS Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) as an optional feature for International Priority Airmail (IPA) to more accurately reflect timing, payment and procedures related to USPS DDP.
The Postal Service will revise the country group assignments for PMEI, PMI, IPA, and First-Class Package International Service (FCPIS) in, and to the format of, Part D Country Price Lists for International Mail so that it can price these products more effectively.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-12-08, which applies to all Airbus Helicopters Model AS350B2, AS350B3, EC130B4, and EC130T2 helicopters. AD 2026-12-08 requires revising the airworthiness limitations section (ALS) of the existing maintenance manual (MM) or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA) and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. Since the FAA issued AD 2026-12-08, a determination was made that new and more restrictive airworthiness limitations and maintenance tasks are necessary. This proposed AD would require incorporating these airworthiness limitations and maintenance tasks into the ALS of the existing MM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Background
The FAA issued AD 2026-12-08, Amendment 39-23378 (
91 FR 36077
, June 16, 2026), (AD 2026-12-08), for all Airbus Helicopters Model AS350B2, AS350B3, EC130B4, and EC130T2 helicopters. AD 2026-12-08 was prompted by an MCAI originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2025-0137, dated June 27, 2025; corrected October 29, 2025, (EASA AD 2025-0137).
AD 2026-12-08 requires revising the ALS of the existing MM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. The FAA issued AD 2026-12-08 to prevent failure of critical parts and primary structural components, which if not addressed, could result in loss of control of the helicopter.
Actions Since AD 2026-12-08 Was Issued
On May 26, 2026, EASA superseded AD 2025-0137 and issued EASA AD 2026-0101 (EASA AD 2026-0101) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations and maintenance tasks have been developed. Additionally, the MCAI states that the airworthiness limitations are identified as mandatory for continued airworthiness and that Airbus Helicopters has issued applicable ALS revisions to specify new and more restrictive life limits and maintenance tasks.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13818.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2026-0101, which specifies replacing components before exceeding their life limits and accomplishing all applicable maintenance tasks within thresholds and intervals specified in the ALS. Depending on the results of the maintenance tasks, EASA AD 2026-0101 specifies accomplishing corrective action(s) or contacting Airbus Helicopters for approved instructions and accomplishing those instructions.
In addition, EASA AD 2026-0101 specifies revising the Aircraft Maintenance Programme (AMP) by incorporating the limitations, tasks, and associated thresholds and intervals described in the specified ALS, as applicable. Revising the AMP constitutes terminating action for the requirement to record accomplishment of the actions of replacing components before exceeding their life limits and accomplishing maintenance tasks within thresholds and intervals specified in the applicable ALS as specified in EASA AD 2026-0101, for demonstration of AD compliance on a continued basis.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2026-0101, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. See “Differences Between this Proposed AD and the MCAI” for a discussion of the general differences included in this proposed AD.
Differences Between This Proposed AD and the MCAI
Where EASA AD 2026-0101 specifies revising the approved AMP within 12 months after the effective date of EASA AD 2026-0101, this proposed AD would require revising the ALS of the existing MM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, within 30 days after the effective date of this proposed AD.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate EASA AD 2026-0101 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2026-0101 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2026-0101 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2026-0101. Material required by EASA AD 2026-0101 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13818 after the FAA final rule is published.

SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters on the Hackensack River, in Kearny and Secaucus, NJ. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the demolition of the existing Portal Bridge. When subject to enforcement, entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector New York, or their designated representative.
DATES:

This rule is effective without actual notice from 6 a.m. November 19, 2026 through 11:59 p.m. on May 27, 2027. For purposes of enforcement the Coast Guard will use actual notice from 6 a.m. on November 17, 2026, through 6 a.m. November 19, 2026 The Coast Guard will only enforce this temporary safety zone during periods during which barges are within the channels at the existing bridge and demolition operations are in progress.
Comments due date:
Comments and related material must be received by the Coast Guard on or before December 21, 2026.

II. Background and Authority
On September 28, 2026, the Coast Guard received sufficient information to be able to fulfill a request from the Skanska Traylor Portal North Bridge Joint Venture for a safety zone on the Hackensack River while demolishing the existing Portal North Bridge (PNB) span (River Mile 5.0). Hazards from this project include but are not limited to deployment of heavy equipment and anchored barges which will continuously obstruct vessel traffic through the navigable channel, during demolition of the existing superstructure, footings, and fender systems, which create hazards for workers and the public. The Captain of the Port, Sector New York (COTP) has determined that potential hazards associated with demolition of the existing bridge are a safety concern for anyone within the work area. Under the authority of
46 U.S.C. 70034
, the COTP is issuing this rule, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone.
The Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As authorized by
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed
(
printed page 74475)
rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable. The Coast Guard was not notified of this schedule and safety zone request with sufficient time to be able to publish this rule by November 17, 2026, when the safety zone must be in place to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment.
For the same reason, the Coast Guard finds that under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This temporary interim rule establishes a safety zone from 6 a.m. on November 17, 2026, until 11:59 p.m. on May 27, 2027. The safety zone will cover all navigable waters of the Hackensack River, surface to bottom, shoreline to shoreline, between the New Jersey Turnpike/I-95 Fixed Bridge (River Mile 5.3) and a line drawn from 40°44′54.52″ N, 74°05′37.59″ W, thence to 40°45′02.07″ N, 74°05′31.69″ W, approximately 1,650 feet south of the existing PNB. These coordinates are based on the World Geodetic System (WGS 84). Vessels and persons will not be allowed to enter the zone during this time, unless authorized by the Captain of the Port.
One full eight-week enforcement period prohibiting vessels or individuals from entering the safety zone is planned from approximately November 17, 2026, through January 29, 2027.
The exact dates and times of the enforcement period, during which all vessel transits through the safety zone will be prohibited, will be published in the Local Notice to Mariners, posted on the Coast Guard Navigation Center Maritime Safety Information Products page at
https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/​msi
,
and issued in a Broadcast Notice to Mariners via marine channel 16 (VHF-FM) as soon as practicable in response to an emergency or hazardous condition.
This rule will remain in effect through May 27, 2027, which should accommodate the possibility of project delays due to unforeseen circumstances. If the project is completed before May 27, 2027, enforcement of the safety zone will be suspended, and notice will be provided via the Local Notice to Mariners.
The Coast Guard Northeast District Local Notice to Mariners can be found at:
https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/​maritime-safety-information
.

Although this regulation is published as a temporary interim rule without prior notice, public comment is nevertheless desirable to ensure that the regulation is both workable and reasonable. Commenters should identify the docket number for the regulation and give reasons for their comments. We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analysis based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.

The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.

Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under

D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act

), the Coast Guard certifies that this rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National

Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (

et seq.
), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment.
This rule is a safety zone. It is categorically excluded from further review under paragraph L60(a) of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1. A Record of Environmental Consideration supporting this determination is available in the docket.

Background: The Coast Guard's Efforts To Comply With the National Historic Preservation Act
The National Historic Preservation Act
Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), codified as
54 U.S.C. 306108
, requires:
[t]he head of any Federal agency having . . . jurisdiction over a proposed Federal . . . undertaking in any State . . ., prior to the approval of the expenditure of any Federal funds on the undertaking . . ., [to] take into account the effect of the undertaking on any historic property.
“Historic property”
[
1
]
includes any historic structure or object included in
or eligible for inclusion
in the National Register of Historic Places. The term “eligible for inclusion” in the National Register includes both properties formally determined as such in accordance with regulations of the Secretary of the Interior and all other properties that meet the National Register criteria.
Applying the National Register criteria, the Coast Guard has determined that the USCG
Smilax
is eligible for inclusion on the National Register. The Coast Guard has also determined that the decommissioning and disposal of the USCG
Smilax
is an undertaking, and that the undertaking is likely to have an adverse effect on the USCG
Smilax.
In accordance with
36 CFR 800.6(a)(4)
, the Coast Guard is now inviting members of the public to express their views on resolving adverse effects of the undertaking.
Short History of the Smilax
USCGC
Smilax
(WLIC 315) was constructed at Dubuque Boat & Boiler Works in Dubuque, IA and was commissioned on 01 November 1944. USCGC
Smilax
was designed for the express purpose of maintaining Aids to Navigation (AtoN) on the inland waterways of the United States, including repair and alterations of fixed AtoN structures and the routine retrieval, servicing and setting of buoys, thereby enabling the safe navigation of waters that support the nation's economy through maritime commerce.
After commissioning, USCGC
Smilax
was homeported in Ft. Pierce, FL from November 1944 to June 1954, then in New Smyrna Beach, FL from June 1954 to November 1965. In 1964 she was re-outfitted with new engines and assigned a 70′ work barge and transferred to Brunswick, GA in 1965 to July 1999. Finally, the
Smilax
was transferred to Atlantic Beach, NC in July 1999, where she remains to the present time.
In March 2011, with 66 years of active service at that time, USCGC
Smilax
became the oldest operational commissioned cutter in the Coast Guard and was designated the “Queen of the Fleet.” She has held this designation for the last 15 years.
Now, with over 80 years of continuous service, the Coast Guard plans to utilize the services of the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) to carry out the final disposition of this ship, the last phase of its life cycle. DLA is a separate Federal agency with the capabilities to carry out the final disposition using the steps of Reutilize, Transfer, Donate, Sales (RTDS) of the vessel to another Federal agency, State or Qualified Local government or sales via the commercial market.
Steps Taken To Identify Historic Attributes of the Smilax
The Coast Guard considered the criteria outlined in
36 CFR part 63
to determine whether the
Smilax
would be considered eligible for listing on the National Register of Historic Places and it consulted with State Historic Preservation Officers (SHPO). Additionally, the Coast Guard referred to the Historic American Engineering Record (HAER) to better understand the
Smilax's
history. The HAER is a collection of documents that provides detailed information with drawings, photographs and historic reports in conformance with the Secretary of the Interior's Standards and Guidelines for Architectural and Engineering Documentation. The HAER study and SHPO Consultations to date are available for viewing in the docket for this notice.
Undertaking's Effects on Historic Properties
The decommissioning and disposition of the vessel was determined to have an adverse effect on this historic property. Upon decommissioning, USCGC
Smilax
will be demilitarized. Military markings will be removed or covered and items that are found to have historical significance will be transferred to the Coast Guard Historians Office. Other gear or materials with Coast Guard markings or decals not in a usable or serviceable condition will be destroyed. Property and parts that are found to be of use will be identified and put back into the Coast Guard supply system for future use. Any other gear will be conveyed with the ship and upon completion of decommissioning, DLA
(
printed page 74595)
will provide disposition services as needed.
National Register Criteria for Evaluation
The National Park Service has developed the National Register Criteria for Evaluation. These criteria, which are set out at
36 CFR 60.4
, are standards by which every property that is nominated to the National Register is judged. The Coast Guard has evaluated the
Smilax
under these criteria to determine whether it is eligible for listing on the National Register.
USCGC
Smilax
was found to be eligible under Criterion “A” with a period of historical significance extending from 1944 to 1976, fifty years before the present. USCGC
Smilax
has performed its mission of maintaining aids to navigation to promote maritime safety for more than 80 years. During this span there have been 5 major military conflicts and dozens of overseas contingency operations and armed conflicts. In 2013, USCGC
Smilax
assisted maritime archaeologists with the North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources to raise a number of artifacts from the site of Queen Anne's Revenge, the pirate Blackbeards's flagship that wrecked just offshore Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina in 1718. Due to the operational longevity, USCGC
Smilax
became the fifth ship to hold the title as “Queen of the Fleet” and it has held this honor for the past 15 years, demonstrating its place in Coast Guard history.
USCGC
Smilax
was found not to meet Criterion “B” since it is not associated with individuals important in United States history.
USCGC
Smilax
was found not to meet Criterion “C” since its original integrity has been compromised by engine refits, equipment upgrades, including the addition of a barge, and the modification of interior spaces.
USCGC
Smilax
was found not to meet Criterion “D,” as it is unlikely to yield information important in prehistory or history.
Summary of Consultations to Date
The Coast Guard has consulted with the Florida, Georgia, Iowa and North Carolina SHPO's concerning the proposed decommissioning and final disposition of USCGC
Smilax.
Florida, Georgia, Iowa, have commented that since USCGC
Smilax
is currently homeported in Atlantic Beach, NC they will agree with any findings or actions that the North Carolina SHPO recommends. The North Carolina SHPO has agreed with the findings of the US Coast Guard regarding the following.
Criteria of Adverse Effects
In accordance with the criteria for assessing whether an undertaking will have an adverse effect enunciated in
36 CFR 800.5
, the Coast Guard has determined its proposed action will have an adverse effect. The steps the Coast Guard has conducted to mitigate the adverse effect of its proposed action are provided in the Evaluation of Alternatives or Mitigation Measures below.
Evaluation of Alternatives or Mitigation Measures
The Coast Guard has mitigated the adverse effects through the preparation of an HAER study, as mentioned earlier. The HAER study will be provided to the Library of Congress, where a copy will be made available for view. See
https://www.loc.gov/​pictures/​collection/​hh/​
for information about the Library of Congress' HAER collection.
Dated: November 13, 2026.

Captain, U.S. Coast Guard, Chief, Office of Cutter Forces.

Background
History, Establishment and Purpose of the Park
Mammoth Cave National Park comprises more than 52,000 acres of land within Edmonson, Hart, and Barren Counties in Kentucky. Within Mammoth Cave National Park is Mammoth Cave. Named for the enormity of its subterranean vaults and the unparalleled extent of its passages, Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world with over 400 miles surveyed to date. The geologic features within the extensive cave system are the product of a unique set of conditions found nowhere else, all of which contribute to the largest, most complex, and best-known karst area in the world. Karst is a geologic term that refers to areas of irregular limestone in which erosion has produced features such as fissures, sinkholes, underground streams, sinking springs, and caverns. The land above the underground formations is characterized by rugged hills, valleys, and forests.
Congress authorized the establishment of the park in 1926, which was officially established in 1941 and added to in 1961 with the acquisition of Great Onyx Cave and Crystal Cave. The legislative history of the establishment of the park recognized the need to protect and conserve the stunning and unique underground formations of the cave system, but also opportunities for recreation that could be provided by lands above ground. The park's enabling legislation directs the NPS to administer the park in accordance with the laws generally applicable to the National Park System, including the NPS Organic Act. That act requires the NPS to promote and
(
printed page 74477)
regulate the scenery, natural and historic objects, and wild life in parks and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means that will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.
54 U.S.C. 100101
.
In 2014, the NPS published the foundation document for the park. The document states that the park's purpose is to preserve, protect, interpret, and study the internationally recognized biological and geologic features and processes associated with the longest known cave system in the world, the park's diverse forested, karst landscape, the Green and Nolin rivers, and extensive evidence of human history; and to provide and promote public enjoyment, recreation, and understanding. Today, visitors are drawn to the park by its caves, scenic river valleys, bluffs, forests, and abundant wildlife. Above ground, the park offers opportunities for ranger-led tours, surface walks, camping, hiking, horseback riding, bicycling, scenic drives, canoeing and kayaking, fishing, accessible trails, and picnicking.
Trail Use in the Park
Bicycling is allowed on approximately 19 of the 85 miles of land-based trails within the park. These multi-use trails are the Connector Trail from the Big Hollow Trailhead to the Maple Springs Trailhead (Maple Springs Connector Trail), the Big Hollow Trail, the Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike & Hike Trail, and the White Oak Trail. Bicycles also are allowed on roads that are open to public motor vehicle traffic and on four administrative roads that are closed to motor vehicle use by the public but open to motor vehicle use by the NPS for administrative purposes (the Crystal Cave, Great Onyx, Three Springs, and Union City administrative roads).
Trails, public roads, and administrative roads that are open to traditional bicycles also are open to two-wheeled electric bicycles (e-bikes). Trail-use of three-wheeled e-bikes is limited to the Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike & Hike Trail and the Maple Springs Connector Trail. The use of traditional bicycles and e-bikes is governed by State law and NPS regulations that address topics such as speed limits, operation during periods of low visibility, obeying traffic control devices, and unsafe operation. See
36 CFR 4.30
.
In addition to opportunities for hiking and bicycling, visitors can ride horses on 54 miles of trail within the park, featuring wooded backcountry routes suitable for different skill levels and ages. The trails include wide, smooth dirt paths that accommodate two riders as well as narrower, single-file ridgeline trails. Horseback riding is prohibited on all park roads pursuant to NPS general regulations that prohibit the use of horses on park roads except in limited circumstances. See
36 CFR 2.16
.
Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment
In 2022, the NPS began developing a new land and river trails management plan for the park. The NPS initiated this planning process because previous plans had become outdated, and the condition of the park's trail system had deteriorated in a way that was adversely impacting park resources and the experience of trail users. The new plan would guide trail management for several decades with the purpose of improving access to high-quality land and river-based recreational opportunities for a diverse group of trail users, including hikers, equestrians, mountain bikers, and paddlers.
After the conclusion of a preliminary planning phase that sought feedback from trail users, community groups, and the general public, the NPS published the “Mammoth Cave National Park Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment” (EA) in 2024. The EA analyzed the potential environmental impacts of a no-action alternative that would have continued current management of the trail system and an action alternative that was identified as the NPS's preferred alternative. Under the action alternative, the NPS would add approximately 66 miles of land-based trails to the park trail system. This 72 percent increase in trail mileage would create new opportunities for hiking, horseback riding, and bicycling.
Specific to bicycle use, under the preferred alternative, the NPS would (1) discontinue bicycle use on the White Oak Trail; (2) close and restore to natural conditions the Maple Springs Connector Trail; and (3) construct eight new multi-use trails where bicycle use would be allowed, resulting in a total of approximately 37 miles of trail open to bicycle use.
As described in the EA, trail construction activities would use sustainable trail techniques to manage water and limit erosion, such as trail hardening, grade reversals, outslopes, and other earthwork strategies that improve drainage. These measures would minimize trail widening and trail braiding on new and rehabilitated trails, resulting in less vegetation trampling. The NPS would implement mitigation measures to minimize the impact on native vegetation during construction.
In addition to evaluating the potential impacts of trail construction and modification activities, the EA evaluated the potential impacts of allowing bicycles on the new trails. The EA and an associated written determination required by NPS regulations evaluate the suitability of trail surfaces and soil conditions for accommodating bicycle use, life cycle maintenance costs, safety considerations, methods to prevent or minimize user conflict, and methods to protect natural and cultural resources and mitigate impacts from bicycle use. Under the preferred alternative, the NPS would convert a one-mile section of the Ugly Creek Road from a public road to an administrative road that is closed to motor vehicle use other than vehicles used by the NPS for administrative purposes. Hiking and bicycling would be allowed on the converted section of this road.
The preferred alternative also would open the Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road (5.4 miles) to horseback riding. This change would improve the experience of equestrians by providing multiple opportunities for shorter loop rides, and a new opportunity to ride to the river and back from the northern boundary of the park. The NPS does not anticipate there will be conflicts between vehicles, equestrian users, hikers, and bicyclists because the road is used rarely by motor vehicles. All other public and administrative roads would continue to remain closed to equestrian use.
The NPS accepted public comments on the EA for 30 days. In December 2024, following a recommendation by the park superintendent, the Regional Director for Interior Region 2, South Atlantic—Gulf, signed a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) that identified the preferred alternative in the EA as the selected alternative. As stated in the FONSI, the NPS believes the selected alternative will improve the conditions and sustainability of the aboveground land and water trail networks in the park and enhance the diversity and quality of visitor experiences while protecting natural and cultural resources. Implementation of the selected alternative will expand opportunities for visitors to enjoy and recreate within the park.
Final Rule
This rule implements part of the selected alternative in the FONSI by amending the special regulations for the park in
36 CFR 7.36
. This rule authorizes the superintendent to
(
printed page 74478)
designate approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails for bicycle use in the park. The rule identifies 12 distinct trails that could be designated for bicycle use. Two trails currently designated for bicycle use—the Maple Springs Connector Trail and the White Oak Trail—are removed, consistent with plans to close those trails to bicycle use under the selected alternative. Another currently designated trail—the Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike & Hike Trail—remains on the list and another—the Big Hollow Trail—is listed as three separate segments as identified on park maps.
The rule adds the following eight new trails that will be constructed under the selected alternative:
Brooks Knob Road Cemetery Trail;
Brooks Knob Road Trail (up to gate);
Crystal Cave Road Trail;
East Entrance Trail;
Little Hope Cemetery Trail;
Sugar Sink Connector Trail;
Sugar Sink Trail; and
West Entrance Trail.
The rule includes the approximate mileage of all the identified trails. The rule requires the superintendent to notify the public of designated trails through one or more of the methods identified in
36 CFR 1.7
, including publication in the Superintendent's Compendium (or written compilation) of discretionary actions and on maps available at the visitor center and on the park website. NPS regulations at
36 CFR 4.30(i)
authorize superintendents to allow electric bicycles on park roads, parking areas, and administrative roads and trails that are otherwise open to traditional bicycles. Accordingly, the superintendent may decide to allow electric bicycles on any of the trails identified in the rule that are open to traditional bicycles and will notify the public pursuant to
36 CFR 1.7
.
NPS general regulations in
36 CFR 2.16(c)
prohibit the use of horses or pack animals on a park road, except where such travel is necessary to cross to or from designated trails, areas, or privately owned property when no alternative trails or routes have been designated, and when the road is closed to motor vehicles. Neither of these exceptions to the general rule apply to riding horses on the Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road, which is called for in the selected alternative. Special regulations for the park, however, can amend, modify, relax, or make more stringent general regulations in
36 CFR parts 1
through
5
and
part 12
. See
36 CFR 1.2(c)
. Accordingly, this rule adds a new paragraph (d) to the special regulations for the park that allows equestrian use on the approximately 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road.
Compliance With NPS Bicycle Regulations
The EA constitutes the planning document and evaluates the criteria required by the NPS's general bicycle regulations at
36 CFR 4.30
. Under the selected action in the FONSI, the NPS will allow bicycle use on approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails in the park. The EA evaluates the suitability of each trail surface and soil conditions for accommodating bicycle use, and life cycle maintenance costs, safety considerations, methods to prevent or minimize user conflict, and methods to protect natural and cultural resources and mitigate impacts associated with bicycle use.
The final trail alignments shown on the maps in the EA are based on field surveys and geographic information system (GIS) analysis. The new trail alignments have been determined at the corridor level, defined as a 60-foot-wide corridor within which the new trail would be constructed. Final trail alignments will be determined on the ground upon implementation and in consultation with park natural and cultural resources specialists, which could result in minor adjustments to the trail locations shown on the maps. If a need existed to align a trail outside of the identified corridor, the amended alignment would undergo additional review to avoid or minimize impacts on sensitive resources, and the change would be documented as an amendment to the trails management plan.
The superintendent of the park signed a written determination that bicycle use on all of the trails identified in this rule and certain administrative roads that will be open to bicycle use under the selected action in the FONSI, is consistent with the protection of the park's natural, scenic, and aesthetic values; safety considerations; management objectives; and will not disturb wildlife or park resources, as required by
36 CFR 4.30
. The NPS made the written determination available on the park's planning website and accepted comments on the written determination during the public comment period for the proposed rule. The Regional Director approved the written determination on August 26, 2026. The written determination is available at the URL listed in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Summary of Public Comments
The NPS published a proposed rule in the
Federal Register
on February 9, 2026 (
91 FR 5700
). The NPS accepted public comments for 60 days via the mail, hand delivery, and the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Comments were accepted through April 10, 2026. The NPS received approximately 150 comments on the proposed rule. Overall, commenters broadly supported expanding recreation opportunities but stressed that effective communication, monitoring, and adaptive management will be essential to protect park resources and ensure safe, enjoyable multi-use trail experiences. Several commenters addressed potential environmental impacts of expanding bicycle use on the trail system, including impacts on soils and erosion, the aquatic ecosystem, plant communities, and park wildlife. These comments are not addressed in this final rule because they raise environmental issues that the NPS considered in the EA and FONSI. The NPS evaluated the environmental impacts of the no-action and preferred alternatives in the EA and explained the reasons for selecting the preferred alternative in the FONSI. The NPS did not identify any new significant environmental issues in the public comments on the proposed rule. After considering public comments and additional review of the proposed rule, the NPS is finalizing the proposed rule without change. A summary of the pertinent issues raised by commenters and NPS responses are provided below:
1. Comment:
Some commenters stated that allowing horses on a shared-use road creates safety risks because horses may react unpredictably to bicycles or vehicles.
NPS Response:
Houchin Ferry Road North experiences very low levels of use which should mitigate the potential for conflicts among vehicles, horseback riders, hikers, and bicyclists. As described in Appendix A of the EA, the NPS employs a monitoring program to track conditions related to visitor experiences, including reports of user conflicts. Monitoring helps assess progress toward desired conditions within the park, such as ensuring that:
visitors can confidently choose appropriate recreational opportunities,
conflicts among user groups are minimized, and
signage and trail markings provide accurate, reliable information.
If monitoring indicates that conditions are trending away from these desired outcomes, the NPS would manage visitor concerns by implementing management strategies listed in Appendix A of the EA, such as providing appropriate trip-planning information to visitors based on
(
printed page 74479)
motivation and separating use types further.
2. Comment:
One commenter expressed concern that transporting horses requires large pickup trucks and trailers (often 25 to 55 feet long) which would necessitate more paved parking and turnaround areas. The commenter stated that during busy periods insufficient parking could lead to parking along road shoulders, which would contribute to soil erosion and create additional traffic hazards.
NPS Response:
As part of the selected alternative in the EA, both the McCoy Hollow and Wildcat Hollow parking areas will be improved to support horse-trailer use. These improvements are designed to enhance maneuverability and safe trailer parking without expanding the footprint beyond what is consistent with desired conditions and resource-protection goals. In addition to physical improvements, the NPS may implement several management strategies if monitoring indicates that parking demand is approaching or exceeding established thresholds. One such strategy is to enforce parking lot capacity limits and prevent overflow parking, including shoulder parking, to avoid soil erosion and maintain roadway safety.
3. Comment:
Some commenters questioned who would be responsible for cleaning up manure from equestrian use on the road.
NPS Response:
The NPS does not have sufficient staff and equipment to collect excrement on trails and roads where horseback riding is allowed. The Superintendent's Compendium for the park states that—at trailheads—manure spilled from the trailering unit and any fresh excrement must be placed in the trailering unit. This requirement will be applied to equestrian use on the Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road to help prevent the introduction of exotic plant seeds into the park and to promote visitor enjoyment of park resources.
4. Comment:
Some commenters opposed constructing new multi-use trails, citing potential impacts on the natural environment and recommending that the NPS focus on maintaining existing trails instead. Others supported creating more pedestrian-only trails due to safety concerns associated with shared-use routes. Several commenters encouraged the NPS to construct purpose-built mountain bike trails rather than additional multi-use trails, while others suggested that equestrian and bicycle use is incompatible and should occur on separate trails.
NPS Response:
The NPS appreciates the range of views on shared use of trail networks within the park. The purpose of the EA was to improve the sustainability of the above-ground trail system, protect natural and cultural resources, and enhance the diversity and quality of visitor experiences. The selected alternative addresses longstanding issues such as inconsistent trail design standards, erosion, trail widening, and visitor-use conflicts and will serve as the guiding framework for trail development, maintenance, and visitor-use management over the long term. Under the selected alternative, the overall mileage of designated trails available for public use in the park would increase substantially. Many existing trails at the park follow old roadbeds or utility corridors that were never designed for recreational use. As a result, they often experience recurring erosion, poor drainage, widening, braiding, and safety issues that cannot be effectively corrected through routine maintenance alone.
A combination of new trails, improvements to degraded existing routes, decommissioning of unsustainable trails, and rehabilitation of visitor-created paths, will allow for greater resource stewardship as the trail system becomes more sustainable overall.
The NPS did not analyze an alternative that would include construction of purpose-built mountain bike trails. The preferred alternative focused on improving and managing a shared-use trail system consistent with the EA's purpose and need. A key element of the selected alternative is the development of shared-use trails designed to safely accommodate multiple user groups—hikers, bicyclists, and in some areas, equestrians. Because these trails must safely serve different types of users, they will be constructed using shared-use design principles rather than incorporating many of the specialized features typical of purpose-built mountain bike trails, such as tight berms, rollers, jumps, or flow-specific technical elements that are not safe or sustainable for hikers or equestrians.
The selected alternative will provide multiple recreational opportunities while applying trail-by-trail decisions to separate uses where safety concerns, resource sensitivities, or known user conflicts warrant it. For example, the selected alternative includes decommissioning the Maple Springs Connector due to documented conflicts between bicycle and equestrian use. Some trails will remain pedestrian-only where terrain or resource conditions make multi-use unsustainable, and equestrian use will remain north of the Green River to protect the park's highly sensitive cave and karst resources concentrated beneath the landscape to the south.
5.
Comment:
Several commenters supported allowing e-bikes on trails open to traditional bicycles, while others raised concerns about potential visitor-safety issues and resource impacts from e-bike use. One commenter stated that e-bikes belong on roads rather than trails. One organization noted that prohibiting e-bikes could hinder economic opportunity and exclude an entire user group.
NPS Response:
Under existing regulations, the Superintendent has discretion to allow e-bikes in locations where traditional bicycles are allowed, including on roads or trails.
36 CFR 4.30(i)
. Among other policy requirements for visitor activities, the Superintedent may allow e-bikes only when doing so will not impede attainment of desired conditions for resource protection or create an unsafe environment for visitors. NPS Management Policies 2006, Section 8.1.1. Since 2021, e-bikes have been allowed on park roads and on trails where traditional bicycles are allowed. The use of e-bikes is subject to the same requirements that apply to the use of traditional bicycles, including requirements to obey traffic control devices, travel no faster than 15 mph, yield the right of way to horses and pedestrians, and avoid travel abreast of another bicycle. After trail construction, the Superintendent will have discretion to allow e-bikes on the new trails, subject to the same policy considerations that apply to all visitor activities. Successful management of visitor use relies on monitoring and informed decision-making. The NPS will use information it gains to manage the use of e-bikes and all other visitor activities to avoid unacceptable impacts to resources and visitors. The NPS will adjust indicators and thresholds for adaptive management as needed, with opportunities for stakeholder engagement when appropriate.
6. Comment:
One commenter observed that, although the rule would increase the total mileage of trails eligible for bicycle use, the Superintendent must designate such trails for bicycle use before they can be used. The commenter recommended that bicycles be allowed on at least 19 miles of trails without the need for designation by the Superintendent and not subject to any closures and restrictions.
NPS Response:
Establishing a fixed minimum mileage would limit the Superintendent's ability to manage trail access based on current conditions and
(
printed page 74480)
informed decision-making for visitor and resource protection. Consistent with the selected alternative, the NPS intends to allow bicycles on the 37-mile trail network identified for bicycle use, subject to closures and restrictions that may become necessary to protect public health and safety, natural and cultural resources, and to meet other management activities and considerations. Some trails have not been constructed and therefore will need to be designated later in time. Allowing the Superintendent to adaptively manage bicycle use is necessary to implement the selected alternative, which requires monitoring and establishes indicators and thresholds for managing visitor use to avoid unacceptable impacts.
7. Comment:
Some commenters emphasized the importance of clear, consistent signage and visitor education to reduce safety conflicts on multi-use trails, including right-of-way information for hikers, cyclists, and equestrians, and guidance for safely navigating trailheads and horse-trailer areas. Many supported additional measures such as speed limits for bicycles, trail-etiquette education, and clear communication of rules, seasonal closures, and user responsibilities.
NPS Response:
As stated above, bicycles and e-bikes are subject to 15 mph speed limits on all roads and trails, and the NPS intends to upgrade parking areas to support horse trailers at trailheads and at the start of the Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road. The selected alternative includes improvements to ensure clear, consistent trail information and to enhance safety for all users. Trail names will be formally designated and used consistently on signs, maps, and other visitor materials to improve wayfinding and create a stronger sense of place. Trailheads will feature standardized signs that clearly describe trail type, allowed uses (hiking, biking, equestrian), difficulty, distance, estimated time, accessibility information, and maps, with additional wayfinding available through on-trail markers or QR codes linking to digital resources. To reduce safety conflicts on shared-use trails, the park will expand education about proper trail etiquette—such as cyclists yielding to pedestrians and pedestrians yielding to horses—and reinforce Leave No Trace principles.
Compliance With Other Laws, Executive Orders and Department Policy
Regulatory Planning and Review (E.O.s 12866 and 14192)
This rule has been determined to be not significant for purposes of
E.O. 12866
. This rule is a “one-time” enabling regulation that will authorize the Superintendent to expand consumption options for the American public by increasing opportunities for access and recreation at the park. As a result, this rule qualifies as an
E.O. 14192
deregulatory action pursuant to M-25-20, “Guidance Implementing Section 3 of
Executive Order 14192
, Titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation'” issued by the Office of Management and Budget, Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, on March 26, 2025.
Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
This rule will not have a significant economic effect on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
). No small entities will be directly regulated by this rule, which will allow bicycle use on approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails throughout the park and allow visitors to ride horses on the 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road. This action will not impose restrictions on local businesses in the form of fees, training, record keeping, or other measures that will increase costs. Rather, this action could lead to a slight increase in park visitation and thereby generate benefits for businesses, including small entities, through increased visitor spending. Therefore, the NPS certifies that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small business entities.
Congressional Review Act
This rule is not a major rule under
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. This rule:
(a) Will not have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more.
(b) Will not cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, Federal, State, or local government agencies, or geographic regions.
(c) Will not have significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S.-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
This rule will not impose an unfunded mandate on State, local, or Tribal governments or the private sector of more than $100 million per year. This rule will not have a significant or unique effect on State, local or Tribal governments, or the private sector. It addresses public use of national park lands and imposes no requirements on other agencies or governments. A statement containing the information required by the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (
2 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
) is not required.
Takings (
E.O. 12630
)
This rule will not effect a taking of private property or otherwise have takings implications under
E.O. 12630
. A takings implication assessment is not required.
Federalism (
E.O. 13132
)
Under the criteria in section 1 of
E.O. 13132
, this rule will not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement. This rule will only affect use of federally administered lands and waters. It will have no direct effects on other areas. A federalism summary impact statement is not required.
Civil Justice Reform (
E.O. 12988
)
This rule complies with the requirements of
E.O. 12988
. This rule:
(a) Meets the criteria of section 3(a) requiring that all regulations be reviewed to eliminate errors and ambiguity and be written to minimize litigation; and
(b) Meets the criteria of section 3(b)(2) requiring that all regulations be written in clear language and contain clear legal standards.
Consultation With Indian Tribes (
E.O. 13175
and Department Policy)
The Department of the Interior strives to strengthen its government-to-government relationship with Indian Tribes through a commitment to consultation with Indian Tribes and recognition of their right to self-governance and sovereignty. The NPS has evaluated this rule under the criteria in
E.O. 13175
and under the Department's Tribal consultation policy. As a result, the NPS determined that Tribal consultation is not required because this rule will have no substantial direct effect on federally recognized Indian Tribes.
Nevertheless, in support of the Department of the Interior's and the NPS's commitment to government-to-government consultation, the NPS initiated Tribal consultation for the EA on April 30, 2024, by sending letters to the following Native American Tribes affiliated with lands and waters within
(
printed page 74481)
the park and inviting consultation: Absentee Shawnee Tribe (Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma); The Chickasaw Nation; Cherokee Nation; Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians; Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma; The Osage Nation; Shawnee Tribe; and United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians in Oklahoma.
Additionally, the NPS developed a phased programmatic agreement to guide the treatment of cultural resources in the different project areas identified in the EA. The NPS invited each of these Tribes to sign on to the phased programmatic agreement. None chose to do so. The Cherokee Nation responded that they would consult with the NPS when there are defined undertakings for any project involving ground disturbance. No other Tribal responses were received.
Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
)
This rule contains no new information collections. All information collections require approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA;
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). The NPS may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA;
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
)
The NPS prepared the EA to determine whether this rule would have a significant impact on the quality of the human environment under NEPA. This rule does not constitute a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment. A detailed statement under NEPA is not required because the EA resulted in FONSI. A copy of the EA and FONSI are available online at the like provided in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Effects on the Energy Supply (
E.O. 13211
)
This rule is not a significant energy action under the definition in
E.O. 13211
. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) determined this rule is not significant under
E.O. 12866
. Consequently, this rule does not meet the first criteria of a significant energy action. Also, the OIRA Administrator has not otherwise designated this rule as a significant energy action. A statement of energy effects in not required.

In consideration of the foregoing, the National Park Service amends

Federal Communications Commission.
ACTION:
Notice; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
As part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork burdens, and as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) invites the general public and other Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on the following information collection. Comments are requested concerning: whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Commission, including whether the information shall have practical utility; the accuracy of the Commission's burden estimate; ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information collected; ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on the respondents, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and ways to further reduce the information collection burden on small business concerns with fewer than 25 employees.
(
printed page 74555)

Written PRA comments should be submitted on or before January 19, 2027. If you anticipate that you will be submitting comments but find it difficult to do so within the period of time allowed by this notice, you should advise the contact listed below as soon as possible.

PRA@fcc.gov
and to
Cathy.Williams@fcc.gov
.

For additional information or copies of the information collection, contact Cathy Williams at (202) 418-2918.
