In the 2006 Adopting Release, the Commission noted that the elements of the two-part analysis were among the factors to be considered in determining whether an item required disclosure as a perquisite. These factors, including the guidance that the first element should be construed narrowly, together with the inclusion of a non-exhaustive list of example items that the Commission had determined constituted perquisites under the two-part analysis, appear to have constrained the analysis by registrants in certain cases, potentially leading to disclosure of items that could reasonably be concluded are not perquisites, and which the board does not consider as part of the executive's compensation.
We propose to revise our guidance as follows:
An item is not a perquisite or personal benefit if it is integrally and directly related to the performance of the executive's duties, as determined by the registrant, so long as such determination is reasonable and made in good faith.
An item is a perquisite or personal benefit if it is determined by the registrant, reasonably and in good faith, that it is not integrally and directly related to the performance of the executive's duties,
and
it confers a direct or indirect personal benefit to the executive, unless it is generally available on a non-discriminatory basis to all employees.
Consistent with the Commission's views in 2006, we continue to believe that the rule should not define perquisites or personal benefits, given that different forms of these items have continued to develop and evolve and that such a definition may become outdated. Consistent with this view, we also believe that registrants, not the Commission, are in the best position to determine what is properly categorized as a perquisite or personal benefit, so long as such determinations are reasonable and made in good faith. Accordingly, we believe it is appropriate to update the prior guidance to state that, in applying the two-part analysis, registrants have flexibility to determine, based on their specific facts and circumstances, whether an item is integrally and directly related to the performance of an executive's duties.
The proposed revisions to the Commission's interpretive guidance are intended to underscore that registrants can utilize the two-part analysis without the outcome being predetermined. For example, in applying the first prong of the analysis, as proposed to be revised, if a registrant acting in good faith reasonably concludes that providing personal security services at all times to a PEO or PFO, or requiring the PEO or PFO to use a company aircraft for personal travel due to security concerns, is integrally and directly related to the performance of the executive's duties, then such security services would not be a perquisite. As under the current guidance, the elements of the second prong of the analysis (
e.g.,
whether there is also a personal benefit or whether the item is generally available to all other employees on a non-discriminatory basis) are irrelevant to the first prong of the analysis. Likewise, if a registrant reasonably determines in good faith that an item is integrally and directly related to the performance of an executive's duties under the first prong of the two-part analysis, then there is no need to proceed to the second prong of the analysis.
As to the second element of the analysis, registrants that determine an item is not integrally and directly related to the performance of an executive's duties should continue to evaluate whether the item confers a direct or indirect benefit that has a personal aspect. If there is no such personal benefit, the item is not a perquisite. If there is such benefit, the registrant should consider whether it is generally available on a nondiscriminatory basis to all employees.
[
201
]
A company may reasonably conclude that an item is generally available to all employees on a non-discriminatory basis if it is
(
printed page 75032)
available to those employees to whom it lawfully may be provided.
[
202
]
The proposed guidance would also eliminate the portion of the current guidance that indicates that whether a benefit is provided for business reasons or the convenience of the company should not be considered in applying this second prong of the analysis. Furthermore, we recognize that, pursuant to the more flexible approach reflected in the proposed guidance, consideration of the benefit to the company and the business purpose is more relevant for the first prong of the analysis and we find that it can be one of the factors that registrants consider in determining whether an item is integrally and directly related to the performance of the executive's duties, and thus not a perquisite or a personal benefit. The elimination of this portion of the guidance in the second prong of the analysis is also consistent with our view that registrants should have flexibility in making this determination under the first prong of the analysis.
Finally, consistent with a more flexible approach to applying the two-part analysis, we are proposing to rescind the Commission's prior statement of examples of items requiring disclosure as perquisites or personal benefits, including security provided at an executive's personal residence or during personal travel. We believe that a registrant is in the best position to determine what benefits are integrally and directly related to an executive's duties, and providing examples of items that would definitively be considered perquisites could be in tension with our view that a registrant should have flexibility to make this determination based on its own set of facts and circumstances.
We believe the primary concern of commenters with the current guidance regarding perquisites is the perceived lack of flexibility in applying the guidance due to prior Commission statements, as opposed to the substantive nature of the guidance itself. We believe the proposed guidance addresses this concern.

de minimis
tracking exclusion for perquisites. Specifically, we are proposing to:
Increase the minimum aggregate reporting threshold for perquisites (below which such perquisites would not be required to be included in the Miscellaneous Compensation Received column of the Earned Compensation Table) to $150,000; and
Add a
de minimis
tracking exclusion for perquisites (below which individual perquisites would be excluded when calculating whether the minimum aggregate reporting threshold had been met and thus would not need to be tracked by the registrant) that would exclude any individual perquisite that is considered a
de minimis
fringe benefit under section
(
printed page 75033)
132(a)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code, or any successor provision.
[
206
]
We continue to believe that disclosure regarding perquisites is important for investors to understand the overall compensation package made available to the PEO and PFO; however, we believe that the current aggregate reporting threshold is unnecessarily low. In addition, because the current rule does not have a
de minimis
tracking exclusion, registrants must compile and track any perquisite, regardless of how small the amount, for purposes of this disclosure item. The proposed amendments are intended to reduce compliance burdens for registrants while retaining disclosure of material perquisites for investors. The proposed increase in the minimum aggregate reporting threshold is intended to modernize the threshold given the passage of time since the 2006 Amendments (including to reflect the impact of inflation), as well as developments in executive compensation over the past decades (as benefits that are only modestly above a $10,000 threshold may often be immaterial in light of modern executive compensation levels).
The addition of a
de minimis
tracking exclusion should further reduce burdens on registrants by eliminating the need for registrants to track small, individual benefits over the course of the year, which investors are unlikely to consider material to an NEO's overall compensation. By using a
de minimis
threshold already applied by registrants for U.S. tax purposes, the proposal also aims to simplify the analysis for registrants.

207
]
We are also proposing to eliminate the requirement that perquisites must be valued on the basis of the aggregate incremental cost to the registrant.
[
208

The 2006 Adopting Release indicated that the amounts attributed to perquisites for Federal income tax purposes should not be used for purposes of our executive compensation disclosure unless, independently of the tax characterization, such amounts constitute the incremental cost to the registrant.

However, we understand from engagement with market participants that there is no uniform way to value certain perquisites, and as a result of the Commission's prior statements, registrants may need to attribute different values to the same perquisite for Federal income tax and Federal securities law purposes, which can be burdensome without a commensurate benefit in the disclosure.
[

]
We are therefore proposing to eliminate the requirement that perquisites must be valued on the basis of the aggregate incremental cost to the registrant so as to provide registrants with greater flexibility in how perquisites are valued, and to reduce burdens on registrants by not requiring them to revalue perquisites already valued for Federal income tax purposes solely for purposes of their executive compensation disclosures under Item 402.

G. Pay-Versus-Performance Disclosure Requirements—Proposed Item 402(f)
We are proposing to amend the pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements in Item 402(v) to simplify and streamline the presentation of executive pay in relation to registrant performance and to reduce compliance burdens while remaining faithful to the statutory mandate. Specifically, the proposed amendments would, among other things, revise the measure of executive compensation for purposes of the pay-versus-performance disclosure and conform the content to track more closely other proposed executive compensation disclosures.

241

Section 953(a) of the Dodd-Frank Act requires the Commission to adopt a rule that directs issuers to disclose the relationship between “executive compensation actually paid” and “the financial performance of the issuer, taking into account any change in the value of the shares of stock and dividends of the issuer and any distributions.”

The rule includes detailed and extensive instructions about the required calculation of Compensation Actually Paid. The current rule also requires registrants to calculate and disclose cumulative TSR for a peer group and describe the relationship between the peer group TSR and the registrant's TSR. (

actually

Adding the fair value (as of the end of the applicable fiscal year) of all awards granted in that year that are outstanding and unvested at the end of that year;
Adding the change in fair value (from the end of the prior fiscal year to the end of the covered fiscal year) of each award granted in any prior fiscal year that was outstanding and unvested as of the end of the covered fiscal year;
Adding the fair value (as of the vesting date) of any awards that are both granted and vest in the applicable fiscal year;
Adding the change in fair value (from the end of the prior fiscal year to either the end of the covered fiscal year or the vesting date, as applicable) of awards granted in any prior fiscal year that vest at the end of or during the covered fiscal year;
Subtracting the fair value (as of the end of the prior fiscal year) of awards granted in any prior fiscal year that failed to meet vesting conditions during the covered fiscal year;
Adding the dollar value of dividends or other earnings paid on awards in the covered fiscal year prior to the vesting date that are not otherwise included in the total compensation disclosed in the Summary Compensation Table; and

A number of commenters further suggested that Compensation Actually Paid may not be used by or useful to investors,
[
268

that proxy advisory firms have their own proprietary methodologies for calculating NEOs' pay-versus-performance,
[
269

and that the five-year horizon does not reflect how boards think about compensation.
[
270

Other letters were supportive of the current rule,
[
271

with many of these indicating that the resulting disclosure is promising
[
272

and useful.
[
273

Some supportive commenters and other sources suggest a correlation between pay-versus-performance disclosure and shareholders' decisions in their say-on-pay votes.
[
274

Several commenters advocated alternative, often simpler, calculations of executive compensation “actually paid” that reflect variations of “realized” or “realizable” pay.
[

The current definition of Compensation Actually Paid begins with the total compensation amount calculated for purposes of the Summary Compensation Table. Since we are proposing to replace Compensation

printed page 75041)
Actually Paid with the amount reflected in the Total Compensation Earned column of the proposed Earned Compensation Table, it is important to note where the individual elements of the Earned Compensation Table may differ from those in the Summary Compensation Table. In general, the same non-equity-related compensation items that are required to be included in the Summary Compensation Table would also be required disclosure in the proposed Earned Compensation Table, as more fully discussed above.
[
276
]
We note, however, that the proposed Miscellaneous Compensation Received column of the proposed Earned Compensation Table, which requires disclosure of certain types of additional compensation and any other compensation that the registrant determines is material or chooses to disclose, may result in disclosure of fewer non-material compensation amounts than are currently required to be included in the Summary Compensation Table “all other compensation” column.
[
277
]
Using the Total Compensation Earned amount in the Earned Compensation Table would eliminate the need to calculate interim valuations for equity awards and instead include stock award values when vested and option award values when exercised. The current Compensation Actually Paid calculation combines changes in unvested equity values,
i.e.,
amounts that may never be paid, and the value of equity upon vesting. The current requirement to revalue unvested equity awards for each year covered by the disclosure provides information about potential pay to which the executive is not yet entitled, rather than amounts to which the executive is immediately entitled.
[
278
]
The Total Compensation Earned amount in the proposed Earned Compensation Table, in contrast, would show equity compensation values only when they have been realized (
i.e.,
for stock awards once they have vested and for option awards once they have been exercised). We believe that this simpler presentation represents an accurate picture of executive pay outcomes, and, as such, addresses the requirement stated in section 953(a) of the Dodd-Frank Act that the disclosure reflect compensation
actually paid.
In addition, Compensation Actually Paid calculations under the current rule can yield negative amounts notwithstanding that the executive does not actually owe money to the employer. For these reasons, in comparison to the current approach, we believe the amount reported in the Total Compensation Earned column of the proposed Earned Compensation Table would better reflect compensation actually paid to and received by NEOs.
[
279
]
In addition, we believe that the Total Compensation Earned amount as determined for purposes of the proposed Earned Compensation Table, when presented in relation to registrant performance, would facilitate an evaluation of executive compensation generally and may provide further insights into the effectiveness of compensation committees and compensation packages.
[
280
]
Specifically, presenting realized compensation values relative to registrant performance may help to reveal whether
ultimate
pay outcomes align with company results.
We are aware that using vesting or exercise date values in the calculation of compensation actually paid may in some instances result in timing misalignment between actual performance and related executive compensation actually paid. Some commenters have expressed the view that, for example, when performance metrics span several years from the grant date to the vesting date, presenting equity values only in the relevant vesting or exercise year would result in spikes in compensation numbers during those years and no potential values during the remainder of the performance period.
[
281
]
Indeed, the Commission was persuaded in part by these views when adopting the current Compensation Actually Paid equity valuation method, stating that “the adopted approach will more effectively allow registrants to describe the relationship between compensation and registrant performance, as the reported amounts of compensation will annually adjust based on the registrant's performance, among other things, in that year.”
[
282
]
However, we note that section 953(a) of the Dodd-Frank Act contemplates disclosure showing “the relationship between executive compensation actually paid and the financial performance of the issuer,” but does not require that the disclosure demonstrate whether there is year over year alignment between the value of unvested pay and executive performance. Further, we believe that questions raised by our proposed approach related to vesting spikes or other perceived mismatches between the timing of pay and performance could be mitigated by the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table, which would provide useful information about stock awards that are not yet vested and option awards that are not yet exercised,
(
printed page 75042)
as well as any additional contextual disclosure a registrant might choose to provide.
We also recognize that
any
practicable approach could result in misalignment based upon the specific facts and circumstances. For example, under the current method for estimating compensation actually paid, the payouts on non-equity incentive awards are recorded only in the year they are paid out, even if they reflect performance over multiple years. In contrast, the payouts on equity incentives are effectively marked-to-market over time as performance is realized. The compensation actually paid values may thereby imply that a registrant relying more heavily on non-equity incentive awards has pay that is less sensitive to performance than a registrant that relies more heavily on equity incentives, even if this is not the case. Given that both the current and proposed approaches result in a degree of misalignment, we believe that the reduced burden on registrants by avoiding the complexity involved in calculating the current version of Compensation Actually Paid would justify a change in approach.
The proposed amendments are intended to simplify and reduce the burden
[
283
]
of producing pay-versus-performance disclosure. By using the information in the Earned Compensation Table, the proposed approach would eliminate the need for a separate set of calculations and provide a clearer integration of the pay-versus-performance disclosure with the remaining executive compensation disclosure under proposed Item 402.
[
284
]
We believe that using the Total Compensation Earned amount set forth in the proposed Earned Compensation Table would continue to meet the Dodd-Frank Act mandate to show the relationship between compensation actually paid and the registrant's financial performance, while providing a clearer picture of the PEO's realized pay.
2. Performance Measures
We are also proposing to simplify the pay-versus-performance presentation by removing required disclosure of several performance measures that can be burdensome to provide, are not mandated by the Dodd-Frank Act, significantly increase the length of the disclosure, and, in some cases, may have little relationship to executive pay. Our proposed amendments would retain a single financial performance measure, registrant cumulative TSR, which we believe would provide shareholders with an easily understandable financial performance measure that ultimately represents the core of shareholder value. Currently, registrants are required to quantify in a table and separately describe the relationship between executive compensation and three financial performance measures: GAAP net income, the cumulative TSR of the registrant, and the Company-Selected Measure. Registrants must also select a peer group and disclose the relationship between the registrant's TSR and the peer group's TSR. Finally, registrants must disclose a Tabular List of three to seven financial performance measures that, in the registrant's assessment, represent the most important financial performance measures used by the registrant to link compensation actually paid to its NEOs to company performance.
[
285
]
Our proposed amendments are intended to shorten and simplify such requirements. Specifically, we propose to retain the registrant's cumulative TSR as the sole required performance measure, with the goal of emphasizing a metric that reflects the registrant's financial performance and frequently impacts executive compensation and investor value. To this end, we propose to remove tabular and relationship disclosure of GAAP net income and peer group total shareholder return, metrics that not only are already available
[
286
]
but also may have a less clear connection to executive pay at many registrants, and to make disclosure of a Company-Selected Measure optional. In addition, we propose to eliminate required disclosure of the Tabular List.
The calculation and presentation of the registrant's cumulative TSR information in our proposed amendments would be the same as the current requirement.
[
287
]
Section 953(a) of the Dodd-Frank Act specifically requires that pay-versus-performance disclosure take into account changes in the value of the shares of stock and dividends of the issuer and any distributions, which TSR does.
[
288
]
In addition, we agree with commenter feedback in the 2022 Pay-versus-Performance Adopting Release that the benefits of using registrant cumulative TSR as a performance measure include that it is well-understood by investors; is widely used by companies in setting compensation; is generally a fair representation of company performance; assists companies in articulating and providing justification for their compensation practices; promotes comparability; and reflects stock price fluctuations that regularly occur in response to publicly known information and company leadership.
[
289
]
As a result, we believe that retaining registrant cumulative TSR as the required financial performance measure both satisfies the statutory requirement and provides investors with the most useful information for evaluating pay-versus-performance while reducing the burdens of preparing the comparative disclosure.
When requiring the disclosure of additional financial performance measures in 2022, the Commission did not indicate a belief that additional measures were necessary to satisfy the Congressional mandate of section 953(a) of the Dodd-Frank Act. The Commission did indicate in the Reopening Release, however, that additional measures “may
(
printed page 75043)
help address concerns that using only TSR may mislead investors or provide an incomplete picture of performance” and “each of the additional disclosures . . . may broaden the picture of financial performance presented in the disclosure . . . [and] could enhance the usefulness of the disclosure by certain registrants or for certain investors.”
[
290
]
We are now proposing to eliminate the additional financial performance measures based on commenter feedback
[
291
]
that TSR provides a well understood measure of shareholder value, and, in practice, the inclusion of the additional measures has not served to substantially enhance the usefulness of the disclosure.
Our goal in eliminating the other required performance measures is to simplify disclosure by removing requirements that may not be necessary to understand the link between executive pay and the registrant's performance. Based on the staff's experience reviewing pay-versus-performance disclosure, we believe that registrants frequently struggle to explain the link between some of these other performance measures and executive pay, which can result in lengthy disclosure explaining why a direct link does or does not exist. Many comments echo this concern, indicating the additional disclosures provide little insight into the pay/performance link.
[
292
]
In the case of net income, for example, it appears that disclosure may often deviate from the rule's requirement by substituting a measure other than GAAP net income (such as adjusted net income or revenue)
[
293
]
or stating that there is no relationship between net income and executive pay. These deviations seem to reflect the viewpoint expressed in many comment letters
[
294
]
received in connection with both the original rule's adoption and the 2025 Roundtable, that “few registrants use GAAP net income as a financial performance measure in their incentive programs.”
[
295
]
Commenters also noted that GAAP net income information can already be found elsewhere.
[
296
]
When adopting Item 402(v), the Commission gave several reasons for including net income as a required financial performance measure, including that it is closely related to other profitability measures that may be used by registrants in setting compensation, is widely understood and standardized, and could complement the market-based performance measure of cumulative TSR.
[
297
]
Based upon staff experience, required pay-versus-performance net income disclosure (including numerical financial statement data and relationship disclosure) is frequently boilerplate and provides little meaningful insight about its relationship, if any, to executive pay. Although net income is widely understood and standardized, its inclusion as a financial performance measure does not appear to have enhanced either investors' understanding of other profitability measures or to have provided a complement to market-based TSR.
Similar to net income, it appears based on the staff's observation that, in many cases, presentation of a Company-Selected Measure may provide little insight into the registrant's executive compensation program because the direct link between the two is unclear.
[
298
]
The Company-Selected Measure is a financial performance measure which the registrant believes represents the most important financial performance measure used by it to link executive compensation to company performance.
[
299
]
In many cases, registrants' compensation programs include complex combinations of multiple financial inputs, over multiple timeframes, without individual weightings or rankings. The staff has observed that registrants often struggle to find a single “most important” financial measure and that disclosure is often rendered less meaningful by attempts to do so. On the other hand, where a registrant
is
able to identify a single most important measure, that disclosure can enhance investors' understanding of the link between executive pay and company's financial performance. As such, we are proposing that registrants would have the option, but not the obligation, to disclose a company-selected measure.
We are also proposing to eliminate the requirement to disclose the Tabular List of three to seven financial performance measures that are used to link compensation with the financial performance of the registrant. The staff has observed that, out of context, the names of these measures alone provide very little information about the relationship between executive pay and registrant performance. In addition, this information is often redundant with disclosures of performance conditions applicable to incentive awards, which appear elsewhere in the executive compensation disclosure.
As with net income and the Company-Selected Measure, we believe that the requirement to disclose the cumulative TSR of a peer group may not measurably and consistently enhance a shareholder's understanding of the link between pay and performance. Currently, registrants are required to provide cumulative TSR for a peer group, either the one used for purposes of Item 201(e) of Regulation S-K,
[
300
]
or the companies it uses as a peer group for purposes of its disclosures under Item 402(b).
[
301
]
While the inclusion of peer group cumulative TSR and relative pay-versus-performance information is not mandated by section 953 of the Dodd-
(
printed page 75044)
Frank Act, in the 2022 Pay-versus-Performance Adopting Release, the Commission noted that registrant TSR alone may not be a sufficient basis for comparison between companies, and that inclusion of peer group TSR could facilitate an assessment of whether the registrant's performance was driven by factors common to its peers or instead by the registrant's own strategy and other choice.
[
302
]
While side-by-side comparisons of peer and registrant TSR may provide such information, it is not clear that the disclosure has supplied peer-to-peer pay for performance comparability, since such a comparison would necessarily involve presenting peer companies'
pay
information as well.
[
303
]
A requirement to present such relative pay-versus-performance disclosures would increase not only registrant burdens, but also the volume of information in the proxy, running counter to our goal of streamlining and simplifying disclosure.
In addition, to the extent investors seek to analyze peer stock performance or relative pay and performance data, public company, industry and line of business stock performance, as well as peer executive compensation, data are readily available in public filings and other sources. As a result, we believe that removing the peer group cumulative TSR disclosure requirement would simplify the pay-versus-performance disclosure without substantially affecting investors' ability to evaluate a registrant's executive compensation.
3. Executives Covered
We are proposing to simplify the pay-versus-performance disclosure by limiting its coverage to the PEO and the PFO to conform to the coverage of the remaining proposed Item 402 executive compensation disclosure requirements. Currently, pay-versus-performance compensation-related disclosure is required to be provided for the PEO and, as a group, the other NEOs. Calculating the average total compensation for the non-PEO NEOs collectively in accordance with the methodology applicable under the pay-versus-performance rule, as currently required, can be especially time-consuming for registrants and obscure specific details about individual NEOs and their compensation.
[
304
]
In addition, based on staff experience, disclosures related to the additional non-PEO NEOs typically double the length of required pay-versus-performance disclosure.
In response to the 2025 Roundtable, many commenters suggested eliminating non-PEO NEOs from required pay-versus-performance disclosure or limiting the disclosure to information about the PEO only or the PEO and PFO.
[
305
]
These commenters reasoned that averaging other NEO compensation can cause distortions due to year-over-year changes in the identities and pay packages of named NEOs,
[
306
]
termination events resulting in spikes (such as accelerated vesting), and other one-time events, like signing bonuses.
[
307
]
These same factors can reduce the utility of such disclosure by obscuring the link between registrant performance and individual NEO pay and minimize insights into NEO pay practices overall.
We recognize that the addition of the average other NEO compensation adds additional burdens to preparing the pay-versus-performance disclosure and we acknowledge commenters' concerns about the burden and potential distortions that may complicate this disclosure. These burdens should be eliminated by our proposal to require compensation disclosure for only the PEO and PFO, without complex averaging. In addition, limiting the required disclosure to the PEO and PFO should help focus the disclosure on the information that is most likely to be material to investors. As discussed in section II.B, we are proposing to limit the NEOs for which Item 402 disclosure is required to only the PEO and PFO. This proposed change alone would reduce the burdens of the pay-versus-performance disclosure, and address many of the commenter concerns with the average other NEO compensation disclosure, because the average other NEO compensation disclosure would simply reflect the compensation of the PFO.
We recognize that the PEO's pay package may receive more scrutiny from investors than the pay packages for the other NEOs, including the PFO.
[
308
]
We note, however, the Commission's stated belief in the 2022 Pay-versus-Performance Adopting Release that “Congress intended for the rules to provide disclosure about both PEOs and the remaining NEOs because Section 14(i) specifically refers to `compensation required to be disclosed by the issuer under [Item 402 of Regulation S-K],' and Item 402 requires disclosure of NEO compensation.”
[
309
]
Since we are proposing to limit Item 402 disclosure to only the PEO and PFO, we also are proposing to require pay-versus-performance disclosure for only the PEO and PFO. Inclusion of the PFO should minimally impact registrant burden since the proposed Earned Compensation Table would include the required compensation information for both executives.
4. Years Covered
We are proposing to simplify the pay-versus-performance disclosure by conforming the number of years it covers, from five fiscal years to three fiscal years, to match the remaining proposed Item 402 executive compensation disclosure. Currently, registrants are required to provide five years of tabular and narrative pay and performance disclosures under the rule,
(
printed page 75045)
and SRCs are permitted to provide only three years instead. In contrast, most other Item 402 disclosures are currently limited to, at most, three years. Better alignment of the years covered by pay-versus-performance disclosure with the other executive compensation information included in the registrant's filing should help alleviate the need to refer to prior proxy statements or other filings to understand compensation for periods prior to what is presented in the current filing. To the extent that investors seek to assess pay and performance over a five-year period, that information would remain available in the registrant's filings with the Commission from prior years. Further, in light of recent studies suggesting a notable increase in PEO turnover rates, a longer time horizon can create substantial burdens for registrants in presenting and describing pay patterns for multiple PEOs.
[
310
]
When adopting the current five-year requirement, the Commission stated that it would “provide a meaningful period over which a relationship between annual measures of pay and performance over time can be evaluated.”
[
311
]
The Commission also noted, when discussing the five-year time period in the 2015 Pay-versus-Performance Proposing Release that “the stock performance graph required by Item 201(e) of Regulation S-K requires disclosure for the previous five fiscal years, although it does not include any compensation information.”
[
312
]
Section 953(a) of the Dodd-Frank Act does not contain a specific period of coverage for the pay-versus-performance disclosure. In light of our goal to simplify and streamline and reduce the compliance burdens of executive compensation disclosure, we are proposing to align the pay-versus-performance disclosure with the remainder of the executive compensation disclosures, rather than with the stock performance chart, which appears outside of the proxy statement and does not include compensation information.

We propose to make conforming changes to Item 18(a)(2) of Form N-CSR, Item 6.F(1)(ii) of Form 20-F, and General Instruction B.19(b)(2) of Form 40-F, which includes the same disclosure requirements as current paragraph 402(w)(1)(ii) of Item 402.

In response to the 2025 Roundtable, some commenters suggested revisions to Exchange Act Rule 10D-1 (“Rule 10D-1”). Rule 10D-1 directs the national securities exchanges and associations that list securities to establish listing standards requiring listed issuers to develop and implement policies providing for the recovery, in the event of a required accounting restatement, of incentive-based compensation received executive officers where that compensation is based on the erroneously reported financial information.

327

We acknowledge the concerns highlighted by these commenters; however, this proposing release is focused on amendments to the disclosure requirements in Item 402. Amendments to Rule 10D-1, such as how and when a registrant's policy to recover erroneously awarded executive compensation should be applied, are outside the scope of this proposal. We nevertheless believe that the changes we are proposing to eliminate certain disclosure requirements regarding the application of a registrant's recovery policy and remove the check boxes from Forms 10-K, 20-F, and 40-F should meaningfully reduce registrant compliance burdens arising from implementation of Rule 10D-1.

I. Pay Ratio Disclosure Requirements—Proposed Item 402(h)
We are proposing to amend the pay ratio disclosure rule to reduce compliance burdens, enhance comparability across registrants, and streamline the requirements.
[
329
]
Current Item 402(u), adopted in 2015 in response to section 953(b) of the Dodd-Frank Act,
[
330
]
requires registrants to disclose the ratio between the annual total compensation of the principal executive officer and that of a median employee, each determined in accordance with the methodology of the current Summary Compensation Table. Under the current rule, the median employee is identified from among all individuals employed by the registrant or any of its consolidated subsidiaries
[
331
]
whether as a full- or part-time, seasonal, or temporary U.S. or non-U.S. worker, but excluding certain independent contractors or “leased” workers.
[
332
]
In addition, registrants must determine the median employee once every three years, or more frequently under certain circumstances,
[
333
]
and each year disclose the median employee's annual total compensation, the annual total compensation of the PEO, and the ratio of the annual total compensation of the median employee to that of the PEO. The rule also requires certain disclosures about the methodology used to identify the median employee and the calculation used to determine total compensation for employees other than the PEO. The rule also provides lengthy guidance related to the use of adjustments, estimates, and sampling in determining the median employee and the treatment of employees resulting from recent acquisitions.
[
334
]
Due to the rule's inclusion of foreign, part-time, temporary, and seasonal workers, identifying the median employee annual compensation can involve numerous steps, such as identifying the world-wide employee population and converting foreign currencies and calculating the median employee compensation using the Summary Compensation Table methodology.
Our proposed revisions to the pay ratio rule would continue to require disclosure of the ratio of the annual total compensation of the median employee of the registrant with the annual total compensation of the PEO of the registrant. As proposed, however, the rule would limit the employee population from which the median employee is identified to those employed on a full-time basis, excluding seasonal and temporary employees, in any jurisdiction of the U.S. or its territories. In addition, because we are proposing to change the tabular presentation of executive compensation under Item 402, including replacing the Summary Compensation Table, we propose to revise provisions in the pay ratio disclosure rule relating to the methodology for determining annual total compensation of the PEO and median employee. Further, we are proposing to change the frequency with which registrants must determine the median employee from once every three years to once every five years. We are also proposing to streamline the rule text and simplify the guidance and disclosure requirements related to the process for identifying the median employee.
1. Employee Population
We are proposing to limit the scope of the population from which the median employee is identified. Specifically, under the proposed rule, the median employee would be determined based upon the annual total compensation of all employees of the registrant or any of its consolidated subsidiaries who are employed on a full-time basis in any jurisdiction of the United States or its territories, which would exclude temporary or seasonal workers. Under the current rule, a registrant must consider the annual total compensation of all its employees, whether they are employed on a full-time, part-time, seasonal, or temporary basis, as well as those of its consolidated subsidiaries, wherever they are located.
[
335
]
For registrants with international employees, determination of the median employee may entail, among other things, collection of compensation data for workers on different payroll systems, and conversion of compensation data from foreign currencies to U.S. dollars.

For purposes of determining the median employee, we propose eliminating the current lengthy definition of “employee,” which presently includes all global full-time, part-time, seasonal, and temporary workers, with limited exceptions. Our proposed revision would require the registrant to identify the median employee from among all employees of the registrant or any of its consolidated subsidiaries who are employed on a full-time basis in any jurisdiction of the U.S. or its territories, excluding temporary or seasonal workers. In addition, consistent with our principles-based approach to these amendments, “employees” will not expressly carve out independent contractors or “leased” workers. We believe that it is well understood that these categories of workers are not employees. In addition, we do not wish to create a special definition of employee for purposes of Item 402. As the Commission indicated in a 2017 interpretive release related to pay ratio disclosure, “registrants already make determinations as to whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor in other legal and regulatory contexts, such as for employment law or tax purposes, . . . [and] we believe it would be consistent with Item 402(u) for a registrant to apply a widely recognized test under another area of law that the registrant otherwise uses to determine whether its workers are employees.”

We believe that this same guidance would continue to apply when determining whether a worker is an employee under our proposed pay ratio rule, and, as such, our proposed rule does not provide for extensive carve-outs or other detailed guidance on this topic. The proposed amendments are intended both to increase the value of the disclosure to investors by enhancing comparability across registrants and to reduce compliance burdens for registrants.

a. Full-Time Employees
We propose to exercise our exemptive authority to exclude part-time, seasonal, and temporary employees from the determination of the median employee.
[

When adopting the current rule, the Commission determined to include part-time, seasonal, and temporary employees because it believed that their inclusion would be more reflective of the actual composition of the registrant's workforce and would help provide shareholders with relevant information about a registrant's compensation practices.
[

As noted above, in the years since its adoption, it has appeared that the usefulness to investors of the disclosure is not grounded in the specific pool of employees used in computing the ratio. Comments in support of the rule generally mention its usefulness as a tool in assessing things like employee morale and productivity
[
362

or impact on registrant performance.
[
363

We do not believe that the benefits to investors of pay ratio disclosure would be diminished by limiting its application to full-time employees. Indeed, commenters frequently point to the considerable variation in global workforce composition as a weakness of the rule, potentially causing significant year-over-year fluctuations in a registrant's pay ratio
[
364

and hindering useful comparisons among registrants.
[

As proposed, the rule would focus only on full-time employees other than temporary or seasonal workers, eliminating such variability and complexity in favor of a simple, easy-to-apply standard that would still provide the kinds of insights that investors seek. We believe that this change would both reduce the burdens associated with producing this disclosure and result in more comparability across registrants. Even among those registrants that would have a smaller pool of full-time employees from which to identify the median employee under the proposed rule, the median employee would presumably represent a more stable datapoint over time than the part-time, seasonal, or temporary workforce.
Based on our experience with the current rule and commenters' expressed concerns regarding its usefulness, and in spite of the broad scope of the term “
all employees
” set forth in section 953(b) of the Dodd-Frank Act, we are proposing to limit the scope of the rule to full-time employees other than temporary or seasonal workers, which we believe would better reflect a registrant's compensation practices within a more stable, consistent employee population.

In considering recent U.S. employment data, most U.S. employees work on a full-time basis.
[

Although we acknowledge that different industries may have different average concentrations of full-time employees, the proposed rule would allow for more comparability across industries even with such variability, and, as noted above, we believe that facilitating cross-registrant comparisons may add benefits to investors in spite of the contrary suggestion in the 2015 Pay Ratio Adopting Release.

In addition, a ratio comparing the pay of employees who work on a full-time basis without a specific endpoint of employment to that of the PEO (also typically a full-time employee with an open-ended term of employment) would compare full-time employees to each other, creating a more meaningful comparison than one that likely requires supplemental disclosure to explain factors that could reduce the usefulness of quantitative pay ratio information.
[
369
]
(
printed page 75052)
Considering the wide variability in employee populations, we believe that the median pay of full-time employees other than seasonal or temporary workers may provide the most consistent and stable measure across registrants for assessing the ratio of PEO to employee compensation, at a lower burden and with improved comparability; and that exclusion of part-time, seasonal, and temporary employees would not significantly alter the overall substance of the disclosure and accordingly still serve the purpose Congress intended for this rule. Specifically, as noted above, we believe that the usefulness of the disclosure to investors would not be diminished, and may be enhanced by the proposed amendment that would limit its application to full-time employees with an open-ended term of employment, since we believe that these employees' compensation should represent a stable, consistent signal of the registrant's pay practices for non-PEO employees. This proposed amendment is also expected to provide significant relief to registrants. For example, excluding part-time, seasonal, and temporary employees should reduce registrant costs created by integrating their non-full-time pay and, for seasonal and temporary employees who work on a full-time basis, their pay for a shorter time period than other full-time employees into the median employee determination, as well as supplementary narrative disclosures necessary to explain the impact of such integration. Overall, we believe that this proposed exemption would be necessary and appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors.

Furthermore, the compensation-setting process for employees located in foreign jurisdictions, where highly disparate norms, employment and contract laws, expectations, local and national government rules, and practices, as well as differences in economic and labor market conditions may apply, is likely to be very different from the process used for U.S. employees. As such, the inclusion of foreign employees could reduce the comparability of pay ratio disclosure across registrants and provide less useful information to investors about the compensation setting process.

(

At the same time, the burden on registrants resulting from the broad scope assigned to the term “all employees” at the time of the current rule's adoption does not appear to be necessary in order to retain the intended benefit to investors. We believe that investors should be better positioned to evaluate and engage with executive compensation and related say-on-pay votes if the pool of employees from which the median employee is identified are all subject to the same laws and standards affecting terms of employment and compensation (for example. minimum and overtime wage laws, anti-discrimination laws, including those protecting wages of employees with disabilities, and retirement income related laws), thereby enhancing comparability. Accordingly, we believe the proposed amendment to limit the determination of the median employee to employees located in the U.S. and its territories is necessary and appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors.

2. Determination of Annual Total Compensation
We are proposing to align the approach to the determination of the PEO's and median employee's annual total compensation for purposes of the pay ratio disclosure rule with the proposed revisions to the tabular presentation of executive compensation.
Section 953(b)(2) of the Dodd-Frank Act requires that annual total compensation under the pay ratio rule be determined “in accordance with [current Item 402(c)(x)] as in effect on the day before the date of enactment of this Act,” referring to the then-current calculation of total compensation in the Summary Compensation Table. As described above, our proposed revisions to Item 402 would remove Item 402(c)(x), and the proposed amendments would not contain an equivalent table to the current Summary Compensation Table. Rather than retaining the substance of Item 402(c)(x) simply for purposes of the pay ratio rule, which we believe would be unduly burdensome, we are proposing to use our exemptive authority to look instead to the closest corollary to current Item 402(c)(x) in the proposed amendments.
We continue to believe that the principal compensation elements that are currently used to calculate annual total compensation for purposes of the pay ratio disclosure, including salary, bonus, and equity awards valued as of the grant date, are appropriate. Because we are proposing to replace the Summary Compensation Table with new tables and the proposed Granted Compensation Table would include
(
printed page 75054)
most of the same compensation elements as the Summary Compensation Table needed to calculate annual total compensation, we propose to use the information from the proposed Granted Compensation Table as the basis for determining annual total compensation for the PEO and median employee for purposes of the pay ratio disclosure. For example, for the PEO's annual total compensation, registrants would use the Total Compensation Granted amount from the proposed Granted Compensation Table (column (g)). With respect to the determination of compensation of the median employees, registrants would correspondingly apply the methodology of the proposed Granted Compensation Table.
We recognize that the proposed Granted Compensation Table does not include all of the elements included in the current Summary Compensation Table, including those related to pension benefits and compensation that is not reportable under another column of the table (
i.e.,
the all other compensation column); however, we believe that the total compensation amount included in the proposed Granted Compensation Table would provide the material elements of PEO compensation, for purposes of determining the pay ratio, and thus serve as a reasonable basis upon which to compare PEO and median employee compensation.
[
380
]
In addition, eliminating these elements (pension benefits and miscellaneous compensation items) would further reduce the burden on registrants since tracking these items for non-executive employees is generally not standard practice. Furthermore, we believe that using the proposed Granted Compensation Table as the basis for annual total compensation would not create additional burdens for registrants because the proposed rules do not change the current method of valuing employees' equity awards (using grant date fair value). In contrast, using the Earned Compensation Table valuation method for calculating pay ratio total compensation could require registrants to track employee grants of equity awards beyond the grant date to determine their values upon vesting or exercise.
In light of the proposed changes to the tabular presentation of executive compensation in Item 402, which we believe would improve executive compensation disclosure generally but also would eliminate current Item 402(c)(2)(x), we believe that the corresponding proposed changes to the determination of annual total compensation in the pay ratio disclosure rules are necessary and appropriate in the public interest, and consistent with the protection of investors.

3. Elimination of Certain Instructions; Timing of Determination of Median Employee
In keeping with the principles-based approach to these amendments, we propose to retain flexibility for registrants relating to the identification of the median employee but to eliminate the detailed requirements and instructions about the use of estimates and exclusion of certain employees. The current rule requires certain disclosures about the identification of the median employee, and provides lengthy guidance related to the use of adjustments, estimates, sampling, the treatment of employees resulting from recent acquisitions, and other matters. We believe that registrants should continue to have flexibility, but we propose to eliminate some of the detailed guidance from the current rule because we believe it may have resulted in disclosure that is unnecessary to an understanding of pay ratio disclosure and unintentionally constrained registrants' flexibility in preparing the disclosure. We also propose removing the disclosure requirements related to the identification process for the median employee because we believe the additional disclosure is not necessary for investor understanding of the pay ratio disclosure.
Specifically, we propose to remove the following current instructions to the pay ratio rule and incorporate some of their components into the proposed rule:
Instruction 1 to Item 402(u)
—
Disclosing the date chosen for identifying the median employee.
(Requiring disclosure relating to the date chosen for identifying the median employee.)
Instruction 2 to Item 402(u)—Identifying the median employee.
(Requiring, in part, that the registrant identify its median employee once every three years but also indicating that, every year, the registrant must determine if there has been a change in its employee population or employee compensation arrangements that the registrant reasonably believes would result in a significant change to its pay ratio disclosure and, if the registrant concludes there is no such a change, the registrant must include disclosure about that determination and use of the same median employee.)
Instruction 3 to Item 402(u)

L. Compensation of Directors—Proposed Item 402(k)
We are proposing to continue to require qualitative and quantitative disclosure of the cash, equity and other material compensation amounts earned by members of the board of directors (or similar governing body) for the registrant's last completed fiscal year, but to amend the rule in favor of a more principles-based approach. The proposed rules would eliminate certain prescriptive requirements, including mandatory disclosure related to the change in value of pension plans, earnings on nonqualified deferred compensation and total director compensation; mandatory tabular presentation requirements; and a list of “all other compensation” amounts. Consistent with a principles-based approach, we are proposing to require that registrants describe the material aspects of the registrant's director compensation program and disclose any material information necessary to an understanding of the compensation amounts disclosed pursuant to the rule. Because, in many cases, director compensation is less structurally complex than PEO and PFO compensation, we believe there may be less need to require, in all cases, highly detailed disclosure for directors. By providing this flexibility, registrants with relatively simple director compensation arrangements would not be compelled to prepare detailed (but potentially immaterial) compensation information but could still choose to disclose the information in a tabular format if they prefer. We recognize, however, that there is value to investors in knowing how directors are compensated, for example, to understand their alignment with shareholder interests. We believe that the more principles-based approach we are proposing that also retains basic compensation elements (cash and equity), and which is rooted in materiality, will continue to ensure that investors receive key information about director pay.
We acknowledge that moving to a more principles-based approach for director compensation disclosure could lead to less standardization of the disclosure and could make it more difficult for investors to compare director compensation across registrants. M. Scaled Disclosure—Proposed Item 402(a)(6)
As noted above, in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release, we proposed streamlining the filer statuses for reporting companies and extending to the proposed NAF category all accommodations currently available to SRCs and EGCs.
[
423
]
If those rules are adopted as proposed, they would accordingly extend to NAFs all the Item 402 accommodations currently available to SRCs and EGCs.
[
424
]
In light of the expansion of scaled disclosure in that release, we are not here proposing new accommodations. We are however proposing to streamline Item 402 by identifying the rule provisions governing the disclosure requirements and accommodations applicable to SRCs and EGCs respectively into paragraphs (a)(6)(i) and (ii) of Item 402, thereby eliminating the need for a separate set of executive compensation disclosure provisions for SRCs and EGCs. If the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release is adopted as proposed, we would consolidate these provisions into one paragraph (a)(6) applicable to NAFs.
Currently, SRCs and EGCs may elect to provide executive compensation disclosure that is generally subject to scaled disclosure accommodations as set forth in a parallel set of disclosure rules under Item 402. Current Item 402(
l
) provides that SRCs and EGCs may use the scaled requirements in paragraphs (m) through (r) of Item 402, instead of reporting pursuant to paragraphs (a) through (k), (s), and (u), which apply to registrants that are not SRCs or EGCs.
[
425
]
Under the scaled executive compensation disclosure requirements currently set out in paragraphs (m) through (r) of Item 402, SRCs and EGCs may, among other things:
Provide executive compensation disclosure for three NEOs in most cases (specifically including the PEO but not the PFO), rather than at least five as required of larger companies;
Provide the Summary Compensation Table disclosure for only the last two completed fiscal years, rather than the three years required of larger companies;
Provide only two of the six primary executive compensation tables required of larger companies; and
Provide only a narrative description of the material terms of potential payments and benefits to an NEO for the payment of retirement benefits and upon termination or a change-in-control event contracts, agreements, plans, or arrangements, not the prescriptive quantitative and qualitative requirements that apply to larger companies.
Further, SRCs and EGCs are currently not required to provide the following:
CD&A (Item 402(b));
Narrative disclosure of compensation policies and practices as they relate to risk management (Item 402(s)); or
Pay ratio disclosure (Item 402(u)).
Additionally, EGCs are currently not required to provide golden parachute compensation disclosure under current Item 402(t) or the pay-versus-performance disclosure under current Item 402(v), while SRCs may provide scaled pay-versus-performance disclosure rather than the more extensive disclosure required for larger companies.
[
426
]
As noted above, we are proposing to consolidate the various provisions that address the scaled disclosure rules available to SRCs under Item 402 into proposed Item 402(a)(6)(i) and to EGCs under proposed Item 402(a)(6)(ii). Proposed Item 402(a)(6)(i) would specify that a registrant that qualifies as an SRC would be deemed to comply with Item 402 if it provides the information required by:
Proposed Item 402(a) (General);
Proposed Item 402(b) (Earned Compensation Table) for each of its last two completed fiscal years;
Proposed Item 402(c) (Granted Compensation Table) for each of its last two completed fiscal years;
Proposed Item 402(d) (Status of Equity Awards Table);
Proposed Item 402(f) (Pay-versus-performance);
Proposed Item 402(g) (Disclosure of a registrant's action to recover erroneously awarded compensation);
Proposed Item 402(i) (Potential payments upon termination or change-in-control);
Proposed Item 402(j) (Golden parachute compensation); and
Proposed Item 402(k) (Compensation of directors).
Proposed Item 402(a)(6)(ii) would specify that a registrant that qualifies as an EGC would be deemed to comply with Item 402 if it provides the information required by:
Proposed Item 402(a) (General);
Proposed Item 402(b) (Earned Compensation Table) for each of its last two completed fiscal years;
(
printed page 75063)
Proposed Item 402(c) (Granted Compensation Table) for each of its last two completed fiscal years;
Proposed Item 402(d) (Status of Equity Awards Table);
Proposed Item 402(g) (Disclosure of a registrant's action to recover erroneously awarded compensation);
Proposed Item 402(i) (Potential payments upon termination or change-in-control); and
Proposed Item 402(k) (Compensation of directors).
Accordingly, as proposed, SRCs and EGCs would continue to be exempt from:
Proposed Item 402(e) (Compensation Discussion and Analysis); and
Proposed Item 402(h) (Pay Ratio Disclosure).
EGCs would continue to be exempt from:
Proposed Item 402(f) (Pay-versus-Performance); and
Proposed Item 402(j) (Golden parachute compensation).
[
427
]
The proposed amendments would reduce the length and complexity of Item 402 by addressing the treatment of SRCs and EGCs each in a single paragraph, rather than repeating a large quantity of text for SRCs and EGCs (in scaled form) as the current rule does.
[
428
]
The proposed amendments would not change the nature of the scaled disclosure accommodations available to SRCs and EGCs. SRCs and EGCs would, like all other registrants under the proposed rules, be required to provide executive compensation disclosures for only two NEOs in most circumstances (
i.e.,
just the PEO and PFO), as compared to at least three (
i.e.,
the PEO and at least the two most highly compensated executive officers other than the PEO) required under the current rule for SRCs and EGCs. Also, like all other registrants, SRCs and EGCs would be required to describe potential payments upon termination or a change in control under proposed Item 402(i).
[
429
]
Overall, the proposed amendments in this release are intended to streamline the rules that apply to SRCs and EGCs (or NAFs, if the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release is adopted as proposed), and reduce burdens on SRCs and EGCs (or NAFs, if the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release is adopted as proposed).

17 CFR 229.402(s)

Where compensation expense is a significant percentage of the unit's revenues.

439

440

When the Commission proposed the current rule in 2009, it noted concerns from some commentators that, at some companies, compensation policies had become insufficiently aligned with the long-term well-being of the company and that “in some cases, the structure and the particular application of incentive compensation policies can create inadvertent incentives for management and employees to make decisions that significantly, and inappropriately, increase the company's risk, without adequate recognition of the risks to the company.”

For example, the management's discussion and analysis requirement in Item 303 of Regulation S-K requires registrants to provide material information relevant to an assessment of the financial condition and results of operations of the registrant, and Item 105 of Regulation S-K requires a discussion of the material factors that make an investment in the registrant or offering speculative or risky.

P. Timing of Executive Compensation Disclosure in Registration Statements
We are proposing to amend certain registration statement requirements to address the timing requirements for providing Item 402 disclosure that covers the last completed fiscal year. Currently, “long form” registration statements on Securities Act Forms S-1, S-4, and S-11, and Exchange Act Form 10, as well as Form N-2 under the Securities Act and Investment Company Act, enumerate Item 402 among the line-item disclosure requirements that must be included.
[
452
]
Because Item 402 requires disclosure for “each of the registrant's last three completed fiscal years,” any of these “long form” registration statements filed on or after the first day of a registrant's fiscal year must include Item 402 disclosure for the immediately preceding fiscal year.
[
453
]
Even when a registrant files a registration statement on the first day of its fiscal year, for example, it is required
(
printed page 75067)
to include Item 402 disclosure for the fiscal year ended on the previous day. Registrants that are only eligible to use “long form” Securities Act registration statements are therefore limited in their ability to offer securities in the public capital markets until they can provide Item 402 disclosure for the immediately preceding fiscal year, which can impact capital formation. This requirement effectively acts as an impediment to the ability of a registrant using a long form Securities Act registration statement to raise capital or conduct business combination transactions through a registered offering until it can provide that executive compensation disclosure.
[
454
]
For an Exchange Act registration statement, a registrant might need to delay important actions, like the voluntary registration of a class of equity securities under section 12(g) of the Exchange Act when seeking to have securities quoted on certain over-the-counter markets, until it has had adequate time to prepare Item 402 disclosure for the last completed fiscal year. In addition, we see no compelling reason to apply a different standard for disclosure timing based upon whether the registration statement is filed under the Securities Act or Exchange Act.
By contrast, registrants using registration statements that do not specifically enumerate Item 402 among the required disclosures, such as Form S-3 and Form S-8, may delay their Item 402 disclosure for the last completed fiscal year until they make a filing with a line item that specifically requires that disclosure.
[
455
]
That filing typically is the Form 10-K and, depending on the filer status of the registrant, the Form 10-K must be filed within either 60, 75, or 90 days of the end of a fiscal year.
[
456
]
In addition to that period of time, General Instruction G.(3) of Form 10-K permits a registrant to delay Item 402 disclosure. Specifically, a registrant may omit the information called for by Part III of Form 10-K, which includes Item 402 disclosure, as long as the information is disclosed within 120 days of the end of the fiscal year in either the registrant's definitive proxy or information statement involving the election of directors or an amendment to its Form 10-K.
[
457
]
As a result, unlike with a “long form” registration statement, an eligible registrant could file a short form registration statement (
e.g.,
Form S-3) without Item 402 disclosure for the most recently completed fiscal year and have that registration statement declared effective without that disclosure for up to 120 days after the end of the fiscal year.
[
458
]
We are proposing to amend Forms S-1, S-4,
[
459
]
S-11, 10, and N-2 to address this disparity and mitigate the resulting implications for capital raising and other actions that may depend on a “long form” registration statement. We propose to amend long form registration statements so that a registrant is not required to provide updated Item 402 disclosure for the most recently completed fiscal year until the later of the date the registrant otherwise discloses that information in a document filed pursuant to section 13(a), 14, or 15(d) of the Exchange Act or 120 days after the end of that fiscal year. The Item 402 disclosure in any filing from which a registrant omits the most recently completed fiscal year pursuant to the proposed amendments should still include the number of fiscal years required by proposed Item 402
[
460
]
using the time-period immediately preceding the omitted fiscal year.
[
461
]
The proposed amendments would further require, however, that, if a registrant files a registration statement without the Item 402 information for the immediately preceding fiscal year as permitted by the relevant Item, and the registration statement would go effective after the deadline for providing Item 402 information for that fiscal year, the registrant must file a pre-effective amendment to the registration statement which includes such Item 402 disclosure.
[
462
]
The proposed changes would provide registrants using long form registration statements the same period of time to prepare their Item 402 disclosures for the most recently completed fiscal year that is currently available to registrants using short form registration statements. We believe that this proposed change appropriately balances registrants' disclosure obligations and burdens with the informational needs of investors and investor protection.
In light of our proposal to amend long form registration statements to provide registrants up to 120 days after their fiscal year end to provide updated Item 402 disclosure, we are proposing to remove certain Item 402 and Form 8-K provisions that relate to extended time to provide salary and bonus information in certain circumstances, as these would be duplicative and unnecessary. A. Introduction
Certain information about the compensation of a registrant's key executives is likely to be material to investment and voting decisions, as detailed in the Broad Economic Considerations section (section IV.B) below. Mandating the disclosure of such information can help to reduce agency problems
[
465
]
and information
(
printed page 75069)
asymmetries
[
466
]
that could result if registrants were permitted to disclose details about their executive compensation on a purely voluntary basis. At the same time, the compliance burden and volume of required executive compensation disclosures have grown substantially over time, and certain of these requirements may call for disclosure that is of limited importance to investors' voting and investment decisions. Many registrants and investors have reported difficulties in producing and in digesting many aspects of current executive compensation disclosures.
[
467
]
The proposed amendments would focus required executive compensation disclosures on the information that is most likely to be material so that investors can continue to make informed voting and investment decisions, while reducing the total amount of disclosure that registrants are required to provide.
[
468
]
For example, registrants would no longer be required to provide disclosure about the compensation of any executive officers other than the PEO and PFO or to undertake significant computations with respect to outstanding equity awards for purposes of certain disclosures. They would also be able to reduce the detail disclosed about executive benefits, such as retirement plans and perquisites. Registrants would still be required to disclose certain standardized quantitative information about the compensation of their PEO and PFO, organized into a new, more condensed set of tables. Larger registrants
[
469
]
would continue to be required to make some further disclosures about their executive compensation programs, including CD&A and pay ratio disclosures, although these requirements are also proposed to be simplified and/or made more principles-based than the current requirements for these disclosures.
[
470
]
The proposed requirements are also intended to better reflect the way many registrants view their compensation programs. By more closely aligning the requirements with the registrant perspective, simplifying the required disclosures, and permitting a degree of flexibility in the content and presentation of disclosures, the proposed amendments may reduce the extent of voluntary supplementary disclosures that some registrants currently provide to clarify certain mandated elements of the disclosures.
The proposed amendments are expected to reduce the costs of producing executive compensation disclosures by a substantial fraction relative to current expenditures while maintaining the disclosure of the information about executive compensation that is most likely to be material.
[
471
]
We expect that the proposed disclosures would be significantly less burdensome for registrants to prepare than current disclosures.
[
472
]
Our monetized estimate of these compliance cost savings is approximately $244,000 per year per registrant, on average across registrants.
[
473

The cost savings are expected to be driven by three key factors. First, reducing the scope of the disclosures as proposed—particularly with respect to the scope of named executive officers, the employees included in the pay ratio determinations, and certain
de minimis
perquisites—would reduce registrants' need to undertake data collection and tracking. Second, the proposed amendments would eliminate current requirements to make certain complex computations such as valuations of outstanding equity awards (after grant but prior to vesting or exercise) for the purpose of the disclosures. Finally, the overall lower total volume of required disclosures (including proposed reductions in the number of tables as well as the extent of narratives and footnotes) should reduce the burdens involved in registrant staff, board, and external advisor review of the disclosures. The resulting compliance cost savings may be redirected to other, potentially more productive uses including being returned to shareholders.
The proposed amendments may also eliminate some incentives to deviate from the practices that the registrant would otherwise determine to be most appropriate. For example, they would limit the likelihood that registrants would feel reluctant to provide security services that are integrally and directly related to the performance of an executive's work duties only because of the implications for compensation disclosure or to pay a bonus to one executive officer only because the amount would change the composition of the registrant's group of NEOs. To the extent that these considerations distort
[
474
]
decisions by registrants,
[
475
]
the proposed amendments would allow registrants to make these types of decisions based on their view of what best serves the company, without needing to weigh the disclosure implications of those decisions. Even when registrant decisions would be unchanged, the proposed amendments may simplify compensation committee
(
printed page 75070)
deliberations and reduce any perceived encumbrance on registrant discretion.
[
476

The effects on investor search and analysis costs are more difficult to predict. Some of the proposed amendments may make it easier for investors to review registrants' executive compensation programs, particularly with respect to tracking the status of a given equity award. Other elements of the proposed amendments, such as the elimination of disclosures about the valuation of these equity awards as performance is realized but before the award status changes (to vested or exercised), may make the review somewhat more difficult. The additional flexibility that would be afforded to registrants to tailor their disclosures to reflect their perspective on their executive compensation program and their individual circumstances could increase the efficiency of investors' review, by highlighting the most important elements in the context of a particular registrant's compensation program. Alternatively, this added flexibility could reduce efficiency by making it harder for investors to find the information they are looking for or to compare disclosures to those of other registrants.
The proposed amendments overall represent a significant change from current disclosure requirements and would likely generate some short-term adjustment costs for both registrants
[
477
]
and investors. Also, while the proposed disclosures would continue to provide the information that we understand to be most broadly relied on by investors, investors would face a loss of some information relative to what is provided in current disclosures. While some of the information that would be forgone may be of little consequence, the elimination of some currently required disclosure may reduce the precision with which investors evaluate executive compensation programs. This less precise understanding of executive compensation by some or all investors may introduce noise
[
