into investment and voting decisions and may increase information asymmetries between investors and management or among investors.
The proposed amendments would also reduce the extent of public disclosure about certain executive benefits and could thus incentivize some executives to request, and/or some registrants to provide, more generous executive benefits than might currently be the case. Any increase in expenditures on executives could at least partially offset the compliance cost savings associated with the proposed amendments. However, the proposed executive compensation disclosures are, taken as a whole, intended to reflect the material elements of compensation that are included in current disclosures in some form, making it difficult to obscure large transfers of value to executives. The proposed amendments may also introduce new disclosure considerations that could distort executive compensation design. For example, the proposal could encourage a greater use of some types of equity awards than others, relative to what would be chosen in the absence of disclosure considerations, because the proposed valuation approach at grant date may value certain similar instruments differently.
[
479

The proposed amendments could also lead to an increased reliance on non-equity incentive awards because of their reduced transparency relative to equity awards under the proposed amendments. That said, given the degree to which current compensation structures common among registrants rely on equity-based incentives, apparently reflecting a strong investor and registrant preference for the use of equity awards, we believe that large-scale market-level shifts in executive compensation structures as a result of disclosure considerations under the proposed requirements would be unlikely in the near term.
Below, we discuss in more detail the anticipated economic effects of the proposed amendments and of significant alternatives to the proposed amendments, including how these effects may vary depending on how registrants, investors, and third-party service providers react to any changes that may be adopted.
B. Broad Economic Considerations
Our economic analysis of the proposed amendments reflects our consideration of the broader utility and consequences of executive and director compensation disclosures. In particular, we recognize that investing in a registrant involves a basic agency problem: it requires delegating decision-making authority to a management team, whose interests may not align perfectly with those of investors.
[
480
]
Executive compensation disclosures help to address this agency problem in two ways. First, transparency around executive compensation can help to ensure that investor resources are used appropriately. While executive compensation typically represents a relatively small percentage of a registrant's total expenses,
[
481
]
the determination of the level of compensation paid to management involves a direct conflict between the managers' personal interests and their responsibilities to shareholders, in that an additional dollar of pay directly benefits a manager while the costs of such pay are borne by investors in the registrant.
[
482
]
Disclosure of the amount of executive compensation can help to address this conflict by allowing investors to directly monitor the extent of registrant resources used to compensate senior management. A
(
printed page 75071)
similar case can be made with respect to the transparency of director compensation.
Second, executive compensation disclosures can provide insights into executives' monetary incentives to take particular corporate actions. This benefit of executive compensation disclosure may be more consequential for shareholder value than the first.
[
483
]
Specifically, recognizing the risk of misalignment between manager and shareholder interests, registrants may design executive compensation packages to encourage executives to exert effort and make decisions that enhance shareholder value. Indeed, a large body of literature (discussed below in this section) provides evidence that various aspects of compensation design—including the level of pay, its performance sensitivity, and other components and terms of compensation—can be used to predict how executives will run the business and how registrants will perform. Disclosure about the design of executive compensation thus allows investors to understand the incentives of the managers to whom they entrust their capital and to assess registrants' future performance. When considering the double-layered agency problem (wherein shareholders delegate oversight of managers to the board of directors, and the board of directors delegates management to the executives), executive compensation disclosures also allow investors to evaluate the strategic priorities and effectiveness of boards of directors in overseeing these executives, while director compensation disclosures allow investors to evaluate the monetary incentives of the board itself.
All of these factors—the responsible use of investor resources, the incentives of managers and directors, and the strategic priorities and effectiveness of boards of directors—may be material and thus relevant to investment and voting
[
484
]
decisions. The disclosure of material information about executive and director compensation allows investors to evaluate these factors and make informed decisions.
A compensation package can reward or penalize certain managerial traits, actions, or outcomes. The level and structure of an executive's compensation may thereby affect such executive's behavior, including the executive's expenditure of effort, degree of risk-taking, prioritization of goals, and likelihood of remaining at a registrant.
[
485
]
Information about the design of executive compensation can, therefore, allow investors to form more informed expectations about executive decisions and a registrant's future performance. For this purpose, investors would generally seek to understand the executives'
ex ante
incentives—that is, the potential rewards and motivations in place before performance is realized
[
486
]
—because they are the drivers of future performance; by the time
ex post
payoffs are made, the performance outcome will also generally be known.
[
487
]
That said, it may be difficult to disclose complete information in advance about these incentives.
[
488
]
Interim “in flight” updates about the progress towards achieving compensation outcomes and
ex post
realized compensation outcomes from the recent past can thereby help to refine investors' understanding of executives' incentives.
[
489
]
Academic research has found that various key aspects of the level and structure of compensation can affect expectations of registrant and executive performance. For example, based on survey evidence, researchers have found that the motivation of CEOs to perform well is sensitive to their perception of the fairness of the level of their pay.
[
490
]
Regarding the structure of pay, the primary sources of monetary incentives are generally believed to stem from compensation's sensitivity to stock prices (also known as “delta”), its sensitivity to volatility (that is, the degree of variation) in stock prices (also known as “vega”), its vesting horizon, and the choice and rigor of performance goals.
[
491
]
The linkage of executive compensation to a registrant's stock price through equity compensation is, in most cases, the dominant source of variation in compensation outcomes,
[
492
]
and stronger equity incentives have been associated with actions that enhance or preserve shareholder value.
[
493
]
Researchers have also
(
printed page 75072)
demonstrated that a higher sensitivity of CEO compensation to volatility in the registrant's stock price is predictive of less conservative strategic choices, such as a greater investment in R&D or in higher risk business segments.
[
494
]
Others have found that the vesting horizon of a CEO's outstanding equity awards is associated with whether the CEO's actions appear to prioritize short-term goals at the expense of long-term value creation, such as in the context of investment and acquisition decisions,
[
495
]
or, separately, with the likelihood that the CEO voluntarily departs from that role.
[
496
]
The choice of performance metrics and the difficulty of performance goals have also been shown to predict elements of registrant
[
497
]
and executive
[
498
]
performance.
While the elements of compensation design mentioned above (which we refer to broadly in this economic analysis as the level and performance sensitivity of pay) are generally believed to provide an executive's primary monetary incentives, other elements (which we refer to as other components and terms of compensation) can provide additional insight into executive decision-making and performance.
[
499
]
For example, researchers have found that executives with high pension (or deferred compensation) balances manage registrants more conservatively,
[
500
]
and that bond prices rise and stock prices fall when investors become aware of such compensation (and thus, presumably, adjust their expectations about managerial risk-taking).
[
501
]
Others have found that the incidence and/or size of severance plans and golden parachutes are associated with reduced managerial conservatism, registrant acquisition likelihoods and premiums, and shareholder value.
[
502
]
The terms of executive equity grants with respect to their entitlement to dividends or the sensitivity of performance metrics to share repurchases have been found to be associated with registrant payout policy and shareholder value.
[
503
]
Even certain perquisites have been found to provide meaningful signals about registrant performance.
[
504
]
Altogether, this body of research provides evidence that various aspects of executive compensation design are associated with executive behavior and registrant performance in ways that may be relevant to investors' voting and investment decisions.
Information about executive pay packages may also be used by investors to evaluate the effectiveness of board oversight over the registrant and its executives, as the board (generally through or with the involvement of its compensation committee) is responsible for designing and approving executive compensation. While the board has certain fiduciary duties, the ability of shareholders to evaluate how well the board is upholding its duties and to make informed voting decisions in director elections is central to maintaining the accountability of directors.
[
505
]
Compensation decisions have been termed the “acid test” of corporate governance; they can provide insight into the board's effectiveness at addressing a direct conflict between shareholders' and managers' interests.
[
506
]
For example, depending on
(
printed page 75073)
the context, a relatively high level of executive compensation could provide insight into the board's assessment of the executive's skill and contribution,
[
507
]
or could reflect a weak board that may be a less effective steward of investor capital.
[
508
]
The design of executive compensation also provides insights into the priorities and goals of the board, based on how compensation is linked to registrant or executive performance (or other factors) and which performance metrics and thresholds are emphasized. Consistent with the hypothesis that executive compensation information is relevant for evaluating the board's performance, researchers have found an association between reduced shareholder support for directors and concerns about a registrant's executive compensation,
[
509
]
and such concerns are commonly cited in investors' self-reported rationales for their voting decisions in director elections.
[
510
]
The effectiveness of boards
[
511
]
and the nature of the relationship between a board and the CEO
[
512
]
also have potential implications for registrant performance and, thus, for informed investment decisions.
Disclosures about the directors' own compensation provide further information that may be relevant to voting
[
513
]
and investment
[
514
]
decisions. For example, some market participants as well as academics have expressed the view that granting some equity-based compensation for directors can provide “skin in the game” to align the interests of boards with shareholders, affecting the board's expected monitoring intensity.
[
515
]
On the other hand, certain compensation levels or structures may raise concerns from an investor perspective as to whether they may compromise director independence
[
516
]
or create incentives that are not consistent with long-term shareholder value maximization.
[
517
]
Because, under State corporate law, the board of directors generally has authority to determine the pay of its own members, subject to oversight by shareholders as provided under applicable law, transparency around director compensation can also help to ensure integrity in the director pay-setting process.
[
518
]
Information about executive and director compensation is also used by registrants (either directly or through compensation consultants) to benchmark their own pay decisions and practices.
[
519
]
The availability of publicly disclosed compensation data reduces the need for registrants to base their compensation decisions on third party survey data, which may be less reliable, less detailed, or less comprehensive than data disclosed in public filings. Executives themselves may also use peer compensation data to evaluate their compensation relative to that of other executives to assess, for example, whether they view their own compensation as fair.
[
520
]
They may use this information in negotiating their compensation packages and in making decisions about their own careers.
The disclosure of executive compensation also has indirect effects. By facilitating the monitoring of compensation committee decisions, such disclosure may lead to more effective compensation design and better executive performance.
[
521
]
Further, transparency around executive compensation can discourage excessive pay or pay practices that investors view unfavorably. For example, a study of the initial institution of executive compensation disclosure requirements upon the enactment of the Exchange Act found that disclosure had a moderating effect on the level of CEO pay at the most extreme outliers, with pay at the top end dropping by about eighty percent, despite average CEO pay increasing.
[
522
]
In more recent times, studies of the practice of retroactively assigning an earlier grant date to an option award (to assign a lower exercise price) found that this practice of backdating was greatly diminished after executives were required to disclose grants of stock options within two business days of the grant (rather than
(
printed page 75074)
up to 40 days after the grant, prior to the rule change).
[
523
]
Executive compensation disclosures can also help investors to better interpret broader corporate disclosures through an understanding of how executives' monetary incentives may affect their exercise of discretion over the content or timing of disclosures, such as in the issuance of management earnings forecasts.
[
524
]
Executive and director compensation disclosure also has costs, including the direct costs of producing the disclosures and the unintended consequences of such disclosure. The direct costs to registrants include the use of internal resources and expenditures on outside advisors for the purposes of, for example, information collection; computations; the design of any principles-based elements; the drafting of tables, narratives, and footnotes; and review of the disclosure.
[
525
]
With respect to unintended consequences, the disclosure of executive compensation information has been tied to “ratchet” effects, whereby registrant practices of benchmarking executives' compensation to be above the median among peers lead pay at all registrants generally to increase.
[
526
]
This “ratchet” effect may be reinforced by cross-registrant comparisons made by executives themselves, with potential discontent and demotivation resulting from comparisons to pay at a registrant's peers that make an executive feel relatively underpaid, even if these peer registrants do not reflect the executive's actual potential alternative employment opportunities.
[
527
]
Benchmarking practices and shareholder scrutiny of executive compensation disclosures can also lead to more uniform pay structures, which might come at the expense of compensation incentives that are more optimally designed for the individual circumstances of different registrants.
[
528
]
Further, historical disclosure requirements treating certain elements of pay or benefits (such as options or deferred compensation) differently than others were associated by researchers with distortions in compensation, with growth in compensation in the form of those elements that were less transparent, even if such compensation were not otherwise optimal from a registrant's perspective.
[
529
]
The users of executive and director compensation disclosures generally seek to compare data about such compensation across registrants.
[
530
]
Without the ability to compare these data, it can be difficult to gauge its appropriateness, because the broader labor market for executives and directors plays a key role in determining the pay level and incentives for performance that may be necessary to attract, retain, and motivate these individuals.
[
531
]
A registrant's executive and director compensation data can therefore be more effectively evaluated by investors if it can be generally understood in comparison to the disclosures of other registrants. Comparability is also likely to be important for registrants and executives to the extent they seek to benchmark pay practices.
While the consistency and comparability of data across registrants' compensation disclosures facilitate these uses of the disclosures, the ability of registrants to otherwise tailor disclosures to their own individual circumstances can also contribute to the effective communication of executive compensation information. Such flexibility may be particularly likely to contribute to more effective disclosure when, for example, compensation packages have unique features that may be harder to understand from information presented in standardized formats or when compensation structures evolve such that prescriptive requirements designed in the past no longer clearly convey their material elements.
In addition, while many of the current executive and director compensation disclosures may, as discussed above, individually provide certain relevant information to the market, the utility of the disclosures may not be uniform. Some disclosures may be more relevant to investors' voting and investment decisions than others, and a given disclosure's contribution may be limited where it adds little to information conveyed elsewhere. With respect to some registrants, certain disclosures may be essentially irrelevant given their compensation structures or specific circumstances. Reducing redundancies and disclosure of immaterial information, while preserving the disclosure of information about executive compensation practices that is more likely to be material, could improve the overall effectiveness of compensation disclosures by concentrating investor attention on the information most relevant to their decisions.
[
532
]
Taking into account all of these considerations on both the utility and cost of executive and director compensation disclosure, we analyze the benefits and costs of the specific provisions of the proposed amendments in detail below.

6. Market Practice
In this section we provide a brief overview of current practices by registrants and investors and recent market developments that are relevant to our consideration of the economic effects of the proposed amendments.
Registrants prepare executive compensation disclosures, often with the help of external advisors. For example, we understand that registrants' securities counsel may often work closely with registrant staff in preparing the proxy statement. Compensation consultants may draft, review, or otherwise provide advice on the CD&A and other compensation disclosures. Consultants, accountants, valuation experts, or other specialists may be retained to aid in producing the required tables and quantitative disclosures, particularly in constructing required valuations and making necessary computations.
In addition to the mandatory executive compensation disclosures required by Item 402, some registrants currently include voluntary disclosures that they believe may better explain their pay practices.
[
599
]
For example,
(

[

Other registrants may present “total direct compensation” and/or other measures intended to demonstrate how the compensation committee views the compensation granted or earned that year. Both registrants and investors have indicated that the flexibility to include registrant voluntary disclosures can be helpful.
[
601
]
Such disclosures can allow registrants to better communicate their specific circumstances or provide context for standardized disclosures that they believe do not convey a complete picture of their compensation programs.
[
602
]
For investors, such voluntary disclosures can make it easier to understand how the board approaches its compensation decisions and programs.
[
603
]
However, the market does not seem to have coalesced around consistent definitions and formats for, or indeed the consistent inclusion of, such voluntary disclosures. Thus, while they may provide investors with useful context, the ability of investors to systematically evaluate these voluntary disclosures or to compare them to peer company disclosures may be limited.
[
604
]
It is possible that some of these additional disclosures were introduced in connection with say-on-pay votes or in response to increased investor engagement associated with such votes.

To the extent that the LAF and NAF filer categories that we have proposed in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted, they would reduce the population of registrants required to hold such votes as that requirement would only apply to LAFs. The incentive to include these disclosures could thereby be reduced in the future, assuming the exempted registrants do not voluntarily conduct say-on-pay votes.
[
606

We understand that investors currently approach the review of executive compensation disclosures in different ways. Investors often review large numbers of proxy statements and related filings over the relatively condensed proxy season every year.

607

To aid in this process, many investors, particularly institutional investors, use analyses of executive compensation disclosures produced by third parties, such as proxy advisory firms.

608

These products synthesize the information disclosed by a large number of registrants and present standardized computations, comparisons, and highlights for more efficient review.
[
609

Other investors undertake their own analyses based directly on registrant disclosures or information extracted from these disclosures by third-party data aggregators, or design bespoke analyses that are produced with the help of compensation consultants.

610

Recent advances in information technology may increase the feasibility of such direct review of large volumes of filings.

Currently, some investors likely combine these approaches, for example, using third-party analyses to identify registrants whose executive compensation warrants further analysis, and then examining and analyzing those registrants' disclosures directly in more detail. Given the resources required for accessing third-party research and undertaking detailed quantitative computations and analysis of large numbers of proxy statements, smaller investors, particularly retail investors, are less likely to use the approaches mentioned above but may directly review executive compensation disclosures. The current definition of NEO for registrants other than SRCs and EGCs includes a registrant's (a) PEO and PFO, including all individuals serving in either of these capacities during the last completed fiscal year, (b) three most highly compensated individuals other than the PEO and PFO who served as executive officers as of the end of the fiscal year and whose adjusted total compensation was at least $100,000, and (c) up to two additional individuals who would have been included under (b) if they had still served as executive officers at fiscal year-end. For SRCs and EGCs, the NEOs include a registrant's (a) PEO, including all individuals serving in this capacity during the last completed fiscal year, (b) two most highly compensated individuals other than the PEO who served as executive officers as of the end of the fiscal year and whose adjusted total compensation
[

was at least $100,000, and (c) up to two additional individuals who would have been included under (b) if they had still served as executive officers at fiscal year-end. Thus, the core number of NEOs is five, scaled down to three for SRCs and EGCs, but the total number of NEOs for a given registrant can range from one (in the case of an SRC/EGC with no executive officers other than the PEO with adjusted total compensation of at least $100,000) to seven (or potentially more, in cases of PEO or PFO transitions within a fiscal year) individuals.
The proposed amendments would limit the group of NEOs for which disclosure must be provided to a registrant's PEO and PFO (including individuals who served in these capacities for any part of the year).
1. Benefits
As detailed in the Baseline section (IV.C above), registrants have a median of five NEOs, with 15 percent of registrants in the sample reporting four or fewer and 31 percent of registrants with available data reporting six or more.
[
645
]
Limiting the NEO definition to individuals serving as PEO or PFO would therefore significantly reduce the number of executives for which compensation disclosure is required at most registrants. Such a reduction in the coverage of Item 402 disclosure and Form 8-K Item 5.02(b)
[
646
]
and (e) disclosure (regarding departures and compensatory plans, contracts, or arrangements, as discussed earlier in this section) would, in turn, be expected to generate significant compliance cost savings for those registrants relative to their current expenditures on such disclosures.
Most directly, reducing the number of NEOs at most registrants (by 60 percent, from five to two for the typical registrant that is not an SRC or EGC
[
647
]
) would reduce the volume of executive compensation disclosure that needs to be prepared (including the registrant's data collection and monitoring of information). The volume of some components of the disclosures, such as the individual-by-individual compensation information presented in tables, is directly proportional to the number of NEOs and would thus decrease proportionally to the reduction in that number. Narrative disclosures, such as those in the CD&A, may decrease less than proportionally with the number of NEOs if the same discussion can currently apply to multiple NEOs, but may decrease significantly at registrants where compensation design varies sufficiently across the executive roles that incremental NEOs necessitate significant additional narrative.
[
648
]
Overall, the length of most components of executive compensation disclosures would likely decrease to some extent with each fewer NEO. A smaller group of NEOs would thus be expected to significantly reduce the amount of information needed to be collected, reviewed, and presented in disclosures by registrants.
Beyond this volume-related reduction in disclosure burdens, we anticipate that limiting the NEOs to the PEO and PFO, as proposed, would also reduce burdens associated with yearly volatility in a registrant's list of NEOs. Registrants may currently expend resources on tracking, computing, and reviewing the compensation of a large group of executive officers for the purpose of identifying who among them will qualify as the three most highly
(
printed page 75095)
compensated by fiscal year-end.
[
649

The NEOs may vary from year to year as the various amounts and components of compensation for different executives fluctuate over time (including changes due to varying bonuses and equity awards), and ad hoc payments such as severance pay or relocation payments can cause unexpected changes in the list of NEOs. Thus, the incremental impact of narrowing the scope of the NEO definition beyond the effects of the other proposed amendments may be somewhat smaller than the effects of this proposed revision considered in isolation.
The benefits of this proposed revision to the NEO definition are expected to vary across registrants based on two factors: (1) their current number of NEOs (which would drive any reduction in the volume of required disclosure); and (2) the size of the pool of executive officers whose compensation is high enough that they could potentially be classified as an NEO at the end of the fiscal year (which would drive savings due to registrants no longer tracking who might become the most highly compensated executive officers other than the PEO and PFO). Registrants currently disclosing compensation for the largest number (such as seven or more) NEOs, or those registrants with many highly paid executive officers whose similar pay levels create uncertainty about the final list of NEOs, would likely experience the greatest savings. In contrast, SRCs and EGCs, which currently typically disclose compensation for three NEOs, would generally realize more modest benefits from moving to an NEO group of only the PEO and PFO as proposed, though they may still experience substantial savings in tracking executive compensation to the extent they have a

2. Costs
Narrowing the NEO definition to only PEOs and PFOs, as proposed, would reduce the information available to investors about the compensation of registrants' other top executives.
[
657

The significance of this information loss is expected to vary across registrants depending on, among other factors, the degree to which executives other than the PEO and PFO (such as a president or chief operating officer) play a pivotal role in a registrant's strategic decisions. Registrants and investors, directly or through costs passed along by their third-party advisors, may also incur limited short-term transition costs to adapt to the new requirements.
Disclosure about executive compensation can provide information that is likely to be material to investment and voting decisions by allowing investors to, among other things, develop informed expectations about executive decision-making and registrant performance.
[
658

Because the PEO typically has the most direct input into a registrant's direction and strategy, disclosure that conveys an understanding about the PEO's incentives is the most likely to be material for forming these expectations. As the most senior and likely most influential executive, the PEO may also set the tone for the overall dynamic between the board and management. Thus, PEO compensation may also be an important factor in evaluating the effectiveness of boards of directors.
In practice, as indicated by the feedback from commenters, the compensation of PEOs is generally more closely monitored and scrutinized than that of other NEOs.
[
659

For example, some analyses used by investors in reviewing compensation disclosures focus primarily on the compensation of the PEO.
[

We therefore believe that investors generally find PEO compensation to be the most important element of executive compensation disclosure when making investment and voting decisions.
Nonetheless, there are reasons why the compensation of other key executives may also be relevant to investors' investment and voting decisions and therefore the amendment to the definition of NEO may, in some cases, result in a loss of information likely to be material to investors. For example, strategic decision-making responsibilities may be concentrated in a PEO at one registrant but dispersed across several executive officers at a different registrant. Attaining the same degree of understanding about the economic incentives that could affect key decisions might involve information about the compensation of more executive officers at the latter registrant than at the former. Information about the compensation of other executive officers would also demonstrate the similarities and differences between the compensation of the PEO and that of other executives and across the non-PEO executives, allowing investors to more fully evaluate the effectiveness of the compensation committee.
[

Compensation information about other executive officers can also provide insight into the dynamics of a registrant's management team. For example, the differential between a PEO's compensation and that of other executives may provide insights about registrant performance that may relate to the influence of the PEO relative to the rest of the management team,
[

about expected synergies or teamwork among executives,
[

The design of non-PEO executive compensation can also provide information about the likelihood that these important employees will choose to stay at the registrant.

Additionally, some commenters referenced investors' consideration of non-PEO compensation,
[

Registrants may also use compensation disclosures to obtain compensation benchmarking data.

The proposed amendment to the definition of NEOs could reduce the amount of public data available to compensation committees about the compensation of executive officers other than PEOs and PFOs at peer registrants or could increase the reliance of these committees on third-party survey or consultant data (potentially at an incremental cost) when designing compensation for these executives.
[

Finally, investors may also receive less information and/or less timely information about the departure of, or material contracts, plans, or arrangements with, the executive officers for whom Item 5.02(b) and (e) Form 8-K disclosure would no longer be required due to the proposed amendment to the definition of NEO.
[

While some of this information (
e.g.,
regarding executive changes) would generally be disclosed eventually by the registrant, such as in the list of executive officers in its Form 10-K,
[

or may become available through other sources (such as the registrant's website or individual executives' profiles on social media), under the proposed amendments much of the compensation-related information regarding these individuals may not be publicly available to investors and the release of information about these individuals' departures may be delayed.
Including the PFO in the proposed NEO definition partially mitigates these potential reductions in available information. For example, including the PFO may provide partial insight into executive team dynamics and how the compensation committee makes pay decisions for different executive roles. Compensation committees would also continue to have uniform benchmarking data for setting PFO compensation. The executive officers for whom compensation data would no longer be disclosed are those for whom such data are less uniformly available or comparable across registrants under the current rule, because the roles of the other NEOs (beyond PEO and PFO) may vary significantly. That said, such data can still be informative to investors under the baseline for the reasons discussed above, and the reduction in disclosure under the proposal may thereby, for some registrants, reduce the amount of information incorporated into registrant security prices and increase information asymmetries between registrant management and investors or among investors.
Transparency into executive officers' compensation may also encourage more effective compensation design for those executives, which could translate into enhanced executive performance.
[
673

It is therefore possible that reducing the transparency of the compensation of some highly paid executive officers by narrowing the scope of the definition of NEOs could, over time, lead to less effective incentives and thus suboptimal performance by top executives other than PEOs and PFOs. Continuing the disclosure of PEO and PFO compensation should partially mitigate this risk by maintaining transparency of the compensation packages that may set the tone for the design of other executives' compensation and maintaining scrutiny of the compensation of the PEO, who likely bears the greatest responsibility for the performance of other managers and of the registrant and who often plays a role in setting the compensation of the other, non-PEO executives.
Registrants may bear some short-term adjustment costs to update their compliance and disclosure processes. Investors may bear some short-term adjustment costs to adapt their review practices and analyses of executive compensation to a narrower definition of NEO. In both cases, these costs may be borne directly or via payments to third parties. We expect these costs to be minor relative to other adjustment costs discussed in this release because it should be relatively straightforward to identify what to remove from current disclosures or compensation analyses in connection with this proposed revision.
Like the potential benefits of the proposed revision to the definition of NEO, the potential costs of this proposed revision are expected to vary across registrants. The costs to investors may be particularly significant in the case of registrants at which one or more highly paid executive officers who are not the PEO or PFO have a significant role in many strategic decisions (which could include a president or chief operating officer), as, under the proposed amendments, those executive officers' economic incentives may no longer be fully disclosed to investors. Beyond such cases, the costs to investors are generally expected to be the greatest in the context of registrants that report five to seven (or more) NEOs under the current rule, because transparency around the compensation of top executives other than the PEO and PFO would decrease the most in such cases. In contrast, in the context of SRCs, EGCs, and other registrants currently reporting fewer NEOs, the proposed revision to the definition of NEOs would have a more limited effect on the amount of available information about executive officer compensation. If the amendments proposed in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted, depending on timing, a much larger group of registrants would be subject to the same NEO definition applicable to SRCs and EGCs and would thus similarly be associated with more limited costs from the proposed revision to the definition of NEO.
3. Reasonable Alternatives
We considered an alternative definition of NEO that would include either three or four executive officers, with one or more of these individuals being the most highly paid executive officers after the PEO (or PEO and PFO), as recommended by some
(
printed page 75098)
commenters.
[

Such an approach would preserve more of the information currently available about the compensation of top executives, and may be particularly valuable in the case of registrants with, for example, a chief operating officer or president with significant strategic decision-making responsibilities (in light of the relative importance of the third executive to registrant performance). More generally, this approach may provide investors with a broader understanding of the registrant's overall managerial incentives, executive team dynamics, and the compensation committee's and board's compensation philosophy and relationship with the management team. It would also make more data available to compensation committees of peer registrants for the purpose of benchmarking pay. However, such an approach would not reduce compliance costs as significantly as the proposed approach. As discussed in section IV.D.1 above, identifying the most “highly compensated” executive officers under this alternative may require tracking the compensation of a larger group of executive officers than the group of NEOs, particularly for registrants with many highly paid executive officers whose similar pay levels create uncertainty about the final list of NEOs. This task could be simplified by, for example, requiring the determination of the most “highly compensated” executive officers to be based on a limited number of compensation components (such as salary and bonus). Regardless, this alternative tends to introduce at least some uncertainty and volatility into the determination of the group of NEOs due to the uncertainty and volatility in final pay levels (as is the case under the baseline), which in turn would disproportionately increase the compliance burden of adding an additional executive officer to the definition relative to the proposal. Including a most “highly compensated” executive officer without regard for that officer's role would also increase the likelihood that the officer's compensation design differs significantly from that of the PEO, likely expanding the extent of explanatory disclosures a registrant may feel necessary to an understanding of the individual's pay package. Further, given that the additional NEOs under this alternative would not have consistent roles or titles across all registrants, the additional information included under this alternative would be less comparable and thus somewhat more difficult to evaluate for investors than the information pertaining to the PEO and PFO as proposed.
We also considered limiting the definition of NEO to include only the PEO,
[
675

given the primary interest in, and scrutiny of, PEO compensation. However, as discussed in section IV.D.2 above, including the PFO provides insight into issues such as executive team dynamics and how the compensation committee tailors pay to specific roles. The PFO, who has oversight of the registrant's financial management and financial disclosure, also has a unique role at the registrant. Including the PFO provides investors with compensation information that may allow them to gauge the incentives of this key executive and, thereby, the reliability of the registrant's financial disclosures and the soundness of its financial decisions.

Under this alternative, the required disclosures would be further simplified and compliance costs would be further reduced in years of executive transition. This approach would also reduce the volatility in disclosed compensation caused by severance or other departure payments. However, as discussed in the Baseline section (section IV.C. above), PEO and PFO transitions are quite common: approximately twenty percent of PEOs, and thirty percent of PFOs, at registrants with readily available data had less than three years of compensation history in proxy year 2025. Limiting compensation disclosures to PEOs and PFOs serving at the end of a fiscal year, under the alternative, would therefore result in frequently incomplete years of compensation and gaps in the compensation data, making it difficult for investors to analyze pay patterns and evaluate the full cost of executive compensation, including by making it more difficult to compare disclosures across registrants and across years for the same registrant.
E. Primary Tabular Disclosure, Perquisite Disclosure, and Compensation Actually Paid Disclosure Requirements and Flexibility in the Manner of Tabular Presentation
A number of provisions in the current rule and proposed amendments pertain to the standardized quantitative data that registrants must disclose about executive compensation. Because the proposed amendments would substantially revise and reorganize the content that is disclosed in the current set of tables and narrative disclosures into a different set of tables and associated supplemental disclosures, we address all of these provisions in this section. We include consideration of the Compensation Actually Paid measure from existing pay-versus-performance disclosures in this section because it represents quantitative data about executive compensation and because the proposed amendments replace this measure with a measure from one of the new primary compensation tables, but we discuss the other pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements separately in section IV.G. below.
As discussed in the Baseline section (section IV.C. above), most section 12 and section 15(d) registrants
[
678
]
are currently required to disclose annual data about each of their NEOs' compensation in tabular format. For registrants that are not SRCs or EGCs, the executive compensation information is currently presented in six primary tables.
[
679
]
Additional disclosures are either required or delineated as items that must be included if material in footnotes and/or supplementary narrative disclosures to the tables. SRCs and EGCs are currently eligible to use a scaled version of these requirements, including only two primary tables, two rather than three years of disclosure in the Summary Compensation Table, and the exclusion of any amounts or tabular
(
printed page 75099)
disclosures associated with pensions (except when benefits are accelerated).
A subset of the registrants required to provide the primary tabular compensation disclosures
[
680
]
are also required to provide pay-versus-performance disclosures. These disclosures include, among other things, tabular disclosure of five years of Compensation Actually Paid to the PEO and, collectively as an average, to the other NEOs. The current rule defines Compensation Actually Paid based on a computation that is intended to quantify how the value of an executive's total compensation package changed that year, including changes in the value of outstanding equity awards. Other pay-versus-performance requirements are discussed separately in section IV.G below.
The proposed amendments would condense and reorganize the information required in the current primary tabular disclosures into three new tables that would apply to all of the affected registrants. The Granted Compensation Table would present the primary elements of compensation generally at the targeted values initially granted by compensation committees or boards. The Earned Compensation Table would present the value of compensation ultimately earned by executives and provide more comprehensive coverage of the primary as well as other elements of compensation. Both of these tables would present three years of compensation data, or two years for SRCs and EGCs. The Status of Equity Awards Table would provide certain factual details about each outstanding, newly granted, or newly vested (or exercised) equity award, such as the range of shares underlying each award and the current status of each award with respect to vesting or exercise.
In addition to reorganizing certain of the information included in the current tables, the proposed new tabular disclosures would reduce the degree of detail provided, particularly about non-equity incentives, deferred compensation and perquisites, and certain other components of miscellaneous compensation, and would eliminate many currently required computations in favor of focusing on factual disclosure and computations already produced by registrants for other purposes. While the value of the primary elements of pay and certain key terms of incentive awards would be explicitly required to be disclosed, registrants would be subject to a higher dollar threshold below which perquisites need not be reported, would have additional flexibility to include some elements of miscellaneous compensation only if they are material, and would have discretion to determine what additional footnotes or other supplementary disclosure are material information necessary to an understanding of the information disclosed in the primary tabular disclosures. For example, when an amount reported in one of the proposed tables represents an aggregation of multiple individual amounts (such as multiple non-equity award payouts or various miscellaneous items), registrants would have discretion whether to identify the individual components and their values. The proposal would also eliminate the disclosure of Compensation Actually Paid and require that registrants instead use total compensation from the Earned Compensation Table in pay-versus-performance disclosures.
The proposed amendments would also give registrants more flexibility in the manner in which they present their tabular disclosures, such as by splitting a single column into multiple columns (or into a supplemental table) so long as the multiple columns (or supplemental table) are clearly labeled and in the aggregate cover all items of compensation required to be reported in that single column. A registrant would also be permitted to provide any supplemental information in any format it determines to be appropriate, including in additional columns in an existing table.
1. Comparison of Information Environment
Given the significant reorganization and revision of the quantitative executive compensation information that would be required to be disclosed under the proposed amendments, we first identify the most significant changes in the information that registrants would disclose as a result of the proposed changes to the primary tabular disclosures of executive compensation information (and the disclosure of Compensation Actually Paid) in order to facilitate the discussion of potential benefits and costs of these aspects of the proposed amendments.
The proposed amendments would generally reduce the amount of data about executive compensation that is either explicitly required or specifically suggested as possibly meriting inclusion in registrant disclosures. These reductions are expected to decrease the compliance costs associated with producing the disclosures and to enable more streamlined disclosures that registrants would have greater flexibility to tailor to their specific circumstances. The proposed amendments are also intended to better align executive compensation disclosures with the way many registrants view their compensation programs. However, they will likely result in less information being disclosed to the public than under the baseline.
Potential changes to the information environment may stem from the proposed revisions to certain bright-line standards (such as the proposed revised minimum aggregate reporting threshold for perquisites) as well as the proposed movement to more principles-based standards for other provisions. The proposed amended bright-line requirements are intended to retain the information that is most likely to be material to investors, but as they would apply consistently across registrants it is possible in some circumstances that they could result in information that is important to voting and investment decisions no longer being disclosed. There is also information required in current disclosures that would not be explicitly required under the proposal and which may be outside the scope of the proposed principles-based disclosure requirements. For example, the aggregate balances of executive pension and deferred compensation plans are reported currently but are not required under the proposal and, even if material, may not be within the scope of the materiality catch-all provisions discussed in more detail below.
Other information would no longer be explicitly required to be disclosed, or would no longer be delineated in lists of examples of potentially material items for consideration in registrant disclosures, but would still be the subject of a duty to disclose if material given a registrant's specific facts and circumstances. Some of this information may thereby still be disclosed by some registrants under the proposed principles-based disclosure requirements but may no longer be as consistently available (or as consistently presented) across registrants.
The principles-based requirements are intended to continue to require registrants to disclose material information, thereby preserving investor access to this information, but may still result in some information that is within the scope of the principles-based disclosure requirements and relevant to
(
printed page 75100)
voting and investment decisions no longer being disclosed. In the next subsection, we discuss how this may happen. In the following subsections, we then discuss the potential changes that could result from the proposed amendments in three broad categories of information: information about the level of executive compensation (also known as the “amount” or “quantum” of pay), information about the performance sensitivity of such compensation, and information about other components and terms of compensation. We consider changes in information in these three categories because we understand that they are consistent with the factors that investors most commonly evaluate with respect to executive compensation.

a. Sources of Potential Information Loss Under Materiality-Based Standards
The proposed amendments introduce several new materiality-based standards for the disclosures.
[
682
]
Pursuant to proposed Item 402(a)(1), the objective of Item 402 disclosures would be to provide investors with material information relevant to an assessment of the compensation of the registrant's named executive officers and directors. Pursuant to proposed Item 402(a)(5)(i), registrants would be required to disclose any material information necessary to an understanding of the information disclosed in the primary tabular disclosures, namely the proposed Earned Compensation Table, Granted Compensation Table and Status of Equity Awards Table. Also, specifically with respect to the components of pay included in the proposed Earned Compensation Table, outside of certain delineated items, registrants would be instructed to include any other compensation that the registrant determines is material (or otherwise elects to disclose).
[
683
]
As discussed in the previous section, the scope of these materiality-based disclosure standards would not encompass all of the information that is required to be disclosed in current Item 402 disclosures. Nevertheless, we expect that these materiality-based disclosure provisions—including one applying broadly to information material to an understanding of the information disclosed in the primary tabular disclosures and one applying specifically to the inclusion of dollar values of material compensation to the NEOs—would preserve the disclosure of material information that falls within these categories. At the same time, there are several factors, discussed in the following paragraphs, that may result in investors having access to a reduced amount of relevant information when making their investment and voting decisions.
First, the materiality determinations would be made at the registrant level, but investors often consider information about compensation practices in the broader market when evaluating and making decisions about a particular registrant.
[
684
]
For example, when evaluating whether the performance conditions applied to a PEO's non-equity incentive award appear appropriate, investors may consider how these conditions compare to the performance conditions attached to non-equity incentive awards of peer PEOs. Under the proposed amendments, an element of compensation that is disclosed by all registrants under the baseline might be disclosed, for instance, by one registrant, because it is material given that registrant's circumstances, but might not be disclosed by other registrants, because it is not material based on their own facts and circumstances. While all of these registrants would be properly disclosing material information, investors may have less context with which to precisely evaluate the first registrant's disclosures than they would under the baseline.
Second, materiality determinations are fact-specific for a given time. Item 402 compensation disclosures are generally made annually, and the underlying facts may change at a time when there is not a present duty to disclose or update information about an executive's compensation and monetary incentives. In contrast, investors evaluate registrants and make decisions throughout the year, the materiality of information may change at any point during the year.
[
685
]
For example, at a company that has not historically paid dividends, it may not be material whether or not the PEO is entitled to dividends on unearned equity; but if the company newly begins paying dividends during the year, factors that could help investors to better understand the context and ramifications of this corporate action may become more important to their investment or voting decisions. Under the baseline, information about (for example) certain terms of incentive awards or certain components of compensation is generally disclosed by all registrants regardless of materiality. Under the proposed amendments, if this information (such as whether the PEO is entitled to dividends on unearned equity, or any specific terms of non-equity incentive awards) is not material at the time that a registrant's annual compensation disclosure is made, the information might not be available to investors if it becomes material thereafter.
Third, there may be information in current executive compensation disclosures that is important to investment or voting decisions that registrants deem to be immaterial.
[
686
]
(
printed page 75101)
The materiality of executive compensation depends on multiple complex factors. For example, a small quantum of pay, which could look immaterial by typical quantitative standards, may still be material because of the outsize effects executive actions (and, by extension, their incentives) can have on registrant performance.
[
687
]
There is thus a risk that information in current disclosures that appears to be immaterial but may, in fact, be material to investor decisions may not be disclosed under the proposal.
While materiality-based standards may increase the likelihood of the loss of important information relative to what would be available under a more prescriptive disclosure standard, they also have benefits, including reducing the risk of immaterial disclosures. The potential loss of information under the proposal may be partially mitigated by investor expectations for more detailed information, as expressed through their voting support or direct engagement with registrants, and the development of market practices or norms for disclosure. It is also possible that some registrants respond to the proposed principles-based requirements with an over-disclosure of information beyond what is material in order to limit the risk of omitting material information, thus reducing any information loss relative to the baseline.
[
688
]
In summary, while the proposed amendments are intended to retain the disclosure of the information about executive compensation that is most likely to be material, some reduction in information will nevertheless result. In characterizing the effects of the proposed amendments on the information available to investors in the following subsections we therefore identify some of the information that may no longer be available (or consistently available) to investors even though we believe that aspects of the proposal would mitigate the loss of material information.

The proposed amendments would require stock and option awards with performance-based vesting or other such contingencies to be included in the Granted Compensation Table at their fair value under the assumption that the award's target outcome will be achieved. For awards with only service conditions that affect whether or not an award vests, there should be no difference in the valuations. Awards with service conditions that affect factors other than whether or not an award vests (such as, for example, an exercise price that varies with years of service) are generally rare, and the degree to which the value reported for such awards they would differ under the proposed amendments would depend on the nature of the service condition and how the award is structured. For awards with performance conditions, we understand that the proposed and baseline valuation approaches should generally give similar results because the target outcome is usually closely aligned with the probable outcome.
[
701
]
That said, it is possible that registrants could respond to the proposed amendments by setting target outcomes that differ more significantly from probable outcomes than in current practice, which could introduce greater imprecision into the reported valuations. For awards with market conditions, the current and proposed valuations may differ significantly. Because reasonable techniques for valuing the effects of market conditions currently exist and account for all of the possible outcomes of an award, we expect that the simpler approach of assuming the target outcome is achieved would generally provide a less precise estimate of award value than the values disclosed currently.
The second difference delineated above should reduce the volatility in reported pay caused by the change in value of all previously accumulated pension benefits with changes in interest rates and other actuarial assumptions. This reduction in reported pay volatility would only affect registrants whose NEOs receive pension benefits, which are a minority of registrants among which larger registrants are disproportionately represented.
[
702
]
While we understand that pension plans are more prevalent among larger registrants, the inclusion of pension service costs even for SRCs and EGCs, which are not currently required to disclose pension-related compensation, should increase the precision with which investors can measure the level of executive compensation for any EGCs and SRCs that provide pension benefits to their NEOs.
[
703
]
That said, the proposed change in the treatment of pensions would obscure the effects on pension benefits of any unexpected increases in pay,
[
704
]
which are not reflected in computations of pension service costs.
With respect to the third point of difference listed above, if compensation practices were to remain unchanged, the exclusion of perquisites below the proposed threshold would reduce the precision with which investors can measure the level of executive compensation to a modest degree. As demonstrated in this table, the proposed threshold would result in the vast majority of perquisites that total no more than 2.5 percent of total compensation no longer

If the use of perquisites were to expand as a result of reduced scrutiny, such that our random sample is not representative of expected practices, the proposed disclosure threshold could introduce a larger amount of noise into measures of the level of executive compensation, particularly at smaller registrants. As demonstrated in Table 4 of the Baseline section (section IV.C) above, we estimate that about five percent of registrants currently pay their PEOs $500,000 or less in total compensation. For such registrants, the proposed threshold could result in perquisites representing 30 percent or more of a PEO's compensation not being disclosed.
The proposed miscellaneous category of compensation may also introduce a small degree of imprecision into measures of the level of pay given that what items (beyond the delineated list of items) are material and therefore included in this category may vary across registrants. We expect any resulting noise to be minor, but it may be difficult for investors or third parties to make adjustments to enhance comparability because specific information about the components of miscellaneous compensation received (and thus what is either included or excluded) may not be available.
Under the proposed amendments, the ability to construct the alternative measures of the level of pay currently in use that involve revaluing equity awards under alternative assumptions or removing certain components of compensation would depend on the extent to which registrants disclose all of the terms of equity awards necessary for such computations and identify the amounts of each of the components of compensation that would be deducted.
c. Information About the Performance Sensitivity of Compensation
Equity awards, non-equity incentive awards, and certain bonuses deliver varying amounts of value to NEOs depending on registrant and/or NEO performance. While other components of pay tend to vary less with performance,
[
706
]
the amount of pay delivered through these other components can also fluctuate in a way that can serve to either enhance or partially offset these performance incentives.
Current executive compensation disclosures include information about the
ex ante
contingencies that affect future compensation payouts, information about outstanding equity awards and how the expected value of these “in flight” awards has changed, and information about the
ex post
value eventually realized by the NEOs from all of the elements of their compensation. The “in flight” and
ex post
values cannot be perfectly constructed based on the disclosure about
ex ante
compensation structure because, for example, specific performance thresholds are often not disclosed
[
707
]
and incremental compensation decisions made while awards are outstanding may affect the total amount of compensation that is eventually realized. The progress toward outcomes reflected in “in flight” valuations and the actual
ex post
outcomes provide insight into the rigor of performance goals and how the board's compensation decisions during a given performance period may have magnified, dampened, or otherwise modified the executive's monetary incentives. Under the proposed amendments, we believe that most of the information about
ex ante
incentives and
ex post
outcomes would still be disclosed in some form, while disclosure about “in flight” values would be limited.
Regarding the
ex ante
contingencies that affect future payouts, the primary terms that are set in advance to provide direct performance incentives and establish the horizon of these incentives are (with varying applicability depending on the award): vesting schedules; performance or market conditions (or service conditions affecting factors other than vesting), including the associated formula or range of payouts and performance period; and option exercise prices and expiration dates. Registrants (including SRCs and EGCs) are currently required to disclose option exercise prices and expiration dates in tabular format;
[
708
]
equity vesting schedules in footnote disclosures;
[
709
]
and non-equity incentive award vesting schedules and performance-based conditions (whether for equity or non-equity awards) in narrative disclosures.
[
710
]
Registrants other than SRCs and EGCs are also currently required to disclose the range of potential payouts of newly-granted incentive awards in the Grants of Plan-Based Awards Table.
Under the proposed amendments, the range of potential payouts under equity awards and the exercise prices of any option awards would be reported in the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table, while all of the other primary
ex ante
equity award terms other than option expiration date would be explicitly required to be disclosed pursuant to proposed Item 402(d)(3), but could be provided in footnotes, narrative, or tabular disclosure at the registrant's election. Option expiration dates would be disclosed to the extent material given a registrant's facts and circumstances.
[
711
]
Under both the
(
printed page 75104)
current rule and the proposed amendments, registrants are not required to disclose specific target levels or goals that affect compensation outcomes if doing so would result in competitive harm to the registrant.
The current rule requires disclosures about outstanding equity awards in the Outstanding Equity Awards at Fiscal Year-End Table, with, for registrants other than SRCs and EGCs, additional information in the Grants of Plan-Based Awards Table. Current disclosures also provide information about the updated value of “in flight” equity awards in two places. For equity awards with performance-based vesting, all registrants are required to compute and report in the Outstanding Equity Awards at Fiscal Year-End Table a number of shares or units as well as an estimated dollar payout value based on either the actual achievement of performance goals (for awards that have been earned but not yet vested) or how actual performance to-date compares to upcoming performance goals (for unearned, unvested awards).
[
712
]
More broadly, in the computation of Compensation Actually Paid for the purpose of pay-versus-performance disclosures, registrants other than EGCs (and those not filing proxy or information statements)
[
713
]
are required to calculate and include (and separately identify) the updated fair value of all new equity awards as of the end of the fiscal year and the change in fair value relative to the prior fiscal year-end of any outstanding equity awards through the end of the fiscal year (or, in both cases, as of their vesting date, if earlier). These computations are provided for the PEO and, as an average, for the other NEOs as a group. The measure of compensation actually paid in these disclosures can be used directly as an aggregate measure of “realizable pay” reflecting these “in flight” values.
The proposed amendments would not require any “in flight” valuations of incentive awards. However, the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table would provide an overview of all of an NEO's equity awards, including those granted in previous years that are still “in flight” as well as those newly granted, newly vested, or newly exercised or expired. Investors or their advisors may be able to construct approximate estimates of the value of “in flight” awards, as some do currently,
[
714
]
with the potential precision of such estimates depending on the extent to which registrants disclose all of the terms and performance goals necessary to compute a precise fair value for such awards. The greatest sources of imprecision in these estimates relative to registrant-produced estimates are likely to be (i) a lack of access to the specific performance goals underlying awards
[
715
]
and therefore how performance is tracking relative to those goals
[
716
]
and (ii) any simplifications used by investors or third parties to make these computations for a large number of registrants.
[
717
]
The current rule also requires the disclosure of certain
ex post
realized amounts of pay based on actual performance outcomes. As in the case of measures of the level of pay, measures of realized pay in use by investors and third parties differ in what components they include and how they value them (particularly with respect to whether they consider options at vesting or at exercise).
[
718
]
Currently, in the case of salary, bonuses, non-equity incentive payouts, and items categorized in “all other compensation” (such as perquisites and registrant contributions to deferred compensation plans), the realized amounts are reported in the Summary Compensation Table for all registrants and can be included or excluded based on the particular definition of realized pay being used. With respect to equity, depending on the definition of realized pay, the realized amounts can be obtained directly from the Option Exercises and Stock Vested Table or can be constructed based on the award terms disclosed in other tables or narrative.
[
719
]
(
printed page 75105)
For SRCs and EGCs, which are not required to include the Options Exercises and Stock Vested Table, information about the realized value on option or stock grants can be derived based on information in Form 4 disclosures with potential reference to Item 402 disclosures to compute realized equity values under the desired definition.
[

]
The proposed amendments would make one measure of realized pay—the total presented in the proposed Earned Compensation Table—directly accessible for all of the affected registrants. The measure would be similar to one that can currently be constructed relatively easily for registrants other than SRCs and EGCs,
[
721
]
but not so easily for SRCs and EGCs.
[

The ability of investors or third parties to construct alternative measures of realized pay that involve valuing options upon vesting or removing certain components of compensation would depend on the extent to which registrants disclose all of the terms of equity awards necessary for such computations and separately identify and quantify each of the components of compensation.
d. Information About Other Components and Terms of Compensation
Beyond the information about the level of pay and the primary performance incentives provided by equity and non-equity awards, there are details about a number of other components of compensation and about other terms of incentive awards that are currently required to be disclosed and that investors may evaluate today. Examples of some of these other compensation components and terms are provided throughout this subsection. While information about some of these factors would still be required to be reported by registrants if it is material information necessary to an understanding of the information disclosed in the tables pursuant to proposed Item 402(a)(5)(i), and may be reported voluntarily in additional cases, the proposed amendments are expected to result in reduced disclosure about at least some of these compensation components and terms by some registrants.
For registrants other than SRCs and EGCs, current disclosures provide significant detail about the balances of and annual changes in NEO retirement plans in the Pension Benefits Table and Nonqualified Deferred Compensation Table. Because these tables would be eliminated under the proposed amendments, information about the NEOs' present value of accumulated benefits in any pension plans and aggregate balance in any non-qualified deferred compensation plans may no longer be disclosed.
[
723
]
Similarly, actual payments and distributions under any of these plans to NEOs who already qualify to receive such amounts, as well as years in service and any contributions made by NEOs themselves, might not be disclosed. SRCs and EGCs are not currently required to provide the tables specific to retirement benefits but are required to disclose the material terms of each plan that provides for the payment of retirement benefits; these disclosures might also not be provided under the proposed amendments. While pension service costs and prior service costs, employer contributions to defined contribution or other deferred compensation plans, and any above-market or preferential earnings on non-qualified deferred compensation plans would be included in dollar terms in the aggregate in the Miscellaneous Compensation Received column of the proposed Earned Compensation Table, they may no longer be separately identified.
Beyond these retirement-related amounts, other elements of the current “other compensation” category that could be included in the proposed “miscellaneous” category may also be less likely to be separately identified than under the current rule. Currently, registrants other than SRCs and EGCs are required to identify and quantify any item that is not a perquisite whose value exceeds $10,000, while SRCs and EGCs are required to identify and quantify any item of “other compensation” to the extent material, where identification of an item is not considered material if it does not exceed the greater of $25,000 or 10 percent of all items of a given type.
[
724
]
Under the proposed amendments, while an aggregate amount of miscellaneous compensation to an NEO would be disclosed, it may be unclear to what extent, for example, the miscellaneous compensation consists of tax gross-ups, retirement contributions, a discount for purchases of the registrant's securities, or another item included in the miscellaneous category. It also may be unclear which elements the registrant has included (because they are material or because the registrant otherwise elects to include them) versus which have been excluded as immaterial.
Current disclosures also include significant detail specific to perquisites. For registrants other than SRCs and EGCs, if the total value of perquisites to an NEO exceeds $10,000, these registrants must identify each perquisite by type (regardless of its amount, but without quantification). All registrants, including SRCs and EGCs,
[
725
]
generally
(
printed page 75106)
also quantify the value of each perquisite that exceeds the greater of $25,000 or 10 percent of the NEO's total perquisites in footnote disclosure. Given the proposed higher threshold for disclosing perquisites and no longer requiring individual perquisites to be identified or quantified, we expect that most of these details would no longer be disclosed under the proposed amendments. Further, the proposed changes in interpretive guidance to determine whether an item is a perquisite would give registrants greater flexibility to identify certain benefits as not constituting perquisites. Additionally, the proposed changes to perquisites would specifically rescind a prior Commission statement that security services provided at an executive's personal residence or during personal travel are always perquisites. These changes may result in reduced disclosure of certain items, such as the provision of security services, relative to what is currently reported.
Registrants (including SRCs and EGCs) are also currently required to disclose the material terms of all incentive awards with respect to NEOs, which the current rule defines to include certain delineated terms beyond those pertaining directly to the performance contingencies and horizons discussed in the previous subsection. For example, these delineated terms include any tandem features
[
726
]
and whether dividends will be paid on stock awards, and if so, the applicable dividend rate and whether that rate is preferential. Registrants might not disclose all such terms of incentive awards in Item 402 disclosures under the proposed amendments. It is possible that some of these terms may be disclosed in relation to compensatory plans, contracts or arrangements and material grants thereunder filed pursuant to the current reporting requirements under Item 5.02 of Form 8-K.
