2. Benefits
The proposed amendments to the tabular disclosures and associated footnotes and narrative disclosures are expected to reduce compliance costs, make certain information more readily available to the users of disclosure, and reduce the risk of certain distortions in executive compensation due solely to the nature of current disclosure requirements.
The primary sources of compliance cost savings would be a reduction in the need to track and collect certain data, the elimination of certain complex computations, and a reduced volume of disclosure that would have to be produced and reviewed.
With respect to tracking and data collection, the proposed amendments would introduce a new
de minimis
tracking exclusion below which registrants would not be required to track perquisites. Several commenters indicated that the tracking, recordkeeping, and analysis of even very minor potential perquisites imposed significant burdens on registrants.
[
728
]
The proposed
de minimis
tracking exclusion would align with the threshold used to identify fringe benefits for tax purposes, and should thus limit the need to track small benefits beyond what would already have to be tracked for these other purposes.
[
729
]
The
de minimis
tracking exclusion would thereby reduce burdens on a registrant's internal time and resources and could reduce the costs of consulting outside advisors to analyze, even for very minor benefits, whether they are perquisites. The revised interpretive guidance with respect to identifying perquisites could also reduce the items that must be tracked (to the extent that registrants determine certain items are not properly categorized as perquisites) and could, in some circumstances, further align which benefits must be tracked with benefits that would, regardless, be tracked for tax purposes. The proposed amendments would also require items of miscellaneous compensation that are not specifically delineated in proposed Item 402(b)(2)(vii) to be included only if material (or if the registrant otherwise opts to include them), in contrast to the current requirement to include all other compensation regardless of amount, which may reduce the need to track other immaterial forms of compensation.
The proposed amendments would also eliminate the need for registrants to perform certain complex computations that we understand are not used for any other purpose beyond compensation disclosures. For example, the calculation of Compensation Actually Paid for the purpose of pay-versus-performance disclosures has been cited as a particularly burdensome element of the current requirements.
[
730
]
Commenters particularly highlighted the burdens of revaluing equity awards every year and at every vesting date
[
731
]
and tracking accrued dividends,
[
732
]
and noted that many registrants must rely on external consultants to construct the measure.
[
733
]
While some commenters
(
printed page 75107)
indicated that costs have come down since the initial years of the disclosure,
[
734
]
this computational burden still represents an incremental cost on registrants other than EGCs (and other registrants that do not file a proxy or information statement in a given year), and removing the requirement to make this computation should result in meaningful cost savings.
Other complex computations that would be eliminated by the proposed amendments currently apply to a broader group of registrants. Specifically, several commenters stated that producing the Outstanding Equity Awards Table, which is required in executive compensation disclosure for all registrants and requires a different set of equity award valuations than any other table, is burdensome.
[
735
]
The most complex computations required in this table are likely those involving the determination of the number of shares or units and the dollar payout value of outstanding awards with performance-based vesting based on how the performance goals compare to recent performance. Such computations would no longer be required under the proposed amendments; the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table would instead present only factual information about equity awards and whether they have vested or been exercised. The proposed interpretive guidance with respect to the identification of perquisites and the elimination of the requirement that perquisites must be valued on the basis of the aggregate incremental cost to the registrant could also reduce the computational burden on registrants. In particular, the need to undertake complicated calculations could be reduced to the extent that (i) registrants determine that certain items which required complex computations to derive the value to be reported in compensation disclosure were not properly categorized as perquisites (given their specific circumstances) and/or (ii) the greater flexibility in how perquisites are valued allows registrants to use simpler computations than they do currently or to rely on computations already produced for tax or other purposes.
[
736
]
The proposed amendments with respect to the primary tabular compensation disclosures are also expected to significantly reduce the volume of disclosure that must be prepared and reviewed by registrant staff, the board and, often, external advisors. Registrants other than SRCs and EGCs are currently required to include six primary tables, each of which is often associated with detailed footnotes and/or narrative disclosure and is time-consuming to produce.
[
737
]
Under the proposal, only three primary tables would be required of all registrants. Additional reductions in the volume of disclosures may result depending on how registrants use the flexibility afforded to them. For example, the proposed tabular disclosures would have no explicit footnote requirements, which may allow registrants to condense disclosures and limit duplication of any material information that is required to supplement the data in the tables. Also, to the extent that the proposed tables are substitutes, or close substitutes, for some disclosures that registrants currently provide on a voluntary basis to supplement the mandated disclosures, registrants may reduce the extent of supplementary disclosures they provide. Overall, the proposed amendments to the primary tabular disclosures are expected to substantially reduce the volume of disclosures (via the number of tables, the length of accompanying narrative and footnotes, and potentially the extent of voluntary supplemental disclosures) and thereby reduce the time and resources required to produce and review the disclosures.
[
738
]
Certain aspects of the proposed amendments to the tabular and associated disclosures would also provide investors with more ready access to certain information. For example, investors would have more direct access to a target-based measure of the level of the primary components of pay in the proposed Granted Compensation Table. In some cases, this measure may be something that investors could easily construct based on existing disclosures, but in other cases, it could provide access to compensation values that investors currently may have difficulty estimating. Specifically, to the extent that registrants include information about performance-stock units granted soon after the end of the fiscal year, the total column in the proposed Granted Compensation Table may provide a more up-to-date picture of the level of granted pay than can often be gleaned from current disclosures.
[
739
]
To the extent that some SRCs and EGCs provide pension benefits to their NEOs, the proposed amendments would also allow for the construction of a more consistent measure of the comprehensive level of compensation for such issuers relative both to larger issuers that award and currently report pensions and to SRCs and EGCs that do not provide pensions.
With respect to the performance sensitivity of pay, while the proposed amendments would not require any valuations of “in flight” equity awards, the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table would provide a single, more uniform (given that it would apply to all registrants) source of award-by-award information about the status of all new, in flight, and recently vested or expired awards.
[
740
]
Because this information is
(
printed page 75108)
spread across multiple tables in current compensation disclosures and is sometimes aggregated across awards of the same type, the proposed table may reduce search costs for investors seeking to track the status of particular awards or to understand how the actual and potential outcomes of awards granted in recent years layer together to provide performance and retention incentives.
[
741
]
The proposed tabular disclosures would also provide more direct access to a measure of
ex post
realized compensation, in the total column of the proposed Earned Compensation Table. For investors interested in evaluating how the board's design of executive compensation granted some years in the past translated into pay outcomes based on actual performance,
[
742
]
this proposed table would likely make the inputs required to perform this analysis more accessible, particularly in the case of SRCs and EGCs.
[
743
]
The reduced volume of disclosures and additional flexibility afforded to registrants to tailor their primary tabular and associated disclosures under the more principles-based approach of the proposed amendments could also increase the efficiency with which some investors review the disclosures. By allowing registrants to split the prescribed columns or tables to more clearly present their specific compensation programs, to focus any supplementary disclosure to the tables on material information, and to format these supplementary disclosures in the way they believe to be most effective, the proposed amendments may allow investors reading disclosures linearly to more readily understand registrants' unique compensation programs.
The proposed amendments to the primary tabular and associated disclosures may also reduce the risk of certain distortions in board and/or compensation committee decision-making. In particular, registrants' decisions to provide their NEOs with certain benefits or services may be influenced by considerations of the impact of such decisions on executive compensation disclosure.
[
744
]
Separately, the increased complexity of calculating Compensation Actually Paid for pay-versus-performance disclosure when awards have frequent (such as monthly or quarterly) vesting schedules may discourage such vesting schedules solely because of the associated computational burden.
[
745
]
The proposed revised interpretive guidance regarding the identification of perquisites and the proposed elimination of the requirement to compute the current measure of Compensation Actually Paid would reduce the risk of such distortions or, even in the absence of actual distortions, would enable boards and/or compensation committees to focus on more substantive considerations when making these decisions.
The benefits of the proposed amendments to the primary tabular and associated disclosures are expected to vary across registrants. Specifically, any compliance cost savings are likely to be lower for SRCs and EGCs given that they are not currently required to include many of the tables and associated disclosures that would no longer be required under the proposed amendments. If the proposed amendments in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted as proposed, a larger subset of registrants (
i.e.,
NAFs) would be subject to all of the accommodations currently available to SRCs or EGCs. Under those circumstances, the compliance costs savings attributable to the proposed amendments to the tabular and associated disclosures would be lower than they would be with the current filer status framework in place. At the same time, investors may benefit more from the proposed amendments to the primary tabular and associated disclosures in the context of SRCs and EGCs (or, if the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted as proposed, the broader group of NAFs) than in the case of other registrants, given the increased accessibility and comparability of the information in the proposed Earned Compensation Table relative to similar information in these registrants' current disclosures.
[
746
]
The proposed narrowing the scope of NEOs would also directly reduce the degree of perquisite tracking, the number of computations, and the volume of disclosure produced in the tabular and associated disclosures. Thus, when considered in combination with that proposed change, the incremental compliance cost savings of the proposed amendments to the tabular and associated disclosures would be lower than when considered independently.

3. Costs
The proposed amendments to the primary tabular and associated disclosures are expected to result in short-term adjustment costs for multiple parties, ongoing search and analysis costs for investors, a reduction in the precision with which executive compensation is evaluated (and thus an increased risk of suboptimal investment and voting decisions), costs to registrants in determining materiality and tailoring disclosures, and a risk of distortions in compensation structures.
Registrants and investors, either directly or through third parties (such as compensation consultants, proxy advisors, and executive compensation data aggregators), are expected to experience short-term adjustment costs in adapting to the proposed primary tabular and associated disclosures. The proposed amendments represent a significant overhaul of the executive compensation disclosures with which these parties have developed experience—in many cases, over the past two decades.
[
747
]
As a result, these parties may all have to revise their technological systems, internal processes, and contracts with other parties to adapt to a new set of disclosures, all of which may entail costs. For registrants, making materiality determinations and deciding how best to tailor disclosures may require extra effort in the first year of compliance with new disclosure requirements. Registrants may also expend some resources to engage with investors, other registrants, and third parties, including external advisors and trade groups, to develop market practices and norms relating to some of the more principles-based elements of the proposed amendments. For investors and other users of executive compensation disclosure, in the short term, comparisons across years may be more likely to span the current and proposed new disclosure regimes and may thus be complicated by the changes in data and presentation format. Similarly, comparisons across registrants may be complicated in the short term by differences in the interpretation and application of the rules across registrants, until the development of market practices and norms relating to varied compensation features and structures in the proposed tables.
For the investors and other users of executive compensation disclosure, more condensed and principles-based disclosures may entail ongoing incremental search and analysis costs to find, organize, and evaluate material information.
[
748
]
Specifically, investors, other registrants, and third parties (such as compensation consultants and proxy advisors) may bear increased search costs to the extent that information that they currently have experience finding in relatively consistent locations (whether in tables, footnotes, or narrative) would be inconsistently available under the proposed amendments or presented in different formats and locations by different registrants, which is a risk of any principles-based disclosure requirement. Sections V.E.1.b, c, and d above identify information about the level of pay, its performance sensitivity, and other factors with respect to executive compensation that may be used currently by investors or other registrants (directly or via compensation consultants or proxy advisors) that may be less readily or less consistently available under the proposed amendments.
For example, the proposed amendments do not prescribe how or where in the disclosure (and at what level of detail or aggregation) information about certain terms of incentive awards should be reported, so the time required to locate, understand, and organize this information may be greater than in the case of current disclosures. Also, the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table would, like the current Grants of Plan-Based Awards Table, include certain terms of newly granted equity awards, but, unlike the current table, would not be required to include information about non-equity incentive awards. Depending on where the material terms of these awards are disclosed it may therefore take additional time to understand the nature of non-equity incentive awards.
[
749
]
The flexibility afforded to registrants under the proposal to split columns or tables may further increase the variation in location of similar information across filings of different registrants and thus entail additional search costs. These search costs may be partially mitigated, over time, by the potential development of any market practices or norms (or investor requests) that increase the consistency of the inclusion and location of information in disclosures.
Elements of the proposed amendments that condense the disclosures could also contribute to search costs. For example, under the current rule, the Options Exercised and Stock Vested Table can currently be used to identify options that have been exercised or stock that has vested in this fiscal year. Under the proposed disclosures, identifying these amounts would require comparing items in the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table to the similar table in the previous year's disclosure. Sections V.E.1.b, c, and d above also identify information that may excluded from a particular registrant's executive compensation disclosures under the proposal but may be included in other filings (such as a Form 4 or an Item 5.02 8-K); users of executive compensation disclosure who seek such information would also bear search costs to access and review these additional disclosures.
[
750
]
The proposed amendments could also increase the resources users of disclosures expend on analyzing the information in the disclosures, particularly to the extent they seek measures or analyses reflecting the “in flight” valuations of outstanding awards to get a more real-time and comprehensive sense of how compensation is tracking performance than possible using
ex post
realized pay.
[
751
]
As discussed in section IV.E.1.c
(
printed page 75110)
above, the proposed disclosures would no longer require such valuations and would thus reduce access to registrant-computed values, though some investors or third parties already produce their own related estimates.
[
752
]
To the extent that additional investors begin to construct such estimates or rely more heavily on third parties for such analysis if the proposed amendments are adopted, those investors may bear direct or indirect costs of such computations.
[
753
]
The costs of analysis may also increase for investors or third parties who rely on measures of the level of pay or realized pay outcomes other than those that can be directly extracted from the proposed disclosures, to the extent that these measures are more readily constructed based on current disclosures, as discussed in section IV.E.1.c above.
The proposed amendments to the primary tabular and associated disclosures would also result in less detailed and comprehensive information about executive compensation being available to investors. Some of the information that may no longer be disclosed or that may be less consistently or readily available under the proposed amendments to the primary tabular and associated disclosures may be of little consequence. For example, some of this information may be highly granular and thus unlikely to be material, such as the individual identification of extremely low-value perquisites. But other information that may be unavailable or less consistently available under the proposed amendments may, particularly when considered in aggregate, reduce the precision of investor evaluations of executive compensation and thus introduce noise into decisions that are made in reliance on information about executive compensation.
[
754

F. Compensation Discussion and Analysis
Certain registrants are required to provide a CD&A discussing the compensation granted to, earned by, or paid to the NEOs. The current stated purpose of the CD&A is “to provide investors material information that is necessary to an understanding of the registrant's compensation policies and decisions regarding the NEOs,” which can reduce information asymmetries between registrants and investors about how the registrant approaches its executive compensation program. Currently, the rules include seven required topics to be covered in CD&As, as well as a list of fifteen example topics that may be material for inclusion depending on a registrant's facts and circumstances.

Specifically, the proposed reduction in the number of required topics and elimination of the non-exhaustive examples of potential topics may allow registrants to reduce the inclusion of boilerplate, repetitive, or superfluous content to the extent that it was merely being included to ensure a response to some or all of these potential topics despite such topics having been already sufficiently covered or not being material in the context of their compensation programs. 3. Reasonable Alternatives
As an alternative to the proposed amendments to CD&A requirements, we could amend the rule to replace all of the current required topics and example topics with a fully principles-based requirement that registrants discuss any material information necessary to an understanding of the registrant's compensation policies and decisions regarding the NEOs. This approach would maximize flexibility to registrants and could result in even more focused, tailored disclosure. However, this approach could be more burdensome for registrants, who may need to spend a significant additional amount of time determining the scope of information to disclose in the absence of any required items for the disclosure. This approach could also lead to over disclosure (reducing the size of any potential reductions in disclosure volume and compliance cost savings), if, in the absence of guidance, registrants produce excess disclosures in order to reduce the risk of missing any potentially material topics. The resulting disclosures could also be less efficient for investors to process, if different registrants interpret the scope of the CD&A very differently.
We could, alternatively, retain a select number of example topics from the current rule (with the same or revised language) targeted at more consistently retaining disclosures in which investors have shown the greatest interest. However, such an approach would reduce registrant flexibility and increase the risk of boilerplate disclosures and could reduce the extent to which CD&As are shortened and streamlined to focus on material information.

The tabular disclosure must include the two compensation measures for both the PEO and, collectively on an average basis, the non-PEO NEOs, and is required to be accompanied by detailed footnotes demonstrating how Compensation Actually Paid was derived from total compensation from the Summary Compensation Table and providing (or cross-referencing) equity valuation assumptions. Under a principles-based requirement, the registrants subject to pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements are also currently required to describe the relationship between Compensation Actually Paid (for the PEO and, collectively on an average basis, the other NEOs) and each of the three registrant performance measures in the tabular disclosures (where the description of the relationship with the TSR of the registrant must include a comparison of the registrant's TSR to the reported peer group TSR). The pay-versus-performance disclosures are also required to include a table listing the names of the three to seven “most important” financial performance measures that are used to link Compensation Actually Paid to performance (the Tabular List). SRCs are subject to a scaled version of these requirements with three years of disclosures, fewer quantified performance measures, no peer group disclosure, no Tabular List, and the exclusion of amounts associated with pension plans in the computation of Compensation Actually Paid.

]
These requirements are proposed to be amended to reflect a more simplified requirement to relate the PEO's and PFO's total compensation from the Earned Compensation Table to registrant TSR over the past three years, with no prescriptive tabular elements or mandated formats.
1. Benefits
The proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements are expected to reduce compliance costs, provide registrants with greater flexibility in their disclosures of how their executive compensation relates to performance, and simplify compensation disclosures.
The greatest compliance costs savings from these amendments are expected to result from the elimination of the disclosure of the Compensation Actually Paid measure. As discussed previously in section IV.E, this computation is often quite complex and has been associated with significant burdens, though these computational costs may have decreased since the initial years of disclosure.
[
804
]
The proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements are also expected to reduce costs by reducing the volume of disclosure that must be prepared and reviewed by registrant staff, directors, and external advisors such as legal counsel and compensation consultants. The current pay-versus-performance disclosures require two tables and very extensive footnotes reconciling computations and providing valuation assumptions, all of which would no longer be required. Based on staff experience, eliminating these footnotes alone would typically reduce pay-versus-performance disclosure by a full page. Replacing the disclosure comparing two compensation measures to each of three performance measures, as well as a comparison of TSR to peer
(
printed page 75117)
TSR—that is, a narrative or graphical description of seven total relationships—with a description of two relationships (namely, for each of the PEO and PFO, between the executive officer's total earned compensation and the registrant's TSR) should also significantly reduce the volume of disclosure that must be produced.
While the current requirements have principles-based elements, they are also quite prescriptive. By reducing the prescribed elements of the current requirements, such as by eliminating the required tables and the required inclusion of multiple compensation and performance measures, the proposed amendments provide registrants with greater flexibility to tailor their disclosure to more effectively communicate how their executive compensation relates to their performance. Under the proposal, some registrants may voluntarily continue to include performance measures other than TSR in the pay-versus-performance disclosure or to provide voluntary supplemental disclosures with other compensation measures (such as Compensation Actually Paid or realizable pay), while others may produce simpler disclosures.
The simplification of the pay-versus-performance requirements and associated reduction in disclosure volume may benefit some investors, such as retail investors, who may read disclosures linearly. Given that some of the currently prescribed disclosures (such as narratives comparing compensation to net income regardless of whether a registrant is profitable or ties compensation to any measures of profitability) may not be particularly relevant for a given registrant, removing some of this disclosure may also reduce the likelihood that less sophisticated investors are confused by some of the disclosure.
The proposed pay-versus-performance disclosures would provide somewhat different information than current disclosures, because of their focus on
ex post
rather than in flight compensation values. The inputs into such an analysis are relatively easier to construct from other executive compensation disclosures because more complete information is available under the current rule (and would become even more readily available under the proposal) for equity awards that have vested or been exercised than for those that are still in flight. The proposed pay-versus-performance disclosures are therefore not anticipated to provide significant additional information beyond the other proposed disclosures, but, if registrants use their flexibility to present this information effectively, it may help investors to more easily evaluate whether ultimate pay outcomes align with registrant performance than would be possible otherwise.
As discussed above, the benefits of the proposed amendments to pay-versus-performance disclosures are likely to vary across investors of different types, with investors that read executive compensation linearly benefiting the most from any simplification of the disclosures. The benefits of the proposed amendments are also expected to vary across registrants. EGCs and certain other registrants (such as section 15(d) registrants)
[
805
]
are not currently subject to these requirements and thus would not be affected by the proposed changes. Among other registrants, those with the most complex equity compensation structures (particularly those that use option compensation and that have frequent vesting, such as monthly vesting schedules) likely incur the greatest burdens in computing Compensation Actually Paid currently and are thus likely to experience the greatest compliance cost savings as a result of the proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements. Registrants that voluntarily continue to disclose Compensation Actually Paid or similar measures or that voluntarily continue to include and explain multiple performance measures in their pay-versus-performance disclosures may experience lower compliance cost savings than other registrants.
The proposed narrowing of the scope of NEOs would also directly reduce the number of computations required to produce the current pay-versus-performance disclosures and simplify the required descriptions of relationships between pay and performance. Under the proposed definition of NEO, the current pay-versus-performance requirements would no longer require computing Compensation Actually Paid for multiple non-PEO NEOs and then taking the average, as the only non-PEO NEO would be the PFO. The relationship of the Compensation Actually Paid of the PFO with the registrant performance measures may be easier to describe than that of the average Compensation Actually Paid across multiple NEOs, given that the latter would reflect changes in the composition of the NEOs over time as well as factors such as registrant performance. Thus, when considered in combination with the proposed amendment to the definition of NEO, the incremental compliance cost savings and degree of disclosure simplification expected to result from the proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements would be lower than when considered independently.
If the amendments in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted as proposed, a much smaller group of registrants (
i.e.,
LAFs, to the extent they disseminate proxy or information statements) would be subject to pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements, which would reduce the incremental benefits of the proposed amendments to these requirements relative to what they would be with the current filer status framework in place.
2. Costs
The proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements may make it somewhat more difficult for investors to evaluate the sensitivity of executive compensation to registrant performance, which may result in increased analytical costs for some investors (either directly or through third parties) and increased noise in investment and voting decisions. Registrants may also bear some short-term adjustment costs to determine how to present the disclosure given the proposed flexibility in format and change in content of the pay-versus-performance disclosures.
The elimination of the disclosure of the Compensation Actually Paid measure would represent a loss of some information, and particularly of readily available analysis, for investors. As discussed above in section IV.E, this computation provides insight into how the value of an executive's overall compensation package changes from year to year (including for awards that are “in flight”), allowing investors to relate registrant performance with concurrent changes in the value of compensation.
[
806
]
While investors and
(
printed page 75118)
third parties can construct estimates of Compensation Actually Paid or similar “realizable pay” measures based on other disclosed information, these estimates would lack the precision of registrant-constructed measures,
[
807
]
and may result in duplicative analytical effort by multiple parties. Investors with fewer resources to allocate towards evaluating executive compensation disclosures may lose access to any such measure. These factors may reduce the accuracy of investors' understanding of the sensitivity of executive compensation to performance and, at times, may lead some investors to make different investment or voting decisions than they would with more precise information.
[
808
]
To the extent that some registrants voluntarily continue to disclose Compensation Actually Paid, realizable pay, or similar measures, these effects on the precision with which investors evaluate executive compensation may be mitigated at such registrants.
The proposed elimination of prescribed tabular disclosures for the purpose of pay-versus-performance disclosure may make it harder for investors to extract the underlying information for the purpose of comparative analysis. This cost may be mitigated by the proposed simplification of the disclosures, in that there is less such information that could be extracted and such information (such as registrant TSR) can be collected from other readily available sources.
Much of the other information that would no longer be required in the proposed pay-versus-performance disclosures may be of only minor consequence. For example, some of this information, such as the values of net income and peer cumulative TSR or the list of company-selected additional financial performance metrics, would generally remain available in other registrant disclosures or other readily available sources.
[
809
]
Other information that may no longer be reported may be irrelevant, such as narratives comparing compensation actually paid to net income at registrants that are not profitable and do not link compensation to net income. That said, removing this information from pay-versus-performance disclosures could, in some cases, increase the time that investors spend referring to other disclosures or other sources in order to interpret the pay-versus-performance disclosure, or could lead some investors to overlook important context about the broader performance or pay-for-performance programs of a registrant when evaluating the pay-versus-performance disclosure.
[
810
]
Registrants required to provide pay-versus-performance disclosure may bear some short term adjustment costs to transition to the proposed amendments. While the proposed requirements would be substantially more limited than current requirements, they would retain the same flexibility in presentation format for the description of the relationship between pay and performance as the current requirements. Registrants may initially need to reconsider the best way to present the pay-versus-performance disclosure given the proposed shift in focus of these disclosures from Compensation Actually Paid to a measure of realized pay (Total Compensation Earned from the Earned Compensation Table) and the different nature of the relationship of each of these pay measures with registrant TSR.
The costs of the proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements are expected to vary across investors. As discussed above, investors who do not have access to third party analyses, have fewer analytical resources, or are less adept at interpreting current disclosures on their own may be the most likely to have a less precise understanding of how pay relates to performance under the proposal than under the current requirements. In contrast, investors who do have access to third party analyses or who undertake their own detailed analyses of executive compensation disclosures are the most likely to bear increased analytical burdens as a result of the proposal.
The costs of the proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements are also expected to vary across registrants. EGCs and certain other registrants (such as section 15(d) registrants)
[
811
]
are not currently subject to the pay-versus-performance requirements, so investors would not bear costs with respect to these registrants (and these registrants would bear no transition costs). Among other registrants, the information in current pay-versus-performance disclosures would be the hardest to replicate by investors or third parties for the registrants with the most complex equity compensation structures or those that would not disclose specific performance targets and thresholds in performance or market conditions applied to their awards under the proposal. The proposed amendments would thereby be the most likely to result in increased analytical burdens for investors and increased imprecision in the understanding of how NEO pay relates to performance at these registrants.
The proposed narrowing of the scope of NEOs would also directly affect the scope of the current pay-versus-performance disclosures. However, given the significant investor focus on PEO compensation and the difficulties in interpreting the average compensation actually paid to a group of NEOs, we do not expect the incremental costs of the proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements to be significantly different when considered in combination with the proposed definition of NEO than when considered independently.
Should the amendments in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release be adopted as proposed, the incremental costs associated with the proposed amendments to the pay-versus-performance requirements would be
(
printed page 75119)
reduced. In that scenario, the pay-versus-performance requirements, and thus the effects of any changes to these requirements, would be limited to LAFs that disseminate proxy or information statements, a smaller group of registrants than the group subject to these requirements under the baseline.
3. Reasonable Alternatives
As an alternative to the proposed amendments, we could retain the disclosure of Compensation Actually Paid and use this measure rather than total compensation from the Earned Compensation Table in the pay-versus-performance requirements, while eliminating the prescriptive tables, footnotes, and other compensation and performance measures included in the current disclosures. This approach may provide investors with clearer and more timely insights into how executive compensation varies with registrant performance. However, given that the construction of the Compensation Actually Paid measure represents a large share of the burdens of the current requirements, this approach would provide very limited compliance cost savings for registrants relative to the baseline.
Another alternative would be to propose a more fully principles-based pay-versus-performance disclosure requirement, under which registrants would be required to provide a clear description of the relationship between executive compensation and registrant performance, without specific measures of compensation and performance being prescribed for this purpose. Such an approach would increase the flexibility of registrants to tailor the disclosure to their specific compensation structures, but may make it more difficult for investors to evaluate the disclosures by increasing the variation in the nature and content of the disclosures across registrants.
We also considered using our exemptive authority to eliminate pay-versus-performance disclosure requirements in the context of the PFO's compensation. Limiting the pay-versus-performance disclosure to the PEO would further reduce compliance costs while continuing to provide the disclosure for the executive officer whose pay is most scrutinized by investors.
[
812
]
However, given the simplified pay-versus-performance requirements under the proposed amendments, the incremental costs of providing this disclosure are expected to be modest, and investors may benefit from disclosures highlighting how the PFO's eventual pay outcomes have aligned with registrant performance, both to better understand the PFO's compensation structure and to understand how the alignment of such pay outcomes with performance may differ for other senior executives as compared to the PEO.
H. Pay Ratio Disclosure Requirements
Each registrant subject to the pay ratio disclosure requirements currently must disclose, each year, the ratio between the annual compensation of its PEO and that of its median employee identified in accordance with the rule. This pay ratio must be computed using total compensation based on all elements included in such total in the Summary Compensation Table. The median employee is to be identified based on the distribution of compensation across all of the registrant's full- and part-time, seasonal, and temporary U.S. and non-U.S. employees. A data privacy exemption permits registrants to exclude any individual employed in a foreign jurisdiction in which the data privacy laws or regulations are such that the registrant is unable to obtain or process the required information without violating those laws or regulations. A
de minimis
exception is also available in that registrants whose non-U.S. employees represent five percent or less of their total U.S. and non-U.S. employees may exclude those employees from the computation. This disclosure is not required of SRCs or EGCs, but is required of all other registrants that must make Item 402 disclosures.
[
813
]
The proposed amendments would simplify the computation of this ratio by limiting the population used to identify the median employee to full-time, U.S.-based employees, excluding seasonal and temporary employees, and changing the definition of total compensation used in the ratio to that reflecting the total from the proposed Granted Compensation Table (which contains fewer elements than the Summary Compensation Table). Under the proposed amendments, registrants would be required to determine the median employee once every five years (as compared to three years under the baseline). The proposed amendments would also remove certain requirements to make disclosures about the selection process for the median employee (such as requirements to disclose the compensation measure used and the date chosen for identifying the median employee).
[

]
1. Benefits
Limiting the population from which the median employee is drawn to full-time, U.S.-based employees, excluding seasonal and temporary employees, is expected to significantly reduce the costs of preparing pay ratio disclosures relative to the compliance costs of producing these disclosures under the current rule.
[
815
]
In particular, excluding non-U.S. based employees from this computation would eliminate the need to, for example, test whether the
de minimis
exemption applies, make foreign exchange computations, integrate data from the potentially different payroll systems often used to track compensation for employees in disparate foreign locations, and comply with the potentially complex requirements of local data privacy laws when integrating such data.
[
816
]
Commenters have highlighted the inclusion of employees in foreign jurisdictions in the determination of the median employee as a source of significant compliance costs.
[
817
]
For example, when the pay ratio rule was first proposed, commenters submitted
(
printed page 75120)
the results of a survey of registrants that indicated that requiring only U.S. employees to be used when estimating the pay ratio would decrease the costs of the disclosure on average by 40 percent.
[
818
]
Excluding part-time, seasonal, or temporary employees from the computation of the pay ratio is expected to provide additional cost savings by reducing the number of employees whose compensation data must be integrated to identify the median employee. Such a change could also reduce the likelihood that registrants feel the need to provide supplementary narrative disclosures explaining that their pay ratio may be skewed due to the inclusion of employee compensation that is not on a full-time basis.
[
819
]
The survey results submitted to the comment file when the pay ratio rule was first proposed indicated that requiring only full-time employees, excluding seasonal and temporary employees, to be used when estimating the pay ratio would decrease the costs of the disclosure on average by 11 percent.
[
820
]
These savings are smaller in magnitude than those associated with excluding foreign workers, and the two estimates should not be treated as fully additive given potential overlap in the underlying cost drivers.
Because wages outside of the U.S. and unadjusted part-time, temporary, and seasonal pay are likely to be lower on average than full-time, annual U.S.-based wages, excluding these employees from the median calculation is likely to raise the reported median employee wage for registrants with such employees, thereby lowering the reported pay ratio. To the extent that the inclusion of part-time, temporary, seasonal, and non-U.S. employees—without time-equivalent or purchasing-power-parity
[
821
]
adjustments—currently inflates reported ratios, the revised computation may produce a ratio that more accurately represents the compensation structure of a registrant's domestic full-time workforce. Research indicates that higher reported pay ratios can be associated with less favorable investor,
[
822
]
employee,
[
823
]
and public
[
824
]
perceptions. If the current ratio overstates a registrant's pay disparity, correcting this may reduce perceptions that are not warranted by the registrant's actual compensation practices.
Requiring that the median employee be determined once every five years instead of once every three years should further reduce the compliance costs borne by registrants to produce pay ratio disclosure. In particular, identifying the median employee may be the most burdensome aspect of producing the disclosure given the large compensation datasets and the various processing steps that may be required. Reducing the frequency of this process should therefore reduce compliance costs.
With regard to benefits to investors, to the extent the proposed amendments reduce registrant costs, these savings may ultimately benefit the shareholders of the affected registrants. Investors may also benefit from more comparable pay ratio disclosures under the proposal. Registrants take varying approaches to foreign operations and fluctuating labor needs, with some outsourcing these labor needs to other entities while others directly employ non-U.S. and/or part-time, seasonal, or temporary workers. Some may employ such part-time, seasonal, or temporary workers at consolidated subsidiaries while others do so through unconsolidated subsidiaries (whose employees are not included in pay ratio computations). These differences in approaches to fulfilling similar labor needs can lead to variation in pay ratios that does not reflect true differences in underlying labor costs. Further, because the current rule does not permit the compensation of a part-time employee to be converted to a full-time equivalent or seasonal or temporary worker pay to be annualized, including their pay in comparison to the full-time, annual compensation of a PEO can artificially inflate pay ratios.
[
825
]
Amending the definition of total compensation to be used in the ratio to reflect the definition used in the proposed Granted Compensation Table could result in further cost savings for some registrants. In particular, to the extent that a registrant's median employee receives benefits or miscellaneous compensation that would otherwise be included in a total compensation measure based on the Summary Compensation Table (but not in a measure based on the proposed Granted Compensation Table)—such as participation in a registrant pension plan or registrant contributions to a defined contribution plan—the registrant's computation of the median employee's total compensation may be simplified under the proposed amendments because these components would not be required to be included under the proposal.
Eliminating requirements to make supplementary disclosures related to the selection process for the median employee may lead to additional cost savings by reducing the volume of necessary disclosure that must be prepared, reviewed, and included in registrants' filings. Relative to the expected savings from excluding non-U.S. based employees and part-time, temporary, and seasonal workers from the computations, these savings are expected to be more marginal.
The benefits of the proposed revisions to the pay ratio disclosure requirements are expected to vary across registrants. Because EGCs and SRCs are exempt from the pay ratio disclosure requirements, they would not experience any incremental benefits. For other registrants required to provide Item 402 disclosures, those expected to benefit the most from the proposed revisions are the registrants with significant foreign operations, particularly those with employees in a large number of different countries or whose employees are otherwise tracked in many separate payroll systems. Registrants in industries that are more likely to employ part-time, temporary, or seasonal workers, such as retail or agricultural industries, are also likely to experience greater savings (and potential positive reputational effects from lower reported pay ratios) than other registrants. Finally, those with broad-based retirement plans or other employee benefits that are included in the Summary Compensation Table definition of total compensation but omitted from the proposed Granted Compensation Table may benefit from simpler computations of median employee compensation.

826
]
(

In addition, if the amendments proposed in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted, a much smaller group of registrants would be subject to pay ratio disclosure requirements, which would reduce the overall incremental benefits of the proposed amendments to these requirements. However, we note that the large registrants that would continue to be subject to pay ratio disclosure requirements are the most likely to be multinational, with employees in a large number of countries, and may thus individually benefit the most from the proposed amendments.
2. Costs
The proposed amendments to the pay ratio disclosure requirements are expected to reduce the amount of underlying information summarized in registrant pay ratios. However, given our understanding of how these ratios are currently used, as discussed below, we do not expect significant adverse effects on investors' ability to use and interpret pay ratios relative to the baseline.
While there is some indication that pay ratios are not relied on by investors to the same extent as many other executive compensation disclosures,
[
827
]
researchers have found evidence that at least some investors seem to consider pay ratio information when making voting
[
828
]
and investment
[

decisions. Investors have expressed that pay ratio disclosures can provide information relevant to understanding a registrant's human capital management and associated risks.
[
830
]
For these uses, we expect a pay ratio limited to U.S., full-time employees, excluding seasonal and temporary employees, to suffice for most investors. In fact, as discussed in the context of benefits above, this proposed revision could make the ratio more easily interpretable. That said, the exclusion of part-time, seasonal, and temporary workers, as well as the use of a less comprehensive compensation measure in the ratio, may add new sources of imprecision into the ratios, in that the proposed ratios would reflect less complete information than current ratios. Requiring that the median employee be determined once every five years instead of once every three years (and eliminating the instruction explicitly requiring registrants to update the median employee sooner under certain circumstances)
[

may introduce a further source of imprecision into the ratio, by increasing the likelihood that the median employee reflected in the disclosure is an outdated reflection of the registrant's current workforce. However, pay ratios already reflect a number of factors that complicate cross-registrant comparisons, such as differences in industry and business type; in the degree of vertical integration; in the reliance on contract and outsourced workers; and in corporate structure with respect to ownership and consolidation.
[
832
]
We therefore do not expect the incremental imprecision that could result from simplifying the ratio to be significant relative to the baseline level of imprecision in the ratio due to existing factors.
The proposed amendments would also remove certain requirements to make disclosures about the selection process for the median employee. There is evidence that some registrants may use their discretion in how the median employee is identified to lower their reported pay ratios.
[

The proposed amendments could make it more difficult for investors to identify such behavior, complicating investors' interpretation of the disclosures. However, at least some of the elements of discretion, included in both the current and proposed rule, such as the choice of a date for identifying the median employee, may be less consequential in the context of the proposed amendments, where, for example, temporary and seasonal employees are excluded. Further, as discussed above, the structural imprecision inherent in pay ratio disclosures (arising from workforce composition and other factors) means that any additional variation caused by the application of this discretion may not significantly affect investors' ability to interpret pay ratios.
While we expect limited costs of the proposed revisions to pay ratio disclosures, the potential costs are expected to vary across investors depending on how they use pay ratio disclosures and will vary across registrants based on their characteristics. Specifically, SRC and EGCs are not subject to pay ratio disclosure requirements and thus they and their investors bear none of these incremental costs. The greatest costs may be associated with registrants in any industries with significant reliance on part-time, seasonal, or temporary workers, or with registrants with variation in employee compensation structure among otherwise similar registrants, which could make it more
(
printed page 75122)
difficult for investors to identify outliers based on the revised disclosures. If the amendments proposed in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted, a more limited subset of registrants would be subject to pay ratio disclosure requirements, thus limiting the scope of any costs of the proposed amendments.
3. Reasonable Alternatives
As an alternative to limiting the population used to identify the median employee to full-time, U.S.-based employees, excluding seasonal and temporary employees, we could limit the population to all U.S.-based employees regardless of employment status (
i.e.,
including part-time, seasonal, or temporary workers) and permit registrants to convert their pay to full-time, annual equivalents in the pay ratio computations. This approach could lead to somewhat more comparable pay ratios across registrants with respect to domestic workforces. However, including these workers and allowing annualization and full-time equivalent computations would likely increase costs for registrants relative to the proposal, because of the greater number of employees whose compensation data must be integrated to identify the median employee and because the registrant may need to perform annualization and full-time-equivalent computations for large numbers of employees. Alternatively, we could include only full-time employees, excluding seasonal and temporary workers, but include non-U.S.-based employees. Under this alternative, we could, for example, expand the
de minimis
exemption provided in the current rule (such as to 10 or 25 percent) and permit purchasing-power-parity adjustments for non-U.S. based employees. Including non-U.S. workers for registrants at which these employees constitute a larger fraction of the workforce, but allowing adjustments to factor in variations in wages across countries, may increase comparability of these registrants' pay ratios with those of registrants that meet similar labor needs using primarily U.S. employees. However, as discussed above, commenters have highlighted integrating foreign and domestic compensation systems for this purpose to be a significant source of compliance costs,
[
834
]
and some of these costs may be borne even by registrants that are able to avail of an expanded
de minimis
exemption because of the need to determine whether the
de minimis
threshold is met. Separately, the extent to which either of these alternatives (including additional types of domestic employees or including foreign employees) would improve the comparability of pay ratios across registrants would be limited by the substantial existing imprecision in pay ratios arising from other sources, as discussed in section IV.H.2 above.
We also considered using the annual total compensation calculation methodology from the proposed Earned Compensation Table (rather than from the Granted Compensation Table, as proposed) for purposes of the pay ratio disclosure. The Earned Compensation Table provides a more comprehensive measure of compensation, including components that are not reflected in the Granted Compensation Table (such as retirement benefits and perquisites), and could thus enhance comparability of pay ratio disclosures across registrants that rely to a different degree on, for example, retirement or other benefits to compensate their PEO. However, as in the case of the currently required Summary Compensation Table methodology as discussed above, computing a measure based on Earned Compensation Table methodology for the median employee may be more burdensome than computing the measure as proposed. Further, as in the case of the other alternatives discussed above, the extent to which this alternative would improve the comparability of pay ratios across registrants would be limited by the substantial existing imprecision in pay ratios arising from other sources.
I. Compensation of Directors
Registrants are currently required to provide tabular disclosure regarding the compensation of directors for the last completed fiscal year in a Director Compensation Table that largely mirrors the Summary Compensation Table, with cash fees instead of salaries in the first column of the table. The Director Compensation Table does not include a bonus column, but includes stock awards, option awards, non-equity incentive plan compensation, change in pension value
[
835
]
and nonqualified deferred compensation earnings,
[
836
]
and all other compensation columns that parallel the columns in the Summary Compensation Table. The delineated list of items to be included in “all other compensation” in the Director Compensation Table includes some items in the equivalent category in the Summary Compensation Table (such as perquisites, tax gross-ups, and contributions to defined benefit retirement plans) but also includes items that are specific to the director context (such as consulting fees and costs associated with director legacy programs). In all cases, the tabular disclosure is required to be accompanied by a narrative description of any material factors necessary to an understanding of the director compensation disclosed in the table.
The proposed amendments would continue to require certain qualitative and quantitative disclosure of the material compensation of directors, including disclosure of compensation at the individual director level, but would eliminate (1) mandatory disclosure of certain specified categories of compensation (such as retirement contributions, tax gross-ups, consulting fees, and costs associated with director legacy programs) regardless of materiality and (2) prescriptive tabular presentation requirements, in favor of a more principles-based approach. The proposed amendments would also change the focus of disclosure with respect to equity awards at the individual director level from the grant date fair value reported in the current Director Compensation Table to a combination of disclosure of the value of any earned (
i.e.,
vested or exercised) equity and the size and material terms of any outstanding equity awards. In addition, registrants would be required to describe the material aspects of the director compensation program in general (
i.e.,
not in the context of individual named directors), including quantification of cash and equity retainers for different roles. Registrants would also be required to disclose any material information necessary to an understanding of the information otherwise disclosed. Further, unlike the current rule, the proposed amendments would require that registrants include compensation to NEOs for any services they provide as directors in the director compensation disclosure and require that registrants exclude that compensation from the executive compensation tables.
1. Benefits
The proposed amendments to the director compensation disclosure requirements are expected to reduce repetitive disclosures and the costs of preparing disclosures. It is also possible
(
printed page 75123)
that the proposed principles-based requirements could increase the information available to investors about how directors are compensated.
As discussed in the Baseline section above, the structure of director pay is generally simpler than that of executive pay. Registrants often describe this structure, such as the level of annual director fees and how these base fees are augmented by additional fees for board leadership positions or committee service as well as how stock grants are sized, in narrative and supplemental tabular disclosures. This information, as well as information about other items of director compensation, is then also summarized at the director level in the Director Compensation Table. The proposed amendments, by not prescribing a presentation format, may allow registrants to more succinctly describe the material aspects and quantified elements of the compensation of directors. By requiring the disclosure of any amounts of NEO compensation that are attributable to service on the board in this section alone, and not in the tabular disclosures of executive compensation, the proposed amendments may also reduce any duplicative explanations of the director pay structure that may currently be made in the executive compensation disclosures.
Reducing any redundant disclosures should reduce, to a modest extent, the costs of preparing director compensation disclosures as well as the overall length of disclosures and thus the cost of disclosure review by registrant staff, outside advisors, and the board. To the extent that some of the elements of compensation included in the current tabular disclosures are not material in the context of a particular registrant or a particular director, there may be additional savings associated with no longer tracking and/or reporting these elements. Consistent with these expectations, some commenters stated that the current tabular disclosure requirement is costly and suggested that narrative disclosure of material information about director compensation would be less burdensome to produce.
[
837
]
Finally, researchers have raised concerns that directors may receive certain benefits as a result of their board position that are not currently disclosed as compensation.
[
838
]
To the extent that there are material director benefits that are not encompassed by the current disclosure requirements, the proposed more principles-based approach to the disclosure of director compensation, together with the materiality standards applied in proposed Item 402(k) and the objective put forth in proposed Item 402(a)(1), could potentially result in increased information being disclosed, to the benefit of investors, about how individuals are compensated for their service as directors.
2. Costs
The proposed amendments to the director compensation disclosure requirements may, because of the transition to a different disclosure framework with more principles-based standards and presentation flexibility, generate some new (primarily short-term) costs for registrants to evaluate materiality and decide how to present their disclosures and may increase search costs for the users of disclosure. The proposed amendments may also reduce the amount of information available to investors (and registrants) for the purpose of evaluating (and benchmarking) director pay.
The proposed requirements rely on registrants to identify the material aspects of their compensation of directors in order to define the scope of the disclosure beyond the minimum required quantified elements (such as any cash and equity retainers for board, committee, chairmanship, and other director services). Registrants may need to expend some effort to determine what factors to disclose, and they may choose to consult with outside advisors to assist them in making this determination. We expect that the relatively simple structure of director compensation should simplify this task in most cases, but the materiality determinations may be more complicated for those with relatively more complex director compensation, such as those with directors receiving pay in the current “all other compensation” category.
[
839
]
Given that the proposed amendments would not mandate a specific disclosure format, registrants would also have to decide how to present the information, and they may potentially consult with outside advisors to assist them. Additional costs may be associated with engaging with investors, other registrants, external advisors, and trade groups to develop market practices or norms for presenting the disclosures. That said, while there may be some ongoing costs associated with evaluating the materiality of various elements as the directors and their circumstances or the director compensation program as a whole change over time, most of the costs associated with determining the content and presentation format for the disclosures should be limited after the initial years of experience with the proposed amendments.
To the extent that registrants respond to the proposed amendments by employing a wide range of alternative presentation formats, or by relying on narrative rather than organized tabular presentations, or by excluding some information currently in the disclosures but that can be computed
[
840
]
or found in other filings or locations,
[
841
]
the search and analysis costs expended by investors, peer registrants, and/or third parties such as compensation consultants and proxy advisors to understand, extract, and compare director compensation information across registrants may be increased.
[
842
]
As discussed in section IV.E.1.a above, there are various reasons why a principles-based disclosure standard may result in investors being less informed despite registrants disclosing all material information. For example, there may be elements of such compensation that are not material to some registrants and thus may appropriately not be disclosed under the proposed amendments, resulting in less consistent peer information to judge the reasonable level of these elements at other registrants. While we expect that the materiality standard, together with concern about litigation risks, should limit the loss of information about director compensation, we note that researchers have found that even modest variation in their compensation
(
printed page 75124)
may impact director behavior.
[
843
]
It is therefore possible that the proposed amendments may result in an increase in the imprecision of investors' understanding of director compensation at some registrants, introducing some noise into investment and voting decisions.
3. Reasonable Alternatives
As an alternative to the proposed amendments, we considered retaining more prescriptive presentation requirements. For example, we could have designed a new Director Compensation Table with simplified requirements and columns to reflect factors that are currently commonly disclosed in narrative or supplemental tables (such as separate columns for base director fees and fees associated with board leadership or committee positions). Relative to the proposed approach, a prescriptive tabular disclosure requirement would reduce the need for registrants to decide how to present their disclosures and would make the data more readily extractable and comparable for investors, peer registrants, and third parties. However, a revised tabular disclosure could still result in duplicative disclosure to the extent that it does not fully align with how registrants prefer to describe their director pay practices. Under the proposed approach, it is possible that market norms for director compensation disclosure may develop to provide similar benefits to this alternative without lengthier or repetitive disclosure.
We also considered requiring program-level disclosure about the material aspects of director compensation while no longer requiring director compensation disclosure on an individual, director-by-director basis. Requiring only program-level disclosure could further reduce the volume of director compensation disclosure that would have to be produced and reviewed. However, given potential variation across directors in elements of compensation outside of the basic retainers and potential differences in equity exposure due, for example, to when different directors joined the board, director-level compensation information may be material to investors in assessing director incentives.
The proposed amendments would require quantitative disclosure of the value of any earned equity (
i.e.,
vested stock or exercised options) and the size and material terms of any outstanding equity awards as of the end of the fiscal year. Alternatively, we could instead require the disclosure of the grant date fair value of equity (and the material terms of any grants). It is possible that investors may be most directly interested in the grant date fair value and material terms of equity when it is initially awarded to a director given that this amount and these terms may be most relevant to an understanding of the performance sensitivity of awarded compensation and thus the director's
ex ante
incentives—such as their degree of “skin in the game.”
[
844
]
While grant date fair values could be computed (and material terms of grants could likely be identified) based on the proposed disclosure of the material aspects of the director compensation program in general, obtaining this information may involve more search and analysis costs for investors and other users of the disclosure than if it is directly disclosed (as under the current rule).
Requiring the disclosure of information about granted rather than earned and outstanding equity may also enhance comparability by resulting in more equivalent disclosure for director compensation structures that have similar economic implications. For example, disclosure of granted equity would result in similar disclosure for stock awards that cliff-vest in one year (and are thus earned after a year) and stock awards that vest immediately (and are thus earned immediately) but that are subject to a holding requirement, which have similar economic implications (in that the stock cannot be sold for at least a year after it is granted) and are both common structures for director equity.
[

]
