J. Scaled Disclosure
Currently, SRCs and EGCs may elect to provide executive compensation disclosure that is generally subject to scaled disclosure accommodations. For example, among many other accommodations, as discussed above,
[
848
]
SRCs and EGCs typically have three rather than five NEOs, have two rather than six required tables under the primary tabular disclosure requirements, may include fewer years of data in certain prescribed tables, and are not currently required to include a CD&A or pay-ratio disclosure. SRCs and EGCs may also provide only a narrative description of the material terms of retirement plans and of potential payments and benefits to an NEO in the case of certain termination and change-in-control events, in contrast to the more detailed and prescribed disclosures on these topics currently required of other registrants.
Some aspects of the proposed amendments (such as the proposed, more narrow NEO definition or the proposed streamlined tabular disclosure requirements) would apply more limited disclosure requirements to all registrants, thereby reducing the extent of differences between the requirements that apply to SRCs and EGCs and all other registrants. Other aspects of the proposed amendments would maintain current accommodations for SRCs and EGCs, such as the exemptions for these registrants from CD&A and pay ratio disclosures. The proposed amendments would also eliminate the current Item 402(q)(1) narrative disclosure requirement (with respect to retirement plans) that applies to these registrants.
(
printed page 75125)
1. Benefits
Because compliance costs generally do not scale perfectly with size, in that they have some fixed cost components, the same disclosure requirement can result in disproportionate burdens on smaller companies. While the proposed amendments would reduce and streamline the extent of disclosure required by all registrants, they would also maintain a scaled disclosure regime for SRCs and EGCs. As under the baseline, the continuing accommodations would help to limit the disproportionate burden that disclosure requirements can otherwise place on smaller registrants.
Maintaining scaled disclosure accommodations for SRCs and EGCs may help to support the potential capital formation benefits of the proposed amendments. In particular, these smaller and younger registrants may be more likely than other registrants to face constraints in their financial or managerial resources and may thus be more likely to redirect any additional compliance cost savings towards strategic planning or capital investment.
The nature of the proposed revised requirements for SRCs and EGCs may also benefit investors. While these registrants would remain eligible to elect scaled requirements, they would, in contrast to the current requirements, produce the same set of tabular disclosures (though with two rather than three years of data where applicable) with the same content (including with respect to pensions) as other registrants. These more consistent disclosures may facilitate investors' review and comparison of the disclosures across registrants of different types. The proposed disclosures would also make certain information about SRCs and EGCs, particularly with respect to stock vesting or option exercises, more accessible than under current rule.
If the proposed amendments in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted, SRCs would no longer be subject to the pay-versus-performance requirements or golden parachute disclosure (and voting) requirements. Further, the proposed exemption from Item 402(q)(1) (
i.e.,
narrative disclosure about retirement plans) and other executive compensation disclosure accommodations would be extended to all new NAFs, a much larger group of filers (with a broader range of individual characteristics) than current SRCs and EGCs. While the larger registrants among the new NAFs might not benefit as significantly from accommodations as current SRCs and EGCs (because they are less likely to face the same resource constraints as these smaller registrants) they may also benefit from incremental compliance cost savings and investors would benefit from more consistent disclosures than would be available if the new NAFs avail themselves of the accommodations under current executive compensation disclosure rules.
2. Costs
The proposed amendments, by applying more consistent tabular disclosure requirements across all registrants, may generate some incremental compliance costs for SRCs and EGCs. In particular, these registrants would newly have to reflect in the proposed Earned Compensation Table stock that vested or options that were exercised. They would also have to include, in this table, the service costs and prior service costs associated with pension plans. However, we expect the collection of this information to impose minimal costs because equity outcomes are likely tracked for other purposes and pension service costs are reported for accounting purposes. Also, the proposed amendments would eliminate the current Item 402(q)(1) narrative disclosure requirement pertaining to pension and other retirement compensation, which would reduce other compliance costs for these registrants.
For investors, the proposed elimination of the current Item 402(q)(1) narrative disclosure requirement with respect to retirement plans would reduce the amount of information available with which to assess the overall monetary incentives of NEOs at SRCs and EGCs. As discussed in section IV.B above, pensions and deferred compensation can affect, for example, the likelihood that managers will be more or less conservative in their strategic choices.
If the proposed amendments in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted, SRCs would no longer be subject to the pay-versus-performance requirements and the golden parachute disclosure (and voting) requirements. Further, the proposed elimination of Item 402(q)(1) disclosure would be extended to all new NAFs, likely increasing any costs to investors of somewhat less detailed information about the pensions and other retirement compensation of NEOs of these registrants.
3. Reasonable Alternatives
As an alternative to the proposed accommodations for SRCs and EGCs, we considered expanding these accommodations. For example, we could allow these issuers to exclude the Status of Equity Awards Table or to provide disclosure only for the PEO rather than both the PEO and PFO. Further accommodations could reduce the volume of disclosures produced by SRCs and EGCs and provide additional compliance cost savings for these registrants, which could be directed toward other purposes.
However, the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table would require the disclosure of factual information, with no incremental computations, and should not be overly burdensome to produce. Similarly, we expect that the proposed disclosure of the PFO's compensation, given the proposed simplified requirements and that the PFO is easily identifiable, would require limited tracking, data collection, or computation for SRCs and EGCs beyond what we expect is produced for other purposes (though it would still contribute to the overall volume of disclosure that would need to be produced). On the other hand, as discussed in sections IV.D and IV.E above, these disclosures may be material to investors' understanding of the executive compensation structures at these registrants.

We also could have required LAFs or all registrants to block text tag or detail tag any footnotes to the tabular disclosures or other narrative disclosures made under proposed Item 402. Relative to the proposed approach, these approaches would have made executive compensation data more readily accessible to investors and increased disclosure processing efficiency. However, a broader tagging requirement would have increased compliance costs for registrants, particularly for SRCs, if the requirement applied to them. Further, because the proposed requirement replaces the existing tagging requirements with tagged information that makes up a substantial portion of the proposed executive compensation disclosure overall, any incremental benefit to investors for tagging additional compensation disclosures could be limited given such disclosures are largely being simplified and streamlined under the proposal.

1. Disclosure on Actions To Recover Erroneously Awarded Compensation
Clawback disclosures related to a registrant's actions to recover certain erroneously awarded compensation from executive officers (not limited to the NEOs) are required for any section 12 or section 15(d) registrant that has securities listed on a national securities exchange, including U.S.-listed FPIs and certain listed registered investment companies.

Specifically, these requirements include (i) the disclosure of certain information if the restatement required the recovery of erroneously awarded compensation and (ii) the disclosure of certain information if the registrant concluded that the restatement
did not
require recovery of erroneously awarded compensation.

Registrants other than registered investment companies are also currently required to indicate, in two check-boxes on the cover pages of Forms 10-K, 20-F, and 40-F, (1) whether the financial statements in the filing reflect the correction of an error to previously issued financial statements (regardless of whether such correction was required or voluntary) and (2) whether any such error corrections are restatements that required a recovery analysis under the registrant's clawback policy.

The proposed amendments would eliminate the disclosure requirements that apply when the registrant concludes that a restatement
did not
require recovery of erroneously awarded compensation (
i.e.,
Item 402(w)(2) and the corresponding elements of Forms 20-F, 40-F, and N-CSR) and would eliminate the check-box requirements that flag for investors whether the filing reflects restatements and whether a recovery analysis was required. The rule would still require registrants to disclose an action to recover erroneously awarded executive compensation stemming from an accounting restatement, including information where an amount was determined to be recoverable but recovery would be impracticable. The proposed amendments would, however, remove the current requirement that amounts determined to be recoverable but for which recovery would be impracticable be separately disclosed for each current and former NEO and all other current and former executive officers as a group.
The proposed amendments to the disclosure requirements associated with clawbacks may generate limited compliance cost savings and contribute to more streamlined disclosure. More importantly, such elimination would reduce the likelihood that the need to check the first box even in the case of restatements that are not required may cause registrants to avoid voluntarily making and reporting these restatements. Reducing any incentive to avoid voluntary restatements could decrease the likelihood of less reliable financial statements and larger restatements in the future.
The removal of the check-boxes and the disclosures currently required when a registrant concludes that a restatement did not require the recovery of compensation would reduce, somewhat, the transparency around restatements and the application of clawback policies. Specifically, the disclosures that would be eliminated may currently make it easier for investors to identify when a “little r” restatement has been made (given that such restatements, unlike “big R” restatements, do not trigger Item 4.02 Form 8-K disclosure)

Removing the current requirement that amounts determined to be recoverable but for which recovery would be impracticable be separately disclosed for each current and former NEO and for all current and former executive officers as a group may also reduce the granularity of the information available to investors to monitor how registrants are applying clawback policies in practice, but it is not clear whether, or to what extent, this level of detail is relied upon by investors.

4. Compensation Policies and Practices Related to the Registrant's Risk Management—Item 402(s)
Under the current Item 402(s), to the extent that risks arising from a registrant's compensation policies and practices for its employees (including non-executive officers) are reasonably likely to have a material adverse effect on the registrant, the registrant is required to discuss its policies and practices as they relate to risk management practices and risk-taking incentives. The proposed amendments would eliminate this requirement for all registrants.
While the preparation of this disclosure may not be as resource-intensive as other executive compensation requirements, registrants must still devote time and effort to assess whether their compensation policies and practices create risks that could have a material adverse effect, draft or update narrative disclosures, and review these disclosures with internal stakeholders and external advisors. Removing the requirement would reduce the time and resources spent on these activities. Given the reported policies and practices may not change significantly from year to year, thus requiring only modest preparation costs after the first year of compliance, removing Item 402(s) is expected to yield modest compliance cost savings relative to the total expenditures on producing compensation disclosure. The proposed changes may also reduce boilerplate or repetitive disclosure to the extent that other disclosure requirements (
e.g.,
Item 105 of Regulation S-K) already require discussion of material risks.
The direct costs of information loss from the elimination of Item 402(s) are expected to be limited, given that to the extent that a registrant's compensation policies and practices create risks that are reasonably likely to have a material adverse effect, the disclosure of such risks would generally continue to be required, if material, pursuant to other disclosure requirements.

N. Effects on Efficiency, Competition, and Capital Formation
While the preceding sections of this economic analysis focused on the detailed effects of the proposed amendments on the affected parties, in this section we consider the broader market-level effects on efficiency, competition, and capital formation.
(
printed page 75136)
The proposed amendments, in aggregate, are expected to significantly reduce the compliance costs required to produce executive compensation disclosures, relative to the current burdens on registrants associated with these disclosures. The resulting savings of cash flow as well as registrant staff, board, and management time and attention may facilitate capital formation by redirecting these resources from compliance efforts toward other, more productive uses.
[
919
]
In particular, for companies that face financing constraints or limited managerial capacity, such savings may be redirected to strategic planning or capital investments that would not otherwise have been undertaken.
[
920
]
In other cases, the savings may be returned to shareholders, who may direct them to other investment opportunities. A reduced disclosure burden on reporting issuers could also be a positive factor in encouraging additional companies to raise capital through registered securities offerings or to become or remain a public company,
[
921
]
which may also enhance capital formation.
[
922
]
There is also a possibility that reduced transparency with respect to executive and director compensation could increase the cost of capital for reporting companies or reduce trust in markets, which could have offsetting effects on capital formation.
[
923
]
The proposed amendments would be expected to generate some short-term inefficiencies due to the adjustment costs that would be borne by registrants and investors (directly and/or via third parties) to adapt to the significant proposed changes (such as by designing new disclosures or revising disclosure review practices) relative to the current executive compensation disclosure requirements, as discussed above.
[
924
]
The potential inefficiencies would also include, for investors, any time and resources that may be expended to express to registrants their requests for disclosure and, for registrants, to engage with investors and potentially work with external advisors and other entities, including trade groups, to develop market practices and norms relating to some of the more principles-based elements of the proposed amendments.
[
925
]
Beyond these short-term adjustment costs, the effects of the proposed amendments on efficiency depend on the extent to which the proposal would affect investor search and analysis costs, would reduce the precision with which investors can evaluate executive compensation, and/or would contribute to distortions in compensation programs relative to the compensation design that would be optimal for shareholder value maximization.
[
926
]
In particular, for investors that review large numbers of executive compensation disclosures, the more principles-based approach of the proposed amendments may increase search and analysis costs (borne either directly or via third parties such as proxy advisors and data aggregators) by reducing the consistency of format, location, and inclusion of certain information. The proposed amendments would afford registrants substantial discretion with respect to, for example, what information about director compensation and about potential payments to executives upon termination is material and how to report it;
[
927
]
what amounts of executive compensation beyond the types that are explicitly delineated are material and must thus be included;
[
928
]
how to format the required tabular disclosures;
[
929
]
what supplementary information is necessary or appropriate to understand the tabular disclosures;
[
930
]
where to present and how to format any such supplementary information as well as the performance, market and service conditions of equity awards;
[
931
]
what specific topics should be covered in CD&As;
[
932
]
and, broadly, what information is material to an assessment of the registrant's executive and director compensation.
[
933
]
To the extent that the flexibility afforded to registrants would result in significant variation in the format, organization, and content of disclosures across registrants (or across time for the same registrant), investors (directly or via third parties) may require more time and resources than they expend today to identify, understand, extract, and compare information about executive compensation. Registrants (directly or via third parties) may also bear increased search costs in their benchmarking exercises. Certain other aspects of the proposed amendments that may help to condense the disclosures may, at the same time, increase the likelihood that some of the users of disclosures would need to refer
(
printed page 75137)
to other filings to access information that is currently contained in a single filing, further increasing potential search costs.
[
934
]
In other ways, search costs may be reduced by the proposed amendments. In particular, the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table may make it easier to assess the complete set of equity awards that have been newly granted, remain outstanding, or have newly vested or been exercised, on an award-by-award basis. Today, this information is spread across multiple tables and presented at different levels of aggregation. For example, for SRCs and EGCs, some of this information (regarding the final outcomes of awards) may have to be accessed in different filings, as these registrants are not currently required to include an Option Exercises and Stock Vested Table. To the extent that registrants use the flexibility afforded to them to include information about grants or award outcomes that occurred after the end of the last completed fiscal year in the proposed Status of Equity Awards Table, such up-to-date information may also become easier to access without referring to other filings. The proposed requirement that LAFs tag the proposed primary tabular disclosures in Inline XBRL may also reduce the costs of extracting information from the disclosures of this subset of registrants.
The net effect on investor search costs, and thus the efficiency of the process by which investors and the market as a whole digest the disclosures, would likely depend on how registrants would use the flexibility afforded to them and whether the potential increases or decreases in search costs are associated with the information that is most frequently sought and most resource-intensive to find.
The proposed amendments may also increase the costs of analysis for some investors (either directly or via third parties). Current disclosures include certain registrant-computed measures of the value of in flight awards, both in the Outstanding Equity Awards at Fiscal Year-End Table (for all registrants) and in more detailed form in the disclosure of Compensation Actually Paid (for registrants required to provide pay-versus-performance disclosures). Removing the requirement that registrants compute these measures may increase analytical burdens on investors (directly or via third parties) who use such computations to evaluate how compensation is tracking performance over time.
[
935
]
For those registrants required to include a CD&A, the disclosure of, for example, compensation peer groups would no longer be explicitly required. To the extent that some such registrants would no longer disclose peer groups, investors and/or third parties may bear greater analytical burdens to identify appropriate peers against which to judge the appropriateness of a registrant's executive compensation design without input from the registrant. Inefficiencies may result from these analytical burdens in that there may be an increased risk of duplicative analytical effort by investors and/or third parties.
Any increased search and analytical burdens are likely to be borne primarily by those investors who most actively review executive compensation disclosures in detail and allocate the greatest resources to such review, which are likely institutional investors and larger investors.
[
936
]
Other investors, such as retail investors or smaller investors for whom it is not possible or cost-effective to allocate significant resources to such review, would be less likely to bear such costs but would, in the absence of taking on such search and analysis, be more likely to have less information and analysis available when making investment and voting decisions. Given recent governance changes that increase the delegation of voting to the end holders of securities,
[
937
]
the role of this group of investors may become more important to voting outcomes in the future, which may exacerbate any effects of reduced access to information and analysis. That said, these investors may be the most likely to read executive compensation disclosure linearly. As such, these investors are also the most likely to benefit from the expected reduction in the volume of disclosure; while they may have less detailed information and analysis at their disposal, they may find the information that remains easier to digest than current disclosures. Given the limited time and resources these investors allocate to reviewing executive compensation disclosures, the cost of their review is unlikely to change meaningfully. However, information asymmetries about executive compensation between investors of different types could either increase or decrease or remain unchanged depending on the extent to which the more principles-based approach would result in information being more readily understood by retail and smaller investors, offsetting the increased asymmetries that may arise from differences in the degree of additional search and analysis undertaken.
The proposed amendments would reduce the detail and comprehensiveness of executive compensation disclosure and may thus lead, overall, to a less precise evaluation (by even the investors with more significant experience or resources for disclosure review) of the appropriateness of the level of pay and of the full set of monetary incentives provided to executive officers.
[
938
]
For example, the proposed amendments are expected to reduce the amount of detailed information available about certain terms of incentive awards (including information about the rigor of performance goals that, in some cases, is currently only available via in flight estimates provided by registrants), certain miscellaneous components of pay (including perquisites and retirement benefits), and potential payments upon termination. The proposed amendments are expected to reduce the comprehensiveness of information about, for example, the compensation of a larger group of executive officers, all amounts of compensation paid to NEOs (however small), and director compensation. Any increase in search and analysis costs could further increase the imprecision of investor evaluations to the extent that some investors would be unwilling to bear additional costs to more closely approach the current precision with which they understand executive compensation.
[
939
]
Any such reduced precision in investors' understanding of the executive compensation at registrants may introduce noise into their voting and investment decisions, in that these decisions may be more likely to vary
(
printed page 75138)
from the decisions that would be made with more detailed and comprehensive information. Such noise may reduce allocative efficiency in the capital market, in that investors' ability to direct capital to its most productive uses may be negatively affected by a diminished ability to reliably evaluate different investment alternatives. A reduction in the detail and comprehensiveness of executive compensation would also be expected to reduce the amount of information incorporated into stock prices, and thus the informational efficiency of markets. Noise in voting decisions may reduce productive efficiency, in that less informed voting outcomes in director elections, say-on-pay votes, votes on equity incentive plans, and other relevant votes may result in less optimal board composition, compensation design, and other registrant-level decisions than otherwise, which could affect the performance and productivity of registrants.
The proposed amendments may also affect compensation design because of the influence disclosure considerations can have on compensation decisions. Some aspects of the proposed amendments reduce factors that could contribute currently to distortions in compensation design (such as in the consideration of whether to provide personal security services to executives or whether to pay a bonus that could change the composition of the NEOs). However, other aspects of the proposed amendments may contribute to new potential distortions, through reduced transparency of some elements (such as perquisites, non-equity incentive pay, retirement benefits, and termination pay) relative to the transparency of other elements of compensation or through differences in how similar awards may be valued (in the case of options versus stock with market conditions). Any distortions associated with disclosure considerations rather than shareholder value optimization may reduce the optimality of executive compensation design and thereby affect the productive efficiency of registrants.
The potential effects of the proposed amendments on efficiency and capital formation may be influenced by other concurrent changes in market practices and regulation. On one hand, other regulatory initiatives to reduce disclosure burdens may, together with the proposed amendments, result in aggregate compliance cost savings that are more likely to have meaningful impacts on capital formation and the decision of companies to go (or stay) public. On the other hand, these initiatives, in totality, may also be more likely to reduce transparency to an extent that there may be offsetting effects on the cost of capital and overall trust in public markets. Market and regulatory environment changes around other governance mechanisms, as discussed in section IV.C.7 above, may also increase the relative importance of executive compensation information to investors' voting and investment decisions and may thus exacerbate the effects of any noise that would be introduced into these decisions as a result of the more condensed and less detailed disclosures that would result from the proposed amendments. A recent trend towards more fragmented shareholder voting, also discussed in section IV.C.7 above, may result in an increase in the number of individuals separately evaluating executive compensation disclosures and in the variety of approaches used for such evaluations. Such a trend could increase the costs associated with a reduction in registrant-provided computations or in the accessibility of certain information, while also increasing the potential benefits of a reduced volume of disclosure given the more limited resources these investors may expend in reviewing the disclosure.
We anticipate limited competitive effects of the proposed amendments on registrants. Because compliance costs generally do not scale perfectly with size, in that they have some fixed cost components, the same disclosure requirement can result in disproportionate burdens on smaller companies. The scaled accommodations currently available to SRCs and EGCs may encourage competition by reducing the risks of such disproportionate burdens. Some aspects of the proposed amendments (such as the proposed NEO definition or the proposed tabular disclosure requirements) would reduce the extent of differences between the requirements that apply to SRCs and EGCs and all other registrants by applying more limited disclosure requirements to all registrants. However, the proposed amendments would also maintain an exemption for SRCs and EGCs from some of the disclosure requirements under the proposal that we expect to be relatively more costly to produce, such as CD&A and pay ratio disclosures. The proposed amendments would thereby maintain a scaled disclosure regime for SRCs and EGCs (or for NAFs, if the proposed amendments in the 2026 Filer Status Proposing Release are adopted) and are thus not expected to meaningfully affect competition among registrants on the whole.

This IRFA relates to the proposed amendments to rules and forms described in section II above.
A. Reasons for, and Objectives of, the Proposed Action
The proposed amendments are intended to make the Commission's executive compensation disclosure requirements more principles-based and the disclosures clearer, more concise, and less complex. In addition, the proposed amendments are intended to reduce compliance burdens for registrants and focus the disclosure on information that is likely to be material to investors. To this end, the proposed amendments would primarily (1) consolidate the main tabular disclosure requirements of Item 402 into three new tables, (2) reduce the number of NEOs for whom executive compensation disclosure is required from five or more to two in most circumstances, (3) provide registrants more flexibility in identifying and reporting perquisites, (4) make compensation disclosure generally, including the CD&A, more principles-based, (5) narrow the required scope of pay-versus-performance, pay ratio and clawbacks disclosures, (6) eliminate prescriptive requirements to disclose potential payments and benefits to an NEO in various termination or change-in-control scenarios, making them more principles-based, (7) simplify and make more principles-based the existing golden parachute compensation disclosure, (8) eliminate mandatory tabular disclosure for director compensation, and (9) extend the period of time available to registrants for providing Item 402 disclosure regarding the last completed fiscal year in registration statements that require Item 402 information. A discussion of the proposed amendments, including a high-level tabular comparison of certain elements of the proposal to current requirements, is set forth in section II above. We discuss the economic impact and potential alternatives to the amendments in section IV, the estimated compliance costs and burdens of the amendments under the PRA in section V, and the present values and annualized values of monetized benefits and costs in section IV.M, above.

C. Small Entities Subject to the Proposed Amendments
The proposed amendments to Item 402 and the related forms, rules, and schedules under the Securities Act, the Exchange Act and Investment Company Act would apply to registrants that are small entities, either as issuers or as investment companies. The RFA defines “small entity” to mean “small business,” “small organization,” or “small governmental jurisdiction.”

For purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act, currently under our rules, an issuer, other than an investment company, is a “small business” or “small organization” if it had total assets of $5 million or less on the last day of its most recent fiscal year and is engaged or proposing to engage in an offering of securities that does not exceed $5 million.

We expect the proposed amendments to reduce burdens associated with preparing executive compensation disclosure for
all

F. Significant Alternatives
The RFA directs us to consider alternatives that would accomplish our stated objectives, while minimizing any significant adverse impact on small entities. In connection with the proposed amendments, we considered the following alternatives:
Establishing different compliance or reporting requirements or timetables that take into account the resources available to small entities;
Clarifying, consolidating, or simplifying compliance and reporting requirements under the rules for small entities;
Using performance rather than design standards; and
Exempting small entities from all or part of the requirements.
As noted, we expect that all or nearly all small entities would be permitted to take advantage of any existing accommodations, to the extent retained in the proposed rule, that allow smaller registrants to provide reduced disclosure in certain areas as compared to other registrants or to be exempt from certain disclosure requirements. The proposed rules would continue to exempt small registrants from substantially the same executive compensation disclosure requirements from which they are exempt under the current rules, as discussed in more detail in section II.M above. In addition, as with all registrants, under the proposal small entities would only be required to provide disclosure for their PEO and PFO, which for SRCs and EGCs is a reduction from the current requirement to provide the PEO, PFO, and next most highly paid executive officer.
With regard to the non-scaled portions of the proposed rule, we believe that the expected benefits of the proposed amendments, including a more principles-based approach and greater flexibility in regard to certain provisions, will accrue to all registrants, including small entities. These expected benefits would result from, among other things:
Requiring registrants to determine and disclose compensation information only for the PEO and PFO, instead of three or more executives (for small entities);
A consolidated, more streamlined approach to tabular disclosure of executive compensation;
Eliminating mandatory tabular disclosure for director compensation;
Eliminating required disclosure related to grants of certain equity awards close in time to the release of material nonpublic information; and
Simplifying disclosure requirements related to a registrant's action to recover erroneously awarded compensation.
After taking into account transition costs, we do not expect that the requirements included in the proposed amendments would increase burdens on any registrants, including small entities. We do not anticipate that small entities would experience any significant adverse impact from the proposal.
We have used both performance standards and design standards in connection with the proposed amendments. Where performance standards supported the goals of the proposed rule amendments, we sought to provide registrants with flexible, principles-based opportunities to meet related disclosure requirements. Where necessary or appropriate to achieving the goals of the proposed rule amendments to elicit specific information, we included design standards, requiring more prescriptive content and/or format to promote clarity and comparability. We believe that, in those areas where we have used design standards, the objectives of the proposed rules are unlikely to be met using performance standards. In these instances, we do not believe that small entities would be disproportionately affected by the proposed prescriptive requirements, some of which they are already complying with under the current rule.
We did consider several alternatives to certain provisions of the proposed rules, which we discuss in detail in section IV above. Some of these alternatives include:
Reducing the NEOs covered to only the PEO (section IV.D.3). Because the elimination of the PFO may not significantly reduce costs, while the information loss to investors could be significant, we are not proposing this alternative.
Requiring alternative presentations for the primary tabular disclosures, such as additional prescriptive requirements to disclose certain factual information about the terms of incentive awards in a standardized form or further delineation of Miscellaneous Compensation Received items (section IV.E.4). Because such additional prescriptive measures would likely increase costs, and not prescribing a presentation method could allow market practices or norms or company-specific approaches to develop under which this information may be presented in a more efficient manner, we are not proposing these alternatives.
The proposed amendments are intended to make the executive compensation disclosure requirements more principles-based, reduce compliance burdens for registrants, and focus the disclosure on information that is likely to be material to investors. We expect that the proposed amendments will generate compliance cost savings for registrants generally, including small entities. As indicated above, the proposed amendments include or retain a number of scaled disclosure accommodations for small entities, which encompass different compliance or reporting requirements, simplified compliance and reporting requirements, and certain exemptions.

                             Staff reviewed filings using the Intelligize database and identified 11,967, 11,116, and 11,053 Item 5.02 Form 8-K filings in each of calendar years 2023, 2024, and 2025 respectively. The number of unique registrants making such filings in each of these years was 4,819, 4,526, and 4,469 respectively. Staff used a large language model (“LLM”) to analyze the Item 5.02(b), 5.02(e), and 5.02(f) disclosures from EDGAR in 2025. The LLM model used was OpenAI GPT-OSS-120B-1:0 with temperature set to 0. The model does not have access to the internet. We converted the filings to text and queried the LLM with the following prompt: “Task: extract Item 5.02 structured records from the filing text. | Regulatory reasons for Item 5.02 filings include and are limited to |: a: Director resignation/removal due to disagreement/cause; | b: Departure of director or principal officer (standard/non-dispute); | c: Appointment of a new principal officer (not applicable to continuation of existing appointments); | d: Election of a new director; | e: New/amended material compensatory arrangement; | f: Determination of previously uncalculable salary/bonus. | Note: an individual being appointed as both a principal officer and a director should result in two extractions: one for `c—appointment of a new principal officer' and one for `d—election of a new director'. However, an existing officer being elected to a director position should not result in a new extraction for c, just for d. | Note: some filings are merely descriptions of changing compensation plans or agreements, not related to any individual, and should be labeled with reason e or f as applicable, but with null for name and role if none are specifically mentioned. | Output schema provided as (strict JSON object): | “extractions” | name, | role, | board_member, | reason_text, | reason_label, | date_effective, material_terms, and evidence. | Rules: Keep each extraction focused on a single person or single event. | Use null for unknown values; do not invent values. | Standardize role names where obvious (
e.g.,
CEO, CFO, Director). | Set board_member=true only when the focused individual is clearly stated to be a board member or director. | reason_text should be concise and quote-near to source wording. | evidence should be a short supporting excerpt from the filing text. | If nothing relevant is found, return an empty extractions array with filing_notes: `No Item 5.02 content found'.” We note that an LLM analysis can result in both false positives and false negatives, and that this analysis is stochastic in nature. Hence, re-running the same algorithm could yield different results. To assess and improve the accuracy of the results, we also conducted a manual validation of a random sample of 100 filings. This review identified five flagged items as potent errors. Two of the five flagged errors could be attributed to errors in prompting when isolating the Item 5.02 disclosures (in one instance the LLM extracted a table of contents and in another instance, the LLM extracted incorporation by reference language from Item 1.01). Of the three substantive errors, two involved 8-Ks with ambiguities in the source (
e.g.,
8-K amendments and 8-Ks that used incorporation by reference language) and one error involved language that the LLM missed. The results reported above reflect the LLM's extraction output for the successfully processed filings with refinement using manual processing to further restrict the filings identified as containing type (b) or type (e) content to those where the focused individual was not identified to be only a board member (and not an executive officer).

November 16, 2026.
On May 11, 2026, the Depository Trust Company (“DTC”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change SR-DTC-2026-007 (“Proposed Rule Change”) pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”)

to consolidate and update the documentation for Agents processing Participant instructions for a corporate action offer, election, solicitation or tabulation (each, an “Offer”) through the DTC Automated Tender Offer Program (ATOP) or DTC Automated Subscription Offer Program (ASOP). The Proposed Rule Change was immediately effective upon filing with the Commission pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Exchange Act.

[
10
]
provides that, after initiating proceedings, the Commission shall issue an order approving or disapproving the proposed rule change not later than 180 days after the date of publication of notice of filing of the proposed rule change. The Commission may extend the period for issuing an order approving or disapproving the proposed rule change, however, by not more than 60 days if the Commission determines that a longer period is appropriate and publishes its reasons for such determination.
[
11
]
As noted above, the Proposed Rule Change was published for public comment in the
Federal Register
on May 22, 2026.
[
12
]
November 18, 2026 is 180 days from that date, and January 15, 2027 is 240 days from that date.
The Commission finds it appropriate to designate a longer period within which to issue an order approving or disapproving the Proposed Rule Change so that the Commission has sufficient time to consider the Proposed Rule Change and its comments. Accordingly, pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Act,

13

Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),

notice is hereby given that on November 3, 2026, Texas Stock Exchange LLC (“Exchange” or “TXSE”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend TXSE Rule 14.001 to: (1) add express cross-references to TXSE Rules 3.007 and 3.021; (2) delete Rule 14.001(b)(1), thereby removing the requirement that the Exchange distribute a product-specific information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product that generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular provided by the listing exchange; (3) amend Rule 14.001(b)(2)(B) to require that any written description be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities; (4) renumber Rules 14.001(b)(2) through (6) as Rules 14.001(b)(1) through (5), respectively, and (5) removing the specific reference to subparagraph (2) from current Rule 14.001(b)(2). The Exchange has designated the proposed rule change as non-controversial pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii)
[
3
]
of the Act and has provided the Commission with the notice required by Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii).
[
4
]
The proposal is based on and substantially similar to recent proposals filed by Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe BZX”), MIAX PEARL, LLC (“MIAX Pearl”), Investors Exchange LLC (“IEX”), and MEMX LLC (“MEMX”).

https://www.txse.com/​reuglations/​rules-filings

(
printed page 74631)
and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to eliminate the requirement in Rule 14.001(b)(1) that the Exchange distribute an information circular to Members prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product. The information circular generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular provided by the listing exchange. The Exchange also proposes to add express cross-references to Rules 3.007 and 3.021 in Rule 14.001(a), amend the written description provision in Rule 14.001(b)(2)(B), and make conforming renumbering changes.
Rule 14.001(b) governs the trading of UTP Exchange Traded Products on the Exchange. UTP Exchange Traded Products are derivative securities products listed on another national securities exchange that trade on the Exchange pursuant to unlisted trading privileges (“UTP”). Under current Rule 14.001(b)(1), the Exchange must distribute an information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product that generally mirrors the information circular provided by the listing exchange, including: (a) the special risks of trading the UTP Exchange Traded Product; (b) the Exchange Rules that will apply to the product, including Rule 3.007; (c) information about the dissemination of the value of the underlying assets or indices; and (d) the applicable trading hours for the UTP Exchange Traded Product and the risks of trading during the period from 8:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. and from 4:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. due to the lack of calculation or dissemination of the underlying index value, the IIV or a similar value. The Exchange proposes to delete Rule 14.001(b)(1) in its entirety.
The product-specific information circular requirement is unnecessary because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members
[
6
]
with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to reproduce. Members have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes.
[
7
]
Requiring the Exchange to prepare and distribute a separate circular containing duplicative information serves no independent investor-protection function.
The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 14.001(a) to add express cross-references to Rule 3.007 (Recommendations to Customers) and Rule 3.021 (Customer Disclosures). These rules already apply to Members by operation of the Exchange's rulebook. The cross-references are intended to preserve the visibility of the applicable customer-protection framework in the context of UTP Exchange Traded Products after deletion of Rule 14.001(b)(1). Rule 3.007 independently requires a Member recommending a UTP Exchange Traded Product to have reasonable grounds for believing the recommendation is suitable for the customer based on the facts disclosed by the customer after reasonable inquiry into the customer's other securities holdings, financial situation, and needs. Similarly, Rule 3.021 independently requires Members to disclose the material risks of extended-hours trading before accepting a customer order for execution in the Pre-Market or Post-Market Session. These standing obligations are not contingent on the Exchange's issuance of a product-specific circular.
Because Rule 14.001(b)(1) has historically served as the mechanism through which the Exchange informs Members of the application of the written-description provisions in Rule 14.001(b)(2)(B), the Exchange proposes a conforming amendment to that paragraph. The Exchange will continue to inform Members of the application of the written-description provisions by information circular, but proposes to require that any written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange, rather than the Exchange, or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing the securities. The Exchange will notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange. This amendment is consistent with the broader purpose of the proposed rule change: where the listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the information necessary to assess a UTP Exchange Traded Product, a duplicative written description obligation serves no independent investor protection function. Members may rely on the listing exchange's information circular in the same manner and to the same effect.
The Exchange also proposes to renumber existing Rules 14.001(b)(2) through (6) as Rules 14.001(b)(1) through (5), respectively.
Finally, the Exchange proposes to delete the reference to subparagraph (2) in current Rule 14.001(b)(2) (as proposed to be re-numbered to Rule 14.001(b)(1) herein) such that instead of reading “this subparagraph (2) apply only to” it would read “this subparagraph apply only to.”
The proposal is based on and substantially similar to the Cboe BZX proposal and the subsequent MIAX Pearl, IEX, and MEMX proposals.
[
8
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
9
]
in general, and specifically with the objectives of Section 6(b)(5),
[
10
]
in that it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange also believes the proposal is consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b)(5) that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
[
11
]
The proposed deletion of Rule 14.001(b)(1) is consistent with the Act because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures that the Exchange's information circular would contain. The investor protection functions historically served by the product-specific circular requirement are independently addressed by the primary listing exchange's information circular and by the Member-level obligations imposed by Rules 3.007 and 3.021, which the Exchange proposes to cross-reference expressly in Rule
(
printed page 74632)
14.001(a). Members will therefore continue to have access to the relevant product information and remain subject to the same suitability, disclosures, supervisory, and trading obligations after the proposed deletion.
The proposed amendment to Rule 14.001(b)(2)(B) is also consistent with the Act because it requires any written description referenced therein to be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing the securities. The amendment aligns the Exchange's requirement with the disclosure framework of the primary listing market and eliminates duplicative Exchange review without reducing the information available to Members or customers. The proposed renumbering of Rules 14.001(b)(2) through (6) as Rules 14.001(b)(1) through (5), respectively, and the deletion of the specific reference to paragraph (2) in current Rule 14.001(b)(2) are ministerial.
As discussed above, the proposal is substantially similar to rule changes previously filed by other national securities exchanges and does not raise novel regulatory issues.
[
12
]
For these reasons, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposal eliminates a duplicative procedural obligation applicable to the Exchange in its capacity as a UTP trading venue. It does not alter the terms or conditions under which UTP Exchange Traded Products may be traded on the Exchange, impose any new requirement on Members, or affect the ability of any market participant to access the Exchange's market. Members will continue to have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes as the Exchange's current circular.
The proposed amendment to Rule 14.001(b)(2)(B) aligns the written-description obligation with the primary listing market's disclosure framework and does not impose a burden beyond the requirements applicable to the product on its listing market. Accordingly, the Exchange does not believe the proposed rule change imposes any burden on intramarket or intermarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange has neither solicited nor received written comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
13
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
14
]
thereunder. Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; or (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
15
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
16
]
thereunder.
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
17
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b4(f)(6)(iii),
[
18
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposed rule change may become operative immediately upon filing. The Exchange states that the proposed rule change eliminates duplicative procedural obligations applicable to the Exchange in its capacity as a UTP trading venue because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce.
[
19
]
The Exchange also notes that the proposed rule change does not alter the terms or conditions under which UTP Exchange Traded Products may be traded on the Exchange. For these reasons, the Commission finds that waiver of the 30-day operative delay is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. Therefore, the Commission hereby waives the 30-day operative delay and designates the proposed rule change to be operative upon filing.
[
20
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-TXSE-2026-048  on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-TXSE-2026-048. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection.  All submissions should refer to file number SR-TXSE-2026-048 and
(
printed page 74633)
should be submitted on or before December 10, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
21
]
Vanessa A. Countryman,
Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106908; File No. SR-ICC-2026-011]
November 16, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Securities Exchange Act” or the “Act”),
15 U.S.C. 78s(b)(1)
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
17 CFR 240.19b-4
, notice is hereby given that on November 3, 2026, ICE Clear Credit LLC (“ICC” or “ICE Clear Credit”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II and III below, which Items have been prepared primarily by ICC. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The principal purpose of the proposed rule change is to make revisions to ICC's Treasury Clearing Rules (“Treasury Rules” or “Rules”) and certain Treasury Clearing Service policies and procedures (“Treasury Risk Documentation”), including the Treasury Clearing Service Initial Margin Approach Model Description Document (“IM Approach Model Description”), Treasury Clearing Service Guaranty Fund and Stress Test Approach Model Description Document (“GF and Stress Test Approach Model Description”), and Treasury Clearing Service Risk Parameter Setting and Review Policy (“Risk Parameter Policy”).
[
1
]
II. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, ICC included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change, security-based swap submission, or advance notice and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change, security-based swap submission, or advance notice. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. ICC has prepared summaries, set forth in sections (A), (B), and (C) below, of the most significant aspects of these statements.
(A) Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
(a) Purpose
ICC proposes changes to the Treasury Rules and Treasury Risk Documentation. As background, ICC filed an application on Form CA-1 (“Application”) under Section 17A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”)
[
2
]
with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) to register as a clearing agency to provide central counterparty services for transactions involving U.S. Treasury (“Treasury”) securities on August 1, 2025. Notice of ICC's Application was published in the
Federal Register
on August 21, 2025.
[
3
]
The Application contained the Treasury Rules and certain other policies and procedures governing the Treasury Clearing Service, including the GF and Stress Test Approach Model Description, IM Approach Model Description, and Risk Parameter Policy. The Commission issued an order granting ICC's Application for registration as a clearing agency to provide central counterparty services for transactions involving Treasury securities on January 30, 2026.
[
4
]
ICC proposes additional changes to the Treasury Rules and Treasury Risk Documentation to facilitate the clearing of Treasury repurchase and reverse repurchase (“repo”) contracts and to make additional clarifications. The proposed changes to the Treasury Rules (i) update and clarify the rules for Variation Payments, (ii) introduce a new margin and settlement model for eligible money funds (the “Money Fund Margin Model” or “Fund Model”), (iii) expand the rules governing Treasury physical settlement to include triparty settlement, (iv) expand the contract terms applicable to repo contracts, and (v) make additional clarification or clean-up changes. The proposed
(
printed page 74620)
changes to the Treasury Risk Documentation provide detail on ICC's risk management approach for repo contracts and make general clarifications throughout the documentation. ICC believes that such revisions will facilitate the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions. ICC proposes to make such changes effective following Commission approval of the proposed rule change. The proposed revisions are described in detail as follows.
Treasury Rulebook Changes
Variation Payments
ICC proposes revising Rule 404 to update and clarify the rules for calculating Variation Payments. The proposed amendments expand the definition of Variation Payment in paragraph (a) to include additional payment types and clarify that Variation Payment calculations may differ for contracts subject to the different Treasury physical settlement provisions in Chapters 22 through 24.
ICC proposes to introduce new defined terms and revise certain existing defined terms in Rule 404. A new defined term, Variation Payment Cycle, is introduced in Rule 404(a)(i) referring to each time as of which ICC determines Variation Payment Requirements.
[
5
]
The definition of Variation Payment Requirement would be revised in Rule 404(a)(ii) to refer to the Variation Payment Cycle. As amended, a Treasury Participant's Variation Payment Requirement for a margin category (“Variation Payment Category”) for a Variation Payment Cycle would be the net sum of applicable components, further described below. The revised definition of Variation Payment Requirement also lists specific components that may be included in the variation calculation, depending on the particular contract and manner of settlement. ICC also proposes to specify in Rule 404(a) which Variation Payment-related amounts are expressed as negative or positive values.
ICC proposes to rename Mark-to-Market Price to Mark-to-Market Amount in Rule 404(b) and provide additional detail on such calculation. Currently, Mark-to-Market Price generally refers to a price determined by ICC pursuant to its procedures. The revised definition provides greater specificity. The Mark-to-Market Amount for an open position means the difference between the position's current value and the value of the position determined by reference to the price, rate and other economic terms agreed by the original parties to the trade.
Pursuant to Rule 404(b), for a repo contract, Mark-to-Market Amount would consist of three components capturing the change in value of the repo contract attributable to (i) the change in value of the Purchased Securities
[
6
]
(“MTM Collateral Component”); (ii) the prevailing spot repo rate applicable to that repo contract and the remaining term thereof (“MTM Spot Repo Rate Component”); and (iii) the forward repo rate specified in the repo contract and the prevailing repo rate determined by ICC for comparable collateral and residual tenor (“MTM Forward Repo Rate Component”). Additional provisions clarify when such components apply. For example, Rule 404(b)(iv) provides that, in respect of a spot contract,
[
7
]
only the MTM Collateral Component applies, because a spot contract does not involve a repurchase contract for which repo rates that would be captured in the MTM Spot Repo Rate Component or the MTM Forward Repo Rate Component are relevant.
ICC proposes MTM Change Payments as a new defined term in Rule 404(c) to refer to the net amount of the Mark-to-Market Amount as of the current Variation Payment Cycle less the Mark-to-Market Amount as of the immediately preceding Variation Payment Cycle. Under Rule 404(c)(i), for the first Variation Payment Cycle for a position, the Mark-to-Market Amount as of the immediately preceding Variation Payment Cycle will be zero, as no Mark-to-Market Amount has previously been determined for that position (and as a result the first MTM Change Payment for that position will equal the full current Mark-to-Market Amount). Each MTM Change Payment transfer would constitute a settlement of the Mark-to-Market Amount, as further described in Rule 404(c)(ii) and (iii).
Rule 404(d) would introduce Price Alignment Amount Payments, calculated using a Price Alignment Rate that is defined as the overnight interest rate determined by ICC for the relevant currency. The Price Alignment Amount Payment means the amount determined by ICC on each Variation Payment Cycle by applying the Price Alignment Rate to the cumulative MTM Change Payments of that Treasury Participant for that Variation Payment Category, as set out in further detail in Rule 404(d). As specified in Rule 404(d)(iii), Price Alignment Amount Payments are determined and settled to account for the funding effect of settling Mark-to-Market Amounts under Rule 404(c), so that the pricing of contracts cleared by ICC is not distorted by reason of such settlement relative to equivalent transactions that are not cleared.
ICC proposes to define Coupon Adjustment Payments and Redemption Adjustment Payments in Rules 404(e) and (f), respectively. ICC would determine a Coupon Adjustment Payment where a coupon or other periodic distribution is paid in respect of Purchased Securities during the term of a repo contract in an amount equal to that coupon or distribution. ICC would determine a Redemption Adjustment Payment where Purchased Securities are redeemed at maturity during the term of a repo contract in an amount equal to the redemption proceeds of those Purchased Securities. Amended Rule 404(g) would revise the definition of Transaction Adjustment Payment, which would reflect the difference between the relevant transaction price and the current ICC Settlement Price.
[
8
]
Additional variation payment provisions are added in Rules 404(h) through (l). Where a settlement obligation is not settled on its scheduled settlement date and the related obligations constitute a fail position, ICC would determine a Fail Settlement Adjustment Payment under paragraph (h) in order to preserve the original economic terms of the failed delivery or receipt obligation. A Fail Charge Payment, as specified in paragraph (i), would be determined under existing Treasury Rule 2205, in the case of certain failures in DVP settlement. Miscellaneous Adjustment Payments would be defined in paragraph (j) as any other amount payable by or to a Treasury Participant for contracts settled through Variation Payments. ICC would maintain a record of the Variation Payment balance of each Treasury Participant for each Variation Payment Category, as specified in paragraph (k). In paragraph (l), ICC would clarify that Variation Payments described in Rule 404 constitute final settlements.
(
printed page 74621)
Money Fund Margin Model
ICC proposes to amend the Treasury Rules to introduce the Money Fund Margin Model, which is intended to facilitate access for registered funds to participate in the Treasury Clearing Service. ICC proposes to adopt a new Treasury Rule 411 to introduce a new margin model. ICC designed this Money Fund Margin Model to be consistent with applicable regulatory requirements for registered funds under the Investment Company Act of 1940,
[
9
]
including the full collateralization requirements for repos by registered funds pursuant to Rule 5b-3 and related existing market practices for repos by registered funds.
[
10
]
To facilitate participation by registered funds in the Treasury Clearing Service, the Money Fund Margin Model makes certain modifications to the standard margin model applicable to other market participants. Additional details are described below.
Under new Treasury Rule 411(a), ICC may, on written request of a Non-Participant Party (
i.e.,
a customer of a Treasury Participant) that is an Eligible Money Fund, permit such Eligible Money Fund to comply with the Money Fund Margin Model with respect to Eligible Money Fund Transactions (such an Eligible Money Fund, a “Covered Money Fund”).
New Treasury Rule 411(b) sets out key defined terms applicable to the Money Fund Margin Model. Such terms include Eligible Money Fund, defined as an investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940
[
11
]
and such other types of investment funds as ICC may permit; Eligible Money Fund Transactions, which are eligible repo contracts in which the Covered Money Fund is acting as the Repo Buyer;
[
12
]
and Money Fund Custodial Account, which is an account in the name of the Covered Money Fund at a triparty bank acceptable to ICC (the “Money Fund Custody Bank”).
Rule 411(c) through (l) set out additional legal, risk, operational, and default management provisions for the Money Fund Margin Model, as follows.
Paragraph (c) describes how an Eligible Money Fund may be designated as a Covered Money Fund. Each Covered Money Fund must enter into an agreement with ICC in such form designated by ICC.
Paragraph (d) requires each Covered Money Fund to establish a Money Fund Custodial Account, subject to an agreement entered into by the Covered Money Fund, the Money Fund Custody Bank, ICC, and such other persons as ICC may designate.
Paragraph (e) requires each Eligible Money Fund Transaction to specify an initial haircut (the “Initial Haircut”) agreed between the Covered Money Fund and its original counterparty (the “Original Counterparty”).
Paragraph (f) describes the settlement of the delivery of the Purchased Securities to and from the Money Fund Custodial Account.
Paragraph (g) restricts a Covered Money Fund generally from transferring, using, rehypothecating or otherwise disposing of any securities transferred to or credited to the Money Fund Custodial Account.
Paragraph (h) provides for a first priority lien and security interest granted by each Covered Money Fund to ICC in (i) its Money Fund Custodial Account, (ii) the Purchased Securities transferred to such Covered Money Fund, (iii) all securities, financial assets, cash and other property that may be transferred, credited to, or held in the Money Fund Custodial Account, and (iv) all cash or non-cash proceeds of any of the foregoing (collectively, the “Money Fund Account Collateral”), to secure the obligations in favor of ICC.
In light of the security interest provided under paragraph (h), paragraph (i) provides generally that neither the Covered Money Fund nor its Treasury Participant is obligated to provide Initial Margin (“IM”) or Variation Payments, and ICC is not obligated to provide Variation Payments.
Paragraph (j) describes how, upon authorization and direction from the Covered Money Fund and its Treasury Participant, ICC effects settlement of the Final Leg of an Eligible Money Fund Transaction by instructing the Money Fund Custody Bank to transfer the relevant securities from the Money Fund Custodial Account against payment of the applicable cash amount.
Paragraph (k) provides that the Covered Money Fund is obligated as principal for the performance of its settlement obligations to ICC and the Covered Money Fund's Treasury Participant is not obligated to ICC to perform such obligations. For the avoidance of doubt, Eligible Money Fund Transactions of a Covered Money Fund are considered Client-Related Positions of that Covered Money Fund's Treasury Participant (subject to the provisions in Rule 411), and accordingly are taken into account in determining the Treasury Participant's Treasury Guaranty Fund (“GF”) requirements.
[
13
]
This provision also sets out when ICC's obligations to the Treasury Participant and Covered Money Fund in respect of settlement obligations are discharged.
Paragraph (l) sets out default management provisions and corresponding default management actions to be taken by relevant parties, including in the case of a client default with respect to a Covered Money Fund, a default of the Covered Money Fund's Treasury Participant, and a default of the Original Counterparty or its Treasury Participant. In the case of a client default with respect to a Covered Money Fund, ICC manages such default with respect to any Eligible Money Fund Transactions and is entitled to apply the Money Fund Account Collateral to the settlement obligations of the Covered Money Fund (against payment of any amount owed to the Covered Money Fund in respect of such settlement). In the case of a default of the Covered Money Fund's Treasury Participant, ICC may, to the extent it is legally permitted and otherwise feasible to do so on a timely basis, apply the Money Fund Account Collateral to the settlement obligations of the Covered Money Fund in respect of Eligible Money Fund Transactions as and when they become due (against payment of any amount owed by ICC to the Covered Money Fund in respect of such settlement). Otherwise, ICC may terminate the Eligible Money Fund Transactions of the Covered Money Fund in accordance with the Rules applicable to client positions of the defaulting Treasury Participant and determine the net cash amount owed in respect thereof by the Covered Money Fund or ICC. In the case of a default of the Original Counterparty (or its Treasury Participant), upon receiving notice from ICC, the Covered Money Fund may, to the extent permitted by applicable law on a timely basis, elect to terminate its Eligible Money Fund Transactions, in which case (i) the corresponding transaction between ICC and the Original Counterparty will simultaneously terminate, (ii) the Covered Money Fund will be entitled to
(
printed page 74622)
withdraw the Money Fund Account Collateral, (iii) ICC will have no further obligation in favor of the Covered Money Fund or its Treasury Participant in respect of the Eligible Money Fund Transactions, and (iv) ICC will have no further obligation to the Original Counterparty (or its Treasury Participant) in respect of the Eligible Money Fund Transactions. If the Covered Money Fund does not timely make such election, ICC may terminate the Eligible Money Fund Transactions of the Covered Money Fund and determine the net cash amount owed by the Covered Money Fund or ICC. In such case, ICC may liquidate the Money Fund Account Collateral of such Covered Money Fund. ICC may apply such collateral or the proceeds thereof to any amount owed in respect of such termination.
Treasury Physical Settlement
ICC proposes to expand its Treasury physical settlement rules by amending existing Chapter 22 and introducing new Chapters 23 and 24.
[
14
]
Amended Chapter 22 would govern DVP physical settlement and would be renamed from “Treasury Physical Settlement” to “Treasury DVP Physical Settlement.” In general, DVP physical settlement refers to a settlement mechanism around the delivery of securities against payment. ICC proposes new Chapter 23, titled “Treasury Standard Triparty Settlement” which would govern transactions designated under the Rules for standard triparty settlement. While largely mirroring the structure of Chapter 22, Chapter 23 would establish a framework for triparty settlement of cleared repo transactions through a designated Triparty Bank. As noted above, in general, DVP physical settlement refers to a settlement mechanism providing for the delivery of securities to the account of the receiving party at its custodian against payment (without any restriction on the use of such securities by the receiving party). In contrast, triparty settlement is affected through accounts of both relevant parties at a designated Triparty Bank, which facilitates the settlement of deliveries and payments, on terms in which securities are generally not removed from the Triparty Bank absent a default by a relevant party. New Rule 2301 introduces key definitions, including Triparty Bank, the bank ICC designates to establish triparty accounts; Triparty Settlement Accounts, which include any of the CP House, CP Client, or Individual Client Triparty Settlement Accounts;

ICC Triparty Settlement Account, which is an account maintained by ICC at the Triparty Bank; and Triparty Settlement Obligation, which refers to a gross or net settlement obligation to deliver or receive Eligible Triparty Securities.

Rule 2302 sets out the methodology for calculating Triparty Settlement Obligations for Settling Open Positions subject to net triparty settlement. Based on the Required Securities Value
