As described below, the Exchange proposes that depending on which Prepayment Fee they elect to pay, Participants of the Program may become eligible to earn either (i) the right to purchase both Original Equity and Additional Equity or (ii) the right to purchase Additional Equity only.
ii. Prepayment Fee
The Exchange proposes that current Participants of the Program who have already paid the $500,000 Prepayment Fee will be automatically eligible to earn the right to purchase Additional Equity for any Measurement Period in which the Program thresholds are met, as long as those Participants continue to meet the other Program eligibility requirements. The Exchange also proposes that any Participant who joins the Program after the proposed rule change goes into effect can either (i) prepay $500,000 in Exchange fees to become eligible to earn the right to purchase both Original Equity and Additional Equity, or (ii) prepay a reduced amount of $250,000 in Exchange fees to become eligible to earn the right to purchase Additional Equity only. The Prepayment Fee must be tendered by the first day of each quarter of the Program Period to participate in the Program as of such quarter until April 1, 2028.
The following are examples of the timing of participation in the Program:
If Participant A joined the Program by tendering the $500,000 Prepayment Fee and executing the required documentation on October 14, 2025 (the date trading commenced on the Exchange), then Participant A's trading starting on October 14, 2025 would be counted toward the Target Volume for Year 1 and thereafter until the end of the Program Period. Participant A would be eligible to earn the right to purchase both Original Equity and Additional Equity for the entire Program Period.
If Participant B joined the Program by tendering the $500,000 Prepayment Fee and executing the required documentation on October 22, 2026, then Participant B's trading starting on January 1, 2027 would be counted toward the Target Volume for the first quarter of Year 3 (
i.e.,
the first Measurement Period for Year 3) and thereafter until the end of the Program Period. Participant B would be eligible to earn the right to purchase both Original Equity and Additional Equity starting with the Measurement Period that begins on January 1, 2027 throughout the end of the Program Period.
If Participant C joined the Program by tendering the $250,000 Prepayment Fee and executing the required documentation on October 22, 2026, then Participant C's trading starting on January 1, 2027 would be counted toward the Target Volume for the first quarter of Year 3 (
i.e.,
the first Measurement Period for Year 3) and thereafter until the end of the Program Period. Participant C would be eligible to earn the right to purchase Additional Equity only starting with the Measurement Period that begins on January 1, 2027 throughout the end of the Program Period.
If Participant D joined the Program by tendering the $500,000 Prepayment Fee and executing the required documentation on October 1, 2027, then Participant D's trading starting on October 1, 2027 would be counted toward the Target Volume for the fourth quarter of Year 3 (
i.e.,
the last Measurement Period in Year 3) and the first quarter of Year 4 (
i.e.,
the only Measurement Period in Year 4). Participant D would be eligible to earn both the right to purchase Original Equity for the last Measurement Period in Year 3 and the right to purchase Additional Equity for the last Measurement Period in Year 3 and the only two Measurement Periods in Year 4. No Member may become a Participant that is eligible to earn Original Equity after October 1, 2027.
If Participant E joined the Program by tendering the $250,000 Prepayment Fee and executing the required documentation on April 1, 2028, then Participant E's trading starting on April 1, 2028 would be counted toward the Target Volume for the second quarter of Year 4 (
i.e.,
the second Measurement Period in Year 4). Participant E would be eligible to earn the right to purchase Additional Equity for the second Measurement Period in Year 4. No Member may become a Participant after April 1, 2028.
All other terms regarding the Prepayment Fee would remain unchanged as described in the Warrant Program Releases.
iii. Target Volume Calculation
As described in the Warrant Program Release, the Target Volume that Participants must meet in order for their warrants to vest is 5% of the average daily trading volume on the Exchange, where the daily trading volume is calculated based on total aggregated average daily volume traded over each Measurement Period.
[
15
]
The Exchange proposes that with respect to Additional Equity only, Target Volume for each Measurement Period will be calculated based solely on Participants' maker volume (
i.e.,
trading volume which adds liquidity to the Exchange). Target Volume will continue to be calculated based on total trading volume with respect to Original Equity.
Pursuant to the Program requirements, the Non-Voting Common Units subject to the Program would be allocated among Participants who have met or outperformed the Target Volume during each Measurement Period on a pro rata basis based on volume contributions to the 24X market. As described in the Warrant Program Release, the volumes for each Participant are calculated for each of the Measurement Periods,
[
16
]
and the Non-Voting Common Units indicated are allocated among Participants after the end of each Measurement Period. With respect to Additional Equity only, the Exchange proposes to add two Measurement Periods during the first and second quarters of Year 4.
(
printed page 74617)
Therefore, the Non-Voting Common Units that would be available to be purchased for the first Measurement Period of Year 4 in accordance with the Program will be allocated among Participants that meet the Target Volume on or before April 5, 2028 and after March 31, 2028, based on trading during the first Measurement Period of Year 4, which is the quarterly period from January 1, 2028 through March 31, 2028. The Non-Voting Common Units that would be available to be purchased for the second Measurement Period of Year 4 in accordance with the Program will be allocated among Participants that meet the Target Volume on or before July 5, 2028 and after June 30, 2028, based on trading during the second Measurement Period of Year 4, which is the quarterly period from April 1, 2028 through June 30, 2028. All other terms regarding Target Volume would remain unchanged as described in the Warrant Program Releases.
b. Proposed Changes With Respect to Both Original Equity and Additional Equity
i. Elimination of 24X Minimum Overall Market Share Threshold
As described in the Warrant Program Releases, the 24X Minimum Overall Market Share is a designated target percentage of the CADV for all NMS Stocks eligible for trading on 24X for each relevant Measurement Period.
[
17
]
The CADV is calculated based on the volume reported by all exchanges and trade reporting facilities to a consolidated transaction reporting plan for the relevant Measurement Period.
In order to incentivize participation in the Program and bring greater volume and liquidity to the Exchange, the Exchange proposes to eliminate the 24X Minimum Overall Market Share requirement with respect to Original Equity, and to not implement a 24X Minimum Overall Market Share requirement with respect to Additional Equity. Elimination of the requirement would make Program outcomes more predictable for Participants because Exchange market share depends on the trading activity of all Members and on changes in overall U.S. equity market volume, rather than the individual actions of each Participant. By allowing Participants to determine whether their warrants will vest solely by choosing to meet the Target Volume and not having to rely on other factors outside their control, the proposed revised Program would both attract more new Participants and encourage existing Participants to increase the amount of liquidity they contribute to the Exchange. The Exchange also notes that another national securities exchange offers a warrant program that does not include an exchange market share threshold as a warrant vesting condition.
[
18
]
ii. Exclusion of Dates
With respect to both Original Equity and Additional Equity, the Exchange also proposes to exclude the following dates from the calculation of the Target Volume that Participants must meet in each Measurement Period in order for their warrants to vest:

On equivalent rebalance and reconstitution dates in the past, a significant percentage of consolidated trading volume has occurred during the closing auctions on the primary listing exchanges. Because these auction executions were not available to the Exchange or Program Participants, they artificially increased consolidated market volume while providing no realistic opportunity for Participants to increase trading volume on 24X. The Exchange therefore proposes to exclude the above dates from the calculation of Target Volume given that their inclusion would create a diluting effect that would make it more difficult for Participants to achieve Target Volume through ordinary trading activity.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Exchange Act
[
19
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Exchange Act
[
20
]
in particular, in that it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanisms of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5) of the Exchange Act
[
21
]
requirement that the rules of an
(
printed page 74618)
exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange also believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Exchange Act,
[
22
]
which requires that Exchange rules provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among its members and other persons using its facilities.
The Exchange believes that the proposed changes to the Program are consistent with the Act. Making the Additional Equity available for purchase through the Program at a reduced Prepayment Fee and based on maker volume only would both encourage additional Participant enrollment in the Program, and encourage Participants to provide additional volume and liquidity to the Exchange. The Exchange believes that an increase in volume and liquidity would benefit all market participants by providing more trading opportunities and tighter spreads, even to those market participants that do not participate in the Program, thereby perfecting the mechanism for a free and open market and national market system.
Moreover, the elimination of the 24X Minimum Overall Market Share requirement and exclusion of certain dates from the calculation of Target Volume with respect to both Original Equity and Additional Equity would make it more likely that Participants' warrants would vest in any given Measurement Period. As described above, elimination of the 24X Minimum Overall Market Share requirement would allow Participants to have more control over whether their warrants vest in any given Measurement Period,
[
23
]
and exclusion of certain dates from the calculation of Target Volume would remove a potential diluting effect that otherwise would hamper Participants' ability to achieve Target Volume through ordinary trading activity. These incentives would promote the long-term interests of the Exchange by attracting new Participants and encouraging existing Participants to contribute to the growth and success of the Exchange via actively providing liquidity on the 24X market, and to provide additional investment and funding which could be used for the regulation and operation of the Exchange. The Exchange believes that the additional funds provided as a result of these changes would enable the Exchange to have greater capacity to carry out the purposes of the Act and to comply with the provisions of the Act, the rules and regulations thereunder, and the rules of the Exchange, which, in turn, would protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes that the proposed changes are equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because all Participants may earn the right to purchase both Original Equity and Additional Equity on the same terms and conditions. The additional Measurement Period, Prepayment Fee schedule, and Target Volume modification with respect to Additional Equity are objective and the same for all Participants. Likewise, the elimination of the 24X Minimum Overall Market Share requirement and exclusion of certain dates from the calculation of Target Volume with respect to both Additional Equity and Original Equity are based on objective standards and would have the same effect for all Participants.
A Participant's total equity ownership of 24X US Holdco Units, including any purchased through the exercise of vested warrants via the Program, shall be subject to the ownership limitations of the 24X US Holdco LLC Agreement.
[
24
]
Accordingly, a Participant will not be able to exercise warrants for Non-Voting Common Units to the extent that such exercise would violate such ownership limitations.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act. The Exchange believes that the Program as amended by this proposed rule change would increase both intermarket and intramarket competition by incentivizing Participants to add liquidity to the Exchange, which will enhance the quality of quoting and increase the volume of securities traded on the Exchange. To the extent that there is an additional competitive burden on non-Participants, the Exchange believes that such burden is appropriate because the Program should incentivize Participants to add liquidity to the Exchange and thus enhance the volume of securities traded on the Exchange. To the extent that this purpose is achieved, the Exchange believes that all of the Exchange's market participants would benefit from the improved market liquidity.
Given the robust competition for volume among equities markets, implementing a program to attract liquidity addition like the one proposed in this filing is consistent with the abovementioned goals of the Exchange Act. This is especially true for the smaller exchange markets, such as 24X, which are competing for volume with much larger exchanges that dominate the equities trading industry. As a new exchange, 24X will likely continue to have a nominal percentage of the average daily trading volume in equities in the near term, so it is unlikely that the Program could cause any competitive harm to the equities market or to market participants. Rather, the Program is a modest attempt to attract order volume away from larger competitors by adopting an innovative pricing strategy. The Exchange notes that if the Program results in a modest percentage increase in the average daily trading volume on 24X, while such percentage would represent a large volume increase for 24X, it would represent a minimal reduction in volume of its larger competitors in the industry. I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (“BZX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to amend the Invesco Galaxy Bitcoin ETF (the “Bitcoin Trust”) and the Invesco Galaxy Ethereum ETF (the “ETH Trust” and, together with the Bitcoin Trust, the “Trusts”), shares (“Shares”) of which have been approved by the Commission to list and trade on the Exchange pursuant to BZX Rule 14.11(e)(4) under approval orders, to permit the Trusts to list and trade under the generic listing standards of that rule.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​bzx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Commission has previously approved the listing and trading of shares for the Bitcoin Trust
[
3

4

The Exchange now proposes to transition the Trusts to operate under the recently Commission-approved generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares pursuant to Rule 14.11(e)(4) (“Amended Rule 14.11(e)(4)”).
[
5
]
Each Trust will meet the requirements of Amended Rule 14.11(e)(4) and will be required to comply with the continued listing requirements set forth in such Rule.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
6
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
7
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
8
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is designed to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest because it would provide for the transition of the Trusts from being listed pursuant to the Approval Orders to Amended Rule 14.11(e)(4) instead. The proposed change would allow the Shares to continue listing and trading on the Exchange and permit the Trusts to operate in reliance on the generic listing standards in Amended Rule 14.11(e)(4) instead of the terms of the Approval Orders, thereby facilitating the continued listing and trading of exchange-traded products that will enhance competition among market participants, to the benefit of investors and the marketplace. Each Trust will meet the requirements of Amended Rule 14.11(e)(4) and will be required to comply with the continued listing standards set forth in Amended Rule 14.11(e)(4).
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purpose of the Act. As discussed above, the proposed change is intended to facilitate the continued listing and trading of the Fund on the Exchange, thereby promoting competition among exchange-traded products to the benefit of investors and the marketplace.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
9
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
10
]
thereunder. Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; or (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
11
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
12
]
thereunder.
(
printed page 74630)
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
13
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
14
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposed rule change may become operative immediately upon filing. The Commission believes that waiving the 30-day operative delay is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest because it will allow the Exchange to implement the proposed rule change without delay, thereby providing for the continued listing and trading of the Trusts' Shares, and does not introduce any novel regulatory issues. Accordingly, the Commission designates the proposed rule change to be operative upon filing.

]

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106912; File No. SR-OCC-2026-012]
November 16, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act” or “Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule
(
printed page 74639)
19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 4, 2026, The Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared primarily by OCC. OCC filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)
[
3
]
of the Act and paragraph (f) or Rule 19b-4
[
4
]
thereunder, such that the proposed rule change was immediately effective upon filing with the Commission. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
This proposed rule change would implement a fee holiday for the period beginning December 1, 2026, and ending December 31, 2026. Pursuant to OCC's Capital Management Policy, which the Commission has approved as an OCC rule, when OCC's liquid net assets funded by equity (“LNAFBE”) exceed 110% of OCC's Target Capital Requirement and other approved capital needs, OCC may use tools it deems appropriate to lower costs for clearing members including by implementing a fee holiday. OCC has filed proposed changes to its schedule of fees as Exhibit 5 to File Number SR-OCC-2026-012. Material proposed to be added to OCC's schedule of fees as currently in effect is underlined and material proposed to be deleted is marked in strikethrough text. All capitalized terms not defined herein have the same meaning as set forth in the OCC By-Laws and Rules.
II. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, OCC included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. OCC has prepared summaries, set forth in sections (A), (B), and (C) below, of the most significant aspects of these statements.
(A) Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
Founded in 1973, OCC operates as a central counterparty (“CCP”) under the jurisdiction of both the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”). As a registered clearing agency under the SEC's jurisdiction, OCC is the sole clearing agency for equity options listed on national securities exchanges. As a registered Subpart C DCO under the CFTC's jurisdiction, OCC clears and settles transactions in futures and options on futures. OCC also provides central counterparty clearing and settlement services for securities lending transactions. In its role as a CCP, OCC guarantees the performance of its Clearing Members for all transactions cleared by OCC by becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. Given OCC's critical role, OCC has been designated by the Financial Stability Oversight Council as a systemically important financial market utility (“SIFMU”) under Title VIII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, entitled the Payment, Clearing and Settlement Supervision Act of 2010 (“Clearing Supervision Act”).
[
5
]
Beginning in January 2025, OCC increased its clearing fee to $0.025 per contract in part to cover increased capital expenditures and decreasing interest income. Over the past several years, OCC has incurred significant expenses due to investments in a modernized technology infrastructure tied to the development and future launch of OCC's new clearing system, Ovation. This new system will improve efficiency both for the industry and OCC. This has come with increased costs, however, with expense growth in cloud technology, hardware, software, data centers, and disaster recovery; headcount increases and wage inflation; and increased costs related to regulatory obligations. However, given the high clearing volumes over the first half of 2025, OCC implemented a fee holiday for December 2025 effectively returning excess capital to market participants. Clearing volume during the first half of 2026 has been similarly strong and OCC's LNAFBE exceeds 110% of its Target Capital Requirement and appears likely to remain above that mark for the remainder of 2026 and 2027. OCC is therefore using the tools outlined in its Capital Management Policy and returning capital to market participants by implementing a fee holiday for December 2026.
1. Purpose
Background
As the sole clearing agency for standardized equity options listed on national securities exchanges registered with the Commission, and with respect to OCC's clearance and settlement of futures and stock loan transactions, OCC maintains policies and procedures to manage the risks borne by OCC as a central counterparty. One such risk that OCC manages is general business risk, that is, the risk of potential impairment to OCC's financial position resulting from a decline in revenues or an increase in expenses. To manage this risk and help to ensure that OCC can continue operations and services as a going concern if general business losses materialize, OCC has adopted its Capital Management Policy,
[
6
]
which provides the framework by which OCC manages its capital. Amending OCC's schedule of fees is one action used by OCC to manage its capital.
Pursuant to OCC's rule-filed Capital Management Policy, and as required by Exchange Act rules applicable to OCC,
[
7
]
OCC must maintain LNAFBE
[
8
]
sufficient to cover at least six months of operating expenses, among other measures
(
printed page 74640)
(“Target Capital Requirement”). Because OCC is required to maintain such funds, the LNAFBE used to meet the Target Capital Requirement cannot be used to cover operational expenses and any increase in expenses must be covered by current revenue or cash held in excess of the Target Capital Requirement. The Capital Management Plan further sets 110% of the Target Capital Requirement as an early warning threshold. If LNAFBE falls below the early warning threshold, OCC management and Board must discuss whether a fee increase is necessary.
In the filing to implement the 2025 fee increase (“2025 Fee Filing”),
[
9
]
OCC projected that its LNAFBE would fall below OCC's Target Capital Requirement by the end of Q1 2025 and took action prior to hitting the early warning threshold. At the time, OCC stated it did not believe it would be prudent, given its designation as a SIFMU, to allow its LNAFBE to decline past the early warning threshold prior to taking action to ensure that OCC maintains sufficient LNAFBE to satisfy its regulatory requirements and so that it may continue to operate as a going concern if it were to experience general business losses.
[
10
]
However, in the 2025 Fee Filing, OCC emphasized its commitment to aligning its revenues with its costs and capital needs and stated that, consistent with its past practice, if revenues exceed costs and OCC's LNAFBE is above the early warning threshold, OCC would consider utilizing tools to lower the cost of clearing for market participants, as provided under its Capital Management Policy.
[
11
]
Later in 2025, OCC followed through and implemented a fee holiday for December 2025 to help lower clearing costs for market participants.
[
12
]
Today, OCC is continuing this practice and instituting a fee holiday for December 2026.
Proposed Fee Holiday
OCC proposes to implement a fee holiday for the month of December 2026. OCC has in place policies and procedures, including the Capital Management Policy, to control costs and regularly review fees and operating expenses, including during its annual budgeting process. Consistent with the Capital Management Policy, OCC set its clearing fees based on factors including OCC's annual budgeted or forecasted operating expenses and projected revenue. However, clearing volume, and therefore revenue, have outpaced projections and OCC currently has LNAFBE in excess of its early warning threshold. In addition to clearing fees, OCC receives revenue from the interest paid on the cash margin collateral it holds with the Federal Reserve System and elsewhere. In October 2026, OCC began paying Clearing Members interest on their margin cash at a rate based on the interest rate OCC receives from the Federal Reserve, less a cash management fee. For budgeting purposes, OCC assumed it would begin paying interest on margin cash in July 2026. Therefore, OCC had three fewer months of interest expenses than anticipated, further contributing to the amount of LNAFBE OCC has in excess of the early warning threshold. The fee holiday will allow OCC to return excess capital to market participants and clearing members while still maintaining sufficient capital to maintain compliance with the Capital Management Policy and regulatory requirements.
In evaluating its current LNAFBE and projections for 2027, OCC determined that a fee holiday is warranted for December 2026. Based on recent volumes, OCC estimates that the fee holiday for the month of December will lead to approximately $77 million in lost revenue. Despite this, OCC believes it will remain above the 2026 early warning threshold ($355.3 million) as well as its projected early warning threshold for 2027 ($390.8 million). To make this determination, OCC evaluated revenue and LNAFBE under a wide range of volume scenarios including current average daily volume (“ADV”), 60 million ADV, and -4% ADV growth. In all scenarios except the negative growth scenario, OCC remained above its early warning threshold through the end of 2027 even with the fee holiday. OCC, however, does not believe the negative growth scenario is realistic, and it would result in ADV decreasing by 50% to 35.5 million contracts a day by the end of 2027. The scenario was selected to illustrate the level of volume decrease that would cause OCC to drop below its early warning threshold. Nonetheless, under this extreme scenario, OCC remained above its early warning threshold through October 2027, meaning OCC would have time to react if the negative ADV growth scenario becomes more realistic.
[
13
]
To enact the proposed changes, OCC would update its schedule of fees as set out below.
Current fee schedule
                             (Clearing fees)
Proposed fee schedule
                             (fee Holiday December 2026)
All Transactions $0.025/contract
All transactions $0.00/contract.
Minimum Monthly Clearing Fee $200
$0.00.
OCC proposes to make the removal of the $.025 fee per contract effective December 1, 2026. The removal of the minimum monthly fee of $200 will be made once OCC receives all necessary regulatory approvals. Effective the first trading day of 2027, clearing fees will revert to the fee schedule in effect before December 1, 2026 and OCC will remove the fee holiday from its schedule of fees.
2. Statutory Basis
OCC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act
[
14
]
and the rules and regulations thereunder.
Compliance With Section 17A(b)(3)(D) of the Act
In particular, OCC believes that the proposed fee change is consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(D) of the Act,
[
15
]
which requires that the rules of a clearing agency provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its participants. OCC believes that the proposed fee holiday is reasonable because it is designed to decrease the cost of clearing while maintaining sufficient LNAFBE to cover OCC's operating expenses and address potential business or
(
printed page 74641)
operational losses so that OCC can continue to meet its obligations as a SIFMU. The reasonableness of the proposal is supported by oversight, transparency, and OCC's past practice, wherever circumstances allow, to utilize tools to lower the cost of clearing for participants.
First, OCC's funding and operations are subject to oversight by OCC's Board and the Commission. OCC's annual budget, compensation for senior management, and capital initiatives are reviewed and approved by its Board-level CPC. OCC's Board is made up of a broad cross-section of options market participants, including public representatives, Clearing Member representatives from Clearing Members of various sizes, and options exchange representatives. At least a majority of the CPC is composed of independent directors, consistent with Commission Rule 17ad-25(e)
[
16
]
and the judgment of the Board.
OCC is also supervised by the Commission throughout the year. Pursuant to Section 807(a) of the Clearing Supervision Act, the Commission's Division of Examinations conducts annual examinations of OCC to determine, among other things, (1) the nature of the operations of, and the risks borne, by OCC; (2) the financial and operational risks presented by OCC to financial institutions, critical markets, or the broader financial system; and (3) the resources and capabilities of OCC to monitor and control such risks.
[
17
]
In addition, changes to OCC's rules, procedures and operations that could materially affect the nature or level of risk presented by OCC are also subject to review by the Commission, in consultation with the Federal Reserve, under Section 806(e) of the Clearing Supervision Act.
[
18
]
Furthermore, the SEC publishes such proposed changes for public comment.
Second, OCC's commitment to reasonable funding is further supported by the transparency it provides on an ongoing basis regarding its financial performance. Each year, OCC publishes its Annual Report, inclusive of its audited financial statements prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. OCC maintains a dedicated website that consolidates its annual reports in a readily accessible place.
[
19
]
On a quarterly basis, OCC also provides unaudited information concerning its total revenues, average daily contract volume and LNAFBE on its “Schedule of Fees” website to aid Clearing Members in assessing the risk associated with a potential Operational Loss Fee in accordance with OCC's capital replenishment plan under its Capital Management Policy.
[
20
]
Third, OCC is committed to aligning its revenues with its costs and capital needs. Consistent with OCC's past practice, if revenues exceed costs and OCC's LNAFBE is above the early warning threshold, OCC would consider utilizing tools to lower the cost of clearing for market participants, as provided under its Capital Management Policy. Such tools may include fee decreases like those OCC implemented in 2020 and 2021,
[
21
]
fee holidays like the one OCC implemented from November through December of 2021 and December 2025
[
22
]
and proposed to be implemented in December 2026, or fee refunds like the $156 million refund in 2020 and the $76.3 million refund in 2021.
Finally, OCC believes that the fee holiday would be equitably allocated because it applies equally to all transaction types and clearing members.
Compliance With Rule 17ad-22(e)(15)
In addition, OCC believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Rule 17ad-22(e)(15), which requires that OCC establish, implement, maintain and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify, monitor, and manage OCC's general business risk and hold sufficient LNAFBE to cover potential general business losses so that OCC can continue operations and services as a going concern if those losses materialize.
[
23
]
The Rule also requires OCC to hold LNAFBE equal to at least six months of OCC's current operating expenses, among other measures.
[
24
]
As described above, OCC will be able to continue to meet its ongoing obligations and hold the required amount of LNAFBE following the fee holiday. OCC estimates that the fee holiday will result in approximately $77 million in missed revenue. Nonetheless, based on a wide range of trading volume projections, OCC expects to remain above its Target Capital Requirement and early warning threshold throughout 2026 following the fee holiday.
[
25
]
(B) Clearing Agency's Statement on Burden on Competition
Section 17A(b)(3)(I) of the Act
[
26
]
requires that the rules of a clearing agency not to impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. OCC does not believe that the proposed rule change would have any impact or impose a burden on competition. OCC believes that the proposed rule change would not disadvantage or favor any particular user of OCC's services in relationship to another user because the proposed fee holiday would apply equally to all Clearing Members. Accordingly, OCC does not believe that the proposed rule change would have any impact or impose a burden on competition.
(C) Clearing Agency's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants or Others
Written comments were not and are not intended to be solicited with respect to the proposed change and none have been received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
27
]
and paragraph (f) of Rule 19b-4
[
28
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
The proposal shall not take effect until all regulatory actions required with respect to the proposal are completed.
[
29
]
(
printed page 74642)
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-OCC-2026-012 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-OCC-2026-012. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of such filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of OCC and on OCC's website at
https://www.theocc.com/​Company-Information/​Documents-and-Archives/​By-Laws-and-Rules
.
Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to File Number SR-OCC-2026-012 and should be submitted on or before December 10, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.

DATES:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In compliance with
44 U.S.C. 3507
, FDA has submitted the following proposed collection of information to OMB for review and clearance.
National Youth Tobacco Survey 2027-2029
OMB Control Number 0910-0932—Revision
This information collection supports the development and implementation of the National Youth Tobacco Survey (NYTS), which is a key component of FDA's youth tobacco surveillance. By providing national estimates of youth tobacco use, the NYTS directly contributes to FDA's ability to effectively regulate tobacco use and prevent youth access to tobacco products in the United States. FDA's Center for Tobacco Products (CTP) was created to carry out the authorities granted under the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act (Tobacco Control Act) (
Pub. L. 111-31
) to educate the public about the dangers of tobacco use and to serve as a public health resource for tobacco and health information. CTP's tobacco surveillance research, including the NYTS, directly contributes to advancing the goals of
Executive Order 14212
: Establishing the President's Make America Healthy Again Commission, including the Make Our Children Healthy Again assessment, in three ways. First, the NYTS helps FDA CTP evaluate the effect of policies and regulations on efforts to reduce tobacco use, the leading cause of chronic disease and mortality in the United States. Second, the NYTS protects the health of children by influencing policies, regulatory action, public education campaigns, and compliance and enforcement efforts designed to decrease the likelihood of youth tobacco initiation and reduce youth tobacco use. Third, the NYTS gathers information about youth tobacco use by means of rigorous scientific methods.
The NYTS has been conducted since 1999 and serves as the gold-standard source of nationally representative estimates of youth tobacco use in the United States. In 2025, FDA assumed leadership of the NYTS from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The collection was previously approved under OMB Control No. 0920-0621. The NYTS supports FDA's CTP in its efforts to reduce tobacco related disease and protect the health of children.
The survey will be conducted among a nationally representative sample of students attending public and private schools in grades 6-12. The survey will be digital, web-based, anonymous, self-administered, and will be taken on school or personal computers, tablets, or mobile devices. Information supporting the NYTS also will be collected from state-, district-, and school-level administrators and teachers. Information collected through the NYTS will be used to identify trends in youth tobacco use over time, and to inform the development of public education campaigns, policies and rules, and compliance and enforcement programs for tobacco products.
The survey will examine the following topics: use of e-cigarettes, cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco (chewing tobacco, snuff, dip), hookahs, pipes, snus, nicotine pouches, other oral nicotine products, bidis, heated tobacco products, and roll-your-own cigarettes; knowledge and attitudes; media and advertising; access to tobacco products and enforcement of restrictions on access; secondhand smoke and e-cigarette aerosol exposure, and cessation.
In the
Federal Register
of May 4, 2026 (
91 FR 23995
), FDA published a 60-day notice requesting public comments on the proposed collection of information. Eight comments were responsive to the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) information collection topics solicited.
(Comment) Seven commenters expressed support for the continuation of the NYTS, with several describing it as the “gold-standard” and only nationally representative, school-based survey focused exclusively on youth tobacco use. Commenters emphasized the survey's value in tracking product trends, identifying emerging tobacco products, informing regulatory and enforcement actions, and supporting public health programs at the federal, state, and local levels. The State Attorneys General specifically endorsed the proposed sample size increase to maintain statistical rigor in light of declining school-based response rates.
(FDA response) FDA acknowledges and appreciates the strong support for NYTS continuation expressed across all comments. The NYTS has been administered since 1999 and has served as an essential surveillance tool for identifying trends in youth tobacco and nicotine product use, informing regulatory action, guiding public health programs, and supporting enforcement at the federal and state levels. FDA remains committed to the annual administration of the NYTS and to maintaining the scientific rigor necessary for the data to serve these functions.
(Comment) One commenter expressed support for the continuation of the NYTS and urged FDA to publish the 2025 NYTS analysis and results consistent with prior years, noting that the release of raw data without an accompanying analysis limits the
(
printed page 74588)
accessibility and utility of the data for clinicians, public health practitioners, and policy makers. The commenter also made recommendations regarding FDA's review of premarket tobacco applications for flavored electronic nicotine delivery systems.
(FDA response) FDA appreciates the commenter's support for the NYTS and acknowledges the concern regarding the timely publication of analysis and results. FDA is committed to ensuring that NYTS findings are made publicly available in a timely manner. To comply with
Executive Order 14303
, titled “Restoring Gold Standard Science,” FDA plans to simultaneously release the public use dataset to coincide with the first publication for a given year of the NYTS. The commenter's recommendations regarding premarket tobacco product applications are outside the scope of this information collection request and will not be addressed here.
(Comment) One comment raised methodological concerns regarding declining school-based response rates, which fell from 77.2% in 2019 to 36.0% in 2025. This decline was attributed in part to the proliferation of state laws requiring active parental consent for youth surveys and expressed concern about potential nonresponse bias and diminished representativeness of recent NYTS estimates. The commenter recommended FDA: (1) conduct and publish an updated nonresponse bias analysis; (2) explore passive (opt-out) parental consent procedures where permissible; (3) evaluate alternative or complementary sampling approaches, such as address-based sampling; (4) enhance transparency around methodology changes and data limitations; and (5) support triangulation with other national and subnational data sources to validate findings.
(FDA response) FDA shares the concern about declining response rates and recognizes that this trend may have meaningful implications for the representativeness and comparability of NYTS data. The proposed increase in the total numbers of schools and students sampled for 2027-2029 reflects FDA's effort to accommodate declining response rates in school-based surveys and continue producing nationally representative data. Responses to each recommendation are as follows:
(1)
Nonresponse bias analysis:
FDA conducts a nonresponse bias analysis each year in accordance with OMB requirements. While the full nonresponse bias report is not made publicly available due to concerns about the potential disclosure of school-level information that could compromise respondent confidentiality, the publicly available methodology report provides a detailed description of the development of nonresponse bias-adjusted weights and calibration procedures. Additionally, a recently published paper reported findings from a nonresponse bias analysis assessing the impact of early termination of the 2025 NYTS data collection (Park-Lee et al., 2026).
(2)
Passive parental consent:
NYTS already employs passive parental consent as its default procedure. Unless a school requires active parental permission, NYTS follows passive parental consent procedures. Based on recent NYTS data collection cycles, approximately 10% of respondents are estimated to require active parental consent. FDA will continue to monitor developments in state-level consent requirements and their potential effects on survey participation and representativeness.
(3)
Alternative or complementary sampling:
Meaningful changes to the NYTS sampling design would need to be evaluated carefully against potential impacts on data comparability, the financial and logistical resources required, and the ability to maintain the precision of national estimates and estimates of population groups. FDA will consider assessing the feasibility of alternative or complementary sampling strategies, including address-based sampling (ABS).
(4)
Transparency around methodology and data limitations:
FDA remains committed to transparency regarding methodological changes and data limitations. The annual methodology report published with the public-use files provides clear guidance on the appropriate interpretation of NYTS data, including the implications of weighting adjustments and changes in sampling procedures.
(5)
Triangulation with other data sources:
As part of its nonresponse bias analysis and dissemination efforts, FDA triangulates with other national and subnational data sources to validate and contextualize estimates. These include both school-based and household surveys, including the Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS), Monitoring the Future (MTF), the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study, and the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH). Continued cross-survey triangulation enables FDA to identify potential nonresponse bias and assess consistency of trend estimates.
(Comment) Another comment suggests FDA to: (1) include brand-specific product images alongside brand-name response options for e-cigarette use questions, citing published studies and original analyses of NYTS 2024-2025 data demonstrating substantial discordance between self-reported brand use and reported device type and flavor; and (2) reinstate the 2024 NYTS follow-up question on the age of social sources of e-cigarettes, which was removed from the 2025 survey, to help assess the potential impact of device-access restrictions.
(FDA response) FDA appreciates the recommendations regarding the visual presentation of product options and the reinstatement of a follow-up question on social sources of e-cigarettes.
(1)
Brand-specific product images:
FDA acknowledges the evidence of discordance between self-reported brand use and reported device type and flavor. However, NYTS includes selected non-branded product images because a brand encompasses a wide variety of products, and it is not feasible to include every product available on the market. Non-branded images representing commonly recognizable device types are intended to aid respondent comprehension of the product category, and respondent burden is considered when evaluating expansions to the image set.
(2)
Reinstatement of the follow-up question on age of social sources:
Question-level decisions reflect careful consideration of scientific priority, policy relevance, and respondent burden. FDA will consider the recommendation as part of its ongoing review of the NYTS questionnaire for future data collection cycles.
(Comment) One commenter expressed support for the continuation of the NYTS and raised concerns about the timeliness and transparency of the NYTS data dissemination, recommending that FDA publish a prospective calendar of NYTS milestones, including questionnaire availability, fielding periods, data release dates, and report publication timelines, and that datasets be released concurrently with initial findings rather than in a piecemeal fashion. With respect to survey content, it was recommended that FDA incorporate emerging product categories and brands as response options more quickly and increase stakeholder engagement to inform timely survey updates; consider a supplemental fall NYTS to provide more frequent trend monitoring; add consumption frequency and initiation questions across all product categories; expand reasons-for-use questions to cover heated tobacco products, nicotine pouches, and oral nicotine products; and refine access source measures to
(
printed page 74589)
better distinguish between commercial and social sources of tobacco products.
(FDA response) Regarding the timeliness of survey results and data dissemination, there are several factors that affect how quickly analysis results are released, including the peer-review process for publications and several levels of internal and external review. Because publication schedules and timelines vary across products we cannot always predict publication dates in advance. To comply with
Executive Order 14303
, titled ‘Restoring Gold Standard Science,’ FDA plans to simultaneously release public-use datasets to coincide with the first publication for a given year of the NYTS. FDA will also explore opportunities to improve transparency around the NYTS process and timeline to the extent practicable. Additionally, as part of the PRA review process, the proposed survey instrument is made publicly available in the docket, allowing the public to view the instrument. A copy of the questionnaire is also included with the release of the public-use dataset and its accompanying documentation, providing further transparency and access for researchers and other data users. With respect to incorporating emerging product categories, NYTS is a federal survey subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act and regulated by OMB. Thus, NYTS is not designed as a rapid surveillance tool with the opportunity to add new items quickly in response to emerging products. FDA conducts environmental scans using a variety of sources to predict potential items to add or remove in advance of seeking OMB approval and consults with subject matter experts and stakeholders. Regarding the recommendation for a supplemental fall NYTS, any meaningful change to the frequency or structure of NYTS data collection would require additional OMB approval and careful evaluation of associated burden and resource implications. Within these constraints, FDA will take the commenter's survey content recommendations under consideration for future data collection cycles.
(Comment) One commenter recommends that FDA add a standalone NYTS measure for “premium cigars” as a distinct product category, using the definition codified at
21 CFR 1107.12
, accompanied by plain-language descriptors and respondent clarifications to help youth distinguish premium cigars from cigarillos, filtered cigars, flavored cigars, and other mass-market cigar products. The commenter argues that the current aggregation of premium cigars with other cigar product types is inconsistent with FDA's own regulatory treatment of premium cigars and produces data of insufficient utility for FDA's current regulatory functions.
(FDA response) FDA appreciates the commenter's recommendation and acknowledges that premium cigars are treated as a distinct product category under
21 CFR 1107.12
. However, FDA does not believe it is appropriate or feasible to incorporate this regulatory definition into the NYTS instrument. The definition requires that a product satisfy eight specific technical criteria. Even with plain-language descriptors and clarifications, it is unlikely that youth could reliably identify whether a product they used meets this definition, introducing significant measurement error. The explanatory text necessary to operationalize this definition for youth would also substantially increase respondent burden. Additionally, available evidence suggests that premium cigars, as defined under
21 CFR 1107.12
, represent a small share of cigar use among youth, who are more likely to use mass-market products such as cigarillos and filtered cigars.

Good Laboratory Practice Requirements for Nonclinical Laboratory Studies
OMB Control Number 0910-0119—Extension
Sections 409, 505, 512, and 515 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (
21 U.S.C. 348
,
355
,
360b
, and
360e
) and related statutes require manufacturers of food additives, human drugs and biological products, animal drugs, and medical devices to demonstrate the safety and utility of their product by submitting applications to FDA for research or marketing permits. Such applications contain, among other important items, full reports of all studies done to demonstrate product safety in man and/or other animals. In order to ensure adequate quality control for these studies and to provide an adequate degree of consumer protection, the Agency issued good laboratory practice (GLP) regulations for nonclinical laboratory studies in part 58 (
21 CFR part 58
). The regulations specify minimum standards for the proper conduct of safety testing and contain sections on facilities, personnel, equipment, standard operating procedures (SOPs), test and control articles, quality assurance, protocol and conduct of a safety study, records and reports, and laboratory disqualification, and include information collection provisions.
Part 58 requires testing facilities engaged in conducting toxicological studies to retain, and make available to regulatory officials, records regarding compliance with GLPs. Records are maintained on file at each testing facility and examined there periodically by FDA inspectors. The GLP regulations require that, for each nonclinical laboratory study, a final report be prepared that documents the results of quality assurance unit inspections, test and control article characterization, testing of mixtures of test and control articles with carriers, and an overall interpretation of nonclinical laboratory studies. The GLP regulations also require written records pertaining to: (1) personnel job descriptions and summaries of training and experience; (2) master schedules, protocols and amendments thereto, inspection reports, and SOPs; (3) equipment inspection, maintenance, calibration, and testing records; (4) documentation of feed and water analyses and animal treatments; (5) test article accountability records; and (6) study documentation and raw data.
Description of Respondents:
Respondents to the collection of information are sponsors of nonclinical laboratory studies that support or are intended to support applications for research or marketing permits for products regulated by FDA.

I. Background
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is responsible for administering the Medicare and Medicaid programs and coordination and oversight of private health insurance. Administration and oversight of these programs involves the following: (1) furnishing information to Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, health care providers, and the public; and (2) maintaining effective communications with CMS regional offices, State governments, State Medicaid agencies, State survey agencies, various providers of health care, all Medicare contractors that process claims and pay bills, National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), health insurers, and other interested parties. To implement the various statutes on which the programs are based, we issue regulations under the authority granted to the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services under sections 1102, 1871, 1902, and related provisions of the Social Security Act (the Act) and Public Health Service Act. We also issue various manuals, memoranda, and statements necessary to administer and oversee the programs efficiently.
Section 1871(c) of the Act requires that we publish a list of all Medicare manual instructions, interpretive rules, statements of policy, and guidelines of general applicability not issued as regulations at least every 3 months in the
Federal Register
.
II. Format for the Quarterly Issuance Notices
This quarterly notice provides only the specific updates that have occurred in the 3-month period along with a hyperlink to the full listing that is available on the CMS website or the appropriate data registries that are used as our resources. This is the most current up-to-date information and will be available earlier than we publish our quarterly notice. We believe the website list provides more timely access for beneficiaries, providers, and suppliers. We also believe the website offers a more convenient tool for the public to find the full list of qualified providers for these specific services and offers more flexibility and “real time” accessibility. In addition, many of the websites have listservs; that is, the public can subscribe and receive immediate notification of any updates to the website. These listservs avoid the need to check the website, as notification of updates is automatic and sent to the subscriber as they occur. If assessing a website proves to be difficult, the contact person listed can provide information.
III. How To Use the Notice
This notice is organized into 15 addenda so that a reader may access the subjects published during the quarter covered by the notice to determine whether any are of particular interest. We expect this notice to be used in concert with previously published notices. Those unfamiliar with a description of our Medicare manuals
(
printed page 74560)
should view the manuals at
http://www.cms.gov/​manuals
.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Administrative Conference Act,
5 U.S.C. 591-596
, established the Administrative Conference of the United States. The Conference studies the efficiency, adequacy, and fairness of the administrative procedures used by federal agencies and makes recommendations to agencies, the President, Congress, and the Judicial Conference of the United States for procedural improvements (
5 U.S.C. 594(1)
). For further information about the Conference and its activities, see
www.acus.gov
.
Policies on the Use of Generative Super Intelligence by Agency Adjudicators and Other Agency Personnel
Generative super intelligence (GenSI) systems are SI “models that are able to generate new content.”
[
2
]
Unlike other SI models—which classify data or make predictions, recommendations, and decisions—GenSI systems create “various outputs, including texts, images, videos, computer code, or music” based on user-input prompts.”
[
3
]
There has been a rapid expansion in the availability and use of GenSI tools since the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022. Today, more than half of Americans regularly use chatbots and virtual assistants such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini to “create responses using algorithms that are trained often on open-source information, such as text and images from the internet.”
[
4
]
Adoption rates also continue to rise among legal service providers,
[
5
]
and the number of GenSI use cases within the federal government “increased about nine-fold” between 2023 and 2024.
[
6
]
When used responsibly, GenSI has the potential to help agencies perform adjudication-related tasks more efficiently and accurately. Adjudicators and other agency personnel might use GenSI to assist in preparing written communications such as notices, orders, and decisions; summarizing and analyzing lengthy written submissions and voluminous evidence; conducting legal and nonlegal research; transcribing hearings; and translating documents.
[
7
]
At the same time, agencies must consider potential risks, including how the use of GenSI might affect adjudicators' analysis of the law and facts of individual cases and how the use of non-secure GenSI tools might affect privacy and other sensitive interests.
Agencies are required to “develop a policy that sets the terms for acceptable use of [GenSI] for their missions and establishes adequate safeguards and oversight mechanisms that allow [GenSI] to be used in the agency without posing undue risk.”
[
8
]
This project will identify best practices to help agencies develop specific policies regarding the use of GenSI by adjudicators and other agency personnel involved in agency adjudications. In addition to identifying best practices for developing, disseminating, and periodically reevaluating such policies, it will identify practices that promote the effective use of GenSI and innovation in adjudication while guarding against misuse and undue risks.
Policies on the Use of Generative Super Intelligence by Parties and Representatives
GenSI also has the potential to benefit parties and their representatives, who can use the technology to assist in conducting legal research and analysis more efficiently and prepare pleadings, briefs, and other written communications more effectively. GenSI
(
printed page 74535)
may be especially useful for self-represented parties by offering “new, highly accessible tools that provide answers to basic questions, including where to find templates and court forms, how to fill them out, and where to bring them for presentation to the judge—all without leaving home.
[
9
]
At the same time, there are potential risks associated with parties' and representatives' use of the developing technology. Most prominently, GenSI tools can hallucinate (generating false or misleading information), and there have been well-publicized instances in which parties and representatives cited nonexistent legal authorities, inaccurately represented legal authorities, or relied on false or misleading information.
[
10
]
The use of GenSI tools may implicate representatives' responsibilities to engage fairly, truthfully, and ethically with tribunals and clients.
[
11
]
And concerns have been raised that GenSI tools could be used to fabricate deepfake evidence.
[
12
]
Agencies have taken different approaches to regulating the use of GenSI by parties, representatives, and other participants in agency adjudications. The Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) and U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, for example, have published specific policies on parties' and representatives' use of GenSI.
[
13
]
Some adjudicators independently inform parties and representatives about proper and improper uses of GenSI. Adjudicators at some agencies affirmatively require representatives to disclose when and how they used GenSI. Some adjudicators require representatives to certify that they did not use GenSI or that they analyzed its output before relying on it. Adjudicators at several agencies have considered alleged misuse of GenSI in the context of individual proceedings, including how existing rules of representative conduct should apply in such cases.
This project will identify best practices to help agencies develop specific policies regarding the use of GenSI by parties, representatives, and other participants in agency adjudications. In addition to identifying best practices for developing, disseminating, and periodically reevaluating such policies, it will identify practices that promote the effective use of GenSI and innovation in adjudication while guarding against misuse and undue risks.
Specific Topics for Public Comment
ACUS welcomes views, information, and data on all aspects of the development of policies regarding the use of GenSI by agency adjudicators, other agency personnel, parties, representatives, and other participants in federal agency adjudications. ACUS also seeks specific feedback on the following questions:
1. How are you using, or have you considered using, GenSI to accomplish any tasks associated with federal agency adjudications, such as drafting filings, conducting legal or nonlegal research, summarizing evidence, conducting discovery, transcribing depositions? What GenSI tools do you use? What benefits and drawbacks have you experienced in using GenSI to accomplish tasks associated with agency adjudications?
2. How do you feel about how agency adjudicators and other agency personnel are using, or might someday use, GenSI to assist in adjudicating cases? What are the benefits and drawbacks of agency adjudicators and other agency personnel using GenSI tools?
3. Do existing agency rules and policies regarding the qualifications and conduct of representatives—such as rules regarding competence, diligence, communication, confidentiality, fees, and candor with the tribunal—provide sufficient guidance regarding proper and improper uses of GenSI in agency adjudications?
4. Do you think it would be useful for agencies to issue specific rules, regulations, policies, guidance, practice guides, benchbooks, standing orders, or other materials regarding the use of GenSI in agency adjudications? Why or why not?
5. Have you encountered any agency rules, regulations, policies, guidance, practice guides, benchbooks, standing orders, or other materials regarding the use of GenSI in agency adjudications? If so, what do they do well, and how could they be improved?
6. Do you have thoughts on rules, regulations, policies, guidance, practice guides, benchbooks, standing orders, and other materials adopted or considerd by federal courts, state courts, state and local agencies, and state bars and other professional associations?
7. What restrictions, if any, should agencies place on the use of GenSI by agency adjudicators, other agency personnel, parties, representatives, and other participants in agency adjudications?
8. Should agencies require parties and/or representatives in agency adjudications to disclose when and how they used GenSI, or at least require parties and/or representatives to certify that they reviewed any content generated by a GenSI tool for accuracy? Why or why not?
9. What consequences, if any, should parties and/or representatives face for using GenSI improperly in agency adjudications?
10. Should the same or different rules apply to private representatives who are lawyers, private representatives who are not lawyers, self-represented parties, and lawyers who represent an agency in agency adjudications?
Authority:

.

Pursuant to section 1009 of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended, notice is hereby given of a meeting of the Advisory Council on Parkinson's Research, Care, and Services (ACPRCS).
This is the fourth meeting of the ACPRCS, which was established by the Dr. Emmanuel Bilirakis and Honorable Jennifer Wexton National Plan to End Parkinson's Act of 2024 (
Pub. L. 118-66
). The Advisory Council is charged with providing advice to the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) on issues that affect people with Parkinson's and related disorders (PDRDs), which include progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, corticobasal degeneration, and Lewy body dementias.
The meeting will focus on strategies to provide timely and responsive care to PDRD patients, including how care teams can improve care across settings. The meeting is virtual and will be open to the public to view via HHS Live Streaming:
www.hhs.gov/​live
.
Registration is not required.
Name of Committee:
Advisory Council on Parkinson's Research, Care, and Services (ACPRCS).
Date:
December 7, 2026.
Time:
9:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
Agenda:
Improving care for Parkinson's and related disorders; public comments; discussion and next steps for PDRD priorities.
Address:
National Institutes of Health, Neuroscience Center, 6001 Executive Boulevard, Rockville, MD 20852.
Meeting Format:
Virtual Meeting.

The meeting is free and open to the public.

Public Comment Due Date: November 30th by 5:00 p.m. ET. For public comment instructions and guidelines, see below.
Contact Person:
Jordan Gladman, Ph.D., Deputy Executive Officer, National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD 20892,
nationalPDplan@nih.gov
.
(
printed page 74593)
Public Comments:
The ACPRCS welcomes written and oral/virtual public comments and asks the public to review and adhere to its Public Comment Guidelines provided at
https://www.ninds.nih.gov/​current-research/​trans-agency-activities/​national-plan-end-parkinsons-act/​parkinsons-council
.
Submissions are accepted in writing via email addressed to
NationalPDplan@nih.gov
.
Please include the phrase “public comment” in the subject line as well as the body of the message. A limited number of slots are available for individuals to provide a 2-3-minute oral summary or excerpt of their written comment to the Council during the meeting in person or via videoconference. For those interested in that opportunity, please indicate “Interested in providing oral/virtual comment” in your written submission, along with your name, email, and professional/organizational affiliation so that Council support staff can contact you if a slot is available.
Note that in order to provide oral public comment, requesters must register for the meeting using the instructions above.
For any given meeting, comment slots will be assigned on a first-come, first-served basis, with priority given to individuals and organizations that have not previously provided comments. This will help ensure that as many individuals and organizations as possible have an opportunity to share comments. Commenters going over their allotted 3-minute slot may be asked to conclude immediately to allow other comments and the rest of the meeting to proceed on schedule.
Public comment submissions received by 5:00 p.m. ET on November 30th will be provided to the Council prior to the meeting for their consideration; all comments received after the deadline will be included in the next Council meeting's materials. The Council is not able to respond individually to comments. All public comments become part of the public record. Attachments of copyrighted publications are not permitted, but web links or citations for any copyrighted works cited may be provided.
Technical issues:
If you experience any technical problems with the webcast, please email
nationalPDplan@nih.gov
.
Disability Accommodations:
All ACPRCS Full Council Meetings provide Closed Captioning through
www.hhs.gov/​live
.
Individuals whose full participation in the meeting will require special accommodations (
e.g.,
sign language or interpreting services) must submit a request to the Contact Person listed on the notice at least seven (7) business days prior to the meeting. Such requests should include a detailed description of the accommodation needed and a way for the ACPRCS to contact the requester if more information is needed to fill the request.
Meeting schedule subject to change.

https://www.ninds.nih.gov/​news-events/​events/​december-2026-advisory-council-meeting-parkinsons-research-care-and-services
.

AGENCY:
National Institute of Health.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
National Center for the Advancement of Translational Sciences of the National Institute of Health has modified its organizational structure.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Part N, National Institutes of Health (NIH), of the Statement of Organization and Functions for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), is amended as set forth below to reflect the reorganization of the National Institute of Health, National Center for the Advancement of Translational Science (NCATS) by retitling and updating the functional Statements (1) the Chemical Genomics Branch to the Translational Models Branch under the Division of Preclinical Innovation within NCATS, (2) revise functional statement of the Office of Special initiatives, (3) abolishing the Office of Drug Development Partnership Programs, and the Office of Translational Medicine under the Office of the Director within NCATS.
Section N,
Organization and Functions,
is amended as follows:
(1) In the
Division of Preclinical Innovation (N92, formerly HN92)
retitle the following:
Chemical Genomics Branch (N924, formerly HN924)
to
Translational Models Branch (N924, formerly HN924).
(1) Develop and advance human-based Non-Animal Models (NAMs) as transformative drug discovery and biomedical research tools; (2) Accelerate therapeutic discovery and regulatory science for rare and common diseases using predictive human model systems; (3) Accelerate target discovery using predictive human model systems; (4) Establish the predictive value and usefulness of human-based NAMs as pharmacology and toxicology assessment tools to reduce reliance on animal models; (5) Generate high-quality human biological data to enable AI-driven predictive modeling of drug efficacy and toxicity; (6) Integrate stem cells, tissue engineering, functional genomics, toxicology and data science into a unified human-based translational research enterprise; and (7) Serve as an NIH-wide resource for advancing human-based models research and technologies.
(
printed page 74592)
(2)
In the Office of the Director (N91, formerly HN91)
revise functional statement of the following:
Office of Special Initiatives (N917, formerly HN917).
(1) Provides transformative programs extramurally that address barriers and bottlenecks to pre-clinical and clinical translation; (2) Drives development and dissemination of novel and disruptive technologies, approaches, and solutions for issues that impede translational research through promotion to the scientific, research, and industry sectors; (3) Incentivizes groundbreaking expansion of the therapeutic landscape for rare and chronic diseases through discovery and exploration of novel therapeutic targets and programs; and (4) Promotes and engenders partnerships and interagency collaborations with key stakeholders including government, industry, and academia, to advance innovation in early-stage clinical trials.
(3) In the
Office of the Director (N91, formerly HN91)
remove the following:
Office of Drug Development Partnership Programs (N918, formerly HN918)
Office of Translational Medicine (N919, formerly HN919)

44 U.S.C. 3101
Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.,
Secretary, Department of Health and Human Services.
