The Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria threshold of $5 million is substantially lower than the market capitalization initial listing standard threshold on NYSE American.
[
65
]
For example, the total value of market capitalization required in applicable standards for
initial listing
is at least $50 million.
[
66
]
Similarly, the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria threshold is substantially lower than the average global market capitalization threshold for the existing
continued listing
standard thresholds on NYSE American.
[
67
]
The average global market capitalization standard for continued listing requires at least $50 million for a consecutive 30 trading-day period.
[
68
]
Accordingly, a company persistently and consistently trading at levels below an average $5 million market capitalization for approximately six calendar weeks (
i.e.,
30 trading days) would be trading significantly below such initial and continued listing requirements for NYSE American-listed companies, raising questions about the company's suitability for continued listing on NYSE American. Further, it is likely that a company that substantially declines from the market capitalization at which it initially listed on NYSE American to the average $5 million market capitalization level will most likely find itself in that position without surprise and, accordingly, will have had the opportunity to raise capital, explore business opportunities, or explore other options to increase assets, reduce liabilities, and increase revenues before crossing the average $5 million market capitalization threshold and remaining below that level for a consecutive 30 trading days.
[
69
]
The Exchange has identified risks pertaining to securities with a market capitalization below $5 million, including a heightened susceptibility to manipulation. The results of the Commission's analysis support approval of the Exchange's proposal to impose the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria. The increased number of securities with an average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period below $5 million in recent years, along with the significant likelihood that such securities will eventually be delisted, warrants the Exchange's consideration of the continued listing of securities with a low level of market capitalization.
[
70
]
Moreover, when securities fall below an average market capitalization of $5 million for a consecutive 30 trading-day period, there is a significant likelihood that they will continue to have an average market capitalization below $5 million for another 180 calendar days, which is a significant period of time.
[
71
]
While the delisting process sometimes affords companies experiencing truly temporary financial or business issues a cure period for them to regain compliance with continued listing standards, they necessarily prolong the delisting process which also prolongs the exposure of investors to potential harm for a company that ultimately is likely to be delisted. The Exchange's proposed $5 million market capitalization threshold and 30-day time parameter reflects a reasonably balanced approach for a continued listing requirement that provides companies with time to recover from short-term unexpected declines without prolonging the delisting process.
In the Commission's view, securities with a small market capitalization may be more prone to manipulation.
[
72
]
When a security has a smaller market capitalization, the cost required to accumulate a position that is large enough to influence the price of the security is reduced. Accordingly, a would-be manipulator may find it less costly to manipulate the price of the security. Thus, the continued listing of companies with small market capitalization raises concerns that these securities may have heightened susceptibility to manipulation. These concerns are exacerbated if companies with low market capitalization lack sufficient natural trading interest that could otherwise mitigate the susceptibility to manipulation by promoting fair and orderly markets in the security. The Commission, certain exchanges, and FINRA have allocated resources to identify and address manipulation in securities of companies with small market capitalization.
[
73
]
Despite these efforts, the Exchange's concerns about the potential for manipulation persist.
[
74
]
Manipulative schemes that target the securities of companies with small market capitalization, like “ramp and dump” and “pump and dump,” are often identified and responded to after the fact. The Exchange's proposal represents a reasonable approach to address concerns that companies with a persistent (
i.e.,
at least 30 consecutive trading days) market capitalization below $5 million may be susceptible to types of manipulation that result in harm to investors. The immediate suspension and delisting of these securities with a small market capitalization, as measured by considering average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period, is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, and more broadly, the rule is reasonably designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade and to protect investors and the public interest.
[
75
]
The proposal is reasonably designed to enhance the Exchange's listing standards by immediately suspending trading and commencing delisting proceedings for securities that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria, which facilitates the continued listing of securities of issuers that are financially sound. As noted above, the imprimatur of listing on a particular exchange correlates to investors' expectations that the listed issuer meets certain standards set by the exchange and that a listing exchange will use its judgment regarding the level at which to set those standards. Those standards are informed by an exchange's regulatory and commercial considerations and exchanges have discretion, subject to the requirements of the Act, to set those standards as they see fit.
Moreover, the addition of the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is not unfairly discriminatory because
(
printed page 74650)
the proposed standard is reasonably tailored to the Exchange's goal of addressing the risks that it has identified with respect to securities with a small market capitalization. The $5 million market capitalization threshold will provide for a level of market capitalization below which there may be a heightened susceptibility to manipulation and difficulties maintaining fair and orderly markets in these securities. And the requirement that a security have an average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period of less than $5 million before being subject to immediate suspension and delisting will target instances where securities have demonstrated a significant longevity of these risks. Therefore, the Commission finds that the Exchange's proposal to immediately suspend and delist companies that fail to comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is reasonably designed and consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act that the rules of the Exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, protect investors and the public interest, and not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
[
76
]
A. Comments Regarding the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria
One commenter stated that issuers with a sustained market capitalization below $5 million “is often a leading indicator of broader financial and compliance concerns that demand disproportionate regulatory oversight and pose significant risks to investors, who generally view companies that meet the requirements to be listed on an exchange as more financially sound and less risky than OTC securities.”
[
77
]
This commenter stated that a bright line continued listing threshold of $5 million in market capitalization “provides an objective, quantitative marker that is reasonably related to initial listing standards and appropriately identifies companies whose ongoing exchange listing, after failing to meet this threshold for 30 consecutive trading days, is no longer consistent with maintaining fair, orderly, and efficient markets.”
[
78
]
This commenter further stated that the Exchange's proposal to utilize an average market capitalization threshold as measured over a consecutive 30 trading-day period would “reduce[] the risk of gaming the threshold through short term price spikes and better reflect[] the sustained market value of the issuer.”
[
79
]
Several commenters stated that the proposed Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria could result in the delisting of companies based on broader market- or sector-wide conditions that may cause temporary fluctuations that are not related to their underlying business or financial condition.
[
80
]
Commenters also raised concerns that the proposal would disproportionately burden microcap and emerging growth issuers.
[
81
]
One commenter stated that the proposed rule disproportionately impacts microcap and emerging growth issuers because these types of issuers “frequently experience temporary fluctuations in market capitalization resulting from broader market conditions, financing cycles, sector-specific developments, and investor sentiment rather than long-term business performance.”
[
82
]
Another commenter stated that the Exchange does not demonstrate that the $5 million market capitalization threshold “is a reliable predictor of sustained financial distress, manipulation risk, or future non-compliance with existing listing standards.”
[
83
]
This commenter attached a report by Professor Craig M. Lewis that presents an empirical study raising concerns that the proposal may prematurely delist companies that would otherwise regain compliance.
[
84
]
The Lewis Report analyzed approximately 190 companies that fell below the $5 million average market capitalization threshold between 2006 and 2025, and concluded that “a temporary decline below the $5 million average market capitalization threshold does not reliably predict business failure or inevitable delisting.”
[
85
]
The Lewis Report stated that of the 190 companies that would have been delisted based on the proposal, 64% recovered at least once above the $5 million threshold during the time period studied, 28% of the 190 companies have not been not delisted, and 37 companies are still trading with market capitalizations above $5 million, representing an average market capitalization of $61.6 million.
[
86
]
One commenter stated that these arguments opposing the adoption of a $5 million continued listing threshold “rest on a misunderstanding of the purpose of continued listing standards and do not undermine the investor protection rationale supporting NYSE American's proposal.”
[
87
]
This commenter stated that listing standards are designed to protect investors and maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets, “not to maximize issuer survival or ensure uninterrupted access to exchange listing.”
[
88
]
This commenter also stated that whether a subset of issuers recover does not negate that periods below $5 million in market capitalization are linked to “thin liquidity, elevated spreads, heightened volatility, and disproportionate susceptibility to manipulative trading activity,” which are conditions that exchanges must address through risk-based listing standards.
[
89
]
This commenter also raised concerns regarding a reliance on backward-looking data, arguing that “[c]ontinued listing standards must operate ex ante, based on observable risk indicators” rather than “ex post based on whether a company eventually stabilizes.”
[
90
]
Finally, this commenter asserted that the Act's framework relies on exchanges “to set and refine listing standards based on front line surveillance of trading activity, issuer behavior, and market quality.”
[
91
]
In response to commenters, the Exchange states that the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is a “measured approach to address concerns about volatility and potential manipulation in low priced stocks.”
[
92
]
According to the Exchange, “microcap stocks are more susceptible to manipulation because it necessarily requires a smaller capital investment to
(
printed page 74651)
transact in a substantial percentage of a microcap issuer's securities, thereby opening the door to a wider range of potential bad actors.”
[
93
]
The Exchange states that, based on the Lewis Report, while only 28% of the companies that fell below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria remain listed today on the Exchange, 72% of such companies are no longer listed on the Exchange, and this data is consistent with the Exchange's historical observation that companies falling below the $5 million average market capitalization standard frequently face additional financial challenges that require a substantial amount of regulatory oversight and make them unsuitable for public market trading.
[
94
]
The Exchange further states that its proposal is not premised on the notion that a company with an average market capitalization below $5 million is without value and instead is seeking to address problematic trading in extremely small companies, which are frequently below other Exchange listing standards.
[
95
]
While the overall conclusion of the Lewis Report is that the Exchange's proposal to immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings for securities that fail to comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria may result in delisting of companies that later recover and that some of those companies may otherwise have remained listed on the Exchange, the possibility of a meaningful recovery is not indicative that the Exchange would be acting unreasonably in determining to delist such a security, and ultimately is not determinative that the proposed rule change is inconsistent with the Act. Both the Commission's analysis and the Lewis Report agree that a significant number of companies that fell below an average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period of $5 million did not recover.
[
96
]
Moreover, as discussed above, the Commission's analysis shows that 59% of the companies that fell below the Market Capitalization Analysis Threshold had an average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period under $5 million after 180 days.
[
97
]
Even if some of the companies that remained below $5 million average market capitalization after 180 days eventually recovered, this analysis indicates that such companies persisted with an average market capitalization below $5 million for an extended period of time. The Commission interprets these results as indicating that, similarly, companies that fall below the Minimum Market Capitilization Criteria would likely remain below that threshold for an extended period of time.
[
98
]
Given the risks that securities with a small market capitalization have heightened susceptibility to manipulative trading activity, which could be exacerbated by a lack of trading interest sufficient to promote fair and orderly markets, the Commission finds that it is not unfairly discriminatory and is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act's requirements that the rules of the Exchange prevent fraud and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, and protect investors and the public interest for the Exchange to immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings for securities that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria.
[
99
]
One commenter expressed concern that factors influencing trading price, and in turn market capitalization, “may fluctuate significantly over relatively short periods without any corresponding change in the issuer's underlying business, financial condition, governance, or compliance with other continued listing standards.”
[
100
]
Further, this commenter stated “a bright-line $5 million market capitalization requirement creates a framework in which immediate suspension and delisting may be triggered by temporary market dislocations rather than meaningful deterioration in an issuer's suitability for continued exchange listing,”
[
101
]
and that the proposed 30 trading-day measurement period is not meaningful in distinguishing between such temporary market dislocations from sustained issuer deficiencies.
[
102
]
Another commenter stated that “the proposal creates a cliff effect: issuers trading anywhere near the threshold will face persistent delisting risk based on ordinary market volatility.”
[
103
]
In addition, commenters stated that a company's market capitalization can be impacted by directional pressure exerted by opportunistic traders and short sellers.
[
104
]
Several commenters expressed concern that the “rigid, time-bound” $5 million average market capitalization threshold could create incentives for manipulative trading activity and market abuse, contrary to the Act's goals of preventing fraud and manipulation.
[
105
]
In particular, commenters stated the mechanical trigger could incentivize coordinated short selling pressure that could force a company below the $5 million market capitalization threshold for long enough to trigger delisting.
[
106
]
One commenter stated that the trigger itself would cause downward price pressure because investors will discount issuers trading near the threshold, lenders would assign additional risk premiums or tighter covenants, and counterparties may hesitate to transact.
[
107
]
One commenter stated that the concerns that automatic delisting could create a “cliff effect” or incentivize strategic short selling “do not reflect actual market dynamics.”
[
108
]
This commenter stated that exchanges already use “bright line, quantitative triggers—such as bid price, public float, and market value of publicly held shares requirements—without evidence of systemic cliff effects or widespread manipulation designed to force delisting.”
[
109
]
This commenter further stated that “sustaining depressed prices for 30 consecutive trading days requires significant capital and is constrained by market maker liquidity provision, natural buying interest, and existing anti
(
printed page 74652)
manipulation rules.”
[
110
]
Another commenter stated that commenters that oppose the proposal are “unable to explain” why the Exchange should be prohibited from setting a $5 million market capitalization listing requirement when that level is far below the $15 million minimum market capitalization imposed by its affiliate, the New York Stock Exchange, and based on its direct experience regarding trading activity on the Exchange.
[
111
]
In response to commenters, the Exchange states that minimum market capitalization continued listing standards have existed for many years—for example, the New York Stock Exchange requires that listed companies maintain a minimum average market capitalization of at least $15 million over a consecutive 30 trading-day period—and the Exchange is not aware that they have had an outsized detrimental effect on listed companies.
[
112
]
Market capitalization, as a combination of the quantity of total common stock outstanding (excluding treasury shares) as well as any common stock that would be issued upon conversion of another outstanding equity security, if such other security is a “substantial equivalent” of common stock,
[
113
]
and their market value, is a reasonable measure to be used in a quantitative listing standard to determine whether a company should continue to be listed on the Exchange because it provides an indication of the issuer's size and how the market values the issuer's securities. The Exchange and other national securities exchanges rely on market capitalization or other measures of market value in existing initial and continued listing standards.
[
114
]
While commenters expressed concern that the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria would create an incentive for opportunistic trading behavior, or for bad actors to manipulate the price of a company's securities to trigger automatic suspension and delisting (including that the consecutive 30 trading-day period may contribute to this risk), commenters have not provided any data showing that similarly structured, existing listing requirements based on market capitalization or other quantitative metrics have created such incentives. Moreover, the requirement to immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings for securities that fall below $5 million average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period would help mitigate the risk of actual opportunistic or manipulative activities in securities that may have a heightened susceptibility to manipulative trading activity. Therefore, the Commission finds that the Exchange's proposal to immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings for securities that fail to comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is reasonably designed and consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act that the rules of the Exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, and protect investors and the public interest.
[
115
]
B. Comments Regarding the Lack of a Cure Period or Exchange Discretion
One commenter raised concerns about the proposal's absence of a cure period that would allow companies that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria to regain compliance before being delisted.
[
116
]

[
117
]
Another commenter stated that the Exchange has historically maintained discretion in administering its continued listing standards in a manner that allows individual circumstances to be considered and that preserving Exchange discretion would better serve investors.
[
118
]
Another commenter raised concerns about the lack of discretion on the part of the Exchange in administering the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria based on facts and circumstances.
[
119
]
For example, according to the commenter, an issuer experiencing long-term operation deterioration may be distinguishable from an issuer that is experiencing temporary market dislocation or a pending financing transaction.
[
120
]
This commenter stated that the proposal would largely eliminate the Exchange's ability to exercise judgement developed from decades of experience evaluating whether individual issuers remain suitable for continued listing.
[
121
]
One commenter, however, stated that “protracted appeals and cure periods” are among the factors that can make listing standards “susceptible to circumvention.”
[
122
]
Another commenter stated that the proposal's immediate suspension and delisting requirement “appropriately recognizes that, at such low market capitalization levels over an extended period, the challenges facing these companies are generally not temporary and are unlikely to be resolved within a conventional compliance period.”
[
123
]
This commenter also stated that continued listing of such issuers can impair the Exchange's ability to maintain fair and orderly markets by making it more difficult for market makers to provide stable liquidity and for investors to rely on the exchange listing as a signal of issuer quality.
[
124
]
In response to commenter concerns about eliminating Exchange discretion, the Exchange states that “transparent bright-line rules . . . enable investors to
(
printed page 74653)
clearly evaluate and understand an issuer's listing status.”
[
125
]
The Exchange also states that continued listing requirements on the Exchange related to minimum price, stockholders' equity, and filing of periodic reports all mandate “non-discretionary regulatory action” for issuer noncompliance.
[
126
]
The Exchange further states that “[o]bjective application of listing rules promotes predictability and transparency which benefits issuers and investors alike.”
[
127
]
In addition, the Exchange states that it disagrees that the proposal does not account for temporary market downturns.
[
128
]
The Exchange states that the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is calculated over a consecutive 30 trading-day period (
i.e.,
at least six weeks of trading activity), thus covering only companies with a prolonged period of noncompliance with the proposed rule.
[
129
]
The Exchange also states that it proactively engages with companies whose average market capitalization falls below $15 million over 30 trading days, and therefore companies would receive meaningful advance notice of their potential noncompliance with the proposed rule.
[
130
]
While the Commission acknowledges that Exchange rules provide for a cure period for noncompliance with certain continuing listing standards, other Exchange rules provide that the Exchange will immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings, without a cure period, for violation of other continued listing standards.
[
131
]
The Exchange's practice of engaging with companies when their average market capitalization falls below $15 million over 30 trading days, along with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria's use of an average market capitalization over a consecutive 30 trading-day period, will provide listed companies with a period of time within which to raise their average market capitalization before they fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria. The requirement's focus on a consecutive 30 trading-day period also means that a security would have a small market capitalization for a prolonged period of time before being subject to immediate suspension of trading and commencement of delisting proceedings.
The Exchange has proposed to immediately suspend and delist companies that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria, without any opportunity to cure, based on concerns that such companies have a heightened susceptibility to manipulation.
[
132
]
The decline of a company's average market capitalization below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria may be indicative of serious difficulties within such company that are likely to continue to put downward pressure on the stock price. As discussed above, according to the Commission's analysis, 59% of the issuers that fell below $5 million market capitalization continued to have a market capitalization under $5 million after 180 days, with the median market capitalization under $4.1 million. The Commission's analysis indicates that the likelihood of companies regaining $5 million market capitalization within 180 days after failing to comply with such market capitalization threshold is limited.
[
133
]
Accordingly, the Commission expects that a significant number of companies that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria either will not recover or will persist with an average market capitalization for a prolonged period of time. Companies that remain below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria may have heightened susceptibility to manipulative trading activity, as discussed above, and requiring their delisting is consistent with the goal of protecting investors and the public interest. Thus, the Exchange's proposal is reasonably designed to protect investors by preventing the prolonged trading of companies with a small market capitalization that may be more susceptible to fraud and manipulation and seeks to help ensure that only financially sound issuers remain listed on the Exchange. Therefore, the Commission finds that the Exchange's proposal to immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings for securities that fail to comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is reasonably designed and consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act that the rules of the Exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, and protect investors and the public interest.
[
134
]
The proposal is also consistent with Section 6(b)(7) of the Act in that, while the Exchange will immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings without a cure period when an issuer's securities fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria, Exchange rules will continue to provide a fair procedure for the prohibition or limitation by the Exchange of any person with respect to access to services offered.
[
135
]
As discussed above, existing Exchange rules provide for immediate suspension of trading and commencement of delisting proceedings, without a cure period, when a security is out of compliance with continued listing requirements.
[
136
]
Pursuant to the Exchange's proposal, a listed company whose security is subject to immediate suspension of trading and the commencement of delisting proceedings after falling below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria will be able to appeal the delisting decision pursuant to Part 12 of the Company Guide.
[
137
]
Depending on the level of proceeding under Part 12 of the Company Guide, a Listing Qualifications Panel, the Committee for Review, or the Exchange Board of Directors will continue to have the authority to consider any failure to meet any quantitative standard for continued listing, and the company will continue to be given a notice of such consideration and an opportunity to respond.
[
138
]
A Listing Qualifications Panel, the Committee for Review, or the Exchange Board of Directors, as part of its respective review, may consider, among other things, the issuer's stock price or any information that the issuer
(
printed page 74654)
releases to the public, including any additional quantitative deficiencies or qualitative considerations reflected in the released information.
[
139
]
Therefore, the Commission finds that the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(7) of the Act in that it provides a fair procedure for the prohibition or limitation by the Exchange of any person with respect to access to services offered.
C. Comments Regarding the Need for the Proposed Rule Change
One commenter stated that the Exchange has not demonstrated the incremental benefit of its proposal against the backdrop of its recently strengthened initial listing standards.
[
140
]
In particular, this commenter stated that the Exchange should explain how the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is justified on its own terms, particularly given that the Exchange originally presented the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria and the Minimum Bid Price Criteria
[
141
]
as addressing the same underlying concern.
[
142
]
This commenter stated that the Exchange must explain the incremental work of the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria or, if the Exchange's proposal is intended to work together with the Minimum Bid Price Criteria, the Exchange must analyze their combined effects.
[
143
]
In addition, this commenter stated that the Exchange has not explained why its existing, conduct-focused tools are inadequate to address concerns about manipulation.
[
144
]
While existing Exchange continued listing requirements may address some similar concerns, as discussed above, the risks of heightened susceptibility to manipulative trading activity and difficulty maintaining fair and orderly markets in the securities of companies that are not able to sustain an average market capitalization of at least $5 million support the adoption of the proposed Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria.
[
145
]
The addition of a non-discretionary, objective metric for continued listing on the Exchange is reasonably designed to enhance its existing conduct-focused regulatory tools to promote administrative predictability and transparency that will benefit issuers and investors alike. Further, the Exchange has separately proposed, and the Commission has approved with separate, independent justification, certain price-based continued listing requirements that reduce the period of time for a company to regain compliance based on investor protection concerns, including the Minimum Bid Price Criteria recently implemented by the Exchange.
[
146
]
That the Exchange previously filed a proposal that included both the Minimum Bid Price Criteria and a proposed continued listing requirement that was substantially similar to the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria, the latter of which was removed before the Commission approved the Minimum Bid Price Proposal, does not alter the Commission's required analysis regarding whether the proposal is consistent with the Act, because the two rules operate independently, and each must be independently approved if the Commission finds that it is consistent with the Act.
[
147
]
The current proposal and prior Commission-approved rules address different continued listing requirements that independently operate to address similar Exchange concerns with lower-priced securities, while taking different approaches to target securities that another continued listing requirement may not capture. For example, the Commission stated, in the context of removing compliance periods for securities that have had excessive reverse stock splits and securities that are trading at very low prices,
[
148
]
that there were investor protection concerns with allowing the securities identified in that proposal to have an extended period of time to regain compliance with the relevant requirements.
[
149
]
Similar to the Reverse Stock Split Proposal, with respect to its current proposal, the Exchange states that companies identified in this proposal may have financial concerns that render them inappropriate for trading on the Exchange for investor protection reasons.
[
150
]
Moreover, while a reverse stock split increases a company's stock price and thus could help a security comply with the Minimum Bid Price Criteria or other continued requirements related to minimum bid price, it does not directly change the company's market capitalization.
[
151
]
If a company is trading at a price compliant with the relevant bid price requirements, but has a very small market capitalization, it could continue to be susceptible to manipulative trading. Similarly, if a company has a large market capitalization but its securities fail to meet the relevant bid price requirements, the low trading price of the securities may make these securities more prone to manipulation.
[
152
]
Therefore, the Commission finds that the Exchange's proposal is reasonably designed and consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act that the rules of the Exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, and protect investors and the public interest.
[
153
]
(
printed page 74655)
D. Comments Regarding Effects on Companies and the Market
One commenter stated that delisting from the Exchange does not eliminate an issuer's ability to access public capital markets as they can continue to trade in the OTC markets, which operate under a “regime that emphasizes disclosure, risk flagging, and heightened scrutiny of low priced and thinly traded securities.”
[
154
]
This commenter further stated that, “[f]rom an investor protection standpoint, this is an appropriate outcome: exchange listing is reserved for companies that meet robust quantitative and qualitative standards, while OTC markets provide an alternative venue for public trading in higher risk or less established issuers, subject to tailored safeguards.”
[
155
]
Other commenters stated that the proposal would negatively impact capital formation for small public companies and increase risk to investors.
[
156
]
One commenter discussed the benefits of exchange listing for both smaller companies and investors in the context of cost of capital.
[
157
]
Specifically, this commenter stated that exchange listing provides smaller companies access to a larger set of investors and greater liquidity through access to secondary markets and allows investors to benefit from a set of Commission rules designed to enhance and organize the flow of information to investors.
[
158
]
The commenter concluded that this lowers the cost of capital because investors “are willing to pay a premium for the ability to trade easily” and “are more willing to make long-dated investments when they know their positions can be readily transferred to other investors.”
[
159
]
This commenter also stated that investors are less inclined to invest in, and lenders are less willing to extend financing, to companies trading close to the bright-line threshold, which intensifies the downward price pressure.
[
160
]
Another commenter stated that the proposal would not only impact companies with a market capitalization under $5 million, but also companies between $5 million and $50 million, as those companies could face a risk of being delisted as a result of temporary market fluctuations.
[
161
]
Several commenters discussed the negative consequences of trading in the OTC market upon immediate delisting and suspension.
[
162
]
These commenters stated that when a security is delisted and moves from a national securities exchange to the OTC market, trading occurs with reduced liquidity, diminished analyst coverage, wider bid-ask spreads, lower institutional participation, fewer financing opportunities, and reduced oversight.
[
163
]
One commenter also stated that retail shareholders may face difficulty purchasing and selling securities efficiently.
[
164
]
This commenter stated that trading in the OTC market would materially impact issuers' ability to access capital, make strategic acquisitions, attract institutional investment, and ultimately regain compliance with exchange listing standards.
[
165
]
Another commenter discussed the benefits of the regulatory framework for exchange-listed securities, which are NMS securities.
[
166
]
The Commission acknowledges that there are many benefits to companies and their shareholders related to being listed on a national securities exchange, including increased access to capital formation and promotion of market efficiency. Commenters have raised concerns that delisting companies that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria may lead to several negative outcomes, including, but not limited to, making raising capital more difficult for small companies.
[
167
]
However, the benefits of listing and possible consequences of delisting for issuers and their shareholders do not override the need for an exchange to maintain and enforce continued listing standards such as the proposed rule, which is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act.
[
168
]
As discussed above, the immediate suspension and delisting of companies that do not comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria will address identified risks of heightened susceptibility to manipulative trading activity, and it is not unfairly discriminatory to impose a standard that is reasonably tailored to address those risks. Moreover, companies that fail to comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria and are subsequently delisted will be able to trade in the OTC market, which provides a viable alternative for the trading of companies that do not meet the requirements for Exchange listing. While companies that are no longer eligible to list on the Exchange may apply to list on another national securities exchange, other national securities exchange may choose to impose similar continued listing requirements, as is the case with the Nasdaq MVLS Proposal. However, the OTC market remains a viable trading venue for securities that are not eligible for listing on any national securities exchange. As such, competition among issuers and national securities exchanges would not be unnecessarily or inappropriately burdened as a result of this proposed rule change. These companies may also apply for Exchange listing in the future. Therefore, the Commission finds that the Exchange's proposal to immediately suspend and delist companies that fail to comply with the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and
(
printed page 74656)
manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, and protect investors and the public interest, consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act.
[
169
]
The Commission also finds that the Exchange's proposal is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers, consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act;
[
170
]
and will not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act, consistent with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act.
[
171
]
E. Comments Suggesting Alternatives
Commenters suggested alternatives to the proposal.
[
172
]
One commenter suggested providing a reasonable cure period and adopting a “graduated compliance framework” similar to other continued listing standards.
[
173
]
This commenter also recommended authorizing the Hearing Panel to consider issuer-specific circumstances.
[
174
]
Another commenter suggested that the Exchange develop a targeted, risk-based response based on characteristics such as public float, insider ownership, and limitation to U.S. regulatory access; provide a meaningful cure period; or consider delisting based on the existence of an additional compliance deficiency.
[
175
]
This commenter also stated that the Exchange could employ graduated supervisory responses, such as enhanced monitoring, watch-list status, or disclosure obligations to distinguish temporary volatility from structural deficiencies.
[
176
]
Further, this commenter suggested providing a twelve-month implementation delay for the proposed rule change to allow issuers, investors, and lenders time to adjust their capital structures, contractual arrangements, and risk assessments in an orderly manner.
[
177
]
The Act governs the Commission's review of SRO-proposed rules. Section 19(b)(2)(C)(i) provides that the Commission “shall approve” a proposal if it finds that the rule is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations applicable to the SRO—including requirements in Section 6(b).
[
178
]
The statute does not give the Commission the ability to make any changes to the rule proposal as submitted, or to disapprove the rule proposal on the ground that the Commission would prefer some alternative rule on the same topic and the Exchange has not amended its proposal in response to commenters' suggestions. The Commission must evaluate the proposal before it and approve if it finds the proposal is consistent with the Act and the rules thereunder. Even if commenters' suggestions could provide alternative, potentially preferable means to address concerns that securities with small market capitalization are susceptible to manipulative trading activity and may present difficulties with the maintenance of fair and orderly markets in these securities, these suggestions are not part of the Exchange's proposal. For the reasons discussed herein, the Commission finds that the Exchange's proposal to immediately suspend trading and commence delisting proceedings for companies that fall below the Minimum Market Capitalization Criteria is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and to protect investors and public interest, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers, consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act.
[
179
]
The Commission also finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(7) of the Act,
[
180
]
which requires, among other things, that the rules of an exchange provide fair procedure for the prohibition or limitation by the exchange of any person with respect to access to services offered by the exchange. In addition, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act,
[
181
]
which requires that the rules of an exchange do not impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.

pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Act,

182
]
that the proposed rule change (SR-NYSEAMER-2026-17) be, and hereby is, approved.

                         The stock price data, which is at the security level, was sourced from Center for Research in Security Prices (“CRSP”) and accessed through Wharton Research Data Services. This data covers the time period from 2006 to 2025. The data provider calculated the daily market capitalization of each security by multiplying the closing price by the number of shares outstanding. If a closing trade was not available, the closing price was calculated as the midpoint of the best bid and ask quotes at the end of the regular trading session. The Commission analyzed the stock price data at the company level, excluded non-corporate issuers, and only kept issues of common equity (including American Depositary Receipts). The total equity market capitalization of each company was obtained by aggregating the market capitalization of each of the company's issues. The delistings data was sourced from CRSP. The delisting analysis included only cases where the listing exchange dropped the issue (

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is considering a proposal to change approximately 15.78 acres of airport land from aeronautical use to non-aeronautical use and to authorize the sale of airport property located at Marquette Sawyer Regional Airport, Gwinn, Michigan. The aforementioned land is not needed for aeronautical use. The subject property is located east of the commercial terminal and parking lot generally bounded by Avenue G. and 11th Street to the north, Kelly Johnson Memorial Drive to the east, 10th Street to the south and Gerry Corkin Drive to the west. The property proposed to be released for sale contains a portion of a non-aeronautical manufacturing facility with the remainder vacant land. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On July 16, 2026, Commerce published the
Preliminary Results
of the 2024-2025 administrative review of the antidumping duty order on citric acid and certain citrate salts (citric acid) from Thailand
[
1
]
in the
Federal Register
and invited interested parties to comment.
[
2
]
The deadline for the final results of review is November 13, 2026. We received no comments from interested parties on the
Preliminary Results,
and we made no changes to the
Preliminary Results
. Accordingly, no decision memorandum accompanies this
Federal Register
notice. The
Preliminary Results
are hereby adopted as the final results. Commerce conducted this administrative review in accordance with section 751(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
Scope of the Order
The products covered by this
Order
include all grades and granulation sizes of citric acid, sodium citrate, and potassium citrate in their unblended forms, whether dry or in solution, and regardless of packaging type from Thailand. For a full description of the scope of the
Order, see
the
Preliminary Results
PDM.
Rate for Non-Selected Company
The Act does not directly address the establishment of a rate to be applied to individual companies not selected for examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(c)(2) of the Act. However,
19 CFR 351.109(g)
states that Commerce will determine the rate for non-selected companies by applying the methodology set forth in
19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)-(2)
, which generally parallels the methodology for determining the all-others rate in an investigation under section 735(c)(5) of
(
printed page 74541)
the Act. Under
19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)
and section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act, the all-others rate is normally “an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any zero or de minimis margins, and any margins determined entirely {on the basis of facts available}.” Where the weighted-average dumping margin for each of the individually examined companies is zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available,
19 CFR 351.109(f)(2)
and section 735(c)(5)(B) of the Act provide that Commerce may use “any reasonable method” for determining the all-others rate, including averaging the margins of the individually examined companies.
In this administrative review, we determined a zero percent rate for the non-examined company, based on the rates calculated for the two mandatory respondents. No party commented on this rate, and therefore it remains unchanged in these final results.
Final Results of Review
We determine that the following weighted-average dumping margins exist for the period July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025:

Disclosure
Normally, Commerce discloses to interested parties the calculations of the final results of an administrative review within five days of a public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of the notice of final results in the
Federal Register
, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.224(b)
. However, because we have made no changes to the
Preliminary Results,
there are no calculations to disclose.
Assessment Rates
Consistent with section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)
, upon completion of the administrative review, Commerce shall determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise covered this review. Because the respondents' weighted-average dumping margins or importer-specific assessment rates are zero or
de minimis
in the final results of review, we intend to instruct CBP to liquidate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
[
3
]
The final results of this administrative review shall be the basis for the assessment of antidumping duties on entries of merchandise covered by the final results of this review and for future deposits of estimated duties, where applicable.
[
4
]
In accordance with Commerce's “automatic assessment” practice, for entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by each respondent which did not know that its merchandise was destined for the United States, we will instruct CBP to liquidate entries not reviewed at the all-others rate established in the original less-than-fair value (LTFV) investigation (
i.e.,
11.25 percent)
[
5
]
if there is no rate for the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of these final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
of the notice of final results of administrative review for all shipments of citric acid from Thailand entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication as provided for by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for the companies listed above will be equal to the weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review (
i.e.,
0.00 percent); (2) for merchandise exported by a company not covered in this review but covered in a prior completed segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published in the completed segment for the most recent period; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review or another completed segment of this proceeding, but the producer is, then the cash deposit rate will be the company-specific rate established for the completed segment for the most recent period for the producer of the merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers or exporters will continue to be 11.25 percent, the all-others rate established in the less-than-fair-value investigation.
[
6
]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Notification to Importers
This notice serves as a final reminder to importers of their responsibility under
19 CFR 351.402(f)(2)
to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during the POR. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties.
Administrative Protective Order
This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an administrative protective order (APO) of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with
19 CFR 351.305(a)(3)
. Timely written notification of the return or destruction of APO materials or conversion to judicial protective order is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
Commerce is issuing and publishing the final results of this review in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and
19 CFR 351.221(b)(5)
.

Background
On October 19, 2026, Commerce published the
Final Results

[

On October 15, 2026, Commerce notified interested parties of the deadline for the submission of ministerial error comments concerning the

[

On October 20, 2026, Commerce received a timely filed allegation of a ministerial error from Resolute FP Canada Inc. (Resolute).
[
4
]
No other interested party filed an allegation or commented on Resolute's allegation.
Legal Framework
A “ministerial error” is defined as an error “in addition, subtraction, or other arithmetic function, clerical error resulting from inaccurate copying, duplication, or the like, and any other similar type of unintentional error which {Commerce} considers ministerial.”
[
5
]
Any issue raised by an interested party as a ministerial error which is, in fact, the result of a methodological decision by Commerce will not be considered a ministerial error because it would not meet the definition of the term in the controlling regulation and under the Act.
[
6
]
Commerce's regulations stipulate that the agency will disclose its calculations to parties to the proceeding and that those parties may submit comments concerning any ministerial error in such calculations in the final results of a review.
[
7
]
Commerce will analyze any comments received and, if appropriate, correct any ministerial error by amending the final results of review.
[
8
]
Ministerial Errors
Resolute alleges that Commerce made a ministerial error in the calculations underlying the
Final Results
. Commerce reviewed the record and agrees that the error alleged by Resolute constitutes a ministerial error within the meaning of section 751(h) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.224(f)
.
[
9
]
Specifically, for Resolute, Commerce made an inadvertent error by using an incorrect figure in the final calculations.
[
10
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.224(e)
, Commerce is amending the
Final Results
to reflect the correction of the ministerial error, as described in the Ministerial Error Memorandum.
[
11
]
Based on the correction, Resolute's final subsidy rate changed from 12.42 percent to 12.35 percent, and the non-selected companies' final subsidy rate changed from 14.11 percent to 14.08 percent. The amended net subsidy rates are listed in the “Amended Final Results” section below.
For a complete discussion of the ministerial error allegation, as well as Commerce's analysis,
see
the Ministerial Error Memorandum. The Ministerial Error Memorandum is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.

Abstract:
The Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) Section 7(a) requires that any person who produces pesticides, active ingredients or devices subject to the Act must register with the Administrator of EPA the establishment in which the pesticide, active ingredient or device is produced. This section further requires that applications for registration of any establishment shall include the name and address of the establishment and of the producer who operates such an establishment. EPA Form 3540-8, Application for Registration of Pesticide-Producing and Device-Producing Establishments, is used to collect the establishment registration information required by this section.
FIFRA Section 7(c) requires that any producer operating an establishment registered under Section 7(a) report to the Administrator within 30 days after it is registered, and annually thereafter by March 1st for certain pesticide or device production and sales or distribution information. The producers must report which types and amounts of pesticides, active ingredients, or devices are currently being produced, were produced during the past year, or sold or distributed in the past year. The supporting regulations at
40 CFR part 167
provide the requirements and time schedules for submitting production information. EPA Form 3540-16, Pesticide Report for Pesticide-Producing and Device-Producing Establishments, is used to collect the pesticide production information required by Section 7(c) of FIFRA.
Establishment registration information, collected on EPA Form 3540-8, is a one-time requirement for all pesticide-producing and device-producing establishments. Pesticide and device production information, reported on EPA Form 3540-16, is required to be submitted within 30 days after the company is notified of its pesticide-producing or device-producing establishment number, and annually thereafter on or before March 1. Pesticide-producing and device-producing establishments may electronically submit their establishment registration information and pesticide production information through EPA's Central Data Exchange (CDX).

).

Changes in the Estimates:
There is a decrease of 1,065 hours in the total estimated respondent burden compared with the ICR currently approved by OMB. This decrease is due to a reduction in the number of forms submitted. full_text:

Department of Justice
Drug Enforcement Administration
On May 6, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Dave Allen Wright, M.D., of Cincinnati, Ohio (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 1, at 1, 3. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration No. BW4012720, alleging that Registrant is “currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the State of Ohio, the state in which [he is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2 (citing
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
).
The OSC notified Registrant of his right to file a written request for hearing, and that if he failed to file such a request, he would be deemed to have waived his right to a hearing and be in default.
Id.
at 2 (citing
21 CFR 1301.43
). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds him to be in default. RFAA, at 2.
[
1
]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
.
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to
21 CFR 1301.43(c)
,
(f)
, and
1301.46
. RFAA, at 3;
see also
21 CFR 1316.67
.
Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted.
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
. According to the OSC, on October 1, 2025, Registrant's Ohio medical license expired by its own terms. RFAAX 1, at 1. According to Ohio online records, of which the Agency takes official notice, Registrant's Ohio medical license remains expired.
[
2
]
eLicense Ohio Professional Licensure License Lookup,
https://elicense.ohio./​oh_​verifylicense
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice medicine in Ohio, the state in which he is registered with DEA.
[
3
]
Discussion
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
, the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under
21 U.S.C. 823
“upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.”
With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. 802(21).”).
[
4
]
The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., Lawrence Rudolph, D.M.D.,
89 FR 79310
(2024);
Henry-Norbert O. Ndekwe, M.D.,
90 FR 15990
(2025);
Benson Sergiles, P.A.,
90 FR 32016
(2025).
According to Ohio statute, “[n]o person shall knowingly obtain, possess, or use a controlled substance or a controlled substance analog,” except pursuant to a “prescription issued by a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs if the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose.” Ohio Rev. Code §  2925.11(A),
(
printed page 74608)
(B)(1)(d) (2025). Further, a “`[l]icensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs or `prescriber' means an individual who is authorized by law to prescribe drugs or dangerous drugs or drug therapy related devices in the course of the individual's professional practice.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I)(2026).
[
5
]
The Ohio statute further defines an authorized prescriber as “[a] physician authorized under Chapter 4731. of the Revised Code to practice medicine and surgery, osteopathic medicine and surgery, or podiatric medicine and surgery.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I)(5)(2026). Additionally, Ohio law permits “[a] licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs, if acting in the course of professional practice, in accordance with the laws regulating the professional's practice” to prescribe or administer schedule II, III, IV, and V controlled substances to patients.
Id.
§ 3719.06(A)(1)(a)-(b)(2025).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks a license to practice medicine in Ohio. As already discussed, an individual must be a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in order to handle controlled substances in Ohio. Thus, because Registrant is not a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in Ohio, and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Ohio, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration in Ohio. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
Order
Pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 824(a)
, I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. BW4012720 issued to Dave Allen Wright, M.D. Further, pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
, I hereby deny any pending applications of Dave Allen Wright, M.D., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Dave Allen Wright, M.D., for additional registration in Ohio. This Order is effective December 21, 2026.
Signing Authority
This document of the Drug Enforcement Administration was signed on November 6, 2026, by DEA Administrator Terrance C. Cole. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DEA. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DEA Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of DEA. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the
Federal Register
.
Heather Achbach,
Federal Register Liaison Officer, Drug Enforcement Administration.
Footnotes
1.
    
                         Based on the Government's submissions in its RFAA dated August 5, 2026, the Agency finds that service of the OSC on Registrant was adequate. The included declaration from a DEA Diversion Investigator (DI) indicates that on May 14, 2026, the DI attempted to contact Registrant via his registered telephone number because the DI had previously found out that Registrant was no longer employed at his registered address and had retired on or around September 2025. RFAAX 2, at 1-2. On the same date, the DI attempt to contact Registrant via his registered email address.
Id.
at 2. Later, on the same date, Registrant returned the DI's phone call and informed the DI that he was no longer domiciled in Ohio or practicing at his registered location, nor was his registered email address a valid means of contact.
Id.
Upon the DI's request to provide an alternative address to personally serve or mail the OSC to Registrant, Registrant declined to inform DEA where he was currently residing for the purposes of updating his registration or receiving mail.
Id.
Registrant did, however, provide the DI with an alternative email address and stated that he could be contacted at this alternative email address.
Id.
Following the telephone conversation, the DI emailed a copy of the OSC to the alternative email address that Registrant had provided and later received an e-receipt confirming successful delivery of the email.
Id.; see also id.,
Appendixes A-B. Here, the Agency finds that Registrant was successfully served the OSC by email and that the DI's efforts to serve Registrant by other means were “`reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise [Registrant] of the pendency of the action.'”
Jones
v.
Flowers,
547 U.S. 220, 226 (2006) (quoting
Mullane
v.
Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.,
339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950)). Therefore, due process notice requirements have been satisfied.
See Mohammed S. Aljanaby, M.D.,
82 FR 34552
,
34552
(2017) (finding that service by email satisfies due process where the email is not returned as undeliverable and other methods have been unsuccessful);
Emilio Luna, M.D.
,
77 FR 4829
,
4830
(2012) (same).
Back to Citation
2.
    
                         Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency “may take official notice of facts at any stage in a proceeding—even in the final decision.” United States Department of Justice, Attorney General's Manual on the Administrative Procedure Act 80 (1947) (Wm. W. Gaunt & Sons, Inc., Reprint 1979).
Back to Citation
3.
    
                         Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 556(e)
, “[w]hen an agency decision rests on official notice of a material fact not appearing in the evidence in the record, a party is entitled, on timely request, to an opportunity to show the contrary.” The material fact here is that Registrant, as of the date of this Order, is not licensed to practice medicine in Ohio. Accordingly, Registrant may dispute the Agency's finding by filing a properly supported motion for reconsideration of findings of fact within fifteen calendar days of the date of this Order. Any such motion and response shall be filed and served by email to the other party and to the Office of the Administrator, Drug Enforcement Administration, at
dea.addo.attorneys@dea.gov
.
Back to Citation
4.
    
                         This rule derives from the text of two provisions of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). First, Congress defined the term “practitioner” to mean “a physician . . . or other person licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by . . . the jurisdiction in which he practices . . . , to distribute, dispense, . . . [or] administer . . . a controlled substance in the course of professional practice.”
21 U.S.C. 802(21)
. Second, in setting the requirements for obtaining a practitioner's registration, Congress directed that “[t]he Attorney General shall register practitioners . . . if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.”
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
. Because Congress has clearly mandated that a practitioner possess state authority in order to be deemed a practitioner under the CSA, DEA has held repeatedly that revocation of a practitioner's registration is the appropriate sanction whenever he is no longer authorized to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which he practices.
See, e.g., Elias Garcia Garcia, P.A.,
90 FR 31242
(2025);
Jason Weakley, R.N., A.P.R.N.,
90 FR 10085
(2025);
Khursheed Haider, M.D.,
90 FR 21950
(2025).
Back to Citation
5.
    
                         Section 4729.01 of the Ohio Revised Code was updated on October 9, 2026, but does not change any of the material parts or alter the Agency's decision in this matter.
