AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
This proposed rule would revise provisions regarding provider enrollment, medical review, investigations, and other program integrity oversight provisions to greatly strengthen our ability to crush fraud, enhance program integrity efforts across Medicare, Medicaid, Children's Health Insurance Program, and the Marketplace and maximize regulatory authorities to address inappropriate payments.
DATES:
To be assured consideration, comments must be received at one of the addresses provided below, by January 19, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
In commenting, please refer to file code CMS-6098-P.
Comments, including mass comment submissions, must be submitted in one of the following three ways (please choose only one of the ways listed):
1.
Electronically.
You may submit electronic comments on this regulation to
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​CMS-2026-0826
.
Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions.
2.
By regular mail.
You may mail written comments to the following address ONLY: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-6098-P, P.O. Box 8013, Baltimore, MD 21244-8013.
Please allow sufficient time for mailed comments to be received before the close of the comment period.
3.
By express or overnight mail.
You may send written comments to the following address ONLY: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-6098-P, Mail Stop C4-26-05, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, MD 21244-1850.
For information on viewing public comments, see the beginning of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Eli Boone, (227) 232-6768, or Katie O'Malley, (410) 786-8987.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Inspection of Public Comments:
All comments received before the close of the comment period are available for viewing by the public, including any personally identifiable or confidential business information that is included in a comment. We post all comments received before the close of the comment period on the following website as soon as possible after they have been received:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the search instructions on that website to view public comments. CMS will not post on
Regulations.gov
public comments that make threats to individuals or institutions or suggest that the commenter will take actions to harm an individual. CMS continues to encourage individuals not to submit duplicative comments. We will post acceptable comments from multiple unique commenters even if the content is identical or nearly identical to other comments.
Plain Language Summary:
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a plain language summary of this rule may be found at
https://www.regulations.gov/​
.
I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose
On June 6, 2025, President Trump issued a Presidential Memorandum on Eliminating Waste, Fraud, and Abuse in Medicaid, expressing this Administration's commitment to preserve and protect the integrity of government programs. Similarly, President Trump, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Kennedy (the HHS Secretary), and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Oz (the CMS Administrator) have strongly demonstrated this Administration's dedication to crushing fraud in Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and the Marketplace. In alignment with this strategic objective, as well as in line with our statutory authorities to undertake rulemaking, CMS is issuing this proposed rule to solicit stakeholder feedback on proposed regulatory changes that would strengthen CMS' ability to address vulnerabilities that make Federal health programs attractive targets to fraudsters, with the ultimate goal of ensuring greater affordability and sustainability of these programs for generations to come.
B. Summary of the Major Provisions
1. Strengthening State Medicaid and CHIP Oversight
CMS intends to enhance Federal oversight of State Medicaid programs through proposed measures that would, if finalized as proposed, expand its authority to enforce program integrity and strengthen State accountability. These initiatives include: (1) facilitating States' ability to rapidly suspend Medicaid payments based on credible allegations of fraud and strengthening State fraud reporting requirements; (2) establishing consistent provider identification requirements to increase State and Federal oversight capabilities; (3) increasing oversight of Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility determination errors; and (4) establishing strengthened State program integrity corrective action plan requirements to ensure compliance with Federal requirements. Additional provisions include:
Requiring prompt reporting and return of Medicaid overpayments
Enhancing managed care integrity reporting
Broadening grounds for Medicaid provider denials and terminations
Increasing data reporting on provider ownership
Requiring electronic visit verification (EVV) data review for specific activities
Collectively, these enhancements aim to strengthen CMS' and States' ability to detect and address fraud, waste, and abuse in Medicaid and CHIP, while fostering improved collaboration between State and Federal efforts in program integrity.
In addition, we are including a request for information within this proposed rule. Specifically, CMS is requesting additional information and public comment regarding deductions from Medicaid payments for benefits such as union dues.
2. Reinvigorating the Medicare Advantage (MA) Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) Program and Introducing New Ways To Hold Plan Sponsors Accountable
CMS proposes MA RADV program reforms to ensure oversight of a program responsible for $21 billion per year in overpayments due to the improper inflation of beneficiary risk scores, and proposes provisions to make referrals of substantiated or suspicious fraud, waste, and abuse mandatory for MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors,
(
printed page 74681)
as well as to expand the required reporting of credible allegation of fraud payment suspensions by pharmacies to all provider and supplier types.
3. Establishing Enhanced Medicare Provider Enrollment and Oversight Requirements
CMS proposes to tighten provider enrollment safeguards across Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP by strengthening identity verification, accelerating reporting of changes in enrollment information, expanding grounds for enrollment denial and revocation, and adding a requirement that all providers and suppliers billing MA be enrolled in Original Medicare.
4. Stopping the Bleeding in the Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS) Benefit
CMS proposes strengthening protections against fraudulent and high-pressure marketing by DMEPOS suppliers, including expanding the prohibition on unsolicited contact and ensuring transparency regarding domestic and foreign marketers. CMS also proposes reinforcing DMEPOS surety bond requirements to reduce Medicare Trust Fund losses when overpayments occur.
5. Crushing Marketplace Fraud
CMS proposes to greatly strengthen its authority to suspend or terminate agents, brokers, and web-brokers engaging in abusive conduct and to exclude or terminate agents, brokers, and web-brokers who pose an unacceptable risk of fraud, waste, and abuse, including those convicted of certain felonies or misdemeanors. Additionally, CMS proposes to increase transparency in enforcement actions following findings of agent, broker, and web-broker noncompliance with regulatory standards and enhance the security of Exchange systems and consumer information.
C. Summary of Costs and Benefits
Currently, the CMS Office of the Actuary (OACT) has not completed a quantitative score of the Federal budgetary or trust fund impacts of this proposed rule. OACT will score the rule and provide detailed financial impact projections in the final rule once policy parameters are finalized and public comments have been evaluated. We specifically request data and feedback from commenters regarding potential administrative, operational, and utilization impacts to assist OACT in developing its final estimates.
We estimate that, taken together, the quantified provisions of this proposed rule would result in approximately $379 million in costs from 2027 to 2036. This estimate does not include the over $90 billion in transfers expected between the Federal government and State governments or private entities that may result from this proposed rule. CMS is seeking public comment on the accuracy of all cost and burden estimates included in this proposed rule.
II. Background
A. Authority
CMS' authority to issue program integrity rules flows primarily from the Social Security Act (the Act), as amended. The general authorities described here are in addition to the specific statutory authorities discussed with respect to each proposal. Sections 1102(a) and 1871(a)(1) of the Act provide general authority for the Secretary to prescribe regulations for the efficient administration of the Medicare program.
Section 1102(a) of the Act likewise provides general authority for the Secretary to prescribe regulations for the efficient administration of the Medicaid program and CHIP, while with respect to Medicaid, section 1902(a)(4) of the Act requires State plans to provide such methods of administration as are found by the Secretary to be necessary for the proper and efficient operation of the plan.
For MA, the Secretary has authority under section 1856(b)(1) of the Act to adopt standards consistent with, and to carry out, Part C. The Secretary also has authority under section 1857(e)(1) to establish new MA contract terms and conditions where necessary and appropriate and not inconsistent with Part C. For Medicare Part D, section 1860D-12(b)(3)(D) provides that the Secretary's authority under section 1857(e) of the Act also applies to Part D.
For Medicaid, section 1902(a)(4) of the Act requires State plans to provide such methods of administration as are found by the Secretary to be necessary for the proper and efficient operation of the plan. For the Exchanges, section 1312(e) of the Affordable Care Act provides the Secretary with the authority to establish procedures under which a State may allow agents or brokers to (1) enroll qualified individuals and qualified employers in QHPs offered through Exchanges, and (2) assist individuals in applying for advance payments of the premium tax credit (APTC) and cost sharing reductions (CSRs) for QHPs sold through an Exchange. Section 1321(a) of the Affordable Care Act directs the Secretary to issue regulations setting standards for meeting the applicable requirements of title I of the Affordable Care Act and the amendments made by that title. These standards concern the establishment and operation of Exchanges, the offering of qualified health plans through Exchanges, and such other requirements as the Secretary determines appropriate. Section 1313(a)(5) of the Affordable Care Act further directs the Secretary, with respect to activities carried out under title I, to provide for the efficient and nondiscriminatory administration of Exchange activities. It also directs the Secretary to implement any measure or procedure that the Secretary determines is appropriate to reduce fraud and abuse in the Administration of title I and has authority to implement under title I or another Act.
B. This Administration's Fight To Crush Health Care Fraud
Health care fraud, waste, and abuse is a pervasive issue that this Administration is tackling in an unprecedented fashion. For example, on March 16, 2026, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14395
, establishing the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. Similarly, the HHS Secretary and the CMS Administrator have strongly demonstrated this Administration's dedication to crushing fraud in Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), the Basic Health Program (BHP), and the Marketplace. In June 2026, the Secretary and the Administrator joined the then-Acting Attorney General to announce the Justice Department's 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown, which resulted in charges against 455 defendants, including 90 doctors and other licensed medical professionals, for their alleged participation in health care fraud and opioid abuse schemes involving over $6.5 billion in false claims and significant patient harm.
[
1
]
This is an example of the significant steps this Administration has taken to crush fraud since President Trump began his second term in January 2025.
During his first term, on October 3, 2019, President Trump issued Executive Order (E.O.) 13890 on Protecting and Improving Medicare for Our Nation's Seniors. This order directed CMS to annually promulgate regulatory or subregulatory changes to Medicare to enhance program integrity and promote
(
printed page 74682)
payment accuracy and efficiency. CMS subsequently finalized a program integrity rule in 2023 (
88 FR 80141
) that required the disclosure of certain ownership, managerial, and other information regarding Medicare skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and Medicaid nursing facilities (NFs). While CMS has issued many program integrity provisions in various rules or direction through subregulatory guidance, subsequent annual stand-alone program integrity rulemaking has not taken place.
Crushing fraud has been a central tenet of President Trump's second term, and undertaking rulemaking to address fraud vulnerabilities is a critical component of that fight. On February 27, 2026, CMS issued a Request for Information Related to Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH RFI) (
91 FR 9803
) to solicit interested parties' feedback on potential regulatory changes that might be included in this proposed rule, as well as other programmatic changes that could be implemented to make CMS more effective in crushing fraud.
Working tirelessly to crush waste, abuse, and fraudulent activities in our health care system remains a key CMS strategic priority. This includes leveraging new techniques, authorities, and policies that will enable CMS to continue shifting away from pay and chase methods to “stop and caught” approaches that allow us to swiftly remove bad actors from our programs which prevents dollars from going out the door towards fraud. We are issuing this Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH) proposed rule to solicit interested parties' feedback on proposed regulatory changes to make CMS more effective in crushing fraud to protect taxpayer dollars and the Americans we serve.
C. Severability
CMS proposes that if any provision of the CRUSH proposed rule, if or when finalized, were held to be invalid or unenforceable—facially or as applied to any person, plaintiff, or circumstance—or stayed pending further judicial or agency action, such provision shall be severable from other provisions finalized, and from rules and regulations otherwise in effect, and not affect the remainder of provisions finalized. It was and continues to be our intent that, unless such provision shall be held to be utterly invalid or unenforceable, it be construed to give the provision maximum effect permitted by law including in the application of the provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other, dissimilar circumstances from those where the provision may be held to be invalid or unenforceable. The CRUSH proposed rule addresses numerous stand-alone proposals that can largely operate independently of one another. We seek public comments on these proposed approaches to severability and whether similar regulatory text should be added to additional proposals within this proposed rule.
D. Effective Dates
We propose that, unless we specify otherwise with respect to a particular a provision, the effective date would be 60 days after the publication of the CRUSH final rule. We request public comment on the feasibility of effective dates for each provision.
III. Medicaid and CHIP Program Integrity Proposals
Medicaid and CHIP are Federal-State partnerships, and these partnerships are central to the programs' success. CMS provides States with guidance; technical assistance, including tools and data; Federal matching funds for expenditures; and other resources to use in meeting statutory and regulatory requirements.
The Federal Government and each State jointly fund each State's Medicaid and CHIP programs. The Federal Government matches State Medicaid program expenditures at a specified percentage, called the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP), which has a statutory minimum of 50 percent and maximum of 83 percent, though enhanced FMAP exceeding 83 percent is available for certain covered populations and services (for example, the 90 percent FMAP available for expenditures attributable to the Medicaid expansion population under section 1905(y) of the Act).
[
2
]
State CHIP expenditures are matched at an enhanced FMAP equal to the State's regular FMAP increased by 30 percent, but bounded by an upper limit as section 2105(b) of the Act provides that the CHIP enhanced FMAP may not exceed 85 percent.
[
3
]
Total Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 Medicaid and CHIP spending exceeded $962 billion, or over 18 percent of total national health expenditures.
[
4
]
The FY 2024 Federal share of Medicaid expenditures constituted 64.7 percent of total Medicaid spending
[
5
]
—in other words, nearly 
                        2/3

Although existing statutory and regulatory requirements provide a strong foundation for Medicaid and CHIP program integrity when properly executed, CMS continues to identify vulnerabilities that limit States' and CMS' ability to effectively oversee Medicaid expenditures and address evolving fraud, waste, and abuse risks. Despite State and Federal efforts, Medicaid and CHIP improper payment rates have also remained persistently high. Improper payments are not always directly attributable to fraud, waste, or abuse, but they remain an important indicator of payment integrity challenges. For example, in FY 2025, eligibility errors specifically accounted for approximately 72 percent of all Medicaid and CHIP improper payments, resulting in an estimated $27 billion in projected Federal improper payments.

CMS has recently intensified its efforts to crush fraud in Medicaid and CHIP nationwide. B. State Payment Suspension Updates and Reporting Requirements
Sections 1903(i)(2) and 2107(e)(1) of the Act relate to limitations on payment. In 2010, section 6402(h)(2) of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) amended the Act to provide that State payments to a Medicaid provider under investigation for a credible allegation of fraud are not eligible for Federal matching funds unless a good cause exception is met. Specifically, section 1903(i)(2)(C) of the Act provides that Federal payment shall not be made with respect to any amount expended for items or services furnished “by any individual or entity to whom the State has failed to suspend payments under the plan during any period when there is pending an investigation of a credible allegation of fraud against the individual or entity,
as determined by the State
[emphasis added] in accordance with regulations promulgated by the Secretary for purposes of section 1395y(o) [1862(o)] of this title and this subparagraph, unless the State determines in accordance with such regulations there is good cause not to suspend such payments[.]”
Our experience working on payment suspension matters has demonstrated to us that States often apply this important administrative tool inconsistently and frequently underutilize it. Although our existing regulations do establish certain “floor” requirements, we also recognize that States have varying standards and processes with their respective Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs) and other law enforcement partners, reflecting individual State policies on how payment suspensions are determined, applied, and maintained, as well as the applicability of these requirements to CHIP. Some of this variation is a feature rather than a flaw: it allows States to develop best practices tailored to their own legal and administrative environments, which can then be shared with and adapted by other States. States' legal frameworks differ and we expect and respect that variation; however, we believe that all States, pursuant to their statutory and regulatory program integrity oversight obligations, should be identifying and investigating credible allegations of fraud, making referrals to law enforcement, and issuing payment suspensions when appropriate to prevent inappropriate payments. CMS expects all States to design and execute payment suspension strategies adapted to that State's fraud risk profile; both the strategies and the risk profile generally will be fluid as fraud is rarely static by location, point in time, or any other factor as fraudsters attempt to leverage and exploit vulnerabilities and points of weakness wherever they discern them. Especially given that the target is ever evolving and the administration of the programs varies based on State laws and policies within Federal contours, our goal is not attaining inter-State uniformity (indeed, among our objectives is fostering and promoting effective creativity), but instead for each State to work within its own legal landscape to maximize the effectiveness of payment suspensions as an administrative tool. States must utilize payment suspensions when appropriate and should draw on the experience of States that have implemented them successfully. States should also ensure they have the funding, staffing, data analytics, and other support needed to identify potential fraud, issue payment suspensions, and make appropriate referrals to law enforcement when potential fraud is uncovered.
At the same time, we are mindful that the consequences of a payment suspension on a provider can be significant and may adversely affect business operations well before any allegation is resolved, and that sometimes what originate as genuine credible allegations ultimately may not be indicative of fraud, waste, or abuse. We recognize that the threshold for establishing a credible allegation of fraud is intentionally lower than the evidentiary standards required for a formal fraud finding, as it is a temporary intervention to stop payments from going out the door to a potentially fraudulent actor. A payment suspension imposed against a legitimate provider, even if only temporarily, can jeopardize that provider's viability and, in turn, disrupt beneficiary access to care, which might be most acutely felt in rural or underserved areas with few alternative providers. The current regulatory framework around good cause exceptions under § 455.23(e) and the additional proposals discussed in this section help ensure that payment suspensions remain a targeted, well-supported program integrity tool.
The following proposals outline how, consistent with statutory and regulatory authority, States may rely on other agencies for credible allegation of fraud determinations and for conducting investigations of such allegations, and the roles that CMS and law enforcement agencies play along with State Medicaid Agencies (SMAs) and CHIP agencies in determining when to issue and maintain payment suspensions.
Specifically, we propose that a State may choose to rely on credible allegation of fraud determination made by CMS or by other Federal agencies. These proposed changes would aim to streamline CMS', SMAs', and CHIP agencies' efforts to ensure Medicaid and CHIP integrity by allowing States to more quickly stop payments where a credible allegation of fraud exists. The regulatory proposals in this rule would be essential to help States quickly and correctly determine whether allegations of fraud are credible so that they could
(
printed page 74685)
rapidly stop payments to individuals and entities and in connection with schemes under investigation for credible allegations of fraud, thus protecting the financial integrity of the Medicaid and CHIP programs and Federal taxpayer dollars.
1. Allowing States To Rely on CMS or Other Federal Agencies' Credible Allegation of Fraud Determinations
Under current regulations at § 455.23(a), an SMA must suspend all Medicaid payments to a provider after the agency determines there is a credible allegation of fraud against such provider for which an investigation is pending, unless the agency has good cause to not suspend payments or to suspend payment only in part. When an investigation leads to the initiation of a payment suspension in whole or part, § 455.23(d) requires the SMA to also make a fraud referral to either the State's MFCU or, in States with no certified MFCU, to an appropriate law enforcement agency. If the MFCU, or law enforcement agency accepts the fraud referral for investigation, the payment suspension may continue until such time as the investigation and any associated enforcement proceedings are completed. There is a similarly defined path for a MFCU to refer a credible allegation of fraud for payment suspension to the SMA at § 1007.9(e). In CHIP, § 457.915 requires the CHIP agency to refer suspected fraud and abuse cases to the CHIP program integrity unit (if such a unit is established) and to appropriate law enforcement officials.
The current payment suspension regulatory framework has led to differing interpretations of what the statutory language “as determined by the State” in section 1903(i)(2)(C) of the Act requires of each State. This has led to variation as to what additional verification steps SMAs or CHIP agencies take when receiving referrals from outside sources, such as CMS or a Federal law enforcement agency, with States handling this process in different ways: some accept a referral as a credible allegation of fraud and immediately impose a payment suspension, while others independently determine the credibility of the allegation(s) before imposing a payment suspension. These divergent approaches create exploitable loopholes that bad actors may use to continue receiving Medicaid and CHIP payments and that make recoupment of improperly paid funds difficult. This is particularly problematic in those States that may not have the internal resources to independently investigate and establish a credible allegation of fraud in every instance. The longer payment suspensions are delayed, the greater the chance of payments continuing to flow to actors potentially defrauding the program.
To address these issues, we propose to add subparagraph § 455.23(a)(1)(i) to specify that a State may rely on a determination by CMS or any other Federal agency that a credible allegation of fraud exists for purposes of imposing a payment suspension and may rely on these agencies' investigations to satisfy the statutory requirement that there is pending an investigation of a credible allegation of fraud against an individual or entity. This would include, for example, investigations conducted by CMS or another Federal agency, such as the U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG), or the Department of Veterans Affairs. We believe this proposal would ease the burden on SMAs or CHIP agencies and reduce the time between when a credible allegation of fraud is referred and a payment suspension is implemented, translating into potential monetary savings for those States and for State and Federal taxpayers, as well as additional protections for those who could experience bodily or financial harm due to the possible underlying fraudulent activity. As stated under the proposed definition of credible allegation of fraud at § 455.2, a State may rely on such other agency determinations as a credible allegation of fraud unless the State has specific information indicating that reliance on the CMS or other agency determinations would be unreasonable under the circumstances. Thus, when accepting credible allegations of fraud from CMS or Federal agencies, SMAs and CHIP agencies may choose to adopt those agencies' determinations as their own.
2. Aligning Modifications to the Definition of Credible Allegation of Fraud
“Credible allegation of fraud” is a statutory term as reflected in section 1903(i)(2)(C) of the Act. On February 2, 2011, CMS published a final rule with comment period (CMS-6028-FC) implementing the new Medicaid payment suspension requirements with an effective date of March 25, 2011. As part of that 2011 final rule, we declined to provide a more precise definition of the term, recognizing that different States may have different considerations in determining what may be a credible allegation of fraud. Instead, we specified at § 455.2 that a credible allegation of fraud may be an allegation verified by the State from any source, and that allegations are considered to be credible when they have an indicia of reliability and the State Medicaid agency has reviewed all allegations, facts, and evidence carefully and acts judiciously on a case-by-case basis. However, as discussed in III(B)(1) of this proposed rule, although the statutory language says that a credible allegation of fraud should be “determined by the State,” it is left to each State in accordance with the Secretary's regulations to decide what that determination must entail. Currently, § 455.2 states that a credible allegation of fraud may arise from sources like fraud hotline tips, claims data mining, or patterns identified through audits and investigations, with credibility established through a State's review for indicia of reliability. In cases where CMS or another Federal agency has already made a credible allegation of fraud determination, requiring the State to independently re-verify that determination is duplicative, time consuming, and oftentimes not necessary. Moreover, the current definition does not explicitly address whether a State may rely on a credible allegation of fraud determination or investigation by CMS or another Federal agency. Without an explicit basis for relying on another agency's determination, we understand that some States duplicate investigative work, delay action, or forgo payment suspensions even when a credible referral already exists. Therefore, we are proposing several changes to the definition of “credible allegation of fraud” at 455.2 to make the Medicaid payment suspension process more efficient and to provide States with clarity as to when the imposition of a payment suspension is appropriate.
First, we propose to revise the definition to explicitly recognize determinations from CMS or another Federal agency as a potential source of a credible allegation of fraud. We are not including State agencies within this new provision; the existing referral pathway at § 1007.9(e) already addresses this category of State-level finding and is not amended by this rule. We believe this proposal would give States a clearer, faster path to act on well-supported referrals from CMS and other Federal agencies, while leaving the established MFCU referral process undisturbed and without need for a conforming amendment to the MFCU regulations at
42 CFR part 1007
.
Second, we are proposing to reorganize the language of the credible allegation of fraud definition at § 455.2 to alleviate duplicative effort that we
(
printed page 74686)
believe the phrase “which has been verified by the State” has caused. We propose that the definition instead provide that a credible allegation of fraud is an allegation that has indicia of reliability that may come from any source, including but not limited to fraud hotline tips verified by further evidence, claims data mining, patterns identified through provider audits, civil false claims cases, and law enforcement investigations, or a determination by CMS or by another Federal agency that an allegation of fraud against a provider is credible.
Third, we propose at § 455.2 that an allegation has indicia of reliability through one of two pathways, depending on its source. For allegations arising from fraud hotline tips, claims data mining, or patterns identified through audits, civil false claims cases, and law enforcement investigations, an allegation has indicia of reliability when the State Medicaid agency has reviewed all allegations, facts, and evidence carefully and acts judiciously on a case-by-case basis, consistent with the existing standard. For allegations based on a determination by CMS or another Federal agency, we propose that the State may adopt the referring agency's determination as its own without conducting an independent redetermination of credibility, unless the State has specific information indicating that reliance on the referring agency's determination would be unreasonable under the circumstances. We believe this presumption would appropriately reduce duplicative State effort while preserving a State's ability to decline reliance where it has a concrete basis to question the referring agency's determination.
We are not proposing to further define “indicia of reliability” in this rule. We have historically left this term undefined to preserve State flexibility to evaluate allegations according to the facts and circumstances presented, consistent with our approach in the 2011 final rule. We recognize, however, that the absence of further definition may create inconsistency across States in how allegations are evaluated, particularly as States begin to rely on determinations made by CMS or other Federal agencies under this proposal, where the referring agency's own application of “indicia of reliability” may not be transparent to the State relying on it. We solicit comments on the following questions:
Should CMS further define “indicia of reliability” in regulation, and if so, what specific factors or criteria should that definition include?
Would a non-exclusive list of factors, for example, the specificity of the allegation, the existence of corroborating documentation, the source's track record of reliability, or the existence of a related law enforcement referral provide useful guidance without unduly constraining State discretion on a case-by-case basis?
Are there existing State-level frameworks for evaluating indicia of reliability that CMS should consider as models if it were to adopt further criteria in future rulemaking?
What burden, if any, would a more detailed definition impose on States, and would that burden be offset by increased consistency?
What additional internal controls, if any, States should be required to maintain to ensure that payment suspensions sustained under this provision are subject to adequate oversight, including the appropriate length of the law enforcement notice-and-objection period?
3. Maintaining a Medicaid and CHIP Payment Suspension During an Investigation
Currently, § 455.23(d)(4) directs that a payment suspension be discontinued if law enforcement declines the fraud referral, unless the SMA has alternative Federal or State authority to impose a suspension or make a referral to another law enforcement agency.
Payment suspensions are temporary measures, subject to defined procedural timeframes, and must be terminated upon specific triggering events specified at § 455.23(c) and (d), and through cross reference at § 457.935(b)(1). However, in practice CMS has observed that payment suspensions may be terminated prematurely, potentially causing at-risk funds to go unrecovered and taxpayer dollars to be lost. For instance, law enforcement agencies may decline State or Federal referrals for various reasons unrelated to the quality of the referral, such as personnel or other resource constraints or competing priorities. As the Medicaid payment suspension regulations currently stand, we did not directly account for the extent of resource constraints that law enforcement agencies may have in accepting a referral for investigation, nor the SMA resources it may take to refer a credible allegation of fraud to multiple agencies for an investigation to commence.
Therefore, we propose revising our regulations to specify that a SMA or CHIP agency may maintain a payment suspension when a credible allegation of fraud is present while the SMA or CHIP agency completes its own investigation, regardless of whether Federal or State law enforcement accepts the referral, if the SMA or CHIP agency documents in writing that the credible allegation of fraud remains under active investigation by the SMA or CHIP agency or by another State or Federal agency. We believe this proposal would appropriately preserve State flexibility to maintain suspensions in cases where the underlying credible allegation of fraud has not been resolved to ultimately determine whether payment should be made, or whether the provider's ability to bill the Medicaid or CHIP programs should be terminated. This would allow the SMA conducting the active investigation to act on its findings, such as by determining that a claim should be denied, that an overpayment exists and can therefore be recouped, or that a provider should be terminated.
However, we are mindful that Congress tied the payment suspension authority under sections 1903(i)(2)(C) and 2107(e)(1)(O) of the Act to the existence of a pending investigation of a credible allegation of fraud, and that the new authority provided by this regulation is not intended to function as an indefinite or open-ended tool. To ensure that a suspension maintained on this basis would remain pursuant to an active ongoing investigation, we are also proposing a requirement that the SMA or CHIP agency redetermine and document in writing, at least quarterly, whether the credible allegation of fraud continues to be under active investigation warranting continuation of the suspension. We propose that, where a Federal or State law enforcement agency accepted the referral and is conducting the investigation, prior to each quarterly redetermination taking effect, the SMA or CHIP agency notify the Federal or State law enforcement agency investigating the alleged fraud of its intent to continue or terminate the suspension, and afford that law enforcement agency the right to request that the payment suspension be kept (or terminated). Should the referring agency timely make such a request, the SMA or CHIP agency would consider the request in its decision to maintain or terminate the payment suspension for that quarter. This approach would give the referring law enforcement agency a direct and time-limited mechanism to provide the least interference with a law enforcement investigation or prosecution. Where no law enforcement agency accepted the referral and the SMA or CHIP agency is conducting its own investigation, its quarterly written redetermination alone would satisfy this
(
printed page 74687)
requirement. Furthermore, should an SMA or CHIP agency be unable to make a finding that there remains an active investigation at any such redetermination, we propose that it must immediately terminate the suspension. We believe this would ensure payment suspensions remain time-limited and subject to meaningful review while protecting Medicaid and CHIP dollars.
We note that this redetermination and termination authority would rest with the SMA and CHIP agency, and that their conclusions could sometimes diverge from those of the agency or agencies that referred the credible allegation of fraud in the first place. We have observed that defendants in Federal matters have, in some instances, cited a State's decision to decline to impose or its decision to subsequently terminate a payment suspension following a credible allegation of fraud referral as evidence that their conduct was believed to be permissible, potentially undermining an ongoing Federal investigation or prosecution involving substantially the same conduct. We encourage coordination between the SMA or/and CHIP agency, and the referring agency before a payment suspension maintained on the basis of that agency's referral is terminated. This would not give the referring agency veto power over the redetermination of a payment suspension at an SMA or CHIP agency, but, instead, would ensure the referring agency would have notice and a meaningful opportunity to share relevant information. For example, a law enforcement agency could share that a matter remains under active investigation and that terminating a payment suspension could adversely affect a related enforcement proceeding.
4. Verifying Good Cause Exceptions to Payment Suspension Requirements
Sections 455.23(e) and (f) currently specify bases for good cause exceptions to payment suspensions. In our experience, good cause exceptions are often invoked when a MFCU or other law enforcement agency requests that a payment suspension not be imposed to prevent a provider from being made aware they are under investigation, which could jeopardize a civil or criminal case and possibly even the safety of the law enforcement officials conducting an investigation. Though that is a laudable and important goal, in recent years we have seen instances in which States seem to invoke good cause exceptions to avoid imposing payment suspensions for other reasons that do not meet the criteria outlined at § 455.23(e)(1). For example, CMS believes that some States may use the (e)(1) clause to avoid provider abrasion (that is, friction, frustration, and administrative stress) to retain providers within the State's Medicaid and/or CHIP network. Other States may want to avoid the administrative burden of implementing a payment suspension or the subsequent litigation risk inherent when payment is paused.
Data analysis bolsters our belief that States are over-relying on exercising § 455.23(e) and (f) payment suspension good cause exceptions. In CY 2025, for example, approximately 75 percent of credible allegation of fraud cases reported to CMS pursuant to State Medicaid payment suspension reporting requirements at § 455.23(g)(3) did not proceed to a payment suspension because an SMA invoked a good cause exception. Good cause exceptions have a legitimate place in payment suspension decision-making, but States should not use them as a blanket policy to reduce litigation risk or avoid their administrative responsibilities. Similarly, we encourage States to provide the most accurate good cause exception reasons and not solely rely—potentially inaccurately—on law enforcement exceptions. And while we expect variability among States, State-reported data revealed that several States had over 90 percent of their potential payment suspensions end with the exercise of a good cause exception, with some States exercising hundreds of good cause exceptions while instituting only a handful of payment suspensions. Such outlier scenarios potentially could be explained in very limited situations by events such as large law enforcement take-down operations in a State, but in no event should they, as we have seen, recur year-over-year. Instead, such patterns warrant our exercising additional oversight to ensure good cause exceptions are applied in accordance with regulatory requirements.
To address this concern, we propose to require additional verifications as to whether the exercise of a good cause exception is appropriate. Specifically, we propose to modify § 455.23(e) to require States to evaluate, and document in writing, that the specific criteria for the exception invoked have been met in each instance. Further, we propose to modify § 455.23(e)(1) to require States to verify the reasons for good cause exceptions with law enforcement and send CMS the basis for each invocation of a good cause exception. Good cause exceptions must be invoked on a case-by-case basis, and SMAs and CHIP agencies must affirmatively verify with the relevant law enforcement agency that the exception is warranted for each individual case. A general or standing request from a law enforcement agency would be insufficient to satisfy this requirement.
We would not intend for this provision, if finalized as proposed, to serve as a categorical bar to good cause exceptions in all cases involving an active law enforcement investigation, nor would we expect SMAs or CHIP agencies to receive or ask for confidential, privileged, or legally protected information from law enforcement. But we would expect the case-specific merits for a good cause exception to be reviewed, confirmed or denied, and communicated by the MFCU or other law enforcement agency to the SMA or CHIP agency. At a minimum, the shared Federal and State goals—and, we believe, universally shared goals—should be to ensure that fraudulent providers are not inappropriately paid, while being circumspect and prudent with exercising authorities to best ensure legitimate providers are not inadvertently ensnared.
5. Updating Payment Suspension Reporting Requirements
Under our current regulations at § 455.23(g)(3), States are required to annually report to CMS summary information on the State's payment suspensions, including the nature of the suspected fraud, the basis for suspension, and the outcome of the suspension. In the 2011 regulation update of the Medicaid payment suspension regulations, we contemplated balancing SMA burden and transparency as they determine whether to implement payment suspensions. At that time, we did not believe it would be necessary to review information on individual payment suspensions by a State with any regularity, and that an annual cadence would allow sufficient oversight over States' payment suspension activities. As discussed previously, however, we have observed over the past several years significant inconsistencies between States, and sometimes within each State over time, in payment suspension utilization. We understand and expect a degree of variability among States as this is a State-implemented program and States vary in program integrity risk profiles, but also expect a consistent level of due diligence in ensuring payments are made appropriately and that inappropriate payments are avoided. Important in that calculus, technological advancements
(
printed page 74688)
over the past decade—including greatly improved data analytics yielding the ability to act on data in near-real time—have altered how businesses and governments run and make more regular reporting more feasible without commensurate burden.
We therefore propose to update § 455.23(g) reporting requirements to increase the reporting cadence from annual to quarterly, and to remove the word “summary” from the description of information to accommodate the increased detail that States would need to report to CMS. As we encourage States to appropriately utilize payment suspensions to halt potentially fraudulent payments, we strive for closer-to-real-time data and analytics on how those decisions are being made. As part of our oversight duties, if finalized as proposed, we would utilize this data to foster deeper discussions within SMAs and CHIP agencies on potential payment suspensions, and provide technical assistance and guidance, when requested or needed. We believe that more frequent reporting of payment suspension data would help States use this tool more effectively and obtain the necessary guidance from CMS.
We also believe that more frequent reporting would enable CMS to compile and analyze program-wide data on payment suspension activity within and across States more effectively. This information would be used to identify systemic trends and patterns in the use of payment suspensions as a program integrity tool. Similar to how we use the data today, should our proposals be finalized as proposed, we would use this data to assess whether States are maintaining effective processes for evaluating credible allegations of fraud and making timely suspension decisions consistent with the proposed updates in §§ 455.23 and 457.935(b)(8), to inform CMS' State auditing activities, and to support aggregate reporting on Medicaid and CHIP program integrity outcomes. More frequent State reporting would also enable CMS to provide States more timely technical assistance to address any inconsistencies or other concerns.
We do not believe that more frequent reporting of this information would be substantially more burdensome to States than their current data sharing. For example, much of the data that States currently share annually with CMS already is shared quarterly, and perhaps even more frequently, between SMAs and their MFCUs through States' existing case tracking systems. In fact, § 1007.9(h) already requires MFCUs to send certain information regarding payment suspensions to SMAs, which the SMA must request quarterly per § 455.23(d)(3)(ii). Accordingly, we believe that any additional burden on States to supply such information to CMS would be nearly negligible. Similarly, while we expect that the shift to quarterly reporting would modestly increase CMS' administrative burden, we believe this increase would be negligible relative to our existing oversight infrastructure and be offset by the program integrity benefits of more timely reporting.
The proposed enhanced reporting requirements would not be intended to enable CMS to substitute its judgment for that of the State in individual cases, nor would they expand CMS' authority by permitting enforcement action based solely on disagreement with a State's individual suspension determination. Rather, CMS would use the reporting data to identify potential systemic deficiencies in a State's program integrity processes, which then could be examined through additional oversight activities, such as audits, and addressed through technical assistance or existing enforcement mechanisms, including deferral and disallowance of Federal Financial Participation (FFP) under §§ 430.40, 430.42, and 457.628(a), where appropriate.
We also propose a technical edit to update the title of § 455.23(g) to include reporting, to more accurately reflect all the subparagraphs.
6. Applicability to CHIP
Current regulations at § 438.608(a)(8) require that Medicaid managed care contracts include a provision for the suspension of payments to a network provider when the State determines there is a credible allegation of fraud, in accordance with § 455.23. Through the cross-reference at § 457.1285, we note that the requirements in § 455.23 are already applicable to CHIP managed care organizations (MCOs), prepaid inpatient health plans (PIHPs), and prepaid ambulatory health plans (PAHPs). Accordingly, any finalized provisions to § 455.23 would also apply to CHIP MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs.
However, we are concerned that the existing regulatory framework does not fully address payment suspensions in the CHIP fee-for-service (FFS) context. We therefore propose to update § 457.935(b) to include a cross-reference to § 455.23. This change would ensure that standalone CHIP programs would be held to the same standards as Medicaid MCOs, PIHPs, PAHPs, and FFS. We believe that including the cross-reference to § 455.23 would close potential program integrity gaps in the CHIP program and support stronger, more consistent program administration.
We seek comments on whether the proposed update to § 457.935(b) and current cross-references to § 455.23 provide sufficient clarity regarding the applicability of payment suspension requirements to CHIP. We also seek comments on whether additional regulatory text or cross-references would be needed to ensure that State CHIP agencies and their managed care partners have clear and actionable guidance on implementing these requirements.
C. Enhanced Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) Requirements
Personal care services (PCS) and home health care services (HHCS) that are delivered during an in-home visit are particularly vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse due to the limited direct oversight of services furnished in beneficiaries' homes. PCS are services that support beneficiaries with Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs) and generally include, but are not limited to, meal preparation, grooming, dressing, and bathing.
[
8 9
]
PCS can be agency-based or self-directed. Under agency-based models, a personal care agency provides oversight, management, and supervision of a beneficiary's PCS. By contrast, self-directed PCS allows individuals, or their representatives, to exercise decision-making authority in the planning, accessing, managing, and purchasing of their PCS with available necessary supports and subject to applicable State oversight requirements, including, as applicable, the requirements specified at §§ 441.464 and 441.585(a).
[
10
]
Regardless of the PCS delivery model, the SMA is responsible for monitoring the quality of services.
PCS fraud and abuse schemes have been well documented in Federal oversight actions and prosecutions. Common PCS fraud and abuse schemes include personal care attendants (PCAs) billing for services not rendered, billing for excessive units, and billing for medically unnecessary services. In FY 2025, MFCUs reported 326 PCA fraud convictions, significantly higher than any other provider type.
[
11
]
PCS fraud and abuse leaves beneficiaries at risk for harm and neglect, and in severe cases
(
printed page 74689)
has resulted in hospitalizations and deaths.
HHCS include, at a minimum, nursing services; home health aide services; and medical supplies, equipment, and appliances. At a State's option, HHCS can include physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech pathology and audiology services. HHCS is a mandatory State plan benefit for specified individuals under section 1902(a)(10)(D) of the Act and is described in section 1905(a)(7) of the Act. Under specific circumstances, HHCS may also be provided under a waiver of the plan. HHCS are generally susceptible to many of the same fraud and abuse schemes as PCS, including but not limited to providers billing for services not rendered, excessive units, or medically unnecessary services, and services provided by unqualified providers.

12

Like PCS, HHCS fraud and abuse can result in significant harm to beneficiaries.
In CY 2023, home and community-based services (HCBS) accounted for 63.8 percent of total Medicaid long-term services and supports (LTSS) expenditures.
[
13
]
Individuals who receive HCBS have significantly lower average expenditures than individuals who receive institutional care, but PCS and HHCS represent a substantial and growing share of HBCS spending.
[
14
]
Of the $145.9 billion in total HCBS expenditures in 2023, PCS spending totaled at least $36.1 billion and HHCS at least $6.9 billion.
[
15

When utilized and delivered appropriately, these services provide important supports that allow individuals to remain in home and community settings. However, they also present unique program integrity challenges because services are furnished in locations allowing for limited, if any, direct oversight.
EVV is a system used for in-home services, including PCS and HHCS, to electronically verify the service type, service recipient, date, location, provider, and service start and end time. Congress enacted EVV requirements in section 12006(a) of the 21st Century Cures Act, which added section 1903(l) of the Act, requiring States to implement an EVV system for Medicaid PCS and HHCS requiring an in-home visit by a provider. The requirements were established, in part, to reduce fraud, waste, and abuse in PCS and HHCS by increasing States' ability to validate that services are provided and monitor the accuracy of payments to providers.
[
16
]

[
17

[
18

Section 1903(l) of the Act does not require States to use a particular type of EVV system, affording States significant discretion in their EVV design and operation. There is also no statutory requirement for States to use global positioning system (GPS) data with respect to their EVV systems, and States are required only to collect the location of service delivery and the time the service begins and ends. States may, however, elect to collect additional information to mitigate fraud, waste, and abuse.
[
19

[

Although CMS has published guidance on how States can use EVV to enhance quality monitoring and oversight of Medicaid services,

In this proposed rule, we propose two related but distinct regulatory changes to require SMAs to use collected EVV data for program integrity and payment oversight. First, we propose to amend § 455.14 to require that SMAs incorporate a review of EVV records as part of preliminary investigations into potential Medicaid fraud or abuse involving in-home service providers subject to EVV requirements in a State. Accordingly, this requirement would apply to Medicaid providers furnishing services subject to Federal EVV requirements, as well as those subject to State

Second, we propose to amend § 447.45(f)(1) to require that SMAs verify that billed Medicaid services are supported by EVV records, where applicable under Federal or State requirements, during prepayment claims review. Together, these proposals are intended to maximize States' existing EVV systems for improved program integrity oversight and better position States to crush Medicaid fraud and abuse within high-risk services.
1. Use of EVV Data in Preliminary Investigations
In accordance with § 455.14, when a SMA receives a complaint of potential Medicaid fraud or abuse from any source or identifies any questionable practices, it must conduct a preliminary investigation to determine whether the complaint warrants a full investigation. States currently have broad flexibility in establishing procedures for preliminary investigations, including for those investigations conducted by managed care plans.
[
25

When a State receives an allegation or complaint of potential Medicaid fraud, the State should review all allegations, facts, and evidence carefully to determine their validity; act on a case-by-case basis; and consider the totality of the facts and circumstances associated with any allegation.
[
26

In accordance with § 455.15, should a State believe that an incident of provider fraud or abuse has occurred based on the findings of a preliminary investigation, it is required to refer the case of suspected fraud or abuse to the State's MFCU for investigation, except in limited cases where no referral to the MFCU is required, in which case the State must conduct a full investigation or refer the case to the appropriate law enforcement agency.
[
27 28

[

We propose to amend § 455.14 to require that SMAs incorporate a review of EVV records, where EVV use is required with respect to the underlying Medicaid service(s) in question under applicable Federal or State requirements, as part of preliminary investigations into potential Medicaid fraud or abuse. Specifically, we propose at new § 455.14(a)(1) that States be required to review and analyze the associated EVV records to attempt to verify the validity of an allegation of fraud or abuse or any identified questionable practice(s). This requirement would apply to any preliminary investigations of allegations of Medicaid fraud or abuse involving Medicaid services subject to EVV requirements under Federal or State requirements and the related providers suspected of such fraud or abuse.
The primary goal of this proposal would be to ensure that SMAs analyze and compare EVV records and claims to identify any discrepancies that warrant further investigation of providers subject to EVV requirements with fraud or abuse allegations or identified questionable practices. For example, during a preliminary investigation of an applicable provider, the SMA would be expected to review a sample of the provider's EVV records for the period under investigation to attempt to verify that services were delivered as billed, including for the appropriate duration and at the appropriate location, or determine if a full investigation pursuant to § 455.15 was warranted. This proposal seeks to enhance State identification and oversight of fraudulent and abusive activities by in-home service providers, including billing simultaneously for two beneficiaries in different locations, billing for improbably large volumes of services, and billing for services on the same day that would be geographically impossible to perform.

2. EVV Data in Prepayment Claims Review
Section 1902(a)(37)(B) of the Act requires States to have procedures for prepayment and post-payment claims review to ensure the proper and efficient payment of claims and management of the program. Regulations at
42 CFR 447.45
implement this statutory requirement. In accordance with § 447.45(f)(1), SMAs are currently required to conduct prepayment reviews for all claims consisting of: (1) verification of beneficiary and provider eligibility; (2) checks that services delivered are consistent with beneficiary characteristics and circumstances; (3) verification that the claim does not duplicate or conflict with other claims; (4) verification that payment does not exceed State plan payment rates or limits; and (5) checks for third party liability.
We propose to amend § 447.45 by adding § 447.45(f)(1)(vi) to require that SMAs verify, during prepayment review, that billed in-home Medicaid services subject to Federal or State EVV requirements are supported by an EVV record, where applicable. Specifically, we propose that for home-based services subject to the requirements of section 1903(l) of the Act, and additional Medicaid services that the State independently subjects to EVV requirements, States verify during prepayment claims review that the following data elements are supported by an EVV record: (1) the type of service performed; (2) the individual receiving the service; (3) the date of service; (4) the location of service delivery; (5) the individual providing the service; and (6) the time the service begins and ends.
With this proposal to require that States use EVV data to verify applicable service claims during prepayment review prior to payment, we aim to encourage States to begin applying automated prepayment claims edits that take into consideration EVV data to stop inappropriate payments on the front-end, an approach we have long labeled “cost avoidance” and that is far more effective than “pay and chase.” We believe this proposal, if finalized as proposed, would ensure States address Medicaid fraud in some of the highest risk services areas using technology, data analytics, and automated systems. We also believe this proposal is consistent with States' existing obligations under section 1902(a)(37) of the Act to maintain procedures for prepayment claims review to ensure the proper and efficient payment of claims. We also note that this proposal would
(

complement our proposed amendment to § 455.14 described earlier in this proposed rule, as well as our proposal to require consistent use of NPIs for eligible Medicaid providers described in section E of this proposed rule. Together, these proposals, if finalized as proposed, would create a more integrated and effective framework for program integrity oversight of home-based services.
CMS would not condition claiming for FFP for EVV-required services on compliance with this provision. However, evidence of noncompliance (for example, as identified in a CMS audit) could cause CMS to reassess a State's compliance determination related to Section 1903(l) of the Act (as added by Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act), which could result in FMAP reductions until compliance was achieved. Under section 1903(l) of the Act, States were required to attest that EVV use was required for all Medicaid-funded PCS (for calendar quarters beginning in 2020) and HHCS (for calendar quarters beginning in 2023) or otherwise be subject to FMAP reductions up to 1 percent. Although section 1903(l) does not specifically require EVV as a prepayment condition, substantive evidence that a State's claims for EVV-required services were not supported by EVV records could indicate that the State was not sufficiently requiring EVV use for those services. Similarly, CMS could take compliance with this provision into account during the certification process for States requesting enhanced FFP for their EVV systems.

Additionally, we acknowledge that, because the prepayment and post-payment review requirements in § 447.45 do not apply to risk-based managed care plans (as there is no cross-reference to § 447.45(f) in § 447.46(c)), the proposals in this section would only apply to Medicaid FFS; however, we are considering extending this proposed requirement to Medicaid managed care as a part of this rulemaking and explicitly seek comments on this approach. Applying this proposed requirement to managed care would necessarily require first extending the established prepayment and post-payment claims review requirements at § 447.45(f) to MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs.
