To ensure States have more complete address information, sections 71103(a)(2)(B) and 71103(b)(2) of the WFTC legislation amend sections 1932 and 2103(f)(3) of the Act, respectively, to require that, beginning January 1, 2027, each contract under a State plan that a State has with MCOs, primary care case managers (PCCMs), PIHPs, or PAHPs include a provision requiring the entity or plan to promptly transmit to the State any address information received directly from enrollees or verified by the entity or plan directly with the enrollee.
Also, effective January 1, 2027, section 71104 of the WFTC legislation requires that States and the District of Columbia, but not territories, screen all Medicaid enrollees against the Death Master File (DMF) (or a successor system) no less than quarterly to determine whether Medicaid enrollees are deceased. States will be required to treat such information as factual, disenroll deceased beneficiaries with notice of fair hearing rights provided no later than the date of action consistent with
42 CFR part 431 subpart E
, and discontinue any payments for medical assistance on the individual's behalf. Prior to the provisions of the WFTC legislation becoming effective on January 1, 2027, pursuant to eligibility verification regulations at §§ 435.945 and 435.952, SMAs are prohibited from acting on DMF data alone and must seek to independently verify a beneficiary's death prior to disenrollment. Once verified, an SMA can terminate coverage immediately, but not retroactively to the date of death and not for items or services furnished prior to death. Section 71104 of the WFTC legislation removes the requirement for additional verification beyond the DMF effective January 1, 2027; however, if an SMA determines that an individual was misidentified as deceased, the SMAs must reenroll the individual immediately and reinstate coverage retroactive to the date of disenrollment.
2. Proposed Policies
a. Standard Contract Requirements Relating to Capitation Payments Retention
Authority for the contracting requirements at § 438.3 is based on section 1903(m)(2)(A)(iii) of the Act (for MCOs) and section 1902(a)(4) of the Act (for PIHPs and PAHPs). Section 1903(m)(2)(A)(iii) of the Act permits Federal matching dollars for State expenditures to a risk-bearing entity for Medicaid services when “such services are provided for the benefit of individuals eligible for benefits under this title in accordance with a contract between the State and the entity under which the prepaid payments to the entity are made on an actuarially sound basis and under which the Secretary must provide prior approval for contracts.” We are proposing to amend § 438.3(c)(2) to retain the requirement that capitation payments may only be made by States and retained by MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs for Medicaid-eligible enrollees, while adding provisions that would permit States to recover capitation payments made for certain periods following an individuals' death or out-of-State relocation. We propose to add § 438.3(c)(2)(i) providing that, following the provision of notice of action with fair hearing rights in accordance with §§ 435.917 and 435.918 and part 431 subpart E, a State must recover capitation payments from MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs for any payment periods following the death of an enrollee when verified through the DMF, and may recover capitation payments from MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs for any payment periods following the date of out-of-State relocation of an individual. We note that these recovery actions would be limited to financial transactions between the State and the managed care plan and would not create any liability for Medicaid beneficiaries. At § 438.3(c)(2)(ii), we propose to add that States would be required to reimburse CMS an amount equal to the Federal share of all capitation payments subject to recovery described in proposed § 438.3(c)(2)(i), taking into account applicable differences in the Federal matching rate(s) applicable to the population, benefit, and Federal Fiscal Year. We note that under § 438.3(c)(2)(ii) States would be required to return the Federal share of capitation payments for any payment periods following the enrollee's death or date of relocation regardless of whether the State elects to recover or require the plan to return the capitation payment. The CHIP regulations at §§ 457.1201(c) and 457.1285 require CHIP managed care plans to comply with all Medicaid managed care rules established within § 438.3(c); therefore, the proposed changes to § 438.3(c)(2), if finalized, would apply to CHIP managed care plans.
This proposal would ensure that States have clear authority to recover capitation payments attributed to individuals who are deceased or who have relocated out-of-State, while the contractual provisions would establish the operational mechanism for implementing those recoveries, regardless of when the State ultimately terminated Medicaid eligibility. This proposal would make clear that existing notice, fair hearing, and eligibility-redetermination requirements would continue to apply before a State may terminate coverage and initiate capitation payment recovery from a managed care plan. As such, States would have to continue to redetermine eligibility in accordance with requirements at §§ 435.916(d) and 457.343, consider all bases of eligibility before making a determination of ineligibility as required by § 435.916(f), and furnish benefits until the individual is found to be ineligible for Medicaid and provided advance notice, as applicable, as described in §§ 431.211 and 435.930(b). Following completion of notice of action with fair hearing rights and termination of coverage,
(
printed page 74712)
States would initiate recovery actions from the applicable managed care plan.
Since the 2016 Managed Care final rule, most States have included sufficiently robust contract language to adequately recover capitation payments associated with deceased individuals, but some States have shared with us that they experience challenges recovering capitation payments from managed care plans for enrollees who have relocated out-of-State. When an enrollee has relocated out-of-State, and the State makes a determination of ineligibility and disenrolls the individual after providing advance notice, covered services under the managed care plan's contract should no longer be available to the enrollee because the enrollee is no longer eligible for Medicaid within the original State. Similarly, associated capitation payments would not be consistent with the requirement that capitation rates reflect reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs under the contract (§ 438.4(a)) because a State may only make payment to a managed care plan for “covered services to Medicaid-eligible individuals in a manner compliant with contractual requirements” (§ 438.3(c)(1)(ii)). Therefore, a payment made for an ineligible enrollee would not be compliant with the contract between the State and the managed care plan. While most SMAs recover capitation overpayments from plans when they are identified, some SMAs are unable to recover such payments because of insufficiently robust managed care contract language.
These challenges are largely related to an inability to identify a date on which to base the recovery. Unlike a date of death, which is recorded in national or State-based sources, such as the Social Security Administration's DMF or States' Departments of Vital Statistics, residential address changes are not routinely tracked and reported. PARIS alerts notify States when a beneficiary has relocated to another State by matching certain State and Federal data, but such alerts are generated quarterly and only if the individual interacts with certain entities in that new State such as the SMA or the Department of Motor Vehicles. In addition, States have reported challenges using PARIS because they may receive a high volume of false positive alerts,
[
97
]
the alerts may be based on delayed data,
[
98
]
or the PARIS system does not retain accessible historical data. All SMAs are required to conduct PARIS data matches, but data matching agreements do not prescribe which of the three PARIS matches (the Veterans Administration Match, Department of Defense/Office of Personnel Management Match, and the Interstate Match) SMAs must conduct, nor the frequency with which any match must be conducted.
[
99
]
Prior to initiating capitation payment recoveries based on an out-of-State relocation, States must first define feasible policies and procedures within their managed care contracts for how they will identify when an out-of-State residential change occurs, what documentation sources can be used to establish a relocation date, and how they will resolve cases of disputed residency. The “date of out-of-State relocation” means the date the State determines, consistent with § 435.403 and applicable State residency requirements that the individual ceased to be a resident of the State. States would also need to include clear terms in their managed care contracts that would define how they would determine which capitation payments would be subject to recovery in instances where individuals would not report the timing of their relocation. Further, these policies should align with the Federal requirements regarding State residency at § 435.403(d), and any applicable State-based residency requirements.
SMAs must treat these types of recoveries like all other recovered overpayments resulting from situations other than fraud as outlined generally at § 433.300, which is to refund all recoveries, including ones relating to changes in circumstance, to CMS within 1 year from the date of discovery.
We believe adding a new paragraph (i) to § 438.3(c)(2) within the standard contract requirements provisions would clarify States' obligation to recover capitation payments for any payment periods following a beneficiary's date of death and States' ability to recover capitation payments for any payment periods following the date of out-of-State relocation—after making a determination of ineligibility and the provision of notice of action with fair hearing rights—and would ensure that SMAs update their managed care contract terms to clearly specify their intent to recover inappropriate capitation payments. We invite comment on these proposals.
b. Prompt Reporting of Beneficiary Changes in Circumstances (§ 438.608(a)(3))
The provision added by the 2016 Managed Care final rule at § 438.608(a)(3) did not define “prompt” reporting or specify how changes should be reported, and we subsequently observed considerable variation in how States implemented the regulation. To ensure uniformity, we propose to amend § 438.608(a)(3) to require that Medicaid and CHIP managed care plans and Primary Care Case Management (PCCMs) report to a State changes in an enrollee's circumstances (specifically including enrollee deaths and all verified address changes) within 30 calendar days of when a plan receives information about a change that may affect the enrollee's eligibility for or access to services covered under the contract. We also propose to amend § 438.608(a)(3)(i) to require managed care plans and PCCMs to report residence changes if provided by the enrollee or verified directly with the enrollee, including both out-of-State and in-State address changes, which would protect from improper disenrollment. In the 2016 Final Rule, we finalized “§ 438.608(a)(3) so that managed care plans
would
notify the State of changes in the enrollee's residence and death,” in an effort to not trigger a required notification by the managed care plan when returned mail is received because the administrative burden on States outweighed the value.
[
100
]
At the same time, we acknowledged that managed care plans “have more direct communication with enrollees than the State and can serve as valuable sources of information relevant to the enrollee's eligibility for Medicaid.”
[
101
]
In the decade since the 2016 Final Rule, managed care plans have expanded communication from mail and telephone to text messages, email, and member portals and mobile applications. With these additional means of communication, managed care plans and PCCMs are in a better position to verify changes in residence with less burden than the State, thus making notification to the State of the verified change in residence beneficial without being overly burdensome.
The proposed change to § 438.608(a)(3) would also implement sections 71103(a)(2)(B) and 71103(b)(2)
(
printed page 74713)
of the WFTC legislation, which mandates that States include a provision in their managed care plan and PCCM contracts that requires managed care plans to promptly transmit to the State any address information for Medicaid and CHIP enrollees that is provided to the managed care plan or PCCM directly from, or that the managed care plan or PCCM verified directly with, the enrollee. We propose to amend § 438.608(a)(3) to define this prompt-transmission requirement as requiring transmission within 30 calendar days of when a managed care plan or PCCM receives information about a change in an enrollee's circumstances, which would add clarity and consistency to the implementation of the provisions in section 71103. The CHIP regulations at §§ 457.1201(c) and 457.1285 already require CHIP managed care plans to comply with all Medicaid managed care rules established within §§ 438.3(c) and 438.608, respectively; therefore, no additional regulatory changes would be necessary to implement such changes within CHIP.
In addition, we are proposing to revise § 438.608(a)(3) to require SMAs to define the procedures for prompt notification to the State when changes in an enrollee's circumstances are to be reported, which would ensure that managed care plans and PCCMs report such changes consistently to the appropriate contacts within the SMA or delegated entity. We believe that establishing a uniform timeframe of 30 calendar days would adequately position States and managed care plans and PCCMs to comply with section 71103(a)(2)(B) and 71103(b)(2) of the WFTC legislation, which requires States to include within the managed care contract a requirement that the MCOs, PIHPs, PAHPs, and PCCMs promptly transmit verified address information for enrollees. When a State receives information indicating an enrollee may have moved out-of-State through this process, it must treat such information as a potential change in circumstances and promptly redetermine eligibility in accordance with §§ 435.916(d), 457.343, and 435.952(d). We believe 30 calendar days is a reasonable amount of time for a managed care plan or PCCM to transmit any new address information to the State and would allow States to initiate timely redetermination procedures and potentially prevent transmitting to managed care plans and PCCMs inappropriate capitation payments for enrollees who have a change that may affect their eligibility, or to facilitate enrollment into a new plan for enrollees who continue to be State residents but have moved out of their current plan's service area. However, we are seeking comments on whether 30 calendar days is an appropriate length of time or if the time period should be increased or decreased. In addition, we interpret section 71103(a)(2)(B) of the WFTC legislation's use of “promptly” to apply this reporting rule to enrollees with new address information that differs from prior address information, and we would encourage States to leverage their experience from unwinding the Medicaid continuous enrollment provision at the end of the COVID-19 PHE to inform the development of these procedures and protocols.
Prompt reporting of an enrollee's death by managed care plans would also support provisions included within section 71104 of the WFTC legislation. Beginning January 1, 2027, section 71104 of the WFTC legislation requires States on at least a quarterly basis to review the DMF, or a successor system that provides beneficiary death data, and disenroll any deceased beneficiaries. The WFTC legislation also requires that States reinstate Medicaid coverage for a beneficiary who was erroneously disenrolled. We believe that managed care plans may learn of potential deaths or erroneous disenrollments before State or Federal entities. However, Section 71104 of the WFTC does not permit States to treat death information from managed care plans as factual, and States will still be required to verify beneficiary death consistent with §  435.952(d).
Section 438.608(a)(3) currently requires States to require managed care plans' prompt reporting to them when the managed care plan receives information about changes in an enrollee's circumstances that may affect the enrollee's eligibility, including change of address and death. We believe that adding a 30-calendar-day timeframe to report out-of-State moves and deceased beneficiary status would strengthen existing requirements and enhance program integrity and eligibility verification in Medicaid.
We propose that these revisions would be applicable for rating periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027. We believe this would also provide sufficient opportunity for States to include these new reporting requirements and recovery provisions in their new or renewed managed care contracts. We invite comment on these proposals.
c. Standard Contract Requirements Relating to Overpayments
We also propose to revise § 438.608(d)(1)(iv) to clarify that the overpayment retention policies specified under § 438.608(d)(1) do not apply to amounts recovered and retained under the False Claims Act or through other Federal or State audits or investigations, including those conducted by Federal agencies, such as CMS, or their contractors. This clarification is intended to ensure that recoveries resulting from fraud, waste, or abuse audits and investigations are treated consistently with existing authorities governing such actions and are not subject to duplicative recovery or return requirements under this section. As stated in the 2016 final rule, “[a]lthough States have the flexibility to implement overpayment retention contract provisions, the policies in the contract would not prohibit the Federal government from retaining the appropriate share of recoveries of overpayments due to their own audits and investigations”.

M. Request for Information on Payment Deductions Under
42 CFR 447.10(i)
CMS is issuing this request for information (RFI) to solicit public input on strengthening consent, documentation, and recordkeeping requirements related to payment deductions made under
42 CFR 447.10(i)
. This regulation governs deductions from certain Medicaid provider payments to make payments to third-parties, including labor unions, on behalf of the provider. CMS is concerned that existing State practices for obtaining and documenting practitioner consent to such deductions may be insufficient to protect practitioners' First Amendment rights and the financial integrity of the Medicaid program. CMS is also considering how to implement a related statutory prohibition enacted under section 71121 of
Pub. L 119-21
, the WFTC legislation. The information received in response to this RFI could inform potential future agency action.
1. Background
Section 1902(a)(32) of the Act generally prohibits Medicaid payment for care or services furnished to an individual to anyone other than the individual or the provider furnishing the care or services, unless a statutory exception applies. CMS' implementing regulation at § 447.10 identifies the
(
printed page 74714)
persons to whom State Medicaid payments may be made and the limited circumstances under which payment may be made to others.
Under CMS' current interpretation of section 1902(a)(32) of the Act, as established in a 2022 final rule
[
103
]
and pursuant to regulations at §  447.10(i), the payment prohibition in section 1902(a)(32) of the Act does not apply to State payments to third-parties on behalf of individual practitioners for those individual practitioners' health insurance and welfare benefits, skills training, and other benefits customary for employees, in the case of a class of practitioners for which the Medicaid program is the primary source of revenue, if the individual practitioner voluntarily consents to such payments on their behalf.
The preamble to the 2022 final rule noted that “most commenters stated support for the 2021 proposed rule.”
See
87 FR 29675
,
29679
(May 16, 2022). But, at the same time, the 2022 final rule also noted that, in response to the 2021 proposed rule,
[
104
]
some commenters expressed concerns about bad actors and questionable practices for diverting Medicaid money to unions without providers' express consent, as the agency noted and described in the 2022 final rule, and argued that the consent requirements in § 447.10(i) were insufficient to protect practitioners and the financial integrity of the Medicaid program.
See
87 FR at 29682-29683, 29686. Some commenters raised concerns about the potential for what they called the practice of “dues skimming,” in which a State automatically deducts union dues from a practitioner's Medicaid payment without the practitioner's affirmative consent.
Id.
at 29686. Some commenters cited
Harris
v.
Quinn,
573 U.S. 616 (2014), and
Janus
v.
American Federation of State, County, & Municipal Employees, Council 31,
585 U.S. 878 (2018), as examples supporting their view that such practices are impermissible and raise First Amendment concerns.
Id.
Some commenters further described specific practices they viewed as coercive or inconsistent with the consent standard articulated in
Janus,
including so-called “captive audience” meetings, high-pressure tactics associated with union enrollment, and limited ability to disenroll from the union.
Id.
Commenters also expressed concern that finalizing the rule could permit States to divert Medicaid payments to unions and political campaigns.
Id.
Despite these comments, at the time of the 2022 final rule, CMS believed the requirements at §  447.10(i), particularly the voluntary consent requirement, were sufficient from the Federal perspective and deferred to States to oversee and operationalize this requirement.
See, for example,
87 FR at 29682-29686, 29689. Specifically, we declined to prescribe in regulation a uniform method for obtaining or documenting consent, including a written consent requirement, out of concern that doing so could conflict with State law, and we deferred to States regarding which methods of obtaining and documenting consent are sufficient.
Id.
However, since the 2022 final rule took effect, CMS has received reports suggesting that these concerns have materialized in practice. In June 2026, CMS sent letters to nine SMAs reminding them of their obligations under § 447.10(i) and of the Supreme Court's holding in
Janus.
In those letters, CMS stated that deductions made without a practitioner's voluntary and affirmative consent are inconsistent with
Janus
and may violate § 447.10. CMS directed States to review their Medicaid payment arrangements involving union dues and requested documentation sufficient to allow CMS to assess compliance.
Although the Supreme Court has not reached the specific question, the First Amendment principles articulated in
Harris
and
Janus
would appear to apply to union deductions from Medicaid payments to homecare workers and would appear to bind States in that context independently of any Federal regulation. Assuming that our understanding of the decisions is correct in this regard, any rule CMS issues with respect to union dues deductions from Medicaid payments must be consistent with those decisions and States' existing constitutional obligations are not optional: that is to say that a State's deduction of union dues from a practitioner's Medicaid payment without the practitioner's clear and affirmative prior and voluntary consent is unconstitutional regardless of whether CMS' regulations separately require it.
We are concerned that current practices in some States may not reliably ensure that consent to the deduction of union dues is obtained in a manner free from coercion or pressure. We note that § 447.10(i) applies broadly to deductions for a range of benefits, not solely union dues, but CMS believes that in the context of union dues, greater regulatory specificity regarding consent, documentation, and recordkeeping may be warranted to ensure voluntary and verifiable consent from practitioners, consistent with applicable First Amendment principles, and to ensure consistent Federal oversight across States.
Separately, section 71121 of the WFTC legislation amended section 1915(c) of the Act by adding a new paragraph (11), which establishes a new HCBS waiver option, available to States beginning July 1, 2028, under which States may provide HCBS to individuals without requiring them to meet the institutional level-of-care requirement otherwise applicable under section 1915(c). Section 1915(c)(11)(C) of the Act provides that no payments made to carry out that paragraph may be used by a State to make payments to a third-party on behalf of an individual practitioner for benefits such as health insurance, skills training, and other benefits customary for employees, in the case of a class of practitioners for which the Medicaid program is the primary source of revenue. CMS is using this RFI, in part, to inform implementation of this statutory provision.
2. Issues for Public Input
CMS continues to receive reports from practitioners and other stakeholders raising concerns regarding compliance with § 447.10(i) and applicable First Amendment principles, including practitioners reporting that consent to union dues deductions was obtained as a condition of provider enrollment, and practitioners reporting difficulty withdrawing previously given consent. These reports, together with the responses to CMS' June 2026 compliance letters, raise questions regarding whether existing State oversight and implementation of § 447.10(i) consistently ensures compliance with the voluntary consent requirement.
CMS is concerned that deduction of union dues, or other third-party payment under § 447.10(i) may in some circumstances occur without the practitioner's voluntary consent. CMS is considering whether more prescriptive Federal requirements addressing how consent to such deductions must be obtained, documented, and maintained, and how States must demonstrate compliance to CMS, are necessary to ensure the financial integrity of the Medicaid program and to safeguard practitioners' constitutional rights, consistent with
Harris
and
Janus.
CMS is seeking additional information from States, practitioners, beneficiaries, unions, and other stakeholders to better understand current practices, the scope of the
(
printed page 74715)
potential problem, and the range of approaches that could address it, including in the context of consumer-directed service programs, where the beneficiary rather than a traditional employer may perform functions relevant to consent and payment.

IV. Medicare Advantage and Medicare Part D Proposals
The Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (BBA),
Pub. L. 105-33
, established a new Part C of the Medicare program, known then as the Medicare+Choice (M+C) program, which became effective in January 1999. As part of the M+C program, the BBA authorized CMS to contract with public or private organizations to offer a variety of health plan options for Medicare beneficiaries. These health plans provide all Medicare Part A and Part B (also known as “Original Medicare,” or “Medicare Fee-for-Service (FFS)”) benefits, and most offer additional benefits beyond those covered under the Medicare FFS program. The M+C program in Part C of Medicare was renamed the Medicare Advantage (MA) program under the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 (MMA) (
Pub. L. 108-173
), enacted in December 2003. The MMA updated and improved the choice of plans for beneficiaries under Part C and changed the way benefits are established and payments are made. As of calendar year 2025, over 34 million individuals receive their Medicare benefits through MA, which represents over half of the total Medicare beneficiary population.
[
105
]
(
printed page 74716)
The MMA also established the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit under Part D, which began providing prescription drug coverage to Medicare beneficiaries in 2006. The Part D program operates through private plan sponsors that contract with CMS, offering coverage either through stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) to supplement Original Medicare, or through Medicare Advantage prescription drug (MA-PD) plans that integrate drug coverage with all other Medicare-covered benefits. The original Part D benefit design included risk-abating mechanisms—including direct subsidy risk corridors, risk adjustment, and Federal reinsurance—enabling CMS to implement a market-based program that maintained affordable premiums over time and promoted high enrollee satisfaction. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) subsequently made significant structural changes to the Part D benefit, including establishing a hard cap on annual out-of-pocket spending and authorizing the Federal Government to negotiate certain drug prices directly with manufacturers, with those changes being phased in through 2026.
Program integrity is fundamental to the proper administration of both the Part C and Part D programs. While CMS has robust program integrity controls in place, bad actors continue to find the Medicare program a financially lucrative target and use creative tactics to evade detection and adverse consequences. Accordingly, the potential for fraud, waste, and abuse (FWA) is significant, making rigorous oversight of MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors, providers, and suppliers essential to protecting both the Medicare Trust Funds and the beneficiaries who depend on these programs. Compliance oversight of our partners is also important to ensure appropriate expenditures of taxpayer dollars. For example, CMS conducts ongoing oversight of MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors through audits, monitoring, data analysis, and other program integrity activities to ensure compliance with Federal requirements and identify program vulnerabilities. In accordance with
42 CFR 422.504(h)(1)
and
423.505(h)(1)
, MA organizations, Part D plan sponsors, and their employees, governing body members, and first-tier, downstream, and related entities agree to comply with Federal laws and regulations designed to prevent or ameliorate fraud, waste, and abuse. Through these oversight activities and its experience administering the Part C and Part D programs, CMS has identified opportunities to strengthen existing regulatory requirements to improve accountability and clarify program integrity standards.

B. Mandatory Reporting of Fraud, Waste, and Abuse
1. Introduction
All MA organizations (including MA organizations offering prescription drug plans (MA-PD plans)) and standalone Part D plan sponsors (collectively referred to herein as “plan sponsors”) are required to adopt and implement effective compliance programs to oversee provider networks, benefits, and payments. Compliance programs must include measures that prevent, detect, and correct non-compliance with CMS' program requirements, as well as measures that prevent, detect, and correct fraud, waste, and abuse.
[
106
]
As part of these requirements, plan sponsors must establish and implement procedures and systems for promptly responding to compliance issues as they are raised, investigating potential compliance problems as identified in the course of self-evaluations and audits, correcting such problems promptly and thoroughly to reduce the potential for recurrence, and ensuring ongoing compliance with CMS requirements.
An important part of plan sponsors' fraud, waste, and abuse initiatives involves sharing potential leads, trends,
(
printed page 74717)
or schemes resulting from the plan sponsors' own data analytics and investigative findings through referrals to CMS, which helps accomplish the following objectives:
Enables CMS to perform data analysis to identify fraud schemes;
Facilitates and increases transparency among CMS and plan sponsors through the exchange of information;
Provides information and education to plan sponsors on potential fraud, waste, and abuse issues, enabling plan sponsors to investigate and take action based on such data;
Improves fraud detection across the Medicare program, allowing for increased recovery of taxpayer dollars and enrollee expenditures (for example, premiums, co-insurance, other plan cost-sharing);
Provides more effective support, including fraud leads, to plan sponsors and law enforcement; and
Increases beneficiary safety through increased oversight measures.
In this proposed rule, CMS proposes to expand upon the existing requirements in sections 2008 and 6063 of the Substance Use Disorder Prevention that Promotes Opioid Recovery and Treatment for Patients and Communities (SUPPORT) Act that CMS previously addressed in the Contract Year 2022 Medicare Advantage and Part D Final Rule (referred to as the “January 2021 final rule” (CMS-4190-F2)). Beginning January 1, 2022, the requirements finalized in the January 2021 Final Rule allowed CMS and plan sponsors to share data and information regarding unscrupulous actors, take swift action based on such data and information, and achieve enhanced outcomes in our efforts to fight the opioid crisis. In addition, the January 2021 Final Rule paved the way for more effective referrals to law enforcement based on plan sponsor reporting, ultimately resulting in reduced beneficiary harm and greater savings for the Medicare program.
2. SUPPORT Act Sections 2008 and 6063
The SUPPORT Act was signed into law on October 24, 2018, and amended sections 1860D-12(b) and 1859 of the Act to alleviate the nationwide opioid crisis by: (1) reducing the abuse and supply of opioids; (2) helping individuals recover from opioid addiction and supporting the families of these persons; and (3) establishing innovative and long-term solutions to the crisis. Part of CMS' role in overseeing the Medicare program is to ensure that payments are made correctly and that fraud, waste, and abuse is stemmed; failing to do so endangers the Trust Funds and can result in harm to beneficiaries. For example, a practitioner engaging in abusive behavior by prescribing unnecessary opioids to Medicare patients poses a threat to the health and safety of the affected beneficiaries, and Trust Fund dollars paid for drugs that were not needed. As a result, several of the SUPPORT Act provisions addressed important program integrity and payment safeguard topics.
Sections 2008 and 6063 of the SUPPORT Act authorized plan sponsors to suspend payments to pharmacies based on credible allegations of fraud; required plan sponsors to report such payment suspensions to CMS through a secure program integrity portal; and clarified that a fraud hotline tip, without further evidence, does not constitute sufficient evidence of a credible allegation of fraud. The SUPPORT Act also required CMS to establish a secure program integrity portal to facilitate referrals and data sharing related to fraud, waste, and abuse among CMS, plan sponsors, and Medicare program integrity contractors; define, through rulemaking, substantiated or suspicious activities of fraud, waste, or abuse and inappropriate opioid prescribing; establish reporting requirements for plan sponsors related to fraud investigations and inappropriate opioid prescribing; and provide plan sponsors with regular program integrity information and fraud, waste, and abuse trend reports.

1. Introduction
a. General Overview of Risk Adjustment Payments in the MA Program
Section 1853(a)(1)(C) of the Act requires that CMS adjust payments made to MA organizations based on risk. Risk adjustment ensures that CMS is able to make appropriate and accurate payments for enrollees with differences in costs. Making accurate payments to MA organizations also ensures we are safeguarding Federal taxpayer dollars.
The risk adjustment model employed to adjust MA payments is known as the CMS Hierarchical Condition Category (CMS-HCC) model. This model functions by categorizing the International Classification of Disease, Clinical Modification (ICD-CM)
[
111
]
diagnosis codes into disease groups called Hierarchical Condition Categories, or HCCs. Each HCC includes diagnosis codes that are related clinically and have similar cost implications. MA enrollee HCCs are assigned based on data submitted to CMS by MA organizations. The HCCs contribute to an enrollee's risk score, which is used to adjust a base payment rate. Essentially, the higher the risk score for an enrollee, the higher the expected health care cost for the enrollee and the greater payment that is received by the MA organization.
The CMS-HCC model was first used for payment in 2004 and has been recalibrated numerous times since then. When CMS recalibrates the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model, it uses data from Medicare FFS claims, using diagnoses in one year to predict the following year's expenditures. Claims data from beneficiaries enrolled in the Medicare FFS program are used to calibrate the CMS-HCC model, which produces a set of coefficients that represent the marginal (additional) cost of each medical condition and demographic factor reported for a given beneficiary. (For additional information, see the Medicare Managed Care Manual, CMS Pub. 100-16, Chapter 7, section 70.1.)
[
112
]
These coefficients are then divided by the average predicted expenditure for the population, also known as the model denominator, to generate relative factors that reflect expected costs relative to the average cost FFS beneficiary. Each beneficiary's relative factors are added together to yield a risk score for that beneficiary that is used to adjust the base payment rate for that beneficiary.
For a diagnosis to be acceptable for risk adjustment, it must be from an acceptable provider type (that is, hospital inpatient facilities, hospital outpatient facilities, or physicians), coded in accordance with ICD-CM coding guidelines, result from a face-to-face visit, and be documented in a medical record, and MA organizations are required to ensure the accuracy and integrity of risk adjustment data submitted to CMS.
[
113
]
CMS uses diagnostic information submitted by MA organizations to calculate risk scores. MA organizations are required to submit data that is accurate, complete, and truthful to the best of their knowledge. CMS pays prospectively and issues final payment through a reconciliation run. As such, the diagnosis data the MA organizations submit do not undergo CMS validation prior to use for risk score calculation and payment. CMS validation audits occur post payment reconciliation. CMS conducts post-payment audits of MA organization-submitted diagnosis data from a selection of MA organizations for specific payment years to ensure that the diagnoses they submitted are supported by their enrollees' medical records. These audits are called contract-specific MA RADV program audits. While RADV audits are intended to identify improper risk adjustment payments, they are not specifically designed to detect fraud,
[
114
]
nor are they intended to identify all improper diagnosis submissions made by MA organizations for risk adjustment payment.
[
115
]
b. Purpose and Description of Contract-Specific RADV Audits
The improper payment measurements conducted each year by CMS that are included in the HHS Agency Financial Report, as well as audits conducted by the HHS-OIG, have demonstrated that the MA program is at high risk of improper payments. In Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 (based on calendar year 2023
(
printed page 74721)
payments), we estimated that CMS made over $21 billion in Part C overpayments, a figure representing over 5 percent of total Part C payments.
[
116
]
The HHS-OIG has also released several reports over the past few years that demonstrate a high risk of improper payments in the MA program,
[
117
]
and for several years has identified the MA program as one of the top management and performance challenges facing HHS due to the high amount of improper payments.
[
118
]
The Medicare program, including MA, has also been identified by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) as a high-risk program due to the risk of substantial improper payments and actions were needed to reduce these risks.
[
119
]
RADV audits are our main corrective action for overpayments made to MA organizations when there is a lack of documentation in the medical record to support the diagnoses reported for risk adjustment. We select MA organizations for RADV audits using a risk-based approach that focuses on HCCs that are more likely to be in error as identified by prior RADV audits, Part C Improper Payment Measurements, OIG findings, and other vulnerability analyses. RADV audits occur after the final risk adjustment data submission deadline for the MA contract year and after CMS calculates final payments, as described at § 422.310(g).
[
120
]
RADV audits are intended to confirm that risk adjustment conditions (that is, diagnoses that map to HCCs) reported by MA organizations are supported by medical record documentation. RADV audits confirm the presence of the diagnoses related to the enrollee's HCC profile through the review of medical records submitted by the MA organizations for the purpose of a RADV audit; specifically, medical records from hospital inpatient facilities, hospital outpatient facilities, and physicians/practitioners (excluding suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies). Risk adjustment discrepancies are identified when an enrollee's HCCs used for payment, which are based on MA organization self-reported data, differ from the HCCs assigned based on the medical record review performed by CMS through the RADV audit process. Risk adjustment discrepancies for sampled enrollees can then be aggregated to determine an average change in risk score as a result of RADV for sampled contract enrollees. The average change in risk score can be used to calculate an estimated total payment error amount for the larger universe of enrollees within an MA organization contract from which the sample is drawn, within specified confidence intervals using statistical extrapolation.
c. History of the Contract-Specific RADV Audits
RADV audits have existed in various forms and approaches for over 20 years. RADV audits began for payment year (PY) 1999, when the payment amounts made to MA organizations on a risk-adjusted basis were small (10 percent). During the period from PY 1999 until PY 2003, our RADV activity had an educational focus and was primarily intended to provide information that could be used by MA organizations to improve the accuracy of the risk adjustment data submitted to CMS for payment. Payment adjustments (recoveries) were limited to enrollee-level adjustments for those enrollees sampled in the audits and were not extrapolated to the overall contract. As a result, for the few MA contracts we audited, payment recovery amounts were small.
Risk adjustment payments using the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model began for the first time in PY 2004.
[
121
]
Because of various risk adjustment payment methodology changes required in the BBA and the Benefits Improvement and Protection Act of 2000 (BIPA) (
Pub. L. 106-554

(2) Informal Proposal Comments and the FFS Adjuster
In response to the December 2010 informal proposal, some MA organizations suggested that CMS could not lawfully enforce the requirement of medical record documentation for diagnosis codes while making payments at the published rates. These MA organizations stated that there is a difference in auditing standards between Medicare FFS and MA diagnosis data because, in contrast to the MA organization-submitted diagnoses data, Medicare FFS data is “unaudited” by CMS. This difference purportedly exists because most FFS payments are made on the basis of the item or service provided and not the beneficiary's diagnosis or diagnoses. For example, an office visit is paid based on whether the evaluation and management service billed met Medicare coverage and payment rules, not based on what diagnoses are listed on the claim or in the medical record. As a result, they stated, the Medicare FFS data used to calculate MA organization payments will understate the cost of treating various conditions and, because erroneous diagnoses in the FFS claims data are used to calibrate the MA payment model, CMS must either adjust payment rates (by raising them) or adjust documentation standards (by loosening them) to resolve the alleged incompatibility between the payment rates and documentation standards. This proposed adjustment to the MA organization payment rates and/or documentation standard was referred to as an “FFS Adjuster.”
These MA organizations ground their arguments in section 1853(a)(1)(C)(i) of the Act, which requires the Secretary to adjust payments to MA organizations for demographic and health related risk factors so as to ensure “actuarial equivalence.” As described previously, the Act requires that we calculate risk-adjusted payments to MA organizations to ensure that MA organizations are paid appropriately based on the enrollees' health status and demographic characteristics. The 2012 methodology included the following components:
Sampling Technique:
Under the 2012 methodology, up to 201 enrollees from each audited MA contract would be selected according to certain criteria. These criteria included, but were not limited to, the enrollees': (1) continuous

The RADV-eligible enrollees would then be ranked by risk score and divided into three equal strata (low risk score, average risk score, and high-risk score), with an equal number of enrollees randomly selected from each stratum (for example, 67 enrollees per stratum in the case of an audit of 201 enrollees).

After medical records were reviewed, payment errors would be calculated for each selected enrollee based on the number of months the person was enrolled in the selected MA contract (and was not in ESRD or hospice status) during the payment year. A payment error amount for each stratum would be calculated, which could include both RADV-identified overpayments and underpayments, and an overall payment error estimate for the audited contract would be derived, along with a 99 percent confidence interval around the payment error estimate.

2. Discussion of Proposals
a. Extrapolation of RADV Audit Findings
(1) Use of Extrapolation in the Medicare Program
Extrapolation, or the act of estimating a value (such as an overpayment amount for a Medicare provider) based on a statistically valid sample of units (such as Medicare claims), has historically been a standard part of auditing practice at CMS. There is significant guidance, including case law and best practices from HHS and other Federal agencies, stating that extrapolation may be utilized as a valid part of calculating improper payments. Courts have held that sampling and extrapolation is a valid method of calculating improper Medicare payments, so long as statistically valid methods are used.
See United States
v.
Lahey Clinic Hosp., Inc.,
399 F.3d 1, 18 n.19 (1st Cir. 2005) (noting that “sampling of similar claims and extrapolation from the sample is a recognized method of proof” for the United States in an affirmative case seeking recovery under a common-law theory);
see also Ratanasen
v.
California Dep't of Health Servs.,
11 F.3d 1467, 1469-71 (9th Cir. 1993) (collecting cases in which sampling and extrapolation have been approved in the Medicaid context, and “join[ing] other circuits in approving the use of sampling and extrapolation as part of audits in connection with Medicare and other similar programs”);
Chaves Cnty. Home Health Serv., Inc.
v.
Sullivan,
931 F.2d 914, 917-23 (D.C. Cir. 1991). The authority to use sampling and extrapolation in Medicare audits is grounded in our statutory and regulatory authority to audit providers and recoup improper payments.
See Chaves,
931 F.2d at 919 (interpreting the Medicare statute to allow for a “sample adjudication procedure” followed by extrapolation from that sample, which “is reasonable given the logistical imperatives recognized by courts in other comparable circumstances”).
Sampling and extrapolation have been used to calculate improper payments in Medicare FFS (Part A and Part B) for decades. CMS formally approved of this technique in 1986 (HCFA Ruling 86-1), but Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs), which are responsible for determining medical necessity and paying Medicare FFS claims, have been using it “at least since 1972.”
Chaves,
931 F.2d at 921;
see also id.
at 913 (explaining that “sample adjudication has been used in previous instances involving post-payment review of `coverage determinations' under Part A,” and that HCFA Ruling 86-1 “simply reiterated [the agency's] belief that it had the latitude to employ sample audits on post-payment review to efficiently recoup overpayments for non-covered services”). Medicare contractors currently use established sampling and extrapolation techniques when determining overpayments in accordance with Chapter 8 of the Medicare Program Integrity Manual. In 1991, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, in
Chaves,
upheld the use of this audit methodology against arguments that the Medicare statute required individualized review of claims submitted by providers.
Id.
at 922.
The MMA imposed limits on the use of sampling and extrapolation in Medicare payment decisions in the context of Part A and Part B. Since 2003, Medicare Part A and Part B extrapolation under section 1893(f)(3) of the Act has been limited to instances in which the Secretary determines either that “there is a sustained or high level of payment error” or that “documented educational intervention has failed to correct the payment error.” No similar limitation applies to the MA program, and CMS announced its intention to use extrapolation in RADV audits in the 2012 notice.
As previously discussed, sampling and extrapolation is a generally accepted audit technique in the Medicare context, and the Act does not apply any limits to the use of extrapolation in the MA program. Therefore, we believe that CMS has the authority to implement this audit methodology in RADV audits for any case in which a RADV audit identifies
(
printed page 74724)
unsupported medical diagnoses resulting in improper risk-adjusted payments. We further believe that extrapolation is a reasonable approach to our RADV audits, given the sustained and high level of risk adjustment payment errors, as previously described, and volume of diagnosis data submitted by MA organizations.
(2) Extrapolation Proposal
CMS proposes extrapolating contract-specific RADV audit findings using statistically valid random sampling techniques. Given the volume of diagnosis data submitted by MA organizations, amount of improper payments identified under the MA program, interest in determining an accurate recovery amount for each audited MA plan, and importance of protecting the overall integrity of the program, we believe that it is in the public interest for CMS to apply extrapolation to PY 2018 and all subsequent years. Implementation of extrapolation and the other audit methodologies in this proposed rule will allow CMS to act in compliance with the improper payment obligations under the Act (most recently updated as part of the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA),
Pub. L. 116-117
, 134 Stat. 113 (2020)), as well as our fiduciary responsibility to recover funds due to the Medicare Trust Funds.
CMS proposes to employ statistical methods to determine statistically valid sample sizes, accurately identify payment error, and extrapolate to the universe of enrollees from which the sample is selected. These statistically valid methods may include applying one or more RADV audit methodologies for any given RADV audit. In addition, while CMS views extrapolation as a statistically valid methodology for RADV audits, the agency may, at times, use its discretion to not utilize extrapolation in a particular instance. For example, there may be unforeseen circumstances in which the statistical validity of the sample is disturbed (such as the need to exclude a large number of cases from the sample due to the loss of medical records in a natural disaster) and extrapolation is no longer possible, despite the initial intent to do so. There may be other limited instances in which CMS seeks to collect overpayments associated only with enrollees in a given sample or wishes to perform only a probe sample of RADV reviews without the use of a statistically valid sample and yet will seek to recover any identified, non-extrapolated overpayments. The OIG may also independently decide not to extrapolate for reasons outside the control of CMS, and CMS will still recover those overpayments in accordance with requirements. To account for this, we are proposing § 422.311(a)(2) to read, “CMS may apply extrapolation to audits for payment year 2018 and subsequent payment years.” However, CMS intends for extrapolation to be the standard practice for RADV audits beginning with PY 2018.
Any sampling and extrapolation methodologies adopted by CMS for RADV audits will be focused on MA organization contracts and enrollees' HCCs that, through statistical modeling and/or data analytics, are identified as being at highest risk for improper payments. This is an appropriate approach to any Federal MA audit that seeks to recoup taxpayer dollars that have been inappropriately paid to MA organizations for diagnoses that are not supported in the medical record. This approach was also recommended by the GAO in a 2016 report titled “Fundamental Improvements Needed in CMS' Effort to Recover Substantial Amounts of Improper Payments.”
[
128
]
The GAO recommended that CMS “modify [its] selection of contracts for contract-level RADV audits to focus on those contracts most likely to have high rates of improper payments by taking actions such as the following: selecting more contracts with the highest coding intensity scores; excluding contracts with low coding intensity scores; selecting contracts with high rates of unsupported diagnoses in prior contract-level RADV audits; if a contract with a high rate of unsupported diagnoses is no longer in operation, selecting a contract under the same MA organization that includes the service area of the prior contract; and selecting some contracts with high enrollment that also have either high rates of unsupported diagnoses in prior contract-specific RADV audits or high coding intensity scores.”
[
129
]
CMS is not required to set forth all potential sampling methodologies for calculating an extrapolated payment error through regulatory provisions. However, in the interest of transparency, we are choosing to inform MA organizations about our plans to use various sampling and extrapolation methodologies in RADV audits, as CMS deems appropriate, through rulemaking.
In the 2018 proposed rule, we stated that, given the amount of improper payments identified under the MA program, interest in determining an accurate recovery amount for each audited MA plan, and importance of protecting the overall integrity of the program, we believed that it was in the public interest for CMS to apply the RADV payment error methodology or methodologies adopted through this rulemaking to PY 2011 and all subsequent years. In the 2023 final rule, we announced that extrapolation would instead begin with the PY 2018 RADV audits rather than PY 2011, as proposed. This change was made due to our fiduciary duty to protect taxpayer dollars from overpayments, certain operational considerations, and public comments on the timeliness of RADV audits.
We also note that our publication of audit methodologies for PYs 2018-2021 put MA organizations on further notice that CMS plans to calculate a contract-specific payment error for PY 2018 and subsequent payments year by extrapolating from its review of a statistically valid sample of enrollees, and that MA organizations have never been entitled to receive or retain payments associated with HCCs that cannot be validated by medical records.
In addition to codifying our existing authority to use contract-specific extrapolation techniques in the RADV context, we also propose to use potential methodologies for sampling and extrapolation that are based on a particular sub-cohort or sub-cohorts in a given payment year. For example, a sub-cohort could be the enrollees for whom a particular HCC or one of a related set of HCCs (such as HCCs for diabetes conditions) was reported. After choosing an MA contract and a sub-cohort or sub-cohorts to audit, we would select a statistically significant sample of enrollees in the sub-cohort or sub-cohorts. After reviewing these enrollees' medical records that are submitted by the MA organization, we would use statistical extrapolation to calculate and recoup the improper payments made to the audited MA contract for all enrollees in the sub-cohort or sub-cohorts in that payment year.
Using a sub-cohort methodology, such as one focused on enrollees with high-risk HCCs, would allow us to use a smaller sample size to calculate a statistically valid extrapolated improper payment amount. This is possible because, when selecting a sample from a smaller population (that is, a sub-cohort of enrollees), one can still achieve an acceptable level of statistical confidence with that smaller sample size. This sub-cohort-based audit methodology would also allow us to spread our audit resources across a wider range of MA contracts and focus
(
printed page 74725)
on cohorts of enrollees that raise programmatic concerns, while also reducing operational burden on both CMS and the MA organizations due to the reduced sample size needed to calculate improper payments.
We emphasize that neither proposed methodology is meant to displace our longstanding authority to audit the medical records of specific enrollees who we believe may be associated with improper payments or to use any statistically valid audit methodology on a case-to-case basis. If we finalize one or more sampling and extrapolation methodologies through this rulemaking, we will announce any future changes to that methodology (or those methodologies) through the Health Plan Management System (HPMS) or other appropriate means.
We also propose that MA organizations would be required to remit extrapolated recovery amounts from RADV audit findings in a manner specified by CMS, typically through CMS' payment system, the Medicare Advantage and Prescription Drug system (MARx), as offsets to MA plans' monthly capitation payments. In the event that the recovery amount exceeds the payment in one month, we propose that the recovery be spread across adjustments for multiple months until the full amount plus applicable interest is recouped. In some situations, payment by wire transfer may be necessary. We also propose that CMS might likewise require MA organizations to remit such recovery amounts based upon audit findings by the HHS-OIG.
We also propose to reissue our RADV dispute and appeals regulations in § 422.311, to conform with the proposed audit methodology provisions. Specifically, consistent with our other proposed policies, we propose to reissue § 422.311 by including language to clarify that recovery of improper payments from MA organizations will be conducted according to the Secretary's payment error calculation methodologies and recovery procedures, and that CMS will apply extrapolation to RADV audits beginning with PY 2018.
b. Fee-For-Service Adjuster Concept
(1) Description of an FFS Adjuster
As previously described, risk adjustment ensures that MA organizations are paid appropriately for their plan enrollees, and section 1853(a)(1)(C) of the Act requires that we calculate risk-adjusted payments to MA organizations based on specific criteria, such as age, disability status, sex, institutional status, and health status. As discussed earlier, MA organizations' payments are calculated using the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model, which is published each time it is updated (see section 1853(b) of the Act).
[
130
]
Additionally, an MA organization may only report a diagnosis, and claim the associated payment, when that diagnosis is properly supported by the beneficiary's medical records. Medical records properly support a reported diagnosis when they comply with all CMS data and documentation requirements, which are described in current agency regulations and policy documents, including Chapter 7 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual and those on the Customer Service and Support Center website.
[
131
]
Plans are also required to submit a sample of medical records for the validation of this risk adjustment data (
see
§ 422.310(e)).
Some MA organizations have suggested that CMS cannot lawfully enforce the requirement of medical record documentation for diagnosis codes while making payments at published rates. These MA organizations state that there is a difference in auditing standards between Medicare FFS and MA diagnosis data. In contrast to the MA organization-submitted diagnosis data, these MA organizations claim that Medicare FFS data is “unaudited” by CMS and presumably contains erroneous diagnosis codes not properly supported by beneficiaries' medical records. As a result, they state, the Medicare FFS data used to calculate MA organization payments will understate the cost of treating various conditions. MA organizations state that CMS must raise payment rates to MA organizations or relax the documentation standard that CMS applies to reported medical diagnoses to address what they refer to as the presence of erroneous diagnoses in the FFS claims used to calibrate the CMS-HCC model. MA organizations refer to this concept of a proposed adjustment to the payment rates and/or documentation standard for MA organizations as an “FFS Adjuster.” These MA organizations ground their arguments in section 1853(a)(1)(C)(i) of the Act, which requires the Secretary to adjust payments to MA organizations for demographic and health related risk factors to ensure “actuarial equivalence.” According to these MA organizations, an FFS Adjuster would either adjust payment rates (by raising them) or adjust documentation standards (by loosening them) to resolve the alleged incompatibility between the current rates and current documentation standards. In the 2012 methodology, using the term somewhat differently, CMS said that it would “apply a Fee-for-Service Adjuster (FFS Adjuster) amount as an offset to the preliminary recovery amount” calculated for RADV audits under that methodology.
(2) FFS Adjuster Proposal
We are proposing to not apply an FFS Adjuster to RADV audits. The “actuarial equivalence” and “same methodology” provisions in the statute do not apply to the obligation of an MA organization to report and return improper payments for diagnoses lacking medical record support, including those improper payments identified during a RADV audit, as discussed in detail later. We also believe that it would not be reasonable to interpret the Act as requiring a reduction in payments to MA organizations by at least a statutorily set minimum percentage pursuant to the coding pattern adjustment, while at the same time prohibiting CMS from enforcing longstanding documentation requirements by requiring an offset to the recovery amounts calculated for CMS audits, as discussed in detail as follows.
(3) Actuarial Equivalence
Some MA organizations have contended that an FFS Adjuster is required in RADV audits to ensure “actuarial equivalence” between payments to MA plans and payments under the Medicare FFS program. Some have also contended that the “same methodology” provision of section 1853(b)(4)(D) of the Act requires the application of an FFS Adjuster in RADV audits.
We believe that the “actuarial equivalence” requirement under section 1853(a)(1)(C) of the Act and “same methodology” provision under section 1853(b)(4)(D) of the Act do not require the use of an FFS Adjuster in RADV audits. As described by the D.C. Circuit, these provisions do not apply to the obligation to return improper payments for MA organization diagnosis codes that are unsupported by medical records.
See UnitedHealthcare Ins. Co.
v.
Becerra,
16 F.4th 867, 869, 891-92 (D.C. Cir. 2021),
cert. denied,
142 S. Ct. 2851 (U.S. June 21, 2022). Although the D.C. Circuit did not address the RADV
(
printed page 74726)
audit context in its decision in
UnitedHealthcare,
our position is consistent with the D.C. Circuit's reasoning in that case.
Id.
In
UnitedHealthcare,
a group of MA organizations challenged the Secretary's Part C Overpayment Rule (the “Overpayment Rule”) (
79 FR 29844
), which implemented section 6402 of the Affordable Care Act (
Pub. L. 111-148
) and required MA organizations to self-report and return payments associated with MA organization diagnosis codes not supported by medical record documentation. The district court invalidated the Overpayment Rule.
See UnitedHealthcare Ins. Co.
v.
Azar,
330 F. Supp. 3d 173, 192 (D.D.C. 2018).
However, the D.C. Circuit reversed the district court, holding that the actuarial equivalence provision applies only to how CMS risk adjusts the payments it makes to MA organizations, and not to the obligation of MA organizations to return improper payments for diagnosis codes, submitted by MA organizations to CMS, lacking medical record support.
See UnitedHealthcare,
16 F.4th at 883-887. The D.C. Circuit also held that even if the actuarial equivalence provision applied, plaintiffs' claims would still fail because they did not meet their burden in showing, either through empirical evidence or persuasive logic, that application of the Overpayment Rule would lead to systematic underpayment of MA organizations.
Id.
at 887 through 891.
While the D.C. Circuit decision pertained only to the Overpayment Rule and declined to address RADV audits, its reasoning applies just as strongly in the RADV context and supports our proposed conclusion that an FFS Adjuster is neither required nor appropriate to reduce a RADV audit overpayment. “The role of the actuarial-equivalence provision is to require CMS to model a demographically and medically analogous beneficiary population in Original Medicare to determine the prospective lump-sum payments to [MA organizations].”
Id.
at 870. The RADV audit program, like the Overpayment Rule, arises post-payment to require MA organizations to refund any payment to which they are not entitled, based on diagnoses that lack support in the medical record. The purpose of RADV audits is to recover payments that were made improperly based on diagnoses not supported by medical record documentation. If a payment is made to an MA organization based on a diagnosis code not supported by medical record documentation, the entire payment for that code is in error and should be recovered in full because the payment standard has not been met.
We also believe it would be unreasonable to interpret the Act as requiring a minimum reduction in payments in one provision (the coding pattern provision), while at the same time prohibiting CMS in an adjacent provision (the actuarial equivalence provision) from enforcing those longstanding documentation requirements (by requiring a reduction to the recovery amount calculated for CMS audits). To the contrary, because the Act requires CMS to reduce payments to MA organizations by at least a specific minimum percentage, the only reasonable interpretation of the Act is that CMS would pay MA organizations at those reduced rates, under the existing payment model,
[
132
]
and enforce the longstanding documentation requirements.
Our proposal is consistent with the conclusion of the D.C. Circuit, which is that the actuarial-equivalence requirement is not an “entitle[ment] . . . to a precise payment amount” for a Medicare Advantage insurer, but only “an instruction to the Secretary regarding the design of the risk adjustment model as a whole . . . describ[ing] the type of `payment amount[s]' that the risk adjustment model should produce”; “[i]t does not directly govern how CMS evaluates the validity of diagnoses or defines `overpayment.' ”
UnitedHealthcare,
16 F.4th at 885-86.
(4) Coding Pattern Adjustment
Section 1853(a)(1)(C)(ii) of the Act requires the implementation of a minimum coding pattern adjustment to reduce risk scores of MA beneficiaries, and therefore MA payment rates, until the Secretary implements risk adjustment using Medicare Advantage diagnostic, cost, and use data. This minimum coding pattern adjustment accounts for differences in coding patterns between MA and Medicare FFS, given that MA organizations have a greater incentive than FFS providers to report diagnoses. To meet this requirement, each year, CMS has implemented an adjustment to offset the effects on MA risk scores of higher levels of coding patterns in MA relative to FFS. (See section 1853(a)(1)(C)(ii) of the Act.) Under section 1853(a)(1)(C)(ii)(III) of the Act, the minimum adjustment factor for 2019 and each subsequent year is 5.90 percent. CMS has, each year, implemented the minimum coding pattern adjustment reduction required by statute.
Some MA organizations have expressed concern that using extrapolation without applying an FFS Adjuster to payment recoveries achieved through RADV audits will overlap with coding pattern adjustments or create a double recovery by CMS. As CMS has explained in its annual MA Advance Notices and Rate Announcements, the coding pattern adjustment, unlike RADV, is not intended to address unsupported or inaccurate codes reported by MA organizations in particular instances but only the general practice, relative to Medicare FFS, of identifying more diagnosis codes, including codes that are nonetheless accurate.

Pub. L. 111-152

(5) Documentation Requirements
Some MA organizations have stated in prior rulemaking comments that not using an FFS adjuster imposes new documentation standards on them, but CMS audits reinforce longstanding documentation requirements. The purpose of RADV audits is to recover improper payments resulting from diagnoses that are not supported in the medical record documentation, which is a longstanding documentation standard that applies to all plans equally and regardless of whether the plan is subject to a RADV audit. The objective of an audit is to promote fair and impartial recovery of improper payments due to insufficient documentation in accordance with regulations. This proposal would not impose a new documentation standard on MA organizations, nor is there a distinction in the documentation standards between the MA and FFS Medicare programs. Under section 1857(d)(2), each MA contract provides the Secretary with the right to audit and inspect any books and records of the MA organization that pertain to services performed or determinations of amounts payable under the contract.
