c. Improving the Hardship Exceptions Process
MA record retention requirements incorporated in MA contracts have been in place since the beginning of the MA program. Under § 422.504(d), MA organizations are required to maintain records and other documentation for 10 years to accommodate the periodic auditing of financial records for such purposes as determining Medicare utilization, costs, and amounts payable under the contract. Further, § 422.504(i) extends these record retention requirements to providers of health care services under contract with the MA organization. This regulation further specifies that the Federal Government has the right to audit an MA organization through 10 years from the end of the final contract period.
However, CMS understands that there may be extraordinary circumstances beyond MA organizations' control that may make it difficult to meet medical record submission or other audit requirements. CMS historically implemented a hardship exception process through sub-regulatory guidance for prior payment year audits. We are now proposing to codify this process in regulation by adding a new subparagraph § 422.310(e)(1) to allow MA organizations to request a hardship exception, as prescribed by CMS, if they cannot submit medical records timely as required.
First, we propose that MA organizations may submit a hardship exception request for: (1) the entire MA contract; (2) a sampled enrollee and all the related audited HCCs; or (3) specific audited HCCs. An MA organization may submit multiple hardship exception requests, if necessary, but all supporting documentation must be submitted before the hardship exception request submission deadline. Deadlines to request a hardship exception would be specified in sub-regulatory guidance issued prior to the start of a payment year audit. An MA organization would be required to withdraw a specific hardship exception request before resubmitting it with modifications. For example, if an MA organization submitted a hardship exception request for one or more audited HCCs for a specific enrollee, the MA organization would be required to withdraw that existing hardship exception request submission prior to adding another HCC to the hardship exception request and resubmitting the request to CMS. If an MA organization submits a valid medical record (MR) for an audited HCC(s) for which it has submitted a hardship exception request, then the hardship exception request and any decision made by CMS (for the related audited HCC(s)) for the request would be rendered moot. In other words, the
(
printed page 74728)
valid MR submission would supersede any hardship exception request.
Second, we propose that an MA organization would be required to submit supporting documentation with a hardship exception request that clearly demonstrates an extraordinary circumstance(s) exists and includes all relevant details required for CMS to comprehensively assess the incident or issue. Supporting documentation includes, but is not limited to, any communications associated with the incident and all available evidence substantiating that the incident occurred. MA organizations still have an obligation to pursue all potential medical record sources before submitting a hardship exception request and should review relevant record retention requirements. MA organizations should actively pursue and submit an alternative medical record that supports an audited HCC(s) when the initial medical record sought is unavailable or insufficient to support the audited HCC(s).
If an MA organization is unable to obtain the relevant medical record(s) and submits a hardship exception request for a sampled enrollee's, or group of sampled enrollees', audited CMS-HCCs, we propose that the MA organization would be required to submit documentation (such as verification of a United States Postal Service certified mail delivery or that a delivery attempt was made, or similar verifiable evidence) that it sought medical record documentation from all providers associated with diagnosis data that the MA organization submitted to CMS for the purpose of receiving risk adjusted payments for the sampled enrollee(s). Additionally, MA organizations should be aware of State requirements for medical records to be placed in the care of a custodian for a period of time when a health care provider's office closes. When a health care provider has closed, retired, passed away, changed ownership, or otherwise undergone a change that, according to State law, should have required their medical records to be placed in the care of a custodian, MA organizations should contact the custodian to request the relevant medical records. We propose that CMS would deny a hardship request if the MA organization failed to submit sufficient supporting documentation, including documentation of the MA organization's pursuit of all possible medical record sources. We also propose that hardship exception requests decisions would be final and not subject to appeal.
The following are examples of extraordinary circumstances that may meet CMS' definition of an extraordinary circumstance that may impede an audited MA organization's timely acquisition of medical records and the types of supporting documentation that CMS would expect to be submitted by the MA organization to substantiate the circumstances:
Natural Disaster or Declared Emergency:
Events such as hurricanes, wildfires, floods, or other declared emergencies that disrupt provider operations or access to records. Supporting documentation includes FEMA or State emergency declarations, provider attestations, news releases, and facility closure notices associated with the natural disaster or declared emergency.
Public Health Emergency:
Public health events that significantly impact staffing, operations, or access to medical records. Supporting documentation includes government-issued emergency declarations, internal contingency plans, and provider attestations.
Legal or Regulatory Restrictions:
Court orders, subpoenas, or legal constraints preventing access to records within required timeframes. Supporting documentation includes court orders, legal correspondence, attestation from legal counsel, and any proof of seizure or unavailability including official documentation showing records were seized.
Major System or Technology Failure:
Significant IT outages or cybersecurity incidents. Supporting documentation includes incident reports, vendor outage notices, and other documentation such as system logs, error reports, security audit reports, data recovery attempts, incident documentation, and/or breach or loss of data reports.
Provider's Office Closed and Custodial Requirements Lapsed:
A provider retired, sold, or closed their practice preventing access to records within the required timeframe and the State law custodial requirements have lapsed. Supporting documentation includes an announcement, news report, or signed attestation indicating closure. Submissions regarding provider office closures would take into consideration State law custodian of record requirements, and evidence that the enrollee's record cannot be accessed by any other provider or practice.
Other Extraordinary Circumstances:
Circumstances beyond the organization's control that materially impact the retrieval of medical record documentation. Supporting documentation includes a detailed written explanation and third-party attestations or corroborating documentation.
These examples are not exhaustive and would not guarantee approval of a submitted hardship exception request. Furthermore, MA organizations failing to submit sufficient supporting documentation, including documentation of the MA organization's pursuit of all possible medical record sources, will result in CMS denying a hardship exception request.
CMS would not consider the following scenarios to be justification for granting a hardship exception:
Reliance solely on State law record retention periods that are shorter than CMS' 10-year record retention requirement.
Health care providers not responding to a request.
Issues related to lost records.
Provider office closures, or retired or deceased health care providers where State law custodial requirements have not lapsed.
Medical practice transfers.
Human resource issues.
Ordinary IT issues (for example, system upgrade issues, routine data migration issues, incomplete vendor handovers) that result in missing or inaccessible records.
MA organizations are reminded of their obligation to pursue alternative medical records in these situations. We seek comments on the hardship exception request process and MA organizations' requirement to submit supporting documentation.
d. Retroactivity
We do not believe that the RADV audit policies proposed in this rule impose any new requirements on MA organizations that could be construed as retroactive. We may begin to conduct new RADV audits or finalize results from existing audits for multiple payment years before finalizing the policies in this rule, pursuant to our longstanding authority under § 422.310(e) to review the medical records of any MA enrollee and recoup improper payments identified.
As discussed in the Discussion of Proposals section, CMS has a long-established historical record of using extrapolation in the Medicare program. There is significant guidance, including case law and best practices from HHS and other Federal agencies, stating that extrapolation may be utilized as a valid part of calculating improper payments. CMS first announced its intention to use extrapolation in RADV audits with the publication of an informal proposal in 2010 and reaffirmed this intention in
(
printed page 74729)
the 2012 methodology.
[
136
]
This intention was again announced in the 2018 RADV proposed rule (
83 FR 54982
) and subsequently finalized in the 2023 RADV final rule (
88 FR 6643
). CMS has also announced its intention not to apply an FFS adjuster in RADV audits since the 2018 RADV proposed rule and this policy intention was finalized in the 2023 RADV final rule.
Even if our proposal was determined to be a retroactive application of policy, a position with which we do not agree, it is in the public interest for CMS to apply extrapolation to past payment years, and, therefore, is authorized under the Act. CMS has the authority, in accordance with section 1871(e)(1)(A) of the Act, to apply retroactive changes in regulations, manual instructions, interpretative rules, statements of policy, or guidelines of general applicability to items and services furnished before the effective date of the change, if the Secretary determines that “such retroactive application is necessary to comply with statutory requirements or failure to apply the change would be contrary to the public interest.” Since the early development of RADV, CMS has repeatedly notified MA organizations and the public of its intent to extrapolate RADV audits results and published a methodology in 2012. We believe that recovering extrapolated improper amounts is necessary to comply with statutory requirements and advances the public interest by protecting the overall integrity of the Medicare program. As mentioned earlier, in fiscal year (FY) 2025 (based on calendar year 2023 payments), we estimated that CMS made over $21 billion in Part C overpayments, a figure representing over 5 percent of total Part C payments.
[
137
]
Due to significant growth in the MA program and the large volume of diagnosis data submitted by MA organizations, we are unable to recover this significant amount of overpayment without the use of extrapolation. We have a statutory mandate under the PIIA to reduce improper payments and a fiduciary responsibility to recover funds due and owed to the Medicare Trust Funds.
As previously discussed, CMS, HHS-OIG, and the GAO have identified a significant volume of improper payments in the MA program,
[
138
]
and RADV audits are the primary way CMS ensures payment accuracy to MA organizations. As further discussed in the Regulatory Impact Analysis section of this proposed rule, CMS estimates extrapolated improper payment recoveries of approximately $9 billion per audit year beginning with the PY 2018 audits. We also believe that extrapolation will foster an additional sentinel effect of RADV audits on the improper payment rate as MA organizations improve their processes to report only those diagnoses that meet CMS requirements to be documented in the medical record in accordance with ICD-CM coding guidelines.
The core component of a RADV audit is to ensure that all diagnoses are properly supported by medical records. We only seek to recover improper payments received by MA organizations for HCCs that are not substantiated by enrollees' medical records. MA organizations have never been entitled to receive or retain payments associated with HCCs that cannot be validated by medical records, and it is impossible for MA organizations to submit, and CMS to audit, every medical record. CMS has never calculated or applied an FFS adjuster to any RADV audit findings and allowing MA organizations to retain Medicare funds for unsubstantiated diagnoses on this basis runs contrary to the statute. Therefore, applying the rule under the public interest exception in section 1871(e)(1)(A) of the Act would not upset any settled or reasonable reliance interests. This all serves the public interest by reducing the improper allocation of taxpayer dollars that can otherwise be used for other purposes within the Federal Government, including solvency of the Medicare Trust Funds. Thus, a retroactive application of the rule is in the public interest within the meaning of section 1871(e)(1)(A) of the Act.
If a court were to find that any provision of this rule is impermissibly retroactive, we believe that the rule should remain in effect for any payment year that has not yet occurred or for other provisions not found to be retroactive. For example, if our proposed use of extrapolation for payment years prior to the publication of a final rule is determined to be impermissibly retroactive, the final regulation would still allow collection of extrapolated recoveries for subsequent payment years depending on what payment year is determined to be the triggering date for retroactive application.
To the extent a court may ultimately enjoin one provision of this section as finalized, CMS proposes that the other provisions should remain in effect, ensuring the continuity of the regulations. We propose that any provision of the requirements of this rule that is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms or as applied to any person, entity, or circumstance would be construed so as to continue to give maximum effect to the provision permitted by law, unless such holding is one of utter invalidity or unenforceability, in which event we propose that the provision would be severable from the other provisions of this rulemaking and would not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the provision to persons or entities not similarly situated or to dissimilar circumstances.
We propose that if any section, subsection, sentence, clause, phrase, word, provision, or application of this proposed rule as finalized shall be found to be invalid, illegal, unconstitutional, or unenforceable, that finding shall not affect or undermine the validity of any other section, subsection, sentence, clause, phrase, word, provision, or application which can be enforced without the use of the offending provision. We request comments from the public on severability, particularly which policies could be severable, if finalized, and how the other policies in a final rule would operate absent those particular provisions.
V. Provider Enrollment Proposals
A. Provider Enrollment Background
1. Introduction
Section 1866(j)(1)(A) of the Act requires the Secretary to establish a process for the enrollment of providers and suppliers into the Medicare program. The overarching purpose of the enrollment process is to help confirm that providers and suppliers (hereafter collectively “providers” unless otherwise noted) seeking to bill Medicare for services and items furnished to Medicare beneficiaries meet all applicable Federal and State requirements to do so. The process is, to
(
printed page 74730)
an extent, a “gatekeeper” that prevents unqualified and potentially fraudulent individuals and entities from entering and inappropriately billing Medicare. It has proven invaluable in this regard and is a vital component of Medicare program integrity.
Under
42 CFR 424.510
, a provider or supplier must complete, sign, and submit to its assigned Medicare contractor the appropriate Form CMS-855 (OMB Control No. 09380685) application in order to enroll in the Medicare program and obtain Medicare billing privileges.
[
139
]
The Form CMS-855, which can be submitted via paper or electronically through the internet-based Provider Enrollment, Chain, and Ownership System (PECOS) process, captures information about the provider or supplier that is needed for CMS or its contractors to determine whether the provider or supplier meets all Medicare requirements. Data collected during the enrollment process include but are not limited to: (1) general identifying information (for example, legal business name, tax identification number (TIN), and National Provider Identifier (NPI)); (2) licensure data; (3) practice locations; and (4) information regarding the provider's or supplier's owning and managing individuals and organizations.
The application is used for a variety of provider enrollment transactions, including the following:
Initial enrollment—
The provider or supplier is: (1) enrolling in Medicare for the first time; (2) enrolling in another Medicare contractor's jurisdiction; or (3) seeking to enroll in Medicare after having previously been enrolled.
Change of ownership—
The provider or supplier is reporting a change in its ownership.
Revalidation—
The provider or supplier is revalidating its Medicare enrollment information in accordance with § 424.515.
Reactivation—
The provider or supplier is seeking to reactivate its Medicare billing privileges after it was deactivated in accordance with § 424.540.
Change of information—
The provider or supplier is reporting a change in its existing enrollment information in accordance with § 424.516.
Our provider enrollment regulations are generally codified in
42 CFR part 424, subpart P
(currently §§ 424.500 through 424.575 and hereafter occasionally referenced as subpart P). B. DMEPOS Supplier Provisions
Among the types of providers and suppliers that must enroll in Medicare to bill the Medicare program are DMEPOS suppliers. Such suppliers include, but are not limited to, the following:
Medical supply companies that exclusively furnish DME like wheelchairs, walkers, and canes.
Physicians and practitioners who provide DMEPOS to their own patients.
Home health agencies (HHAs) and hospitals that provide DMEPOS to their own patients.
Oxygen and oxygen equipment suppliers.
Prosthetists and orthotists.
Pharmacies.
DMEPOS suppliers enroll in Medicare via the Form CMS-855S application (Medicare Enrollment Application—Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics and Supplies (DMEPOS); OMB Control No. 0938-1056). Per
42 CFR 424.57(b)(1)
—and excluding locations it utilizes solely as warehouses or repair facilities—the supplier must separately enroll each physical location it uses to furnish Medicare-covered DMEPOS.
Suppliers of DMEPOS have long presented to the Medicare program an elevated risk of fraud, waste, and abuse—historically, perhaps the highest of all Medicare provider and supplier types. Numerous HHS-OIG reports since 1998 have noted serious program integrity problems with DMEPOS suppliers, and we recently outlined a significant number of DMEPOS supplier criminal and False Claims Act cases.
[
140
]
Recognizing this threat, CMS over the years has established particularly stringent requirements that DMEPOS suppliers must meet to enroll and maintain enrollment in Medicare. To illustrate, DMEPOS suppliers under
42 CFR 424.518(c)
are one of only a few provider and supplier types subject to the highest and strictest level of screening during the enrollment process. (In fact, they were one of only two types originally assigned to this high-risk screening category in 2011—the other being HHAs). This level of screening includes: (1) a site visit; and (2) submission of fingerprints of the supplier's 5 percent or greater owners for a Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) criminal background check. There are other regulatory provisions besides the basic provider enrollment requirements in
42 CFR part 424, subpart P
(§§ 424.500 through 424.575) that DMEPOS suppliers must meet. These requirements include, but are not limited to, the following:
Compliance with the DMEPOS supplier standards in § 424.57(c).
Acquisition and maintenance of a surety bond consistent with §  424.57(d).
Compliance with DMEPOS quality standards.
Accreditation by a CMS-approved DMEPOS accrediting organization.
The foregoing underscores the serious and continued payment safeguard challenges associated with DMEPOS suppliers. We accordingly propose several regulatory revisions related to DMEPOS supplier enrollment.
1. Medicare Surety Bonds
a. Introduction
On January 2, 2009, we published in the
Federal Register
(
74 FR 166

The rule established a new § 424.57(d) requiring DMEPOS suppliers that were not otherwise exempted to submit a surety bond in the amount of at least $50,000 to the National Supplier Clearinghouse (now the National Provider Enrollment Contractors (NPECs)) to enroll in and maintain their enrollment in the Medicare program. The surety bond requirements of § 424.57(d) have been in effect since 2009. DMEPOS suppliers presently are the only Medicare provider or supplier type required to submit and maintain a surety bond as a condition of enrollment.
Section 6402(g)(1) of the Affordable Care Act amended section 1834(a)(16) of the Act by adding a provision regarding the volume of DMEPOS billing as it relates to the surety bond requirement. Section 1834(a)(16)(B) of the Act now provides that a DMEPOS supplier must furnish a surety bond of at least $50,000 that the Secretary determines is commensurate with the volume of the supplier's billing. Consistent therewith, and as discussed further, we are proposing changes to § 424.57(d) to improve the overall surety bond process.
b. Issues With Existing § 424.57(d)
In general, a surety bond—in the context of Medicare DMEPOS supplier enrollment—represents a promise by a surety that it will pay CMS a certain sum amount if the DMEPOS supplier to whom the surety issued the bond fails to repay a debt it owes to CMS; these debts include overpayments, civil money penalties, and assessments. Indeed, debt recoupment is the principal goal of CMS' surety bond requirement. The bond requirement has other benefits, too. One is that it facilitates additional screening of the DMEPOS supplier beyond that performed under § 424.518(c). Before deciding whether to issue a surety bond, the surety reviews the finances and other aspects of the DMEPOS supplier that CMS may currently lack the means to assess. This is critical given the program integrity threats that DMEPOS suppliers pose. The other is that suppliers may learn that CMS has referred their unpaid debt to the surety. Concerned that the surety might cancel the supplier's bond if the surety has to pay the debt to CMS—leaving the supplier at risk of revocation if it is unbonded—the supplier finally pays the debt. Since 2012, in fact, two of CMS' DME Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) jurisdictions have collected a combined $171.3 million in DMEPOS supplier payments in this manner. Hence, § 424.57(d) is not only a means of collection from sureties but also from the suppliers themselves.
Over the years, though, our surety bond collection efforts have encountered challenges. A particular difficulty has been that sureties sometimes do not make payment to CMS notwithstanding their obligation to do so under both § 424.57(d) and the surety bond's terms. To illustrate, of the approximately $32 million in DMEPOS supplier debts that CMS referred to sureties for payment between CY 2016
(
printed page 74732)
and CY 2018, CMS collected only $2.85 million from the sureties.
[
141
]
To help address this issue, we proposed in a March 1, 2016, provider enrollment rule that CMS could reject an enrolling or enrolled DMEPOS supplier's surety bond if the surety that issued the bond failed to make a required payment to CMS pursuant to § 424.57(d).
[
142
]
Though we did not finalize this provision, the problem remains very serious. To illustrate:
CMS data from 2025 showed that a combined $37.5 million in DMEPOS supplier debts had been referred to seven sureties for payment. The sureties collectively paid only $540,000. Although the affected suppliers paid about $5.5 million of the $37.5 million amount once their debts were referred to the sureties, it is extremely disconcerting that the sureties—despite their obligation to do so under the bond's terms—paid no more than 1.5 percent of the amount of debt referred to them.
The two previous-referenced DME MAC jurisdictions also informed CMS that since 2012 they have referred a combined $229.2 million in DMEPOS supplier debts to sureties. Of this total, sureties paid only $35.7 million.
In sum, sureties' failures to make required payments to CMS have resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid DMEPOS supplier debts. Sureties should not be able to avoid fulfilling their legal and financial obligations to CMS. Given the resulting harm to American taxpayers and the need to protect the Trust Funds, we propose the following changes to § 424.57(d).
c. “Sufficient Evidence” Standard and Review of Overpayment Calculations
Section 424.57(d)(5)(i) states that the DMEPOS surety bond must guarantee that the surety will—within 30 days of receiving written notice from CMS containing “sufficient evidence” to establish the surety's liability under the bond of unpaid claims, civil money penalties (CMPs), or assessments—pay CMS a total of up to the full penal amount of the bond. Section 424.57(a) defines “sufficient evidence” as documents CMS may supply to the surety to establish that the supplier had received Medicare funds exceeding the amount due and payable under the statute and regulations, the amount of a CMP, or the amount of some other assessment against the DMEPOS supplier.
One reason a surety sometimes cites for refusing to pay CMS is that, in the surety's view, CMS did not furnish “sufficient evidence” that the surety is, in fact, liable for payment. This, in many cases, is incorrect, and there have been numerous instances where no matter how many documents CMS furnishes to the surety that conclusively establish the supplier's debt and the surety's obligation, the surety continuously—and, we believe, inappropriately—maintains that the evidence is insufficient. Nonetheless, and to clarify its scope, we propose to revise the “sufficient evidence” definition such that the term would mean that CMS has furnished documentation to the surety that establishes all of the following:
The amount and basis of the overpayment, CMP, or assessment that the DMEPOS supplier owes.
That it is an unpaid claim.
A valid surety bond exists.
The request to the surety for payment satisfies the surety bond requirements, specifically:
++ When a bond is in effect, that the unpaid claim, CMP, or assessment occurred during the term of the bond. This includes when a DMEPOS supplier changes its surety during the term of a bond; or
++ When the DMEPOS supplier fails to furnish a bond, submit a rider
[
143
]
when required, or if the DMEPOS supplier's billing privileges are revoked, that the unpaid claims, CMPs, or assessments are asserted or imposed against the DMEPOS supplier during the 2 years following, and they are based on overpayments or other events that took place during the term of the bond or rider.
This clarification is not intended to change which surety is responsible when a DMEPOS supplier obtains a bond from a new surety; in that circumstance,
42 CFR 424.57(d)(9)
determines which surety is responsible. Rather, we believe these revisions would remove any ambiguity about the surety's responsibility to make payment to CMS, and we expect sureties to do precisely this after receipt of this documentation.
In addition, some sureties have declined to make required payments to CMS because: (1) CMS did not furnish documentation to the surety as to how CMS calculated the overpayment, CMP, or assessment; or (2) the supplier's appeal rights regarding the overpayment have not been exhausted. This is improper because neither the existing definition of “sufficient evidence” nor any other provision in current § 424.57(d) (including paragraph (d)'s required bond terms) have ever required such documentation or the exhaustion of appeal rights. Regarding the former, “sufficient evidence” only requires documentation “that the DMEPOS supplier had received Medicare funds in excess of the amount due and payable under the statute and regulations, the amount of a CMP, or the amount of some other assessment against the DMEPOS supplier.” The surety's obligation under the bond to make payment is the critical consideration, not the details of how CMS calculated the debt amount. 2. Medicare DMEPOS Supplier Relationship Reporting
A significant challenge CMS has faced in stemming DMEPOS fraud, waste, and abuse has been our lack of upfront knowledge of certain outside entities with which the supplier may have business relationships. While DMEPOS suppliers have for decades been required to report on the Form CMS-855S their 5 percent or greater owners, general and limited partners, managing employees and organizations, and corporate officers and directors, the supplier need not disclose various other parties with which they are associated, such as the following:
Marketing companies, which perform services for the supplier such as advertising, mail and email solicitation to beneficiaries, and generating leads.
Wholesalers that purchase supplies from manufacturers and then sell them to the supplier.
Fulfillment companies, which generally are entities with which the supplier contracts to deliver items to beneficiaries (rather than the supplier directly delivering them).
Considering the excessive program integrity risk DMEPOS suppliers have long posed and the need to ensure that the products they distribute to beneficiaries are quality items, we believe we must understand the full chain of the supplier's acquisition and eventual distribution and delivery of these goods. Without knowing, for instance, the entity from which the supplier purchased its products, we may lack important information to help us ascertain the seller's credentials. Indeed, we have seen instances where certain wholesalers distribute low-quality supplies that can harm beneficiaries, sometimes with the knowledge of questionable DMEPOS suppliers seeking to limit costs at the expense of patient care. In a similar context, it can be difficult for us to verify whether a supplier will properly deliver supplies to beneficiaries if we do not know whether the supplier uses a fulfillment company for this function and, if it does, which company. Some fulfillment entities may have poor records regarding supply delivery (with beneficiaries sometimes never receiving needed items) or have participated in fraud schemes.
Awareness of these companies' identities would help CMS: (1) safeguard beneficiaries; (2) validate the supplier's compliance with the enrollment standards in § 424.57(c); (3) vet these entities for program integrity risks; and (4) ascertain whether the supplier may be acting with other entities in a larger fraud scheme, an especially important consideration given that we have seen an alarming number of such instances over the years. We also note that some of these entities may have as much (or more) involvement with the supplier's regular operations as certain parties that must currently be reported, such as indirect owners and various members of boards of directors. This, in our view, further warrants the collection of data about wholesalers and fulfillment companies.
Marketing entities are of particular concern to us. Section 424.57(c)(11) currently states that—with three exceptions outlined in § 424.57(c)(11)(i) through (iii)—suppliers may not contact a beneficiary by telephone when supplying a Medicare-covered item.

3. Beneficiary Consent for Items
An especially disturbing DMEPOS supplier practice over the years has been the shipping of supplies to beneficiaries without the latter having requested them, followed by the supplier billing Medicare for the items. Indeed, we have seen fraud schemes involving stolen beneficiary information, which enables the supplier to report a beneficiary's data on the claim with a fictitious diagnosis and date of service and a random referring provider's information; in some cases, the supplier never even sent the item to the beneficiary. The following are several recent examples of this conduct (as noted previously, we generally use the term “supplier” to refer to DMEPOS suppliers and the term “provider” to refer to other provider and supplier types):
A supplier submitted approximately a dozen claims for items it claimed to have sent to various beneficiaries. All of the beneficiaries: (1) denied the diagnoses the supplier reported; (2) confirmed that they never received the items; and (3) denied knowing the supplier or the referring provider.
A beneficiary received orthotics from a supplier via shipment. The beneficiary stated that he did not know why he received the items, and that the reported diagnosis was incorrect. While he stated that he was scheduled for an appointment with the reported referring provider, he had not yet seen said provider.
A beneficiary received a call from a party identifying itself as Medicare, advising her that she would receive orthotics for free. The beneficiary informed the caller that she did not need them, but she ultimately received the supplies. The beneficiary later told CMS that she never saw or spoke with the referring provider and had never used the services of the supplier listed on the claim.
Another beneficiary received a call from a supplier: (1) asking her questions about her medical diagnosis; and (2) stating that she was qualified to receive DMEPOS items at no cost to her. She received the items but informed CMS that she had neither requested nor needed them; she also had never discussed needing the items with her primary care provider.
We believe that requiring prior confirmation from the beneficiary that the item was requested and needed before it is sent to the beneficiary would help stem this improper activity. Suppliers could not simply send unauthorized items to patients and receive payment for them. To this end, we propose an additional DMEPOS supplier standard in new § 424.57(c)(32) that would require DMEPOS suppliers to have a process for obtaining prior beneficiary consent for items the supplier sends to the beneficiary at their home or residence. For purposes of this standard:
The standard only applies to the initial order the supplier receives, not to refills.
The process must, at a minimum, include the following:
++ After receiving a valid order for the item from the ordering or prescribing provider (for example, physician), the supplier must telephone or email the beneficiary (or, if applicable, their representative (such as a caretaker or guardian)) and ask whether the beneficiary or representative: (1) is aware of the order or prescription; (2) whether the beneficiary needs the item; and (3) consents to receiving the item. The item cannot be delivered until these three conditions are met, even if the beneficiary or representative cannot be reached. If only the representative can satisfy the requirements, the supplier's process must include a means of confirming that said individual is authorized to act on the beneficiary's behalf.
++ For each such item, the supplier must document in a written log: (1) the beneficiary's or representative's name and either their phone number or email address (whichever means of communication was used); (2) time(s) and date(s) of the contact(s); and (3) a statement that the three conditions were met.
We solicit comments on any additional minimum requirements that should be included in this process.

Section 424.58(e)(8)(i)(A) states that a DMEPOS accreditation organization (AO) must perform a survey of all DMEPOS supplier locations for which the supplier seeks accreditation or reaccreditation with the AO. (This includes, but is not limited to, accreditations: (i) for a new item type the supplier has not previously furnished; or (ii) as required under § 424.551.) Surveys help determine whether the supplier meets the DMEPOS quality standards. These standards address matters such as: (1) administration; (2) financial, human resources, and information management; (3) equipment and item delivery and set-up; (4) patient and caregiver training and instruction; and (5) patient follow-up. The standards are both extensive and detailed because of the need to confirm the supplier's legitimacy. Compliance with the quality

Given the importance of DMEPOS supplier surveys in protecting beneficiaries and facilitating program integrity, the following proposed changes to § 424.58(e)(8)(i)(A) would expand the instances in which a survey must be performed.
First, § 424.551 states that a DMEPOS supplier undergoing a CIMO—which is defined as an individual or organization acquiring more than a 50 percent direct ownership interest in the supplier within 36 months of its initial enrollment (or within 36 months of its most recent CIMO)—must enroll as a new DMEPOS supplier, undergo a survey, and obtain a new accreditation. There are three supplier exceptions to this “36-month rule” in § 424.551: (1) the supplier's parent company is undergoing an internal corporate restructuring; (2) the supplier's owners are changing the supplier's business structure, and the owners remain the same; and (3) an individual owner of the supplier dies. We are concerned that the lack of a supplier survey in these three exempted situations—as well as with suppliers that undergo CIMOs beyond the 36-month window—leaves CMS unable to confirm whether the supplier under its new majority ownership is compliant with the quality standards and is committed to patient care. To us, the central issues are the change in the supplier's controlling interest itself and the potential involvement of the new majority owner(s)—rather than the timing (for instance, more than 36 months after initial enrollment) or whether an exception applies.
We therefore propose to revise § 424.58(e)(8)(i)(A) such that any DMEPOS supplier in which an individual or organization acquires more than a 50 percent direct ownership interest requires a survey. This survey requirement would thus apply a modified version of the definition of CIMO in § 424.551(a); that is, it would apply even if the CIMO: (1) occurred more than 36 months after initial enrollment or the supplier's most recent CIMO; or (2) qualifies for an exception under § 424.551(c). We note that this change would only involve the performance of a survey. A supplier undergoing a CIMO that is excepted or occurs outside the 36-month period would not have to enroll as a new supplier or receive a new accreditation based solely on the CIMO.
Second, we propose to also include practice location changes within § 424.58(e)(8)(i)(A). If a supplier moves to another site, we have no means of ascertaining whether it is compliant with the quality standards in that new physical environment. To illustrate, several standards pertain to personnel qualifications. Since the new location may result in new employees, we must ensure that said personnel meet, for instance, licensure or certification requirements. Accordingly, we believe this proposed revision is needed to help safeguard beneficiaries.

5. Ordering Unnecessary DMEPOS Services or Items
Several of the criminal cases cited earlier—as well as other criminal cases and situations we have seen—involve physicians ordering DMEPOS services and items that were either not reasonable or not necessary. This is sometimes done as part of a fraud scheme, with the physician receiving remuneration from the supplier that will be providing the services and items. Millions of Medicare dollars are at risk from such behavior. While we have various means of addressing these situations, a significant program integrity gap remains; specifically, our existing authority to immediately revoke the physician is limited in certain circumstances. To illustrate, under § 424.535(a)(8)(i) and (a)(21), respectively, we can revoke:
A provider or supplier that submits a claim or claims for services that could not have been furnished to a specific individual on the date of service.
A physician or eligible professional who has a pattern or practice of ordering, certifying, referring, or prescribing Medicare Part A or B services, items, or drugs that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries, or otherwise fails to meet Medicare requirements.
In our aforementioned scenario, though, § 424.535(a)(8)(i) could only apply to the DMEPOS supplier (that is, the supplier submitting the claim), not to the doctor who ordered the item (Dr. X). While § 424.535(a)(21) could apply to Dr. X as the ordering physician, it may require multiple instances of Dr. X's non-compliant ordering. This effectively means we might have to wait until Dr. X engages in this behavior a second or third time (or more) before we can take revocation action, thus allowing Dr. X to continue said misconduct and threaten the Trust Funds. This would run counter to our obligation to protect taxpayer dollars and, equally important, Medicare beneficiaries from unnecessary and potentially dangerous services and items. We must be able to take swift action on the physician's enrollment. We thus propose in new § 424.535(a)(29) that CMS have the authority to revoke a physician's or practitioner's enrollment if the individual ordered a DMEPOS item or service that was not reasonable or not necessary. The revocation effective date under proposed new § 424.535(g)(1)(xxix) would be the date on which CMS determines that the supplier should be revoked under § 424.535(a)(29).
We stress that this proposed revocation ground is not restricted to demonstrated DMEPOS fraud schemes. No prior finding of fraud would be required. On the other hand, stakeholders should not assume that CMS intends to revoke every physician or practitioner who orders a DMEPOS service or item that is later determined not to be reasonable or necessary. CMS would only take revocation action when, after careful consideration of the facts and circumstances, said action is warranted. In addition, § 424.535(a)(29) would be limited to the ordering of DMEPOS items or services, in large part because of the longstanding program integrity threat that DMEPOS suppliers have posed—higher, perhaps, than any other Medicare provider or supplier type.
C. Factors for Consideration for Denial and Revocation Decisions
As already alluded to, CMS under § 424.535(a) may revoke a provider's enrollment for any reason specified in that paragraph. These reasons include, for instance, the provider's: (i) failure to adhere to Medicare enrollment requirements; (ii) exclusion by the HHS OIG; (iii) felony conviction within the previous 10 years; (iv) pattern of improper or abusive billing; and (v) termination by another Federal health care program. A revocation helps safeguard the Medicare program, the Trust Funds, and beneficiaries by removing (and preventing payment to) Medicare providers that have engaged in problematic or otherwise non-compliant behavior. When a provider is revoked, it is generally barred from reenrolling in Medicare for a period of 1 to 10 years. The length of this “reenrollment bar” is determined based upon the severity of the basis of the revocation.
(
printed page 74738)
CMS also has reasons in § 424.530(a) for which it can deny a provider's enrollment application, some of which duplicate our revocation grounds in § 424.535(a) (for instance, OIG exclusion). The general rationale for a denial mirrors that for a revocation: to protect the Medicare program and its beneficiaries from potentially fraudulent or abusive activity.
For several of our denial and revocation grounds, CMS in its determination must consider various criteria outlined within the applicable denial/revocation reason in §§ 424.530 and 424.535. As an example, § 424.535(a)(9) permits revocation if the provider fails to report a change in their enrollment information (such as a change in practice location) within the required timeframe. Section 424.535(a)(9)(i) through (iv) lists the following factors that CMS must consider in its decision: (i) whether the data in question was reported; (ii) if the data was reported, how belatedly; (iii) the data's materiality; and (iv) any other information that CMS deems relevant to its determination.
Such specified criteria have, in our view, hindered CMS' denial and revocation authority—even to the point where we could not deny or revoke the provider in a particular instance even though CMS believed that it was justified under the circumstances. Consider these two § 424.535(a)(9) scenarios:
Scenario 1
—A provider was required to report a certain change to us within 30 days but did not do so until Day 50.
Scenario 2
—A supplier failed to report a change involving information that, on the surface, might not appear as crucial as that in Scenario 1.
Revocation might prove challenging in both situations. In the former, the data was ultimately submitted 20 days after the deadline. This may weigh against a revocation per § 424.535(a)(9)(i) and (ii)—even if the information was material. The end result could be incorrect payments being made to the provider due to the lack of timely, updated information. For Scenario 2, an apparent lack of materiality per § 424.535(a)(9)(iii) could, in some circumstances, override the failure to disclose the change.
We outlined our concerns regarding factors in the aforementioned CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule (
91 FR 72022

One particular concern we discussed involved the criterion in several of our denial and revocation grounds that requires CMS to consider whether the provider has any history of final adverse actions as defined in § 424.502 (such as felony convictions). We stated that most aberrant billing we have seen is done by providers with no history of adverse actions. Yet the adverse action factor essentially requires us to weigh against a denial or revocation for such providers. It aids non-compliant providers so long as the provider lacks an adverse history (which it often will), hence obstructing our program integrity efforts.
The point is that the facts of every potential denial and revocation case are very different. We must accordingly have the maximum possible flexibility to address them without criteria that might effectively compel us to enroll (or maintain the enrollment of) a non-compliant provider—something that could seriously harm the Trust Funds, the taxpayers, and beneficiaries.
We proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule to remove the factors in § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) and § 424.530(f) (the latter addresses reapplication bars). Given the scope of the foregoing problem, though, we believe we must go much further and remove all factors from our denial and revocation reasons. D. Faster Enrollment Change Reporting for Medicare Providers
Providers must report changes to their enrollment data within the timeframes specified in our regulations. DMEPOS suppliers under § 424.57(c)(2) must disclose all such changes within 30 days of the change. All other provider and supplier types must report changes within 30 days or 90 days, depending on the data involved. Changes in ownership, practice location, and final adverse actions are typically subject to a 30-day timeframe, with 90 days for most others.
We propose to require that all changes of information—regardless of the type of
(
printed page 74739)
data involved or the provider or supplier type—be reported within 30 days. While ownership, practice location, and final adverse action changes are important (hence their general 30-day timeframes), other data changes are, too. A failure to timely report a new managing employee or corporate officer, for example, could result in CMS unknowingly paying a provider with a high-level official who poses a program integrity risk based on past or current conduct. Too, if we do not timely learn of a provider's new bank, billing agency, doing business as name, or correspondence address, CMS risks sending funds or information to—or receiving claims from—the wrong entity or individual; this could lead to incorrect payments or the inadvertent release of confidential data. In short, any outdated or erroneous enrollment information can threaten the Trust Funds, making, in our view, a 90-day reporting period much too long. We believe that a shorter, across-the-board reporting timeframe would help ensure more accurate data. It would also eliminate uncertainty as to whether a particular data element is subject to the 30-day period or, instead, the 90-day period. We note that DMEPOS suppliers are well-accustomed to the 30-day period, and we believe all other provider and supplier types will also become accustomed; this has been our past experience when we have reduced certain reporting timeframes from 90 to 30 days.
This proposal does not mean that CMS now intends to revoke every provider that fails to meet these reporting timeframes. Our authority to revoke enrollment under § 424.535(a)(9) for failing to timely report changed data is discretionary (not mandatory), and we sometimes use other vehicles to address failures to timely disclose changes, such as stays of enrollment under § 424.541 and deactivations under § 424.540.
Our specific regulatory revisions are as follows:
In § 410.33(g)(2), which pertains to independent diagnostic testing facilities, we propose to delete the existing second and third sentences. The new second sentence would state that all changes in enrollment information must be reported within 30 days of the change.
In § 424.205(c)(5), which addresses Medicare diabetes prevention programs, we would remove the current language and state that all changes in enrollment information must be reported within 30 days of the change.
Sections 424.516(d)(1), (d)(2), (e), (e)(1) and (e)(2) address reporting requirements for other provider and supplier types. We propose to delete all these paragraphs and revise § 424.516(d)'s lone sentence such that all changes in enrollment information must be reported within 30 days of the change. We would also change the title of paragraph (d) from “Reporting requirements for physicians, nonphysician practitioners, and physician and nonphysician practitioner organizations” to “Reporting requirements for all other provider and supplier types”.
Section 424.516(e)(3) addresses requirements for ambulance suppliers to report license or certification revocations or suspensions. We propose to re-designate paragraphs (e)(3), (e)(3)(i), and (e)(3)(ii) as new paragraphs (e), (e)(1), and (e)(2), respectively. In addition, we would change paragraph (e)'s title from “Reporting requirements for all other providers and suppliers” to “Special air ambulance supplier reporting requirements.”
E. New Bases for Medicare Provider Enrollment Denial/Revocation
1. CY 2027 HH PPS Proposed Rule Grounds
Among the denial and revocation reasons we proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule were the following—
Proposed new § 424.535(a)(24) would permit CMS to revoke enrollment if the provider's or supplier's enrollment presents a high risk of fraud, waste, or abuse due to the provider's or supplier's location within a limited geographic area that has an excessive number of providers and suppliers.
Proposed new § 424.530(a)(19) would allow denial of enrollment if the provider's or supplier's practice location is in the same suite or office as another provider or supplier whose Medicare enrollment has been revoked or denied under § 424.535 or § 424.530.
Proposed new § 424.530(a)(20) would permit denial of a hospice's enrollment if any of the following apply—
++ The hospice's medical director: (1) is the medical director of multiple other hospices; or (2) practices at such a distance (for example, in a different State) from the enrolling hospice that the medical director cannot realistically perform all medical director functions required under
42 CFR part 418
.
++ The hospice's administrator: (1) is the administrator of multiple other hospices; or (2) practices at such a distance (for example, in a different State) from the enrolling hospice that the administrator cannot realistically perform all administrator functions required under
42 CFR part 418
.
++ The hospice's medical director does not have an active physician medical license in the State in which they are practicing.
We explained at great length in the proposed rule the reasons for these provisions and briefly summarize them here.
Regarding proposed § 424.535(a)(24), we noted the alarming increase in situations where numerous providers and suppliers—sometimes of the same type—are simultaneously operating within a very small geographic area (for instance, a multi-block sector), the same complex or building, or even the same office. We cited as examples: (1) 18 HHAs operating within the same building in Columbus, Ohio; and (2) hundreds of HHAs and hospices having enrolled in Los Angeles County over the span of several years. There was no medical need for such increases, which were entirely out of proportion with any increase in the region's beneficiary population and could be a strong indicator of fraud. As for proposed § 424.530(a)(19), sharing a suite or office with a provider who has been deemed non-compliant with Medicare enrollment requirements could spur concerns about the newly enrolling provider's own willingness to maintain compliance if enrolled. This is particularly true when—in cases we have seen—several providers in the same suite engage (or seek to engage) in a fraud scheme, have their Medicare enrollments revoked or denied, and another provider aims to enroll in that same office. Proposed § 424.530(a)(20), meanwhile, reflected the longstanding program integrity issues involving hospices. Of special concern were instances where an individual is a medical director or administrator of numerous hospices, sometimes at a great distance from the hospice location. This raises questions as to whether such persons are actually fulfilling these roles consistent with our regulations.
We recognized in the proposed rule—and do so again here—that some of these situations do not automatically mean fraud, waste, and abuse is occurring. Many medical facilities and complexes have a large number of providers and suppliers located therein. For example, a medical center comprising of three adjacent buildings may have seven physician practices with different specialties, two laboratories, etc.; some neighborhoods may have several types of providers and suppliers within them. Too, a physician operating in the same suite as a revoked provider is not automatically indicative of fraud. Nevertheless, some of the fraud schemes we have encountered have similarities to the situations addressed in these three proposed provisions.
(

Considering the hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars that such schemes can threaten, we need the discretion to deny or revoke providers and suppliers in the three proposed circumstances if warranted. So concerned are we about such situations that we believe these three denial or revocation grounds should be both denial and revocation bases, rather than only a denial reason or only a revocation reason (for instance, the § 424.535(a)(24) scenario only permits revocation).
Thus, we propose the following provisions. First, proposed new § 424.530(a)(23) would permit denial in the circumstances described in § 424.535(a)(24) in the July 1, 2026, proposed rule. Second, proposed new revocation grounds in § 424.535(a)(26) and (27) would duplicate the §§ 424.530(a)(19) and (20) denial grounds in the July 1, 2026, proposed rule. Third, the effective dates of proposed new § 424.535(a)(26) and (27) would, under proposed new § 424.535(g)(1)(xxxiii) and (xxvii) be the date on which CMS determines that the provider should be revoked under these paragraphs; said date would align with our previously mentioned proposal in the CY 2027 HH PPS to make the remainder of our prospective revocation grounds retroactive.
2. Change in Hospice Administrators
We have already noted in the present and the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rules the serious program integrity risks posed by hospices in recent years. Among the hospice fraud schemes we have seen involves administrators opening clusters of hospices within a small geographic area—sometimes even in the same building—without any corresponding need for such an increase in hospice services. The administrator inappropriately bills Medicare through these hospices, departs the hospices, and then repeats the pattern as administrator of other hospices the individual opens. Even if the administrator does not start up the hospices, the person may engage in misconduct at several hospices, and his or her successors as administrator may do the same. Constant changes of administrators can raise questions as to the hospice's legitimacy and stability and, more importantly, whether the provider is engaged in fraud, waste, or abuse.
While we acknowledge that administrators may depart hospices for entirely legitimate reasons (for example, retirement, taking a different position, etc.), we must protect the Medicare program against situations where the administrator turnover reflects improper conduct. We hence propose in new §§ 424.530(a)(24) and 424.535(a)(28) to have the authority to deny or revoke a hospice's enrollment if the hospice changes its administrator within 36 months following the hospice's initial enrollment or its most recent change in administrator. The revocation effective date under § 424.535(g)(1)(xxviii) would be the date on which CMS determines that the hospice should be revoked under § 424.535(a)(28). We emphasize that our proposal would not represent an across-the-board prohibition against administrator changes within 36 months, for, again, we recognize that many such changes have no nefarious intent. It would simply afford us the authority to take measures should the situation warrant it.
3. Denial and/or Revocation of Old and New Owner in Ownership Changes
We earlier referenced § 424.551, which requires DMEPOS suppliers to enroll as a new supplier and obtain a survey and accreditation if they undergo a non-exempt CIMO. A similar 36-month CIMO provision is in § 424.550(b)(1) for hospices and HHAs. The main purposes of this “36-month rule” are twofold. First, it helps prevent “flipping”, whereby a provider enrolls in Medicare after receiving a survey and/or accreditation and then promptly sells the business to another party such that the latter need not receive a survey/accreditation. This makes it harder for CMS to confirm that the provider under its new ownership meets all Medicare requirements. Second, and even if “flipping” is not involved, the 36-month rule enables CMS to fully scrutinize the provider and the new owner via the initial enrollment and survey/accreditation processes.
Considering the failures of some providers to comply with the 36-month rule as well as efforts to circumvent it (such as by concealing the ownership change from CMS), we proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule to give CMS the authority to deny or revoke enrollment under §§ 424.530(a)(22) or 424.535(a)(25) if the provider does not comply with the provisions of, as applicable, § 424.550(b)(1) or § 424.551. Yet other ownership changes—depending on their particular facts—can at times pose program integrity risks, such as: (1) HHA, hospice, and DMEPOS supplier CIMOs occurring outside the 36-month period; and (2) CIMOs involving provider types that are not subject to a 36-month rule (such as skilled nursing facilities). Of considerable concern to us are situations where the owner of a provider that presents serious program integrity risks attempts to sell the business to another party, perhaps as part of a larger fraud operation. The following examples are illustrative:
Example 1
—U owns Ambulance Supplier V, which has 20 employees. V was recently reactivated after having been deactivated for non-compliance with enrollment requirements. Both U and V are now under investigation for potential fraud. U decides to sell the company to W, who has previously been revoked from Medicare and intends to change V's name but retain its employees. A Form CMS-855B enrollment application is submitted to report the planned sale, though the sale is not scheduled to occur for another 60 days.
Example 2
—X has owned Hospice Y for 5 years (outside of § 424.550(b)'s 36-month window). X sells Y to Z, but neither X nor Z report the sale to CMS, in violation of the requirement to report ownership changes within 30 days. X thus remains on record with CMS as the owner even though Z is the actual owner.
Both scenarios are disconcerting. In the first: (i) U might be selling V in hopes that doing so would end the investigation of U's activities; and (ii) the company—which remains under investigation—is being sold to a party with a prior revocation. In the second, the failure to report means that Medicare monies may be going to an entity whose new owner has not been vetted by CMS—at potentially significant risk to the Medicare program. The apparent risks that U, V, and W (for W, based on its prior revocation) pose and the non-compliance of X and Z raise serious questions as to whether any of them can be relied upon as current or future partners of the Medicare program. Since neither of these two situations is directly covered by §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551, we believe additional safeguards are needed to address problematic ownership changes. We accordingly propose the following in new § 424.536.
In paragraph (a), we propose that CMS, as applicable to the situation, may deny or revoke the enrollment of any provider or supplier involved in a change in majority ownership if CMS determines that the—
The seller, buyer, or any provider or supplier involved in the change in majority ownership failed to comply with Medicare enrollment requirements; or
The change in majority ownership, the seller, the buyer, or any provider or supplier involved in the change of majority ownership poses an undue risk
(
printed page 74741)
of fraud, waste, and abuse to the Medicare program.
Using our two examples, CMS could revoke V's enrollment due to U's attempt to forestall the investigation into U's activities if CMS determines this presents an undue fraud, waste, or abuse risk; if the sale of the business to W proceeds and W tries to reenroll V, CMS could deny the enrollment on the same “undue risk” basis. Regarding the second, neither the seller nor the buyer reported the change. This means that Y's enrollment could be revoked. Too, if Z tries to reenroll Y, CMS could deny the enrollment: (1) because Medicare requirements involving the CIMO were not met; and/or (ii) if CMS determines that an undue risk exists.
We recognize that previously proposed §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25)—as well as existing § 424.535(a)(9), which permits revocation for failing to timely report changes in ownership—may address some problematic CIMO situations. Yet proposed § 424.536 would go further in two ways. First, and unlike §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25), it would cover all CIMOs regardless of the provider or supplier type or the sale's timing. Second, denial or revocation under § 424.536 would be permitted based on an undue risk of fraud, waste, and abuse. Section 424.536 would hence enable CMS to address a greater number of circumstances surrounding a CIMO, although CMS could still utilize §§ 424.530(a)(22), 424.535(a)(9), or 424.535(a)(25) in lieu of or in conjunction with § 424.536 if the conditions for invoking any of the three former provisions exist.
In new § 424.536(b), we propose that paragraph (a) could be applied regardless of whether the provider's or supplier's name, identity, or location changes due to the CIMO. While CIMOs are sometimes accompanied by such changes, this does not negate the risk or non-compliance involved. Indeed, if we exempted § 424.536's application if the buyer changed the entity's name or identity, buyers might do precisely this to avoid a § 424.536 revocation. This concern of ours is why a number of our current denial and revocation reasons permit revocation under any of the provider's current or former names, numerical identifiers, or business identities.
In paragraph (c), we propose that a CIMO under § 424.536 occurs when a party acquires more than a 50 percent direct ownership interest in a provider (including via the cumulative effect of asset sales, stock transfers, consolidations, or mergers); this comports with the general CIMO definition in § 424.502. However, and consistent with our prior discussion, a § 424.536 CIMO could take place regardless of the provider type involved (for example, ambulance suppliers, HHAs), whether the CIMO occurred within 36 months of initial enrollment or the most recent CIMO, or whether the change in majority ownership requires a new, initial enrollment.
In paragraph (d), we propose that nothing in § 424.536 would negate the requirement that an HHA, hospice, or DMEPOS supplier enroll as a new provider or supplier and be surveyed/accredited if §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551 applies. This would merely remind stakeholders that the latter two provisions are separate and distinct from proposed § 424.536's denial and revocation authority.
Sections 424.530 and 424.535 contain procedures for denials and revocations (in addition to the denial and revocation grounds listed in §§ 424.530(a) and 424.535(a)). These procedures include, for example, reapplication and reenrollment bars, revocation effective dates, and specifications for submitting claims for services furnished before a revocation. To ensure these procedures apply to § 424.536 actions—that is, to directly tie § 424.536 to §§ 424.530 and 424.535, we propose to add new §§ 424.530(a)(27) and § 424.535(a)(32) by which CMS could deny or revoke under § 424.530 or § 424.535 if it determines that denial or revocation (as applicable) is warranted under § 424.536; the revocation effective date per new § 424.535(g)(1)(xxxii) would be the date on which CMS determines that the provider should be revoked under § 424.535(a)(32). Due to the breadth of § 424.536's provisions (such as its distinct definition of change in majority ownership), we believe our proposed approach is sounder than including all of § 424.536 within § 424.530 and § 424.535.
4. Other Improper Activity
Section 424.535(a)(7) permits revocation if the provider knowingly sells to or allows another individual or entity to use its billing number. (This does not include providers or suppliers who enter into a valid § 424.80 reassignment of benefits or a § 489.18 change of ownership.) While this provision has existed for many years, we have long been concerned about its narrowness. It only addresses a specific, unique scenario without capturing other very concerning situations directly or indirectly related to the provider's improper use of its enrollment, billing number, electronic funds transfer (EFT) arrangement, or other aspect of its relationship with Medicare. For example, there have been instances where an enrolled provider secures access to Medicare Beneficiary Identifiers and sells them to outside parties for nefarious purposes. Yet no existing revocation reason explicitly addresses such behavior. We believe § 424.535(a)(7) must be expanded to incorporate a wider range of inappropriate conduct. We thus propose to revise this paragraph to permit revocation if the provider engages in improper activity related to its Medicare enrollment, any billing number or identifier, or EFT arrangement. We would also change the paragraph title from “Misuse of billing number” to simply “Improper activity.” (For purposes of § 424.535(a)(7), the term “improper” would have its plain language meaning.) In addition, the § 424.535(a)(7) effective date would be that which we proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule at revised § 424.535(g)(1)(vii)—namely, the date on which the conduct resulting in the revocation occurred.
We acknowledge that this is a broad expansion of § 424.535(a)(7). We do not intend for this provision to supplant other current revocation grounds addressing inappropriate conduct (for example, abusive or non-compliant prescribing under § 424.535(a)(14)). In fact, we expect to utilize revised § 424.535(a)(7) only in exceptional circumstances. Nonetheless, the vast array of potential scenarios involving such conduct requires that we close all regulatory gaps that could permit the provider to remain enrolled and continue its behavior, hence the need for § 424.535(a)(7).
F. Verification of Identity and Risk Posed by Foreign and Domestic Owners and Managing Employees
Although CMS has means of validating the identities of enrolling physicians, enrolling practitioners, and an organizational provider's individual owners and managing employees, such means are mostly limited to reviewing the individual's legal name and social security number (SSN) against the Social Security Number Verification Service (SSNVN). This presents two significant problems.
One is that we have seen a disturbing increase in Medicare provider identity theft. Unscrupulous individuals and entities have attempted to: (1) enroll in and bill Medicare using the SSNs (and other identifiers) of bona fide physicians and practitioners; and (2) shield their actual (and problematic) owners and managing employees by instead listing on the Form CMS-855 application the
(
printed page 74742)
stolen identities of other persons as their owning and managing individuals. This has in certain instances permitted nefarious parties to enroll in Medicare—either directly or through an organization in which the party is the actual owner—and commit fraud because CMS' identity verification vehicles are limited.
The second dilemma is that providers sometimes list foreign owners and managing employees/organizations on the Form CMS-855. While there is no existing Medicare provider enrollment prohibition against a provider having a foreign owning or managing party, validation of the party's identity becomes difficult if no SSN or tax identification number (TIN) is included as many foreign parties lack one. The foreign status of such parties also makes it hard to confirm their specific location and any adverse legal history the party has (such as a criminal conviction or sanction). All this, in turn, can leave us unable to ascertain whether said foreign party poses a program integrity risk to Medicare—a vital consideration given the Medicare fraud schemes we have seen involving foreign nationals. Accordingly, although we are not seeking to bar foreign ownership or management of Medicare providers at this time, we still must strive to prevent potential threats to Medicare.
We believe the foregoing situations require that CMS have additional means of validating domestic and foreign identities and of reviewing possible risks posed by such parties. We hence propose the following regulatory revisions.
First, § 424.510(d)(2) outlines documentation that providers must submit as part of the enrollment process. Paragraph (d)(2)(ii) addresses documents that may be needed to uniquely identify the provider (though specific types of documents are not listed). To ensure our ability to verify the provider's identity and other data beyond what we currently require (such as the IRS CP-575 for TINs and legal business names), we propose the following:
A new provision in paragraph (d)(2)(ii) by which CMS could require an individual provider, owner, managing employee, general or limited partner, or corporate officer or director to submit a copy of their driver's license, passport, social security card, birth certificate, or similar documentation if CMS determines it is needed to validate their identity. We emphasize that we would not ask for any of these documents as a matter of course but only if: (1) other verification means are unsuccessful; or (2) we suspect a possible case of identity theft. The overwhelming majority of providers would not have to submit them.
To revise paragraph (d)(2)(iii), which permits CMS to require any other documentation needed to validate the data on the enrollment application, including, but not limited to, “documentation regarding the provider's or supplier's ownership or management.” In paragraph (C) thereof, we would insert “domestic or foreign” between “provider's or supplier's” and “ownership.” This would supplement our change to paragraph (d)(2)(ii) by reiterating our ability to request any documentation needed to validate ownership or management, including foreign.
Second, we propose in new §§ 424.530(a)(25) and 424.535(a)(30) that we may deny or revoke a provider's enrollment if the provider has a domestic or foreign owner, managing employee, managing organization, general or limited partner, or corporate officer or director: (1) whose identity or location cannot be confirmed; or (2) that CMS determines poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, or abuse to Medicare. An example of such a risk might be that the foreign party is based in a nation in which other persons and entities have been (or suspected to have been) involved in Federal health care program (including Medicare) fraud—though we emphasize that there are other factual scenarios in which an undue risk could arise, including with respect to domestic owners, managers, etc., as well as situations not involving identity verification. To a degree, our proposal is similar to existing §§ 424.530(a)(13) and 424.535(a)(19), albeit perhaps with a greater emphasis on risks posed by owners and managers themselves than on affiliations involving those parties. Indeed, it would be somewhat illogical to permit denial or revocation based on affiliations but not on individual threats that the parties in those relationships might present.
The effective date of a § 424.535(a)(30) revocation would, under § 424.535(g)(1)(xxx), be the date on which CMS determines that the provider should be revoked under this paragraph.
G. Medicaid and CHIP Provider Enrollment Reforms
As previously described, the Medicaid program (title XIX of the Act) is a joint Federal and State health care program that covers approximately 67 million low income-individuals.
States have considerable flexibility when administering their Medicaid programs within a broad Federal framework, and programs vary from State to State. CHIP (title XXI of the Act) is a joint Federal and State health care program that provides health care coverage to over 7 million children in families with incomes too high to qualify for Medicaid, but too low to afford private coverage.
In operating Medicaid and CHIP, and as required by sections 1902(a)(78) and 2107(e)(1)(D) of the Act, respectively, each State requires providers to enroll in order to furnish, order, prescribe, refer, or certify eligibility for Medicaid or CHIP items or services in that State.
[
155
]
States may also establish their own provider enrollment requirements, which must be met in addition to the applicable Federal provider enrollment requirements. Similar to Medicare provider enrollment, the purposes of the Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment processes are to ensure that providers: (1) meet all Medicaid or CHIP requirements (and any other State-specific or Federal requirements); (2) are qualified to furnish, order, prescribe, refer, or certify Medicaid and CHIP services, items, and drugs; and (3) are eligible to receive payment, where applicable.
Different States may have different provider enrollment processes in operating their Medicaid and CHIP programs. However, all States must comply with Federal Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment statutory and regulatory requirements, including those in part 455, subparts B and E.
