1. Principal Purposes of Medicaid and CHIP Provider Enrollment Proposals
There are several key reasons for our proposed Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment revisions in this proposed rule.
First, we have not updated part 455's provider enrollment provisions in a comprehensive, wide-ranging fashion since the previously noted February 2, 2011, final rule. As certain enrollment terminology and requirements have become outdated or otherwise need enhancement given this long passage of time, we believe revisions to part 455 are warranted.
Second, the February 2, 2011, final rule emphasized the value of consistency between programs by establishing, for all three programs,
(
printed page 74743)
common provider enrollment screening levels (limited, moderate and high) and application fee requirements. We also in that rule based other new Medicaid enrollment provisions partly on our stated desire for greater conformity to Medicare enrollment requirements. This included, for example, § 455.104(b)(1)(ii), in which we required disclosing entities, fiscal agents, and managed care entities to disclose the date of birth (DOB) and social security number (SSN) of any person with an ownership or control interest in the entity. (We similarly require owning and managing individuals of Medicare providers and suppliers to disclose their DOBs and SSNs.)
Various statutory provisions also emphasize consistency among programs. For example, under section 1902(kk)(3) of the Act, States must require providers to comply with the same requirements regarding disclosure of certain affiliations that also apply to Medicare under section 1866(j)(5) of the Act. Section 2107(e)(1) of the Act, meanwhile, makes the requirements of section 1902(kk) of the Act—including the screening, enrollment, and disclosure requirements—applicable to CHIP.
Yet the issue is not merely consistency between Medicare and Medicaid/CHIP. As already noted, and while all States must comply with the enrollment provisions in part 455, States often have different State-based Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment requirements and processes. This can prove challenging for providers located in multiple States, for this could necessitate adherence to different requirements for many different State programs. We believe that harmonizing certain requirements via updates to part 455 could ease the burden on providers enrolling in (or enrolled in) multiple States' Medicaid programs and CHIPs. We emphasize, though, that our revisions are not intended to remove the States' traditional and general discretion over the requirements and operations of these programs.
Third, we believe it is critical to provide States with further means of preventing and combating potential and actual fraud, waste, and abuse. We presently have numerous grounds for which we can deny or revoke a Medicare provider's enrollment under §§ 424.530 and 424.535, respectively. These grounds address a broader range of circumstances than the Medicaid and CHIP denial and termination reasons specified at § 455.416. While some States may have State-specific denial and termination grounds beyond those in § 455.416, we are uncertain whether they adequately cover the many situations that could justify taking denial or termination action against a provider. To help States address such cases and protect Medicaid and CHIP monies and beneficiaries, we are proposing additional grounds for the State to deny or terminate a provider's Medicaid or CHIP enrollment, most of which mirror the existing Medicare grounds in §§ 424.530 and 424.535.
The proposed changes in section V.G. of this proposed rule are generally discussed in the numerical order of the applicable regulatory provision in part 455. Unless noted otherwise, all references to Medicaid (for example, “Medicaid provider enrollments”) should be read to include CHIP.

Section 1902(kk)(1), under which the State must comply with the process for screening providers and suppliers under this title, as established by the Secretary under section 1866(j)(2) of the Act.
Section 1902(a)(27) of the Act provides general authority for the Secretary to require provider agreements under the Medicaid State Plans with every person or institution providing services under the State plan. Section 2107(e) of the Act, which provides that certain title XIX and title XI provisions apply to States under title XXI.
3. Definitions (§§ 455.2 and 455.101)
We propose to: (1) revise several definitions in §§ 455.2 and 455.101 to clarify existing processes and enhance conformity to Medicare enrollment definitions; and (2) add several definitions to § 455.101.
a. “Conviction or Convicted”
The current definition of “Conviction or Convicted” in § 455.2 reads, “a judgment of conviction has been entered by a Federal, State, or local court, regardless of whether an appeal from that judgment is pending.” We propose to change this to, “has the same meaning as the definition of `convicted' in
42 CFR 1001.2
.” That definition states:
A judgment of conviction has been entered against an individual or entity by a Federal, State or local court, regardless of whether—
++ There is a post-trial motion or an appeal pending; or
++ The judgment of conviction or other record relating to the criminal conduct has been expunged or otherwise removed.
A Federal, State or local court has made a finding of guilt against an individual or entity;
A Federal, State or local court has accepted a plea of guilty or nolo contendere by an individual or entity; or
An individual or entity has entered into participation in a first offender, deferred adjudication, or other program or arrangement where judgment of conviction has been withheld.
We believe this definition is more detailed, thorough, and robust than that currently in § 455.2; it would accordingly provide greater clarity as to the types of convictions falling within § 455.2's purview. Moreover, we reference the § 1001.2 definition in §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3), which permit, respectively, denial or revocation of Medicare enrollment based on a felony conviction. Since, as we discuss later, we are proposing similar felony provisions in this rule, we believe that a concomitant definition of “Conviction or Convicted” in part 455 is warranted.
b. Definitions Related to Disclosures
As later addressed in greater detail, a “disclosing entity” is required under § 455.104(b) to report certain information to the State. These data include but are not limited to:
Any person (individual or corporation) with an ownership or control interest in the disclosing entity.
Whether the person (individual or corporation) disclosed in the previous

bullet is related to another person with an ownership or control interest in the disclosing entity as a spouse, parent, child, or sibling.

A central purpose of this information is to help the State confirm that the provider is not under the direct or indirect control of an excluded party. Various definitions in current § 455.101 apply to this disclosure requirement. These include:
“Disclosing entity,”
which means “a Medicaid provider (other than an individual practitioner or group of practitioners), or a fiscal agent.”
“Other disclosing entity,”
which means “any other Medicaid disclosing entity and any entity that does not participate in Medicaid but is required to disclose certain ownership and control information because of participation in any of the programs established under titles V, XVIII, or XX of the Act.” This includes:—

++ Any Medicare intermediary or carrier; and
++ Any entity (other than an individual practitioner or group of practitioners) that furnishes, or arranges for the furnishing of, health-related services for which it claims payment under any plan or program established under title V or title XX of the Act.
“Person with an ownership or control interest,”
which means a person or corporation that:

We propose to revise or supplement several of these definitions as follows:
c. Addition of “Managing Organization”
We propose to add a definition of “managing organization” to § 455.101 that states: “Managing organization means an entity that exercises operational or managerial control over or that directly or indirectly conducts the day-to-day operations of a provider, either under contract or through some other arrangement.” This definition, which mirrors § 424.502's definition of this term, would be used for our proposed requirement (discussed later) that providers furnish data on entities that manage them.
d. Revisions to the Definition of “Person with an Ownership or Control Interest”
The opening language of this definition states: “Person with an ownership or control interest means a person or corporation that . . . .” We propose to change this to read: “Person or organization with an ownership or control interest is one that . . . .” We do not believe organizational interests should be limited to corporations; any organizational interest in a provider is pertinent regardless of whether it is a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, etc.
We are not proposing to concomitantly revise paragraph (e) of this definition, which includes officers and directors of disclosing entities that are corporations as “person[s] with an ownership or control interest”. As previously noted, sections 1124 and 1124A of the Act require providers to disclose certain information about various persons and entities associated with the provider. Per section 1124(a)(3)(B) of the Act, this includes “officer[s] or [director[s] of the entity if the entity is organized as a corporation.” To remain consistent with section 1124(a)(3)(B) of the Act, only officers and directors of corporations (rather than, for example, of limited liability companies) would fall within paragraph (e).
4. Expanded Medicaid and CHIP Provider Enrollment Disclosure Requirements
We propose the following changes to § 455.104:
The current version of § 455.104(b)(1)(i) requires the disclosure of the name and address of any person (individual or corporation) with an ownership or control interest in the disclosing entity, fiscal agent, or managed care entity. The addresses for corporate entities must include (as applicable) the primary business address, every business location, and P.O. Box address. We propose two changes to this paragraph.
First, we would change the language that reads “any person (individual or corporation) with an ownership or control interest” to “any person or organization with an ownership or control interest.” We believe that disclosures of owning or controlling organizations should be made irrespective of whether the entity is a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, or other form of organization. It is important that States can screen all owning and controlling parties for potential program integrity issues. Second, we propose to remove the word “corporate” from the second sentence of paragraph (b)(1)(i). This is to clarify that the addresses of any organization under paragraph (b)(1), regardless of the entity's structure, must be disclosed.
Section 455.104(b)(1)(iii) requires in part the disclosure of an “Other tax identification number (in the case of a corporation) with an ownership or control interest in the disclosing entity (or fiscal agent or managed care entity) . . .” We propose to change this to reference the tax identification number of any organization with an ownership or control interest in, or that serves as a managing organization of, the disclosing entity (or fiscal agent or managed care entity). This revision would: (1) accord with our proposed change to § 455.104(b)(1)(i) by removing the reference to corporations so that the paragraph applies to all organizations, regardless of type; and (2) add managing organizations to the paragraph's purview.
As we stated in the earlier noted September 10, 2019, final rule, a managing entity often has as much (or more) day-to-day control over a provider or supplier as an owner. Given the important roles that managing organizations have over providers' operations, we believe that States must know the organizations' identities to help ensure that Medicaid and CHIP program integrity is maintained. We note that Medicare providers and suppliers have long been required to disclose managing organizations as part of the enrollment process.
Section 455.104(b)(2) generally requires disclosure of the identities of persons reported per paragraph (b)(1) who are related to each other. We propose to change the language “person (individual or corporation) with an ownership or control interest” in that paragraph to “person or organization with an ownership or control interest.” This change would conform to our proposed revision of the definition of “person with an ownership or control interest” in § 455.101.
(
printed page 74745)
Section 455.104(b)(4) requires the disclosure of “the name, address, date of birth, and Social Security Number of any managing employee of the disclosing entity (or fiscal agent or managed care entity).” We propose to redesignate this as new § 455.104(b)(4)(i) and to add new § 455.104(b)(4)(ii) to read: “The name, address, and tax identification number of any managing organization of the disclosing entity (or fiscal agent or managed care entity).” This is consistent with our proposed revisions to § 455.104(b)(1) involving managing entities.
Meanwhile, paragraph (a) of § 455.106 states that before the Medicaid agency enters into or renews a provider agreement, or at any time upon written request by the Medicaid agency, the provider must disclose to the Medicaid agency the identity of any person who:
Has ownership or control interest in the provider, or is an agent or managing employee of the provider (§ 455.106(a)(1)); and
Has been convicted of a criminal offense related to that person's involvement in any program under Medicare, Medicaid, or the title XX services program since the inception of those programs (§ 455.106(a)(2)).
We propose to revise paragraph (a) to expand the types of adverse actions that must be reported to the State. We would require that before the State enters into or renews a provider agreement, or at any time upon written request by the State, the provider must identify whether the provider, any person or organization with an ownership or control interest in the provider, or any agent, managing employee or managing organization of the provider, under any current or former name, numerical identifier, or business identity—
Was, within the preceding 10 years, convicted of a Federal or State felony offense (regardless of type);
Has been revoked or terminated, or is currently suspended, from participation in any State Medicaid program, CHIP, Medicare, or any other Federal health care program;
Is currently subject to a payment suspension under § 455.23 or under CHIP or Medicare; or
Has had its health care license revoked—or whose license is currently suspended—in any State. (This includes situations where the individual or entity voluntarily surrendered the license in lieu of disciplinary action.)
These four actions would be included in revised paragraph (a)(1) and new paragraphs (a)(3), (4), and (5). We also would expand existing paragraph (a)(2)'s scope to include misdemeanors involving sexual assault or financial misconduct; this is because we proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule to permit denial or revocation of a provider's enrollment based on a misdemeanor conviction involving sexual assault or financial misconduct.
There are two main reasons for this proposal. First, these data—some of which, in the Medicare context, must currently be reported on the applicable Medicare provider enrollment application (OMB Control No.: 0938-0685)—would give States greater insight into potential program integrity threats that the disclosed party may pose. This, in turn, could further safeguard the Medicaid program, CHIP, and their beneficiaries. Second, and as already noted and discussed in more detail later, we are proposing a number of new Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment denial and termination reasons. Since several of these grounds involve the reportable actions under proposed revised § 455.106(a), we believe this information would help the States determine whether a denial or termination is warranted.
We particularly note the proposed addition of the language “under any current or former name, numerical identifier, or business identity.” This language has been used with several existing Medicare denial and revocation reasons in §§ 424.530 and 424.535 for a number of years. The purpose is to enable us to take action against problematic parties notwithstanding any identity change. We believe States must have the same ability. We do not believe a party's demonstrated program integrity risk disappears upon a mere change in name, especially when the entity or person makes this change to circumvent an existing adverse action. Indeed, we previously saw situations where a revoked Medicare provider changed its name to evade its revocation and subsequent bar against reenrolling in Medicare. In our view, the party's risk remains, and States must base their payment safeguard actions more on said risk than on the party's current name or identity.
Existing § 455.106(c) states that the Medicaid agency may refuse—
To enter into or renew an agreement with a provider if any person who has an ownership or control interest in the provider, or who is an agent or managing employee of the provider, has been convicted of a criminal offense related to that person's involvement in any program established under Medicare, Medicaid, or the title XX Services Program; or
To enter into or may terminate a provider agreement if it determines that the provider did not fully and accurately make any disclosure required under § 455.106(a).
We propose to delete this paragraph because these and all other denial and termination reasons in subpart B would, per this proposed rule, be included in revised § 455.416. This would ensure that all denials and terminations are addressed in one section rather than split between multiple sections.
5. New Bases for Medicaid and CHIP Provider Enrollment Denial and Termination
a. Introduction
Pursuant to the Secretary's general authority under section 1102 of the Act to prescribe regulations for the efficient administration of the Medicaid program and CHIP, we are proposing a number of additional denial and termination reasons. Our proposed grounds would—
Be mandatory, meaning the State (except as discussed in the next bullet) would be required to deny or terminate enrollment if the facts of the case fall within those covered by the applicable denial or termination reason; and
Permit the State in most cases to forgo mandatory denial or termination if the State determines that the denial or termination would not be in the best interests of its Medicaid program or CHIP.
We recognize that virtually all of our Medicare denial and termination grounds are discretionary. Yet we believe that making our proposed Medicaid denial and termination reasons mandatory—with the best interests exception—is advisable, in part because it would be consistent with the mandatory nature of (and best interests exceptions within) most of
42 CFR part 455
's existing denial and termination grounds. Moreover, and notwithstanding our desire for greater consistency between Medicare and State Medicaid provider enrollment programs, we maintain that substantial conformity between States in how they interpret and carry out Part 455's denial and termination reasons is also important. Indeed, this was a principal consideration behind the aforementioned February 2, 2011, final rule's establishment of additional provider enrollment requirements in subparts B and E of Part 455. We believe that having consistent, uniform interpretations of Federal Medicaid provider enrollment provisions in Part 455 is preferable to inconsistent ones and would reduce provider uncertainty
(
printed page 74746)
regarding the meaning of these requirements.
b. Listing of Current Denial and Termination Reasons in § 455.416
The following denial and termination reasons are in existing § 455.416:
Under paragraph (a), the State must terminate the enrollment of any provider where any person with a 5 percent or greater direct or indirect ownership interest in the provider did not submit timely and accurate information and cooperate with any screening methods required under this subpart.
Under paragraph (b), the State must deny or terminate enrollment if a person with a 5 percent or greater direct or indirect ownership interest in the provider has been convicted of a criminal offense related to that person's involvement with Medicare, Medicaid, or title XXI of the Act in the last 10 years.
Under paragraph (c), the State must deny or terminate enrollment of any provider that is terminated under Medicare or under the Medicaid program or CHIP of any other State and is currently included in the termination database under § 455.417.
Under paragraph (d), the State must deny or terminate enrollment if the provider or a person with an ownership or control interest or who is an agent or managing employee of the provider fails to submit timely or accurate information.
Under paragraph (e), the State must deny or terminate enrollment if the provider, or any person with a 5 percent or greater direct or indirect ownership interest in the provider, fails to submit sets of fingerprints in a form and manner to be determined by the Medicaid agency within 30 days of a CMS or State Medicaid agency request.
Under paragraph (f), the State must deny or terminate enrollment if the provider fails to permit access to provider locations for any site visits under § 455.432.
Under paragraphs (g)(1) and (2), the State may deny or terminate enrollment if CMS or the State Medicaid agency—
++ Determines that the provider has falsified any information provided on the application; or
++ Cannot verify the identity of any provider applicant.
Paragraphs (b), (d), (e) and (f) state, however, that the State is not required to deny or terminate enrollment if it determines that denial or termination of enrollment is not in the best interests of the Medicaid program, and the State documents that determination in writing.
Also, under § 455.107(g), the State must deny a provider's enrollment if it determines under § 455.107 that a particular affiliation (as that term is defined under § 455.101) poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, or abuse.
We are proposing to delete existing § 455.416(a) through (g). This is primarily because some of these provisions fall within the larger scope of our proposed grounds. To avoid duplication and confusion by having two separate reasons involving similar conduct, we would incorporate the existing grounds within the proposed ones to the maximum extent possible. Those current § 455.416 grounds not falling within one of our proposed reasons would remain in § 455.416, though under a different paragraph designation and, in some cases, with revisions.
To summarize, revised § 455.416 would include: (1) the incorporation of several existing provisions within our proposed reasons; (2) the retention of several existing grounds with modifications; (3) the transfer of several denial and termination reasons from §§ 455.104, 455.106, and 455.107 to § 455.416; and (4) the incorporation of a number of Medicare denial and revocation grounds into Medicaid within § 455.416, though in most cases with the former's required factors and discretionary application replaced by the “best interests” exception referenced in current § 455.416.

Excluded from Medicare, Medicaid, and any other Federal health care program, as defined in § 1001.2 of this chapter, in accordance with section 1128, 1128A, 1156, 1842, 1862, 1867, or 1892 of the Act.

In addition, revised § 455.416(e) would effectively incorporate existing § 455.106(c)(2), which permits denial or termination if the provider fails to make a required disclosure under § 455.106(a).
(6) Felony Convictions (§ 455.416(f))
In revised paragraph (f), we would mirror the current Medicare denial and revocation reasons in §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3) regarding felony convictions. We propose that the State must deny or terminate enrollment if the provider, any person or organization with an ownership or control interest in the provider, or any managing employee or managing organization of the provider was, within the preceding 10 years, convicted (as that term is defined in § 1001.2) of a Federal or State felony offense that the State determines is detrimental to the best interests of its Medicaid program or CHIP and their beneficiaries. Offenses would include, but not be limited in scope or severity to—
Felony crimes against persons, such as murder, rape, assault, and other similar crimes for which the individual was convicted;
Financial crimes, such as extortion, embezzlement, income tax evasion, insurance fraud and other similar crimes for which the individual was convicted;
Any felony that placed the Medicaid program or CHIP or its beneficiaries at immediate risk, such as a malpractice suit that results in a conviction of criminal neglect or misconduct; and
Any felony that would result in mandatory exclusion under section 1128(a) of the Act.
We have long believed that any felony conviction, regardless of the type, raises questions as to whether the provider can be a reliable participant in Medicare. We believe the same concern would apply in the Medicaid program or CHIP. States thus must do whatever possible to prevent unnecessary risks to Medicaid or CHIP and those programs' beneficiaries. Nonetheless, under our proposal the State would have discretion to determine what types of convictions are “detrimental to the best interest of the Medicaid program or CHIP or their beneficiaries” and could utilize the “best interests” exception if it deems warranted.
(7) False or Misleading Information (§ 455.416(g))
Under existing § 455.416(g)(1), the State may deny Medicaid or CHIP enrollment if CMS or the State determines that the provider has falsified any information provided on the application. Per existing § 424.530(a)(4), we can deny Medicare enrollment if the provider or supplier has submitted false or misleading information on the enrollment application to gain enrollment in the Medicare program; offenders may be referred to the OIG for investigation and possible criminal, civil, or administrative sanctions.
We propose to redesignate § 455.416(g)(1) as revised § 455.416(g), combine it with § 424.530(a)(4)'s language, and add further clarification. Under revised § 455.416(g), the State must deny or terminate Medicaid or CHIP enrollment if the provider submits false or misleading information to (or omits information from) the Medicaid program or CHIP to gain or maintain enrollment.
We believe that providers submitting false or misleading data or omitting data to become or remain enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP potentially pose the same level of risk to these two programs as they do to Medicare. The language “in order to gain or maintain enrollment” is particularly important because it clarifies two aspects of existing practice in the Medicare context. First, the requirement to submit complete and truthful information is not restricted to initial applications but also applies to revalidations, changes of information, and all other application types. Our proposed inclusion of “maintain” (as opposed to merely gaining enrollment, which implies initial submissions) is therefore necessary; providers must always submit truthful and accurate information to Medicaid and CHIP. Second, we believe that any false, misleading, or omissive submission to Medicaid or CHIP—regardless of whether it was made via the enrollment application, supporting documentation,
(
printed page 74748)
or otherwise—should constitute grounds for denial or termination. The specific format of submission, in our view, is less crucial than the actual submission.
Under current § 455.416(g)(2), States may deny or terminate the provider's Medicaid or CHIP enrollment if CMS or the State Medicaid agency cannot verify the identity of any provider applicant. We propose to delete this provision because we would include it within the general “Non-compliance” category in § 455.416(e)(1)(iv)).
We note that while current paragraph (g)(1) is discretionary, we propose to make revised paragraph (g) mandatory (though with the “best interests” provision in proposed (g)(2)) to be consistent with most of our other proposed denial and termination grounds.
(8) Drug Enforcement Administration Certificates (§ 455.416(h))
The DEA implements and enforces titles II and III of the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970, and the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act, as amended, and collectively referred to as the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) (
21 U.S.C. 801-971
); the implementing regulations for these statutes are in
21 CFR parts 1300
through
1321
. The CSA makes possession of authority under State law to dispense controlled substances a requirement for both obtaining and maintaining a DEA Certificate of Registration.
Sections 424.530(a)(11) and 424.535(a)(13) state, in part, that we may deny or revoke a physician's or eligible professional's Medicare enrollment if the individual's DEA Certificate of Registration to dispense a controlled substance is currently suspended or revoked or is surrendered in response to an order to show cause. We believe that a DEA Certificate of Registration to prescribe controlled substances is akin to a State's requirement that a physician or eligible professional be licensed or certified by the State to furnish health care services. The loss of the ability to prescribe drugs via a suspension or revocation of a DEA Certificate indicates that the physician or eligible professional may be misusing or abusing their authority to prescribe such substances.
Yet those concerns are not limited to Medicare. Improper prescribing activities can harm Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries and program integrity as much as Medicare patients and program integrity. Hence, we propose in new § 455.416(h) that a State must deny or terminate enrollment if the physician's or practitioner's DEA certificate is currently suspended or revoked or is surrendered in response to an order to show cause, with the “best interests” provision included. The only difference would involve our use in § 455.416(h) of “practitioner” instead of “eligible professional,” since the former term is broader than
42 U.S.C. 1396b(t)(3)(B)
's somewhat narrow definition of the latter.
(9) Misuse of Enrollment (§ 455.416(i))
Under current § 424.535(a)(7), we may revoke Medicare enrollment if the provider or supplier knowingly sells to or allows another individual or entity to use its billing number. (This does not apply to providers or suppliers who enter into a valid reassignment of benefits as specified in § 424.80 or a change of ownership outlined in § 489.18.) This provision is meant to prevent providers from permitting others to utilize their Medicare enrollment. A provider's enrollment is restricted and unique to that provider. Each provider must individually meet and maintain compliance with the legal requirements specific to it and cannot use the credentials of other providers, suppliers, or other parties to do so. To permit another party to bill Medicare via the provider's enrollment would entirely undercut this principle; it could lead to fraudulent individuals and entities (or other parties that Medicare has not screened) billing the program and receiving payment under the provider's enrollment.
We have the same concerns regarding Medicaid and CHIP. Each Medicaid or CHIP enrollment is specific to the enrolled provider and does not extend to any other party. To help protect against the improper use of a provider's enrollment by other persons or entities, we propose in new § 455.416(i) that the State must terminate enrollment if the provider knowingly sells or allows another individual or entity to use its enrollment to bill Medicaid or CHIP. We believe the language “use its enrollment to bill Medicaid or CHIP” is more appropriate than “use its billing number.” The former is broader and can encompass any activity by which the other party bills Medicaid or CHIP via the provider's enrollment.
As with § 424.535(a)(7), there would be two exceptions to § 455.416(i). One would be for Medicaid and CHIP assignments of payment. Under § 447.10(g), payment for services provided by an individual practitioner may be made to—
The employer of the practitioner, if the practitioner is required as a condition of employment to turn over the practitioner's fees to the employer;
The facility in which the service is provided, if the practitioner has a contract under which the facility submits the claim; or
A foundation, plan or similar organization operating an organized health care delivery system, if the practitioner has a contract under which the organization submits the claim.
We believe these provisions are akin to those under § 424.80, whereby the physician or practitioner permits a party with whom it has an employment or contractual relationship to bill for and collect payment for the services the individual provides. We thus conclude that an exception for payments permitted under § 447.10(g) is appropriate.
The second exception involves changes of ownership. Because State laws vary regarding: (1) what constitutes a change of ownership; (2) the consequences of such a change; and (3) the vetting and screening process for ownership changes, we propose that a State would not be required to terminate a provider under § 455.416(i) if State law permits another individual or entity to bill Medicaid or CHIP under the provider's enrollment in a change of ownership situation.
As with most of our other proposed grounds, the “best interests” exception would be included within § 455.416(i).
(10) Abusive Prescribing or Ordering of Services, Items, or Drugs (New §§ 455.416(j) and (k))
Existing §§ 424.535(a)(14) and (21) permit revocation of Medicare enrollment if we determine that the physician or eligible professional has a pattern or practice of—
Prescribing Medicare-covered drugs that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries, or fails to meet Medicare requirements. (§ 424.535(a)(14)); or
Ordering, certifying, referring, or prescribing Medicare Part A or B services, items, or drugs that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries, or otherwise fails to meet Medicare requirements (§ 424.535(a)(21)).
We outlined our concerns about improper prescribing in our discussion of proposed § 455.416(h). The inappropriate ordering, certifying, or referring of services and items is equally concerning to us. If a physician or practitioner is improperly performing these activities, patient harm can ensue. For instance, a physician ordering tests that patients do not require could subject beneficiaries to dangerous and
(
printed page 74749)
unnecessary procedures. Moreover, Medicaid and CHIP funds would be unnecessarily spent on these tests.
We believe States should take action against these individuals, not only to protect Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries but also to safeguard the financial integrity of these programs. Accordingly, we propose to duplicate existing §§ 424.535(a)(14) and (21) in new § 455.416(j) and (k), though we note the following. First, all references in §§ 424.535(a)(14) and (21) to Medicare would be changed to “Medicaid or CHIP.” Second, to avoid overlap, we would not include improper prescribing within new § 455.416(k) because we believe § 455.416(j) would adequately address this situation. Section 455.416(k) would be limited to services and items. Third, any references in §§ 424.535(a)(14) and (21) to eligible professionals would be changed in § 455.416(j) and (k) to physician or practitioner. Fourth, both paragraphs would include the “best interests” exception.
6. Additional Medicaid and CHIP Provider Enrollment Proposals
a. Database Reviews (§ 455.436)
Section 455.436 lists databases that States must review when (1) enrolling Medicaid and CHIP providers and (2) confirming their eligibility to remain enrolled. Section 455.436(b) lists the Excluded Parties List System (EPLS) as one of these databases. As this database is now named the System for Award Management (SAM), we propose in § 455.436(b) to replace “Excluded Parties List System” with the former term. For the same reason, we propose to change “EPLS” in § 455.436(c) to “SAM.”
b. Screening Levels (§ 455.450)
Section 424.518 discusses the different levels at which Medicare must screen initial applications, revalidation applications, and other application submissions. The levels are limited, moderate, and high. The categories are generally based on the assessed degree of program integrity risk each provider or supplier type poses; those types presenting the highest risk (for example, hospices) are in the “high” category.
Section 455.450 addresses the screening levels applicable to Medicaid enrollment. The first sentence in its opening paragraph states: “A State Medicaid agency must screen all initial applications, including applications for a new practice location, and any applications received in response to a re-enrollment or revalidation of enrollment request based on a categorical risk level of `limited,' `moderate,' or `high.” Consistent with section 1902(kk)(1) of the Act—and as explained in the preamble to the aforementioned February 2, 2011, final rule—for provider types that exist in both Medicare and Medicaid, the State must assign providers to the same or higher risk category applicable under Medicare in accordance with § 424.518. To codify this requirement in regulatory text, we propose to amend the opening paragraph of § 455.450 to add the following language between this paragraph's two existing sentences: “For provider types that also exist in Medicare, the State must assign such providers to the same or higher risk category applicable under Medicare in accordance with § 424.518.”
c. Application Fees (§ 455.460)
Under § 455.460(a), the State must “collect the applicable application fee prior to executing a provider agreement from a prospective or reenrolling provider other than either of the following” persons or entities, which are listed in § 455.460(a)(1) and (2). We propose several changes to this section.
First, we propose to change the language “a prospective or re-enrolling provider” in paragraph (a) to “a prospective, revalidating or re-enrolling provider” to clarify that revalidating institutional providers, consistent with section 1866(j)(2)(C) of the Act and current practice, must pay an application fee.
Second, we propose to remove the language “either of” in paragraph (a) because all parties listed in paragraph (2) are, as applicable, exempt from the fee.
Third, the purpose of the application fee is to cover the costs of screening provider applications under subpart E. As already noted, States must screen a provider's application at the same or a higher level than we use for that same provider type in Medicare and as prescribed in § 424.518. For instance, hospitals under § 424.518(a)(1) are subject to the “limited” risk category of screening; under § 455.450, States, too, typically screen hospital applications using the “limited” risk category procedures. However, States have the discretion under § 455.452 to screen an application using additional or more stringent methods than those required by subpart E. This helps States address local or statewide conditions involving provider types that may present a higher risk of fraud, waste or abuse and thus require stricter screening.
Section 455.460(a)(2)(ii) states that providers that have already paid the application fee to a Medicare contractor or to another State are exempt from paying a second fee to the State. This is because the State may rely on the screening results of the Medicare enrollment or the other State enrollment. Yet this becomes problematic when the State believes that a higher level of screening is warranted with respect to the provider's Medicaid or CHIP enrollment. Some States have expressed reluctance to screen at higher levels under § 455.452 because of the inability to collect an application fee under § 455.460(a)(2) to cover the costs of such screening. This has led to instances where the State has been unable, for financial reasons, to use enhanced screening methods when the State believed they were necessary. We are concerned that this has resulted in certain Medicaid providers having been insufficiently screened.
Section 455.460(a)(2)(ii) contains the language “(p)roviders that have paid the applicable application fee to (A) a Medicare contractor, or (B) (a)nother State”. To address the previously mentioned concerns, we propose the following:
Redesignating paragraphs (a)(2)(ii), (a)(2)(ii)(A), and (a)(2)(ii)(B) as, respectively, paragraphs (a)(2)(ii)(A), (a)(2)(ii)(A)(
1
), and (a)(2)(ii)(A)(
2
);
Changing “providers that have paid the applicable application fee” to “Subject to paragraph (2)(ii)(B), providers that have paid the applicable fee. . .”; and
Establishing a revised paragraph (ii)(B) that reads: “Paragraphs (2)(ii)(A)(
1
) and (
2
) do not apply if the State is screening the provider at a higher level under § 455.450 than the Medicare contractor or other State to which the provider paid the fee. In this situation, the State may collect a fee from the provider that represents the cost of this additional screening above and beyond the level of screening the Medicare contractor or State performed under § 455.450. However, the State shall document the reason(s) for the enhanced screening.”
To illustrate how revised paragraph (ii)(B) would work, assume State A screened a fee-paying enrolling provider at the “moderate” level. Said provider now submits an enrollment application to State B, which believes the provider should be screened at the “high” level. State B's “high” level screening typically costs Y dollars and its “moderate” level screening X dollars. State B could require the provider to pay the difference between Y and X to reflect the additional screening activities; States would have the discretion to determine the cost of this additional screening. We believe that
(

We also note that revised paragraph (ii)(B) would only apply to providers that have paid the applicable fee to the Medicare contractor or other State. Providers that, for example, received a hardship exception from paying the fee to the Medicare contractor or other State would not have the pay the costs of the additional screening.
In summary, we believe that revised paragraph (ii)(B) would assist the States in their efforts to appropriately screen Medicaid and CHIP providers by removing the disincentive for elevated screening. This would, in turn, enhance Medicaid and CHIP program integrity. To ensure that States have sufficient grounds for requiring a fee under (ii)(B), though, we believe that States should document the need for the enhanced screening.
d. Monthly Reporting of Denials and Terminations to CMS
Consistent with sections 1902(kk)(8) and 1902(ll) of the Act as well as § 455.417, CMS operates a “termination database.” This database contains information on certain Medicaid and CHIP terminations and Medicare revocations. Per Sections 1902(kk)(8) and 1902(a)(41) of the Act, the State must report to the Secretary all its provider terminations under Medicaid and CHIP that are “for cause” (as defined in § 455.101) within 30 days after the effective date of the termination, which is the later of the effective date specified in the termination notice or the date appeal rights have been exhausted. Although CMS reviews these terminations in the database, the latter does not capture: (1) denials of Medicaid or CHIP enrollment; or (2) situations where the State chose not to deny or terminate enrollment based on a best interests determination. We believe that despite the termination database's usefulness, the lack of certain information about the State's denial and termination decisions hinders our ability to detect and address vulnerabilities in the Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment processes.
To address this gap, we propose in new § 455.418 that each State must submit to CMS on a monthly basis—and in a format required by CMS—the legal business and doing business names, address, TIN, and NPI of each provider (Medicaid or CHIP) whose enrollment, within the applicable monthly period, the State—
Denied or terminated under § 455.416. This must include—
++ The regulatory basis for the denial or termination.
++ The facts of the case and an explanation of how the State reached its decision.
Was required to deny or terminate under § 455.416 but declined to do so based on a best interests finding. This must include—
++ The regulatory basis for the prospective denial or termination; and
++ The facts of the case, an explanation of how the State reached its decision, and reasons for the State's best interests determination.
CMS would issue guidance to States on the required format should this provision be finalized.
In new paragraph (b), we would remind stakeholders that the requirements of § 455.418 would be in addition to, and not in lieu of, the reporting requirement under sections 1902(kk)(8) and 1902(a)(41). That said, they would only apply to denials or terminations pursuant to § 455.416 and not those under separate State authority that might meet the definition of “for cause” for purposes of those provisions.
H. Medicare Advantage Original Medicare Provider Enrollment Requirements
1. Background
a. General Overview
The Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (BBA) established a new Part C of the Medicare program, known as Medicare+Choice (M+C), effective January 1999. As part of the M+C program, the BBA authorized CMS to contract with public or private organizations to offer a variety of health plan options for enrollees, including both traditional managed care plans (such as those offered by HMOs, as defined in section 1876 of the Act) and new options not previously authorized. The M+C program was renamed the Medicare Advantage (MA) program under Title II of the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 (MMA) (
Pub. L. 108-173
), which was enacted on December 8, 2003. The MMA changed how benefits are established and payments are made; under the MMA, enrollees were able to choose from additional plan options. Also, Title I of the MMA established the Medicare prescription drug benefit (Part D) program and amended the MA program to allow most MA plans to offer prescription drug coverage.
All Medicare health plans (but not Program of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) organizations) that specify networks of providers from whom enrollees may obtain services must develop a network of qualified providers that meets CMS network adequacy standards as detailed in § 422.116. CMS reviews MA organizations' network of contracted providers on a routine basis, unless there is a triggering event that would require an expedited formal network review, such as a significant provider termination.
b. The 2016 and 2018 Part C Provider Enrollment Regulations
In November 2016, CMS issued a final rule (
81 FR 80170
) containing various requirements related to provider enrollment,
[
157
]
including the addition of §  422.222. This section required providers and suppliers that furnish health care items or services to a Medicare enrollee who receives their Medicare benefit through an MA organization to be enrolled in Original Medicare (also known as Medicare fee-for-service (FFS)) in an approved status no later than January 1, 2019. (The term “MA organization” refers to both organizations offering stand-alone MA plans and MA plans that provide drug coverage, otherwise known as MA-PD plans.)
The general purpose of this requirement was to ensure that MA providers and suppliers (hereafter collectively “providers” unless otherwise noted) were fully screened via the provider enrollment process used for Original Medicare Part A and Part B providers. As previously noted in this proposed rule, Original Medicare Part A and Part B provider enrollment screening is comprehensive. It involves the collection and verification of critical data such as the provider's identity, address, licensure and other qualifications, practice location, owners, managing employees, and adverse legal history. Depending on the provider type, it can also include site visits and fingerprint-based criminal background checks. The thoroughness of this process was invaluable in protecting the Medicare program from fraud, waste, and abuse as well as Medicare beneficiaries from unqualified providers. Given that many providers at the time underwent less robust screening by their prospective MA organizations before becoming MA
(
printed page 74751)
providers, we believed that our requirement would help safeguard the MA program and its beneficiaries (hereafter occasionally “enrollees”).
We began outreach efforts shortly after the November 2016, final rule's publication. We communicated with provider associations and MA organizations regarding, among other things, the purpose of the enrollment process, the rationale for the new enrollment requirement, and the mechanisms of completing and submitting an enrollment application. While the vast majority of MA providers and suppliers were already enrolled in Original Medicare and thus met the new MA provider enrollment requirement, over 100,000 were not. This led the MA community to raise concerns about the potential burden of this requirement, especially since MA providers also must undergo credentialing by their respective MA organizations.
In response to these concerns, we issued a final rule in April 2018 (
83 FR 16440
) that eliminated the MA provider enrollment requirement at §  422.222.
[
158
]
In its place, we established in § 422.222 a “preclusion list.” The preclusion list for contracted and non-contracted individuals and entities is a list of providers that are precluded from receiving payment for MA services and items they furnish. Per the definition of “preclusion list” in § 422.2, there are three ways individuals and entities can be added to the list:
The individual or entity is currently revoked from Medicare, is currently under a reenrollment bar, and CMS has determined that the underlying conduct that led to the revocation is detrimental to the best interests of the Medicare program.
The individual or entity has engaged in behavior for which CMS could have revoked the individual or entity to the extent applicable if they had been enrolled in Medicare, and CMS determines that the underlying conduct that would have led to the revocation is detrimental to the best interests of the Medicare program.
Regardless of whether they are or were enrolled in Medicare, the individual or entity has been convicted of a felony under Federal or State law within the previous 10 years that CMS deems detrimental to the best interests of the Medicare program. (We proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule (
91 FR 41216
) to expand this to include felony convictions against the individual or entity or an owner, managing employee, managing organization, director, or officer (as those terms are defined in §  424.502) thereof.))
For purposes of burden reduction, the April 2018 final rule also replaced the requirement that prescribers of Medicare Part D drugs be enrolled in Original Medicare with a preclusion list for Part D prescribers, addressed in § 423.120(c)(6).
c. Preclusion List and Part C Program Integrity Issues
The preclusion list for MA providers has been in effect since 2019. For several reasons, though, we are reevaluating its effectiveness in stemming MA fraud, waste, and abuse in comparison to the proven program integrity safeguards of our existing Medicare provider enrollment process.
First, while many MA organizations require providers to be enrolled in Original Medicare as a condition of contracting,
[
159
]
well over 100,000 in-network providers remain unenrolled. In certain cases, a particular MA organization's credentialing process may not be as comprehensive as Original Medicare enrollment screening. The latter, for example, contains the following verification mechanisms that do not necessarily exist in the MA organizations' internal process:
Reviewing the provider and its owners and managing employees against the System for Award Management, which lists debarment actions taken by various Federal agencies.
Reviewing the provider's adverse legal history, such as criminal convictions, health care program revocations and suspensions, and adverse State licensure actions.
Fingerprint-based criminal background checks for 5 percent or greater owners of provider types designated as high-risk under § 424.518.
Reviewing the Medicaid Termination Database under § 455.417 to ascertain whether the provider is terminated under Medicaid or CHIP.
Monthly monitoring to ensure the provider's continued compliance with licensure and other enrollment requirements.
Verifying the validity of the provider's practice location.
Requiring the provider to revalidate its Medicare enrollment information (including upon a CMS request) by submitting a complete Medicare enrollment application.
Most disconcerting of all is that out-of-network providers that bill MA may not be credentialed by any MA organization, meaning they receive little, if any, screening. This leaves the MA program vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse.
As noted, Original Medicare enrollment is the front line of Medicare program integrity. It enables us to detect and stop non-compliant and potentially fraudulent parties from billing MA at the start, rather than after they begin doing so. Without this important vetting, we have limited means of preventing unqualified providers from entering MA and possibly harming the Trust Funds and MA enrollees.
Second, and in this same vein, we see the preclusion list as more of a reactive program integrity measure than a proactive one. For MA providers that are not enrolled in Original Medicare, we sometimes do not learn that the provider has engaged in fraudulent or other improper conduct until the MA organization itself discovers this and informs us. Only then can we begin the process of placing the provider on the preclusion list. By the time all this occurs, many months may have passed, hundreds of thousands of MA organization dollars may have been paid to the provider, and considerable harm to MA enrollees may have taken place. In other words, in such cases CMS effectively must wait: (1) for the inappropriate activity to happen; (2) for the inappropriate activity to be discovered by the MA organization (potentially months after it occurred); and (3) to be notified by the MA organization before CMS can commence action against the provider. This directly contradicts our stated objective of moving away from the “pay-and-chase” program integrity model and towards the far better approach of halting fraud before it begins.
Third, pursuant to § 422.222(a)(3), the following timing conditions apply to the addition of an individual or entity (other than an OIG-excluded party) to the MA preclusion list:
If the individual or entity (hereafter occasionally and collectively referenced as “party”) does not file a reconsideration request under § 498.5(n)(1), the party is added to the preclusion list upon the expiration of the 60-day period in which the party may request a reconsideration; or
If the party files such a reconsideration request, they are added to the list effective the date on which CMS, if applicable, denies reconsideration. OIG-excluded parties
(
printed page 74752)
are added to the preclusion list effective on the date of the exclusion.
This means that even though CMS believes an individual or entity has, for instance, engaged in fraud, beneficiary harm, or felonious conduct, CMS cannot take any action against that individual or entity via the preclusion list for at least 60 days—and if said party files a reconsideration request, CMS action could take considerably longer. Yet with Original Medicare provider enrollment, CMS can immediately revoke the provider's enrollment without having to wait for the expiration of any appeals process, thus providing further protection for Medicare funds and beneficiaries. In addition, many of the Medicare enrollment revocation reasons in § 424.535(a) are retroactive, meaning the revocation effective date—in general and with variations—essentially goes back to the date the provider's non-compliance with Original Medicare enrollment requirements began. This enables CMS to recoup monies paid to the provider while they were non-compliant.
[
160
]
(We also proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule to make the remainder of our Medicare revocation reasons retroactive.) Accordingly, requiring providers that bill MA to enroll in Original Medicare, and hence be subject to retroactive revocations in cases of non-compliance, would likely go further in the MA realm in safeguarding taxpayer monies and protecting MA enrollees than the preclusion list.
Too, we have seen a growing trend of providers foregoing Original Medicare enrollment and instead billing MA organizations as out-of-network providers. This only enhances the need for the comprehensive, up-front screening process that Medicare provider enrollment furnishes.
We recognize that proposing to require MA providers (both in-network and out-of-network) to be Original Medicare-enrolled would, if finalized, be a change in position from our prior decision to have the preclusion list replace the enrollment requirement. We also appreciate providers' likely concerns about the potential burden of having to enroll. Yet we note two things.
One is that several of the aforementioned issues concerning the preclusion list-such as the time it can take for CMS to learn of an MA provider's misconduct-were not as apparent as they are now. In fact, in September 2026, as part of the White House Anti-Fraud Task Force's ongoing efforts to crush fraud in the healthcare system and protect taxpayer dollars, CMS identified and barred via the preclusion list 11 DME companies with more than $3.4 billion in suspected fraudulent billing practices in 2025 and 2026 from receiving future Part C and Part D payments. These 11 DMEPOS suppliers: (1) had submitted no claims prior to 2025; (2) used improper billing practices for their claims; (3) had billed for medical equipment to beneficiaries already deceased; and (4) supplied equipment to beneficiaries who never requested or received it. Four of the suppliers had already been revoked from Original Medicare and began billing MA organizations instead.
[
161
]
This is one illustration of how the preclusion list is a useful tool once potential fraud has been identified but can fall short when fraud is being targeted at MA plans instead of Original Medicare, especially when those targeting MA are out-of-network providers. MA credentialing by itself is often not as rigorous as the Medicare provider enrollment process (as previously shown in the bulleted list of verification activities that some MA plans do not undertake), and the lack of screening for out-of-network providers is an extremely serious vulnerability; the increasing number of out-of-network providers greatly heightens this risk to the MA program. Circumstances have changed, and our obligation to protect the Trust Funds requires us to be flexible in our program integrity activities and to modify them as warranted.
As discussed in more detail in this proposed rule's ICR section, roughly 150,000 MA providers (many being out-of-network) would have to enroll in Medicare. While we again acknowledge this burden, we stress that the payment of MA dollars to fraudulent or otherwise unqualified providers burdens all Americans, including legitimate MA providers. Indeed, a single fraud scheme involving several MA providers that had not been adequately vetted before they began providing MA services—when strict enrollment screening might have kept them out of the MA program—could alone result in tens of millions of dollars in lost taxpayer monies. The point is that the cost burden of MA provider enrollment would, we believe, ultimately be far less than the savings to bona fide MA providers and all other Americans from MA fraud and abuse prevention.
For all these reasons, we propose to require that all providers that bill MA be enrolled in Original Medicare. This proposal is aligned with Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General's September 2026 report on CMS actions to prevent durable medical equipment fraud in MA.
[
162
]
The proposed regulatory changes that follow largely mirror those we finalized in the previously mentioned November 2016 final rule. An important modification, though, would be our proposal to expand the enrollment requirement to include out-of-network MA providers, which were not required to enroll under the November 2016 final rule. CMS is proposing to include out-of-network MA providers in this requirement to address the earlier noted program integrity threats associated with these parties.
To give unenrolled MA providers adequate time to enroll in Original Medicare and MA organizations adequate time to operationalize this requirement, our changes, if finalized, would not become applicable until January 1, 2030. This timeframe is somewhat akin to that which we finalized in November 2016 final rule, which was the first day of the next plan year that begins 2 years after the date of publication of that final rule. Until this January 1, 2030, applicability date, the MA preclusion list requirements would remain in effect.
We are not at this time proposing that Part D prescribers be required to enroll in Original Medicare in lieu of the preclusion list. We may consider doing so in future rulemaking.

2. Specific Regulatory Changes
We propose the following regulatory revisions:

d. New Enrollment Section (§  422.223)
To address some of our new enrollment requirements (including outlining the parties to which they apply), we propose to establish a new § 422.223. We believe that promulgating a new, separate section would be clearer for stakeholders than attempting to incorporate our new provider enrollment provisions within § 422.222. Section 422.223's opening paragraph would state that beginning January 1, 2030, providers that are types of individuals or entities that can enroll in Original Medicare (in accordance with section 1861 of the Act) must be so enrolled in Original Medicare in an approved status to receive payment from an MA organization for health care items or services provided to a Medicare enrollee who receives their Medicare benefit through the MA organization. (For purposes of this requirement, “approved status” means the provider is neither revoked from Medicare under § 424.535 nor deactivated under § 424.540.) As outlined in new § 422.223(a)(1) through (6), this would include the following providers and suppliers:
In-network and out-of-network MA providers.
First-tier, downstream, and related entities (FDR), as these are defined at § 422.2.

Providers in Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs) or Competitive Medical Plans that contract with CMS under section 1876 of the Act.

Locum tenens providers.
Incident-to providers.
With the exception of out-of-network MA providers, these six provider categories were included within our MA enrollment requirement in the November 2016 final rule. e. Excluded, Revoked, and Precluded Providers
Section 422.224(a) states, in part, that an MA organization may not pay for items or services furnished to a Medicare enrollee by an individual or entity that is OIG excluded or on the preclusion list. Section 422.224(b) states, also in part, that if the MA organization receives a request for payment by, or on behalf of, such an excluded or precluded individual or entity, the MA organization must notify the enrollee and the excluded or precluded party that payment will not be made; the paragraph adds that payment cannot be made to, or on behalf of, an excluded or precluded person or entity. We propose to re-designate these paragraphs as new § 422.224(a)(1) and (a)(2). Consistent with our aforementioned revisions, we would also add the following after the paragraph (a) designation: “Before January 1, 2030”. This will clarify these paragraphs' applicability. In new paragraph (b), we would largely duplicate proposed new §§ 422.224(a)(1) and (a)(2) but with two modifications. First, the requirements would apply beginning January 1, 2030. Second, we would leave precluded parties within the scope of these sections but change it to refer to Part D prescribers that are on the preclusion list as defined in § 423.100 and as described in § 423.120(c)(6). We believe that the program integrity risk that all parties on the preclusion list pose—be they MA or Part D—warrants the inclusion of the latter within § 422.224(b). (The existing reference in § 422.224 to precluded MA providers, though, would not be retained in § 422.224(b) because the preclusion list will not be applicable to MA providers beginning January 1, 2030.)
We also would include the language “revoked from Medicare” in revised § 422.224(b). As we stated in the November 2016 final rule and have reiterated in others since then, revoked providers and suppliers pose a significant risk to Medicare beneficiaries
(
printed page 74754)
and the Trust Funds and should not receive Federal dollars. This is why we originally included revoked providers within the scope of § 422.224(a) in the November 2016 final rule and propose to do so in revised § 422.224(b). For this same reason, we are not proposing a “first-time allowance” (FTA)—similar to what we did in the April 2018 MA preclusion list final rule with respect to precluded providers—in which payment could be made the first time the revoked provider submits a claim but not thereafter. The objective behind any FTA would be to prevent beneficiaries from being liable for payment when the first claim is denied due to the provider's revocation. The beneficiary is notified that while payment will be made in this instance, future payments to the provider will not be; this means the beneficiary should seek a different provider to ensure that the beneficiary's services are covered. However, we explained in the November 2016, final rule that beneficiaries would already be protected in these situations per
42 CFR 1001.1901(b)
and §  424.555(b), which prevent OIG-excluded individuals and entities (as well as revoked, deactivated, and denied providers) from recouping payment from beneficiaries. There is accordingly no need for an FTA.
