3. Solicitation of Comments
We recognize that there are certain circumstances in which an MA organization is obligated to pay a provider regardless of that party's contract status with the plan or for a benefit that is not covered under Original Medicare. The following are illustrative.
First, under § 422.113, an MA organization must cover and pay for emergency and urgently needed services, regardless of whether the provider has a contractual relationship with the plan.
Second, MA organizations are required to pay for out-of-network services in certain circumstances, such as:
When an MA organization's provider network is insufficient to furnish a covered service (such that an in-network provider or benefit is unavailable or inadequate to meet an enrollee's medical needs), the organization must arrange for, and pay for, that service from an out-of-network provider; and
When the enrollee is in a PPO plan, which is required to reimburse for covered services obtained out-of-network.
Third, supplemental benefits that MA organizations may offer under section 1852(a)(3) of the Act are, by definition, items and services not covered under Original Medicare Parts A and B; providers furnishing these benefits may not have a basis to maintain Medicare FFS enrollment.
We also recognize that while we believe our proposed provisions are very much necessary, stakeholders—as after the November 2016 final rule was issued—may be concerned about certain aspects of these requirements. These could involve, for example, the potential burden, impact on beneficiary financial liability and access to care, and whether certain provisions might or should be inapplicable to certain situations. We wish to be as responsive as possible to such concerns within the parameters of our program integrity objectives. Accordingly, we welcome and encourage public comments on our proposed provisions, especially concerning the following issues:
Whether § 422.222 should include an exception for providers furnishing: (1) emergency or urgently needed services under § 422.113; (2) services furnished when the MA organization is required under § 422.112(a)(1)(iii) and § 422.4(a)(1)(v)(B) to cover or arrange for out-of-network coverage; and (3) supplemental benefits not covered under Original Medicare. In Moreover, we request feedback on how any such exception should be structured to avoid creating a loophole that could be exploited to circumvent the enrollment requirement's program integrity purpose.
Whether the payment safeguards proposed at § 422.224 should still apply to these three aforementioned illustrations.
Whether there should be any other exceptions to our enrollment requirements and, if so—
++ The reason(s) for the exception(s);
++ The situations in which they should or should not apply; and
++ The sub-category or sub-categories of MA providers to which they should apply.
Whether any of our proposed six categories of applicability in proposed § 422.223 should or should not be included therein—as well as any clarification needed regarding the scopes and meanings of said categories (for example, the scope of the locum tenens and incident-to categories). Conversely, we ask stakeholders whether any provider types not listed in § 422.223—such as PACE providers—should be subject to our enrollment requirements.
We ask stakeholders to be as specific and detailed as possible in describing their recommended exemptions, requested clarifications, etc. Suggested regulatory text—and its location within the CFR—would be appreciated, as well as recommended limitations or clarifications on the scope of any of the proposed categories.
The network adequacy requirements in § 422.116, including whether our provider enrollment proposals would impact the ability of MA organizations to meet network adequacy standards, especially in Rural or Counties with Extreme Access Considerations (CEAC) areas.
The extent of any access to care issues that stakeholders believe might arise, where and why they may occur, and recommendations on how they could be alleviated within the context of our proposal, including any recommended regulatory text.
Suggestions regarding the limitation of beneficiary financial liability for services performed by unenrolled providers—for instance:
++ Whether enrollee liability should be capped at normal in-network cost-sharing whenever the plan is barred from paying a provider under § 422.224 for services the enrollee was otherwise permitted to receive under §§ 422.4, 422.112, or 422.113.
++ Whether and how MA organizations should ensure the MA enrollee is not liable for care provided by unenrolled providers.
++ Additional situations where stakeholders believe that beneficiary liability should be restricted, including suggested regulatory text and their locations with the CFR.
Requested CMS educational activities concerning our proposed requirements (such as those we performed following the November 2016 final rule).
Costs that MA organizations might incur in implementing our provisions.
Any other CFR sections that stakeholders believe should be added, revised, or updated to accommodate our proposed MA enrollment requirements.
VI. Marketplace
In recent years, there has been a substantial increase in complaints from consumers who reported that they were unaware they had been enrolled in Exchange coverage or that their Exchange plan had been switched without their consent by an agent, broker, or web-broker. From 2023 through 2025, CMS received over 624,000 consumer complaints attesting to unauthorized Exchange
(
printed page 74756)
enrollments
[
166
]
or unauthorized plan switching
[
167
]
by agents, brokers, or web-brokers and confirmed by issuer and CMS review; 300,000 of the 624,000 were received in 2025 alone.
[
168
]
These improper enrollments constitute abusive conduct that costs Federal taxpayers billions of dollars. For example, the HHS Agency Financial Report for Fiscal Year 2025 estimates improper payments of Premium Tax Credits totaled about $1.13 billion.
[
169
]
Abusive conduct by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, such as unauthorized enrollments and unauthorized plan switching, can cause significant medical or financial harm to consumers. For example, enrolling consumers in Exchange plans or changing a consumer's Exchange plan without their consent can cause financial harm, such as unexpected tax liabilities and higher copayments and deductibles. It can also cause physical harm by interrupting their access to medical care when an unauthorized new plan does not cover their medications or include their established providers in-network.
[
170
]
CMS has identified an ongoing pattern of unauthorized enrollment, unauthorized plan switching, and other fraudulent, unauthorized, or noncompliant enrollment activity involving a subset of agents, brokers, and web-brokers participating in the Federally-facilitated Exchange (FFEs) and State-based Exchanges on the Federal platform (SBE-FPs).
[
171
]
While CMS has taken a number of steps to address this conduct, the conduct has persisted. For example, on August 31, 2026, CMS canceled approximately 315,000 enrollments covering over 760,000 consumers after following its standard issuer investigation process to confirm that these enrollments were unauthorized. Similarly, CMS is also holding agents, brokers, and web-brokers accountable for violating Marketplace standards. Since January 2026, CMS has issued termination notices to more than 200 non-compliant agents and brokers. Furthermore, in the summer of 2026, CMS issued 569 notices of intent to terminate to agents and brokers who submitted 2026 applications without key-identifying applicant information, such as Social Security Numbers (SSN).
When an agent, broker, or web-broker enrolls someone in a Marketplace health plan without their knowledge or consent, or switches plans without their knowledge or consent, that action can trigger Advance Premium Tax Credit (APTC) payments on behalf of a person who never actually agreed to the coverage — resulting in improper payments, because the subsidy is based on an eligibility determination tied to an application the enrollee did not knowingly submit or a plan the person did not select. These improper payments can result in the improper disbursement of taxpayer dollars. Accordingly, we propose to strengthen the integrity of the vetting and oversight processes for agents, brokers, and web-brokers participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs to reduce waste, fraud, and abuse, protect Exchange consumers, and safeguard Exchange systems.
A. Statutory and Regulatory Authority
Section 1312(e) of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (the Affordable Care Act) provides the Secretary with the authority to establish procedures under which a State may allow agents or brokers to: (1) enroll qualified individuals and qualified employers in qualified health plans (QHPs) offered through Exchanges; and (2) assist individuals in applying for premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions (CSRs) for QHPs sold through an Exchange. Section 1313(a)(5) of the Affordable Care Act provides that, with respect to activities carried out under Title I of the Affordable Care Act, the Secretary shall provide for the efficient and non-discriminatory administration of Exchange activities and implement any measure or procedure that— (A) the Secretary determines is appropriate to reduce fraud and abuse in the administration of Title I; and (B) the Secretary has authority to implement under Title I or any other Act. Section 1321 of the Affordable Care Act also authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations setting standards for meeting the requirements under Title I of the Affordable Care Act with respect to the establishment and operation of Exchanges (including Small Business Health Options Program), the offering of QHPs through such Exchanges, and such other requirements as the Secretary determines appropriate.
Regulations at
45 CFR 155.220
implement the statutory requirements in section 1312(e) of the Affordable Care Act, establishing standards governing Exchange participation by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, including Exchange Agreement(s) requirements, standards of conduct, and enforcement authorities. The proposals in this rule would revise these existing requirements and strengthen oversight, improve enforcement procedures, and better protect consumers and taxpayer dollars.
B. Overview of Proposed Policies
These proposed policies would improve CMS'
[
172
]
ability to prevent abusive conduct by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, better protect consumers within the FFEs and SBE-FPs, and support the efficient, non-discriminatory administration of the FFEs and SBE-FPs. First, this proposed rule would add participation standards to
45 CFR 155.220(g)(3)
that would prevent agents, brokers, and web-brokers from participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs in the circumstances described below, which CMS believes present an unacceptable risk because continued participation may pose a substantial likelihood of consumer harm, improper enrollment activity, misuse of Exchange information, or material program integrity concerns (defined in section VI.B. of this proposed rule). Specifically, agents, brokers, and web-brokers that CMS determines pose such an unacceptable risk would not be permitted to register, complete training, or enter into agreements with the FFEs and SBE-FPs as described in § 155.220(d) (hereinafter referred to as “Exchange agreement(s)”), preventing them from assisting
(
printed page 74757)
consumers with enrolling in Exchange coverage, including insurance affordability programs, through the FFEs and SBE-FPs. Additionally, this proposed rule would update § 155.220(g)(3) to allow CMS to immediately terminate agents, brokers, and web-brokers who the agency determines pose such an unacceptable risk from participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs, without waiting 30 calendar days from the date of notice.
To strengthen oversight and improve fairness in enforcement proceedings arising from findings of agent, broker, and web-broker noncompliance under § 155.220(g)(2), we propose additional revisions to § 155.220. Specifically, we propose to amend § 155.220(g)(3)(i) to replace the existing opportunity for agents, brokers, and web-brokers to “resolve” a noncompliance determination with an opportunity to “refute” before CMS terminates their Exchange agreement(s) for cause or imposes other penalties. As discussed in section VI.C.1. of this proposed rule, this change would clarify that the 30-calendar day period is primarily for submitting information to dispute or rebut a noncompliance determination.
We also propose to codify the factors that CMS would consider when determining whether to terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) with the FFEs and SBE-FPs for cause and to impose other penalties under § 155.220(k)(1) after making a noncompliance determination. In addition, we propose to amend § 155.220(h) to clarify that agents, brokers, or web-brokers may request reconsideration when CMS denies them the right to enter into Exchange Agreement(s) in addition to when CMS terminates their Exchange Agreement(s) for cause.
We also propose to add a new standard in § 155.220(j) to codify a term in the existing FFEs and SBE-FP Exchange agreement(s) requiring agents, brokers, and web-brokers to implement and maintain reasonable safeguards to ensure that access and attempted access to the FFEs and SBE-FPs, systems that support the FFEs and SBE-FPs, and consumer personally identifiable information (PII) obtained through those Exchanges only occur from locations within the United States.
We have also determined changes to § 155.220(g)(5) are necessary and appropriate to enhance transparency measures (for example, the public registration termination list) around program integrity oversight of the FFEs and SBE-FPs and further strengthen our administrative actions against suspected bad actors. Specifically, this proposed rule would make several amendments to § 155.220(g)(5), including moving from a fraud-based standard to an abusive conduct-based framework. This proposed rule would also adjust the standard of proof CMS would apply to suspensions and terminations for cause of an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) under § 155.220(g)(5). Specifically, under § 155.220(g)(5)(ii), CMS could suspend an agent's, broker's, or web-broker's agreements if CMS finds that there is a credible allegation of abusive conduct. Under § 155.220(g)(5)(iii), CMS could terminate those agreements if CMS determines, by a preponderance of the evidence, that abusive conduct occurred. Furthermore, this proposed rule would amend § 155.220(j)(2)(i) and (ii) by adding illustrative, non-exhaustive examples of agent, broker, and web-broker behavior that CMS has observed and considers harmful. CMS would also amend § 155.220(j)(4) to limit its scope as applied to abusive conduct as proposed in § 155.220(g)(5)(1). We seek comment on these proposals.
C. Expand Authority To Deny and Terminate Agents, Brokers, and Web-brokers' Exchange Participation
There are certain instances in which participation by an agent, broker, or web-broker can pose an unacceptable risk to the FFEs and SBE-FPs, including when certain administrative actions have been taken by Federal programs and State licensure authorities, as well as when an agent, broker, or web-broker has been convicted of a Federal or State misdemeanor or felony offense that CMS determines is detrimental to the best interests of the FFEs, SBE-FPs, and their consumers. Similar authorities regarding providers or suppliers with felony convictions have long existed in the Original Medicare program, also known as Medicare fee-for-service.
[
173
]
Medicare suppliers and providers, as well as agents, brokers and web-brokers in the Exchange, are entrusted with safeguarding program integrity, public health, and taxpayer money. Better alignment between the Federal Exchange platform approach with similar longstanding authorities that exist in the Medicare program would create consistency and strength through a unified voice and are necessary to increase program integrity and better protect consumers and taxpayer dollars by preventing agents, brokers, and web-brokers that pose unacceptable risk from participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs.
1. Suspension, Termination, or Debarment From Any Federal Program, or Suspension or Revocation of State Licensure in Any State (§ 155.220(g)(3)(iii))
We propose to add § 155.220(g)(3)(iii) to provide that CMS may deny registration for, or immediately terminate the Exchange Agreement(s) of, any agent, broker, or web-broker who is currently terminated, suspended, revoked, debarred, or excluded from participation in any Federal program, or whose license is currently revoked or suspended for conduct that may cause harm to consumers or program integrity in a State other than that in which the agent, broker, or web-broker is enrolling consumers, regardless of whether any appeals are pending. If the appeal is successful and no other grounds for denial of registration exist, CMS would allow the agent, broker, or web-broker to register (or re-register if they were terminated) with the FFEs and SBE-FPs. Agents, brokers, and web-brokers with a history of these adverse actions imposed by a Federal program or a State licensing entity pose an unacceptable risk for the FFEs, SBE-FPs, and their consumers because they have demonstrated an inability to abide by the rules of other programs to such an extent that serious sanctions were warranted. Accordingly, if codified, we believe this proposal would better protect the FFEs, SBE-FPs, and consumers by preventing agents, brokers, and web-brokers who have a track record of misconduct from participating in the Exchange agent-broker program. We seek comment on the potential need for any exceptions to this proposed bar on participation, as well as if there are any reasons why an agent, broker, or web-broker who is currently terminated, suspended, revoked, debarred, or excluded from participation in a Federal program should not also be barred from participation in the FFEs and SBE-FPs. CMS also believes it is prudent to take such action even if an appeal, which can take months if not years to complete, is pending, and seeks public comment on whether any exceptions to this approach are warranted.

The current regulation at § 155.220(g)(3)(i) governing termination for cause of agent, broker, and web-broker Exchange agreement(s) in FFEs and SBE-FPs for noncompliance states that CMS will notify the agent, broker, or web-broker of the specific finding of noncompliance or pattern of noncompliance made under § 155.220(g)(1), and after 30 calendar days from the date of the notice, may terminate their Exchange agreement(s) if the matter is not resolved to the satisfaction of CMS. Many agents, brokers, and web-brokers have interpreted this 30-calendar day period to mean that if the agent, broker, or web-broker takes corrective action or makes assurances that they will maintain compliance moving forward, that CMS may not proceed with termination. This interpretation is not consistent with our original intent with this regulation: to take enforcement action, as appropriate, in response to noncompliance notwithstanding corrective action or assurances by the agent, broker, or web-broker.
[

Further, if agents, brokers, and web-brokers continue to have this belief, they may not be incentivized to refrain from noncompliant behavior and may instead believe that they can correct it before they are subject to any
(
printed page 74760)
negative consequences. Therefore, we are proposing to reframe the 30-calendar day period as a time for the agent, broker and web-broker to refute the noncompliance rather than resolve the noncompliance, to clarify that nothing prevents CMS from terminating an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) where the agency makes a finding of noncompliance, even if the agent, broker, or web-broker takes corrective action or makes assurances that they will maintain compliance moving forward. Compliance with all terms and conditions of Exchange agreement(s), any State law applicable to agents, brokers or web-brokers, and any Federal law, including HHS regulations implementing those laws, is required at all times under § 155.220. Further, CMS expects compliance at all times with CMS' regulatory enforcement framework.
Further, by framing the 30-calendar-day period primarily as a time to
resolve
the matter to CMS' satisfaction, agents, brokers, and web-brokers have expressed concerns that they cannot refute the noncompliance finding or determination prior to a termination action going into effect. Instead, they can only do so after a termination action goes into effect and the agent, broker, or web-broker is offered a reconsideration in accordance with § 155.220(h). This belief is based on an incorrect reading of the current regulatory text. The existing language at § 155.220(g)(3)(i) frames the 30-calendar-day period as a time to resolve the matter “to the satisfaction of HHS,” which some agents, brokers, and web-brokers have interpreted as being limited to corrective action or assurances of future compliance rather than as a time to dispute the underlying findings of noncompliance. Because the current regulatory text does not explicitly specify this 30-calendar-day period as a time to refute whether noncompliance occurred, agents, brokers, and web-brokers have mistakenly concluded that the reconsideration process under § 155.220(h), which occurs after a termination action goes into effect, is their first meaningful chance to refute the findings themselves.
As such, we have seen that some agents, brokers, and web-brokers choose not to respond during the 30-calendar-day notice period but will request reconsideration to dispute the findings. The intent of the 30-calendar-day notice period is to provide agents, brokers, and web-brokers the chance to provide CMS with information to inform a decision on whether the alleged noncompliance actually occurred. Bypassing this 30-calendar-day period to engage with CMS subverts the intent of the review and enforcement processes and wastes the time and resources of both CMS and agent, broker, and web-broker. If agents, brokers, and web-brokers have information that can refute a noncompliance determination, and they submit that information within the 30-calendar-day period, CMS would be able to make more fully informed decisions on the front end of the process and reduce resources expended on imposing enforcement actions, conducting reconsideration reviews, and in some instances, rescinding previously imposed terminations. This would also protect agents, brokers, and web-brokers from interruptions to their ability to assist consumers with enrollment through the FFEs or SBE-FPs as a result of an avoidable termination that was imposed due, in part, to their failure to refute during the 30-calendar-day period.
While CMS may consider any actions the agent, broker, or web-broker has taken to address or correct the identified noncompliance, these actions alone may not be determinative of whether CMS may proceed to terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) and impose a penalty other than termination. As explained in section VI.D.2. of this proposed rule, under proposed § 155.220(g)(1)(i), CMS may consider the nonexclusive factors identified in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2), to the extent relevant to the facts and circumstances of the particular case, to assess the nature and circumstances of the noncompliance and the impact of that noncompliance before deciding whether termination, another penalty under § 155.220(k)(1), or both are appropriate. This approach would preserve CMS' flexibility to account for unusual circumstances. For example, analysis under the non-exclusive factors would allow CMS to consider an individual's history with the FFEs and SBE-FPs, which could include consideration of any proactive actions taken to address or correct identified noncompliance. CMS may determine, based on consideration of the factors proposed in section VI.D.2. of this proposed rule, that despite corrective action, the noncompliance warrants enforcement action under § 155.220(g)(1) and (k)(1).
In summary, by aligning the regulation text to clarify and mirror the original intent of the policy, this proposed approach would protect the integrity of the FFEs and SBE-FPs and the interests of consumers; clarify that agents, brokers, and web-brokers have an opportunity to refute findings of noncompliance before termination goes into effect or CMS imposes a penalty; and help to ensure that enforcement decisions are based on a complete and accurate assessment of the noncompliance. We seek comment on these proposals.

We propose to revise § 155.220(g)(1) and add a new paragraph at § 155.220(g)(1)(i) to specify how CMS would determine whether to terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) and impose a penalty under § 155.220(k)(1) when CMS has made a determination of noncompliance under § 155.220(g)(1).
Specifically, we propose to remove the “sufficiently severe” language in § 155.220(g)(1) and replace it with a new framework under proposed § 155.220(g)(1)(i). The removal of the “sufficiently severe” language is intended to reduce ambiguity regarding what is sufficient to trigger termination and instead replace it with explicit factors CMS would consider that are clear and transparent. The proposed framework would provide that, except for terminations made in accordance with paragraphs (g)(3)(ii) through (g)(3)(iv) of this section, when CMS makes a noncompliance determination under paragraph (g)(1), CMS would consider the factors identified in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2) to the extent relevant to the facts and circumstances of each case, as well as any additional relevant factors supported by the evidence when it: (A) decides whether to terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) for cause; or (B) selects among the penalties identified in paragraph (k)(1) of this section, including the length of the penalty imposed under paragraph (k)(1)(i) of this section.
The factors listed under § 155.285(b)(1) and (2) are the factors that CMS has established for consideration in determining the amount of a civil money penalty (CMP) imposed against an individual for providing false or fraudulent information to an Exchange. CMPs, terminations, and the imposition of other penalties are all enforcement mechanisms that aim to address and correct noncompliance. Thus, utilizing these factors when making determinations on whether to terminate for cause an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) and the imposition of penalties other than terminations, when relevant, would help to ensure consistency throughout CMS' enforcement mechanisms. Use of
(
printed page 74761)
a single, nonexclusive factor framework across related enforcement decisions would reduce divergence in factors considered, increase consistency in decision making, and promote transparency while preserving CMS' flexibility to terminate Exchange agreement(s) and impose other penalties when supported by the facts of the identified noncompliance. The factors listed under § 155.285(b)(1) and (2) reflect the considerations most relevant to the full range of noncompliance CMS has encountered in overseeing the FFEs and SBE-FPs and are expected to apply in the vast majority of enforcement actions. The nonexclusive nature of the list preserves CMS' flexibility to account for case-specific circumstances not captured by the codified factors. We propose that CMS would consider additional factors to the extent they are relevant to the particular case and supported by the evidence. These additional factors could include, but would not be limited to, failure to cooperate with CMS monitoring, audit, or enforcement activities, or the submission of incomplete, inaccurate, or misleading information to CMS.
As explained in section VI.C.1. of this proposed rule, if CMS were to find that a preponderance of available evidence supports a finding that an agent, broker, or web-broker violated a standard under this section, an applicable Exchange agreement term, or Federal or State law, and that such noncompliance justifies termination of the agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s), or imposition of other penalties based on an assessment of the proposed factors in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2), CMS will make a refutable determination of noncompliance under § 155.220(g)(3)(i). In accordance with proposed § 155.220(g)(3)(i), following the 30-calendar-day refutation period, CMS would review all refutation evidence provided and reassess whether a preponderance of the evidence still supports a finding of noncompliance that, based on an assessment of the proposed relevant factors in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2), justifies termination or imposition of other penalties under § 155.220(k)(1) before moving forward. If the information provided does not refute the noncompliance, meaning that a preponderance of the evidence still supports the noncompliance determination based on CMS' assessment of the proposed factors in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2), CMS may proceed to terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) and impose other penalties. This approach aligns with § 155.285(b)(1)(vii) that contemplates evaluating “any additional information provided by the individual to refute performing the violation.”
Under this proposal, CMS would weigh both mitigating and aggravating facts, but would retain discretion to weigh the proposed factors as appropriate and would not be required to consider all of the factors in every case. CMS would only consider a factor listed in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2) if the factor is relevant to the noncompliance at issue and applicable to the facts and circumstances of the particular case, and would consider both the presence and absence of a relevant factor when making a termination decision and selecting penalties. For example, not all findings of noncompliance as described in § 155.220(g)(2) involve the disclosure of false or fraudulent information as referenced in § 155.285(b)(2)(v). A finding of noncompliance may instead involve, for example, an agent, broker, or web broker's failure to obtain or maintain required consumer consent documentation. Similarly, even if an agent, broker, or web-broker did not receive compensation associated with the violation as described in § 155.285(b)(1)(vi), or CMS is not able to determine whether the agent, broker, or web-broker received compensation, assessment of other relevant factors may still support termination and imposition of a penalty other than termination. In such circumstances, CMS may determine that enforcement action is appropriate based on its assessment of the other factors relevant to the particular case. We have determined that codifying these factors would provide greater transparency into CMS' enforcement decision-making under § 155.220(g)(1) and reflect that enforcement determinations are based on the totality of the circumstances.
Section 155.285(b)(1) provides that CMS may take into account the nature and circumstances of the conduct, including, but not limited to: the number of violations; the severity of the violations; the individual's history with the Exchange, including any prior violations that would indicate whether the violation is an isolated occurrence or represents a pattern of behavior; the length of time of the violation; the number of individuals affected or potentially affected; the extent to which a person received compensation or other consideration associated with the violation; any documentation provided in any complaint or other information, as well as any additional information provided by the person alleged to have committed the violation to refute performing the violation; and whether other remedies or penalties have been imposed on the person alleged to have committed the violation for the same conduct or occurrence.
When considering the number of and length of time of violations, as described in § 155.285(b)(1)(i) and (iv), CMS may look at, among other things, the number of regulatory requirements the agent, broker, or web-broker violated; the number of times CMS identified the agent, broker, or web-broker violated such requirements; compliance with previously provided technical assistance; and for how long the agent, broker, and web-broker sustained the noncompliance. For example, if an audit or other oversight action results in findings of many instances in which an agent, broker, or web-broker failed to document consumer consent and eligibility application information review in accordance with § 155.220(j)(2)(iii) and (j)(2)(ii)(A) for a large number of different consumers and applications, CMS may consider this more significant than an audit that identifies only a few instances of failure to document consumer consent across a small number of consumers and applications.
Similarly, in considering an agent, broker, or web-broker's history with the Exchange, as described in § 155.285(b)(1)(iii), CMS would consider any previously identified violations of agency regulatory requirements, such as those described in §§ 155.220 and 155.221, to assess whether the violation is an isolated occurrence or represents a pattern of behavior. However, the absence of a documented history of noncompliance would not preclude CMS from taking enforcement action as appropriate, including termination of an Exchange agreement required under § 155.220(d), against an agent, broker, or web-broker. If, after assessment of the other factors described in § 155.285(b)(1) and (2), CMS determines that totality of the circumstances warrants enforcement action, CMS would retain authority to terminate the Exchange agreement required under § 155.220(d) and impose a penalty other than termination under § 155.220(k)(1), regardless of whether the agent, broker, or web-broker had a prior history of noncompliance.
In considering the severity of any identified noncompliance with regulatory requirements, as described in § 155.285(b)(1)(ii), CMS would assess the nature and degree to which the agent, broker, or web-broker violated the regulatory requirement(s) at issue, including the extent to which the violation departed from the applicable requirement and whether the
(

Using noncompliance with the consent documentation requirements at § 155.220(j)(2)(iii) as an example, CMS would likely consider less severe a procedural or technical noncompliance in which an agent, broker, or web-broker clearly obtained and documented consumer consent, but the documentation did not include an adequate description of the process by which the consumer or their authorized representative may rescind the consent, as required by § 155.220(j)(2)(iii)(B). This type of violation would likely be considered less severe because the documentation demonstrated that the consumer knowingly consented to the enrollment, which is the core purpose of the consent requirement, and the deficiency was limited to an incomplete description of a procedural right.
In contrast, CMS would likely consider noncompliance with regulatory requirements to be more severe if it impacted the enrollee's ability to provide actual, informed consent before the agent, broker, or web-broker enrolled them in coverage through the FFEs or SBE-FPs, as we would not be able to determine if the consumer named on the application provided such consent. This uncertainty directly undermines the core purpose of the consent requirement to ensure that enrollments are made with the consumer's knowing and voluntary authorization. Another example of a severe violation might include an instance in which an agent, broker, or web-broker failed to document the name of the consumer or consumer's authorized representative providing consent to be enrolled, creating a situation where we cannot determine if the consumer named on the application provided consent to the agent, broker, or web-broker's assistance with this enrollment. As a further example, CMS would likely consider enrolling a consumer in a health plan without
any
documented evidence that the consumer authorized the enrollment to be a severe violation because, as previously described, the consent requirement is a fundamental safeguard that helps ensure enrollments and application updates are authorized by the consumer. Failure to obtain or maintain any consent documentation prevents CMS from verifying that consumer authorization was obtained, undermines the integrity of the FFE and SBE-FP enrollment process, and increases the risk of consumer financial and medical harm. Because maintaining adequate consent documentation is a condition of participation in the FFEs and SBE-FPs, agents, brokers, and web brokers are responsible for retaining records sufficient to demonstrate compliance.
In considering the number of individuals affected by the noncompliance, as described in § 155.285(b)(1)(v), for instances in which the number of affected individuals cannot be readily determined from the documented instances of noncompliance, CMS could, for example, consider the total number of applications submitted by the agent, broker, or web-broker during the relevant period to determine the number of affected individuals should findings suggest a pattern of noncompliance likely existed across a large portion of the agent, broker, or web-broker's book of business. CMS may also consider the nature of the noncompliance because certain types of noncompliance may affect a broader population of consumers than others. For example, if CMS finds that an agent, broker, or web-broker engaged in misleading marketing in violation of § 155.220(j)(3), CMS may consider the potential reach and impact of the misleading marketing to estimate the number of people affected, including the number of advertisements publicly posted, the number and type of platforms on which the advertisements were posted, the length of time the postings were made public or how often they were posted, available information regarding consumer exposure or engagement, complaints or referrals that mention the misleading marketing, and any related application or enrollment activity. CMS would consider such information, as available and appropriate, in assessing the number of individuals potentially affected and may not necessarily presume that all individuals who may have been exposed to a misleading advertisement were actually impacted by the advertisement.
In considering the extent to which a person received compensation or other consideration associated with the violation as an aggravating factor, as described in § 155.285(b)(1)(vi), CMS could, for example, weigh whether an agent, broker, or web-broker received commissions from QHP issuers for enrollments the agent, broker, or web-broker assisted with or facilitated while engaging in noncompliance.

4. Policies To Address Abusive Conduct
a. Purpose and Description of Abusive Conduct Standards
Abusive conduct by agents, brokers, and web-brokers can adversely impact consumers, resulting in significant medical or financial harm. Consumers enrolled in Exchange QHPs without their knowledge or consent can experience interruptions in access to medical care and unexpected tax liabilities associated with receiving APTCs. Through our investigations and data analytics in the FFEs and SBE-FPs, we have identified specific actions and patterns of inappropriate behavior by agents, brokers, and web-brokers that violate the standards of conduct listed in § 155.220(j)(2). These activities ultimately result in consumers being misled about important aspects of their Exchange coverage, including their eligibility for APTC based on their income, the cost-sharing implications (that is, deductibles and copayments) associated with the insurance plans they sign up for, and other material information necessary to make informed enrollment decisions.
Through our investigations of consumer complaints and analyses of enrollment activity in the FFEs and SBE-FPs, we have found that significant consumer harm arises from abusive conduct by agents, brokers, and web-brokers that may not initially rise to the level of fraud under current § 155.220(g)(5). The proposed standard of abusive conduct would better reflect the nature of the misconduct we are seeing that often involves deceptive or coercive enrollment practices, material misrepresentations, unauthorized application or enrollment activity, or the submission of inaccurate application information that misleads consumers and undermines the integrity of Exchange operations. Under the current regulatory framework, the suspension authority at § 155.220(g)(5) is tied in part to a reasonable suspicion of fraud, which may not capture a significant portion of the types of misconduct CMS encounters through its Marketplace oversight activities. Based on this experience, we have determined it is appropriate to propose revising our regulations to establish an enforcement framework that would more directly address the misconduct we are seeing while applying a clear and transparent evidentiary standard.
Accordingly, we believe revisions to our suspension and termination authorities are necessary to better align our enforcement authorities with the types of abusive conduct encountered through our Marketplace oversight. We therefore propose to amend § 155.220(g)(5) by removing reference to a “reasonable suspicion of fraud” in § 155.220(g)(5) and replacing it with a standard under which CMS may suspend an agent, broker, or web-broker when CMS finds there exists a credible allegation of abusive conduct by the agent, broker, or web-broker. We further propose amending § 155.20 to add a definition of “a credible allegation of abusive conduct,” defining it to mean: an allegation from any source, including but not limited to the following: (1) consumer, Marketplace call center, or agent, broker, or web-broker complaints verified by further evidence; (2) data or information identified during investigation; or (3) patterns identified through data analysis. Additionally, the definition would state that allegations are considered to be credible when they have indicia of reliability. The presence of one of these sources alone could be sufficient to meet this standard as a credible allegation of abusive conduct, depending on the facts of each individual case.
Unlike a general finding of noncompliance or pattern of noncompliance under § 155.220(g)(1) and (2), enforcement actions under § 155.220(g)(5) would apply to the most egregious behaviors. Specifically, enforcement actions would apply when the conduct is likely to or has caused harm to the Federally facilitated Exchange, SBE-FP, or their consumers. Conduct that does not meet this harm standard, though it may cause harm, would be addressed through enforcement actions authorized under § 155.220(g)(1) through (3). We seek comment on this proposal.
Likewise, we propose to amend § 155.220(g)(5)(ii) and (iii) to establish standards for suspension and termination based on a finding of abusive conduct. Specifically, we propose that CMS may suspend an agent, broker, or web-broker based on a credible allegation of abusive conduct and may terminate the agreement of an agent, broker, or web-broker based on a preponderance of evidence of abusive conduct. We believe the proposed credible allegation of abusive conduct standard for suspensions is consistent with Medicare's payment suspension authority, which uses a credible allegation of fraud standard, and mirroring these standards is appropriate because the resulting impact is similar

We believe the proposed preponderance of the evidence standard for terminations is appropriate because it is the evidentiary standard generally applied in Federal administrative and civil cases, and it would create a fair, well-established, and transparent basis for final enforcement actions. Adopting these standards would better align our enforcement framework with the nature of these administrative proceedings while providing agents, brokers, and web-brokers with greater clarity regarding the evidentiary standard CMS would apply when determining whether termination is warranted. This proposal would also align with the standards we have used for other enforcement actions against agents, brokers, and web-brokers. We consider these examples to constitute abusive conduct because they are likely to cause harm to consumers or the Exchange. For example, when consumers wrongly believe that the agent, broker, or web-broker that is calling them represents an Exchange, they are unaware of the commission payment incentives that may steer them toward a specific plan or product. As another example, when consumers are misled into believing that coverage on the FFEs and SBE-FPs is free, they may be financially harmed when they are charged a deductible, copayment, and coinsurance, of if they are required to repay excess APTC. For consumers whose incomes are too low for APTC eligibility, the Exchanges are harmed by the outflow of millions of dollars in APTC subsidies that are not authorized by law nor capable of recoupment.

Dual enrollment may also confront consumers with unexpected and confusing procedures for addressing coordination of benefits issues, which may ultimately lead to forgoing or delaying needed medical care.
Thus, we propose to consider situations where agents, brokers, and web-brokers use or project, or ask a consumer to use or project, on the Exchange eligibility application, inaccurate or implausible income projections, to constitute abusive conduct that can trigger the suspension and termination of the agent, broker or web-broker's Exchange Agreement(s) under these proposed revisions to
45 CFR 155.220(g)(5)
.
(5) Inaccurate Household Compositions
We propose in
45 CFR 155.220(j)(2)(ii)(H)
that an agent, broker, or web-broker must accurately enter information provided and confirmed by the consumer pertaining to all tax household members. We also propose that agents, brokers, and web-brokers must ask consumers about their household composition to the same extent consumers are asked about household composition on the Exchange eligibility application and accurately report each consumer response, and that failure to do so may result in suspension and termination for abusive conduct consistent with these proposed revisions to § 155.220(j)(2)(G).
In accordance with § 155.305(f), a consumer may only be eligible for APTC if they are an applicable taxpayer, in accordance with
26 CFR 1.36B-2(b)
, which requires a taxpayer to have household income that is at least 100 percent but not more than 400 percent of the Federal Poverty Level for the taxpayer's family size for the taxable year. Further, in accordance
42 CFR 435.603(h)
, Medicaid financial eligibility for applicants, and other individuals not receiving Medicaid benefits at the point at which eligibility for Medicaid is being determined, must be based on current monthly household income and family size.
Our investigations have shown that some agents, brokers, or web-brokers are entering incorrect tax household compositions on Exchange eligibility applications. Agents, brokers, or web-brokers often fail to ask consumers about members of their household, as required in the eligibility application. For example, we have observed agents, brokers, and web-brokers who omit questions about marital status, spouse's name, spouse's health insurance coverage, and whether the applicant and their spouse are filing income tax returns jointly or separately. We have also seen instances where an agent, broker, or web-broker asks consumers about their household composition but does not include all household members on the Exchange eligibility application. Agents, brokers, and web-brokers are required to include all household members even if those household members are not applying for coverage. Our investigations have also uncovered situations where some Exchange eligibility applications that included an agent, broker, or web-broker's NPN included fictitious household members.
Omitting any part of the household composition information on the eligibility application is likely to cause harm to the affected consumer and therefore constitutes abusive conduct. For example, the consumer may be harmed financially, as APTC is an advanced payment based on projected tax household income and composition. If the consumer's actual household composition differs from the household composition on the eligibility application, the consumer may be required to repay any overpayment of APTC unexpectedly. Moreover, this practice causes harm to the Exchange as a result of the outflow of funds to pay APTC for ineligible consumers. The submission of inaccurate household composition information can also harm a consumer by resulting in denial of a consumer's eligibility for Medicaid, CHIP, APTC, or CSRs. Thus, we propose that agents, brokers, and web-brokers must accurately enter information provided and confirmed by the consumer pertaining to all tax household members, and that failing to do so may result in suspension and termination for abusive conduct consistent with these proposed revisions to § 155.220(g)(5).

(

For example, some agents, brokers, and web-brokers enrolling consumers at addresses where the consumer has never resided (for example, in a State in which they have never resided) or no longer resides. Inaccurate address information is likely to cause harm both to the consumer and the Exchange by interfering with the ability of the Exchange and its QHP issuers to communicate properly with the consumer about their health insurance coverage, upcoming Open Enrollment, or issues with their eligibility determinations. In our investigations, we have also observed the use of inaccurate residential addresses as a means of keeping individuals unaware that their personal information has been used to create a QHP enrollment for which an agent, broker, or web-broker is collecting commission payments. Thus, we propose that agents, brokers, and web-brokers must accurately enter information provided and confirmed by the consumer regarding residence address in accordance with

(7) Deceased Consumers
We propose in
45 CFR 155.220(j)(2)(ii)(F)

Our prior investigative efforts and data analytics have also shown that some Exchange eligibility applications submitted by agents, brokers, or web-brokers are for consumers who were deceased at the time of enrollment. In accordance with § 155.220(j)(2)(ii), agents, brokers, and web-brokers must document that the eligibility application information has been reviewed and confirmed to be accurate by the consumer, or the consumer's authorized representative designated in compliance with § 155.227, prior to the submission of the eligibility application. A deceased consumer cannot review and confirm the accuracy of their eligibility application information. We believe existing § 155.220(j)(2)(ii) makes clear that an agent, broker, or web-broker does not have consent to enroll deceased consumers. However, to increase transparency, we are proposing to add § 155.220(j)(2)(ii)(F) that would explicitly prohibit the enrollment of deceased consumers.
The enrollment of deceased consumers causes harm to Exchange operations in multiple ways. First, enrollment of deceased consumers creates administrative burden for the Exchange to recoup APTC payments to QHP issuers made on these improperly created policies. Second, the recoupment of those APTC payments results in unexpected and unpredictable cash outflows for the QHP issuers who sell insurance on the Exchange. Third, the creation of these policies fundamentally undermines the integrity and reliability of the Exchange as a market, where transactions ought to be reliable and trustworthy when information is passed from consumer to Exchange to QHP issuer.
5. Extension of the Rebuttal Period
Under the existing framework in § 155.220(g)(5), in circumstances where we suspend an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s), the agent, broker, or web-broker may submit evidence in a form and manner specified by CMS to rebut the allegation(s) during the 90-day period following the suspension. We propose in revised § 155.220(g)(5)(ii)(B) that if the agent, broker, or web-broker submits such evidence within 30 days of the suspension, CMS will review the evidence and make a determination on whether to lift the suspension within 90 calendar days of the suspension. This would provide CMS at least 60 calendar days for review of evidence submitted by an agent, broker, or web-broker as such evidence must be submitted within the first 30 days of the 90-day suspension period.
Based on our experience with prior Exchange oversight activities, we believe that extending CMS' review time from the current 45 calendar days to at least 60 calendar days is appropriate to allow CMS more time to review the submitted evidence and make an informed decision about whether such evidence persuades us to lift the suspension. These additional days are needed as the review process can involve parsing complex technical information and data, revisiting consumer complaints, and reaching out to consumers individually. While this proposal adds days to the review process, this minimal additional burden to agents, brokers, and web-brokers strikes the appropriate balance of protecting the FFEs, SBE-FPs, and their consumers from abusive conduct and quickly reviewing and making rebuttal determinations for agents, brokers, and web-brokers. This proposed review period also aligns with the 60-calendar day review period CMS has to review an agent, broker, or web-broker's reconsideration request under the revised 155.220(g)(5)(iii) and (h), which would make this process easier for CMS to administrate and regulated entities to follow.

[
181

The prohibitions in the existing agreements include a prohibition against using a Virtual Private Network (VPN) or other similar technology that routes Exchange system traffic through a server, network, or other point located outside the United States, regardless of whether the agent, broker, or web-broker is physically located inside the United States.
Data, including consumer PII, once transmitted outside the United States, may not be recoverable because it
(
printed page 74770)
becomes subject to a foreign jurisdiction or otherwise falls outside of CMS' enforcement authority. This means CMS loses the ability to ensure deletion, recovery, or continued protection of that data once it is transmitted outside the United States. Additionally, access from outside the United States may occur through networks, devices, or infrastructure that are not subject to the same cybersecurity standards and legal protections applicable to domestic systems, increasing the risk of data breaches and other cyberattacks. Foreign access also significantly complicates CMS' ability to monitor, audit, and enforce compliance with the data security requirements applicable to agents, brokers, and web-brokers assisting consumers with enrollments through the FFEs and SBE-FPs because the relevant systems, devices, records, personnel, or data may be located outside United States jurisdiction or otherwise beyond CMS' direct oversight and enforcement authority. For example, CMS has encountered situations in which an agent, broker, or web-broker routed outbound emails containing consumer PII through third-party email servers located outside the United States. In one such case, CMS determined that consumer PII was accessible to overseas technical teams through shared IT infrastructure, and that the entity's security posture was insufficient to prevent unauthorized foreign access to Exchange Systems. Data breaches and cyber-attacks of consumer PII transmitted outside the United States could result in consumer information getting into the hands of agents, brokers, or web-brokers that are looking to gain commissions through unauthorized enrollments or plan changes or to sell consumer information to other agents, brokers, or web-brokers looking to do so. Thus, these risks may result in significant consumer harm, including interruptions or loss of health coverage, and improper determinations or payments of APTCs or CSRs that may create financial consequences for consumers and taxpayers.
Existing Exchange agreements already prohibit remote connections to the FFEs and SBE-FPs, and systems connected to the FFEs and SBE-FPs from outside the United States, including through the use of technologies such as VPNs.
[
182
]
The prohibition on access routed through technologies such as VPNs also captures situations where an agent or broker may be located in the United States, when accessing Exchange Systems but Exchange system traffic is routed outside the United States, such that consumer PII becomes accessible to foreign actors or subject to foreign jurisdiction.
We are proposing to codify a standard that would require agents, brokers, and web-brokers to implement and maintain reasonable administrative, technical, and contractual safeguards. These safeguards would be designed to ensure that access and attempted access to the FFEs and SBE-FPs, systems that support the FFEs and SBE-FPs, and PII obtained through the FFEs and SBE-FPs by the agent, broker, or web-broker and all employees, contractors, subcontractors, and other downstream entities acting on their behalf occurs only from locations within the United States. For the purposes of this proposal, systems that support the FFEs and SBE-FPs, collectively referred to as “Exchange Systems,” would include, but not be limited to systems used for agent and broker training, registration, and certification; CMS identity and access management; and eligibility and enrollment functions.
Consistent with the existing prohibition in the Exchange Agreements, the proposal further provides that such reasonable safeguards must include safeguards to ensure that VPNs or other similar technologies do not route Exchange system traffic through a server, network, or other point located outside the United States regardless of whether the agent, broker, or web-broker is physically located inside the United States at the time of access, and regardless of whether the technology causes the access to appear to originate from a location inside the United States. Therefore, agents, brokers, and web-brokers would have to implement and maintain reasonable safeguards to ensure that their network architecture and any third-party services they use do not result in Exchange system traffic being routed, stored, or processed on foreign infrastructure.
In addition, we propose that CMS would not find an agent, broker, or web-broker noncompliant with the proposed requirements due to unauthorized activity resulting from compromised credentials or inadvertent network activity that the agent, broker, or web-broker could not reasonably have known about or prevented through reasonable safeguards. Agents, brokers, and web-brokers would be required to implement reasonable safeguards, such as network monitoring, access controls, and contractual restrictions on third-party service providers, to prevent prohibited access, including inadvertent routing. CMS would not find an agent, broker, or web-broker noncompliant with the proposed standard if they implemented such safeguards and a prohibited connection nonetheless occurs that the agent, broker, or web-broker could not reasonably have known about or prevented through reasonable safeguards.
We believe it is appropriate that agents, brokers, and web-brokers implement and maintain reasonable safeguards to prevent prohibited access by all employees, contractors, subcontractors, and other downstream entities acting on their behalf because it would help ensure that the proposed requirement cannot be circumvented by delegating Exchange-related functions to another individual or entity. When CMS determines through its existing monitoring, audit, or enforcement activities that an employee, contractor, subcontractor, or downstream entity accessed the FFEs and SBE-FPs, Exchange Systems, or PII obtained through the FFEs and SBE-FPs from outside the United States on behalf of an agent, broker, or web-broker, CMS would treat such conduct as noncompliance by the agent, broker, or web-broker and pursue appropriate enforcement against the agent, broker, or web-broker under the applicable regulations. However, CMS would not find an agent, broker, or web-broker noncompliant with the proposed prohibition if an agent, broker, or web-broker can demonstrate they had implemented reasonable safeguards related to their contractor, subcontractor, or downstream entity's access to the FFEs and SBE-FPs, Exchange Systems, or PII obtained through the FFEs and SBE-FPs and prohibited access or attempted access nonetheless occurs without their knowledge or authorization. Reasonable administrative, technical, contractual, and oversight measures may include but are not limited to the following:
Contractual measures:
Including express prohibitions on foreign access to Exchange Systems in contracts with employees, contractors, subcontractors, and downstream entities; requiring such individuals or entities to attest to compliance with the foreign access prohibition; and including audit rights allowing the agent, broker, or web-broker to verify compliance by such individuals or entities.
Technical measures:
Implementing network access controls that restrict connections to Exchange Systems to domestic IP addresses; deploying monitoring tools that detect and alert on access attempts from foreign locations or through foreign infrastructure; requiring multi-factor authentication for all Exchange System access; and
(
printed page 74771)
configuring systems to block VPN or proxy connections that route Exchange traffic through foreign servers.
Oversight measures:
Conducting periodic reviews of access logs to identify unauthorized or suspicious connection attempts; requiring employees, contractors, subcontractors, and downstream entities to promptly report any known or suspected foreign access incidents; and maintaining documentation of compliance oversight activities sufficient to demonstrate that reasonable controls were in place.
CMS recognizes that what constitutes reasonable controls will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case, including the nature of the downstream relationship and the type of Exchange System access involved. CMS expects all regulated parties to take meaningful steps commensurate with their resources and the nature of their downstream relationships.
Codifying this requirement would protect the FFEs and SBE-FPs against the risk associated with access to Exchange Systems from outside of the United States and ensure agents, brokers, and web-brokers are notified that CMS may monitor, audit, and conduct enforcement activities related to access to Exchange Systems from outside of the United States in accordance
45 CFR 155.220(j)(2)(ix)
and
155.220(c)(5)

B. Pervasiveness of Medicare DMEPOS Fraud, Waste, and Abuse
DMEPOS fraud, waste, and abuse in the Medicare program has been a serious problem for many years, placing billions of taxpayer dollars at risk and potentially resulting in patient harm when beneficiaries use medically unnecessary or substandard items.
[
190 191
]
CMS' role in overseeing the Medicare program is to ensure that payments are made correctly and that fraud, waste, and abuse is stemmed because failure to do so endangers the Trust Funds and may result in beneficiary harm. Consequently, CMS rigorously scrutinizes DMEPOS suppliers upon enrolling, and to maintain enrollment, in Medicare.
[
192
]
Despite these safeguards, fraudulent billing for Medicare DMEPOS continues to be a major concern, and new schemes continue to emerge.
[
193
]
In fact, in 2026, CMS announced a nationwide temporary enrollment moratorium on newly enrolling Medicare DMEPOS medical supply companies based on evidence that the supplier category presented significant program integrity concerns, including a history of fraudulent billing and other abusive practices. CMS determined that temporarily restricting new enrollments was necessary to protect Medicare while preserving beneficiary access through the substantial number of existing enrolled suppliers. A nationwide approach was taken because it was clear to us that DMEPOS fraud, waste, and abuse was not restricted to certain types of items or particular areas of the country. Rather, it was widespread across DMEPOS types and geographic areas.
Additionally, in March 2025, CMS launched the Fraud Defense Operations Center (FDOC), also referred to as the Fraud War Room, a cross-functional unit combining data analysts, investigators, health policy experts, legal advisors, and law enforcement personnel to identify and interdict fraudulent billing before payment is made. In its first year of operation (March 31, 2025 through March 31, 2026), the FDOC suspended payments to 138 suspect DMEPOS suppliers, and as of August 2026, was holding $1.9 billion through these payment suspensions.
In many fraud schemes, DMEPOS suppliers and their agents target Medicare beneficiaries with unsolicited direct contacts and use high-pressure marketing tactics or deceptive lead generation to obtain information and consent to enable the DMEPOS supplier to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary or unneeded items, or items that are never supplied at all. This unsolicited direct contact may include emails, text messages, direct messages on social media, and door-to-door in person solicitation. Increasingly, these schemes involve third-party organizations, such as telemarketers or independent marketing firms. In some cases, unsolicited outreach to beneficiaries is used to offer free services, medical equipment, or gift cards in exchange for their Medicare number, which is then used to fraudulently bill Medicare.

Advances in technology also allow bad actors to spoof the number that appears on a beneficiary's caller ID so that an incoming call appears to be from a trusted health care provider or government agency.
[

Often, the enticement for the individual is that they are “qualified” for items “at no cost” or “free.” Once the scammers obtain the enrollee's personal information, monthly billing to Medicare will begin for medically unnecessary supplies that may or may not actually be sent to the enrollee.

C. Proposed Revisions to Supplier Standards Pertaining to Beneficiary Solicitation
Despite the existing program integrity controls in place pertaining to beneficiary solicitation by DMEPOS suppliers, fraudulent billing for Medicare DMEPOS continues to be a major concern, and new schemes have emerged. A crucial element in many of these schemes is the targeted, unsolicited contact with beneficiaries by DMEPOS suppliers and their agents, who use manipulative tactics to obtain personal information and consent. Accordingly, CMS has determined that a clarification to make explicit the prohibition on unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers (and third-party entities acting as their agents) when supplying a Medicare-covered item is needed to address these schemes. We believe that making explicit the supplier standards specified in 42 CFR 424.57(c)(11) and the addition of new supplier standard at 42 CFR 424.57(c)(31) would help to ensure that legitimate DMEPOS suppliers furnish items of DMEPOS to Medicare beneficiaries consistent with Medicare requirements.
Specifically, we are proposing to revise the supplier standard at
42 CFR 424.57(c)(11)
to clarify that suppliers must agree that they and their agents shall not contact a beneficiary when supplying a Medicare-covered item by telephone call or message, including text messages unless one of the following applies: (i) the beneficiary has provided written permission to the supplier to contact the beneficiary by telephone concerning the furnishing of a Medicare-covered item that is to be rented or purchased; (ii) the supplier has furnished a Medicare-covered item to the beneficiary and is contacting the beneficiary to coordinate delivery; or (iii) the supplier has previously furnished a covered item to the beneficiary in the 15-month period prior to the date of contact. This clarification would be consistent with the Telephone Consumer Protection Act's
[
200
]
long-standing definition of “telephone solicitation” as the initiation of a telephone call or message for the purpose of encouraging purchases or rentals of property, goods, or services, but excludes such a call or message when express permission for contact has been granted or there is an established business relationship.
In accordance with our authority in section 1834(j)(1)(B) of the Act to establish additional supplier standards, we are also proposing to add a supplier standard at
42 CFR 424.57(c)(31)
that would require that a supplier must agree that they and their agents shall not contact a beneficiary when supplying a Medicare-covered item using direct messages from social media platforms, email messages without opt-out provisions, and door-to-door in-person solicitation unless one of the following applies: (i) the individual has given written permission to the supplier to contact them concerning the furnishing of a Medicare-covered item that is to be rented or purchased; (ii) the supplier has furnished a Medicare-covered item to the individual and the supplier is contacting the individual to coordinate the delivery of the item; or (iii) if the contact concerns the furnishing of a Medicare-covered item other than a covered item already furnished to the individual, the supplier has furnished at least one covered item to the individual during the 15-month period preceding the date on which the supplier makes such contact.
We also propose to clarify that both
42 CFR 424.57(c)(11)
and
(31)
apply to all DMEPOS suppliers, whether the DMEPOS supplier itself or another qualified party is furnishing the item. We believe such clarification is necessary in light of our observations that third-party organizations, such as telemarketers and independent marketing firms, are increasingly working with DMEPOS suppliers to engage in fraudulent schemes targeting Medicare. We note, however, that our proposed clarification that
42 CFR 424.57(c)(11)
would apply to third-party agents and would not expand the existing prohibition. CMS and HHS-OIG have long interpreted the current version of
42 CFR 424.57(c)(11)
as prohibiting DMEPOS suppliers from using agents or other third parties to make unsolicited telephone calls that improperly target consumers.

CMS must take action to safeguard the Medicare program when bad actors exploit advances in technology and engage in coercive, high-pressure marketing tactics that result in the proliferation of fraudulent Medicare DMEPOS billing schemes. In doing so, however, CMS has continuously weighed the impact of additional contact limitations on both program integrity and DMEPOS suppliers' rights to engage in Constitutionally protected speech.
We believe that this proposed rule avoids the overly broad language of previous efforts and, if finalized as proposed, would not prohibit otherwise permissible marketing activity. This proposal is appropriately limited in scope and focuses on targeted communication that has significantly contributed to fraudulent Medicare DMEPOS billing. The proposed changes are designed not to prevent DMEPOS suppliers from engaging in legitimate marketing communications, but, instead, to strengthen CMS program integrity efforts to safeguard the Medicare program by preventing DMEPOS suppliers from utilizing third-party entities to indirectly engage in unsolicited beneficiary contact in which DMEPOS suppliers themselves may not engage when supplying a Medicare-covered item.

To estimate the financial burden on States, it was important to consider the Federal government's contribution to the cost of administering the Medicaid and CHIP programs. The Medicaid FMAP that is established for each State is based on the per capita income in the State as compared to the national average. Medicaid FMAPs range from a minimum of 50 percent in States with higher per capita incomes to a maximum of 83 percent in States with lower per capita incomes, but exceptions to the regular FMAP rate exist for certain States, situations, populations, providers, and services. b. ICRs Regarding PERM CAPs (§§ 431.992(a), (b)(3)(ii)(E), (b)(3)(ii)(F), (c), and (e) and 431.1010(b)(2)(ii))
The following proposed changes will be submitted to OMB for review under control number 0938-1012 (Expiration date: November 30, 2027).
Ensuring that States are taking necessary steps as part of their PERM CAPs is vital to CMS and States being able to reduce improper payments in future years. While we provide guidance to States throughout the entire PERM CAP process, we currently have limited enforcement authority to ensure that States comply with all PERM CAP requirements and effectively attempt to reduce or prevent future PERM errors.
Under new § 431.992(c), this proposed rule would provide us with explicit authority to approve (with required revisions, as needed) or disapprove a State's PERM CAP. This would allow us to ensure that States submit high-quality, effective, and robust PERM CAPs that would reduce future errors, while also allowing us to make more effective “good faith effort” determinations.
Currently, as part of the PERM CAP development process, we review the CAP developed by the State to ensure that it includes all requirements outlined in § 431.992, including the identification of root causes of improper payments, how the State plans to avoid repeat errors, how the State will monitor CAP implementation, and evaluate the effectiveness of the corrective actions. In instances in which this information is missing or deemed insufficient by us, a request for additional information is issued to the State, and the State is expected to make the updates until the information in the PERM CAP is deemed by CMS to meet regulatory requirements. This process would largely be unchanged under these new regulations, as this proposal would simply provide CMS with the authority to approve or disapprove a State's PERM CAP. We do not believe that this proposal to provide CMS with explicit authority to approve or disapprove a State's PERM CAP would lead to an increased workload or costs on States. The request for additional information is exempt from the requirements of the PRA since each request would be non-standardized across the States.
We are also proposing to amend § 431.992(a) to require States to submit a combined PERM CAP that addresses both Medicaid and CHIP PERM errors and deficiencies, as applicable. This provision proposes combining the Medicaid and CHIP CAPs, which would eliminate the need for States to duplicate responses on both CAPs, as the errors and corrective actions are generally similar across programs. This would reduce the time needed for States to meet PERM CAP regulatory requirements, as two separate CAPs would no longer be required. It is estimated that this change would reduce the burden on States' staff processing time by approximately 30 hours (from 60 to 30 hr) at $77.38/hr, which is the approximate time it takes claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators to generate responses on two separate reports. c. ICRs Regarding Requirements for Program Integrity Corrective Action Plans (§ 455.600 et seq.)
The following proposed changes will be submitted to OMB for review under control number 0938-AV97 (CMS-6098).
As discussed in section III. of this proposed rule (Medicaid and CHIP Program Integrity Proposals), CMS conducts program integrity audits to assess State compliance with applicable Federal Medicaid program integrity requirements and identify programmatic vulnerabilities. Although CMS currently works with States to address findings identified through these audits, existing regulations do not establish standardized requirements governing when a State must develop a corrective action plan in response to findings identified through a CMS program integrity audit, the required contents of such a plan, or CMS review and oversight of its implementation.
Therefore, we propose at § 455.602 to establish requirements governing Program Integrity Corrective Action Plans (Program Integrity CAPs). Under the proposal, following a CMS program integrity audit, the final audit report would specify whether CMS requires the State to develop a Program Integrity CAP and would identify the findings of noncompliance that the State must address through the CAP. CMS would determine whether a CAP is required based on the circumstances identified through the audit.
If a Program Integrity CAP is required, the State would be required to develop and submit a single CAP addressing the findings identified by CMS for corrective action. The CAP would be required to include the elements specified in new § 455.602(b), including a root cause analysis; the corrective
(
printed page 74781)
actions the State would implement to address the identified findings and come into compliance; an implementation schedule and monitoring plan; and a plan for evaluating the effectiveness of the corrective actions. States would be required to submit a Program Integrity CAP to CMS no later than 30 calendar days after the date of the final audit report, and CMS would review the CAP to determine whether it satisfies the regulatory requirements and adequately addresses the applicable audit findings. If necessary, CMS could return the CAP to the State with feedback and require revision and resubmission. The State would also be required under § 455.602(c)(2) to provide updates on Program Integrity CAP implementation progress at each milestone timeframe identified in the implementation schedule for each corrective action and upon request by CMS. These updates would include the State's progress in implementing the corrective action in accordance with the approved implementation schedule and information regarding the effectiveness of the corrective action in rectifying the applicable finding or findings of noncompliance.
