f. ICRs Regarding Medicaid Fee-For-Service Overpayment Reporting (60-Day Rule) (§ 455.900, et seq.)
Section 1128J(d) of the Act requires a person who has received an overpayment to report and return the overpayment to the Secretary, the State, an intermediary, a carrier, or a contractor, as appropriate. The Act also requires that a notification be made to the payer, in writing, of the reason for the overpayment. Section 1128J(d)(2) of the Act requires persons receiving overpayments under Medicaid or Medicare to report and return the overpayment by the later of: (1) 60 days after the date on which the overpayment was identified; or (2) the date any corresponding cost report is due, if applicable. Section 1128J(d)(3) of the Act specifies that any overpayment retained by a person after the deadline for reporting and returning an overpayment is an obligation subject to enforcement under the FCA (as defined in
31 U.S.C. 3729(b)(3)
). The term “person” refers to any provider of services, supplier, Medicaid managed care organization, Medicare Advantage Organization, or Prescription Drug Plan sponsor. Section 1128J(d)(4)(C)(ii) of the Act excludes beneficiaries from the definition of person.
As discussed in section I.B.4.f. of this proposed rule, even without a final rule, all interested parties are already subject to the statutory requirements found in section 1128J(d) of the Act and could face potential FCA liability, CMPL liability, and exclusion from Federal health care programs for failure to report and return an overpayment. This proposed rule provides clarity and consistency in the reporting and returning of overpayments in Medicaid FFS by outlining these requirements in regulation. We believe that this change would spur persons to be more diligent in reporting and returning overpayments in the Medicaid FFS program. That would likely increase the overpayments that States collect and the associated FFP they return, as well as the reporting that States must perform related to these returned overpayments.
Despite the absence of a strong basis for estimating the magnitude of this clarification's effect on the reporting and returning of overpayments in the Medicaid FFS program, we believe that we can use existing data to approximate what the potential impact may be, both on persons eligible to receive Medicaid funds (who would be responsible for identifying and returning the overpayments to the State) and on States (which would need to return the Federal share of those overpayments to us through the standard CMS-64 reporting process that is currently approved by OMB under control number 0938-1265). As for the impact on persons eligible to receive Medicaid funds, we believe that the PERM improper payment rates provide us with national context on improper payment rates for the Medicaid FFS component of the PERM measurement, which was approximately 5 percent for FY 2024. Given that the total amount of projected improper payments reported was $31.10 billion, we can calculate the FFS component to be $11.23 billion. Although the actual improper payment rates for individual States can vary quite widely, we believe that it is reasonable for us to use the national numbers to approximate the impact on an average State. The CMS-64 does not track overpayments by providers; however, data exists related to PERM overpayment letters sent to States for reporting on the CMS-64. Under the PERM medical review and data processing recovery process, recovery amounts are based on payments identified in individual sampled claims. The total Federal share of Medicaid PERM overpayments identified for recovery for RY 2025 is $1,264,636. This amount is not extrapolated to the national payment universe. States report the Federal share through CMS-64 adjustments. Eligibility-related improper payments are addressed through the separate disallowance framework under section 1903(u) of the Act, including the 3 percent threshold and the good faith waiver provisions.
This proposed regulation may also have an impact on the States themselves, as they would be responsible for reporting and returning the Federal share through the standard CMS-64 reporting process, but we believe that the impact would be minimal because States already report and reconcile expenditures and recoveries through the CMS-64, which CMS reviews and finalizes quarterly. Given that States are already responsible for reporting and returning the Federal share of overpayments made in their FFS programs, we do not believe that there would be an appreciable increase in burden by clarifying these requirements in regulation, even if the regulation leads to increased reporting by providers. The steps to report this information in the CMS-64 are well established and would not require changes as a result of this regulation. We welcome public comments on our assumptions.

IX. Regulatory Impact Analysis
A. Statement of Need
CMS' current Original Medicare, Medicaid and CHIP, Medicare Advantage, Medicare Part D, and Marketplace program integrity frameworks contain outdated, inconsistent, or incomplete requirements across several regulatory areas. These gaps limit CMS' ability to
(
printed page 74793)
detect fraud, hold States accountable, and recover improper payments. The proposals below address these gaps by modernizing reporting, clarifying enforcement authority, and closing structural vulnerabilities in oversight tools. CMS seeks public comments on all assumptions and estimates related to stakeholders impacted, benefits, costs, and transfers as part of these provisions.
1. Medicaid and CHIP Program Integrity
a. PERM CAPs (§§ 431.992(a), (b)(3)(ii)(E), (b)(3)(ii)(F), (c), and (e) and 431.1010(b)(2)(ii))
Section 431.992 currently requires each State selected for a Payment Error Rate Measurement (PERM) review to develop separate Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) corrective action plans (CAPs) for each improper payment rate measurement. Each CAP must address the State's PERM errors and deficiencies and include an error analysis, corrective actions, an implementation schedule and monitoring plan, and an evaluation of the CAP from the previous measurement. States must submit and begin implementing the CAP no later than 90 calendar days after their improper payment rates are posted and must provide implementation updates annually and upon request. A State with an eligibility improper payment rate above 3 percent for consecutive PERM years must also submit implementation updates every other month.
Although the existing requirements provide an important framework for addressing PERM errors and deficiencies, the current process requires each State to prepare and submit two CAPs—one for Medicaid and one for CHIP—even when the two submissions include similar information. The every-other-month update requirement also results in six responses each year for affected States. In addition, CMS currently reviews State CAPs and requests revisions when a submission does not sufficiently address the applicable requirements, but § 431.992 does not expressly set out an approval, revision, and disapproval process.
To reduce duplicative administrative work and clarify the CAP process, we propose to revise § 431.992(a) to require one combined Medicaid and CHIP PERM CAP while preserving the separate program requirements through program-specific identification of each error, deficiency, and CAP element. We also propose to revise § 431.992(b)(3)(ii)(E) and add § 431.992(b)(3)(ii)(F) to clarify the monitoring and effectiveness-evaluation information included in the CAP; establish at § 431.992(c) a CMS approval, revision, and disapproval process with a defined 90-calendar-day correction period; and revise § 431.992(e) to reduce eligibility corrective action implementation updates from every other month to every 6 months. Under proposed § 455.804, implementation of a CMS-approved Medicaid PERM CAP would be a condition for approval of a good faith waiver of an eligibility-related disallowance, but would not require a separate submission.
b. Medicaid and CHIP Managed Care Oversight Policies
States generally pay Medicaid managed care plans a per member per month capitation payment to provide a specified benefit package. These payments are made for Medicaid-eligible enrollees regardless of whether an enrollee uses services in a given month. Under § 438.3(c)(2), managed care plans may retain capitation payments only for Medicaid-eligible enrollees. States also must ensure that capitation rates are actuarially sound and reflect the reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs of providing services under the contract, as required by § 438.4(a).
Existing requirements provide a foundation for preventing payments on behalf of individuals who are no longer eligible, but they do not fully address how changes in an enrollee's circumstances are reported and how resulting capitation overpayments are recovered. Section 438.608(a)(3) requires managed care plans to promptly notify the State when they receive information about changes in an enrollee's circumstances that may affect an enrollee's eligibility, including a change of address or death. The regulation does not define “prompt” or require states to specify procedures for receiving these reports. As a result, states and plans may learn of or act on changes at different times. An out-of-state move or death may go unreported while capitation payments continue, and an in-state move may leave an enrollee assigned to a plan whose service area no longer includes the enrollee's residence.
Federal oversight has demonstrated the financial significance of these gaps. A Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) review found that Medicaid incurred approximately $117.1 million in capitation costs in August 2020 associated with beneficiaries concurrently enrolled in managed care programs in two states. Separate HHS-OIG audits of 14 states identified more than $249 million in unallowable capitation payments made on behalf of deceased enrollees, including $172 million in Federal funds. CMS has also identified practical barriers to recovery, including uncertainty about the date of an out-of-state relocation and managed care contracts that do not clearly address recovery of the associated payments.
Limited State access to data and the current regulatory ambiguity create a need for clearer, more consistent requirements that allow states to identify these changes, determine their effect on eligibility and plan enrollment, and recover inappropriate capitation payments. To address this need, we propose to amend § 438.608(a)(3) to require managed care plans and PCCMs to report an enrollee's death and verified address changes within 30 calendar days of receiving the information, and to require states to establish procedures for those reports. We also propose to amend § 438.3(c)(2) to clarify the recovery of capitation payments for periods following an enrollee's death or out-of-state relocation and the return of the applicable Federal share to CMS. These recovery actions would occur between states and managed care plans and would not create liability for beneficiaries. Applicable eligibility redetermination, notice, and fair hearing requirements would continue to govern state action affecting an enrollee's coverage.
Finally, we propose to clarify § 438.608(d)(1)(iv) so that the overpayment return flexibilities in § 438.608(d) do not result in duplicative treatment of recoveries retained under the False Claims Act or through other Federal or State investigations. Together, these revisions would strengthen Medicaid and CHIP managed care program integrity, improve the accuracy of capitation payments, and give states and plans clearer procedures for reporting and addressing changes in enrollee circumstances.
c. Revisions to 455.17 Reporting Requirements
States are currently required to report certain provider fraud and abuse information to CMS pursuant to
42 CFR 455.17
. These reporting requirements were established in 1983 and designed primarily to capture basic information regarding provider fraud and abuse investigations. The authority to collect this information expired in 1986. While these reporting requirements may have provided useful information to CMS and its oversight partners, they have not
(
printed page 74794)
been updated to reflect significant changes in law and regulatory landscape. They were, for example, developed decades before the 2006 enactment of the Medicaid Integrity Program at section 1936 of the Act which significantly bolstered our development of nationwide Medicaid program integrity efforts and before the widespread use of modern data analytics, cross-State information sharing, managed care program integrity activities, and many current fraud detection techniques.
Under the expired requirements at § 455.17(a), States were required to report to CMS the number of fraud and abuse complaints that warranted a full investigation. Under § 455.17(b), for cases of suspected provider fraud and abuse that warranted a full investigation, States are required to report: (1) the provider's name and number; (2) the source of the complaint; (3) the type of provider; (4) the nature of the complaint; (5) the approximate range of dollars involved; and (6) the legal and administrative disposition of the case, including actions taken by law enforcement. Consistent with the 1983 final rule (
48 FR 3756
), these reporting requirements applied only to suspected provider fraud and abuse cases and did not extend to suspected beneficiary fraud cases.
These requirements were meant to provide a foundation for Medicaid program integrity reporting for over 40 years, but CMS has determined that they no longer provide the level of detail necessary to support effective national oversight or provide CMS with sufficient information to hold States accountable for lacking program integrity operations. Specifically, the expired existing reporting requirements do not consistently provide information necessary to support national trend analysis, identify emerging fraud schemes, evaluate investigative outcomes, or coordinate oversight activities among Federal and State partners. CMS, State Medicaid Agencies (SMAs), Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs), Unified Program Integrity Contractors (UPICs), managed care plans, and law enforcement entities routinely coordinate activities involving provider investigations and administrative actions, and more detailed and standardized reporting would meaningfully strengthen those efforts.
We have also identified specific data gaps in the prior reporting requirement that limited its usefulness for program integrity purposes. The prior reporting requirement did not consistently capture provider identifiers in a standardized format, limiting CMS' ability to cross-reference reported cases against other data sources or match investigation records across States and programs. It also did not capture the estimated or final overpayment amounts associated with investigated cases, limiting CMS' ability to evaluate the financial impact of fraud and abuse activity or assess the effectiveness of State investigative efforts. Finally, the prior reporting requirement did not capture administrative actions taken by SMAs (such as provider terminations, payment suspensions, and overpayment recovery actions) separately from law enforcement dispositions, limiting CMS' visibility into the full range of program integrity actions States are taking in response to identified fraud and abuse.
To address these issues, we propose to revise § 455.17 to modernize Medicaid fraud and abuse reporting requirements and improve the usefulness of information reported to CMS. Consistent with the prior scope of § 455.17, these proposed revisions would apply only to suspected provider fraud and abuse cases and would not extend reporting requirements to beneficiary cases. Specifically, we propose to amend § 455.17(b) to require States to report the following additional data elements for cases of suspected provider fraud and abuse that warranted a full investigation: (1) the provider's NPI, or Medicaid ID if the provider is ineligible to receive a NPI; (2) the provider's Employer Identification Number or Taxpayer Identification Number (EIN/TIN); (3) the State in which the investigation is being conducted; (4) the investigation status; (5) the type of service involved; (6) the payor (for example, Fee-For-Service, managed care); (7) the relevant claim dates; (8) the estimated overpayment amount; and (9) where available, the final overpayment amount and the approximate time period covered by the investigation. We also propose to renumber the existing § 455.17 (and expand is scope to include additional reporting options to include the disposition of the case to include administrative actions taken by the SMA, including provider termination, payment suspension (including good cause exceptions identified under § 455.23), and overpayment recovery status, in addition to the existing requirement to report actions taken by law enforcement.
We seek comments on these proposals, including on the operational feasibility of the proposed data elements, whether additional data elements should be included, and the timeframe States would need to come into compliance with the revised reporting requirements.
d. Medicaid Payment Suspensions Updates (§  455.23)
This set of proposed provisions would impact all 50 States, the District of Columbia, and the applicable territories. Including all States and territories (hereafter collectively “States”), there are 56 Medicaid programs in the United States.
Consistent with sections 1902(a)(68) of the Act (which requires States to require certain entities to maintain policies and procedures for detecting fraud, waste, and abuse) and 1903(i)(2)(C) of the Act (which prohibits payment of Federal Financial Participation (FFP) with respect to services furnished by a provider to which the state has failed to suspend payment pending investigation of a credible allegation of fraud (CAF)), we are proposing a number of Medicaid payment suspension provisions to strengthen and clarify certain aspects of the payment suspension process.
Medicaid is one of the largest Federal-state partnership programs in the United States. Fraud, waste, and abuse represent a persistent threat to the program's financial integrity. Payment suspensions based on CAFs are among the most powerful tools available to State Medicaid Agencies (SMAs) to halt potentially fraudulent payments before they become unrecoverable, while the CAF is investigated. The proposed regulatory changes are designed to ensure that this tool is used consistently, effectively, and in a timely manner across all States. Medicaid and CHIP fraud undermine the programs' integrity and harm the public. Fraudulent providers exploit gaps in oversight to extract payments from a public insurance program funded by Federal and State taxpayers. The costs are borne broadly by the public, while the benefits accrue to bad actors. The payment suspension provisions described address this failure in distinct and complementary ways.
(
printed page 74795)
(1) Inconsistent State Implementation of CAF Determinations
Under the current regulatory framework, the absence of explicit guidance on whether SMAs must independently redetermine the credibility of a CAF received from an outside agency has produced significant variation in State practice. Some States immediately initiate payment suspensions upon receipt of an externally determined CAF, while others conduct full independent credibility reviews before acting. This inconsistency creates exploitable gaps: bad actors operating in States with more deliberate review processes may continue receiving Medicaid payments for extended periods, increasing the total overpayment amount and reducing the likelihood of full recoupment.
The financial consequences of delayed payment suspensions are compounded by the behavior of fraudulent providers once detected. Upon discovery, such providers frequently cease operations, dissolve business entities, or file for bankruptcy protection, leaving States with limited or no viable pathway to recover funds already disbursed.
(2) Payment Suspension Lapses Due to Law Enforcement Declinations
CMS has observed that payment suspensions may be terminated because MFCUs or other law enforcement agencies have declined fraud referrals due to resource constraints or competing priorities. Under current § 455.23(d)(4), States without alternative Federal or State authority to maintain the suspension are required to terminate it upon law enforcement declination, even when the CAF remains credible and unresolved. This creates a structural vulnerability in the payment suspension framework that is unrelated to the merits of the underlying allegation.
(3) Overutilization of Good Cause Exceptions
CMS data (reported by states) from CY 2025 indicates that approximately 75 percent of CAF cases reported under § 455.23(g)(3) did not proceed to a payment suspension because an SMA invoked a good cause exception. Several States reported good cause exception rates exceeding 90 percent, with some States recording hundreds of good cause exceptions against only a handful of actual payment suspensions. While good cause exceptions serve a legitimate purpose—particularly when a payment suspension could compromise an active law enforcement investigation—the data suggests that some States may be invoking the exception as a blanket policy to avoid provider abrasion, administrative burden, or litigation risk, rather than on a case-by-case basis as required.
(4) Limitations of Annual Reporting
The current annual reporting cadence under § 455.23(g)(3) limits CMS' ability to identify emerging trends, provide timely technical assistance to States, and conduct effective program integrity oversight. Given that much of the relevant data is already exchanged between SMAs and MFCUs on a quarterly basis through existing case tracking systems, the annual reporting requirement represents a missed opportunity for more proactive and responsive oversight.
e. National Provider Identifier (NPI) Requirements for Medicaid Providers (§ 455.440)
Accurate provider identification is fundamental to the effective administration of the Medicaid program and to CMS' ability to oversee program integrity activities. Provider identifiers support virtually every operational component of Medicaid administration, including provider enrollment, claims processing, payment administration, managed care oversight, fraud detection, audit activities, and coordination with Federal and State oversight partners. As Medicaid programs have become increasingly dependent upon electronic data exchange and sophisticated analytical tools, consistent provider identification has become an essential component of effective program administration.
The Department adopted the National Provider Identifier (NPI) as the standard unique health care provider identifier under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) Administrative Simplification provisions. Since its implementation, the NPI has become the nationally recognized provider identifier used throughout Medicare and much of the commercial health care sector. The NPI was specifically designed to improve administrative efficiency by providing a single identifier that could be used consistently across multiple health care transactions and operational systems.
Within Medicaid, however, provider identification practices have evolved incrementally over time rather than through the implementation of a comprehensive enterprise-wide provider identification strategy. Although States generally collect NPIs
(
printed page 74796)
where required for HIPAA standard transactions or specific Medicaid operational functions, current Medicaid regulations do not require States to consistently collect, maintain, and use NPIs throughout all systems for every Medicaid provider eligible to obtain an NPI.
As a result, States have developed differing approaches to provider identification. In many States, multiple provider identifiers continue to exist across separate business functions, with internal provider numbers serving as the primary identifier for some operational activities while NPIs are used only where specifically required. Consequently, the same provider may be represented by different identifiers within provider enrollment systems, claims processing systems, managed care oversight activities, program integrity databases, and reporting systems.
CMS has determined that inconsistent provider identification practices have become an increasingly significant limitation on effective Medicaid program integrity oversight. Over the past decade, CMS has substantially expanded the use of advanced data analytics, predictive modeling, and coordinated Federal and State oversight activities. The effectiveness of these activities depends upon accurate and consistent provider identification.
When provider identifiers differ across operational systems or jurisdictions, CMS' ability to accurately associate provider activity across multiple datasets is diminished. These inconsistencies reduce the effectiveness of automated data matching, increase administrative complexity, and require additional manual review before investigative resources can be effectively deployed.
CMS has also identified specific operational limitations associated with inconsistent provider identifiers that affect several complementary proposals contained elsewhere in this proposed rule. For example, elsewhere in this proposed rule CMS proposes to strengthen State reporting requirements under § 455.17 by requiring additional standardized information regarding provider fraud and abuse investigations. The usefulness of those additional reporting elements depends in significant part upon the availability of a standardized provider identifier.
CMS believes that these considerations collectively demonstrate that existing Medicaid regulations no longer provide sufficient consistency to support modern Medicaid program integrity operations.
f. Requirements for Program Integrity Corrective Action Plans (§ 455.600,
et seq.
)
Effective oversight of Medicaid and CHIP requires that CMS have mechanisms to ensure States address identified vulnerabilities. Despite ongoing efforts to provide effective oversight, we continue to find errors and deficiencies in State program integrity operations that result in repeat findings and recommendations. Currently, our authority to take action for instances of sustained non-compliance with Federal requirements is limited to a small subset of CMS program integrity initiatives. Our ability to require a State to develop and implement a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) in response to our program integrity-related activities is significantly limited.
As a result of these limitations, our existing authorities do not sufficiently allow us to take administrative actions should a State fail to effectuate their CAPs or comply with program integrity requirements. This significantly limits the effectiveness of our oversight efforts and allows known vulnerabilities to persist.
To address these gaps, we propose to amend part 455 by adding a new subpart G (§ 455.600,
et seq.
) titled “Requirements for Program Integrity Corrective Action Plans” that codifies the administrative actions we may pursue when States fail to comply with program integrity requirements. Specifically, we propose adding a new § 455.602 that would require a State to respond to a final audit report by developing and implementing a Program Integrity CAP for each area of non-compliance. The necessary elements of the Program Integrity CAP would be codified in new § 455.602(b) and serve as a basis for CMS to evaluate whether the Program Integrity CAP mitigates program integrity risks in a meaningful and effective way.
g. Medicaid and CHIP Beneficiary Eligibility Audits (§ 455.700,
et seq.
)
This rule proposes to establish a Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audit program under new part 455, subpart H (§ 455.700, et seq). The Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audits provide us with enhanced oversight of States' eligibility determination processes, enable us to focus additional resources on high-risk States, and strengthen our ability to identify and recover erroneous excess payments. By establishing a regulatory framework for our beneficiary eligibility audits, we intend to increase transparency of audit requirements and procedures. If this rule is finalized as proposed, future audit findings could result in disallowances under section 1903(u) of the Act, establishing a new mechanism for overpayment recovery. In addition, beneficiary eligibility audits will be conducted more frequently, with each State undergoing an audit at least once in a five-year period and some States audited multiple times within that period based on their risk score.

Section 1903(l) of the Act requires the use of EVV systems for certain services provided by an in-home provider. Specifically, CMS is proposing to require the reporting of a referral of substantiated or suspicious activities of a provider of services (including a prescriber) or a supplier related to fraud, waste and abuse to initiate or assist with investigations conducted by CMS, or its designee, a Medicare program integrity contractor, or law enforcement partners as well as require the reporting of all payment suspensions based on credible allegations of fraud for all providers and suppliers, rather than only those by pharmacies.
CMS believes that increased reporting is essential to the oversight of the Medicare Part C and Part D programs, as this information is valuable to CMS and assists with investigations, referrals to law enforcement, and trend monitoring. In addition, more stringent reporting requirements allow CMS to anonymously share more robust data on referred providers or suppliers with other MA organizations and Part D contracts on a quarterly basis to assist in their own internal fraud, waste, and abuse efforts. Data transparency and information sharing with our partners are at the core of CMS' strategy to crush fraud. Changes proposed in this rule will affect the Medicare Part C and Part D plan sponsors contracted with CMS to provide Medicare beneficiaries coverage under the Medicare Part C and Part D programs.
b. Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV)
This rule proposes certain program integrity policies in the MA program, specifically, the recovery of improper payments identified during RADV audits, and aligns with the Administration's focus on the fiscal sustainability of the MA program and the interests of Medicare beneficiaries, providers, and MA organizations. 3. Medicare Provider Enrollment Provisions
Consistent with section 1866(j) of the Act, we are proposing several Medicare provider enrollment provisions to strengthen and clarify certain aspects of the provider enrollment process. These include, but are not limited to, adding and modifying grounds for denying or revoking a provider's or supplier's Medicare enrollment. We are also proposing to enhance our DMEPOS supplier surety bond process under § 424.57(d), to collect additional information from DMEPOS suppliers regarding certain relationships they may have, and to require DMEPOS suppliers to have a process for obtaining prior DMEPOS beneficiary consent for items the supplier sends to the beneficiary at their home or residence. We are further proposing to revise subparts B and E of
42 CFR part 455
, which address Medicaid and CHIP provider enrollment, to: (1) add more reasons for which the State must deny or terminate a provider's enrollment; and (2) require Medicaid and CHIP providers to submit certain data regarding their ownership, management, and associated adverse legal history. Too, we are proposing that providers that bill MA for services and items furnished to MA beneficiaries be enrolled in Original Medicare in order to receive payment. All the foregoing changes are necessary to help ensure that payments are made only to qualified Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and MA providers and suppliers, that the Medicare program can recoup monies it is owed, and that the financial integrity and beneficiaries of Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and MA are protected.
4. Marketplace Program Integrity
In recent years, there has been a substantial increase in consumer complaints from individuals who reported they were unaware they had been enrolled by an agent, broker, or web-broker in Exchange coverage. From 2023 through 2025, CMS received over 624,000 consumer complaints attesting to unauthorized Exchange enrollments or unauthorized plan switching by agents, brokers, or web-brokers and confirmed by issuer and CMS review; 300,000 of the 624,000 were received in 2025 alone. These improper enrollments may constitute abusive conduct, costing Federal taxpayers billions of dollars and can cause significant medical or financial harm to consumers.
Consistent with sections 1312(e), 1313, and 1321 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), we are proposing a number of additions and amendments to
45 CFR 155.220
to improve the integrity of the FFEs, reduce abusive conduct by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, and better protect consumers within the FFEs. These proposals include but are not limited to: (1) amending
45 CFR 155.20
to add a definition of “convicted” and “credible allegation of abusive conduct,”(2) adding participation standards for agents and brokers to
45 CFR 155.220(g)(3)
, which would prevent agents and brokers that pose unacceptable risk from participating in the FFE, (3) amending 155.220(g) to replace the existing 30-calendar day opportunity to resolve noncompliance before CMS may terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) for cause with an opportunity to refute identified noncompliance and to codify factors that CMS would consider in determining whether to terminate an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) for cause and to impose other penalties, (4) amending
45 CFR 155.220(g)(5)
to increase transparency around program integrity oversight of the FFE and further strengthen our administrative actions against suspected bad actors, (5) amending
45 CFR 155.220(j)(2)(i)
and
(ii)
by adding specific examples of behavior that CMS considers abusive conduct, and (6) codifying a term in the existing Exchange Agreements with the FFEs and SBE-FPs which would prohibit agents, brokers, and web-brokers from accessing and attempting to access, the FFEs and SBE-FPs, Exchange systems, and personally identifiable information obtained through the FFEs and SBE-FPs from outside the United States. The impacted stakeholders for the provisions described in this section are agents, brokers, and web-brokers participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs, and their downstream entities such as employees of agents, brokers, and web-brokers, contractors engaged by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, and subcontractors engaged by those contractors.
5. Clarifying Existing Requirement and Adding a New Unsolicited Beneficiary Contact Prohibition
This rule includes a provision to clarify the existing prohibition against unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers to make explicit the inclusion of third-party entities acting as the agents of DMEPOS suppliers; and to clarify that the prohibition against unsolicited beneficiary contact by telephone refers to a telephone call or message, including text messages. This rule also includes a provision to add a new supplier standard under
42 CFR 424.57(c)(31)
to prohibit unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers and their agents when supplying a Medicare covered item by direct messages from social media platforms, email messages without opt-out features, and door-to-door in-person solicitation, unless a specified exception applies.
Fraudulent billing for Medicare DMEPOS continues to be a major concern. Despite an existing prohibition on unsolicited beneficiary contact by telephone, DMEPOS suppliers and third parties acting as their agents are targeting Medicare beneficiaries with unsolicited text messages and other direct messages, door-to-door in person solicitation, unwanted telephone calls, and other means to engage in high-pressure marketing tactics and deceptive lead generation that allow DMEPOS suppliers to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary or unneeded items, or items that are never supplied at all. These changes are necessary to help ensure that legitimate DMEPOS suppliers are furnishing medically necessary items of DMEPOS to Medicare beneficiaries consistent with Medicare requirements, which we believe would assist in protecting the Trust Funds and Medicare beneficiaries.

C. Detailed Economic Analysis
As was mentioned in the COI section of this rule, “To estimate the financial burden on States, it was important to consider the Federal Government's contribution to the cost of administering the Medicaid and CHIP programs. The Medicaid FMAP that is established for each State is based on the per capita income in the State as compared to the national average. Medicaid FMAPs range from a minimum of 50 percent in States with higher per capita incomes to a maximum of 83 percent in States with lower per capita incomes, but exceptions to the regular FMAP rate exist for certain States, situations, populations, providers, and services. For Medicaid, all States generally receive a 50 percent FMAP for administration. States also receive higher Federal matching rates for certain systems improvements, redesign, or operations, including a 90 percent match rate for the design, development, and enhancement of Medicaid information technology (IT) systems. We have estimated that States would contribute 10 percent of applicable Medicaid IT costs. For CHIP, Congress created an “enhanced” Federal matching rate for CHIP that is generally about 15 percentage points higher than the Medicaid rate, averaging 71 percent nationally.
To determine the Federal contribution to the costs of administering the Medicaid and CHIP programs for purposes of estimating State burden with respect to the collections of information and reviewing the regulation and training staff, we elected to use the higher end estimate that the States would contribute 50 percent of the costs. This assumption represents the upper bound of potential State burden, recognizing that the actual share is often lower once enhanced Federal match rates are applied.”

++
Faster Payment Suspensions and Reduced Overpayments.
Reducing the time between a CAF referral and the implementation of a payment suspension would directly limit the number of potential overpayments disbursed during the intervening period. The magnitude of this benefit is a function of the volume of CAF referrals received from external agencies and the average payment amounts involved. Even modest reductions in the delay between CAF determination and payment suspension initiation could yield significant savings at the program level. Similarly to what was discussed above, the amount of potential savings is based on expected overpayments resulting from unknown future fraud schemes and the difference between each States' investigative times including the difference between the current and future reliance on CAF determinations made by CMS or other agencies. Since CMS does not dictate State policy and we see the large variability, we cannot estimate the potential savings from decreased overpayments.
++
Uniform National Standards.
Establishing a clear, uniform standard for how SMAs may treat externally determined CAFs would reduce the exploitable variation in State practice
(
printed page 74804)
and create a more consistent national framework for Medicaid program integrity. This benefit is not expected to have measurable outcomes.
++
Deterrence.
A more consistent and rapid payment suspension response to CAF determinations may deter fraudulent providers from targeting Medicaid programs in States that previously had more deliberate review processes. This benefit is not expected to have measurable outcomes.
§ 455.23(d)(4)—Maintaining Payment Suspensions
++
Prevention of Suspension Lapses Due to Law Enforcement Resource Constraints.
By permitting SMAs to maintain payment suspensions when a CAF remains under active investigation—regardless of whether law enforcement has accepted the referral—this provision would close a structural gap that currently allows fraudulent payments to resume solely because of law enforcement capacity limitations unrelated to the merits of the underlying allegation. This would provide policy norms across States.
++
Protection of Medicaid Funds During Ongoing Investigations.
Maintaining payment suspensions throughout the duration of an active investigation would preserve the financial integrity of the Medicaid program and maximize the potential for recoupment of improperly paid funds. Since the number of payment suspension and resources available to law enforcement agencies varies by State, we cannot estimate how much may be saved by this proposal. We also would not want to prescribe a floor or ceiling to the number of payment suspensions that a state should do in any given timeframe, as discussed above.
++
Preservation of State Flexibility.
The proposed provision would preserve State flexibility by allowing—rather than requiring—SMAs to maintain suspensions, while establishing clear procedural guardrails (written documentation and quarterly redetermination) to ensure that suspensions remain tethered to actual, ongoing investigations. This benefit is not expected to have measurable outcomes.
++
Safeguard Against Indefinite Suspensions.
The quarterly redetermination requirement would ensure that payment suspensions maintained under this provision remain time-limited and subject to meaningful review, consistent with the statutory authority under section 1903(i)(2)(C) of the Act. This would protect providers from open-ended suspensions in cases where the underlying investigation has effectively concluded. This is a benefit to providers that is not expected to have measurable outcomes.
§ 455.23(e)(1)(i)—Verifying Good Cause Exceptions
++
Reduction in Improper Good Cause Exception Invocations.
We expect that requiring SMAs to affirmatively verify, on a case-by-case basis, that a good cause exception is warranted for each individual CAF case would reduce the rate of improper or unsupported good cause exception invocations. Based on CY 2025 data showing a 75 percent good cause exception rate, even a modest reduction in improper invocations could result in a meaningful increase in the number of appropriate payment suspensions implemented, with corresponding reductions in fraudulent payments. Since the number of payment suspensions and how States have used the law enforcement good cause exception varies by State, we cannot estimate how much may be saved by this proposal. Similarly, we would not want to direct States to implement a certain number of payment suspensions, as discussed above.
++
Improved Accountability and Transparency.
Requiring SMAs to document the basis for each good cause exception and transmit documentation to CMS would create an auditable record of good cause exception decisions, enabling CMS to identify patterns of potential overutilization and provide targeted technical assistance. This benefit is not expected to have measurable outcomes.
++
Alignment with Existing MFCU Obligations.
This proposed verification requirement would be consistent with existing obligations under § 1007.9(h), which already contemplates MFCUs providing quarterly updates to SMAs regarding payment suspensions for each case. This policy alignment is a benefit that is not expected to have a measurable outcome. The marginal burden of providing case-specific good cause confirmations is therefore expected to be limited.
§ 455.23(g)(3)—Quarterly Reporting
++
Enhanced CMS Oversight Capabilities.
Quarterly reporting would enable CMS to compile and analyze program-wide data on payment suspension activity on a more timely basis, identify systemic trends earlier, and potentially provide technical assistance to States before problematic patterns become entrenched. More granular and timely data on payment suspension activity would enhance CMS' ability to conduct risk-based State Program Integrity reviews and target oversight resources toward States with potential systemic deficiencies. Similarly, quarterly data would support more robust and timely aggregate reporting on Medicaid program integrity outcomes, consistent with CMS' broader commitment to transparency and accountability. More frequent reporting would also enable CMS to identify States that may benefit from technical assistance and provide guidance in a more timely manner, reducing the risk that problematic patterns persist unaddressed for extended periods. Since fraud schemes are variable and how States choose to utilize technical assistance is anticipated to vary, we cannot estimate how much may be saved by this proposal.
We request comments from States on our benefits assumptions for the Medicaid payment suspension provisions.

e. National Provider Identifier (NPI) Requirements for Medicaid Providers (§ 455.440)
(1) Stakeholders Impacted
The States and territories, and individual providers that act as Personal Care Attendants will be impacted by this provision. In the absence of comprehensive national data identifying the number and characteristics of all health care providers that would be newly affected by these requirements, this analysis uses personal care attendants (PCAs) as a proxy for estimating the potential burden on affected providers. PCAs provide a reasonable proxy because they represent a large population of individual providers participating in Medicaid-funded services for whom provider identification, enrollment, and screening requirements vary across states. As a result, the PCA population provides an observable basis for estimating the administrative and financial burden associated with obtaining an NPI and completing related provider enrollment activities.
All 50 States, the District of Columbia, and the applicable territories are subject to this reporting requirement. Including all States and territories (hereafter collectively “States”), there are 56 Medicaid programs in the United States.
(2) Benefits
To address the limitations described above, this rule proposes to require State Medicaid agencies to collect, maintain, and use NPIs for all Medicaid providers eligible to obtain one. Under this proposal, the NPI would serve as the standardized provider identifier used consistently across Medicaid provider enrollment, claims processing, managed care oversight, program integrity, and reporting systems.
The proposed changes would improve the consistency and reliability of provider information available to States and CMS and strengthen the infrastructure supporting Medicaid program integrity activities. Although the proposed revisions would not directly prevent fraud or improper payments, the consistent use of NPIs would improve the ability of States and CMS to match provider information across Medicaid systems, identify potentially suspicious billing patterns, evaluate provider activity across jurisdictions, and coordinate program integrity and oversight activities.
The proposed benefits associated with this provision are primarily assessed qualitatively and include:
Improved Data Quality and Interoperability:
The proposed revisions would establish a standardized provider identifier across Medicaid systems, improving the consistency and reliability of provider information and facilitating more effective data matching. The use of a standardized identifier would also reduce administrative complexity associated with managing multiple maintaining and reconciling multiple provider identifiers.
Enhanced Program Integrity Analytics:
The proposed revisions would improve the ability of States and CMS to analyze provider information, identify potentially suspicious billing patterns, evaluate provider activity across jurisdictions, and support coordination of program integrity and investigative activities with other oversight entities.
(

Strengthened Foundation for Other Program Integrity Initiatives:
The standardized use of NPIs would provide infrastructure that supports other program integrity proposals in this rule, including enhanced fraud reporting under § 455.17 and EVV utilization requirements. More consistent provider identification would also provide a stronger foundation for existing and future Medicaid program integrity and oversight activities.

c. Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV)
This proposed rule creates regulations to govern the collection of extrapolated audit findings in MA. As we develop our approach to statistical sampling and extrapolation, we are taking account of the recommendations of the 2016 GAO report
[
224
]
entitled, “Fundamental Improvements Needed in CMS' Effort to Recover Substantial Amounts of Improper Payments.” The GAO recommended that CMS select plans based on the risk for improper payments. Prior to the GAO report, CMS selected stratified random samples of enrollees during RADV audits, including our 2011 to 2013 audits. However, beginning with audits of MA contracts for payment year 2014, CMS began incorporating the potential risk of improper payments to MA organizations, based on past audit findings and other factors, into selecting enrollee samples for audits. Accordingly, CMS expects to be more effective in identifying improper payments in future audit years.
To clarify in more detail how this proposed rule impacts the recovery audit process, we note the following:
The Part C Improper Payment Measurement program (not RADV audits) measures and reports improper payments in accordance with the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA) Public Law (116-117) in the Medicare Part C program.
[
225
]
After defining the eligible population, a representative sample of beneficiaries from risk adjustment eligible contracts are selected for medical record review. MA organizations submit medical record documentation to substantiate the CMS-HCC payments sampled by CMS for each year's Part C Improper Payment Measurement. Certified coders code the medical records, and the findings are used to recalculate risk scores for each sampled beneficiary. The difference between the payment risk scores and the recalculated risk scores is termed Risk Adjustment Error. Validation results from the sample are extrapolated to the broader Part C population to produce payment error estimates that meet the PIIA requirements for the payment year. No recoveries are made through these audits.
Findings from the Part C Improper Payment Measurement audits and contract-specific RADV audits are used to help identify cohorts of beneficiaries for which CMS may be most at risk for making improper payments to MA organizations. While CMS has flexibility to decide how to focus audits, starting with the PY 2014 audits, CMS took a more focused approach on areas of high risk of improper payments and CMS intends to focus audits on such MA organizations in the future and continue taking a more focused approach on areas of high risk of improper payments.
By better targeting contract-specific RADV audits based on MA organizations' risk of receiving improper payments, CMS expects to have a sentinel effect and reduce the historical Part C improper payment rate over time.
Lastly, CMS understands that there may be extraordinary circumstances beyond MA organizations' control that may make it difficult to meet medical record submission or other audit requirements. In this proposed rule, CMS is adding a provision to allow MA organizations to request a hardship exception, as prescribed by CMS, if they cannot submit medical records timely as required. If CMS approves an MA organization's hardship exception request, the MA organization is not required to submit medical record documentation for the audited CMS-HCC and the audited CMS-HCC will not negatively impact error calculation.

e. Medicaid, CHIP, and MA Provider Enrollment and Other Considerations
(1) Additional Medicaid and CHIP Denial and Termination Reasons (§ 455.416)
We are proposing several new and expanded grounds for which the States must deny or terminate a provider's Medicaid or CHIP enrollment under § 455.416. These include, but are not limited to, the following:
Non-compliance:
Deny or terminate if the provider is non-compliant with any requirement described in subpart B or E of Part 455.
Felony convictions:
Deny or terminate if the provider, any person or organization with an ownership or control interest in the provider, or any managing employee or managing organization of the provider was, within the preceding 10 years, convicted of a Federal or State felony offense that the State determines is detrimental to the best interests of its Medicaid program or CHIP and its beneficiaries.
Prescribing Authority:
Deny or terminate if: (1) a physician's or practitioner's Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Certificate of Registration to dispense a controlled substance is currently suspended or revoked or is surrendered in response to an order to show cause.
Misuse of enrollment:
Terminate if the provider knowingly sells to or allows another individual or entity to use its enrollment to bill Medicaid or CHIP.
Improper prescribing practices:
Terminate the physician or practitioner has a pattern or practice of prescribing Medicaid or CHIP drugs that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicaid or CHIP beneficiaries, or fails to meet Medicaid or CHIP requirements.
Abusive ordering, certifying or referring of Medicaid or CHIP services or item:
The physician or practitioner has a pattern or practice of ordering, certifying or referring Medicaid or CHIP services or items that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicaid or CHIP beneficiaries, or otherwise fails to meet Medicaid or CHIP requirements.
(a) Stakeholders Impacted
The principal impacted parties would be the States and Medicaid and CHIP providers.
(b) Benefits
We believe that our proposed denial and revocation grounds would: (1) facilitate greater consistency between Medicare and Medicaid as well as between State Medicaid agencies and CHIPs; and (2) protect Medicaid and CHIP from non-compliant providers.
(c) Savings, Costs, and Transfers
We are unable to assess the cost impact of these provisions or calculate potential transfers for two main reasons. First, as these are new or expanded grounds, we have no precedent in Medicaid or CHIP upon which we can establish an estimated impact. Second, although most of these bases are duplicated in § 424.535(a) with respect to Medicare, we do not believe that using the annual number of Medicare revocations on these grounds as a basis for calculating the likely number of Medicaid and CHIP terminations is appropriate. This is because the number of situations in which these Medicaid and CHIP termination situations will arise may be very different from that for Medicare. This is particularly true because these grounds are discretionary in Medicare but would be mandatory in Medicaid and CHIP (absent a State finding that the termination would not be in the best of the Medicare program or CHIP). States may therefore have considerably more terminations than Medicare. Too, some States, for instance, may already have several of these denials and termination reasons (or variations of them) under State law, meaning there would be no material increase or decrease in denials or terminations for such provider activity.
Due to this uncertainty, we request comments from interested parties (in particular, the States) on the potential impact of these proposed bases. We are particularly interested in comments regarding whether the States currently use termination reasons similar to those we are proposing and, if so, how frequently.
As with our proposed Medicare revocation reasons, we believe there could be savings or transfers from terminations of Medicaid or CHIP enrollment, though we are unable to estimate a potential amount.
(2) Medicaid and CHIP Application Fee (§ 455.460)
Consistent with § 455.460, States must collect the applicable provider enrollment application fee from a prospective or revalidating provider. There are exceptions, though. These include, but are not limited to, providers identified in § 455.460(a)(2) that—
Are enrolled in either Medicare or another State's Medicaid program or CHIP.
Have paid the applicable application fee to a Medicare contractor or another State.
In general, application fees are intended to cover the State's cost of screening the provider and the application. States screen a provider's application at the same level (limited, moderate, or high) that CMS uses for that same provider type under § 424.518. Some States have expressed reluctance to screen at higher levels under § 455.452 because of the inability to collect an application fee under § 455.460 to cover the additional costs. States therefore have occasionally been unable for financial reasons to use enhanced screening methods when the State believed they were necessary. 4. Marketplace Program Integrity
a. Stakeholders Impacted
The Marketplace provisions would impact insurance agents, insurance brokers, and insurance web-brokers. Some entities within these categories may qualify as small businesses.
b. Expand Authority To Terminate Agents, Brokers, and Web-Brokers' Exchange Participation
We propose to revise
45 CFR 155.220(g)(3)
to add participation standards that would prevent agents, brokers, and web brokers that pose unacceptable risk from participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs. Specifically, agents, brokers, and web-brokers that pose unacceptable risk would not be permitted to register, complete training, or enter into Exchange agreement(s) with CMS.
Additionally, this proposed rule would update § 155.220(g)(3) to allow CMS to immediately terminate agents, brokers, and web-brokers who pose unacceptable risk from participating in the FFEs and SBE-FPs, without waiting 30 calendar days from the date of notice. This proposed rule would also add a definition of “convicted” to § 155.20 in alignment with the Medicare program.
We do not expect the proposed changes to § 155.20 or § 155.220(g)(3) to have a financial impact on agents, brokers, or web-brokers because the changes do not impose any new requirements on them. We also expect these changes to only have minimal impact on CMS' oversight responsibilities because CMS already has systematic access to the data required for implementation. We anticipate that these changes would have benefits, including reducing the amount of taxpayer dollars being inappropriately disbursed, increasing transparency around program integrity oversight of the FFE, and improving public trust with the FFE and the agent, broker, and web-broker community.
We believe disruptions in the broker market will be limited to brokers that pose an undue risk of fraud in FFEs and SBE-FPs. That is, any disruptions in the broker market will be related to fraudulent brokers or dollars that should not have been paid out in the first place. We will analyze feedback submitted in response to the agent-broker moratoria announcement. In addition, we will analyze the comments received from stakeholders to enrich the newly proposed provision when this rule is finalized.

(3) Extension of the Rebuttal Period
In circumstances where we suspend an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange agreement(s) under proposed § 155.220(g)(5), the agent, broker, or web-broker may submit evidence in a form and manner specified by CMS to rebut the allegation(s) within 30 days of the suspension. a. PERM CAPs (§§ 431.992(a), (b)(3)(ii)(E), (b)(3)(ii)(F), (c), and (e) and 431.1010(b)(2)(ii))
We considered maintaining the current requirements in § 431.992. Under this alternative, each of the 17 States in an annual PERM cycle would continue to submit separate Medicaid and CHIP CAPs, and affected States would continue to submit eligibility corrective action implementation updates every other month. This alternative would avoid regulatory changes, but it would preserve duplicative submissions, require 85 additional responses and 714 additional burden hours each year compared with the proposed approach, and leave the current CMS review and revision process unstated in the regulation. We determined that requiring one combined CAP, reducing the update frequency to every 6 months, and formalizing the review and revision process would reduce administrative burden while preserving program-specific requirements and CMS oversight.
b. Medicaid Managed Care Capitation Payments and Reporting of Enrollee Changes in Circumstances (§§ 438.3(c)(2), 438.608(a)(3), and 438.608(d)(1)(iv))
We considered maintaining the current requirements. Managed care plans would continue to notify States promptly when they receive information about an enrollee's death or change of residence, without a specified 30-calendar-day deadline, and States would continue to administer capitation payments and recoveries under existing requirements. This alternative would avoid implementation costs attributable to the proposed changes, but it would leave States and managed care plans without the proposed reporting deadline and recovery clarifications. The burden analysis estimates $1.67 million in one-time setup costs and, for an illustrative 100,000 reports, $1.88 million in annual processing costs under the proposed approach. These amounts should not be treated as the savings from maintaining current requirements because managed care plans and States already perform some reporting and processing, and the number of additional reports is unknown. We determined that a defined reporting deadline and clearer recovery procedures would help States address changes in enrollee circumstances and improper capitation payments more consistently. We cannot quantify the additional recoveries attributable to the proposal.
c. Revisions to 455.17 Reporting Requirements
CMS does not currently collect this information from states. The alternative to updating and adding the updated requirements is to continue not collecting the information or to collect the information without the enhanced reporting requirements.
d. Medicaid Payment Suspensions Updates (§  455.23)
No Action (Status Quo).
Under the status quo, the inconsistencies, gaps, and inefficiencies identified above would persist. States would continue to apply divergent standards for CAF determinations, payment suspensions would continue to lapse due to law enforcement declinations, good cause exceptions would continue to be overutilized, and CMS would continue to receive only annual reporting data. This alternative was rejected because it fails to address the documented program integrity vulnerabilities and does not reflect 15 years of implementation experience.
Mandatory (Rather Than Permissive) Reliance on External CAF Determinations.
CMS considered but did not propose requiring SMAs to accept all externally determined CAFs without any independent review. This alternative was rejected because it would eliminate State flexibility and could result in payment suspensions being initiated based on CAF determinations that may not be fully applicable to the Medicaid context. Moreover, it would not comply with current statutory language referencing CAF determinations by the State. The proposed permissive standard appropriately preserves State discretion while reducing unnecessary duplication.
Mandatory Payment Suspension Maintenance.
CMS considered but did not propose requiring SMAs to maintain payment suspensions in all cases where a CAF remains unresolved, regardless of law enforcement declination. This alternative was rejected because it would eliminate State flexibility and could result in open-ended suspensions in cases where the underlying investigation has effectively concluded. Moreover, it would not comply with current statutory language requiring a pending investigation. The proposed permissive standard with quarterly redetermination requirements appropriately balances these considerations.
Monthly Reporting.
CMS considered but did not propose increasing the reporting cadence to monthly rather than quarterly. This alternative was rejected because the incremental oversight benefit of monthly reporting was not considered sufficient to justify the additional administrative burden on SMAs, particularly given that the primary data sources (case tracking systems) may not be updated this frequently.
e. National Provider Identifier (NPI) Requirements for Medicaid Providers (§ 455.440)
We considered an alternative in which we would encourage, but not require, States to maintain another unique identifier for providers who are not eligible to obtain an NPI. While we encourage this as a best practice, we are not currently proposing it as a requirement, but we may adopt it, or other approaches in the final rule based on comments and evidence received.
Instead, we are focusing potentially mandating NPIs, which are a national standard and covers the vast majority of providers in the majority of states, and we believe the most effective approach to achieving our program integrity goals without imposing unnecessary burden for non-traditional or atypical provider types. We believe the current proposal strikes the right balance by establishing a consistent enterprise-wide identifier where it is most impactful. However, we invite comments on alternative approaches for reliable provider identification, in particular for providers where direct oversight is limited and fraud risk is elevated, for example those providers furnishing services in home- and community-based settings. Please submit supporting data and explain how each approach would address the issues at hand. Depending on the comments and evidence received, the final rule may adopt the proposed approach, the alternative described here, or a variation within the range described in this notice.

a. Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV)
This rule includes transfers from MA organizations to the Federal Government. The aggregate impact of each of these over 10 years is approximately $90.2 billion (see Table C-B8). b. Alternatives Related to the Extrapolation of RADV Findings
As an alternative to our decision to extrapolate our RADV audits beginning in PY 2018, we considered policies whereby we would not extrapolate and would only collect improper payments associated with sampled enrollees as a result of RADV audits. While such a policy would likely be favorably received by MA organizations, it would result in a drastic reduction in potential recoveries and dilute the sentinel impact that the RADV program has on reducing the Part C improper payment rate. More specifically, we estimate that total non-extrapolated overpayment recoveries would be approximately $89.7 billion less than total extrapolated overpayment recoveries for the time period of 2027-2036. Further, the RADV audit program would have a negative return on investment of approximately $3.2 million per calendar year. This assumes the annualized monetized cost of the contract-level RADV audit program is approximately $48 million and annualized monetized non-extrapolated recoveries of $44.8 million. CMS has a fiduciary responsibility to reduce and recover improper payments for the Medicare Trust Funds. Not extrapolating and incurring a negative return on investment for the audit program would be in direct conflict with our responsibilities under the PIIA to reduce improper payments and fiduciary responsibility to recover improper payment from the Medicare Trust Funds, and therefore, this alternative was not an acceptable alternative to CMS.
c. Alternatives Related to the Application of an FFS Adjuster to RADV Improper Payment Determinations
As an alternative to our proposal to not apply an FFS Adjuster to our RADV overpayment determinations, we considered a policy whereby we would apply an FFS Adjuster to RADV overpayment determinations. We believe such an approach through regulatory or other means would be an unsupportable and unreasonable interpretation of the Act.
As previously described, we have determined that the “actuarial equivalence” and “same methodology” provisions do not apply to the obligation of an MA organization to report and return overpayments that they have identified, including overpayments due to lack of medical record support for diagnoses, or their obligation to return overpayments identified based on a RADV audit. 4. Marketplace Program Integrity
Regarding the opportunity to refute determinations of noncompliance, CMS considered retaining the existing “resolved to the satisfaction of HHS” standard in § 155.220(g)(3)(i) without modification but determined providing agents, brokers, and web-brokers with an opportunity to refute determinations of noncompliance or submit information for CMS' consideration before enforcement action is taken improves procedural clarity and fairness as discussed in more detail above in this proposed rule. CMS also considered retaining the existing “sufficiently severe” standard in § 155.220(g)(1) as the sole basis for determining whether to terminate an agreement for cause and impose other penalties after making a finding of noncompliance, with the exception of determinations made in accordance with § 155.220(g)(3)(ii) through (iv) as proposed in this proposed rule. CMS determined that relying solely on that standard may not adequately account for the full range of circumstances relevant to enforcement determinations, including repeated or escalating noncompliance that may collectively result in significant consumer harm or risks to Exchange operations. CMS further considered adopting a more prescriptive framework establishing fixed numerical thresholds or specific categories of violations that would automatically result in termination or other penalties. CMS declined to adopt such an approach because it would reduce flexibility and may not appropriately account for the varying factual circumstances presented in individual cases.
We considered leveraging the existing regulatory standards for abusive conduct cases, which allow enforcement action against an agent, broker, or web-broker engaging in noncompliance under § 155.220(g)(1) through (3). However, the current noncompliance standards do not allow for an immediate suspension of an agent, broker, or web-broker's Exchange Agreement(s), which is critical for abusive conduct cases that often involve high-risk behavior and imminent consumer harm. We determined that updating § 155.220(g)(5) to an abusive-conduct standard from a fraud-based standard would better reflect the types of cases identified during our investigations, improve transparency on CMS' enforcement action processes, allow CMS to address abusive conduct quickly, and reduce consumer harm.
Finally, CMS considered continuing to address restrictions on foreign access solely through agreement terms entered into under § 155.220(d) rather than codifying these requirements in regulation. HHS determined that codifying these standards in regulation would provide greater clarity, transparency, and enforceability regarding the obligations of agents, brokers, and web-brokers and would ensure that violations are subject to the full range of remedial actions available under § 155.220. CMS also considered adopting more technology-specific requirements, such as mandating particular technical controls or security measures, but declined to do so because technical specifications may become outdated over time and may be more appropriately addressed through operational guidance or Exchange agreement(s) requirements.

I. Initial Regulatory Flexibility Act (IRFA)
The IRFA requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small entities. For purposes of the IRFA, HHS estimates that many impacted entities are small entities, as that term is used in the IRFA, either by being nonprofit organizations or by meeting the Small Business Administration (SBA) definition of a small business. Small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions. Individuals and states are not included in the definition of a small entity.
Executive Order 13272
requires that HHS thoroughly review rules to assess and take account of their potential impact on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and small organizations (as mandated by the IRFA).
If a proposed rule has a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, then the proposed rule must discuss steps taken, including alternatives considered, to minimize the burden on small entities. The IRFA does not define the terms “significant economic impact” or “substantial number”. The SBA advises that this absence of statutory specificity allows what is “significant” or “substantial” to vary, depending on the problem that is to be addressed in rulemaking, the rule's requirements, and the preliminary assessment of the rule's impact. Nevertheless, HHS typically considers a “significant” impact to be 3 to 5 percent or more of the affected entities' costs or revenues and a “substantial number” to be greater than 5 percent of entities.
The IRFA requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small entities, if a rule has a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities. For purposes of the IRFA, we estimate that there are some entities that can be considered small entities as that term is used in the IRFA (including small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions). The great majority of hospitals and most other health care providers and suppliers are small entities, either by being nonprofit organizations or by meeting the SBA definition of a small business (having revenues of less than $9.0 million to $47.0 million in any 1 year) as of 2023). The SBA has recently updated this threshold in 2025, which has resulted in more hospitals and health care providers.

1. Objectives and Legal Basis
CMS' current Medicare, Medicaid and CHIP, and marketplace program integrity frameworks contain outdated, inconsistent, or incomplete requirements across several regulatory areas. These gaps limit CMS' ability to detect fraud, hold States accountable, and recover improper payments. The provisions in this rule discuss these gaps by modernizing reporting, clarifying enforcement authority, and closing structural vulnerabilities in oversight tools. Small businesses,

including DMEPOS suppliers, insurance agents, brokers, and web-brokers would face minimal costs for implementing the provisions discussed in this rule. At this time, we cannot determine the cost for each impacted industry, but as can be seen in Table C-B13, if we assume the annualized costs of $46.08 million are distributed evenly over each impact entity, then that cost would be a minimal cost of $127.65. We are seeking comments from the public regarding this assumption.
Thus, we are proposing enhancements to our DMEPOS supplier surety bond process under § 424.57(d). This rule includes a proposal to clarify the existing prohibition against unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers to make explicit the inclusion of third-party entities acting as the agents of DMEPOS suppliers; and to clarify that the prohibition against unsolicited beneficiary contact by telephone refers to a telephone call or message, including text messages. This rule also includes a proposal to add a new supplier standard under
42 CFR 424.57(c)(31)
to prohibit unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers and their agents when supplying a Medicare-covered item by direct messages from social media platforms, email messages without opt-out features, and door-to-door in-person solicitation, unless a specified exception applies. At this time, we cannot determine how much revenue is currently being generated by these practices that are being banned.
Fraudulent billing for Medicare DMEPOS continues to be a major concern. Despite an existing prohibition on unsolicited beneficiary contact by telephone, DMEPOS suppliers and third parties acting as their agents are targeting Medicare beneficiaries with unsolicited text messages and other direct messages, door-to-door in person solicitation, unwanted telephone calls, and other means to engage in high-pressure marketing tactics and deceptive lead generation that allow DMEPOS suppliers to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary or unneeded items, or items that are never supplied at all. These changes are necessary to help ensure that legitimate DMEPOS suppliers are furnishing medically necessary items of DMEPOS to Medicare beneficiaries consistent with Medicare requirements, which we believe would assist in protecting the Trust Funds and Medicare beneficiaries. There could be a large reduction in revenue for these businesses, but at this time we are unable to estimate such reductions.
Additionally, this rule proposes a number of additions and amendments to
45 CFR 155.20
and § 155.220 to improve the integrity of the FFE, reduce abusive conduct by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, and better protect consumers within the FFE. We are proposing to amend § 155.20 to add a definition of “convicted” and “credible allegation of abusive conduct”. We are also proposing to add participation standards for agents and brokers to § 155.220(g)(3), which would prevent agents and brokers that pose unacceptable risk from participating in the FFE.
