4. Medicare Advantage
Each year, MA organizations estimate costs for the upcoming plan year and then submit bids and proposed PBPs to CMS. These bids project payments to hospitals, providers, and staff for covered benefits, as well as the cost of plan administration and profits. Because the provisions proposed in this rule would apply to every MA plan and each MA plan must furnish at least the Medicare Part A and Part B benefits, we assume that the cost of implementing the stated provisions would be built into the administrative component of the basic benefit bid. At this point in time, we are unable to quantify these costs. These bids in turn determine one component of the payments of the Medicare Trust Fund to the MA organizations who reimburse providers and subcontractors for their services. A second component of the Trust Fund payment to MA organizations are the rebates, which are a portion of the difference between the basic benefit bid compared to an administratively set benchmark for the MA plan's service area (currently, based on our past and projected experience, rebates vary by plan and are approximately 66 percent). If the bid is below the benchmark, CMS pays an amount equal to the standard bid of the MA organization. However, if the bid is above the benchmark, CMS pays the portion of the cost up to the benchmark and the MA organization bears the extra cost and must charge enrollees a premium for the remaining amount, as set forth in section 1854 of the Act. As the cost of providing services by these entities is covered by a combination of government funding and in some cases by enrollee premiums, MA and Part D plans are not expected to incur burdens or losses because the private companies' costs are being supported by the government and enrolled beneficiaries. This lack of expected burden applies to both large and small MA health plans. Any MA health plans that are considered “small” would be expected to include the costs of compliance with the proposed regulations in their bids, thus avoiding additional burden, since the cost of complying with any regulation is funded by payments from the government and, if applicable, enrollee premiums. Historically, at most two percent of plans bid above the benchmark, and they contain roughly one percent of all plan enrollees. In the present circumstances, we are unable to quantify this burden and costs estimate.
Table C-B10 reports the percentage of MA organizations bidding above the benchmark and the percentage of affected enrollees in recent years. This table reports aggregates of proprietary bid data collected by the CMS Office of the Actuary (OACT). Unfortunately, this table does not present the direct, compliance burden since data are not available at this time. As shown in Table C-B29, the percentage of plans incurring additional costs by bidding above the benchmark is 0.11 percent in 2024 and 0.07 percent in 2025, while the CMS threshold for what constitutes a significant impact for purposes of the IRFA is 3 to 5 percent. Since at least 99 percent of MA organizations bid below the benchmark in recent years, we estimate that the federal government fully pays these MA organizations their projected costs for providing services to enrollees for the coming year. Unfortunately, we cannot determine at this time if this across-the-board increase in costs would increase the share of bids that bid above the benchmark. The preceding analysis shows that MA plans, whether small or large entities, are not significantly affected by this proposed rule since the vast majority (all but at most 1 percent) will have their costs subsidized by the federal government and would not be materially impacted. 5. Does the Impact on Small Businesses Meet the Two-Part Threshold
As a measure of its significant economic impact on small entities, HHS uses a change in revenue of more than 3 to 5 percent. The agency considers the rule to have a significant impact on a substantial number of small businesses when more than 5 percent of impacted small entities meet the significant economic impact threshold defined above.
According to Table C-A13, the provisions in this proposed rule would have almost no impact (<0.019 percent) on small the small businesses identified.
Moreover, given that the annual revenue for the 5th percentile firm is over $29 billion and 3 percent of this revenue gives a significant impact threshold of a significantly large estimate (>$888 million), then any cost estimates smaller than this estimate will not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small businesses. Assuming the firm size distribution provided in Table C-B13, we expect the annualized costs estimated as a result of this proposed rule to fall below this significant impact threshold. We believe that the threshold for significant economic impact on a substantial number of small businesses will not be reached by the requirements in this proposed rule. At this moment, we are unable to determine the impact of the $90 billion transfers from businesses to the federal government. Even though including the nonemployers from NES data is important, and shows that very small firms make up a much larger share of the size distribution, we are unable to determine the impact on revenue.

J. Alternatives for Small Entities
As was mentioned previously, this proposed rule would update § 155.220(g)(3) to allow CMS to immediately terminate agents, brokers, and web-brokers who pose undue risk from participating in the FFE and SBE-FPs, without waiting 30 calendar days from the date of notice. As an alternative, CMS would terminate agents, brokers, and web-brokers who pose undue risk from participating in the FFE and SBE-FPs, after 30 calendar days from the date of notice.
Additionally, as was also mentioned previously, we are proposing enhancements to our DMEPOS supplier surety bond process under § 424.57(d). This rule includes a proposal to clarify the existing prohibition against unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers to make explicit the inclusion of third-party entities acting as the agents of DMEPOS suppliers; and to clarify that the prohibition against unsolicited beneficiary contact by telephone refers to a telephone call or message, including text messages. This rule also includes a proposal to add a new supplier standard under
42 CFR 424.57(c)(31)
to prohibit unsolicited beneficiary contact by DMEPOS suppliers and their agents when supplying a Medicare-covered item by direct messages from social media platforms, email messages without opt-out features, and door-to-door in-person solicitation, unless a specified exception applies.
1. Identifying Duplication
CMS confirms that the proposed provisions in this rule do not duplicate efforts of previous rulemaking, but rather, they build upon and refine them to ensure that CMS' current Medicaid and CHIP program integrity framework contains updated, consistent or complete or requirements across several regulatory areas. These requirements will greatly enhance CMS' ability to prevent and detect fraud, hold States accountable, and recover improper payments.
2. Conclusion and Request for Public Comments
CMS concludes that the provisions relevant to impacted entities do not produce a significant economic impact on a substantial number of impacted small businesses. CMS seeks public comments on their assumptions related to the number of direct health and medical insurance carriers and government health plans, home health agencies, personal care assistants, DMEPOS suppliers, physicians, hospices, and agents/brokers, and web-brokers, that could be considered small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, or small organizations. We request public comments specifically on how the provisions increase or decrease administrative burden for small entities.
For the purposes of the IRFA analysis, CMS concludes that there is not a significant impact on small entities. As a measure of significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, HHS uses a change in revenue of more than 3 percent. As illustrated by the revenue test in Table C-B13, none of the small firm sizes approached the 3 percent threshold.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 603 of the IRFA. For the purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. Therefore, the Secretary has certified that this proposed rule will not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals, and as a result we are not preparing an analysis for section 1102(b) of the Act.

Parties in a change in majority ownership.

Revision period.
The State must submit revisions that address the identified issues and meet the applicable requirements of paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section within 90 calendar days after the date of CMS' initial written notice under paragraph (c)(2)(i) of this section for the affected portion. A revised submission does not restart that period. CMS works with the State during the revision period and communicates in writing any remaining issues identified through its review. Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2)(iii)(B) of this section, each affected eligibility portion not approved by the end of the revision period will be deemed disapproved for the applicable PERM-review year, without a separate written disapproval determination. Following a deemed disapproval, the State must continue to address the identified issues and seek CMS approval of a revised eligibility portion that meets the applicable requirements of paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section. CMS' subsequent written approval supersedes the earlier deemed disapproval of that portion for the applicable PERM review year, as provided in paragraph (c)(2)(v) of this section.

Pending review.
An eligibility portion is not deemed disapproved while CMS review of the most recent revision submitted within the revision period remains pending. Subpart G: Requirements for Program Integrity Corrective Action Plans
§ 455.600
Purpose.
This subpart establishes administrative requirements governing:
(a) State Medicaid program integrity corrective action plans (CAPs).
(b) This subpart only applies to Medicaid. Corrective action and withholding for failure to comply with CHIP requirements are governed by part 457 of this chapter, including § 457.204.
§ 455.602
Program integrity corrective action plans.
(a) If CMS identifies findings of non-compliance with Medicaid statutory and regulatory requirements as a result of a CMS program integrity audit, the final audit report will specify the findings, if any, for which the State is required to develop a Program Integrity CAP. If the final audit report requires a Program Integrity CAP for one or more findings, the State must develop a single Program Integrity CAP that addresses all such findings, as described in paragraph (b) of this section.
(b) If required under paragraph (a) of this section to develop a Program Integrity CAP, the State must address each finding of non-compliance for which the final audit report requires corrective action through a Program Integrity CAP and take the following actions:
(1) Conduct a root cause analysis to identify the specific programmatic causes to which each finding of non-compliance is attributed.
(2) Identify the specific corrective action(s) that will be implemented to address each finding of non-compliance and bring the State into compliance.
(3) Develop an implementation schedule for each corrective action and implement such corrective actions in accordance with the schedule. The implementation schedule must identify all of the following for each corrective action:
(i) Status of the corrective action.
(ii) Estimated or actual implementation date.
(iii) Contact information for all key personnel responsible for implementation.
(iv) Monitoring plan to track the progress of implementation of the corrective action.
(4) A plan for evaluating the effectiveness of each corrective action and how the corrective action will rectify the finding(s) of non-compliance.
(c) If the final audit report requires a Program Integrity CAP under paragraph (a) of this section, the State must submit the CAP to CMS no later than 30 calendar days after the date of the final audit report, unless CMS grants a good-cause extension.
(1) The Program Integrity CAP developed under paragraph (a) of this section is subject to CMS approval. If CMS determines that a submitted Program Integrity CAP does not satisfy the requirements of paragraph (b) of this section, CMS returns the CAP to the State for revision and resubmission.
(2) The State must provide updates on Program Integrity CAP implementation progress at each milestone timeframe identified in the implementation schedule for each corrective action under paragraph (b)(3) of this section, and upon request by CMS. Such updates must include the State's progress in implementing the corrective action in accordance with the approved implementation schedule and the evaluation of the effectiveness of the corrective action and how the corrective action is rectifying the finding or findings of non-compliance under paragraph (b)(4) of this section.
(d) Nothing in this section limits, delays, or conditions CMS' exercise of any other administrative or financial action otherwise authorized under Federal law. CMS may pursue such action before, concurrently with, or after requiring a Program Integrity CAP under this section, as appropriate.

Subpart H—Medicaid and CHIP Beneficiary Eligibility Audit Program
§ 455.700
Basis and scope.
This subpart establishes requirements for Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audits designed to reduce eligibility errors by reviewing States' eligibility processes and policies, and the appropriateness of eligibility determinations for sampled cases. A State is required to participate in an eligibility audit when selected by CMS, as set forth in this subpart. The statutory bases for this subpart are sections 1903(u), 2105(e), and 1936 of the Act.
§ 455.702
Definitions.
For purposes of this subpart, the following terms have the definitions:
(
printed page 74841)
Corrective action
means a specific action that a State would be required to implement to address identified eligibility errors to achieve compliance with Federal requirements and Medicaid and CHIP State plans (or waiver of such plans).
Eligibility
means meeting the State's categorical, financial, and non-financial criteria for receipt of benefits under the Medicaid or CHIP programs.
Eligibility audit
means a CMS and Federal contractor conducted, primarily risk-based audit of States' Medicaid and CHIP point of application or renewal eligibility determinations, designed to verify compliance with Federal and State eligibility requirements, reduce eligibility errors, and assist States in improving their eligibility determination processes.
Eligibility determination
has the same meaning as at § 435.4 for Medicaid, and § 457.301 for CHIP.
Eligibility error
means an error resulting from the State's improper application of Federal or State requirements, causing an improper determination of a beneficiary's eligibility. For purposes of this definition, an eligibility error could include, but would not be limited to, authorizing an ineligible individual as eligible when they received services, providing certain ineligible services to an otherwise eligible individual, improperly denying an individual's Medicaid or CHIP application, improperly terminating a beneficiary from Medicaid or CHIP, or enrolling in managed care an individual ineligible for managed care.
Erroneous excess payments for medical assistance
means the total of payments under the State plan (or waiver of such plan) with respect to ineligible individuals and families, and overpayments on behalf of eligible individuals and families by reason of errors in determining the amount of expenditures for medical care required of an individual or family as a condition of eligibility.
Observation
means an instance where a beneficiary's or applicant's eligibility was correctly determined notwithstanding the State failing to follow Federal and State eligibility requirements.
§ 455.704
General requirements.
(a) When selected, a State must participate in a Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audit upon written notification by CMS of an audit. In rare cases, CMS may grant a State an audit exemption for demonstrating extraordinary circumstances beyond the State agency's control that make audit participation impracticable during the applicable fiscal year audit period.
(1) Audit selection criteria include all of the following:
(A) Every State will undergo a Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audit at least once every 5 years.
(B) In selecting States for audit, CMS prioritizes States determined to be at high-risk for eligibility errors.
(2) CMS issues an engagement letter to the relevant State Medicaid director, outlining the audit objectives, scope, applicable disallowance authorities, data and documentation request and corresponding data and documentation submission due dates.
(b) State participation during an eligibility audit includes the following:
(1) Providing the requested eligibility and enrollment data and documentation within 10 business days from the date the engagement letter was issued, unless granted an extension by CMS.
(2) Assigning at least two State subject matter experts to navigate the necessary information contained in the State's eligibility and enrollment systems in coordination with the auditors during the case review portion of the audit to allow CMS to verify if eligibility determinations were made in accordance with Federal and State requirements for the sampled cases.
(3) Providing requested copies of additional eligibility case records and any other necessary documentation for sampled cases and documentation within 5 business days of the written request unless granted an extension by CMS.
(4) Responding to the draft report within 10 business days, unless granted an extension by CMS, by providing a written response that indicates whether the State agrees or disagrees with each eligibility error. For any eligibility error with which the State disagrees, the State must provide a detailed written explanation of the basis for disagreement and submit supporting documentation to CMS to substantiate its position.
(5) Submitting a CAP to CMS for approval with proposed corrective actions to address each eligibility error, if applicable, by the deadline specified in the final audit report.
§ 455.706
Audit methods for audits with findings potentially subject to disallowance.
(a) The audit will include four statistically valid stratified random samples of Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries selected from the universes of eligibility and enrollment data provided by the State. Samples are selected from all eligibility categories included in the Medicaid and CHIP programs.
(1)(i) One sample includes individuals who are enrolled in Medicaid whose eligibility was determined or redetermined and for whom the State made payments for services provided during the full fiscal year audit year.
(ii) The second sample include individuals whose Medicaid eligibility was denied or terminated during the full fiscal year audit period.
(iii) The third sample consists of individuals enrolled in CHIP whose eligibility was determined or redetermined and for whom the State made CHIP payments for services provided during the audit period.
(iv) The fourth sample consists of individuals whose CHIP eligibility was denied or terminated during the audit period.
(2) The State's Medicaid and CHIP information systems will be used to obtain data on beneficiaries and applicants in the sampling frames and their associated Medicaid and CHIP payments.
(3) A statistical software package would be used to generate random numbers to select samples from each stratum.
(4) Sample sizes will be designed to support statistically valid extrapolations of individuals associated with eligibility errors and their associated improper payments at a 90 percent confidence level, if applicable.
(b) The total number of individuals associated with eligibility errors extrapolated to the State's entire Medicaid and CHIP populations and the total extrapolated amount of erroneous excess payments made on behalf of individuals who were improperly enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP during the audit period will be estimated based on the lower limit of the 90 percent confidence interval, if applicable, using statistical software.
(c) Extrapolated error rates for the total dollar amount attributable to erroneous excess payments for medical assistance, as defined in section 1903(u)(1)(D)(i) of the Act, is calculated for both the Medicaid program and CHIP during the audit period using the lower limit of the 90 percent confidence interval, if applicable.
(d) The Federal share of payments determined to be inappropriately made for erroneous excess payments for medical assistance during the audit period are subject to potential disallowances if one or both of the calculated eligibility error rates described in § 455.706(c) exceed the allowable 3 percent threshold under
(
printed page 74842)
section 1903(u) of the Act, unless the State meets the good faith waiver requirements defined in § 455.804.
§ 455.708
Protection of applicant and beneficiary information and due process rights.
The State Medicaid agency performing activities for the eligibility audits specified in this subpart must do so in a manner that is consistent with all of the following:
(a) Part 431, subpart F of this chapter concerning the safeguarding of beneficiary and applicant information.
(b)
42 CFR 435.930(b)
,
435.917
,
435.918
;.part 431, subpart E; and 457.1110 of this chapter concerning the continuation of Medicaid of coverage for eligible individuals until the State has made a final determination of ineligibility and provided advance notice and fair hearing rights.
§ 455.710
Access to records.
The State, upon written request, must submit to CMS and its Federal contractors, all necessary records, including complete eligibility case documentation for sampled cases and all other available documents pertaining to eligibility determinations in effect during the audit period.
§ 455.712
Corrective action plans.
(a) The State is required to submit a CAP for approval in accordance with § 455.602, if applicable.
(b) After obtaining approval for a CAP, the State is required to make sufficient progress towards implementing the CAP within the established milestone timeframes as specified in § 455.602.

Subpart I—Medicaid and CHIP Beneficiary Eligibility-Related Disallowances
§ 455.800
Purpose.
This section establishes rules and procedures for disallowing Federal financial participation (FFP) in erroneous medical and child health assistance payments due to eligibility improper payment errors, as identified through the Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audits subject to disallowance established under Subpart H of this part.
§ 455.802
Disallowance of Federal financial participation for eligibility errors.
(a) After the State's eligibility error rates for Medicaid and CHIP have been calculated in accordance with § 455.706(c) during a beneficiary eligibility audit, if applicable, CMS computes the amount of the disallowances and adjusts the FFP payable to the State in accordance with the procedures in § 430.42.
(b) CMS computes the amount to be disallowed for Medicaid and CHIP separately as follows:
(1) Subtract the 3 percent allowable threshold from the lower limit of the State's Medicaid or CHIP eligibility error rate percentage.
(2) If the difference is greater than zero, the corresponding Federal share of medical assistance or child health assistance funds for the period are multiplied by that percentage. This product is the amount of the disallowance of FFP that will be adjusted in a future State expenditure report absent a good faith waiver in accordance with § 455.804.
§ 455.804
Good faith waivers and notice to States.
(a) If CMS is satisfied that the State did not meet the 3 percent allowable threshold despite a good faith effort, CMS may reduce the funds being disallowed, in whole or in part, based on the extent to which the State demonstrates compliance with the criteria in paragraph (b) of this section and the evidence submitted under paragraph (c) of this section.
(b) CMS may find that a State did not meet the 3 percent allowable threshold despite a good faith effort if all of the following requirements are met:
(1) The State implemented the eligibility-related elements of its most recent CMS-approved PERM CAP in accordance with § 431.992.
(2) Where applicable, the State submitted a CAP under § 455.712 in response to previous Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audit findings, obtained CMS approval of that CAP, and is making sufficient progress implementing the approved CAP within its established milestone timeframes at the time of the good faith waiver determination.
(3)(i) The State has taken additional reasonable actions to prevent, identify, or mitigate eligibility errors it believed were necessary to meet the 3 percent threshold.
(ii) In determining whether a State took reasonable actions, CMS considers factors including, but not limited to, the following:
(A) Whether the State maintained reasonable pre-existing eligibility controls.
(B) Whether the same eligibility errors had been identified in previous audits or reviews.
(C) The timeliness and substance of the State's response after error identification.
(Dv) Immediate corrective actions already taken.
(Ev) Cooperation and transparency during CMS audits and reviews.
(c)(1) The State must submit evidence demonstrating its actions under paragraph (b) of this section within 30 calendar days of CMS' issuance of the final Medicaid and CHIP beneficiary eligibility audit report and notification of the associated disallowance amount, unless granted an extension by CMS.
(2) Evidence submission may include all of the following:
(i) Policy manuals.
(ii) Staff training records;
(iii) Documentation of eligibility and enrollment system enhancements.
(iv) Self-audit reports.
(v) Detailed CAPs with proof of implementation and effectiveness.
(d) Notwithstanding paragraphs (a) through (c) of this section, CMS may determine that a State is ineligible for a good faith waiver or is eligible for only a partial waiver where the information and evidence available to CMS demonstrates systemic or persistent program integrity failures inconsistent with a good faith effort during the audit period.
(e) Circumstances that may warrant a determination under paragraph (d) of this section include, but are not limited to any of the following:
(1) Repeated beneficiary eligibility audit or PERM findings involving the same or substantially similar errors.
(2) Failure to address or implement prior CMS audit recommendations related to eligibility determination errors.
(3) Known system defects, operational deficiencies, or policy weaknesses affecting eligibility determinations that remained unaddressed by the State during the audit period.
(4) Patterns of noncompliance identified across multiple Federal oversight activities.
(f) Each State that has an eligibility improper payment rate above the allowable threshold is notified by CMS in writing of the good faith waiver determination, including whether CMS granted a full waiver, a partial waiver, or no waiver, and, where applicable, the amount of the disallowance issued under § 455.802. This written notification would also include the
(
printed page 74843)
information specified in § 430.42(a), as appropriate, including notice of the State's right to request reconsideration of the disallowance.
§ 455.806
Appeals.
If a State disagrees with the determinations set forth in the written notice described in § 455.804(f), the State may request reconsideration or appeal within 60 calendar days of receipt of the notice. All processes regarding the notice of disallowance, reconsideration, retention of funds, and appeals will be governed by the procedures set forth in § 430.42 of this chapter.
Subpart J—Reporting and Returning of Overpayments in Medicaid Fee-for-Service
§ 455.900
Basis and scope.
This subpart sets forth the policies and procedures for reporting and returning self-identified overpayments to the Medicaid Fee-For-Service program as required by section 1128J(d) of the Act.
§ 455.902
Definitions.
For purposes of this subpart only—
Overpayment
means any funds that a person received or retained under title XIX of the Act to which the person is not entitled under such title after applicable reconciliation.
Person
means a provider of services or supplier who participates under a State plan (or waiver of such plan) established under title XIX of the Act.
§ 455.904
Requirements for reporting and returning of overpayments.
(a)
General.
(1) A person that has received an overpayment must report and return the overpayment to the State, including a written reason for the overpayment, in the form and manner specified by the State in accordance with paragraph (c) (1) of this section.
(2) A person has identified an overpayment when the person knowingly receives or retains an overpayment. The term “knowingly” has the meaning set forth in
31 U.S.C. 3729(b)(1)
.
(b)
Deadline for reporting and returning overpayments.
A person who has received an overpayment must report and return the overpayment to the State by the later of either of the following:
(1) The date which is 60 days after the date on which the overpayment was identified.
(2) The date any corresponding cost report is due, if applicable.
(c)
State responsibilities.
A State must do all of the following:
(1) Establish a mechanism for a person to report and return to the State when an overpayment is identified, in accordance with paragraph (b) of this section.
(2) Return the Federal share of overpayments to CMS consistent with the requirements in
42 CFR 433.312
.
(3) Maintain a record of all reported or received overpayments and make such records available to CMS upon request.
(d)
Reporting.
A person must use the mechanism established by the State in paragraph (c)(1) of this section to report and return an identified overpayment to the State. If the person calculates the overpayment amount using a statistical sampling methodology, the person must describe the statistically valid sampling and extrapolation methodology in the report.
(e)
Enforcement.
Any overpayment retained by a person after the deadline for reporting and returning the overpayment specified in paragraph (b) of this section is an obligation for purposes of the False Claims Act,
31 U.S.C. 3729(b)(3)
.
(f)
Lookback period.
An overpayment must be reported and returned in accordance with this section if a person identifies the overpayment, as defined in paragraph (a)(2) of this section, within 6 years of the date the overpayment was received.

Section 155.20 is amended by adding the definitions of “Credible allegation of abusive conduct” and “Convicted” in alphabetical order to read as follows:
Credible allegation of abusive conduct.
A credible allegation of abusive conduct is an allegation from any source, including but not limited to the following:
(1) Consumer, Marketplace call center, or agent, broker, or web-broker complaints verified by further evidence;
(2) Data or information identified during investigation; or
(3) Patterns identified through data analysis.
Allegations are considered to be credible when they have indicia of reliability.
Convicted
means that—
(1) A judgment of conviction has been entered against an individual or entity by a Federal, State or local court, regardless of whether:
(i) There is a post-trial motion or an appeal pending;', or(ii) The judgment of conviction or other record relating to the criminal conduct has been expunged or otherwise removed;
(2) A Federal or State court has accepted a plea of guilty or
nolo contendere
or an Alford plea by an individual or entity; or
(3) An individual or entity has entered into participation in a first offender, deferred adjudication or other program or arrangement where judgment of conviction has been withheld.

PERM program annually measures the national Medicaid and CHIP improper payment rates using a 17-State 3-year rotation process. As such, each State is reviewed once every 3 years, and the year in which a State is measured is known as its “PERM year.” A State is not required to conduct a MEQC pilot during its PERM year. When a State is not under PERM review (that is, in the 2-year interval between a State's PERM review cycles), the State is required to conduct MEQC activities, including one (1) 12-month MEQC pilot. title: HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes To Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens
abstract: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or "Department") is issuing this final rule to modify the Standards for Privacy of Individually Identifiable Health Information ("Privacy Rule") under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) and the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act. These modifications address standards that may impede the nationwide transition to value-based health care by limiting or discouraging individual access or care coordination and case management or posing other unnecessary burdens. The modifications in this final rule promote the essential sharing of individuals' protected health information (PHI) for care coordination and individual engagement while continuing to protect its privacy and security.

AGENCY:
Office for Civil Rights (OCR), Office of the Secretary, Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or “Department”) is issuing this final rule to modify the Standards for Privacy of Individually Identifiable Health Information (“Privacy Rule”) under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) and the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act. These modifications address standards that may impede the nationwide transition to value-based health care by limiting or discouraging individual access or care coordination and case management or posing other unnecessary burdens. The modifications in this final rule promote the essential sharing of individuals' protected health information (PHI) for care coordination and individual engagement while continuing to protect its privacy and security.
DATES:
Effective dates:
The final rule is effective on January 19, 2027.
Compliance date:
Persons subject to this regulation must comply with the applicable requirements of this final rule by July 19, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Marissa Gordon-Nguyen at (202) 240-3110 or (800) 537-7697 (TDD), or by email at
OCRPrivacy@hhs.gov
.

I. Executive Summary
A. Overview
Empowering individuals to take control of their health is critical to delivering on the promise to Make America Healthy Again, which is central to the mission of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or “Department”). Enabling individuals, their personal representatives, their health care providers, and others designated by the individuals to have unfettered access to their information is a necessary first step towards achieving this promise.
Many individuals rely on access to their health information—directly, through their health care providers, through patient or health plan member portals, or through the use of health apps—to monitor their chronic conditions, adhere to their treatment plans, find and address errors in their health records, and track their progress in wellness and disease management programs. This information provides the individual and their care team with insight into the current state of their health and enables them to set goals for improving it. Equally important, the efficient operation of the health care system depends upon the ability of covered entities
[
1
]
and their business associates
[
2
]
(collectively, “regulated entities”) to promptly disclose an individual's protected health information
[
3
]
(PHI) to other regulated entities and certain others (
e.g.,
non-covered health care providers, social services agencies, family members) to ensure that individuals receive timely and appropriate care. For example, such disclosures enable health care providers to avoid ordering duplicative or unnecessary tests, which reduces waste and the overall cost of health care. They also facilitate the ability of health care providers to provide care promptly by avoiding long waits for approvals of coverage by health plans.
To foster electronic access to health information by individuals and health care providers, the Trump Administration has launched a series of initiatives to break down barriers to information sharing and form the building blocks for a digital ecosystem in which patients can view, manage, use, and share their health information through digital applications and other modern solutions. The goal of this digital ecosystem is to expand access to personalized health guidance for patients to improve prevention and chronic disease management, while maintaining the privacy and security of PHI in the ecosystem. For example, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is taking bold steps to modernize the nation's digital health ecosystem with a focus on empowering Medicare beneficiaries through greater access to innovative health technologies.
[
4
]
As another example, the
(
printed page 74852)
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology
[
5
]
(ONC) adopted certification criteria for health information technology (“health IT”) that support real-time verification of an individual's prescription benefits and standardized electronic prior authorization.
[
6
]
The Department also has announced an intention to take an active enforcement stance against health care entities that restrict patients' engagement in their care by blocking the access, exchange, and use of certain health information.
[
7
]
As explained by then-Acting Inspector General Juliet T. Hodgkins, “[p]roviders and certain health IT entities have a legal duty to ensure that information flows where and when it's needed.”
[
8
]
While it is important that individuals have access to their own health information—in a format of their choosing, including through their personal health apps—and covered entities can use and disclose that information for certain purposes, individuals also have an interest in the privacy of this highly personal information, given the potential for harm if it is shared with the wrong person(s). Thus, it is incumbent upon the Department to establish rules that both enable the use and disclosure of an individual's health information for beneficial purposes and protect the privacy (and security) of that information.
Consistent with these goals, this final rule modifies certain provisions of the Standards for Privacy of Individually Identifiable Health Information (“Privacy Rule”), issued pursuant to section 264 of the Administrative Simplification provisions of title II, subtitle F, of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA).
[
9
]
The Privacy Rule
[
10
]
is one of several rules, collectively known as the HIPAA Rules,
[
11
]
that establish the required protections for the privacy and security of individuals' PHI, which is individually identifiable health information
[
12
]
(IIHI) transmitted by or maintained in electronic media or any other form or medium, with certain exceptions.
[
13
]
This final rule supports access by individuals to their PHI and the use and disclosure of PHI by regulated entities for care coordination and case management, discussed in detail below. Specifically, this final rule amends provisions of the Privacy Rule that may present barriers to individual engagement and care coordination and case management—or impose other burdens without sufficiently compensating for, or offsetting, such burdens through privacy protections for PHI. These barriers may impede the transformation of the health care system from a system that pays for procedures and services to one that pays for high-quality health care and empowers individuals to take charge of their health. Consistent with the Department's historical approach to the HIPAA Rules, the amendments generally are technology neutral. Where appropriate, we discuss the application of these amendments, and the Privacy Rule as a whole, to current technology in preamble.
B. Summary of Major Provisions
After consideration of the public comments received in response to the 2021 Proposed Modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule to Support, and Remove Barriers to, Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) (“2021 Privacy Rule NPRM”), the Department is modifying the Privacy Rule to support individual access and improve care coordination and case management by:
[
14
]
Modifying provisions on the individual's right of access to PHI by doing all of the following:
Adding definitions of the terms “electronic health record” and “personal health application” (“personal health app”).
Reducing the amount of time that covered entities have to respond to an access request to no more than 15 calendar days after receipt of the request (reduced from the current 30 days), with the opportunity for an extension of no more than 30 calendar days (retaining the current 30-day extension).
Clarifying the form and format required for responding to individuals' requests for PHI.
Reducing the burden of identity verification on individuals exercising their access rights.
Limiting the individual's right of access to direct the transmission of PHI to a person they designate to electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record (“right of access to direct”), in accordance with a binding court decision.
[
15
]
Requiring covered entities to inform individuals that they retain their
(
printed page 74853)
right to obtain copies of their PHI or direct electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record to another person when a summary of PHI is offered in lieu of a copy.
Amending the permissible fee structure for responding to requests made pursuant to the right of access, including specifying when electronic PHI
[
16
]
(ePHI) must be provided to the individual at no charge.
Requiring covered entities to post estimated fee schedules on their websites for copies of PHI obtained under the right of access and with an individual's valid authorization.
Amending the definition of health care operations to clarify the scope of permitted uses and disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute health care operations.
Clarifying the ability of covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations, home and community-based services (HCBS) providers,
[
17
]
and other similar third parties
[
18
]
that provide health-related services, to facilitate care coordination and case management for individuals.
Eliminating the requirement to obtain an individual's written acknowledgment that they have received a copy of a Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP) from a health care provider with whom they have a direct treatment relationship.
Modifying the content requirements of the NPP to clarify for individuals their rights with respect to their PHI and how to exercise those rights.
Expressly permitting disclosures to Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) communications assistants for persons who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability, and modifying the definition of business associate to exclude TRS providers.
Expanding the permission to use or disclose PHI of Armed Forces members in certain circumstances to all Uniformed Services, which then would include the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS) Commissioned Corps and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Commissioned Corps.
The Department carefully considered the extent to which each of these modifications would affect privacy protections for health information and the likely benefits of making PHI more available for care coordination or case management. These and other considerations are fully described for each modification throughout this preamble and in detail in the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA).

3. Final Rule
The effective date of this final rule is 60 days after publication. Accordingly, the final rule is effective on January 19, 2027.
Regulated entities will have 180 days beyond the effective date of the final rule to comply with its provisions. We understand that some regulated entities are concerned that they may encounter difficulties complying with the modified requirements within an 180-day period. Section 160.104(a) permits the Department to adopt a modification to a standard or implementation specification adopted under the Privacy Rule no more frequently than once every 12 months. D. Severability
The Department intends that any provisions of the Privacy Rule and its subparts that are unchanged by this final rule shall remain in full force and effect, even if other modified or new provisions in this final rule are held to be invalid or unenforceable, or are stayed pending future judicial or agency action.
The Department also believes that, if a court or further agency action deems invalid or unenforceable any language or section of a provision that is newly finalized or modified in this rulemaking, the remaining provisions that reference the language or section held invalid or unenforceable, but that are not directly related to a covered entity's ability to implement the remaining language or section, will remain in effect and be given the maximum regulatory effect permitted under the law.
The Department is finalizing significant changes related to the individual right of access. We believe these changes are severable such that the individual right of access as a whole or aspects of the right, as they existed until the effective date of this final rule, shall remain in effect should any changes finalized in this rulemaking related to the right as a whole or such aspects of that right be held invalid or unenforceable.
For example, the Department is adopting a new definition at
45 CFR 164.501
for the term “electronic health record.” While the Department believes that this new definition will aid in covered entities' and individuals' understanding of the full scope of obligations and rights under the Privacy Rule and the HITECH Act,
[
32
]
a covered entity's obligation to implement the right of access to direct
[
33
]
is not dependent on the adopted definition of electronic health record. Accordingly, the Department believes that the right of an individual to direct an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual, finalized at
45 CFR 164.524(d)
, remains intact should the new definition be held invalid or unenforceable.
Similarly, the Department believes that the new definition of personal health app is severable from the obligation of a covered entity to provide access to the individual in a timely manner by, among other things, transmitting the requested copy of the PHI through the individual's personal health app, as codified at
45 CFR 164.524(c)(3)
.
[
34
]
Even without the definition of personal health app, covered entities and individuals retain the ability to agree to an acceptable form and format for a requested copy of PHI. Prior to this rulemaking, the Privacy Rule already provided individuals with
(
printed page 74855)
a right to an electronic copy of their PHI that is maintained electronically in the electronic form and format requested by the individual, if it is readily producible, or if not, in a readable electronic form and format as agreed to by the covered entity and the individual. The requirement to provide PHI in the individual's chosen form and format, where readily producible, is a longstanding component of the individual right of access. Thus, the Department believes that individuals should retain the right to request copies of PHI through a personal health app, even if the definition of personal health app is held to be invalid or unenforceable.
We are adopting several provisions that address the fees that covered entities may charge to fulfill an individual's request for access to their PHI. II. Statutory and Regulatory Background
A. Statutory Authority and History
1. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA)
In 1996, Congress enacted HIPAA
[
36
]
to reform the health care system to “improve portability and continuity of health insurance coverage in the group and individual markets”
[
37
]
and to support the electronic exchange of health information. To enable health care system reform, Congress included requirements for standards to support the electronic exchange of health information. According to section 261 of HIPAA, “[i]t is the purpose of this subtitle to improve [. . .] the efficiency and effectiveness of the health care system, by encouraging the development of a health information system through the establishment of standards and requirements for the electronic transmission of certain health information.”
[
38
]
Congress applied HIPAA's Administrative Simplification provisions directly to three types of persons referred to in regulation as “covered entities”: health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers who transmit information electronically in connection with a transaction for which HHS has adopted a standard.
[
39
]
Section 262(a) of HIPAA required the Secretary to adopt uniform standards “to enable health information to be exchanged electronically.”
[
40
]
Congress also directed the Secretary to adopt standards for, among other things: transactions and data elements relating to health information,
[
41
]
the security of that information,
[
42
]
and verification of electronic signatures.
[
43
]
Congress recognized that the standardization of certain electronic health care transactions required by HIPAA posed risks to the privacy of confidential health information and viewed individual privacy, confidentiality, and data security as critical for orderly administrative simplification.
[
44
]
One Member of
(
printed page 74856)
Congress acknowledged that individuals should have “control over who actually has access to their medical records.”
[
45
]
According to another Member of Congress, privacy standards would create an additional layer of protection beyond the oath pledged by health care providers to keep information secure and, as described by another Member, would further protect information from being used in a “malicious or discriminatory manner.”
[
46
]
Moreover, Congress considered that health care reform required an approach that would not compromise privacy as health information became more accessible.
[
47
]
Additionally, another Member acknowledged that health plan data was often nonstandard, and the bill “would facilitate the coordination of benefits between different systems.”
[
48
]
Section 264(a) of HIPAA directed the Secretary to submit to Congress detailed recommendations for Federal “standards with respect to the privacy of individually identifiable health information [IIHI]” within 1 year of HIPAA's enactment.
[
49
]
The statute made clear that the Secretary had the authority to promulgate regulations if Congress did not enact legislation covering these matters within 3 years.
[
50
]
Congress directed the Secretary to ensure that the regulations promulgated “address at least” the following three subjects: (1) the rights that an individual who is a subject of IIHI should have; (2) the procedures that should be established for the exercise of such rights; and (3) the uses and disclosures of such information that should be authorized or required.
[
51
]
Additionally, Congress provided a clear statement that HIPAA's provisions would “supersede any contrary provision of State law,” with certain limited exceptions.
[
52
]
One exception to this general preemption authority is for state privacy laws that are contrary to and more stringent than the corresponding Federal standard, requirement, or implementation specification.
[
53
]
Thus, Congress provided for the Department to create privacy standards to safeguard health information while respecting the ability of states to provide individuals with additional health information privacy protections and rights.
Congress required the Secretary to rely on recommendations of the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics (NCVHS or “Committee”) when adopting standards,
[
54
]
thereby ensuring that the Secretary's decisions reflected public and expert involvement and advice in carrying out the requirements of section 264.
[
55
]
On June 27, 1997, NCVHS sent its initial recommendations to the Secretary. Among its recommendations was that legislation for health privacy should include some specific rights for individuals, including a right to be informed about uses of their health information and a right to request amendment of their records.
[
56
]
Additionally, NCVHS recommended that an individual have the right to access their health information.
[
57
]
As the Committee explained, a basic element of fair information practices for “personal records maintained by third party record keepers—is a right of access by the subject of the record.”
[
58
]
NCVHS further asserted that fair information practices for health information would provide secondary users of health information with knowledge about when they could have health information and when they could not, what their obligations would be, and what penalties would result if those obligations were ignored.
[
59
]
NCVHS also supported “limiting use and disclosure of identifiable information to the minimum amount necessary to accomplish the purpose. The Committee strongly believe[d] that when identifiable health information is made available for non-health uses, patients deserve a strong assurance that the data will not be used to harm them.”
[
60
]
NCVHS also believed that users of health information should be required to justify their need for such information and accept reasonable substantive and procedural limitations on access.
[
61
]
Congress anticipated that the Department's rulemaking under HIPAA would not remain static. Congress built in a mechanism to update or adapt the regulations to address evolving technology and health care practices, directing the Secretary to review and adopt modifications to the Administrative Simplification standards as determined appropriate, but not more frequently than once every 12 months.
[

III. Justification for This Rulemaking
A. An Effective Health Care System Requires That Individuals Have Access to Their Health Information and That Others Are Able To Use and Disclose Health Information About Individuals
To further empower individuals and achieve the promise of Make America Healthy Again, as described in the Executive Summary, the Department must take action to create systemic improvements in health care through the appropriate use and disclosure of health information. By building on the existing policy framework for patient access and interoperability, the Department can drive large-scale adoption of health management and care navigation applications, reduce barriers to information access and exchange, realize the potential of recent innovations in health care that promote better health outcomes, and accelerate progress toward a patient-centric learning health system.
[
147
]
The Department's initiatives today build on the work of the Institute of Medicine
[
148
]
(IOM), which, in its 1998 landmark report on the quality of the U.S. health care system, identified six attributes of a high functioning health care system.
[
149
]
According to the IOM, health care should be: safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable because a system with these attributes would enable individuals to obtain care that is “safer, more reliable, more responsive, more integrated, and more available.”
[
150
]
Not only would individuals benefit, but clinicians and others involved in the provision of health care would also experience increased satisfaction because they would be “providing care that was more reliable, more responsive to [individuals], and more coordinated.”
[
151
]
As part of its work, the IOM created a set of ten rules to guide the redesign of the health care system. The IOM's rules and report highlighted the importance of ensuring the bi-directional flow of information, not only between clinicians, but also between individuals and clinicians. According to the IOM, the health care system “must be designed to serve the needs of [individuals], and to ensure that they are fully informed, retain control and participate in care delivery whenever possible, and receive care that is respectful of their values and preferences.”
[
152
]
Additionally, “[it] must facilitate the application of scientific knowledge to practice, and provide clinicians with the tools and supports necessary to deliver evidence-based care consistently and safely.”
[
153
]
The IOM report made clear that, without improved communication and transfer of knowledge, health outcomes would suffer.
One of the IOM's recommendations highlighted the connection between high-quality health care, care coordination, and the timely flow of information. Specifically, Recommendation 4 encouraged stakeholders to redesign the health care process to prioritize the individual by ensuring that individuals are able to obtain the care that they need at a time and location that is convenient for them; in a manner that responds to their choices and preferences; and based on shared decision making that is informed by their access to their PHI, clinical knowledge, and evidence-based science. According to the IOM, this prioritization of the individual should occur while also limiting administrative burden and waste.
When taken together, Recommendation 4 and the goal of HIPAA as described by the Department
[
154
]
ultimately are the same: a health care system that ensures the best possible health outcomes for individuals in a manner that limits the administrative burdens. To achieve that goal, individuals and people involved in their care need to have prompt access to the individual's PHI in a manner that both protects the individual's privacy and minimizes burdens on individuals, health care providers and other participants in the health care sector, and other stakeholders.
1. Individuals Need To Have Access to Their Own Information for Many Purposes, Including Understanding Their Health Status, Coordinating Their Health Care, and Obtaining Government Benefits
As discussed in greater detail above, the right of individuals to access their PHI has been a central component of the Privacy Rule since its inception. NCVHS stated in its initial 1997 recommendations to the Secretary that, while the exact scope of this right—in particular, potential exceptions—was a subject of debate, committee members found universal agreement with the basic principle of individual access rights.
[
155
]
And later that same year, in its recommendations to Congress on the contents of privacy legislation, the Department counseled that individuals should be afforded a certain level of control over their health records. Specifically, the Department recommended that “[p]atients should be able to see and get copies of their records [. . .]”
[
156
]
with limited exceptions.
[
157
]
The Department also recommended that such legislation include a limitation on Federal requirements to disclose health information to anyone other than the individual.
[
158
]
As we explained, “[t]he ability to see one's own record is central to effective control of information [. . .].”
[
159
]
This recommendation was consistent with recommendations from at least as early as the 1970s to provide individuals with the right to access records about themselves.
[
160
]
As explained by the Department:
(
printed page 74862)
[T]he right recommended here is not simply a right to fair procedure in an administrative transaction or criminal or civil legal action (which may be provided in any case by other law); it is a freestanding fair information practice right to see one's record at a time of one's choosing regardless of actual use in a proceeding or for decision making. It should be available unless there is a danger that patient access would impede the investigation.
[
161
]
While Congress did not enact specific legislation on health information privacy, the Department's recommendations served as the underpinnings for its original Privacy Rule. Thus, the Department's recommendations to Congress, and the privacy considerations undergirding them, are instructive here.
Providing individuals with access to their health information is not only a fair information practice; it also is essential for the individual's ability to engage in shared decision making,
[
162
]
a fundamental component of an improved health care system. Shared decision making is “a collaborative process in which [individuals] and clinicians work together to make healthcare decisions informed by evidence, the care team's knowledge and experience, and the [individual's] values, goals, preferences, and circumstances. Families and caregivers also play an important role in [shared decision making].”
[
163
]
Ultimately, this means that, “to effectively manage their health, individuals need to be able to access and use their health information when, where, and how they want, including sending it to the people and tools helping them to become or stay healthy—neighbors, friends, relatives, health care providers who are treating or consulting with the individual, or even third-party software tools used for self-management.”
[
164
]
Thus, it is critical for individuals to be able to obtain access to their information promptly and efficiently.
Not only do individuals need access to their PHI, but research shows that individuals generally want to be able to access it and to have some level of control over the PHI that others are able to access.
[
165
]
According to the qualitative study of individuals with diabetes who engage with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) patient portal, “having access to the patient portal puts control over health information into the hands of patients. When patients want to share information between providers, patients can send information themselves.”
[
166
]
The evolution of the VA's capabilities for providing individuals with electronic access to their PHI also illustrates how technology has increasingly enabled individuals to obtain and use their health information. For example, the study describes how VA's My HealtheVet portal
[
167
]
and Blue Button
[
168
]
functionality enable individuals to access clinical information electronically, and how individuals use that information to support their care, including for care coordination between VA and non-VA health care providers.
[
169
]
Thus, allowing individuals to direct a covered entity to provide access to that individual's PHI to a person designated by the individual, for example, by using the functionalities of a patient or health plan member portal, enables coordination among people involved in the individual's care, including among health care providers. Sharing PHI in this manner can reduce duplicate and unnecessary testing, saving time and health care resources.
[
170
]
Research also demonstrates that individuals are more likely to consent to disclosing their health information electronically through health information exchanges (HIEs)
[
171
]
when they have greater control over what health information is shared and with whom.
[
172
]
When individuals can exercise more control over disclosing their health information, the privacy concerns associated with requests for individuals to share their information are reduced and trust in health care professionals increases, which, in turn, results in higher consent rates.
[
173
]
Thus, providing individuals with greater control over who has access to their information, including the ability to direct copies of their information to another person, is likely to increase their willingness to agree to (or authorize, where required) disclosures of that information for other purposes, such as clinical research. We believe that the Department can foster this increased trust and willingness and the attendant benefits for health care and public health by improving individuals' ability to obtain, and direct the disclosure of, their information in a manner that is timely, efficient, and privacy protective.
2. Persons Involved in Caring for Individuals Need To Use Their PHI
Individuals are not alone in their need to use their PHI. Persons involved in caring for individuals—health care providers, family members, caregivers, community-based organizations, and others—also may need to obtain individuals' PHI to facilitate care coordination and case management and enable such individuals to obtain necessary health care and related services. Some of these persons may be covered entities, but others may not.
a. Improving Cooperation Is a Common Element in Existing Definitions of Care Coordination and Case Management
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, neither care coordination nor case management has a precise, commonly agreed upon definition. However, both terms have been interpreted broadly to refer to activities that are aimed at promoting cooperation among persons involved in caring for an individual, such as family members, caregivers, and community-based organizations, with the goal of ensuring the best possible health outcomes for the individual. For example, the Department's Office of Inspector General (OIG) defines “coordination and management of care” as the “deliberate organization of patient care activities and sharing of information between two
(
printed page 74863)
or more VBE [value-based enterprise] participants, one or more VBE participants and the VBE, or one or more VBE participants and patients, that is designed to achieve safer, more effective, or more efficient care to improve the health outcomes of the target patient population.”
[
174
]
CMS has described care coordination and management as “the foundation of a value-based health care delivery system”
[
175
]
and as including a range of activities that link individuals to services and improve communication flow.
[
176
]
In its 2014 guidance addressing a particular Medicaid benefit, CMS explained that the various definitions of this term share three key concepts:
Comprehensive coordination of all services, including services delivered by systems other than the health system.

b. Care Coordination and Case Management Improve Health Outcomes and Decrease the Cost of Care
While the definitions of care coordination and case management may vary, they consistently recognize that access to an individual's PHI, gathered from disparate sources, is integral to improving health outcomes for individuals. Research on care coordination and case management generally demonstrates the benefits of exchanging PHI for care coordination and case management for individuals and for the health care system. A 2026 qualitative study based on interviews with twenty hospital and health care system leaders found that current HIEs represent an improvement over alternative means of sharing information between settings of care.
[
190
]
According to a 2019 literature review, the annual costs associated with the failure of care coordination (
i.e.,
unnecessary admissions or avoidable complications and readmissions) ranged from $27.2 billion to $78.2 billion, while the annual cost savings associated with five different care coordination interventions, including the use of a HIE, ranged from $29.6 billion to $38.2 billion.
[
191
]
These figures do not include costs associated with unnecessary testing or procedures, nor do they include savings from decreases resulting from related interventions.
[
192
]
A 2019 study of data collected from 2011 to 2014 examined the effects of electronic data exchange by hospitals in Florida with other health care providers on health outcomes for individuals who experienced an acute myocardial infarction and found that hospitals that participated in HIEs performed significantly better than hospitals that did not participate.
[
193
]
The study showed a greater decrease in 30-day all-cause readmissions for participating hospitals than non-participating hospitals and sustained decreases for readmissions at 45 days and 60 days.
[
194
]
The study also found an association between HIE participation, readmission reduction, and increased intensity in the inpatient treatment received by individuals who experienced an acute myocardial infarction, which, according to the study's authors, suggested that HIE participation may play a role in determining the cost trade-offs of inpatient care as opposed to readmission.
[
195
]
This further suggests that electronically exchanging information may have helped participating hospitals evaluate the most appropriate and cost-effective health care for each individual during their initial admission. As another example, a 2021 study found that there was a significant association between the use of an HIE by primary care physicians to obtain the PHI of individuals recently released from the hospital and visits to emergency departments and rehospitalizations.
[
196

In such cases, the individual's likelihood of visiting the emergency department was reduced by 53 percent, while the risk of rehospitalization was reduced by 61 percent.
[
197

Additionally, if the individual was rehospitalized, the median length of time between the hospital visits more than doubled, increasing from 99 days to 238 days.
[
198
]
A 2023 study of 2018 data found that Medicare beneficiaries with Alzheimer's disease were 23 percent less likely to die during a readmission where the readmission was fragmented
[
199
]
and the associated hospitals shared an HIE as compared with fragmented readmissions to hospitals that did not share an HIE.
[
200
]
Additionally, beneficiaries who experienced fragmented readmissions where the hospitals shared an HIE were more likely to be discharged home with home health, as opposed to a skilled nursing facility (SNF), regardless of whether they had Alzheimer's disease.
[
201
]
And in another example, researchers found that individuals enrolled in a certain Medicaid section 1115 demonstration project generally experienced improved health outcomes when participating sites implemented, among other things, health IT that enabled the electronic exchange of PHI.
[
202
]
Not only did health outcomes improve, but the cost of care decreased significantly.
[
203
]
The specific health IT adopted by the sites varied, including EHRs,
[
204
]
case management platforms, cloud-based storage, and
(
printed page 74865)
centralized repositories (
e.g.,
HIEs), but overall, the participant sites reported improvements in the selected health outcomes measured.
[

Accordingly, ensuring that persons involved in caring for individuals have access to the individuals' PHI is a critical component for enabling care coordination and case management.
A study also identified the ability of individuals to directly access PHI as an opportunity for improved program evaluation.
[

A 2019 study of the ties between entities in a network of health care organizations and social services agencies demonstrated the importance of integration between these organizations to network performance. According to study authors, “more cohesive interorganizational networks of health care and social service organizations are associated with lower levels of potentially avoidable health care use and spending among beneficiaries.”
[

The authors of a review of the effectiveness of initiatives to address health-related factors that influence health outcomes concluded that there is a “need for policy incentives to more effectively integrate [such] data into EHR systems and foster stronger community partnerships to ensure broader, sustainable impact.”
[

Thus, to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the health care system, covered entities must be able to partner with and disclose PHI to social services and community-based organizations that are working to address health-related factors for care coordination and case management.
As then-HHS Deputy Secretary Eric D. Hargan explained before the Brookings Institution on January 30, 2019, care coordination is a necessary component of achieving value-based care:
One of [the components of value-based care] is coordinated care and the drive to coordinated care provokes some obvious questions that point towards the need for broad-based regulatory reform in this area. Some of the questions and challenges that we got along the way [. . .] [include]: how can we expect physicians to act as navigators of the health system while also holding them accountable if their decision-making is hamstrung by outdated regulations; or how can we expect providers to get on board with payments based on outcomes if we're not willing to give them the freedom to experiment and coordinate with one another [. . .] how can we really make major steps in preventing and curing disease without also rethinking how regulations [. . .] could impede patients and providers working together in creative arrangements [. . .] ?
[

Former Secretary Azar later praised the advancement of coordinated care with the publication of final rules on interoperability, access to health information, and certification of electronic health record technology.

And, when announcing the publication of a final rule modifying regulations on the confidentiality of substance use disorder (SUD) treatment records to expand care coordination and quality, Secretary Azar explained, “[t]his reform will help make it easier for Americans to discuss substance use disorders with their doctors, seek treatment, and find the road to recovery.”

More recently, Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. noted, in his announcement of expanded enforcement of the information blocking regulations, “[w]hen a patient visits an emergency room, doctors need to access that patient's medical history. And at a recent U.S. Senate hearing, the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, Dr. Thomas Keane explained:

Access to data will [. . .] help inform providers' clinical decision making which can lead to improved care and patient safety [. . .]. In some cases, missing information is not just frustrating, it is dangerous. A patient with a known drug allergy who shows up at a new facility without their records may be prescribed improper medication that could have been avoided if their history were available.

Thus, it is essential that HIPAA not only permit, but also encourage, the coordination of care where appropriate.
B. The Health Care Environment Has Changed Since the Privacy Rule's Right of Access and Care Coordination Provisions Were Last Revised
Over the course of the last decade, the U.S. health care system has changed significantly. The Department has modified the Privacy Rule a few times in the intervening years, but none of those modifications have addressed the reasons for the shift towards the electronic exchange of health information. While the Privacy Rule is technology neutral, the Department must consider the causes of the change in the U.S. health care system, such as the implementation of laws, spread of technology, and the breadth of research that encourage care coordination, to determine how the changes interact with the Privacy Rule and their implications for the goals of HIPAA.

As part of this examination, the Department must determine whether the Privacy Rule accurately reflects the obligations of regulated entities and the rights of individuals, whether regulated entities are correctly interpreting and applying the Privacy Rule, and whether the Privacy Rule unnecessarily imposes real or perceived barriers to the accomplishment of HIPAA's goals.

General Policy Considerations
As discussed in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM and above, the ability of individuals to access and direct disclosures of their own health information, including PHI, is key to care coordination. Section 164.524 of the Privacy Rule generally requires most covered entities

1. Adding Definition of “Electronic Health Record”
a. Issues To Address
Section 13405(e)(1) of the HITECH Act added a new right within the individual right of access that requires covered entities to transmit an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by an individual when directed to do so by the individual
[
390
]
and codified a definition of electronic health record that specifically applies to that Act's privacy and security provisions for regulated entities.
[
391
]
The HITECH Act defines “electronic health record” as “an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff.”
[
392
]
However, the Privacy Rule currently does not define the term “electronic health record.”
b. Proposed Rule
Accordingly, to effectively implement this right, discussed in greater detail below, the Department proposed to add a definition of electronic health record
(
printed page 74877)
in
45 CFR 164.501
that would be consistent with the HITECH Act definition. We also proposed, as part of the definition, to clarify some of the terms used within the definition that are not defined in the statute or the Privacy Rule.
For example, as we discussed in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, the Privacy Rule does not define the term “clinician,” and the Department has not identified a uniform statutory or regulatory definition of the term. To minimize uncertainty about the scope of the term for purposes of the Privacy Rule, we explained that we intended to interpret “authorized health care clinicians and staff” to at least include covered health care providers who are able to access, modify, transmit, or otherwise use or disclose PHI in an electronic health record, and who have direct treatment relationships with individuals; and members of their workforce
[
393
]
who support the provision of such treatment by virtue of their qualifications or job role. Thus, under this interpretation, an electronic health record would include electronic records consulted by any covered health care provider, or a workforce member of such a covered health care provider, so long as the provider has a direct treatment relationship with individuals. The Department did not propose specifically to include covered health care providers who have indirect treatment relationships
[
394
]
with individuals.
With respect to the types of information in an electronic health record, the Department proposed to equate “health-related information on an individual” with the scope of the familiar, defined term, “individually identifiable health information.”
[
395
]
