We also proposed to interpret the term “health-related information” as equating to the Privacy Rule's definition of “health information.”
[
396
]
Further, the Department proposed to interpret “on an individual,” to refer to information that is “individually identifiable.”
c. Overview of Comments
Several commenters expressed support for the Department's proposed definition of an electronic health record. Many commenters urged us to adopt a common definition of electronic health record for the various components of the Department. Some commenters expressed concerns about the proposal to limit the definition of electronic health record to apply only where a health care provider has a direct treatment relationship with individuals because they asserted that health care providers who have an indirect treatment relationship with individuals also maintain electronic health records that contain PHI to which individuals should have access. Some commenters expressed opposition to the Department's proposal to equate “health-related information” to the Privacy Rule's definition of “health information” because it would include both clinical and non-clinical data.
d. Final Rule
The final rule adopts the new term “electronic health record” and its definition with two modifications. Consistent with the statutory definition, we are not including the word “their” in the definition. Thus, the definition will refer to “authorized health care clinicians and staff.” Additionally, we are modifying our interpretation of “authorized health care clinicians” specifically to include health care providers that have indirect treatment relationships with individuals. As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, health care providers who have indirect treatment relationships generally deliver health care based on the orders of another health care provider.
[
397
]
In the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, we also explained that we believed that the direct treatment provider would be the entity documenting information about services, products, or reports provided by an indirect treatment provider, and thus it would be appropriate to limit our interpretation of clinicians to direct treatment providers. However, we are persuaded by commenters that a health care provider who has an indirect treatment relationship with an individual may not provide all of their services, products, or reports to the health care provider who has the direct treatment relationship with the individual. For example, providers who furnish durable medical equipment (DME) generally do not provide all of the data recorded by the DME to the ordering health care provider. The same is true of providers of medical devices. And while clinical laboratories may send laboratory reports to the ordering clinician, the reports may not include every single lab value in their documentation. Thus, PHI in the electronic health record of the provider who has the direct treatment relationship may not include all of the PHI created by an indirect treatment provider. If our interpretation of clinicians is limited to only those providers with direct treatment relationships with individuals, the PHI to which an individual would be entitled to direct to a person they designate is thereby limited. Additionally, according to several commenters, distinguishing between health care providers with direct treatment relationships with individuals and those with indirect treatment relationships would create uncertainty about the scope of PHI included in the right of access to direct because direct and indirect treatment providers may create, receive, maintain, and transmit PHI in the same electronic health record. By including both health care providers with direct treatment relationships with individuals and those with indirect treatment relationships, we eliminate this uncertainty and maximize the amount of PHI included within the right of access to direct. Accordingly, the Department is modifying our interpretation of “clinicians” to include both health care providers that have a direct treatment relationship with individuals and health care providers that have an indirect treatment relationship with individuals.
[
398
]
The HITECH Act does not define an electronic health record to mean a specific electronic information system, application, or software; rather, it defines it as an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff.
[
399
]
Thus, whether information is part of an electronic health record is not dependent on the particular system, application, or place in which the information is maintained, but rather on whether it is health-related information about an individual and on who creates, gathers, manages, and consults it. For example, an electronic record maintained by a business associate for, or on behalf of, a covered entity may be part of the covered entity's electronic health record if the record otherwise meets the definition.
Accordingly, the scope of information included in an individual's electronic health record may vary across different health care providers because covered health care providers have substantial
(
printed page 74878)
flexibility in determining the appropriate composition of that electronic health record for their particular circumstances. Additionally, because the definition includes the term “record,”
[
400
]
which covered entities already understand from the definition of designated record set, this new definition is clear and workable. Accordingly, this definition is intended to provide a clear standard that health care providers can use to identify what PHI is subject to requirements of the HITECH Act that address PHI in an electronic health record. We believe that this new definition will improve understanding of whether certain aspects of a covered entity's electronic records are included in an electronic health record, which will enable a covered entity to assess whether such ePHI is subject to the right of access to direct.
For example, an electronic health record includes the work product of health care providers that have indirect treatment relationships with individuals, such as electronic lab test reports created by workforce members of a large health system who are licensed clinical laboratory personnel, and who perform clinical lab tests for patients treated by the health system. An electronic health record also includes electronic images taken by an imaging technician who is a workforce member of a radiology group practice and electronic reports of a pathologist who is employed by a small hospital where the reports contain the pathologist's analysis of tissue samples taken from an individual. Electronic billing records created, gathered, managed, and consulted by workforce members of a covered health care provider that has a direct treatment relationship with an individual (
e.g.,
a hospital) are included in the term electronic health record because health care billing information is health-related information.
[
401
]
Consistent with the modification we are making to the proposed definition, electronic billing records created, gathered, managed, and consulted by workforce members of a covered health care provider that has an indirect treatment relationship with an individual (
e.g.,
an independent clinical laboratory or single specialty radiology practice) also are included in an electronic health record.
e. Response to Public Comments
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for the Department's proposed definition of an electronic health record. One commenter expressed support for the proposal because they believed that the proposed definition would include all ePHI. Another commenter expressed support because they believed that it would expand upon and align with the way the term is used by health care providers. One commenter recommended that the Department define electronic health record as broadly as possible.
Many commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that it would be overly inclusive. Several commenters asserted that the proposed definition would not align with the common industry definition of an EHR; instead, according to some commenters, the proposed definition would better align with the definition of “health information technology.” Many commenters recommended that the Department limit the definition to one that would be consistent with the HITECH Act. Many also expressed concern that the proposed definition would include non-clinical information, such as billing records, that often is maintained separately from clinical information. According to commenters, combining information that is maintained in separate electronic information systems would be burdensome. One commenter asserted that billing records should be considered as part of an electronic health record only to the extent that such records are included in a designated record set. Another commenter stated that state law may prevent covered entities from disclosing personally identifiable information in billing records. Several commenters requested that the Department exclude certain types of information from the definition or clarify whether certain types of information would be included in the definition.
Response:
The Department is finalizing its proposed definition of electronic health record with minimal modifications, as described above. The definition that we are adopting for the Privacy Rule is consistent with the HITECH Act, which provides a definition of electronic health record that applies specifically to the provisions that address the privacy and security of PHI. As explained above, that HITECH Act definition is “an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff.” Where the HITECH Act did not specifically define terms used in the definition, we rely upon existing definitions of similar terms. For example, while the HITECH Act does not define “health-related information on an individual,” section 13101 of the HITECH Act defines “health information” by reference to section 1171(4) of the SSA,
[
402
]
in a manner that is consistent with the definition of the term contained in the Privacy Rule. Thus, we believe that it is reasonable to interpret the term “health-related information” to be at least as broad as “health information.”
[
403
]
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, “health information” includes not only clinical, but also billing and other data. Accordingly, the broader term “health-related information” could be expected to include such data and not be limited to clinical data.
We understand that other components of the Department may have adopted a variety of definitions of electronic health record or similar terms, such as “certified EHR technology”
[
404
]
or “qualified electronic health record.”
[
405
]
These terms also are defined in the HITECH Act. However, these definitions occur in Subtitle A of the HITECH Act, “Promotion of Health Information Technology,” and are codified in a new title (“Health Information Technology and Quality”) in the PHSA at
42 U.S.C. 300jj
, while the definition of “electronic health record” is codified in
42 U.S.C. 17921
and occurs in Subtitle D of the HITECH Act, “Privacy,” the same subchapter that establishes the right of access to direct.
[
406
]
Because Congress adopted a different term and definition for purposes of the HITECH Act's privacy and security provisions, the rule of statutory
(
printed page 74879)
interpretation against surplusage (generally, a presumption that every clause and word in a statute should be given meaning and not be superfluous) guides us to interpret electronic health record as meaning something different in the context of the HIPAA Rules.
[
407
]
As discussed above, “electronic health record” is defined in the HITECH Act as “an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff.” While both “electronic health record” and “qualified electronic health record” use the term “an electronic record of health-related information on an individual,” the latter definition is then arguably limited by additional descriptors:
[E]lectronic record of health-related information on an individual that—(A) includes patient demographic and clinical health information, such as medical history and problem lists; and (B) has the capacity—(i) to provide clinical decision support; (ii) to support physician order entry; (iii) to capture and query information relevant to health care quality; and (iv) to exchange electronic health information with, and integrate such information from other sources.
[
408
]
The definition of “electronic health record,” moreover, does not reference “certified EHR technology” (which is defined in part as a “qualified electronic health record that is certified pursuant to section 3001(c)(5)” and is, thus, also arguably limited).
[
409
]
In addition, the “health-related information on an individual” “is created, gathered, managed, and consulted” not only by “authorized health care clinicians,” but also by “staff,” which suggests that the electronic record would not be limited to clinical health information, but also would include information that nonclinical staff create, gather, manage, and consult, such as scheduling, prior authorization, referrals, billing, and other administrative information. Based on the statutory definition of “electronic health record” (and how it differs from the definitions of those other terms), we believe that Congress intended for electronic health record, when used in the context of the individual right of access, to refer to an electronic record of an individual's health, rather than a file about an individual in a specific system or technology, and we have interpreted it accordingly.
We clarify that, while the definition of an electronic health record may include PHI that is not part of the designated record set, as discussed below, the right of access, including the right of access to direct, does not extend to such information. Also, as discussed in detail below, it does not extend to psychotherapy notes or information compiled in reasonable anticipation of, or for use in, a civil, criminal, or administrative action or proceeding.
[
410
]
Regulated entities are required to identify and document which records are part of the designated record set.
[
411
]
For example, clinical laboratory test reports become part of the laboratory's designated record set when they are “complete,” which means that all results associated with an ordered test are finalized and ready for release. However, other information concerning the test may be part of the designated record set, and thus accessible to the individual even if the test report has not yet been completed, such as test orders, ordering provider information, billing information, and insurance information.
[
412
]
The definition of electronic health record, like the definition of designated record set, is not dependent on a specific type of system or technology platform or where an organization maintains the information, with the caveat that PHI that is in an electronic health record necessarily is maintained electronically (and, thus, it is ePHI). Accordingly, an electronic health record is not limited to clinical data, but also includes billing and other non-clinical information about the individual. This interpretation is consistent with the scope of the term “record” within the definition of “designated record set.”
[
413
]
Comment:
A few commenters expressed opposition to the Department's proposal to define an electronic health record because they believed that the definition should focus on the information to be protected, rather than the technology used to create, receive, maintain, or transmit the information. One commenter asserted that the Department did not have the authority to interpret the statutory definition. One commenter recommended that the Department adopt a definition that complies with the
Ciox
decision, but that also requires a covered entity to provide—in response to a request from an individual to direct a covered entity to send an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual—PHI that is similar in content and extent to the ePHI that the covered entity would be required to provide in response to an individual's request to obtain a copy of their PHI.
Response:
As discussed above, the Department is adopting a definition of electronic health record to clarify the scope of the right of access to direct. The definition of electronic health record that we are codifying at
45 CFR 164.501
is consistent with the HITECH Act's definition of the term
[
414
]
and the
Ciox
decision. It includes additional language intended only to clarify the terms of the definition for consistency with terms already defined in the HIPAA Rules. The protections provided by the Privacy Rule for PHI are not dependent upon the manner or form and format in which PHI is created, received, maintained, or transmitted, and that remains unchanged by this final rule. Individuals have a right to access PHI in a designated record set, with limited exception. As discussed below, to the extent PHI is within the scope of the individual right of access (including being in the designated record set) and is in an electronic health record, as defined herein, the PHI is within scope of the right of access to direct.
Comment:
More than half of the commenters urged us to adopt a common regulatory framework with one set of definitions to be used across the Department because they believed that having different definitions would be burdensome or confusing for regulated entities. One commenter urged the Department to incorporate the term “electronic health information” into the definition of electronic health record to
(
printed page 74880)
clarify how the proposed definition relates to the information blocking regulations.
Response:
We understand that other components of the Department may have adopted a variety of definitions of electronic health record or similar terms; however, we do not have the statutory authority to adopt such definitions here. The definition that we are adopting for the Privacy Rule is consistent with the HITECH Act, which specifically provides a definition of electronic health record that applies to the provisions that address the privacy and security of PHI. We do not believe that this definition conflicts with other laws. Rather, this definition supports the Department's goals of implementing the statutory right of individuals to direct an electronic copy of their PHI in an electronic health record to a person they designate as part of the right of access and enhancing care coordination and case management. Ensuring that individuals can access their PHI and direct such access to others is critical to monitoring various health conditions and improving patient health outcomes.
[
415
]
We decline to incorporate the term “electronic health information”
[
416
]
into the definition of electronic health record. The definition of EHI references definitions codified in the HIPAA Rules, such as ePHI; thus, incorporating EHI into a definition in the Privacy Rule is unnecessary and likely to increase confusion.
Comment:
Commenters provided a variety of comments on the relationship between the definitions of electronic health record and designated record set. Several commenters recommended that the Department align the definition of electronic health record with the definition of “designated record set” to avoid confusion, to promote clarity, and to align it with the right of access. In contrast, several commenters recommended that the Department not align the definitions of electronic health record and designated record set because they believed that we lacked the statutory authority to do so and it would create confusion. A few commenters recommended that the Department provide additional guidance on the scope of the designated record set. One commenter recommended that the Department add a definition of “electronic designated record set,” rather than aligning the definitions of electronic health record and designated record set, asserting that this alternative approach would avoid confusion. A few commenters stated that the definition of electronic health record should be broader than the designated record set because an electronic health record could include PHI that is not part of the designated record set.
Response:
The definition of electronic health record in
45 CFR 164.501
is consistent with the HITECH Act's definition that applies to its privacy and security provisions,
[
417
]
and includes additional language intended only to clarify the terms of the definition for consistency with terms defined in the HIPAA Rules. We agree with commenters that the right of access to direct should not extend to PHI about the individual that is outside of any designated record set. As discussed below, we are adopting modifications to clarify this within the right of access to direct at
45 CFR 164.524(d)
.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that the Department interpret the definition of electronic health record using existing terms from the HIPAA Rules to avoid confusion.
Response:
We agree with the commenters that relying on existing terms, where appropriate, can help regulated entities better understand new obligations. Thus, we have relied upon existing terms to interpret the HITECH Act's definition of electronic health record to the extent possible and consistent with the statute.
[
418
]
Comment:
Some commenters requested that the Department clarify whether the proposed definition would apply only to covered health care providers or also to health plans.
Response:
As explained above, an electronic health record is an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff. We interpret “authorized health care clinicians and staff” to include health care providers who are able to access, modify, transmit, or otherwise use or disclose PHI in an electronic health record. This includes health care providers that have a direct or indirect treatment relationship with individuals,
[
419
]
as well as members of the health care provider's workforce
[
420
]
who support the provision of treatment. Thus, we intend for the definition of electronic health record to apply broadly, including to electronic records maintained by health care providers and, where applicable, health plans. Where a health plan is integrated with one or more covered health care providers, electronic records created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff of those providers may constitute an electronic health record. A health plan's maintenance of claims, enrollment, utilization management, payment, or other administrative records does not, by itself, cause those records, or the electronic information system in which they are maintained, to constitute an electronic health record. Similarly, consultation of such records by a clinician or other professional employed by the health plan does not, by itself, cause the records to constitute an electronic health record.
Furthermore, the application of the definition in this final rule is limited by the scope of the right of access to direct, which is discussed elsewhere in this final rule.
Comment:
One commenter requested that the Department clarify the scope of “health-related information” to reflect the current understanding of activities that are part of health care, such as information about activities to address the social determinants of health and interactions between individuals and unlicensed workforce members and volunteers. A few commenters recommended that “health-related information” include information about the price of health care. Another commenter recommended that the Department limit “health-related information” to clinical information that is electronically maintained in a designated record set.
Response:
As discussed above, while the HITECH Act does not define “health-related information on an individual,” the Privacy Rule defines “health information”
[
421
]
in a manner that is consistent with the definition of
(
printed page 74881)
the term in section 262 of HIPAA. Thus, we believe that it is reasonable to interpret the term “health-related information” to be at least as broad as “health information.”
[
422
]
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, “health information” includes not only clinical, but also billing and other data. Accordingly, the broader term “health-related information” could be expected to include such data and not be limited to clinical data.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal to limit the interpretation of “authorized clinicians and staff” to those with a direct treatment relationship to individuals because they believed that it would be consistent with the HITECH Act. A few commenters urged the Department to clarify that the proposed definition would include only the records of direct treatment providers. One commenter expressed opposition to the Department's proposal because they believed that it was overly inclusive and suggested that it should be limited to health care providers responsible for providing direct services, alternative care providers, and allied health professionals.
Several commenters expressed concern that the Department proposed to limit the interpretation of “authorized clinicians and staff” to health care providers with a direct treatment relationship to individuals and questioned whether PHI received from providers with indirect treatment relationships would be included in the definition of electronic health record. A few commenters disputed the Department's assumption that PHI provided by indirect treatment providers always would be incorporated into the electronic health record of a direct treatment provider.
Several commenters requested that the Department provide specific examples of “authorized clinicians.” One commenter encouraged the Department to adopt a more plain language definition of “clinician” because other covered entities are facilitating care coordination at a population-level.
According to one commenter, defining the term “clinician” would clarify whether an electronic health record contains information outside of the designated record set.
Response:
We are modifying our interpretation of authorized clinicians to include both health care providers that have a direct treatment relationship with individuals and those that have an indirect treatment relationship with individuals. The Department is persuaded by commenters who asserted that PHI that is created, received, maintained, or transmitted electronically by health care providers that have an indirect treatment relationship with individuals may not be integrated into the electronic health record of health care providers that have a direct treatment relationship with individuals. As a result, limiting the interpretation of authorized clinicians to direct treatment providers would narrow the scope of an electronic health record, and thus the right of access to direct, in a way that we did not intend.
We based our proposal on the assumption that all PHI created by an indirect treatment provider is securely and electronically shared with (and thus incorporated into the designated record set of) the referring or ordering direct treatment provider, and by extension, the individual has ready access to the PHI through the direct treatment provider's electronic health records. We understand that in some cases, PHI from an indirect covered health care provider may be incorporated into the direct treatment provider's electronic health record, without the direct treatment provider's involvement. However, we also understand from comments that, in many circumstances, indirect treatment providers create and share PHI with a direct treatment provider, who does not incorporate the PHI into their electronic health record. Additionally, we also understand that in some cases, the direct treatment provider who originally ordered clinical services, products, or reports that are produced by an indirect health care provider may not receive all PHI created by the indirect treatment provider (
e.g.,
PHI used to prepare a report), and thus that such PHI would not be in the designated record set of the direct treatment provider.
For example, radiologists generally have indirect treatment relationships with individuals because they deliver diagnostic services based on the orders of other health care providers (
e.g.,
internists, cardiologists, nephrologists, neurologists, obstetricians/gynecologists), and the results or products of those services (
e.g.,
reports, interpretations, images) typically are available to the individual through the direct treatment provider. The radiologist often sends only a report of their findings to the direct treatment provider, rather than providing them with access to the images upon which the report is based.
[
423
]
Individuals may seek to access such images for their records or to share with other health care providers or other persons. In such circumstances, the only option for individuals is to request copies of images directly from the radiologist or imaging center, the indirect treatment provider. Similarly, pathologists and clinical laboratories often are indirect treatment providers and generally are in possession of underlying PHI that may not be provided to direct treatment providers. Thus, individuals may need to obtain such PHI directly from pathologists or clinical laboratories, as well.
As another example, a direct treatment provider may be monitoring an individual's DME (
e.g.,
heart monitor), implantable medical device (
e.g.,
pacemaker), or remote monitoring technology. The provider of the DME generally has the complete set of PHI recorded by the monitors, while the direct treatment provider may be sent only summary information or alerts when monitors are malfunctioning. Individuals and direct treatment providers may require access to such PHI for a complete diagnosis and care plan.
To ensure that individuals have the right of access to direct a covered entity to transmit an electronic copy of the full scope of PHI that is consistent with the statute to a person designated by the individual, we believe that it is necessary and appropriate to specify that the definition of electronic health record applies to both health care providers that have a direct treatment relationship with individuals and those that have an indirect treatment relationship with individuals.
Comment:
A few commenters urged the Department to include non-clinical workforce members of health care providers in its interpretation of “staff.” A few commenters expressed concern that the addition of “and staff” would create ambiguity and cause confusion because it would include non-clinicians.
Several commenters recommended that the Department incorporate role-based access into the proposed definition of electronic health record to clarify who is permitted to create, gather, manage, or consult it because they believed that a definition would need to consider workforce members who do not have a direct treatment relationship with individuals, but who may create, gather, manage, or consult the electronic health record for essential purposes (
e.g.,
payment, health care operations).
(
printed page 74882)
Response:
We interpret “staff” to mean workforce
[
424
]
members who support the provision of treatment, either directly or indirectly, by virtue of their qualifications or job role.
[
425
]
Thus, an electronic health record would include electronic records consulted by a workforce member of a covered health care provider where the workforce member is supporting the provision of treatment by the health care provider. Examples of workforce members that would be “staff” include, but are not limited to, medical residents, registration support personnel, schedulers, receptionists, administrative staff who support covered functions (
e.g.,
billing, prior authorization, scheduling, referrals), coding specialists, clinical laboratory personnel, home health assistants, office or practice managers, and care referral coordinators.
2. Adding Definition of “Personal Health Application”
a. Issues To Address
Section 164.524(a) of the Privacy Rule currently establishes, with limited exceptions, the right of an individual to inspect or obtain (or both) a copy of their PHI to the extent such information is maintained in a designated record set of a covered entity. An individual's right of access exists regardless of the format in which the PHI is maintained, and the standards and implementation specifications that address individuals' requests for access and timely action by the covered entity (
e.g.,
provision of access, denial of access, and documentation) apply to an electronic environment in a similar manner as they do to a paper-based environment.
[
426
]
b. Proposed Rule
The Department proposed to adopt and define a new term, “personal health application,” to support the right of an individual to obtain a copy of their PHI through a personal health app pursuant to the right of access, discussed below.
Under the proposed definition, the information in a personal health app would not be managed, shared, or controlled by a covered entity. Additionally, the information would not be managed by the app developer on behalf of or at the direction of a regulated entity (
e.g.,
a patient or health plan member portal used by a covered entity to manage individuals' access to the PHI it maintains) or another party, such as an entity that is not regulated under HIPAA that collects or manages PHI for its own purposes (
e.g.,
research organization). Instead, under the proposed definition, an individual (or their personal representative) would use a personal health app for the individual's own purposes, such as to monitor their health status and access their health information using the app. As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, because the developer of a personal health app would not be acting on behalf of, or at the direction of, a regulated entity, the app developer would not be a business associate, and therefore, would not be subject to the federal privacy and security obligations of the HIPAA Rules. Also as described in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, a personal health app would be a tool used by, or primarily for, the individual, as opposed to other health apps that contain information that is managed, shared, and controlled by other persons for their own purposes (
e.g.,
patient or health plan member portal, research). Thus, the proposed definition would have focused on apps where only the individual or their personal representative manages, shares, and controls the information and apps that enable the information to be managed, shared, and controlled primarily for the individual. It would not have included apps where the information is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for another party.
c. Overview of Comments
Commenters were evenly split in their views of this proposal. Some urged the Department to adopt a broader definition of personal health app (
e.g.,
including apps on the web, mobile devices, and desktop computers, as well as apps that enable individuals to manage and/or to generate insights from their health information), while others recommended that we adopt a narrower one (
e.g.,
to limit the definition to apps that incorporate certain privacy and security protections). Many commenters requested that the Department provide examples of technologies that would meet the proposed definition.
d. Final Rule
We are finalizing our proposal to adopt the new term, “personal health application,” at
45 CFR 164.501
, with modifications for clarity and readability. Specifically, we are separating the clauses of the definition into two paragraphs, one that addresses what the term expressly includes and one that addresses what the term expressly excludes. Additionally, we are separating the clause that addresses what the term expressly excludes into two sub-paragraphs and clarifying that an electronic application is not a personal health app if the health information in such application is managed, shared, or controlled: (1) by or primarily for a covered entity; or (2) primarily for another person.
Further, we are removing the example of an app developer from the definition and replacing “party” with “person.” These modifications are not substantive but are made to align with our preference for providing non-exhaustive lists of examples in guidance, rather than in regulatory text, and using defined terms where possible.
[
427
]
This definition is consistent with, and will help further, the Department's ongoing efforts to promote and support individuals' use of technology to exercise the right of access.
[
428
]
Individuals increasingly are choosing to use technology to access and manage their health information. Technology, such as personal health apps, that individuals can select to manage, share, and control their health information, gathered from one or more sources, empowers them to be more in control of decisions about their health and well-being. For example, individuals with access to their health information are better able to monitor chronic conditions, adhere to treatment plans, find and request that errors in their health records be amended, track progress in wellness or disease management programs, and directly contribute their health information to research.
[
429
]
With the increasing use of and continued advances in health IT, there are novel and increasing ways for individuals to quickly and easily access
(
printed page 74883)
their health information electronically, in real time, and on demand from a variety of sources. The Privacy Rule was designed to be technology neutral and does not mandate the use of any particular technologies, but instead establishes standards that can be met through a variety of means.
[
430
]
This approach enables the Department to address in the preamble how the definition applies to technologies in current use without revising the regulatory text solely to account for each new or developing technology. Accordingly, we decline to provide examples of specific technologies that meet the definition in the regulatory text. Rather, the Department believes that the definition we are finalizing provides flexibility to accelerate innovation,
[
431
]
empower individuals, and improve individual access to their PHI, while encouraging competition among technology developers.
While covered entities (and business associates acting for or on behalf of covered entities) may offer individuals the ability to access their PHI and other information using apps developed by or for the covered entities,
[
432
]
the information in such apps (
e.g.,
patient and health plan member portals) generally is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for those regulated entities.
[
433
]
Such entities determine, among other things, who can access the information in their apps, what information can be entered, and what happens to the information that is entered. In contrast, individuals generally make such decisions when it comes to personal health apps, subject to the app's terms and conditions or consumer privacy policy, which the individual generally has the opportunity to review and consider when they determine which app to use. For example, an individual selects the app that they prefer to use, the information that they wish to maintain in the app, and whether they prefer that information gathered from multiple sources be integrated or viewed separately. Thus, by limiting the definition to apps that provide an individual with the ability to manage, share, and control the health information that is in the app and to apps that enable the health information in the app to be managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual, we ensure that the definition encompasses only apps used by the individual or their personal representative, not other persons. This definition is consistent with how individuals view these technologies and supports individuals' ability to obtain all the PHI to which they are entitled under the right of access using the personal health app of their choosing. In contrast, where an app allows another person (
e.g.,
a medical product company conducting research) to manage, share, and control the individual's health information (but not primarily for the individual), requests from the individual to disclose PHI to the app may constitute a request pursuant to the right of access to direct (and would be subject to that right's limitations), depending on the nature and scope of the request.
A personal health app may not allow an individual to perform all three of the functions included in the definition, that is, manage, share, and control the individual's health information. Thus, the definition also allows for circumstances where one or more of those functions is performed by someone other than the individual (
e.g.,
the developer of a personal health app) primarily for the individual. An app connected to a fitness tracker selected by the individual for their own use generally contains information that is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual, and thus, likely would meet the definition of a personal health app. As another example, a wellness app selected by the individual for their own use likely would meet the definition of a personal health app because the information in the app generally is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual.
We explicitly exclude, from the definition of a personal health app, such apps that are used by individuals to access their health information where the information is managed, shared, or controlled: (1) by or primarily for a covered entity; or (2) primarily for another person. Because business associates, by definition, are acting for or on behalf of covered entities, the term personal health app excludes apps that contain information that is managed, shared, or controlled by a business associate that is acting as a business associate or a subcontractor of a business associate with respect to the app. Thus, by definition, personal health apps are not entities that are regulated under HIPAA.
[
434
]
The same holds true for developers of personal health apps with respect to such apps.
[
435
]
While a regulated entity may provide an individual with an app to access the patient or health plan member portal, the information in that app is not managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual. Rather, the information that resides in the app (generally supplied from the regulated entity's electronic information systems) is managed, shared, or controlled by or primarily for the regulated entity, even though the individual may benefit from it. Similarly, where a fitness tracker is provided to the individual by a covered entity, the developer of the app connected to the fitness tracker likely would be a business associate. Thus, the app would not meet the definition of a personal health app. As another example, while an entity managing clinical trials may provide an individual with an app to collect the individual's health information, the information in that app is not managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual. Rather, the information in such apps is managed, shared, or controlled primarily for the entity that is conducting the clinical trial for research purposes.
e. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for the proposed definition of personal health app. According to a few commenters, the proposed definition would enable workforce members to distinguish individual access requests from requests for disclosures that require an authorization. One commenter asserted that adding a definition of personal health app would provide clarity and account for new technologies with
(
printed page 74884)
minimal effects on the operations of covered entities.
A few commenters recommended that the Department clarify the scope of a personal health app. For example, a few commenters questioned whether the term would include electronic apps that are managed, shared, and controlled by an employer for an individual employee and whether it would apply to online or digital tools, platforms, or services that have the functional capabilities of a personal health app, but are not necessarily considered an app.
Several commenters asserted that the proposed definition would be too narrow. One commenter recommended that the Department expand the proposed definition to include apps on the web, mobile devices, and desktop computers, and apps that enable individuals to manage and/or to generate insights from their health information. One commenter recommended that the Department expand the proposed definition to include any app that offers services to individuals and maintains an individual's health information for their use and to explicitly include the ability to access price information.
A few commenters requested that the Department clarify whether apps recommended by health care providers would be considered personal health apps. One commenter recommended that the Department modify the definition to clarify that a personal health app accesses information for the individual.
A few commenters expressed opposition to the proposed definition because they believed that the Department should rely on the HITECH Act's definition of personal health record. One commenter recommended that the Department use the term “personal health record” because not all tools or services selected by individuals to manage and maintain their health information will be apps as the term generally is understood. The commenter provided examples of such tools and services, such as online platforms that are accessible by individuals through an internet browser. One commenter asserted that the Department should use personal health records and personal health apps as examples of forms and formats for individual access, rather than defining the term personal health app.
Response:
As explained above, we are finalizing the definition of personal health app with a few modifications. Under this definition, a personal health app is a service offered directly to consumers. It is not a service offered to the individual by a covered entity or its business associate, such as an EHR vendor. Neither the covered entity nor its business associate manages, shares, or controls the information, nor does the app developer manage the information on behalf of or at the direction of a health care provider or health plan (
e.g.,
through a patient portal that the regulated entity uses to manage individuals' access to the PHI it maintains). An electronic application also would not be a personal health app where the app developer manages the information on behalf of or at the direction of another person or where another person collects or manages PHI for its own purposes (
e.g.,
a research organization). Instead, an individual (or their personal representative) uses a personal health app (
e.g.,
Individual Access Services
[
436
]
(IAS) provided by an IAS Provider in TEFCA (or other party to TEFCA that offers TEFCA IAS), a “patient facing app”
[
437
]
that connects to CMS Aligned Networks as a participant in the Medicare App Library,
[
438
]
fitness tracker, or wellness app) for the individual's own purposes, such as to monitor their own health status and access their own PHI using the app. For example, an individual might request that their health care providers send weight, vital signs, and other PHI to their chosen personal health app either to store in such app or direct it to others.
As we explained in the proposed rule, the definition of personal health app is similar to the HITECH Act definition of personal health record,
[
439
]
but specifically addresses a category of health apps, some of which also may be personal health records to the extent that they meet both definitions.
[
440
]
The definition of personal health app generally is technology neutral, with the caveat that the app must be electronic. Thus, a personal health app may include electronic software, applications, or successor technologies. Using this technology, the individual (or their personal representative) is able to manage, store, and control their health information, gathered from one or more sources, including entities not regulated by HIPAA. These technologies often are described as “direct-to-consumer,” “consumer-directed,” or “patient-facing.”
[
441
]
They may include mobile apps, online tools, browsers or browser extensions, platforms, or services that provide individuals with the ability to manage, share, and control their own health information.
Some app developers and other technology developers may offer multiple products, including some that are offered directly to consumers and some that are offered to covered entities to provide to individuals. If a technology developer meets the definition of a covered entity or business associate with respect to a particular product (or, in the case of a hybrid entity, a product is offered through a designated health care component), that particular product or technology is not a personal health app; other products or technologies offered by the technology developer may meet the definition of a personal health app if the individual or their personal representative has the ability to manage, share, and control the health information through that product or technology. Technologies that contain an individual's health information would not meet the definition of a personal health app where the health information is managed, shared, or controlled primarily for a person other than the individual or their personal representative.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that the components of the Department align their definitions of a personal health app. One commenter asserted that the proposed definition would align with the information blocking regulations. A few commenters urged the Department to limit the definition to apps that incorporate certain privacy and security protections and/or standards.
Response:
The definition of personal health app that we are finalizing is consistent with definitions of similar terms, such as the HITECH Act definition of personal health record,
[
442
]
but is tailored to the HIPAA Privacy Rule. The definition captures certain
(
printed page 74885)
health apps, some of which also may be personal health records.
Under HIPAA and subtitle D of the HITECH Act, the Department's statutory authority is limited to covered entities and their business associates. A personal health app developer does not meet the definition of a business associate because it is not acting for, or on behalf of, a covered entity or business associate. Instead, the personal health app is a tool that is employed by or primarily for an individual (or their personal representative) to manage, share, and control the individual's health information. The Privacy Rule does not limit an individual's right of access based on the technology that the individual uses to obtain a copy of their PHI or how the information will be used or disclosed once the individual receives it. For instance, a covered entity is not permitted to deny an individual's right of access to their ePHI, where the individual requests that such access be provided through a personal health app, based solely on the covered entity's concerns that the app developer will not adequately protect the privacy of the individual's ePHI or because the app does not encrypt the individual's data at rest. Accordingly, we decline to limit the definition of personal health app to apps that meet certain privacy and security standards.
Comment:
Several commenters asserted that covered health care providers would be unable to confirm who will manage, share, and control the ePHI being transmitted to an app. Several commenters requested that the Department provide guidance, including examples, of how to identify when health information about an individual that is in an app is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual.
Response:
We recognize that app developers may offer some products directly to consumers and some products to covered entities to provide to individuals. We also are aware that there may be situations where an organization has multiple service offerings that use the same technology platform. Covered entities will need to distinguish between requests for PHI submitted through apps that are personal health apps and those that are not, based on the processes and technology that the covered entity implements to enable apps to connect to a covered entity's electronic information systems and transmit requests for disclosures of PHI, including requests for access. For example, for covered entities that have implemented a Health IT Module certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program to, for example, the certification criterion at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)
(“Standardized API for patient and population services”), the health IT developer of that Health IT Module is required to maintain a standardized authentication and application authorization process to register and enable applications for use.
[
443
]
Similarly, a covered entity that participates in TEFCA should be able to identify, based on information provided to it through TEFCA, whether a request is submitted by an IAS Provider, and whether the request was submitted by the individual.
[
444
]
Based on the processes that a covered entity implements and the information provided by an app, covered entities will need to determine whether a request submitted through an app is a request of an individual exercising his or her right of access through a personal health app and, thus, the appropriate response and compliance posture.
3. Strengthening the Access Right To Inspect and Obtain Copies of PHI
a. Current Rule
The Privacy Rule's individual right of access at
45 CFR 164.524(a)
includes an individual's right to inspect their PHI in a designated record set and their right to obtain a copy of that PHI.
[
445
]
Covered entities must arrange with an individual for a convenient time and place to inspect the PHI.
[
446
]
b. Proposed Rule
In the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, the Department proposed to strengthen the right of an individual to inspect their PHI in a designated record set by making it a separate requirement from the right of an individual to obtain a copy of their PHI in a designated record set and adding more detail. Specifically, we proposed to include, within the right of an individual to inspect their PHI in a designated record set, the right to view, take notes, take photographs, and use other personal resources to capture the information.
[
447
]
The Department also proposed to clarify that a covered entity would not be required to allow an individual to connect a personal device to the covered entity's electronic information systems. Additionally, we proposed that a covered entity would be permitted to impose requirements to ensure that the individual's recordings would be limited to only the PHI to which the individual has a right of access.
c. Overview of Comments
Most commenters, regardless of whether they expressed support or opposition, raised concerns about the increased burdens of this proposal, such as the need to develop new policies and procedures to address how to protect the privacy and security of other individuals, workforce members, and EHR systems. Most commenters who expressed opposition to the proposal believed that it would increase risks to patient or workforce safety and create risks for intellectual property rights. Several commenters expressed concern that the proposal would require the dedication of additional resources, such as personnel and space, and interrupt workflows. According to commenters, the proposal was unnecessary because most individuals do not seek to access their PHI in person; rather, they prefer to access their PHI electronically.
d. Final Rule
The Department is not finalizing the proposed modifications to the right to inspect. Although the proposal was intended to reduce requests for covered entities to make copies of PHI, we agree with commenters who asserted that the proposal would be overly burdensome for covered entities to implement. Additionally, the existing right of inspection already permits individuals to inspect their PHI in person at a mutually convenient time and place; it does not preclude inspection from occurring in conjunction with a health care appointment. Further, the
(
printed page 74886)
Department has not received information or complaints from individuals indicating that they frequently face difficulties when they choose to record their health information using their own resources.
e. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for this proposal because it would provide individuals with access to their PHI in a way that did not depend on technology. Several commenters asserted that covered entities often deny caregivers access to PHI and that this proposal would provide an individual's caregiver with an easier path towards obtaining
[
448
]
access.
Response:
The Department agrees that the right of inspection provides an individual or their personal representative with another way of obtaining access to the individual's PHI. Accordingly, we are preserving the right to inspect as it currently exists. Under the right to inspect, an individual or their personal representative may view the individual's PHI in a designated record set at a mutually convenient time and place.
[
449
]
The mutually convenient time and place for inspection may occur during a health care appointment, and a health care provider may voluntarily allow an individual (or their personal representative) to take photos or use other resources to view and capture images.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concerns about the ability of covered entities to establish policies and procedures that would enable individuals to exercise the proposed right to inspect their PHI without infringing on the privacy of others, including workforce members, or the security of ePHI in EHR systems. A few commenters asserted that individuals should not have access to the electronic information technology systems of covered entities.
Other commenters recommended that the Department require individuals to obtain permission before recording conversations with health care providers. Commenters also expressed concerns about the effect of the proposed change on legal protections for intellectual property and the intersection between this proposal and Federal or state recording laws.
Response:
Although the Department is not finalizing the proposed changes to the right to inspect, the existing right does not prohibit covered entities from allowing individuals to use personal resources to capture their PHI. Generally, individuals should be able to use personal resources, such as a smartphone, camera, or other device, to capture information about themselves. However, a covered entity is permitted to establish reasonable policies and safeguards regarding an individual's use of such personal resources for copying PHI to ensure that such use does not interfere with the ability of the covered entity to provide health care to others. These policies and safeguards may also ensure that the individual's personal resources are used in a way that enables the individual to copy or otherwise memorialize only the PHI to which they are entitled under the right of access.
A covered entity is not permitted to establish policies and safeguards that impose unjustified or unreasonable barriers to individual access (
e.g.,
limiting individuals to paper copies of their PHI). However, a covered entity is not required to allow an individual to connect a personal device to the covered entity's electronic information systems (
e.g.,
insert an individual's USB drive into one of the covered entity's workstations, sign an individual's mobile device onto a covered entity's network).
The Department does not believe that individuals capturing their own PHI through video, still camera photos, or audio recordings would be inconsistent with Federal or state recording laws or intellectual property rights protections.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern about the administrative burdens that this proposal would impose on covered entities, such as the potential disruptions to workflow, and the potential implications for the quality of care. Several commenters asserted that the proposed change would require significant resources, such as extra space and personnel.
Several commenters expressed concern that individuals exercising this proposed right would view PHI that has not been validated or reviewed for accuracy or that is incomplete. A few commenters asserted that covered entities could face liability if certain PHI was not included in the medical record when inspected. One commenter stated that requiring a health care provider to provide access to PHI in real-time could damage the integrity of the medical record because health care providers may hesitate to be candid in their documentation and diagnosis in such cases.
Response:
The Department agrees that the proposed changes to the right to inspect could be overly burdensome to covered entities and disruptive to their workflow. Accordingly, we are not finalizing the proposal. The existing right of inspection allows, and the Department encourages, covered entities to provide individuals with on demand, in-person access to requested PHI where appropriate, in whole or in part (if certain access may be denied under the Privacy Rule), including at the point of care.
A covered entity may deny an individual access to all or a portion of PHI requested in only very limited circumstances.
[
450
]
For example, a covered entity may deny an individual access if the information requested is not part of a designated record set maintained by the covered entity (or by a business associate for a covered entity),
[
451
]
or if the information is excepted from the right of access.
[
452
]
As another example, a covered entity may deny an individual access to particular PHI if a licensed health care professional determines in the exercise of professional judgment that the access requested is reasonably likely to endanger the life or physical safety of the individual or another person.
[
453
]
Accordingly, a covered entity may deny an individual experiencing suicidal ideation access to such PHI as a health care provider determines in their professional judgment is reasonably likely to lead the individual to take their own life.
[
454
]
However, we stress that this ground is narrowly construed in order to protect individuals' autonomy interests and their right under the Privacy Rule to obtain information about themselves, which is fundamental in facilitating individuals' active participation in their own health care. General concerns about psychological or emotional harm (
e.g.,
concerns that the individual will not be able to understand the information or may be upset by it) are not sufficient to deny an individual access. In addition, the requested access must be reasonably likely to cause harm or endanger physical life or safety. Thus, concerns based on the mere possibility of harm are not sufficient to deny access.
[
455
]
As a result, we expect this ground for
(
printed page 74887)
denial to apply only in extremely rare circumstances.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that covered entities should be permitted, not required, to allow individuals to inspect their PHI. Several commenters who expressed opposition to the proposal recommended modifications. For example, some commenters recommended that the Department limit an individual's right to inspect their PHI to certain circumstances, while others recommended that the Department permit covered entities to limit the proposed right to inspect in certain circumstances. Still other commenters requested that the Department provide guidance on circumstances in which covered entities would be permitted to limit an individual's right to inspect.
Response:
While in-person, point-of-care access to PHI may not always be appropriate or feasible, the Department declines to limit the existing right of an individual to inspect their PHI in a designated record set. Providing individuals with easy access to their PHI empowers them to make decisions about their health and well-being. Accordingly, as a process matter, covered entities should have in place reasonable procedures to enable individuals to inspect their PHI. The Department believes that responding to requests from individuals to inspect their PHI should impose minimal burden on the covered entity, particularly where the PHI requested is of the type easily accessed onsite or virtually by the covered entity itself in the ordinary course of business, such as during an in-person or virtual visit. The Department encourages covered entities to provide individuals with on demand access to PHI at the point of care where appropriate, in whole or in part (if access to certain PHI may be denied under the Privacy Rule).
Furthermore, where covered entities that are subject to the information blocking regulations employ practices that are likely to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of EHI, such practices may implicate the information blocking regulations.
[
456
]
This includes circumstances where an individual seeks to exercise their right to inspect and the requested PHI also meets the definition of EHI.
[
457
]
Comment:
One commenter recommended that, instead of creating a specific right to take photographs or videos, individuals should be given the option to take video or photographs, if both parties agree, at a mutually convenient time and place; and if the covered entity does not agree, require the covered entity to provide PHI in an alternative format.
Response:
The Department is not modifying the Privacy Rule to include a specific right to take photographs, videos, or use other personal resources to capture PHI as part of an individual's right to inspect. The existing right to inspect does not place limitations on an individual's ability to record their PHI while they inspect it at a mutually convenient time and place. A covered entity may establish reasonable policies and safeguards regarding an individual's use of their own smartphone, camera, or other device for capturing PHI when exercising their right to inspect their PHI to ensure that equipment or technology used by individuals is not disruptive to the entity's operations and is used in a way that enables an individual to copy or otherwise memorialize only the PHI to which they are entitled under the right of access. An individual may inspect PHI in person (whether simply viewing or capturing it using a personal resource consistent with a covered entity's reasonable policies and safeguards), in addition to obtaining copies or in lieu thereof.
Comment:
According to a few commenters, the proposal was unnecessary because individuals usually do not seek to access their PHI in person; instead, individuals generally prefer to access their PHI through patient portals or other electronic means.
Response:
The Department agrees that the proposed changes are unnecessary, especially in light of (1) the burdens the proposal would impose on covered entities; and (2) the ability of an individual to capture their PHI in person using personal resources, to the extent consistent with a covered entity's reasonable policies and safeguards, while exercising the existing right to inspect their PHI in a designated record set. The Department also agrees that many individuals may prefer to access their PHI through patient or health plan member portals or other electronic means. With the increasing use of and continued advances in health IT, individuals often have the ability to access their PHI electronically quickly and easily, in real time, and on demand. Thus, the right to inspect PHI is not limited to in-person inspection. Rather, an individual may seek to exercise their right to inspect a copy of their PHI using remote communications technology (
e.g.,
communication app on a smartphone or other computing device). Accordingly, the right to inspect PHI can be a convenient method for individuals who choose to exercise their right of access in person or remotely.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed support for the idea that covered entities should be permitted to provide individuals with copies of PHI in lieu of in-person inspection when necessary for public health and safety, during emergencies or otherwise.
Response:
As explained above, the Department is not finalizing its proposals to add requirements to an individual's right to inspect their PHI in a designated record set. The Privacy Rule does not provide covered entities with the opportunity to deny or delay (beyond the permitted response period and extension) the right of an individual to inspect PHI, whether in person or otherwise, for public health and safety, during emergencies, or other circumstances. However, it does provide the opportunity for the covered entity to arrange with the individual for a time and place, which may be virtual, for the inspection that is mutually convenient.
[
458
]
Additionally, the covered entity is permitted to discuss the scope, format, and other aspects of the request for access with the individual as necessary to facilitate the timely provision of access.
[
459
]
4. Modifying the Implementation Requirements for Requests for Access and Timely Action in Response to Requests for Access
a. Current Rule
Section 164.524(b)(1) requires a covered entity to permit an individual to request access to inspect or to obtain a copy of PHI about the individual that is maintained in a designated record set. It permits a covered entity to require individuals to make such a request in writing, provided that the covered entity informs individuals of such requirement. Section 164.524(b)(2) requires a covered entity to act on an individual's request for access no later than 30 days after receipt of the request, with an option to extend the time by an additional 30 days if they provide, during the initial 30-day period, a written explanation and the date by which the entity will complete its action on the request. The Department has long maintained that 30 calendar days is an outer limit.
[
460
]
(
printed page 74888)
b. Proposed Rule
The Department proposed to modify the Privacy Rule to clarify that, while a covered entity may require an individual to make a request for access in writing, provided that it informs the individual of such a requirement, it may not impose unreasonable measures that impede the individual from obtaining access when a measure that is less burdensome for the individual is practicable for the entity. We also proposed to clarify that the writing could be in electronic or paper form and to include examples of reasonable and unreasonable measures in regulatory text. The Department proposed to modify the Privacy Rule to require that access be provided as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receipt of the request, with the possibility of one 15-calendar-day extension, provided that certain conditions are met. The Department also proposed that where another Federal or state law requires a covered entity to provide individuals with access to the PHI requested in less than 15 calendar days, we would deem the shorter time period to be practicable for purposes of proposed
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i)
and
(d)(5)
.
Additionally, we proposed to add a new condition for the use of an extension that would require a covered entity to establish a written policy to prioritize urgent or other high-priority access requests (especially requests for health and safety and to support individual decisions about treatment options), to limit the need to use a 15-calendar-day extension for such requests. The Department also proposed to provide expressly at
45 CFR 164.524(c)(3)
and
45 CFR 164.525(b)
that, while a covered entity may discuss aspects of the access request with the individual before fulfilling the request, discussions to clarify the scope, format, and other aspects of the request would not extend the time limit for providing access.
c. Overview of Comments
Most commenters expressed concern that the proposed timeliness requirements would be overly burdensome and insufficiently flexible because of the varying complexity of requests. Even among commenters who were generally supportive, many recommended exceptions for certain types of requests or in certain circumstances (
e.g.,
natural disasters). While some commenters expressed support for the proposal to permit one 15-calendar-day extension if the covered entity adopted a policy to prioritize urgent or high-priority requests, most commenters expressed opposition to this proposal because they believed that it would be confusing and difficult to implement. Some of the commenters who expressed support for the proposal also requested that the Department clarify what would constitute a high priority or urgent request, including examples. Commenters who expressed opposition highlighted the burdens that they believed the proposal would create for both the covered entity and the individual. Commenters provided examples of circumstances that they believed would require additional time. Others expressed their belief that requiring the development and implementation of policies to prioritize responses to requests that are high priority or urgent access was unnecessary because such requests already are addressed by
45 CFR 164.506
, which permits a covered entity to use or disclose PHI for TPO, without the individual's authorization, in certain circumstances.
d. Final Rule
We are adopting, with modification, the proposal to clarify the ability of covered entities to require individuals to make requests for access in writing. Specifically, we clarify, in
paragraph (ii) of 45 CFR 164.524(b)(1)
what we mean by “in writing.” We are not including the phrase “electronic or paper form” in regulatory text because the term “form” could be misinterpreted as requiring a particular form, template, document, or format that an individual must use to request access, which could cause confusion given other uses of the term “form” in
45 CFR 164.524
. Instead, we clarify that “in writing” means that the request itself serves as documentation of the individual's exercise of the right of access, including when the request is submitted electronically or on paper. This language is intended to make clear that requests in writing do not need to be submitted on a particular form or in a particular format.
A request may be in writing when made through one or more written or electronic communications, so long as the communication(s) documents the individual's exercise of the right of access. For example, a request may be submitted using a handwritten letter, a paper form, an email, a secure message, a patient or health plan member portal, or another electronic mechanism. A request also qualifies as “in writing” if a covered entity receives a notification or other electronic transmission from a personal health app that contains the information necessary to document the individual's exercise of the right, such as information identifying the individual, the scope of the requested access, and information about where to send the requested PHI. For example, an access request sent through a Qualified Health Information Network
[
461
]
(QHIN) using TEFCA to a covered entity from an individual using an IAS Provider that is also a personal health app would constitute a written request where it documents the individual's exercise of their right of access. As another example, a request sent to a covered entity from an individual, through a patient facing app that connects to CMS Aligned Networks as a participant in the Medicare App Library, and such app is a personal health app, similarly would constitute a request that is in writing where it documents the individual's exercise of their right of access.
Covered entities are not required to adopt a particular electronic mechanism for receiving access requests or to receive electronic requests in a manner that the covered entity does not have the capability to support. The Department, however, strongly encourages covered entities to allow individuals to make requests for access electronically and to receive requests through electronic mechanisms that the covered entity has the capability to support.
Additionally, we are finalizing a new paragraph at
45 CFR 164.524(b)(1)(iii)
to prevent a covered entity from imposing measures on an individual making requests for access that impede the individual from obtaining access (which includes measures for requesting such access) when there is a measure that is less burdensome for the individual and practicable for the entity. The finalized requirement does not include the term “unreasonable” because the regulatory text expressly describes the circumstances in which a measure is prohibited.
Further, we are not finalizing in regulatory text examples of reasonable or unreasonable measures. Including examples in the regulatory text could create the impression that the list is exhaustive, or that only the enumerated measures are permissible or impermissible. Instead, we reaffirm the examples provided in the 2021 NPRM and provide a non-exhaustive list of
(
printed page 74889)
additional examples in this preamble to illustrate how the standard may apply in particular circumstances. For example, a covered entity may not require individuals to submit written requests or accept individuals' written requests only in a particular form (
e.g.,
only paper, only through a patient or health plan member portal) or delivered in a particular manner (
e.g.,
only in person at the covered entity's facility, only through the covered entity's online portal) when there is another measure for making such requests that is less burdensome for the individual and practicable for the entity (
e.g.,
emailing a request to a member of the covered entity's workforce responsible for handling requests for access). In addition, where a covered entity has the capability to receive requests for access submitted by the individual through a patient or health plan member portal, a personal health app from a secure standards-based API, or an HIO (
e.g.,
a QHIN), requiring the individual to use a more burdensome method to make the same request may impede access if receiving the request through that mechanism is practicable for the entity. When determining whether receiving requests electronically through such mechanisms is practicable, a covered entity may consider its technical capabilities, its obligations to protect the privacy of PHI under
45 CFR 164.530(c)
and the security of ePHI under
45 CFR 164.306
