, and the costs of implementing such technical capabilities. We intend to issue additional guidance on access requests, including illustrative examples, to help regulated entities to understand the various ways in which requests might be made and the types of information that might need to included in different typ.
We also are adopting a modified version of the proposal to reduce the amount of time in which covered entities must respond to requests for individual access. Specifically, we are modifying
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i)
to require that a covered entity provide access to individuals “as soon as practicable,” but no later than 15 calendar days after receipt of a request. Relatedly, we are modifying
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(ii)
to clarify that the 30-day extension that is permissible in certain circumstances refers to 30 calendar days. Additionally, we are adding a new
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(iii)
to clarify that where Federal or state law requires a covered entity to provide an individual with access to the requested PHI in less than 15 calendar days, that shorter time period will be deemed practicable for purposes of
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i)
. This will ensure that individuals receive more timely action on their access requests, while retaining the existing possibility of one 30-calendar-day extension (rather than the proposed 15-day extension) to accommodate more complex or difficult requests (
e.g.,
paper records that are archived offsite and not easily accessible, ePHI that may need to be retrieved from offline archival storage). The finalized requirement reduces the time within which covered entities must provide individuals with access to PHI, empowering individuals to take an active role in their care and facilitating care coordination and case management.
As discussed in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, at least eight states require patients to be provided with copies of their health records in less time than the Privacy Rule's current 30-day limits,
[
462
]
and at least five states require the opportunity to view or inspect the record in fewer than 30 days.
[
463
]
Such requirements generally apply to health care providers, including hospitals and other health facilities, but not to health plans. Because most states do not impose time limits on covered entities that are as short as 15 days, access to PHI in such states will be markedly improved. Additionally, these shorter timelines support the Department's initiatives to implement statutory requirements aimed at empowering individuals to make more informed decisions about health care.
[
464
]
Shorter timelines also are consistent with individuals' needs and expectations. For example, most patients expect immediate online access to health information in their medical records, including tests results and clinician notes.
[
465
]
Easy online access to medical records—through patient or health plan member portals, personal health apps, or other mechanisms—is vital for those managing chronic conditions, new diagnoses, or another's care.
[
466
]
For the same reasons, we also are adopting our proposal to apply these same timeliness requirements to requests from an individual to a covered entity to direct an electronic copy of PHI about the individual in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual at new
45 CFR 164.524(d)(5)
.
Additionally, we are adopting our proposal to modify
45 CFR 164.524(c)(3)
to reflect that discussions between the covered entity and the individual about the scope of an individual's request do not extend the amount of time that covered entities have to provide the requested access.
We are not finalizing the proposal to require that a covered entity implement a policy to prioritize certain types of requests. Based on public comments, covered entities already prioritize requests if an individual communicates the urgency of the request. Additionally, we are concerned that such a requirement could incentivize covered entities to require individuals to provide personal information about why a request is urgent, which would place a burden on individuals and could delay responses to such requests.
e. Response to Public Comments
Comment:
Some commenters expressed support for the proposal for
(
printed page 74890)
reasons such as strengthening an individual's right of access, enabling individuals to obtain PHI more easily, improving care coordination, and enabling plaintiffs in personal injury lawsuits to meet litigation-related deadlines. A few commenters asserted that the fact that some states require covered entities to provide individuals with access to their PHI in less time than is currently required by the Privacy Rule demonstrates that it is possible. Several commenters expressed support for the proposal but recommended that the Department require covered entities to provide access to ePHI more quickly than the proposed timeline because it would benefit individuals to have access to their PHI as quickly as possible and ePHI is easily transmitted by a covered entity to an individual.
Many commenters recommended that the Department include exceptions to the proposed requirement. Commenters recommended exceptions for exigent circumstances or infeasibility (
e.g.,
natural disasters); where a covered entity demonstrates that it has made a good faith effort to retrieve PHI to which it lacks immediate access; for certain health care providers that treat individuals who have been involuntarily committed; and for covered entities that have revenue of less than a certain amount.
Several commenters expressed support for the “as soon as practicable language” but expressed opposition to the 15-calendar-day timeline because of concerns about their ability to gather the requested PHI in less time than they currently have or about the time it takes them to obtain clarification from individuals where the requests that they receive are incomplete.
Many commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that it would be burdensome to implement. Commenters asserted that many covered entities use a manual process for responding to access requests because they rely on legacy systems, requested PHI may be maintained offsite and/or in a form or format that is not easily accessible, or the requested PHI may include sensitive information that is subject to privacy restrictions in other laws. According to these commenters, the manual process can require more than 15 days. Commenters also asserted that the proposal would require extensive changes to workflow, training, orientation, and documentation. One commenter asserted that some hospital records may not be complete within 15 days of an individual's discharge because of delays in completing certain records. Some commenters recommended that the Department adopt alternative timeframes. For example, a few commenters recommended that the Department adopt a 30-day timeliness requirement with the possibility of one 15-day extension. A few commenters urged the Department to modify the proposal to provide different timelines for ePHI and for PHI that is not ePHI.
Several commenters requested that the Department provide guidance on best practices for managing and fulfilling individual access requests within 30 days.
Response:
As discussed above, the Department is adopting a modified version of its proposal to reduce the amount of time that a covered entity has to respond to a request made pursuant to the right of access, including the right of access to direct. The final rule requires a covered entity to respond to an individual's request for access as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request, with the possibility of one 30-calendar-day extension. The Department encourages covered entities to view the 15 calendar days as an outer limit, particularly for requests for electronic copies of ePHI. Indeed, a covered entity may have the capacity to provide individuals with almost instantaneous electronic access to the PHI requested through personal health apps (
e.g.,
a TEFCA IAS Provider, a patient facing app that connects to CMS Aligned Networks as a participant in the Medicare App Library), web portals, or similar electronic means. Further, individuals may reasonably expect a covered entity to be able to respond in a much faster timeframe when the covered entity is using health IT in its day-to-day operations.
[
467
]
For example, individuals may be accustomed to receiving treatment from health care providers who use tools that are embedded in their EHRs to make certain information available quickly.
[
468
]
Similarly, individuals may reasonably expect to obtain electronic access to PHI from their health plan in a faster timeframe when they request to receive their health information through an API.
[
469
]
Additionally, as discussed above, we clarify that where a Federal or state law requires a covered entity to provide individuals with access to the PHI requested in less than 15 calendar days, that shorter time period would be deemed practicable.
[
470
]
We emphasize that the timeliness requirement applies regardless of the circumstances of the request. For example, the timeliness requirement applies without regard to the form or medium (
e.g.,
paper, electronic) in which the requested PHI is maintained. Negotiating with the individual about the form and format of the response does not extend the timeliness requirement. As another example, the
(
printed page 74891)
timeliness requirement also applies to requests for PHI that is on paper, archived offsite and/or offline, and/or not otherwise easily accessible. If a covered entity is unable to provide access within 15 calendar days (
e.g.,
the information is archived offsite on paper and not easily accessible), the covered entity may extend the time to respond by no more than 30 calendar days. To extend the time, the covered entity must, within the initial 15 calendar days, inform the individual in writing of the reasons for the delay and the date by which the covered entity will provide access. Only one extension is permitted per access request.
In certain circumstances, because of the nature of a product or service (
e.g.,
mainstream genetic testing for cancer patients,
[
471
]
comprehensive genomic profiling of solid tumors,
[
472
]
or molecular biomarker testing
[
473
]
), 15 calendar days may not be sufficient to complete the product or service to which the individual has requested access. If the individual submits a request for access to the particular product or service that has not been completed and is not expected to be completed before the end of the 15-calendar-day period, the covered entity may notify the individual in writing within that 15-calendar-day period of the need and specific reason for the delay in providing access to PHI related to the completed product or service and the date by which the covered entity will complete its action on the request, in accordance with
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(ii)(A)
and
164.524(d)(5)(ii)(B)
(
1
). The Privacy Rule permits only one extension on such request, and the extension may not exceed an additional 30 calendar days. In the rare circumstance where 45 total calendar days is insufficient to satisfy the individual's request for access to PHI related to the completed product or service, the covered entity may, at the end of the 45-day period, satisfy the access request by providing the individual with access to the PHI that does exist at the time (
e.g.,
test requisitions, the underlying data being used to generate the reports, other completed test reports) in the designated record set.
However, to avoid this situation to the extent possible, where a covered entity knows that a particular product or service will take longer than the time permitted for responding to a right of access request, we encourage the covered entity to explain this circumstance to the individual. Upon informing an individual of this situation when they request access, the individual may be willing to withdraw or hold their request until a later time to ensure that they get access to the PHI that they want or need. If an individual chooses not to withdraw their request for access, the individual will then have a right, with respect to that request for access, only to obtain PHI in the designated record set at the time the request is fulfilled, which might not include the particular PHI requested because it is not yet available.
[
474
]
The individual can obtain the particular PHI requested by making another request for access at a later date. In these circumstances, we encourage covered entities to retain and respond to individuals' requests when the relevant product or service is completed and becomes part of the designated record set; however, they are not required to do so absent a new request.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern about the ability of small health care providers to comply with the proposal because of limited staffing and other resources. A few commenters asserted that the proposal would have a negative effect on state government and Tribal entities in particular, because of their resource constraints and the associated burdens. These commenters provided examples of reasons why they believed this proposal was uniquely burdensome for them, such as weekend and holiday staffing challenges, their size, language translation needs, special programs, and other laws.
Response:
The Department considered commenters' concerns about the potential burdens that the shorter time period may create. We believe that increasing the length of a possible extension to accommodate more complex or difficult requests from 15 calendar days, as proposed, to one 30-calendar-day extension, alleviates many of these concerns. To the extent that implementation burdens remain, the Department believes that the benefits to individuals (
e.g.,
their ability to direct their own health care, enhanced care coordination) outweigh the potential burdens on covered entities.
As discussed previously, the final rule requires that access be provided as soon as practicable, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after receipt of the request. It clarifies that the Department will deem fewer than 15 calendar days to be practicable where a Federal or state law requires such access to be provided more quickly. Where there is no specific law requiring faster access, the Department strongly encourages covered entities to provide individuals with access to their health information as quickly as possible within the allotted 15 calendar days. Moreover, even if regulated entities that also are subject to the information blocking regulations
[
475
]
fulfill requests for access within the time period required by the Privacy Rule, a practice that delays the fulfillment of such requests could constitute an interference under the information blocking regulations.
[
476
]
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that the Department align timeliness requirements across Federal programs that address aspects of the right of access.
Response:
Implementation of certain requirements of the HITECH Act and Cures Act enables covered entities (and their business associates) that choose to use health IT to respond timelier to individual requests for ePHI. For example, developers of certified API technology must publish certain
(
printed page 74892)
information about their APIs that can be used by individuals to access certain information using a personal health application.
[
477
]
The Cures Act directed the Secretary to require, as a condition of certification and maintenance of certification for the ONC Health IT Certification program, that the developer of certified technology allows health information from such technology to be accessed, exchanged, and used without special effort through the use of APIs or successor technology or standards, as provided for under applicable law, including providing access to all data elements of a patient's electronic health record to the extent permissible under applicable privacy laws.
[
478
]
To achieve such access, exchange, or use without special effort, ONC issued regulations that require certified APIs, and the health care ecosystem in which they are deployed, to be standardized, transparent, and pro-competitive.
[
479
]
Where a developer of certified API technology institutes an authenticity verification process for API users, the developer must complete that process within 10 business days and subsequently register and enable the application for production use within 5 business days.
[
480
]
Accordingly, when regulated entities adopt health IT that includes certified API technology, individuals can more easily access their ePHI and covered entities can more easily respond to right of access requests.
To further encourage the use of ONC-certified and other secure, interoperable health IT with the goal of providing individuals with timelier access to their PHI, this final rule requires that access be provided “as soon as practicable,” but in no case later than 15 calendar days after receipt of the request. It clarifies that the Department will deem fewer than 15 calendar days to be practicable where Federal or state law requires such access to be provided more quickly. Accordingly, where other Federal regulations, such as the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule,
[
481
]
the Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule,
[
482
]
and the Quality Payment Program,
[
483
]
require a covered entity to provide an individual with access to PHI in fewer than 15 days, the Department deems the shorter time period to be “practicable” and expects that covered entities will comply with such other law.
[
484
]
Thus, a failure to comply with such other law also could result in a violation of the timeliness requirements at
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i)
and
164.524(d)(5)(ii)(A)
. Where there is no specific law requiring access in fewer than 15 calendar days, covered entities still must provide individuals with access to their health information as soon as practicable (
i.e.,
in less than 15 calendar days if practicable). Furthermore, where regulated entities that are subject to the information blocking regulations engage in a practice that delays fulfilling access requests, such practice could constitute an interference under the information blocking regulations, even if the requests are fulfilled within the 15-calendar-day period required by this final rule.
[
485
]
The Department strongly encourages covered entities to take advantage of technologies that enable individuals to have faster or even immediate access to the requested information, adoption of which would, in turn, make such expedited access “practicable.”
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that covered entities often take more than the permitted time to let individuals know that their request is incomplete and then reset the “clock” when the individuals submit an updated request.
Response:
The time period for responding to a request for access begins on the date that a covered entity receives the request, and a covered entity must respond within 15 calendar days of receiving it. This 15-calendar-day period includes, for example, the time that it takes a covered entity to obtain any additional information from the individual or personal representative that it needs to act upon a request and the time that it takes a covered entity to obtain pertinent information from a business associate or forward the request to the business associate for action. It also includes the time that it takes to verify an individual or personal representative's identity, and in the case of a personal representative, their authority to obtain access to the requested PHI. Where a request is sent directly to a business associate and the business associate agreement provides that the business associate is responsible for responding to such requests, the 15-calendar-day period begins when the business associate receives the request from an individual.
If the covered entity is unable to act on a request within 15 calendar days of receiving the request, it may extend the deadline for up to an additional 30 calendar days by providing the individual with a written statement of the reasons for the delay and the date by which the covered entity will complete its action on the request. This written statement describing the extension must be provided within the standard (
i.e.,
pre-extension) deadline of 15 calendar days. A covered entity may extend the deadline only once for any given access request.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that the proposal would be burdensome for health plans for a variety of reasons, including that they offer multiple products, requests often require coordination across business associates, the PHI requested may span a long period of time, and they have multiple electronic information systems that maintain PHI. One commenter requested that the Department provide health plans with a longer implementation period for this proposal because it would require administrative and technological changes to implement a new process for responding to access requests.
Response:
We are adopting a modified version of our proposal that requires covered entities to respond to a request for access as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receipt of the request, with the possibility of one 30-calendar-day extension. To the extent that a particular request meets the conditions for a one-time extension, the total amount of time permitted for acting on the request is 45 calendar days from receipt of the individual's request, which we believe is sufficient for most
(
printed page 74893)
requests today even without significant changes in covered entities' policies and procedures. Additionally, to comply with other laws, many covered entities already have implemented patient or health plan member portals and other solutions for providing individuals with access to their PHI in an electronic form and format quickly and easily. Thus, we do not believe that covered entities need additional time to implement this requirement.
The effective date of the final rule is 60 days after publication for all regulated entities. Regulated entities have an additional 180 days until the compliance date to establish and implement policies, procedures, and practices to achieve compliance with any new or modified standards. Regulated entities are permitted to comply earlier than the compliance date, but the Department will not take action against them for noncompliance with the finalized requirements that occur before the compliance date. Thus, regulated entities have 240 days to develop and implement policies and procedures for responding to such requests.
5. Addressing the Form and Format of Access
a. Current Rule
Section 164.524(c)(2) includes the requirements for the form and format of a covered entity's response to an individual's request for access to their PHI. Section 164.524(c)(2)(i) requires a covered entity to provide an individual with access to the individual's PHI in the form and format requested by the individual, if it is readily producible in the requested form and format. Where the covered entity cannot provide PHI in the requested form and format,
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(i)
requires the covered entity to provide the individual with a readable hard copy or such other form and format as agreed to by the covered entity and individual. If the covered entity maintains the PHI electronically,
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(ii)
requires a covered entity to provide the individual with access to the information in the requested electronic form and format, if it is readily producible in that form and format, or if not, in a readable electronic form and format as agreed to by the covered entity and individual.
The Department interprets the phrase “readily producible in that form and format” as referring to (1) how PHI is produced to the individual (or person designated by the individual to receive an electronic copy of the PHI in an electronic health record), and (2) the format of the PHI that is transmitted (
e.g.,
the type of electronic file, etc.). When an individual requests access to PHI in a particular form or format, the question for the covered entity is whether or not the entity is able to readily produce the copy in that format—which is a matter of capability, not willingness.
[
486
]
Thus, if a covered entity has the capability to readily produce the requested format, it is not permissible for the covered entity to deny the individual access to that format because the entity would prefer that the individual receive their PHI in a different format or follow other procedures for accessing records that are more customarily relied upon by the entity.
[
487
]
For example, where an individual requests a paper copy of PHI maintained by the covered entity either electronically or on paper, it is expected that the covered entity will be able to provide the individual with the paper copy requested.
[
488
]
Where an individual requests an electronic copy of PHI that a covered entity maintains only on paper, the covered entity is required to provide the individual with an electronic copy if it is readily producible electronically (
e.g.,
the covered entity can readily scan the paper record into an electronic format).
[
489
]
In the event that an individual requests an electronic copy of PHI and a covered entity maintains PHI electronically, a covered entity is not required to purchase new software or equipment in order to accommodate every possible individual request.
[
490
]
However, the covered entity in this circumstance must have the capability to provide some form of electronic copy of PHI maintained electronically.
[
491
]
Where an individual declines to accept any of the electronic formats readily producible by the covered entity, the covered entity may satisfy the request for access by providing the individual with a readable hard copy of the PHI.
[
492
]
The Privacy Rule also includes requirements that address whether and when covered entities can provide individuals with summaries or explanations of their requested PHI. Section 164.524(c)(2)(iii) permits a covered entity to provide the individual with a summary of the requested PHI in lieu of copies, or an explanation of the PHI to which access has been provided, if the individual has agreed in advance to such summary or explanation, and to the fees imposed, if any, by the covered entity to cover the costs of preparing the summary or explanation.
b. Proposed Rule
In the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, the Department proposed to modify the requirements for covered entities responding to requests for access to PHI in an electronic form and format. Specifically, the Department proposed to add a new subparagraph (iii) to
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)
that would deem PHI to be “readily producible” in a form and format where another applicable Federal or state law requires the entity to provide the access in the particular electronic form and format requested by the individual. To accommodate this new paragraph and address the requirements of the right of access to direct, we also proposed to redesignate
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iii)
as
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iv)
and
164.524(d)(4)
.
Additionally, we proposed to require at
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iv)(B)
and
164.524(d)(4)(ii)
that when a covered entity offers a summary to an individual, or a person designated by the individual, in lieu of copies of the requested PHI, it must inform the individual that they retain the right to obtain a complete copy of the PHI. These proposed requirements would not apply when the covered entity offers a summary because it is denying the individual's request made pursuant to the right of access (including the right of access to direct) on unreviewable or reviewable grounds. For example, a covered entity would not be required to inform an individual that they retain the right to obtain a complete copy of their PHI where the covered entity denies the individual's request for access to PHI because the requested PHI was obtained from someone (other than a health care provider) under a promise of confidentiality and the access requested would be reasonably likely to reveal the source of the information.
[
493
]
In such
(
printed page 74894)
circumstances, the covered entity would be required to implement the specified procedures for such denial.
[
494
]
c. Overview of Comments
Commenters expressed mixed views on these proposals, with most commenters expressing concern or opposition. Some commenters asserted that the proposal to deem ePHI readily producible in a particular form and format in certain circumstances would increase costs for health care providers because it would require changes to their EHRs. Many commenters expressed opposition to the Department's proposal because they believed that it would require covered entities to use secure, standards-based APIs to fulfill requests for access. In contrast, a few commenters expressed support for this proposal because they believed that it would require covered entities to use secure, standards-based APIs to fulfill requests for access.
A few commenters expressed support for the Department's proposals to require that covered entities inform individuals that they retain their right to request access to their PHI (including their right of access to direct) if they do not agree to receive the summary (or to direct the summary to the person designated by the individual) in lieu of a copy of the PHI.
Commenters expressed the need for transparency about the information personal health apps collect on individuals, and what the developers do with that information, and urged the Department to protect individuals' health information from exploitation. These commenters expressed concern that app developers that are not regulated entities may misuse individuals' health information. Many commenters who expressed opposition to providing individuals with a copy of their PHI through a personal health app pursuant to the individual's right of access recommended that the Department require covered entities or an app itself to notify individuals that their information is not protected by HIPAA under such circumstances.
d. Final Rule
The Department is finalizing the proposals to: (1) add a new
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iii)
;
(2)
redesignate existing
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iii)
as
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iv)
and
164.524(d)(4)
without modification; and (3) add new
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iv)(B)
and
164.524(d)(4)(ii)
. New
paragraph (iii) of 45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)
provides that if other Federal or state law requires an entity (which may include a business associate acting on behalf of a covered entity) to implement a technology or policy that has the effect of providing an individual with access to their PHI in a particular electronic form and format, such form and format would be deemed “readily producible” for the purposes of compliance in fulfilling requests for such PHI under
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(i)
and
(ii)
.
The Department believes that aligning the Privacy Rule with other applicable laws facilitates individual access and care coordination, and eases burdens on covered entities and individuals. The Department also believes that these modifications increase transparency about the obligations of covered entities to provide individuals with copies of their PHI. Moreover, we believe that these modifications will result in a more complete understanding of the right of individuals to access their PHI.
Further, we clarify that PHI is readily producible in a form and format where a covered entity makes PHI available in that form and format to other persons (
e.g.,
regulated entities), and where the level of risk to the security of the covered entity's ePHI and electronic information systems (or the business associate's electronic information systems when the ePHI is maintained or transmitted by the business associate for, or on behalf of, the covered entity) is no greater than it is when providing the PHI to such other persons in that same form and format. For example, where a covered entity (or a business associate acting for, or on behalf of a covered entity) provides ePHI to another covered entity through a secure, standards-based API that also is capable of transmitting ePHI to a personal health app without increasing the risk to the security of the covered entity's ePHI or electronic information systems, we consider the ePHI to be readily producible to the individual through their personal health app. Further, where a covered entity transmits a copy of PHI through a personal health app, we interpret this as a transmission to the individual. In other words, the Department interprets a request by an individual to receive a copy of their PHI through a personal health app as an exercise of their right to obtain a copy, rather than an exercise of the right of access to direct (discussed below).
A covered entity is not required to provide an individual with a copy of the individual's PHI to or through a personal health app if a copy is not readily producible to or through such application. In other words, this final rule does not independently require the implementation of technology or policies by covered entities for the purpose of gaining the ability to provide individuals with a copy of their PHI to or through a personal health app. Rather, it requires that covered entities use technology or policies that are required by other Federal or state laws, or that they have otherwise implemented, to provide individuals with copies of their PHI to or through personal health apps where individuals request copies in such form and format.
Relatedly, we encourage covered entities to provide individuals with an electronic copy of their ePHI in another standards-based interoperable electronic format if the requested ePHI is not readily producible in the requested electronic form and format. Where the ePHI is not available in another standards-based interoperable electronic form and format, we encourage covered entities to provide individuals with their ePHI in a machine-readable electronic form and format. This approach aligns with the Manner Exception in the information blocking regulations.
[
495
]
Only if the ePHI is not producible in a machine-readable electronic form and format should covered entities offer individuals a copy of their ePHI solely in a human-readable electronic form and format—unless the individual requests the copy in such form and format.
Additionally,
45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(iv)(B)
and
164.524(d)(4)(ii)
require that, when a covered entity offers a summary in lieu of a copy of PHI, it must inform the individual that the individual retains the right of access, including the right of access to direct if they do not agree to receive the summary. To fully comply with the access provisions, a covered entity remains obligated to ensure that it is the individual, and not the covered entity, who decides whether a summary is an acceptable substitute for a copy or copies of the requested PHI.
e. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
A few commenters expressed support for the proposal because they believed that it would clarify that “readily producible” includes access through secure APIs and personal health apps.
In contrast, many commenters expressed opposition to the Department's assertion that “readily producible” could include the use of implemented secure, standards-based APIs to fulfill access requests if a Federal or state law requires an entity to implement a technology or policy that
(
printed page 74895)
would have the effect of providing an individual with access to their PHI in that form and format. A few commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that such a requirement would exceed the Department's authority under HIPAA and would require reliance upon or changes to other Federal or state laws. These commenters additionally asserted that aligning the Privacy Rule with other laws or policies in this manner could undermine the ability of the Department to exercise enforcement discretion, causing conflicts or requiring modification to the Privacy Rule when such other laws are modified.
Some of these commenters asserted that API technology was not mature and would continue to evolve. According to commenters, this lack of maturity could harm patient care because API technology was not able to fully integrate into other technologies, delaying the ability of covered entities to respond to individuals' requests for ePHI or diverting resources from clinical initiatives. Several commenters expressed opposition to this proposal because they believed that it would require physicians to implement API technology. These commenters asserted that such a requirement would increase costs and burdens for health care providers, especially for small providers, for various reasons, including the complexity of integrating API technology with legacy systems.
Several commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that the proposed modification would increase the burden on covered health care providers.
Other commenters recommended that the Department modify the proposal to clarify that a covered entity would not have to provide access to ePHI in the form or format requested if an exception to information blocking applies.
Response:
The Department believes that providing individuals with easy and prompt access to their PHI empowers them to make informed decisions about their health care, and that supporting the adoption of new technologies that enable such access is essential. The Privacy Rule generally is technology neutral; accordingly, we do not specifically require covered entities to adopt APIs or other technology that enables access through personal health apps. Additionally, we recognize that not all covered entities have implemented technology, such as secure, standards-based APIs that are consistent with ONC's certification criteria and with their Security Rule obligations, to enable access to requested PHI through personal health apps. However, where a covered entity has chosen, or is required by other Federal or state law, to implement such technology or participate in TEFCA or the CMS Aligned Networks to enable access to requested PHI,
[
496
]
we will deem that PHI to be readily producible in that form and format for purposes of the right of access. We recognize that even where covered entities have implemented such technology or elected to participate in networks that enable the electronic exchange of PHI, not all PHI will be readily producible in the requested electronic form and format. For example, today, not all images can be exchanged electronically. Where an individual requests a copy of PHI that includes such images to be sent to their personal health app, the Department would not deem such images to be readily producible through the personal health app. Instead, the covered entity would be required to produce the PHI that is readily producible in that form and format through a personal health app and to provide the individual with the balance of the PHI in a mutually agreed upon form and format.
The provision deeming ePHI to be readily producible in a form and format where other Federal or state law requires that ePHI be available in the particular form and format only implicates covered entities that are subject to such other laws (
e.g.,
the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule).
[
497
]
This provision does not require modifications to other Federal or state laws, nor does it affect the ability of the Secretary to exercise enforcement discretion. Where an exception to or exclusion from a Federal or state law applies to a covered entity, the covered entity would not be obligated under such law to provide access using a particular form or format that otherwise would be required by the law. However, if that form or format is readily producible for the covered entity, the covered entity is still required to provide ePHI in that form or format if requested by the individual under the Privacy Rule.
We clarify that requiring all personal health apps to complete a registration process before the covered entity transmits ePHI to the individual and/or their personal representative through such apps, would not constitute a denial of access in the form and format requested, provided that the registration process does not exclude or prevent a personal health app that is capable of securely connecting to the secure, standards-based API from so connecting.
[
498
]
Additionally, as discussed above, negotiations about the form and format of an individual's request do not extend the amount of time that covered entities have to respond to requests for access. Accordingly, a covered entity's decision to require personal health apps to register through the process described above cannot be used as a basis to exceed the timeliness requirements for requests made pursuant to the right of access. This holds true regardless of whether the request was to provide the individual with their PHI through a personal health app or to transmit it to a person designated by the individual pursuant to the right of access to direct.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concern about potential risks to the privacy and security of identifiable health information in personal health apps. A few commenters urged the Department either to work with private sector entities to develop a privacy and security trust framework or to warn individuals that APIs and health apps currently lack sufficient regulatory and technology-based privacy and security guardrails. One commenter asserted that the proposal would facilitate the development of a national privacy framework that would ensure that health care data obtained by third-party apps is held to high privacy and security standards. One commenter asserted that the Department should limit the ability of personal health apps to be used by others for financial gain. Another commenter recommended that developers of personal health apps be required to provide individuals with transparency about their data collection and use policies.
Response:
As health IT proliferates and matures, the Department must take steps, where possible within its statutory authority, to require that regulated entities implement corresponding privacy and security measures.
[
499
]
However, as we have
(
printed page 74896)
explained elsewhere in this final rule, a personal health app or its developer, by definition, is not acting on behalf of or at the direction of a regulated entity, and therefore would not be subject to the privacy and security obligations of the HIPAA Rules. At the same time, a covered entity must provide an individual with access to their PHI in the form and format requested by the individual, if it is readily producible in such form and format.
[
500
]
As discussed above, we are adopting the proposal to clarify that a requested form and format would be deemed readily producible for purposes of compliance with the Privacy Rule if other Federal or state law requires an entity to implement a technology or policy that has the effect of providing an individual with access to their PHI in a particular electronic form and format (
e.g.,
if a Federal law required the provision of access via secure, standards-based API).
Whether a particular mode of transmission or transfer is readily producible is based on the capabilities of the covered entity and the level of security risk that the mode of transmission or transfer may introduce to the PHI on the covered entity's electronic information systems.
[
501
]

6. Addressing the Individual Right of Access to Direct Copies of PHI to a Person Designated by the Individual
a. Issues To Address
Section 13405(e)(1) of the HITECH Act expanded the individual right of access, codified at
45 CFR 164.524
, to include the right of an individual to direct an electronic copy of their PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual, provided that the direction is clear, conspicuous, and specific.
[
511
]
Under the 2013 Omnibus Rule, which implemented certain provisions of the HITECH Act, the individual's (or their personal representative's) request to exercise the right of access to direct must be in writing, signed by the individual, and clearly identify the designated person and where to send the copy of the PHI.
[
512
]
The 2013 Omnibus Rule also expanded the right of access to direct to encompass all PHI in a designated record set, regardless of whether the PHI is in an electronic health record.
[
513
]
The court in
Ciox
held that the Department had exceeded its authority under the HITECH Act and vacated the Department's expansion of the right beyond electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record. Thus, the Department is revising the Privacy Rule to ensure that section 13405(e) of the HITECH Act is implemented consistent with the court's interpretation of the statute in
Ciox.
b. Proposed Rule
The Department proposed to create a separate set of provisions, within the Privacy Rule section on the right of access, to address the individual's right of access to direct a covered health care provider to transmit an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual. We proposed to require a covered health care provider to respond to an individual's request to exercise this right when the request is clear, conspicuous, and specific and to permit the request to be made orally or in writing (including electronically). Additionally, the Department proposed that only covered health care providers would be responsible for fulfilling an individual's request under the right of access to direct because the Department did not believe that other covered entities would have an electronic health record as we proposed to define it.
The Department also proposed to extend the right of access to direct to require a covered health care provider or health plan (the “Requestor-Recipient”), at an individual's direction, to submit an individual's access request for their ePHI to another covered health care provider (the “Discloser”), requesting that the Discloser transmit ePHI maintained by or on behalf of the Discloser in its electronic health record to the Requestor-Recipient. We proposed that this requirement would apply when an individual was an existing or prospective new patient or a current member (or dependent) of the Requestor-Recipient, and would be limited to directing electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record back to the Requestor-Recipient.
c. Overview of Comments
Many commenters expressed opposition to the Department's proposal to limit the right of individuals to direct a copy of PHI to a designated person to only electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record because they believed that it would eliminate individuals' right of access to direct non-electronic copies of PHI and PHI that is not in an electronic health record. Some commenters expressed concerns that the right of access to direct had been misused by other persons and that individuals sometimes were unaware of what PHI was being disclosed under this right, to whom, and for what purpose. Several commenters expressed support for limiting an individual's right of access to direct as proposed because they believed that it would ease compliance.
d. Final Rule
We are finalizing many of our proposals for
45 CFR 164.524(d)
, with modification, as described below. Consistent with the HITECH Act, the final rule adopts, with modification, the proposal to require a covered entity to transmit an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to the person designated by the individual if directed to do so by an individual. While we do not believe that the definition of an electronic health record is relevant to all covered entities, we recognize that there are some circumstances where a covered entity other than a covered health care provider may have an electronic health record (
e.g.,
where a health plan is integrated with a health care provider and maintains PHI in the same electronic information systems as the health care provider). In such circumstances, both the health plan and the health care provider would be required to respond to requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct. Accordingly, the regulatory text reflects that the right of access to direct may apply to all covered entities that are subject to the right of access.
[
514
]
As required by the HITECH Act, consistent with the court's decision in
Ciox,
the scope of this right is limited to requests for electronic copies and to PHI in an electronic health record. Thus, requests for a non-electronic copy of PHI or for PHI that is not in an electronic health record do not meet the conditions for the right of access to direct. Instead, in such circumstances, in order for the covered entity to transmit the requested PHI to another person, an individual would need to provide a covered entity with a valid authorization to disclose the requested PHI to that other person, absent an applicable Privacy Rule permission.
Section 13405(e) of the HITECH Act places the right of access to direct within
45 CFR 164.524
, which contains the standard for the right of access. Thus, the final rule adopts a revised version of the proposed standard for the right of access to direct—also placing it within the section of the Privacy Rule that addresses the right of access—that more closely mirrors the standard for the individual right of access at
45 CFR 164.524(a)
and incorporates the limitations of the right of access into the right of access to direct. Through these revisions, we clarify that, consistent with the HITECH Act and the
Ciox
decision, the right of access to direct is limited to PHI about the individual that is both in an electronic health record and in a designated record set. PHI that is in an electronic health record but not in a designated record set (
e.g.,
patient safety work product), or that is in a designated record set but not in an electronic health record (
e.g.,
paper records), is not subject to the right of access to direct. We also clarify that this right, like the broader right of access, excepts both psychotherapy notes and information compiled in reasonable anticipation of, or for use in, a civil, criminal, or administrative action or proceeding, from the PHI in an electronic health record that an individual is entitled to direct to a person designated by the individual. Similarly, we clarify that, for purposes of the right of access to direct, an “electronic copy” has the same meaning as we interpret the term under the broader right of access.
[
515
]
The
(
printed page 74898)
requirements of the individual right of access with respect to denials and timing also are mirrored in the right of access to direct. Thus, requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct can be denied for the same reasons as a request made pursuant to the individual right of access and must be addressed within the same amount of time, as discussed below.
Additionally, we eliminate references to a “third party” and replace them with the statutory language of “a person designated by the individual.” Not only does this language mirror the HITECH Act more closely, but it also emphasizes the purpose of the right—to strengthen individuals' control over disclosures of their PHI.
We are not finalizing the proposal to require a covered entity to respond to individuals' requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct when such requests are made orally. We are persuaded by public comments that implementing the proposed requirement for covered health care providers to respond to oral requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct would be difficult, would increase burdens on covered entities because of the work associated with verifying the accuracy of the request, and would increase the likelihood of miscommunication and erroneous responses to requests, leading to potential breaches of unsecured PHI (
e.g.,
misdirected records). Instead, we are finalizing the implementation specification at
45 CFR 164.524(d)(5)
to more closely mirror the implementation specification at
45 CFR 164.524(b)
by including both: (1) instructions for how a covered entity is to identify requests made pursuant to the relevant right; and (2) the amount of time that a covered entity has to act on such requests.
Consistent with the HITECH Act, the final rule adopts a new
45 CFR 164.524(d)(5)(i)
that instructs a covered entity to permit an individual to direct an electronic copy of PHI about the individual in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual where the request is clear, conspicuous, and specific. This section also clarifies that a covered entity is permitted to require an individual to make such a request in writing, provided that it informs the individual of such a requirement. For purposes of the right of access to direct, consistent with new
45 CFR 164.524(b)(1)(ii)
, “in writing” means that the request itself serves as documentation of the individual's exercise of the right of access to direct, including when the request is submitted electronically or on paper.
Individuals who request that a covered entity provide them or a person that the individual designates with access to their PHI are not required to execute a HIPAA authorization. As discussed above, a request to direct an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual is sufficient when it is clear, conspicuous, and specific. Because a HIPAA authorization requires more information than is necessary or that may be relevant for individuals to exercise their access rights, including their right of access to direct,
[
516
]
requiring the execution of a HIPAA authorization may create impermissible obstacles to the exercise of this right. Where it is unclear, based on the form of a request, whether the request is an effort by the individual to exercise their right of access to direct or merely the individual's authorization to disclose PHI as requested by a third party, covered entities may seek clarification from the individual about whether the request was a direction from the individual or a request from the third party. The instructions about the amount of time a covered entity has to respond to a request made pursuant to the right of access to direct are now in
45 CFR 164.524(d)(5)(ii)
, mirroring the instructions for timeliness under the individual right of access at
45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)
. A covered entity's decision to require individuals to execute HIPAA authorizations for all requests for disclosures does not extend the amount of time that it has to respond to a request made pursuant to the right of access, including the right of access to direct. This is true even if the covered entity needs to contact an individual who requests an electronic copy of their PHI in an electronic health record to clarify whether the individual is intending to exercise their right of access to direct.
To eliminate redundancy, we are finalizing the proposal to consolidate the instructions to covered entities about how to address individual requests for a review of a denial of access at
45 CFR 164.524(e)(4)
and clarifying that similar instructions apply where an individual requests a review of a denial of the right of access to direct for a reviewable ground. Accordingly, where a covered entity denies, on a reviewable ground, a request made pursuant to the individual right of access, including the right of access to direct, the covered entity must designate a licensed health care professional who was not directly involved in the denial to review the decision to deny access and promptly refer the request to such designated reviewing official. The designated reviewing official must determine, within a reasonable period of time, whether to deny the access request based on the standards for a reviewable ground for a denial. The covered entity must promptly provide written notice of the determination of the designated reviewing official and take any other required actions to carry it out.
The Department is not finalizing the proposal to require covered health care providers and health plans, at an individual's direction, to submit an individual's request made pursuant to the right of access to direct to another covered health care provider (the “Discloser”), requesting that the Discloser transmit ePHI maintained by or on behalf of the Discloser in its electronic health record to the Requestor-Recipient. We are persuaded by public comments that the proposal would increase the burden on covered entities and be difficult to implement. The disclosures contemplated by the proposal already are permitted under the Privacy Rule (
e.g.,
for treatment purposes). Thus, the Department's decision not to finalize this proposal does not preclude covered entities from assisting an individual by submitting an access request for PHI to another covered entity on the individual's behalf, nor would it preclude the other covered entity from sending the requested PHI to the covered entity who assisted the individual in making the request.
e. Response to Public Comments
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that the proposal to limit the right of access to direct to electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record would decrease the utility of this right by decreasing the amount of PHI available to a person designated by the individual. According to commenters, this would limit the ability of individuals to meaningfully participate in their health care and to determine who has access to their information. A few commenters asserted that limiting the right of access to direct to PHI in an electronic health record would not address requests to direct to a designated person non-electronic PHI or PHI in health IT systems other than an EHR, thus requiring a covered health care provider to obtain an authorization before complying with such requests. A few commenters asserted that it would be difficult to distinguish between requests from an individual to direct an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record to a designated person from requests an individual makes that require an authorization.
(
printed page 74899)
Response:
The Department is finalizing its proposal with minimal modifications, as described above. The court in
Ciox
held that the HITECH Act created a limited right of access to direct and the Department could not expand that right. Therefore, the final rule limits the right of access to direct PHI to an electronic copy of PHI in an electronic health record. The definition of electronic health record further limits the application of the right of access to direct because the HITECH Act specifies that an electronic health record is an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff. As discussed above, we interpret such clinicians to include health care providers that have direct or indirect treatment relationships with individuals. Also as discussed above, we do not believe that the definition of an electronic health record applies to all covered entities, but we recognize that it may apply to more than covered health care providers. Thus, we are not limiting the right of access to direct to only covered health care providers. Furthermore, as explained above, we do not interpret PHI in an electronic health record as limited to PHI in a particular software or application. Rather, we interpret it to include all PHI that is in an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff.
As a process matter, to ensure compliance with the Privacy Rule, covered entities may wish to assume that a clear, conspicuous, and specific request made by an individual to transmit an electronic copy of PHI about the individual in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual is a request made pursuant to the right of access to direct. Covered entities are encouraged to contact the individual making the request if there are any questions or concerns about the request, including about the authority of the person designated by the individual to have access to the PHI.
A request for PHI that is not in an electronic health record, or a request for a copy in a non-electronic format, would not meet the conditions of the right of access to direct. Thus, such requests should be treated as requests made pursuant to an authorization, provided that the request meets the requirements for a valid authorization at
45 CFR 164.508
. Where such requests do not meet the requirements for a valid authorization, the Department encourages covered entities to consider whether another provision of the Privacy Rule would permit the disclosure, and if not, to contact individuals to explain the limitations of the right of access to direct and obtain the information that is needed for the request to constitute a valid authorization.
Comment:
Many commenters asserted that disclosures to personal health apps should be treated as requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct, rather than either of the following: (1) a request made pursuant to the individual right of access, or (2) a request for disclosure pursuant to valid authorization.
Response:
As explained above, we interpret a personal health app to be equivalent to the individual and a request from an individual to receive their PHI in a personal health app to constitute an individual request to obtain a copy of their PHI in a particular electronic form and format. In other words, when employed by the individual (or their personal representative), a personal health app, as defined in this final rule, is a technology or tool used by the individual (or their personal representative); the personal health app is not a person designated by the individual to receive PHI. Thus, when an individual requests that a covered entity transmit the individual's PHI to a personal health app, we interpret the request as being made pursuant to the individual right of access at
45 CFR 164.524(a)
, rather than a request made pursuant to the right of access to direct at
45 CFR 164.524(d)
. Where an individual requests that a covered entity transmit a copy of their PHI in an electronic health record to an app that is not offered by or on behalf of another regulated entity, and does not meet the definition of personal health app (because, for example, the information in the app is not managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual), we would interpret such request as being made pursuant to the right of access to direct (where the request meets the applicable requirements). As discussed above, the processes and technology that a covered entity implements will enable it to differentiate between the different types of apps that transmit requests for PHI through the covered entity's API.
Comment:
Some commenters asserted that the right of access to direct is abused by third parties for commercial purposes. According to some commenters, in some cases, fraudulent requests are submitted to covered entities purportedly on behalf of individuals, creating additional burden for regulated entities because they must verify that the request was initiated by the individual. Some commenters recommended that the Department limit the scope of the proposal, or issue guidance to clarify its application, to specific categories of persons, purposes, or PHI; or limit the liability of health care providers when a request is for disclosure in certain circumstances. A few commenters asserted that Congress intended for section 13405(e) of the HITECH Act to facilitate the disclosure of PHI only for health care purposes and urged the Department to limit the right of access to direct to apply only where the person designated by the individual is a health care provider, social service organization with whom PHI may be shared for care coordination, or caregiver. One commenter expressed concern about their ability to comply with the proposal while also complying with other laws that restrict the disclosure of certain PHI (
e.g.,
state laws that limit the disclosure of records about an individual's mental health).
Many commenters expressed concern that the proposal would result in the disclosure of sensitive information to entities that are not regulated under the HIPAA Rules. Some commenters expressed concern that such disclosures would pose risks to the privacy and security of PHI. One commenter asserted that the proposal would impose an administrative burden and raise liability concerns for health care providers if the PHI is disclosed to a designated person and then used or disclosed inappropriately.
Several commenters requested that the Department either modify the Privacy Rule or issue guidance to clarify covered entities' obligations under the proposed right of access to direct in an environment where PHI is increasingly transmitted electronically and to a wider pool of recipients.
Response:
As discussed above, Congress has enacted several laws that direct the Department to empower individuals by ensuring that they have access to and the ability to share their PHI. For example, as enacted by Congress, section 13405(e) of the HITECH Act provides individuals, as part of the right of access, the right of access to direct a covered entity to transmit an electronic copy of their PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual. The statute placed no limitations on the ability of the individual to choose the person to whom they direct electronic copies of their PHI in an electronic health record. In this final rule, the Department seeks to implement this right, as directed by Congress. Thus,
(
printed page 74900)
consistent with the HITECH Act and the Privacy Rule's longstanding right of access provisions, the purpose of an individual's request for access and/or the designated person to whom they choose to direct an electronic copy are not relevant factors when a covered entity responds to an individual's access request, including a request under the right of access to direct. Accordingly, a covered entity cannot deny an individual's request under the right of access to direct based solely on the covered entity's opinion of the person that the individual designates or the purpose(s) for which the individual requests the disclosure. For example, a covered entity may not deny an individual's request made pursuant to the right of access to direct merely because the covered entity does not agree with the individual's decision to direct a copy of their PHI to an attorney or other person. Prior to disclosing PHI, a covered entity is required to verify the identity of a person requesting PHI and the authority of that person to have access to PHI if the identity or authority of such person is not known to the covered entity. Elsewhere in this final rule, we finalize a prohibition against imposing an unreasonable identity verification requirement on an individual attempting to exercise the right of access and provide examples of both reasonable and unreasonable measures of identity verification. For example, it would be reasonable for a covered entity that receives a request made pursuant to the right of access to direct to contact the individual to verify that they intended to direct the copy to the particular person.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that all requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct should be in writing. Many commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to allow oral requests, with several commenters asserting that the proposal would be inconsistent with the HITECH Act because oral requests are not “conspicuous.” Some commenters expressed concern that the proposal could lead to increased risks to individual privacy, as well as fraud and abuse. Some commenters asserted that the proposal would pose an administrative burden or implementation challenge and provided examples, such as developing new processes for accepting, documenting, and tracking such requests, changing workflows, and training staff on the new processes.
Some commenters expressed concern about their ability to verify the identity of an individual making an oral request. A few commenters recommended that the Department impose limitations on oral requests, such as allowing individuals to make oral requests only in person except where making the request in person would present an undue burden for the individual or in urgent situations, provided that the request is later reduced to writing. A few commenters recommended that health care providers be permitted to verify the identity of individuals making oral requests. A few commenters stated that covered entities should have the flexibility to determine whether to accept oral requests for access.
Some commenters requested that the Department create a safe harbor to shield covered entities from liability for erroneous disclosures that may result from responding to an oral request for access. One commenter asserted that the proposal could create a conflict with state laws that require providers of behavioral health care to adopt additional due diligence practices, such as obtaining written consent from the individual, before disclosing PHI.
Several commenters requested that the Department provide guidance on how to operationalize this proposal and examples of what would constitute “clear, conspicuous, and specific” requests.
Response:
As explained above, based on public comments, we are not finalizing the proposal to require covered entities to accept oral requests made pursuant to the right of access to direct. Instead, consistent with the HITECH Act, we require that the request be clear, conspicuous, and specific. We also are adopting language that permits a covered entity to require that the request be in writing, provided that it informs individuals of such requirement, consistent with the modification that we are making at
45 CFR 164.524(b)(1)(ii)
, which includes the clarification of what constitutes a request in writing.
[
517
]
For example, we would consider a request to be clear, conspicuous, and specific if the individual sends an email to a covered health care provider requesting that the provider send to the individual's family member an email containing a report interpreting diagnostic images where the report is maintained in the provider's electronic health record, provided that the request included the family member's name and email address.
[
518
]
We would not consider this request to be clear, conspicuous, and specific if it did not contain the family member's name or email address. As another example, we would consider a request to be clear, conspicuous, and specific where the individual sends a message through a personal health app to a covered health care provider requesting that the provider send the individual's PHI in the provider's electronic health record to a file-sharing application used by the individual's attorney, provided that the message included the attorney's name and specific information about how and where to send the PHI. We would not consider this request to be clear, conspicuous, and specific if it did not include information about how to send the individual's PHI to the attorney's file-sharing application.
Where a verbal request meets the requirements of clear, conspicuous, and specific, a covered entity is permitted, but not required, to accept the request. For example, where an individual, in a discussion, tells the receptionist that they would like to have their PHI in an electronic health record emailed to a particular family member and the individual dictates the family member's email address or provides the email address in writing to the receptionist, such request could be considered clear, conspicuous, and specific. For such verbal requests, the covered entity would be responsible for adopting reasonable safeguards to document the request in writing to protect the information that is disclosed. For example, a reasonable safeguard would not need to require the covered entity to confirm that the individual provided the correct email address of the designated person, but it would require reasonable procedures to ensure that the covered entity correctly typed the email address.
[
519
]
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for the proposal to require covered entities and health plans, at the individual's direction, to submit an individual's access request to another covered entity. A few commenters expressed support for this proposal because it would facilitate care coordination and access. One commenter requested guidance about how this access pathway would work in relation to the pathway for individuals to obtain access through a personal health app.
Many commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to require covered health care providers and plans, at an individual's direction, to submit to another covered entity the individual's request to transmit an electronic copy of
(
printed page 74901)
PHI in an electronic health record to a person designated by the individual. Some commenters asserted that the proposal would be burdensome or impracticable for health care, create additional paperwork, obligate health care providers to gather PHI that they do not need, potentially cause confusion, and unnecessarily delay responses to requests. We are not finalizing the proposal to require covered health care providers and health plans (“Requestor-Recipient”), at an individual's direction, to submit to another covered entity (“Discloser”) the individual's request to transmit an electronic copy of the individual's PHI in an electronic health record. We are persuaded by the comments asserting that such a requirement likely would create unreasonable administrative burdens without meaningfully contributing to the Department's efforts to facilitate information sharing among entities in the health care system.

]
However, this does not preclude covered entities from assisting an individual by submitting an access request to another covered entity on the individual's behalf.
7. Adjusting Permitted Fees for Access to PHI and ePHI
a. Current Rule
The Privacy Rule allows covered entities to charge a reasonable, cost-based fee to fulfill access requests from individuals for copies of their PHI. Section 164.524(c)(4) limits the allowable fees to the costs of: (1) labor for copying (whether the PHI is in paper or electronic form); (2) supplies for creating the paper copy or electronic media if requested; (3) postage; and (4) preparing any agreed-upon summary or explanation of the requested PHI.
The labor portion of allowable fees for copying includes only labor for creating and delivering the electronic or paper copy in the form and format requested or agreed upon by the individual, after the PHI that is responsive to the request has been identified, retrieved or collected, and compiled and/or collated, and is ready to be copied.
[
521
]
Examples of allowable labor costs include, but are not limited to, costs associated with the following:
Photocopying PHI that is on paper.
Scanning PHI that is on paper into an electronic format.
Converting electronic information in one format to a format requested by or agreed to by the individual.
Transferring (
e.g.,
uploading, downloading, attaching, burning) ePHI from a covered entity's electronic information system to a web-based portal (where the PHI is not already maintained in or accessible through the portal), portable media, email, app, personal health record, or other manner of delivery of the PHI.
Creating and executing a mailing or email with the responsive PHI.
Importantly, we recognized in the 2013 Omnibus Rule that covered entities would continue to improve their technological capabilities over time and that the costs of producing an electronic copy would be negligible.
[
522
]
The labor portion of allowable fees for copying does not include costs associated with reviewing the request for access; searching for and retrieving the PHI, which includes locating and reviewing the PHI in the medical or other record; or segregating or otherwise preparing the PHI that is responsive to the request for a copy. Additionally, a covered entity may not pass on the administrative or other costs associated with outsourcing the function of responding to individual requests for access (
e.g.,
the cost of using a business associate to act on individual requests for access).
[
523
]
b. Proposed Rule
The Department proposed to modify the provisions addressing access fees to establish a fee structure with two elements based on the type of access request.
[
524
]
The first proposed element described categories of access for which covered entities would not be permitted to charge a fee, and the second described the allowable costs that could be included when an access fee is permitted.
[
525
]
(
printed page 74902)
The Privacy Rule does not permit fees to be charged for inspection of PHI by the individual who is the subject of the PHI. The Department believes that a covered entity does not incur labor costs for copying and is unlikely to incur more than
de minimis
costs for supplies when providing the individual with the opportunity to inspect PHI in person. The same is true when an individual who, while inspecting their PHI, takes notes, or uses other personal devices or resources to memorialize, record, or otherwise capture the PHI. Likewise, the Department believes that there are circumstances in which a covered entity can provide an individual with access to PHI using technology without the involvement of their workforce members. We refer to such technologies as “internet-based methods.” When an individual uses an internet-based method to obtain access to their PHI, the covered entity likely incurs no allowable labor costs or expenses. For example, where an individual requests or agrees to access their PHI available through the View, Download, and Transmit (VDT) functionality of the CEHRT, we believe there are no labor costs and no costs for supplies to enable such access.
[
526
]
Thus, for example, a covered health care provider cannot charge an individual a fee when it fulfills an individual's HIPAA access request using the VDT functionality of the provider's CEHRT. Accordingly, at
45 CFR 164.524(c)(4)(ii)
, the Department proposed to specify two situations that would always be free of charge: (1) when an individual inspects PHI in person; and (2) when an individual uses an internet-based method to view or obtain a copy of their ePHI, including access through the covered entity's certified health IT or by a personal health app connecting to a secure, standards-based API, consistent with applicable Federal or state law.
[
527
]
The Department proposed that access requests by an individual for an electronic or non-electronic copy of PHI through a non-internet-based method would remain subject to the individual access fee limitations of a reasonable, cost-based fee.
[
528
]
Accordingly, we proposed to modify
45 CFR 164.524(c)(4)(i)
to permit a covered entity to charge a reasonable, cost-based fee, provided that the fee includes only the following costs:
