Comment:
Some commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that it would lead to breaches of PHI. For example, commenters posed examples of malicious actors creating technology that is able to impersonate individuals or covered entities being unable to verify the identity of a minor's guardian. One commenter expressed concern that relaxing identity verification measures could lead to increased identity theft, fraud, or misidentification, while another commenter recommended that the Department clarify that a covered entity is permitted to reject a request if it is unable to verify a person's identity.
Response:
The final rule does not require covered entities to relax identity verification requirements. Nothing in this final rule changes a covered entity's obligation under
45 CFR 164.514(h)
to take reasonable steps to verify the identity and authority of a person requesting PHI before disclosing the PHI to help ensure that unauthorized persons do not obtain an individual's PHI.
[
594
]
Rather, the final rule prohibits covered entities from imposing measures that impede access requests or imposing unreasonable identity verification measures. Covered entities remain responsible for assessing security risks and are not required to adopt verification methods that would increase the likelihood of identity theft, fraud, or misidentification, nor are they required to fulfill an access request when they cannot verify the identity of the person making the request.
C. Amending the Definition of Health Care Operations To Clarify the Scope of Care Coordination and Case Management
1. Current Rule
The Privacy Rule expressly permits covered entities to use and disclose PHI, without an individual's valid authorization, for treatment and certain health care operations, among other important purposes.
[
595
]
The definitions of both “treatment” and “health care operations” include some care coordination and case management activities.
[
596
]
As explained in preamble to the 2000 Privacy Rule, certain activities may be considered either health care operations or treatment, depending on whether the activities are population-wide or individual-specific activities, and if individual-specific, whether the communication with an individual occurs on behalf of a health care provider or a health plan.
[
597
]
For example, a telephone call by a nurse in a doctor's office to an individual to discuss follow-up care would be a treatment activity; however, the same activity performed by a nurse working for a health plan would be a health care operation.
[
598
]
2. Proposed Rule
Despite the guidance in the 2000 Privacy Rule, we have received anecdotal reports that some covered entities have interpreted the definition of “health care operations” to include only population-based care coordination and case management, which would have the effect of excluding individual-level care coordination and case management by health plans.
[
599
]
In addition, some covered entities have expressed uncertainty about the ability of health care providers to disclose PHI to health plans for individual-level care coordination and case management without an individual's authorization.
Thus, the Department proposed to amend the definition of “health care operations” at
45 CFR 164.501
to clarify that it encompasses all care coordination and case management by health plans, whether individual-level or population-based. The Department explained that, as drafted, the placement of commas separating the list of activities following the term “population-based activities” permitted the interpretation that the term “population-based activities” modifies (
i.e.,
places a condition on) all of the activities listed between the semi-colons, including case management and care coordination, although the Department has not applied that interpretation to the definition of health care operations. Accordingly, the Department proposed to change the commas into semi-colons in paragraph (1) of the definition of “health care operations” at
45 CFR 164.501
to clearly convey that the activities listed are each separate types of health care operations.
3. Overview of Comments
Many individuals and organizations commented on the proposal to clarify the definition of “heath care operations.” Most commenters expressed general support for the proposal because they believed that the changes would clarify the scope of health care operations. They also believed that the proposed modifications would facilitate the sharing of PHI to support care coordination and case management.
Some commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that it would permit the use and disclosure of PHI for individual-
(
printed page 74916)
level care coordination and case management without requiring an individual's authorization, thereby excluding individuals from the process of care coordination.
4. Final Rule
This final rule adopts the proposed clarification of the definition of “health care operations” to facilitate the intended range of care coordination and case management activities. The Department generally has interpreted the existing definition to permit health care providers to disclose PHI to health plans for individual-level care coordination and case management without an individual's authorization. However, covered entities have expressed uncertainty about the extent to which the definition applies to activities such as case management and care coordination by health plans or as part of value-based health care models. Therefore, it is necessary for the Department to expressly confirm that health care operations encompasses all care coordination and case management activities by health plans and covered health care providers, whether individual-level or population-based. Changing the punctuation in the definition accomplishes this goal, thereby improving the likelihood that covered entities will use and disclose PHI accordingly.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Many commenters expressed support for this proposal because it would facilitate both individual-level and population-based care coordination and case management. Several commenters asserted that the proposal would provide certainty to covered entities that are hesitant to disclose PHI for care coordination and case management without an individual's authorization. One commenter stated that clarifying the definition would decrease the burden for workforce members who previously requested individual authorizations for these disclosures. Another commenter suggested that the Department issue guidance to address this concern, rather than notice and comment rulemaking.
Several commenters expressed support for the Department's goal but recommended further revisions. For example, one commenter recommended that the Department add the phrase “individual-level or population-based” in front of the words “case management and care coordination” to provide additional clarity.
Response:
The Department believes that the clarification that we are finalizing here addresses any uncertainty regarding whether PHI may be used or disclosed for individual-level care coordination and case management without an individual's authorization and reduces the burden of obtaining an individual's authorization when not required. This revision to the definition sufficiently clarifies the intended range of care coordination and case management, so it is not necessary to modify it further.
Comment:
A few commenters who expressed support for the clarification to the definition of health care operations recommended that the Department define or provide greater clarity regarding the activities included in “care coordination” and “case management” to allow for more consistent interpretation of the terms. Some commenters requested that the Department explicitly include coordination of social services such as supportive housing for an individual with a disability, in the definition of health care operations.
Response:
We decline to define “care coordination” and “case management” in this final rule. Both terms refer broadly to a set of activities aimed at promoting cooperation among people involved in caring for individuals, including family members, caregivers, and community-based organizations. Rather than proposing limiting definitions, the Department has, instead, provided an extensive discussion and a non-exhaustive list of examples of the types of activities it considers to be care coordination and case management activities.
[
600
]
The Department also declines to include coordination of social services in the definition of “health care operations” in this final rule. Instead, to address questions about whether the Privacy Rule permits disclosures to social services organizations for care coordination and case management, the Department is adding a provision at
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
to expressly permit disclosures of PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations, to certain types of organizations that provide health and human services.
[
601
]
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern that the proposal would increase the ability of covered entities to use and disclose PHI for care coordination and case management without individual authorization. A few commenters expressed opposition to the Department's proposed clarification because they believed that it would exclude individuals from the process of care coordination. One commenter asserted that the proposal would expand access to individual-level PHI without accompanying safeguards and controls to protect an individual's privacy.
Response:
This clarification does not expand the authority of covered entities to use or disclose PHI without a valid authorization. As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, the Department has become aware that some covered entities may be interpreting the definition of health care operations in a manner that is inconsistent with the Department's intent. Thus, the Department does not consider this clarification to be a substantive modification because the final rule does not alter our interpretation of the definition. Rather, the modification to the definition merely clarifies the ability of covered entities to use and disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management. For example, health plans may use and disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management, and covered entities may disclose PHI to health plans for these purposes.
The Department appreciates commenters' concerns about protecting individuals' privacy and emphasizes that covered entities must apply the requirements of the minimum necessary standard for uses and disclosures of PHI for the purpose of health care operations. Additionally, individuals have a right to request restrictions on uses or disclosures for TPO under
45 CFR 164.522(a)
.
[
602
]
(
printed page 74917)
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concern that the proposal could have unintended adverse consequences if implemented in conjunction with the proposal to modify the minimum necessary standard. For example, one commenter asserted that removing the minimum necessary standard for health care operations for care coordination and case management could allow health plans to gain unfettered access to a physician's EHR and empower health plans to make decisions about an individual's health care.
Response:
The Department is not finalizing the proposed exception to the minimum necessary standard for health care operations uses and disclosures of PHI related to individual-level care coordination and case management, as discussed below. Retaining the current minimum necessary standard addresses concerns that the modification to the definition of health care operations weakens individuals' privacy protections. Therefore, covered entities who engage in care coordination and case management as health care operations must limit the PHI that they use or disclose to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the use or disclosure.
D. Creating an Exception to the Minimum Necessary Standard for Disclosures for Individual-Level Care Coordination and Case Management
1. Current Rule
Section 164.502(b) requires covered entities to use, disclose, and request only the minimum amount of PHI necessary for the purposes of TPO, except for disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment, where the minimum necessary requirement does not apply.
The Department has long considered care coordination to be part of an individual's treatment and interpreted the Privacy Rule to permit health care providers to disclose PHI in support of an individual's health care to service providers who may not be covered entities and who may not be health care providers.
[
603
]
Health plans also coordinate an individual's care when managing and paying for health plan benefits; however, these activities are considered health care operations activities (and therefore subject to the minimum necessary standard) because most health plans do not provide treatment.
[
604
]
2. Proposed Rule
The Department proposed to create an exception to the minimum necessary standard for disclosures to, or requests by, a health plan or covered health care provider for care coordination and case management. The proposed exception would apply only to individual-level activities for care coordination and case management activities. In conjunction with the proposal to clarify that the definition of health care operations includes individual-level care coordination and case management described above, this proposed exception would permit health plans to request, use, and disclose PHI without limitation for such health care operations, including disclosures to persons who are not covered entities and who are not health care providers. For covered health care providers, the proposal would specify that the existing exception for disclosures to, or requests by, a health care provider for treatment includes case management and care coordination. The proposed exception would relieve covered entities from the requirement to make determinations about the minimum information necessary when the request is from, or the disclosure is made to, a covered health care provider or health plan to support individual-level care coordination and case management activities.
3. Overview of Comments
Commenters were evenly split in their views of the proposal. Commenters who expressed support for this proposal asserted that it would facilitate care coordination, improve outcomes, and provide clarification, while commenters who expressed opposition did so because they believed that it would decrease an individual's privacy.
4. Final Rule
This final rule does not adopt the proposed exception to the minimum necessary standard for individual-level care coordination and case management. The Department is persuaded by public comments that asserted that providing an exception to the minimum necessary standard for certain health care operations would erode individuals' confidence in the privacy of their PHI and their willingness to fully engage with the health care system. Additionally, we believe that other modifications that we are making in this final rule, such as modification to the definition of health care operations, will facilitate the ability of health plans to perform beneficial individual-level care coordination and case management activities.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Many commenters who expressed support for this proposal asserted that it would facilitate care coordination, improve outcomes, and clarify that disclosures of all PHI, rather than the minimum necessary, is permissible to health care providers and health plans for the purpose of individual-level care coordination and case management. Some commenters provided examples of the types of activities that they believed that this proposal would facilitate. According to one commenter, the proposal would eliminate concerns about determining the purpose of certain requests that could be for either treatment or health care operations. One commenter asserted that this proposal would not alter the practice of covered entities to request the minimum PHI necessary to accomplish their purpose. A few commenters expressed their belief that the proposal would reduce the administrative burden on covered entities. One commenter expressed support for the proposal because they believed that it would reduce impediments to the disclosure of PHI using HIEs. Another commenter asserted that the proposal would enable covered entities to transition from providing care on a fee-for-service basis to providing care based on value.
Response:
The Department agrees with commenters that it is important for the Privacy Rule to permit the disclosure of PHI to facilitate care coordination and improve health care outcomes. However, we have determined that such aims can be achieved by means other than creating a new exception to the minimum necessary standard. Specifically, elsewhere in this rule, we are finalizing
(
printed page 74918)
our proposals to modify the definition of health care operations and to expressly permit the disclosure of PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers,
[
605
]
and other similar entities. We are not convinced that excepting, from the minimum necessary standard, disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management when performed for the purpose of health care operations would provide sufficient benefits to outweigh the interests of individuals in limiting the PHI that is shared with health plans.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because of concerns that it would decrease an individual's privacy. Relatedly, several commenters asserted that the proposal would deter individuals from seeking treatment or erode individuals' trust in their health care providers. Several commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that increasing disclosures of PHI for care coordination or case management could harm individuals in a variety of ways, such as increased disclosures to entities that are not regulated under HIPAA, denials of public benefits, discrimination, and breaches. A few commenters asserted that PHI should not be disclosed for care coordination or case management without an individual's consent. According to a few commenters, obtaining an individual's authorization before disclosing PHI for care coordination or case management does not prevent or delay the provision of health care to an individual.
Several commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because it would permit health plans to have access to more PHI than they currently are able to obtain. Several commenters expressed opposition to the idea that health plans need access to more than the minimum necessary PHI for care coordination and case management. Several commenters asserted that the proposal would lead to an increase in coverage denials by health plans. One commenter expressed opposition to this proposal because they believed that it would lead to an increase in requests from health plans for the disclosure of PHI, leading to an increase in burden on health care providers.
Response:
The Department agrees with the comments expressing concern that allowing health plans to have access to more than the minimum PHI necessary to accomplish their purpose likely would raise concerns for individuals, whether warranted or not, thereby eroding trust in the health care system. We also agree that, where the Privacy Rule permits disclosures of PHI beyond the minimum necessary for a particular purpose, there is the potential for an increase in the risk of unintended adverse consequences (
e.g.,
more PHI exposed in the event of a breach), regardless of who receives the PHI. At the same time, we recognize that health plans need a certain amount of PHI to perform routine functions, such as case management, care coordination, medical review, auditing, and provider credentialing. Therefore, in light of commenters' concerns, the Department believes that existing restrictions on the use and disclosure of PHI (
e.g.,
the prohibition on the use of genetic information for underwriting purposes, limitations on the use and disclosure of psychotherapy notes) strike an appropriate balance of protecting individuals' privacy interests while permitting uses and disclosures of PHI that are needed for health plans' legitimate purposes, including payment and health care operations. Accordingly, we are not finalizing our proposal to provide an exception to the minimum necessary standard for requests by or disclosures to health plans for individual-level activities for care coordination and case management.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concerns about the potential for health plans to use the proposed exception to gain access to large amounts of PHI to create de-identified data sets for sale and potential re-identification. According to these commenters, this would make PHI available for a variety of applications without authorization from individuals. These commenters urged the Department to implement protections to prevent the disclosure of such de-identified datasets and the re-identification of PHI before finalizing this proposal.
Response:
As discussed above, the Department is not finalizing the proposed exception to the minimum necessary standard. With respect to concerns about re-identification of de-identified data, the de-identification standard requires that the information does not identify an individual and there is no reasonable basis to believe that the information can be used to identify an individual.
[
606
]
In other words, PHI is not de-identified under the Privacy Rule if there is a reasonable basis to believe that it can be re-identified.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns about whether health care providers would be able to deny a request for PHI from health plans when the request meets the requirements of the permission for health care operations and the proposed exception to the minimum necessary standard, given the requirements of the information blocking regulations. One commenter recommended that the Department clarify how the information blocking regulations and the HIPAA Rules work in concert to ensure appropriate oversight and enforcement of the information blocking regulations.
Response:
As discussed above, the Department is not finalizing the proposed modification to the minimum necessary standard because we do not believe that it is a necessary or effective mechanism to facilitate the ability of covered entities to support individual-level care coordination and case management. The information blocking regulations exclude from the definition of information blocking reasonable and necessary practices that advance the privacy interests of individuals.
[
607
]
For example, the information blocking regulations accommodate circumstances where the Privacy Rule requires that certain preconditions (
e.g.,
the minimum necessary standard) be met before permitting the use or disclosure of PHI.
[
608
]
For more information about the interaction of the information blocking regulations with the HIPAA Rules and other laws protecting individuals' privacy interests, see the discussion of the Privacy Exception in the Cures Act Final Rule.
[
609
]
E. Clarifying the Scope of Covered Entities' Abilities To Disclose PHI to Certain Third Parties for Individual-Level Care Coordination and Case Management That Constitutes Treatment or Health Care Operations
1. Current Rule
Section 164.506 of the Privacy Rule sets forth the circumstances in which a covered entity is permitted to use and disclose PHI for TPO. Under
45 CFR 164.506(a)
, covered entities are permitted to use or disclose PHI without an individual's authorization for TPO,
(
printed page 74919)
subject to the applicable conditions and other requirements of the Privacy Rule. Section 164.506(b)(1) of the Privacy Rule permits, but does not require, covered entities to obtain an individual's consent to use or disclose PHI for TPO.
[
610
]
The implementation specifications for using and disclosing PHI for TPO are in
45 CFR 164.506(c)
of the Privacy Rule. Under
45 CFR 164.506(c)(1)
, a covered entity may use or disclose PHI for its own TPO. Sections 164.506(c)(2) and (c)(4) permit a covered entity to disclose PHI for the treatment activities of another health care provider and for specified health care operations of another covered entity, respectively, when the applicable conditions are met.
The Privacy Rule's definitions of both treatment and health care operations expressly include care coordination and case management activities.
[
611
]
Consistent with these definitions, the Department previously explained that a covered health care provider may disclose PHI for treatment purposes without an individual's authorization when coordinating or managing an individual's care with third parties that provide services related to the individual's health, including public- or private-sector entities that provide health-related social and community-based services.
[
612
]
For example, a covered health care provider is able to make a disclosure to a provider of HCBS
[
613
]
to treat an individual who is older or has a disability if it is for the coordination or management of that individual's treatment by the health care provider.
[
614
]
As another example, a health care provider may disclose to a senior center or adult day care provider the minimum PHI necessary to help coordinate health-related services for an individual, such as arranging for a home aide or helping the individual with their prescribed at-home or post-discharge treatment protocol. Likewise, the Privacy Rule also would permit the disclosure of PHI to facilitate care coordination and case management as part of a health plan's health care operations, such as when a health plan discloses to a senior wellness center the minimum PHI necessary where the individual is enrolled in the plan's wellness program. For example, if an individual plan member enrolls in a health plan's diabetes management program, the health plan may disclose only the minimum necessary amount of PHI to a senior center that is administering the wellness program for care coordination purposes, such as the member's demographic information and relevant diagnosis. The health plan would not be permitted to disclose PHI beyond the minimum necessary, such as unrelated diagnoses and other nongermane health information.
Section 164.502(b) contains the minimum necessary standard, which governs how much PHI a covered entity is permitted to disclose based on the purpose of the request, and the exceptions to that standard.
[
615
]
Disclosures to, or requests by, a health care provider for treatment purposes are excepted from the minimum necessary standard.
[
616
]
If a disclosure for treatment is made to an entity that is not a health care provider, this exception to the minimum necessary standard does not apply, and the covered entity must limit the disclosure to the minimum PHI necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the use or disclosure. Disclosures for health care operations are likewise subject to the minimum necessary standard, unless an exception applies.
2. Proposed Rule
The Department long has interpreted the Privacy Rule as permitting a covered entity to use or disclose an individual's PHI without authorization for many care coordination and case management activities, even where such disclosure is to a third party that is not subject to the HIPAA Rules. However, as discussed in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, we have become aware that some covered entities are uncertain about whether the Privacy Rule permits disclosures of PHI for these purposes to certain third parties without an individual's authorization and are requiring authorizations for such disclosures.
To address this uncertainty, the Department proposed to clarify that the Privacy Rule permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, and similar third parties that provide health or human services to specific individuals for individual-level care coordination and case management, either as a treatment
[
617
]
activity of a covered health care provider or as a health care operations
[
618
]
activity of a covered health care provider or health plan. The Department proposed to make this clarification by adding paragraph
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
that would identify such entities as permissible recipients of PHI for these purposes. The Department proposed to limit the scope of this permission to disclosures by covered entities for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations, rather than including population-based activities, to ensure that the disclosures made under this permission would be akin to disclosures for treatment, which individuals expect to occur without the need to provide an authorization or consent.
3. Overview of Comments
Most commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal to expressly permit disclosures of PHI to third parties for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations because they believed that it would enhance the ability of health care providers and health plans to provide case management and care coordination for individuals. Commenters who expressed opposition to the proposal recommended that disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management require an
(
printed page 74920)
individual's authorization. A few commenters asserted that this proposal would increase the administrative burden on covered entities because they believed that it would lead to an increase in requests, additional contracts, and difficulties complying with other Federal and state laws. Some commenters expressed concerns about the ability of such organizations to safeguard the privacy and security of the information disclosed to them by regulated entities pursuant to this proposal, as well as their ability to use and redisclose such information because they generally are not subject to the HIPAA Rules.
4. Final Rule
The Department is finalizing its proposal to adopt
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
without modification. This section clarifies that the Privacy Rule permits covered entities to disclose PHI, without an individual's authorization, to social service agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, and similar third parties for individual-level care coordination and case management activities that constitute treatment or health care operations. This clarification will facilitate the treatment and health care operations of the disclosing covered entities in circumstances where a disclosure will serve the health care or health-related needs of individuals.
The Privacy Rule has long permitted disclosures of PHI to such entities for treatment or, in certain circumstances, health care operations.
[
619
]
Rather than changing the Department's interpretation of these permitted disclosures, this final rule adds express language at
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
to provide greater clarity about the scope of these existing permissions. The inclusion of this language in regulatory text ensures that covered entities understand their ability to disclose PHI to coordinate and manage care for individuals across clinical and community-based settings without an individual's authorization, where the Privacy Rule permits such disclosures. This clarification is consistent with the Department's longstanding approach of permitting uses and disclosures of PHI for TPO without authorization to avoid interfering with the ability of individuals to access quality and effective health care, while continuing to protect individuals' privacy.
[
620
]
This express permission to disclose PHI to third parties for care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations eliminates confusion about a covered entity's ability to make such disclosures to improve individuals' health care. For example, a covered health care provider may disclose the minimum necessary PHI of an individual, who is transitioning from a long-term care facility into community living, to a social service agency that arranges housing, day programs, and other health-related services that the individual may need upon discharge. The covered provider also may disclose the minimum necessary PHI, for example, to a community-based organization that facilitates transportation, life skills training, and nutrition services that are needed to support the individual's health care. Likewise, a health plan may disclose the minimum necessary PHI to a transition coordinator
[
621
]
to verify an individual's eligibility for certain services and streamline care coordination.
The Department is limiting the scope of this permission to disclosures by covered entities for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations, rather than population-based activities. The limitation to individual-level activities in
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
does not affect a covered entity's ability to make disclosures for population-based activities where such disclosures are otherwise permitted by
45 CFR 164.506(c)(1)
or another applicable provision of this Privacy Rule. This limitation is intended to ensure that the scope of the permission at
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
remains consistent with the privacy expectations of individuals. Covered entities remain subject to all applicable conditions and requirements of the Privacy Rule, including the minimum necessary standard, as applicable.
Nothing in this final rule alters an individual's right under
45 CFR 164.522(a)
to request restrictions on a use or disclosure of PHI for TPO. While a covered entity generally is not required to agree to such restrictions, it must act in accordance with any restriction to which it does agree. In addition, although covered entities are not required to obtain an individual's authorization or consent for disclosures permitted under
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
, disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management activities that constitute treatment or health care operations should remain consistent with the covered entity's NPP.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Some commenters expressed support for this proposal because they believed that it would remove barriers to care coordination and improve the quality of care. These commenters also asserted that it would reduce the burden on individuals and health care providers because it would reduce reliance on written authorizations where the Privacy Rule already permits disclosures without authorization.
Response:
The Department is adopting the proposal to add an implementation specification for TPO to provide greater clarity regarding covered entities' ability to disclose PHI without an individual's authorization to social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, and other similar third parties for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations. This clarification reduces unnecessary administrative burdens that can delay or impede coordination of care by decreasing the need for consultations with legal or compliance offices about whether authorizations are required for these disclosures. The Department also expects that this clarification will facilitate and encourage greater wraparound support and more targeted care for individuals who need health-related social or supportive services. For example, if a health care provider refers an individual with diabetes to a food bank, the health care provider could disclose the minimum necessary PHI about the individual to the food bank to enable the food bank to provide appropriate dietary accommodation or nutrition support.
Comment:
While many commenters expressed support for limiting the proposal to individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations, several commenters recommended that the Department
(
printed page 74921)
expand the proposal to permit disclosures of PHI to community-based organizations for population-level activities.
Response:
The Department is limiting
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
to disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management activities that constitute treatment or health care operations. The Department believes that the limitation to individual-level activities will ensure that disclosures made pursuant to
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
are consistent with the types of treatment and health care operations disclosures that individuals generally expect to occur without the need to provide an authorization and will protect individuals' privacy interests. Limiting the provision in this manner also preserves existing privacy protections and ensures that the scope of permissible disclosures remains tied to the care of a specific individual.
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that the Department clarify the types of organizations to which covered entities would be permitted to disclose PHI, the circumstances in which such disclosures may be made, or the services contemplated, and provide examples. Some recommended that the types of organizations identified be interpreted broadly to allow for maximum flexibility. One commenter expressed concern that the proposal would restrict who is permitted to receive PHI for care coordination and case management.
Response:
Section 164.506(c)(6) permits disclosures to social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, and similar third parties that provide health or human services to specific individuals for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations. The Department believes that the plain regulatory language provides sufficient clarity to allow covered entities to determine whether a potential recipient of PHI falls within the scope of the provision. This approach preserves flexibility and avoids unintentionally excluding organizations that provide care coordination and case management services in a variety of settings. The Department believes that these categories of entities encompass organizations serving many types of individuals across communities, consistent with the purpose of facilitating individual-level care coordination and case management.
This provision does not restrict the ability of a covered entity to disclose PHI for care coordination and case management. Rather, this provision clarifies that an individual's authorization is not required for disclosures to third parties for individual-level care coordination and case management activities that constitute treatment or health care operations. A covered entity is still permitted, but not required, to obtain an individual's consent to disclose the individual's PHI for TPO.
[
622
]
Comment:
Commenters expressed mixed views about whether the proposal should be limited to circumstances in which a particular service or provider is identified in an individual's care plan or where a screening assessment has been conducted. Commenters who expressed opposition to such conditions generally did so because they believed that additional requirements or conditions would increase the administrative burden for health care providers or community-based organizations, while commenters who expressed support for imposing such conditions generally did so because they believed that it would be more protective of individuals' privacy. A few commenters recommended that disclosures be limited to circumstances where there is shared care planning between individuals and health care providers. Some commenters urged the Department to specify that a covered entity may make disclosures based on their good faith belief that the disclosure is in the best interests of the individual. Another commenter asserted that regulated entities should disclose PHI to a community-based organization only if the organization requests the disclosure.
Many commenters raised concerns about the potential negative effects of disclosures to certain types of organizations on health disparities. One commenter asserted that while they supported screening for social needs and documenting such needs in an individual's care plan, requiring documentation of such information in the individual's care plan would serve to further entrench inequities.
Response:
The Department is not adopting additional conditions or prerequisites on disclosures permitted under
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
that would impede timely coordination of services for individuals. The Privacy Rule already permits uses and disclosures of PHI for treatment and health care operations, subject to existing conditions and limitations, including the minimum necessary standard where applicable. The addition of
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
removes uncertainty and eases care transitions. The Department believes that imposing additional conditions or prerequisites such as care plan documentation, screening assessments, or shared care planning would create barriers to care coordination and case management and increase the administrative burden for health care providers and community-based organizations.
Comment:
Several commenters requested clarification of how the proposal would interact with other laws that regulate the use and disclosure of certain health information about individuals that also may be PHI, such as
42 CFR part 2
(“Part 2”), the information blocking regulations, and state laws. A few commenters requested that the Department expressly state that this provision would not require such disclosures and it would allow covered entities to implement consent processes where required by other laws. One commenter expressed support for this proposal to the extent that it would not affect the obligations of Part 2 programs.
Response:
The Privacy Rule creates a Federal floor of protection for the privacy of PHI. It preempts state laws that are contrary to a standard, requirement, or implementation specification adopted under the Privacy Rule, with certain exceptions. As discussed above, Congress excepted from HIPAA's general preemption authority contrary provisions of state law that impose requirements, standards, or implementation specifications that are more stringent than those of the Privacy Rule.
[
623
]
If a provision of state or other Federal law provides greater privacy protection than a provision of the Privacy Rule, and it is possible for regulated entities to comply with both the state or other Federal law and the Privacy Rule (
e.g.,
where a state or other Federal law requires an individual's authorization for a disclosure that the Privacy Rule would permit without authorization), there is no conflict between the laws, and no preemption as to the state law. Accordingly, nothing in this final rule affects the obligations of covered entities to comply with applicable state or other Federal laws that restrict the disclosure of sensitive information, including information about SUD or other sensitive health issues, nor does it change the compliance obligations of covered entities subject to other Federal laws. For example, the permission in this section does not remove the obligations of covered entities that are also federally funded SUD treatment programs (
i.e.,
Part 2 programs) to
(
printed page 74922)
obtain patient consent when using or disclosing Part 2 records for treatment, payment, and health care operations purposes.
Similarly,
45 CFR 164.506(c)
does not prevent or relieve covered entities from complying with the information blocking regulations. Section 3022(a)(1) of the PHSA generally defines information blocking as a practice that, except as required by law or specified by the Secretary pursuant to rulemaking, is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of EHI.
[
624
]
Section 3022(a)(1)(A) excludes from the definition of information blocking practices that are required by law, circumstances where one or more elements of the definition is not met, and circumstances where the practice is covered by one of the exceptions for reasonable and necessary activities.
[
625
]
For example, if a covered entity is required by a state or Federal law to satisfy a precondition (such as obtaining patient consent or authorization) before providing access to, exchanging, or using EHI, the covered entity may choose not to provide access to, exchange, or use such EHI if the precondition has not been satisfied under certain circumstances.
[
626
]
Comment:
Several commenters raised questions about the ability of social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, and similar entities to exchange information electronically. Some commenters recommended that the Department provide support or guidance to facilitate electronic information exchange or compliance with HIPAA requirements for policies and procedures. Several commenters recommended that the Department provide resources to enable data segmentation. One commenter expressed concern that technical limitations of EHR systems may make it difficult for covered entities to limit the disclosures of PHI to the minimum necessary. Another commenter requested clarification that covered entities would be permitted to disclose PHI electronically, including through HIEs/HINs.
[
627
]
Response:
The Privacy Rule regulates the use and disclosure of PHI maintained in any form or medium. The Department does not prescribe specific means by which covered entities must use or disclose PHI and does not regulate the technical capabilities of entities that are not subject to HIPAA.
A covered entity may use an HIO, such as an HIE/HIN, to facilitate the exchange of PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations, provided that it has a business associate agreement with the HIO that requires the HIO to protect the information.
[
628
]
As discussed above, covered entities remain responsible for complying with the minimum necessary standard, as applicable, when disclosing PHI under
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
. However, some of the requests or disclosures to or through the HIO by a covered entity may not be subject to the minimum necessary standard, such as disclosures for the treatment activities of a health care provider. For electronic disclosures by a covered entity to and through an HIO that are subject to the minimum necessary standard, such as for a payment or health care operations purpose, the Privacy Rule would require that the minimum necessary standard be applied to that exchange and that the business associate agreement limit the disclosures by the HIO of, and requests for, PHI accordingly.
[
629
]
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concerns about the ability of social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, or other similar third parties to safeguard the privacy and security of the information disclosed to them by covered entities pursuant to this proposal. A few commenters recommended that the Department specify that the disclosure of PHI should be limited to persons who have implemented appropriate privacy and security measures or that the Department provide guidance on how the information should be safeguarded after PHI has been disclosed. Several commenters expressed concerns about the ability of third parties to re-disclose an individual's PHI without limitation and urged the Department to take steps to limit re-disclosures of PHI by entities that are not regulated under HIPAA.
Some commenters expressed concerns about potential liability for covered entities if there is a breach after disclosure of PHI to such organizations. A few of these commenters recommended that the Department provide a safe harbor or assurances for covered entities that disclose PHI to social services agencies in the event of a subsequent improper use or disclosure, while another suggested that the Department provide a safe harbor for regulated entities that adopt software that assigns labels to PHI to govern how that PHI may be accessed, used, or disclosed.
Response:
The Department declines to require that disclosures under
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
be limited to entities that have implemented particular privacy or security measures. The Department also declines to establish a safe harbor or impose additional conditions related to the potential liability of covered entities based on actions taken by persons who receive PHI and are not regulated under HIPAA. A safe harbor is unnecessary because a covered entity is not liable for subsequent breaches or improper use of health information by the person who receives it, including a person who is not regulated under HIPAA. We have determined that imposing such conditions could impede timely and effective care coordination and case management because it would require covered entities to assess, verify, or monitor the privacy and security practices of a wide range of persons who are not regulated under HIPAA and may not have standardized or readily assessable frameworks to facilitate such reviews. Requiring covered entities to evaluate privacy or security practices of such persons could not only delay or deter necessary information sharing and
(
printed page 74923)
create barriers to integrated care, but it also could increase the compliance burden for regulated entities.
Regulated entities remain subject to all applicable requirements of the Privacy and the Security Rules. This includes the obligation to implement reasonable safeguards, to limit disclosures to the minimum necessary PHI as applicable, and to determine whether a recipient is acting as a business associate, in which case a business associate agreement must be in place prior to disclosure.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that the Department clarify whether covered entities would be required to enter into business associate agreements with the third parties contemplated in this proposal before making a disclosure. Some commenters recommended that the Department require covered entities to execute written agreements with third parties to limit their use or redisclosure of PHI. A few commenters expressed concern that requiring agreements would increase administrative burden and impede care coordination.
Response:
Section 164.506(c)(6) does not impose any new requirements regarding business associate agreements. A covered entity is required to enter into a business associate agreement with a person or organization only when that person or organization meets the definition of a business associate.
[
630
]
As discussed above, there may be instances where disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations under
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
will be made to business associates engaged by a covered entity to provide health-related services on behalf of the covered entity. In those circumstances, a business associate agreement must be in place prior to the disclosure of PHI. In other circumstances, the person who receives the PHI will not be performing covered functions or activities for or on behalf of the covered entity; it will be providing services to the individual on its own behalf. In such cases, the person who receives the PHI does not meet the definition of a business associate, and a business associate agreement is not required.
Furthermore, the Department declines to require regulated entities to execute additional written agreements with third parties as a condition of disclosures under new
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
. Requiring such agreements would increase administrative burden and risk delaying or impeding care coordination and case management activities. Covered entities remain responsible for complying with the applicable conditions and requirements of the Privacy Rule, including determining whether a person who receives PHI is acting as a business associate and ensuring that a business associate agreement is in place when required.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that the Department add definitions or further clarify certain terms related to the proposed permission. For example, some commenters requested a definition of “social service agencies” with examples of the types of services contemplated.
Response:
The Department is not adopting any additional definitions or exclusions in connection with this provision. The Privacy Rule already defines the terms treatment and health care operations, and those definitions expressly encompass care coordination and case management activities. The Department believes that the robust description and discussion of other definitions for care coordination and case management above affords the regulated community sufficient information with which to determine whether a recipient is engaged in the contemplated activities. As discussed in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, the third parties contemplated by this provision may include a range of organizations that provide health or human services to specific individuals. The third party receiving PHI under this provision does not have to be a health care provider and may instead provide health-related social or other supportive services, such as food or sheltered housing needed to address health risks and conditions. For example, a covered health care provider may disclose the minimum necessary PHI to a senior center or adult day care provider to coordinate health-related services as part of treatment, and a health plan may disclose the minimum necessary PHI to a senior wellness center to coordinate care for an enrolled individual as part of the plan's health care operations.
[
631
]
The Department does not believe that adding definitions or enumerated lists of entities or services would improve clarity and is concerned that doing so could inadvertently limit the application of this provision in varied clinical and community contexts. Covered entities remain responsible for determining whether a disclosure falls within treatment or health care operations and whether the recipient is engaged in individual-level care coordination or case management activities.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern about the potential risks of this proposal to an individual's privacy. Some commenters recommended that an individual's consent or authorization be required before disclosures to social services agencies and similar third parties for care coordination and case management are made or that individuals be given an opportunity to object to such disclosures. According to some commenters, disclosures of PHI without an individual's consent could alienate individuals, lead to lower engagement with care, or result in care avoidance. A few commenters recommended that covered entities be required to notify individuals of such disclosures in advance. One commenter asserted that it would be reasonable for a clinician to explain to the individual the disclosures that would be made and the implications of disclosing PHI to entities not regulated under HIPAA.
Response:
While the Department appreciates commenters' concerns about protecting individuals' privacy interests, we decline to require consent, authorization, advance notice (other than what is required in an NPP),
[
632
]
or an opportunity to object as a condition of disclosures permitted under this provision. The Privacy Rule already permits disclosures without authorization for treatment and, in certain circumstances, health care operations, and this final rule clarifies the applicability of those existing permissions to disclosures that are made for these purposes to social services agencies, community-based organizations, HCBS providers, and similar third parties, consistent with longstanding guidance.
Section 164.506(c)(6) is limited to disclosures for individual-level care coordination and case management that constitute treatment or health care operations, rather than population-level activities, and such disclosures remain subject to the minimum necessary standard, where applicable. The limitation to individual-level activities ensures that the disclosures made under this permission are comparable to disclosures for treatment, which individuals expect to occur without
(
printed page 74924)
their authorization or consent. The right to request restrictions on disclosures for TPO purposes also remains available for individuals to request limitations on such disclosures.
[
633
]
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concern that the proposed provision could permit disclosures of PHI to law enforcement or child welfare agencies. Several commenters identified examples of potential harms that they believed could result from this proposal, including discrimination, increased health disparities and inequities, and loss of privacy.
Response:
This provision does not permit disclosures of PHI to law enforcement or child welfare agencies for law enforcement or investigatory purposes. The Privacy Rule's existing provisions governing disclosures for law enforcement, public health, or other public policy purposes remain unchanged by this final rule and continue to apply independently of
45 CFR 164.506(c)(6)
.
The Privacy Rule does not permit a regulated entity to disclose PHI for law enforcement purposes without an individual's authorization unless the disclosure is made pursuant to process and as otherwise required by law,
[
634
]
or another express permission applies.
[
635
]
Additionally, disclosures to child welfare or protective services agencies are permitted only under the applicable provisions of the Privacy Rule, including disclosures for public health activities and for reports of child abuse, domestic violence, and neglect.
[
636
]
Section 164.506(c)(6) does not expand or alter these existing permissions.
Comment:
Some commenters requested clarification of how this proposal would interact with the proposed modification to the minimum necessary standard or recommended modifications that would require the application of the minimum necessary standard to the proposal.
Response:
As discussed in this final rule, the Department is not finalizing the proposed exception to the minimum necessary standard for health care operations uses and disclosures related to individual-level care coordination and case management.
[
637
]
This final rule does not alter the minimum necessary requirements.
The applicability of the minimum necessary standard for disclosures of PHI to a third party for individual-level care coordination and case management is governed by
45 CFR 164.502(b)
. Disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for the treatment activities of either the requesting health care provider or another health care provider are not subject to the minimum necessary standard. Disclosures of PHI for treatment to third parties that are not health care providers and for health care operations remain subject to the minimum necessary standard. Thus, if the minimum necessary standard applies, a covered entity must take reasonable steps to limit the disclosure of PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose.
[
638
]
F. Encouraging Disclosures of PHI When Needed To Help Individuals Experiencing Substance Use Disorder (Including Opioid Use Disorder), Serious Mental Illness, and in Emergency Circumstances
1. Current Rule
Sections 164.502(g) and 164.510-164.514 of the Privacy Rule permit covered entities to disclose PHI in certain circumstances when an individual is unable to agree or object to the disclosure of their PHI or where a disclosure may be needed to prevent or lessen a threat to health or safety. In such circumstances, the Privacy Rule provides for the exercise of professional judgment when determining whether such disclosure should be made.
Disclosures to Personal Representatives
Under
45 CFR 164.502(g)
, a personal representative generally is a person with authority under applicable law (
e.g.,
state law) to act on behalf of an individual in making decisions related to health care.
[
639
]
In many circumstances, the parent or guardian of an unemancipated minor child is treated as the child's personal representative under applicable law. In circumstances where state or other applicable law does not treat a parent as an unemancipated minor child's personal representative,
45 CFR 164.502(g)(3)(ii)(C)
permits, but does not require, covered entities to provide PHI under the right of access to a parent, guardian or other person acting
in loco parentis,
if the action is consistent with state or other applicable law and the decision to disclose the child's PHI is based on the professional judgment of a licensed health care professional.
Uses and Disclosures Requiring an Opportunity for the Individual To Agree or Object
Section 164.510 of the Privacy Rule generally requires that covered entities must provide an individual with the opportunity to agree or object before using or disclosing the individual's PHI for inclusion in a facility directory or disclosing PHI to family members, caregivers, or others involved in care or payment for care. However, individuals are not always able to agree or object to such uses or disclosures, particularly in emergency situations. Accordingly,
45 CFR 164.510(a)(3)
permits a covered health care provider to disclose in its facility directory certain PHI, including name, location within the facility, general condition, and religious affiliation to clergy and persons who ask for the individual by name, when the individual cannot agree or object because of incapacity or an emergency treatment circumstance, if providing this information meets both of the following conditions:
The disclosure is consistent with a prior expressed preference of the individual, if any, that is known to the covered health care provider.
The disclosure is in the individual's best interests, as determined by the covered health care provider, in the exercise of professional judgment.
For similar reasons,
45 CFR 164.510(b)(2)(iii)
permits a covered entity to disclose relevant PHI about an individual who is present and has decision-making capacity, if the covered entity can reasonably infer, based on the exercise of professional judgment, that the individual does not object to the disclosure. Further,
45 CFR 164.510(b)(3)
permits a covered entity to disclose relevant PHI about an individual who is not present or cannot agree or object because of incapacity or an emergency circumstance to family members and other caregivers involved in the individual's care or payment for care, if the covered entity, based on professional judgment, determines that the disclosure is in the best interests of the individual.
Disclosures To Avert a Threat to Health or Safety
Section 164.512(j) of the Privacy Rule permits covered entities, consistent with applicable law and standards of ethical conduct, to use or disclose PHI when
(
printed page 74925)
necessary to prevent or lessen a serious and imminent threat to the health or safety of a person or the public.
[
640
]
To “lessen” a threat could mean, for example, to reduce the severity of the threatened harm, or the likelihood of the anticipated harm occurring. The permission is intended to accommodate, and be consistent with, a “duty to warn” others of a threat as established in case law (and in some states, statutory requirements).
[
641
]
Certain conditions apply, including that the recipient of the PHI must be reasonably able to prevent or lessen the threat, or the use or disclosure must be necessary for law enforcement to identify or apprehend the subject individual.
[
642
]
In the case of a disclosure to law enforcement, additional conditions include that the individual made a statement admitting participation in a violent crime that the covered entity reasonably believes may have caused serious physical harm to the victim, or that circumstances demonstrate that the subject individual escaped from a correctional institution or lawful custody, as defined in the Privacy Rule.
[
643
]
Identity Verification
Section 164.514(h)(2)(iv) of the Privacy Rule generally requires covered entities to verify the identity and authority of a person requesting PHI.
[
644
]
In certain situations, the circumstances surrounding the disclosure itself may accomplish the verification without having to collect additional documents or rely on a preestablished procedure.
[
645
]
Accordingly,
45 CFR 164.514(h)(2)(iv)
provides that a covered entity's obligation to verify a requestor's identity is met if the covered entity relies on an exercise of professional judgment pursuant to
45 CFR 164.510
, or acts on a good faith belief in making a disclosure pursuant to
45 CFR 164.512(j)
to prevent or lessen certain serious and imminent threats.
2. Proposed Rule
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM,
[
646
]
support from family members, friends, and caregivers is essential for many individuals who are experiencing SUD
[
647
]
or SMI.
[
648
]
However, family members and caregivers need sufficient information to provide this support.
To address these concerns, the Department has issued extensive guidance on the circumstances in which the Privacy Rule permits disclosures of PHI to an individual's friends, family, and others.
[
649
]
For example, guidance issued in 2017 addresses the permission for covered health care providers to disclose PHI to an individual's friends, family, and others involved in the individual's care or payment for that care when the individual has experienced an overdose and is unable to agree or object to uses and disclosures of PHI.
[
650
]
The guidance clarifies that a health care provider may use professional judgment to talk to the parents of an individual who has been incapacitated by an opioid overdose about the overdose and related medical information, but generally cannot share PHI unrelated to the overdose without the individual's agreement.
[
651
]
The guidance further clarifies when a covered health care provider may rely on the permission at
45 CFR 164.512(j)
in an overdose situation. Additionally, in response to the Cures Act,
[
652
]
OCR compiled a full suite of guidance and materials on its website related to mental and behavioral health for health care professionals and consumers.
[
653
]
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, although the guidance focuses primarily on overdose situations, the provisions apply equally to the disclosure of PHI during other health emergencies or dangerous situations.
Despite this extensive guidance, the Department continued to receive reports that covered entities were reluctant to disclose PHI to persons involved in the care of individuals experiencing SUD or SMI, even when the Privacy Rule permits such disclosures. Accordingly, in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, we proposed to replace “exercise of professional judgment” with “good faith belief” as the standard pursuant to which covered entities would be permitted to make certain uses and disclosures in the best interests of individuals in
45 CFR 164.502(g)(3)(ii)(C)
,
164.510(a)(3)
,
164.510(b)(2)(iii)
,
164.510(b)(3)
, and
164.514(h)(2)(iv)
. In these five provisions, the proposed new standard in
45 CFR 164.502(k)
would include a presumption of a covered entity's good faith that could be overcome with evidence of bad faith. Under this proposal, disclosures for any improper purpose, such as crime, fraud, or personal enrichment, would be considered “bad faith” disclosures. Additionally, in
45 CFR 164.512(j)
, we proposed to replace “serious and imminent” threat with “serious and reasonably foreseeable,” define reasonably foreseeable based on an ordinary person's understanding, and add a provision for heightened
(
printed page 74926)
deference to decisions about such disclosures by workforce members with specialized training, expertise, or experience.
3. Overview of Comments
The commenters expressed support for and opposition to these proposals in even numbers. Family members and caregivers of individuals experiencing SUD or mental illness generally expressed support for the proposals about good faith and preventing harm and threatened harm because they believed that the proposed modifications would encourage health care providers to provide PHI to the family members and caregivers without fear of violating HIPAA, particularly during emergencies, crises, and circumstances in which the individual is incapacitated. In contrast, many commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that it would decrease an individual's privacy and autonomy. Many of these commenters asserted that the proposed modifications would lead to discrimination, shame, stigma, interference with efforts to seek care, and care avoidance.
4. Final Rule
The Department is not finalizing the proposed changes to the standards for good faith and professional judgment in
45 CFR 164.502
and
164.510-514
. Upon review and analysis of public comments, the Department is not persuaded that the proposed changes would provide the clarity sought. We also are concerned that finalizing the proposals could increase complexity and burden for covered entities while chilling access to care. The Department believes that additional technical assistance and public education about the Privacy Rule's provisions that permit covered entities to disclose PHI to an individual's family and caregivers would better address any misunderstandings about the scope of the existing permissions.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Many commenters expressed support for the proposal to replace the “professional judgment” standard with a “good faith” standard because they believed that it would reduce barriers that prevent family members and caregivers from assisting loved ones experiencing SUD or SMI. They described challenges under the current rule, including a lack of notification to family members and caregivers when the individual is discharged, difficulty locating loved ones, and their inability to obtain the information that they need to support individuals who cannot care for themselves. Commenters asserted that the proposed changes would improve access to care, enable earlier intervention, and facilitate more effective coordination between families and clinicians.
Response:
The Department recognizes the difficulties families and caregivers face when caring for individuals with SUD and SMI. However, after reviewing the comments, the Department has determined that replacing “professional judgment” with a “good faith” standard likely would introduce ambiguity without improving outcomes. The equal proportion of comments expressing support for and opposition to the proposals reinforces the need for a measured approach to balancing the privacy interests of individuals with the need for disclosure in urgent situations. The Department is persuaded that the existing provisions provide the appropriate balance. Rather than finalizing the proposed changes, the Department intends to emphasize outreach and technical assistance to covered entities to improve their understanding of existing permissions to disclose PHI to family, friends, and caregivers.
Comment:
Some commenters asserted that the proposal to adopt a good faith standard would help health care providers, family members, and caregivers respond effectively during emergencies. According to these commenters, this proposal would reduce providers' concerns about violating the Privacy Rule, alleviate confusion about what the Privacy Rule permits, and facilitate appropriate disclosures of PHI. A few commenters stated that the proposal would reduce the refusal of covered entities to disclose PHI and improve continuity of care.
Response:
The Department acknowledges commenters' interest in reducing uncertainty involving disclosures allowed under
45 CFR 164.502(g)
,
164.510
, and
164.512(j)
. However, the Department has determined that altering the disclosure standard likely will not resolve concerns about the hesitancy of covered entities to disclose PHI and, in fact, could create additional challenges. Instead, we will continue to focus on providing outreach and technical assistance to address these concerns.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended various further modifications, such as applying good faith based on the belief that disclosure will improve the individual's care or benefit the individual. Others suggested that the Department add exceptions that would permit a covered entity to override an individual's prior expressed preference in certain circumstances.
A few commenters requested that the Department clarify what would constitute good faith under the proposed standard and how the proposal would interact with information blocking regulations, protect sensitive PHI, and apply to non-clinical workforce members, such as peer counselors. A few commenters suggested that the Department provide safe harbors for disclosures made in good faith, and a few requested that the Department provide guidance on how to address situations in which an individual's previously expressed disclosure preferences may have changed.
Response:
As discussed above, the Department is not finalizing the proposals to replace the professional judgment standard with a good faith standard. The Department's decision not to finalize the proposed changes to the professional judgment is based, in part, on the lack of clear consensus on whether the modifications would offer meaningful improvements to individuals' health care and access to care.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal to revise
45 CFR 164.512(j)
by replacing “serious and imminent” with “serious and reasonably foreseeable.” These commenters asserted that this proposal would allow for earlier intervention and help prevent escalations in harm. A few commenters requested that the Department give greater deference to harm assessments made by health care professionals with specialized clinical or behavioral health training.
Response:
Rather than providing the certitude sought by commenters, the Department has determined that revising the threat standard in
45 CFR 164.512(j)
could increase uncertainty about when disclosures are appropriate. Accordingly, the Department is not finalizing this proposed revision. Instead, we refer stakeholders to guidance issued by OCR on applying the serious and imminent threat standard for individuals with mental health conditions and SUD.
[
654
]
Comment:
A few commenters who expressed support for the proposals requested that the Department clarify
(
printed page 74927)
the interaction of the proposed changes with state laws or consider preempting stricter state requirements to ensure consistency.
Response:
The preemption provisions of HIPAA are statutory; thus, they are not subject to modification by the Department. HIPAA excepts from its general preemption authority contrary provisions of state law that impose requirements, standards, or implementation specifications that are more stringent than those of the Privacy Rule.
[
655
]
In addition, if a provision of state or other Federal law provides greater privacy protection (
e.g.,
a state or Federal law that requires an individual's consent or authorization before a covered entity is permitted to disclose PHI) than a provision of the Privacy Rule, and it is possible for regulated entities to comply with both the state or other Federal law and the Privacy Rule, there is no conflict between the laws and no preemption of state law.
Comment:
Several commenters urged the Department to better align the HIPAA Rules and Part 2 to reduce barriers to coordinated care for individuals with SUD.
Response:
The Privacy Rule does not conflict with Part 2 in circumstances where it is possible for regulated entities to comply with both Part 2 and the Privacy Rule. Thus, where the HIPAA Rules and Part 2 both apply, the Privacy Rule permissions for disclosure without authorization to family members, caregivers, and others do not negate Part 2's general requirement to obtain a patient's written consent for the disclosure of Part 2 records.
[
656
]
Where an exception to Part 2's general requirement applies, a Privacy Rule permission also may apply, subject to the conditions of the applicable Part 2 exception. For example, Part 2 permits disclosure without patient consent for a bona fide medical emergency, subject to the condition that the disclosure be documented afterwards, while the Privacy Rule permits—but does not require—a broader range of disclosures without an individual's authorization for treatment purposes, including emergency medical treatment. Accordingly, a covered entity that is also subject to Part 2 can be in compliance with both regulations when it makes the more limited disclosure permitted by Part 2 for a bona fide medical emergency and meets the applicable requirements and conditions of both the Part 2 exception and Privacy Rule permission.
To address concerns about the alignment between Part 2 and the HIPAA Rules, the Department published two final rules in early 2024. The Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder (SUD) Patient Records Final Rule, published on February 16, 2024,
[
657
]
and the 2024 Privacy Rule, published April 26, 2024,
[
658
]
implemented section 3221 of the CARES Act and modified the requirements of the NPP to align it with the Part 2 Patient Notice. This final rule makes additional modifications to the NPP, discussed in detail below, to further align it with the Part 2 Patient Notice.
Comment:
A few commenters asserted that the proposal to replace the professional judgment standard would not discourage individuals from seeking care and that a good faith approach could improve care coordination. A few commenters urged the Department to expand the definition of incapacity to include individuals who cannot exercise sound judgment because they have been diagnosed with dementia, psychosis, or another SMI.
Response:
The Department is concerned that modifying the professional judgment standard for disclosing PHI to an individual's family, friends, and caregivers or altering the definition of incapacity could introduce more ambiguity and result in unintended consequences. Although an individual who has been diagnosed with dementia, psychosis, or other SMI may lack decision-making capacity in some circumstances, a diagnosis of SMI, by itself, does not determine whether an individual can make independent decisions.
[
659
]
Neither
45 CFR 164.510
nor
45 CFR 164.512
requires a legal determination of incapacity; instead, an individual's inability to make decisions about uses and disclosures of their PHI may be transient or situational. For example, an individual with SMI may temporarily lack decision-making capacity when their symptoms are untreated, but their decision-making capabilities may resume upon treatment.
[
660
]
Comment:
Some commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to replace the professional judgment standard with a good faith standard because they believed that it would weaken privacy protections for individuals' PHI, increase stigma associated with SUD and SMI, and deter individuals from seeking care. These commenters asserted that broad disclosure permissions could particularly harm individuals in certain situations (
e.g.,
