individuals seeking sensitive health care services such as mental health care and SUD treatment).
A few commenters asserted that the proposal to replace the professional judgment standard was unnecessary because the Privacy Rule already permits appropriate disclosures to family members or caregivers. According to these commenters, it is misinformation, not regulatory limits, that leads to inappropriate refusals to disclose PHI.
Several commenters expressed opposition to the Department's proposal to replace professional judgment with good faith because they believed that clinical expertise should guide decisions about the appropriateness of disclosures of PHI to family, friends, and caregivers. These commenters also asserted that a good faith standard would be subjective and difficult to enforce. Several commenters expressed concern that the proposal would allow non-clinical workforce members to make disclosure decisions without sufficient knowledge of an individual's circumstances. Other commenters observed that covered entities sometimes lack information about family dynamics.
Some commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to include a presumption of good faith and stated that individuals would struggle to prove bad faith without a requirement that covered entities document the rationale for their decision.
A few commenters expressed their opposition to the implementation of a good faith standard for identity verification because they believed that family members would not need to provide proof of their identity under such a standard.
Response:
As discussed above, the Privacy Rule already permits many of the disclosures sought by family members and caregivers. OCR has longstanding guidance on these topics, including those that specifically address circumstances involving individuals that have been diagnosed with mental and behavioral health conditions, such
(
printed page 74928)
as SMI and SUD.
[
661
]
The Department agrees that maintaining trust and confidentiality is essential for individuals to seek health care and that decisions to disclose PHI about individuals in certain circumstances may require the exercise of clinical expertise. The Department is persuaded by concerns about the potential chilling effect of the proposals to replace the professional judgment standard at
45 CFR 164.502(g)
and
45 CFR 164.510-512
with a good faith standard on the willingness of individuals to seek or obtain health care, as well as concerns that the proposals might cause additional confusion or limit an individual's exercise of their autonomy. Accordingly, we are not finalizing the proposed changes to the professional judgment standard in
45 CFR 164.502(g)
and
45 CFR 164.510-512
. Moreover, commenters have convinced us that the current provisions in the Privacy Rule are sufficient to permit appropriate disclosures to family members or caregivers.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed their belief that covered entities should honor the expressed privacy preferences of individuals except in true emergencies.
Response:
The Privacy Rule requires that a covered entity honor an individual's expressed privacy preferences in certain circumstances.
[
662
]
While not required in many circumstances, the Department generally encourages covered entities to take an individual's expressed privacy preferences into consideration before making permitted disclosures.
G. Modifying Notice of Privacy Practices Requirements To Reduce Regulatory Burden and Increase Transparency
1. Current Rule
The Privacy Rule generally requires that certain covered entities provide individuals with an NPP to ensure that they understand how the covered entity may use and disclose their PHI, their rights, and the covered entity's legal duties with respect to PHI.
[
663
]
There are limited exceptions to this general requirement. For example, a correctional institution
[
664
]
that is a covered entity is not required to provide individuals who are inmates
[
665
]
with a copy of its NPP.
[
666
]
Section 164.520(b) of the Privacy Rule describes the contents of the NPP, both required and optional, including descriptions of the types of permitted uses and disclosures of individuals' PHI. For example, the NPP must describe how the covered entity is permitted to use and disclose PHI for TPO,
[
667
]
as well as each of the other purposes for which the covered entity is permitted or required to use or disclose PHI without the individual's written authorization.
[
668
]
Additionally, the NPP must include a statement that the covered entity is required by law to maintain the privacy of PHI and abide by the terms of the current notice.
[
669
]
It also must include a statement of the individual's rights with respect to PHI, including the right to inspect or obtain a copy of their PHI, or both, and a brief description of how the individual may exercise these rights.
[
670
]
If the covered entity intends to use or disclose PHI to engage in certain activities, such as fundraising, the NPP must contain statements informing the individual of such activities.
[
671
]
Section 164.520(c) of the Privacy Rule sets forth the circumstances in which a covered entity must provide the NPP to an individual. Under
45 CFR 164.520(c)(2)(ii)
, a covered health care provider that has a direct treatment relationship with an individual generally must make a good faith effort to obtain a written acknowledgment of receipt of the provider's NPP. If the provider is unable to do so, it must document its good faith efforts and the reason for not obtaining the acknowledgment and maintain such documentation for six years.
[
672
]
Those same requirements apply to an NPP sent electronically.
[
673
]
2. Proposed Rule
The Department has proposed changes to the NPP requirements several times in recent years, including in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM and the 2022 Part 2 NPRM.
[
674
]
Some of those proposals were finalized in the 2024 Privacy Rule, while others remain outstanding. This final rule addresses those outstanding proposals, as summarized below.
Of significance, we proposed to eliminate
45 CFR 164.520(c)(2)(ii)
, which requires a covered health care provider that has a direct treatment relationship with an individual to obtain a written acknowledgment of receipt of the NPP. Removing this provision also would eliminate the requirement that if the covered health care provider is unable to obtain the written acknowledgment, it must document its good faith effort and the reason for not obtaining the acknowledgment.
[
675
]
Similarly, the Department proposed to remove, from
45 CFR 164.520(c)(2)(iii)
,
[
676
]
the same requirements for an NPP sent electronically. We also proposed to remove the requirement at
45 CFR 164.520(e)
to retain copies of such documentation for 6 years, pursuant to
45 CFR 164.530(j)(2)
.
To ensure that individuals are informed about a covered entity's privacy practices, we proposed to replace the written acknowledgment with a right for the individual to discuss the NPP with a person designated by the covered entity. Additionally, we proposed at
45 CFR 164.520(b)(1)(vii)
to require the covered entity to include the designated contact person's email address and a statement specifying that the designated person is available to answer questions about the NPP.
The Department also proposed to modify the prominent and specific language in the NPP header to help increase individuals' understanding of a covered entity's privacy practices and their rights with respect to their PHI. We proposed to modify the required header to specify that the notice provides information to individuals about: (1) how to access their health information; (2) how to file a HIPAA complaint; and (3) their rights to their medical information, including an individual's right to receive a copy of the notice and to discuss its contents with a designated person. Additionally, in preamble, we explained that we were considering adding a requirement that the header specify whether the designated contact
(
printed page 74929)
person is available onsite. The Department also proposed to require that the header include a phone number and email address the individual can use to reach the designated person. And in the 2022 Part 2 NPRM, the Department proposed to make a non-substantive modification to change the word “Medical” to “Health” throughout the header to refer to the type of information covered by the NPP.
[
677
]
Consistent with the proposed language in the header, the Department proposed to modify the required element of an NPP that addresses the right of access. The Department proposed to require that an NPP describe how an individual can exercise the right to obtain a copy of their records at limited cost or, in some cases, free of charge, and the right of access to direct.
Additionally, the Department proposed at
45 CFR 164.520(b)(2)(iii)
to permit covered entities to include in the NPP information to address circumstances in which individuals seek to direct their PHI to a designated person, when the request does not meet the conditions of the right of access to direct under
45 CFR 164.524(d)
.
Finally, in the 2022 Part 2 NPRM, the Department proposed to remove the provision that excepts individuals who are inmates of correctional institutions that are covered entities from the requirement that covered entities must provide individuals with an NPP.
[
678
]
The Department explained that we no longer believed there to be a safety or security risk associated with providing inmates an NPP.
3. Overview of Comments
Most commenters asserted that the requirement to obtain a written acknowledgment increases the administrative burden on covered entities and is misunderstood by individuals. Commenters were evenly divided on their views of the proposed content modifications to the NPP. Several commenters stated that the proposed NPP changes would increase administrative burdens. A few commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to provide individuals with the right to discuss the NPP with a designated contact person because they believed that it would be more burdensome than obtaining the written acknowledgment. According to these commenters, the proposal was unnecessary because individuals always have had the ability to ask questions about the NPP. Several commenters expressed support for creating a right for an individual to discuss the NPP with a designated person because they believed that it would increase individuals' understanding of their privacy rights. Some commenters asserted that the proposed header modifications would draw attention to the items of greatest relevance to the individual.
A few commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal that would eliminate the provision that excepts individuals who are inmates of correctional institutions that are covered entities from the requirement that covered entities must provide individuals with an NPP because they believed that such individuals would benefit from transparency about how their health information is used and disclosed. One commenter asserted that providing the NPP would increase the burden on workforce members with minimal benefit to the individual who is an inmate.
4. Final Rule
The Department is finalizing our proposals to modify the NPP provisions, including certain proposals included in the 2022 Part 2 NPRM, with minor modifications as described below. Specifically, we are removing the requirement at
45 CFR 164.520(c)(2)(ii)
for a covered health care provider with a direct treatment relationship to an individual to obtain a written acknowledgment of receipt of the NPP. Removing this provision also eliminates the requirement that if a covered entity is unable to obtain the written acknowledgment, it must document its good faith efforts and the reason for not obtaining the acknowledgment. Relatedly, we are removing the parallel requirement at
45 CFR 164.520(c)(3)(iii)
for an NPP sent electronically. We also are removing the requirement at
45 CFR 164.520(e)
to retain copies of such documentation for 6 years. Removing these NPP requirements eliminates a significant documentation and storage burden for health care providers and increases the resources available for providing high-quality health care. These modifications also will remove the burden on covered entities to document a good faith effort to obtain the written acknowledgment in situations where the individual is unconscious or otherwise incapacitated or cannot sign the acknowledgment because of communication barriers. Moreover, eliminating these requirements will remove confusion for individuals about the purpose of the written acknowledgment or whether it is required for treatment, in addition to removing confusion for workforce members who may erroneously believe that individuals must sign the acknowledgment to obtain care. Eliminating these requirements does not affect the obligation of a covered entity to document compliance with the notice requirements by retaining copies of the versions of the notice issued by the covered entity consistent with
45 CFR 164.530(j)
.
[
679
]
As discussed above, covered entities must include in the NPP information about individuals' rights under the Privacy Rule and how individuals may exercise those rights with respect to the covered entity.
[
680
]
Thus, to ensure that individuals understand and can make decisions based on the information in the NPP, the Department is finalizing the proposal to replace the written acknowledgment requirement with a new provision at
45 CFR 164.520(b)(1)(iv)(G)
, which requires the NPP to state the individual's right to discuss the NPP with a person designated by the covered entity. A covered entity can satisfy the right to discuss the NPP in a variety of ways. For example, the covered entity could have one or more workforce members with knowledge of the NPP available onsite during business hours to answer questions or could offer to schedule meetings or calls with individuals within a reasonable time period of receiving their requests to discuss (whether a request is made in person, by telephone, or by email). As another example, a covered entity could implement technology, such as super intelligence (SI),
[
681
]
in a manner that is compliant with the Privacy and Security Rules, to receive and triage questions from individuals on its NPP, provided that individuals have the option to discuss the NPP with a workforce member knowledgeable about the covered entity's privacy practices to address their questions. Additionally, we are finalizing language to permit covered entities to name either an office or a specific contact person to align the NPP with the Part 2 Patient Notice.
[
682
]
We believe that having a designated contact person or office with whom an individual can discuss their privacy rights will be more effective for
(
printed page 74930)
enhancing an individual's understanding of their privacy rights than signing an acknowledgment that they received the NPP. Accordingly, we encourage covered entities to identify as the designated person or office responsible for providing further information and answering questions a person or office that is knowledgeable about the covered entity's privacy practices and HIPAA complaint process, rather than a general customer service contact.
Relatedly, the Department is finalizing its proposal to modify
45 CFR 164.520(b)(1)(vii)
, which requires a covered entity to provide contact information for their designated contact person or office, including the person or office's email address. We also are finalizing the proposal to require that the NPP specify that the designated contact person or office responsible for providing further information is available to answer questions about the covered entity's privacy practices and receive complaints as required by
45 CFR 164.530(a)(1)(ii)
.
We adopt our proposal, with a minor modification, to revise
45 CFR 164.520(b)(1)(iv)(C)
to describe how an individual can exercise the right of access to obtain a copy of their records at limited cost or, in some cases, free of charge, and the right of access to direct.
[
683
]
The Department believes that this modification provides individuals with additional information about how to access their PHI to manage their own health care and payment for care, further empowering them. Consistent with modifications made elsewhere to this final rule, we are replacing “third party” with “person designated by the individual.” This language aligns with the language of the HITECH Act and emphasizes that the individual themselves (or their personal representative) is seeking the disclosure, not a third party.
[
684
]
To ensure consistency with how NPP content is presented to individuals, the Privacy Rule requires that covered entities use a specific header for their NPP. Accordingly, to improve clarity in the NPP for individuals, the Department is finalizing the proposal to modify
45 CFR 164.520(b)(1)(i)
to require that the header state that the NPP provides information about: (1) how to access their health information; (2) how to file a HIPAA complaint; and (3) their rights to their health information, including an individual's right to receive a copy of the notice, and to discuss its contents with a designated person or office. Consistent with the modification to permit covered entities to list a specific office as the designated contact rather than a person, the Department also is finalizing the proposal to modify the header to give covered entities the option to include the contact information of an office rather than a person. We are not finalizing our proposal, described in the preamble, to require that the contact be onsite because we believe it is sufficient for individuals to have the contact person or office's telephone number and email address. However, the Department encourages covered entities to have the designated contact person or someone from the designated office available onsite or otherwise easily reachable during operating hours to promptly answer individuals' questions about the NPP and receive HIPAA complaints.
The Department is also finalizing the proposal to modify the header of the NPP to change the word “Medical” to “Health,” to align with the modification to the Part 2 Patient Notice. As discussed in the 2022 Part 2 NPRM, this change does not modify substantive requirements. Instead, it will more accurately reflect and clarify that the information covered by the notice is not limited to the information in an individual's medical record.
The Department believes that providing this information at the beginning of the NPP will improve individuals' awareness of their Privacy Rule rights, what they can do if they suspect a violation of the Privacy Rule, and how to contact a designated person or office to ask questions.
The Department also is modifying
45 CFR 164.520(b)(2)(iii)
to add a new optional element for a covered entity to include information addressing an individual's alternatives when they seek to direct their PHI to a designated person, but their request is outside the scope of the right of access to direct.
[
685
]
This optional element will help increase awareness that individuals retain the right to obtain the PHI directly from the covered entity and give it to a person of their choosing. Alternately, it will inform individuals that they can request that the covered entity send a copy of PHI directly to a designated person using a valid authorization. While this provision is optional, the Department encourages covered entities to include in the NPP information about how an individual can send PHI to a person the individual designates in such circumstances. For example, if an individual requests that a paper copy of PHI in an electronic health record be sent to another person, the covered entity could address in this optional NPP provision how the individual may obtain that information, such as through a request made pursuant to the right of access and send it to the other person themselves, or how to request that the covered entity send the information to the other person pursuant to a valid authorization. We are finalizing this provision as proposed, with one minor modification, replacing “third party” with “person designated by the individual” to ensure consistency with modifications discussed elsewhere in this final rule.
The Department also is finalizing the proposal that we made in the 2022 Part 2 NPRM to remove the exception at
45 CFR 164.520(a)(4)
, “exception for inmates.” Thus, covered entities that serve correctional institutions, and correctional institutions that are covered entities, will be required to provide individuals who are inmates with a copy of the NPP. Consistent with a goal of section 3221 of the CARES Act, this modification aligns the NPP with the Part 2 Patient Notice, which does not include an exception regarding the provision of the notice to individuals who are inmates. Removing this exception ensures that individuals who are inmates receive an NPP that is consistent with what is provided to other individuals while also retaining the limitation on the ability of individuals who are inmates to exercise the right of access to ensure the safety and security of correctional facility personnel and others.
[
686
]
Furthermore, providing individuals who are inmates with an NPP affords inmates greater transparency on how the correctional institution, or a covered entity that serves a correctional institution, may use and disclose their PHI, such entities' legal duties with respect to PHI, and the individuals' rights with respect to their PHI, without changing other rights or duties unrelated to the NPP.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Most commenters expressed support for the proposal to eliminate the requirement to obtain a signed acknowledgment of the NPP, stating that the requirement is an administrative burden and causes confusion for individuals without providing any meaningful benefit. A few commenters recommended that the Department provide covered entities
(
printed page 74931)
with the ability to obtain an individual's acknowledgment through alternative mechanisms, such as verbal and electronic confirmation. A few commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that the acknowledgment requirement ensures that individuals receive the NPP and are aware of the covered entity's privacy practices.
Response:
Eliminating the requirement to obtain a written acknowledgment of receipt of the NPP will reduce the covered entity's administrative burden, improve workflow congestion, and allow more time for individuals to discuss the NPP with the designated person or office. The Department is not replacing the requirement to obtain a written acknowledgment with an alternative mechanism, such as obtaining verbal or written confirmation of receipt, because such requirement would add unnecessary complexity. Importantly, removing the requirement to obtain a written acknowledgment does not remove the requirement for covered entities to provide individuals, including inmates, with an NPP to ensure that they are aware of the entity's privacy practices and know how to contact a designated person or office to answer any questions about the NPP or submit a HIPAA complaint. This modification also does not affect an individual's ability to access an NPP that is posted on a covered entity's website, consistent with the Privacy Rule's requirements for the website posting of NPPs.
[
687
]
Removal of this requirement does not prevent a covered entity from continuing to document that it has provided individuals with an NPP if it wishes to do so.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal to create a right for an individual to discuss the NPP with a designated contact person. A few commenters recommended that the Department permit the designated person to be a group or a department, rather than requiring that it be a particular person, because it would allow the covered entity to identify the specific person who is best able to respond to each inquiry. One commenter recommended that the Department require that the designated contact person meet certain minimum qualifications.
Some commenters expressed opposition to the proposal because they believed that it would be burdensome and unnecessary. According to these commenters, this proposal would replace the documentation burden with an increase in workforce time and burden on workflow.
Response:
The Department is adopting a modified version of the proposal that requires covered entities to designate a person or office as the contact for discussing the NPP with individuals and accepting HIPAA complaints. While the definition of “person” in the HIPAA Rules is broad enough to refer to an office, we are persuaded by public comments that this modification is necessary to clarify that covered entities may designate an office or a workforce member as the contact.
[
688
]
This modification is consistent with other instances in the Privacy Rule that refer to “person or office.”
[
689
]
According to commenters, individuals generally do not ask questions about the NPP. Based on these comments, we do not expect that covered entities will receive many questions about their privacy practices. Thus, the Department believes that having a designated person or office available to answer questions about the NPP will create less administrative burden than obtaining a written acknowledgment of receipt of the NPP or documenting good faith efforts and the reason for not obtaining the acknowledgment. Furthermore, the final rule provides flexibility by permitting covered entities to choose to designate either a person or office as the contact. The Department has long stated that duties may be delegated and shared, so long as there is one point of accountability for the covered entity's privacy practices to ensure that individuals are able to speak to a knowledgeable person.
[
690
]
Thus, although the Department recommends that the designated person or office be versed in the entity's privacy practices and HIPAA complaint process, we are not requiring that the designated contact person or office must meet certain minimum qualifications to answer questions about the NPP or receive HIPAA complaints. Providing a designated contact person or office recognizes the importance of assuring patients that their PHI is being protected and shared appropriately. Additionally, it engenders trust and encourages open dialogue between individuals and covered entities.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed support for the proposal to modify the header because it would draw attention to the items of greatest relevance to individuals, thereby improving individuals' understanding of, and ability to exercise, the rights afforded to them by the Privacy Rule. Some commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to modify the header because of an increased administrative burden associated with modifying the NPP.
Response:
The Department is adopting the proposal to revise the header because it will make it easier for individuals to quickly see and improve their understanding of the entity's privacy practices in the NPP. We acknowledge that updating the NPP will create a one-time burden for covered entities; however, we believe that eliminating the recurring requirement to obtain and document the written acknowledgment, or the covered entity's good faith effort and reason for not obtaining the acknowledgment, will more than offset this burden.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that the Department update the model NPP to: (1) address how an individual's information may be used and disclosed within the health care system and by business associates; and (2) include examples related to health care operations and psychotherapy notes.
Response:
The Department intends to update the model NPPs and model Part 2 Patient Notice, which addresses SUD patient records, to reflect the changes herein prior to the compliance date for this final rule.
[
691
]
Comment:
One commenter expressed support for the Department's proposal to make it optional for covered entities to include in the NPP information about how an individual who seeks to direct a copy of their PHI to a designated person can instead obtain a copy of PHI themselves or request that the covered entity send a copy of the PHI to a designated person using a valid authorization if the request does not meet the conditions of
45 CFR 164.524(d)
because of the variability of options and fees.
Response:
Allowing covered entities to include in the NPP a thorough explanation of individuals' options of obtaining access to and sharing their
(
printed page 74932)
PHI with others informs and empowers individuals to make such decisions in a thoughtful and educated manner. Covered entities that choose to include this information are not required to include in the NPP information about their fees for disclosing such PHI. Elsewhere in this final rule, we discuss the decision to finalize the proposal to require covered entities to make available a fee schedule that applies to requests made pursuant to the right of access and valid authorizations.
Comment:
One commenter expressed opposition to the proposal to remove the exception to the requirement to provide individuals with a copy of the NPP for individuals who are inmates of correctional facilities that are covered entities because they believed issuing the NPP to such individuals would mean that they would have the same health information privacy rights as individuals who are not inmates. The commenter also expressed concern about potential safety and security risks associated with sharing information about scheduled appointments or surgeries with an individual who is an inmate or family or friends of an individual who is an inmate.
Response:
We are finalizing this provision as proposed in the 2022 Part 2 NPRM. Individuals who are inmates are afforded the same health information privacy rights under the Privacy Rule as other individuals, with limited exceptions. For example, a correctional institution that is a covered entity may limit the disclosure of PHI in response to an inmate's right of access request if such disclosure would jeopardize the health, safety, or security of the individual or other inmates, or the safety of any officer, employee, or other person at the correctional institution or responsible for the transporting of the inmate.
[
692
]
And while an inmate's personal representative (which could be a family member or friend) may be able to obtain a copy of PHI on the inmate's behalf in some cases where a covered entity may deny access to the individual, this has been true since the 2000 Privacy Rule.
[
693
]
Additionally, while the NPP is provided to each individual, it does not include information about the individual; rather, it addresses the covered entity's privacy practices and individuals' rights and how to exercise them.
H. Permitting Disclosures for Telecommunications Relay Services for People Who Are Deaf, Hard of Hearing, or Deaf-Blind, or Who Have a Speech Disability
1. Current Rule
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, TRS providers facilitate telephone calls between individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability, and others.
[
694
]
Federally regulated common carriers (
e.g.,
operators of all landline and mobile telephone services) must provide TRS to individuals in the general public who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability.
[
695
]
TRS providers facilitate such communications by using a communications assistant who transliterates conversations (or in some cases, interprets using American Sign Language (ASL)).
[
696
]
The communications assistant relays information, which may include PHI, between a person who uses text or video and another person, who may be communicating by voice or who also may be using TRS.
[
697
]
All TRS providers must comply with standards for operators established by the Federal Communications Commission pursuant to Title IV of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), as amended,
[
698
]
including protecting the confidentiality of all relayed communications.
[
699
]
The Privacy Rule currently does not explicitly permit the use and disclosure of PHI for purposes expressly related to TRS, nor does it explicitly address whether a TRS communications assistant is a business associate. However, the Department previously explained in guidance that a covered entity is permitted to disclose an individual's PHI to a TRS communications assistant when communicating with the individual without the need for a business associate agreement with the TRS provider.
[
700
]
As explained in the guidance, the Privacy Rule permits disclosures to TRS communications assistants under
45 CFR 164.510(b)
because individuals have an opportunity to agree or object to disclosures of PHI to a TRS communications assistant at the beginning of a call, and the individuals are effectively identifying the communications assistant as involved in their care if the individuals do not object. Additionally, the guidance also explains that the TRS provider is not acting for or on behalf of the covered entity when it provides such relay services. Thus, the TRS provider is not a business associate.
Also as explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, the Department has become aware that advances in technology now allow people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability to communicate with the help of a TRS communications assistant in a seamless manner, with immediate connection and instantaneous transliteration of text or interpretation of ASL to voice and vice versa, such that the other party to the call may not know that a person is using a TRS communications assistant. Additionally, TRS is used not only to connect individuals with workforce members of regulated entities, but also to assist in communications between workforce members of regulated entities. For these reasons, the assumption that individuals always would have the opportunity to agree or object to a use or disclosure of PHI to a TRS communications assistant no longer holds when it is a workforce member of the regulated entity, rather than an individual, who needs the TRS services to assist with communications.
2. Proposed Rule
The Department proposed to add a new subsection (v) to paragraph (4) of the definition of business associate at
45 CFR 160.103
that would exclude TRS providers from the definition of business associate. This proposal would ensure that regulated entities would not need to analyze whether they need business associate agreements with TRS providers, nor would they need to enter into and implement such agreements.
(
printed page 74933)
The Department also proposed to add a new paragraph (m) to
45 CFR 164.512
that would expressly permit covered entities to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants, as defined at
47 CFR 64.601(a)(12)
.
[
701
]
This proposed permission would cover all disclosures to TRS communications assistants related to any covered functions performed by, for, or on behalf of covered entities.
Together, the proposed modifications to
45 CFR 160.103
and
164.512
would help to ensure that workforce members and individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability are able to communicate easily using TRS for care coordination and other purposes.
3. Overview of Comments
The Department received relatively few comments on this proposal. Commenters generally expressed support for the proposal because they asserted that it would facilitate care coordination for individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability, as well as enable regulated entities and their workforce members, who may be deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or have a speech disability, to communicate with individuals and each other using TRS.
4. Final Rule
Consistent with the Department's proposal, this final rule modifies the definition of business associate at
45 CFR 160.103
by adding a new subsection (v) to paragraph (4) to expressly exclude TRS providers from the definition of business associate. Additionally, it permits regulated entities to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants to conduct covered functions by adding a new paragraph (m) to
45 CFR 164.512
. Section 164.512(m)(1) permits covered entities to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants to conduct covered functions, while
45 CFR 164.512(m)(2)
expressly permits business associates to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants to conduct covered functions for, or on behalf of, a covered entity. The language that we are adopting is modified from the proposed language for
45 CFR 164.512(m)
to clarify in regulatory text that business associates can make such disclosures regardless of whether their business associate agreements address the ability of the business associates to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants for the purposes described above. This modification is consistent with the intended scope of the Department's proposal, as described in preamble to the 2021 Privacy Rule,
[
702
]
and helps further our goals of reducing administrative burden on regulated entities and facilitating communications for persons who rely on TRS communications assistants.
As of 2024, hearing loss was the third most common chronic physical condition in the United States,
[
703
]
affecting more than 37.9 million Americans
[
704
]
and projected to rise to over 70 million by 2060.
[
705
]
Further, hearing loss that is disabling is experienced by 5 percent of adults aged 45 to 54, 10 percent of those aged 55-64, 22 percent of those aged 65 to 74, and 55 percent of adults over the age of 75.
[
706
]
Moreover, in this same time period, over 17 million adults experienced difficulties using their voice in the 12 months preceding this time period while over 9 million adults experienced the problem for a period of 1 week or longer.
[
707
]
With respect to vision loss, according to estimates from the 2024 National Health Interview Survey, 49.5 million American Adults age 18 and older reported experiencing some degree of vision loss. Of these, 3.8 million adults have a lot of trouble seeing, even when wearing glasses, and 420,000 cannot see at all.
[
708
]
Thus, the need for TRS communications assistants to aid such individuals in communicating with regulated entities, and workforce members of regulated entities in communicating with each other and outside parties, is likely to increase in the near future.
Accordingly, the Department believes that this modification to the Privacy Rule promotes access to health care for individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability and will facilitate the compliance of regulated entities with applicable Federal and state disability laws. Additionally, we believe that clarifying that regulated entities are permitted to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants to conduct covered functions eliminates confusion and enables persons who are deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability to be employed in the health care industry without imposing on regulated entities the need for a business associate agreement, while presenting no real risk to the privacy and confidentiality of PHI.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
Commenters almost universally expressed support for the proposal to exclude TRS providers from the definition of a “business associate” and clarify that regulated entities are not required to enter into business associate agreements with TRS providers in order to disclose PHI to them. According to commenters, this proposal would eliminate the administrative burden associated with implementing a business associate agreement, enabling regulated entities to more easily make necessary disclosures to TRS communications assistants for patient care. Many commenters asserted that it would reduce burden for patients who are deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability. These commenters expressed uncertainty about whether regulated entities must enter into business associate agreements with TRS providers, which has caused some regulated entities to be reluctant to communicate via TRS or to require business associate agreements from TRS providers. According to commenters, this uncertainty has resulted in delays to the timely provision of health care for affected individuals. Commenters asserted that this proposal would alleviate concerns about potential violations of the ADA
[
709
]
and the burdens imposed on affected individuals in circumstances where
(
printed page 74934)
covered entities did not implement accessible telephone systems.
One commenter opined that the proposal would not result in any adverse consequences, such as posing significant risks to individuals' privacy or undue burdens on regulated entities.
Response:
The Department agrees that this modification reduces barriers to both health care for individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability, and employment for such persons. The Department also agrees that eliminating the need to implement a business associate agreement with TRS providers will reduce the administrative burden on regulated entities, namely the amount of time and other resources associated with determining whether a business associate agreement is necessary and implementing such business associate agreements. Additionally, we are unaware of any potential unintended, adverse consequences that would be created by this proposal.
Accordingly, we are finalizing these modifications.
Comment:
One commenter recommended that the Department modify the proposal to permit covered entities to disclose PHI to TRS communications assistants to the same extent as during a traditional voice call. The commenter expressed concern that regulated entities otherwise might conclude that the minimum necessary standard applies to the disclosure of PHI when using a TRS communications assistant.
Response:
The Department declines to modify the proposal as requested because the recommended language could cause uncertainty about the scope of the permission. This final rule permits a regulated entity to disclose PHI when necessary to conduct a function covered by the HIPAA Administrative Simplification provisions but does not permit it to disclose PHI beyond such functions. Further, the Department believes that the finalized text vests discretion with the disclosing regulated entity to ensure that the amount of PHI disclosed is consistent with the purpose for which it is disclosed. I. Expanding the Permission To Use and Disclose the PHI of Armed Forces Personnel To Cover All Uniformed Services Personnel
1. Current Rule
Section 164.512(k) of the Privacy Rule contains the standard for uses and disclosures of PHI for specialized government functions, including U.S. military and veteran activities. Paragraph (k)(1)(i) of this section specifically permits covered entities to use and disclose the PHI of individuals who are Armed Forces personnel for activities deemed necessary by appropriate military command authorities to assure the proper execution of the military mission. Application of the permission requires the military authority to publish notice in the
Federal Register
of the appropriate military command authorities and the purposes for which the PHI may be used or disclosed.
[
710
]
Section 164.512(k)(1)(ii) permits a component of the Departments of Defense or Homeland Security that is a covered entity to disclose to the VA the PHI of an individual who is a member of the Armed Forces upon the separation or discharge of the individual from military service for the purpose of a VA determination of eligibility or benefits entitlement. These permissions enable covered entities to use and disclose the PHI of Armed Services personnel, under certain conditions, to avoid the burden and obstacles of obtaining individuals' authorizations when the balance of privacy interests and societal values weighs toward permitting the use or disclosure of PHI without authorization for specialized purposes.
[
711
]
When taken together, they ensure that the PHI of members of the Armed Forces is made available for operations that tie directly to military and VA operations.
2. Proposed Rule
As we explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM, according to the Directors of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps, the existing provision limits the ability of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps to facilitate care coordination and case management for Commissioned Corps personnel.
[
712
]
Such care coordination and case management are important for ensuring that personnel meet medical readiness standards and are able to fulfill the Commissioned Corps' respective missions. Accordingly, the Department proposed to expand the applicability of
45 CFR 164.512(k)
(1) from the Armed Forces to all Uniformed Services, which—in addition to the Armed Forces—includes HHS's USPHS Commissioned Corps and the Department of Commerce's NOAA Commissioned Corps. This would permit covered entities to use and disclose PHI for mission requirements and veteran eligibility of members of these Services without individual authorization. The Department proposed to modify
45 CFR 164.512(k)(1)(i)
to permit covered entities to use and disclose the PHI of individuals who are members of the USPHS or NOAA Commissioned Corps for activities deemed necessary by appropriate Service authorities to assure the proper execution of the missions of the respective Commissioned Corps. The Department also proposed to modify
45 CFR 164.512(k)(1)(ii)
to permit a component of either the Department of Commerce or HHS that is a covered entity to disclose PHI to the VA concerning members of their respective Commissioned Corps in the same manner that is currently allowed for the Departments of Defense and Homeland Security with respect to the Armed Forces under their respective jurisdictions.
3. Overview of Comments
The Department received relatively few comments on this proposal, but the comments that we received generally expressed support for it.
4. Final Rule
The final rule adopts the proposal to expand the permission for covered entities to use and disclose PHI of members of the Armed Services to include members of all Uniformed Services, with minor modifications to account for the organizational structure of the Department of Defense.
[
713
]
Additionally, because Uniformed Services includes the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps, the final rule adopts the modification to permit a covered component of either the Department of Commerce or Health and Human Services to disclose PHI to the VA at
45 CFR 164.512(k)(1)(ii)
.
The Uniformed Services are composed of the Armed Forces (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Space Force, Coast Guard) plus the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps. While members of the USPHS and NOAA
(
printed page 74935)
Commissioned Corps are not members of the Armed Forces, they maintain similar obligations to those of the Armed Services. For example, for the USPHS,
42 U.S.C. 204(a)
establishes both a Regular Corps and Ready Reserve Corps to be available for deployment in certain specified circumstances.
Paragraph (1) of 42 U.S.C. 402(a)
requires the Secretary to establish requirements to ensure the readiness of both Corps' components for response to urgent or emergency public health care needs that cannot otherwise be met at the Federal, state, and local levels; and any member who fails to maintain fitness is subject to disciplinary actions. Under
42 U.S.C. 217
, the President may, by Executive Order, in time of war, or of emergency involving the national defense, declare the USPHS Commissioned Corps to be a military service. Similarly, section 3007 of title 33 of the U.S. Code requires the Secretary of the Department of Commerce to ensure a “high physical state of readiness” by establishing physical fitness standards for NOAA personnel that are substantially equivalent to those prescribed for Coast Guard personnel. Section 3030 of 33 U.S.C. provides that officers of NOAA shall be subject to the same laws as Navy personnel for purposes of temporary appointment or advancement in time of war or national emergency. Section 3061 of 33 U.S.C. provides that the President may, whenever in the judgment of the President a sufficient national emergency exists, transfer NOAA commissioned officers, ships, and stations to the military departments if the President deems it in the best interest of the country.
Members of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps are obligated to maintain physical fitness to ensure duty readiness in a similar manner to members of the Armed Forces. Members of these Commissioned Corps also enjoy certain benefits linked to their service.
[
714
]
As explained by the directors of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps in their joint comments, the Commissioned Corps are part of the eight Uniformed Services and may be assigned or detailed to the Armed Services. As such, according to the directors, members of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps “must meet medical readiness standards consistent with the various military missions.”
[
715
]
Thus, it is appropriate to permit the use and disclosure of PHI, without authorization, of members of the USPHS Commissioned Corps and the NOAA Commissioned Corps for the same purposes, and in a similar manner as the Privacy Rule currently permits with respect to the PHI of members of the Armed Forces.
Additionally, based on public comments, the Department believes that expanding the Armed Forces permission is likely to facilitate efficient care coordination and case management for members of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps, and thus help the respective Commissioned Corps ensure the health and safety of their officers. As explained by the Directors of the USPHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps, the health and safety of officers is crucial for ensuring that such officers can fulfill the mission of the Corps and protect the health and safety of the nation's population. Accordingly, we are finalizing the proposal with minor modifications to account for the organizational structure of the Department of Defense. The final regulatory text in paragraphs (k)(1), (k)(1)(i), (k)(1)(i)(A), and (k)(1)(ii) hews closely to the original regulatory text but substitutes the term “Uniformed Services” for the terms “military” and “Armed Forces” in certain instances and in others, substitutes “command” for “military” or “military command.” These modifications clarify that “Uniformed Services” refers to the personnel whose PHI may be used or disclosed under this permission, not to the departments, agencies, or components that oversee those personnel. The appropriate command authorities for purposes of
45 CFR 164.524(k)(1)(i)
are those identified in the
Federal Register
notice required by that provision. Thus, this modification enshrines an explicit permission for covered entities to use and disclose the PHI of members of all Uniformed Services for the purposes specified in this provision. The final regulatory text is also consistent with the regulatory text suggested by USPHS and NOAA in their joint comments on the 2018 RFI, as explained in the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM. The final rule does not modify the scope of the permission, nor does it change the requirement at
45 CFR 164.512(k)(1)(i)
that the appropriate authority publish a notice in the
Federal Register
identifying the appropriate command authorities and the purposes for which PHI may be used or disclosed.

The transition provisions for business associate contracts and other written arrangements (collectively, “business associate agreements”) are found in

3. Overview of Comments
While the Department did not specifically propose to provide regulated entities with additional time to modify business associate agreements, several commenters urged the Department to provide additional time for them to do so, citing the administrative burden and costs of implementing the revised business associate agreement provisions.
4. Final Rule
The Department recognizes that regulated entities may have existing business associate agreements that are not set to terminate or expire until after the compliance date, and we understand that a 6-month compliance period may not provide enough time to reopen and renegotiate all business associate agreements. Accordingly, we are modifying
45 CFR 164.532(e)
to allow regulated entities to continue to operate under certain existing business associate agreements for up to 1 year beyond the effective date (
i.e.,
6 months beyond the compliance date) for the revisions to the Privacy Rule made by this final rule.
The Department's authority to provide additional time for regulated entities to comply with certain provisions of the Privacy Rule is set forth in
45 CFR 160.104(c)
, which permits the Secretary to establish the compliance date for any modified standard or implementation specification, considering the extent of the modification and the time needed to comply with the modification. We provided a similar transition period for revising business agreements in the 2002 Privacy Rule
[
717
]
and 2013 Omnibus Rule
[
718
]
for similar reasons.
Specifically, the final rule modifies the transition provisions at
45 CFR 164.532(e)
to allow regulated entities to continue to operate under certain existing business associate agreements for up to 1 year beyond the effective date of this final rule. The additional transition period is available to a regulated entity if, prior to the publication date of this final rule, the regulated entity has an existing contract or other written arrangement with a business associate or subcontractor that complies with the HIPAA Rules, and such contract or arrangement is not renewed or modified between the effective date and the compliance date of this final rule. These transition provisions allow regulated entities that have valid business associate agreements with business associates and subcontractors to continue to disclose PHI to the business associate or subcontractor, or to allow the business associate or subcontractor to continue to create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on behalf of the regulated entity, for up to 1 year beyond the effective date of this final rule, regardless of whether the business associate agreement meets the applicable requirements of this final rule. The Department will deem such business associate agreements compliant with the modifications to the Privacy Rule until the earlier of: (1) the regulated entity either renews or modifies the business associate agreement following the compliance date of this final rule; or (2) the date that is 1 year after the effective date.
Business associate agreements that renew automatically without any change in terms or other action by the parties (also known as “evergreen contracts”) are eligible for the extension, and they will continue to be deemed compliant with the final rule, as described above, when they automatically roll over. These transition provisions apply only to written contracts or other written arrangements, and not to verbal contracts or other arrangements.
These transition provisions apply only to the requirement to amend business associate agreements; they do not affect any other compliance obligations under the HIPAA Rules. For example, beginning on the compliance date of this rule, a business associate that responds to requests for individual access on behalf of a covered entity must respond to such requests as soon as practicable, but not later than 15 calendar days after receiving a request, even if the business associate agreement has not yet been amended to reflect the modifications to the Privacy Rule.
5. Responses to Public Comments
Comment:
A few commenters requested that the Department provide additional time for regulated entities to revise business associate agreements affected by the revised Privacy Rule.
Response:
We agree with commenters that regulated entities may require additional time to update and renegotiate their business associate agreements. The Department is aware that many regulated entities have existing business associate agreements that do not terminate or expire until after the compliance date, and that a 240-day compliance period may be insufficient for regulated entities with many business associate agreements to come into compliance, while also implementing the other modifications finalized in this rule. To reduce this administrative burden, we are revising
45 CFR 164.532(e)
to provide regulated entities with a 1-year transition period during which certain existing business associate agreements may remain in effect beyond the compliance date of this final rule.

iv. Distributing the NPP
Providing the NPP to Individuals Who Are Inmates
This final rule removes paragraph (a)(4) from
45 CFR 164.520
, which excepts inmates in correctional institutions from the right to receive a copy of the NPP and excepts correctional institutions that are covered entities from the obligation of providing it. The Department requested comments about this proposal and did not receive any that addressed quantified costs for implementing it, although one commenter asserted that the proposal would add to workflow without any benefit. The Department is finalizing a new right for individuals who are inmates to receive a copy of an NPP and including an estimate of the costs for covered health care providers to provide such copies in person. We understand that contractors that provide health care in prisons and jails generally serve two roles: (1) managing a provider network and (2) handling claims for payments. To the extent that the contractor is a single covered entity, only one NPP is required. Where the contractor's business arrangements rely on separate covered entities to perform different functions, a joint NPP likely would be sufficient.
[
758
]
Thus, the cost estimates include only one NPP per individual who receives health care while an inmate in a correctional institution.
The Department anticipates that individuals who are newly admitted to prisons and jails will receive a two-page double-sided printed copy of the NPP during their first health care encounter, as will individuals who are already incarcerated when the rule becomes effective, likely upon their next visit to a covered health care provider. The Department estimates that distributing each NPP costs $0.972: $0.042 in paper and toner
[

]
and $0.930 in labor costs.

]

While theoretically possible, there are several reasons why this scenario is unlikely to happen and the number of distributed NPPs will be lower in practice, as explained further below.

First, some of the health care provided to individuals who are inmates is paid for directly by correctional facilities employing staff in prison or jail health clinics, rather than through electronic transactions using standards adopted under HIPAA.

Thus, only a portion of health care is provided by health care providers who are subject to HIPAA. Second, jail admission statistics include repeat offenders. The same individual who is admitted to the same jail multiple times in a year would receive only one NPP when the correctional institution health care provider's records show the individual is not a new patient. Third, unlike prisons that house persons who are serving sentences of longer than 1 year, individuals who are admitted to jails often are there for short periods of time and have less opportunity to receive health care, or may not need health care during that time period.

Second, according to a recent study, “[i]n 2023, there were 7.6 million jail admissions, but 1 in 4 of these admissions was someone returning to jail for at least the second time that year.” For its low-end estimates, the Department assumes that unique jail inmates are 75 percent of the 85 percent of new jail inmates who have rights under HIPAA.
Third, the BJS reports that the average number of days an individual spent in jail was 31.8 in 2023, a number that is likely skewed upward by relatively few (about 30 percent) convicted individuals serving their sentence in jail, while the majority (70 percent) of individuals in jail are there for much shorter times.

4. Consideration of Regulatory Alternatives
The Department carefully considered several alternatives to issuing this final rule, including the option of not pursuing any regulatory changes, but rejected that approach for several reasons. First, the regulatory changes that we are finalizing will further the Administration's goal of reducing regulatory burden on individuals and the regulated community and promoting care coordination. Second, many commenters on the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM believed that the Privacy Rule could be improved and offered comments that expressed support for some of the ideas suggested in the NPRM that are now finalized. Revising the Privacy Rule will clarify covered entities' obligations and flexibilities, improve individuals' access to their PHI, and improve care coordination and case management overall.

C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Department has examined the economic implications of this final rule as required by the RFA.
[

The Department generally considers a final rule to have significant economic impact on a substantial number of small covered entities if it generates a change in revenues of 3 percent or more for at least 5 percent of small covered entities.
[
801

We published an initial assessment of the potential economic implications of the 2021 Privacy Rule NPRM in Section C., RFA, and a factual basis for certifying that the proposed rule would not result in a significant negative impact on a substantial number of small entities. We received no public comments on the small entity analysis or proposed certification under the RFA. We received several comments about the reduced burden resulting from the removal of the requirement for direct treatment providers to make a good faith effort to obtain an acknowledgment of receipt of the NPP and the addition of the permission for disclosures to certain third parties for individual-level care coordination and case management activities that constitute treatment or health care operations. We also received several comments that the number of simultaneous changes needed to update policies and procedures during the coronavirus disease 2019 public health emergency would be overly burdensome for small entities, particularly sole provider practices, such that more time and additional guidance from the Department would be needed to comply. In response to these comments and input from other Federal agencies, we have reconsidered certain aspects of the RFA analysis, including the scope of effects that may be relevant to certification. In this revised analysis, we include a comparison of the average costs by firms with employees (across all firm sizes) and the average yearly revenue of the smallest firms in each industry category that is potentially affected by this final rule. Generally, this approach likely would overestimate any economic effect on small entities because we also expect that the costs would be roughly proportional to entity size. For example, the cost to revise policies and procedures and revise training (representing more than 80 percent of costs in the first year, see Table 13) increases significantly as revenue increases because we assume that only larger businesses will incur expenses for lawyers' time for the revisions and training experts' time to revise training materials. We do not anticipate that small businesses with less than $100,000 in annual revenue will pay for tailor-made revisions to policies and training programs. Instead, we expect that they will adapt resource materials or tools offered by professional and trade associations and free government resources, such as the model NPP, in a manner suitable to their business. Even with these assumptions, we do not identify a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities in the smallest revenue categories. These findings also are generalizable to small entities in larger revenue categories (
e.g.,
firms with annual revenues between $100,000 and $500,000), which will have a lower cost-to-revenue ratio than the cost-to-revenue for the smallest entities. The ratio will be lower because the average costs are the same for smaller entities within the category as they are for the larger entities, but the actual revenue increases for the larger entities. This final regulatory flexibility analysis explains the factual basis for certifying the final rule under the RFA.
In addition to the statistical analysis that follows, the Department believes that the smallest of the small entities will be affected most directly by the final rule's reduced time period for responding to access requests because such entities generally do not have dedicated workforce members (or a business associate) to respond to requests for PHI. § 164.501
Definitions.
*
*
*
*
*
Electronic health record
means an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff. Such clinicians shall include, but are not limited to, health care providers that have direct or indirect treatment relationships with individuals as defined at § 164.501, such as physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and other allied health professionals. For purposes of this definition, “health-related information on an individual” covers the same scope of information as the term
individually identifiable health
(
printed page 74963)
information
as defined at § 160.103 of this subchapter.
*
*
*
*
*
Health care operations
means any of the following activities of the covered entity to the extent that the activities are related to covered functions:
(1) Conducting quality assessment and improvement activities, including outcomes evaluation and development of clinical guidelines, provided that the obtaining of generalizable knowledge is not the primary purpose of any studies resulting from such activities; patient safety activities (as defined in
42 CFR 3.20
); population-based activities relating to improving health or reducing health care costs; protocol development; case management and care coordination; contacting of health care providers and patients with information about treatment alternatives; and related functions that do not include treatment.
(2) Reviewing the competence or qualifications of health care professionals, evaluating practitioner and provider performance, health plan performance, conducting training programs in which students, trainees, or practitioners in areas of health care learn under supervision to practice or improve their skills as health care providers, training of non-health care professionals, accreditation, certification, licensing, or credentialing activities.
(3) Except as prohibited under § 164.502(a)(5)(i), underwriting, enrollment, premium rating, and other activities related to the creation, renewal, or replacement of a contract of health insurance or health benefits, and ceding, securing, or placing a contract for reinsurance of risk relating to claims for health care (including stop-loss insurance and excess of loss insurance), provided that the requirements of § 164.514(g) are met, if applicable.
(4) Conducting or arranging for medical review, legal services, and auditing functions, including fraud and abuse detection and compliance programs.
(5) Business planning and development, such as conducting cost-management and planning-related analyses related to managing and operating the entity, including formulary development and administration, development or improvement of methods of payment or coverage policies.
(6) Business management and general administrative activities of the entity, including, but not limited to, any of the following:
(i) Management activities relating to implementation of and compliance with the requirements of this subchapter.
(ii) Customer service, including the provision of data analyses for policy holders, plan sponsors, or other customers, provided that protected health information is not disclosed to such policy holder, plan sponsor, or customer.
(iii) Resolution of internal grievances.
(iv) The sale, transfer, merger, or consolidation of all or part of the covered entity with another covered entity, or an entity that following such activity will become a covered entity and due diligence related to such activity.
(v) Consistent with the applicable requirements of § 164.514, creating de-identified health information or a limited data set, and fundraising for the benefit of the covered entity.
*
*
*
*
*
Personal health application
means an electronic application used by an individual to access health information about that individual, which can be drawn from multiple sources, provided that all of the following conditions apply:
(1) Such information is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual.
(2) Such information is not managed, shared, or controlled in any of the following manners:
(i) By or primarily for a covered entity.
(ii) Primarily for another person.
